Il est donc évident que le Seigneur a subi la mort, en obéissant au Père, le jour même où Adam est mort, en désobéissant à Dieu. Or, le jour où Adam est mort est aussi celui où il a mangé. Car Dieu a dit : « Le jour où vous en mangerez, vous mourrez de mort. »

C'est donc ce jour que le Seigneur a récapitulé en lui-même en venant à sa passion la veille du sabbat, qui est le sixième jour de la création, celui où l'homme fut façonné ; par sa passion, il lui a ainsi accordé un second façonnement, celui qui le délivre de la mort. D'autres, en revanche, rapportent la mort d'Adam au millénaire, car « un jour du Seigneur est comme mille ans » ; or, Adam n’a pas dépassé les mille ans, mais il est mort avant leur terme, accomplissant ainsi la sentence portée contre sa transgression. Que ce soit donc en raison de la désobéissance, qui est la mort ; ou parce qu'à partir de ce moment ils furent livrés à la mort et en devinrent débiteurs ; ou selon le jour unique et identique où ils ont mangé et sont morts, puisqu'il n'y a qu'un seul jour de la création ; ou selon le cycle hebdomadaire, puisqu'ils sont morts le même jour où ils ont mangé, à savoir la Parascève, que l'on nomme la Cène pure, c'est-à-dire le sixième jour, jour que le Seigneur a mis en lumière en y souffrant sa passion ; ou enfin parce qu'Adam n'a pas dépassé les mille ans mais est mort au cours de ceux-ci : selon toutes ces significations, Dieu est bien véridique. En effet, ceux qui ont goûté de l'arbre sont bien morts. Le serpent, en revanche, s'est révélé menteur et homicide, comme le Seigneur l'a dit à son sujet : « Il est homicide depuis le commencement et ne s'est pas tenu dans la vérité. »
en: ST. IRENAEUS OF LYONS And there are some, again, who relegate the death of Adam to the thousandth year; for since "a day of the Lord is as a thousand years" [1 Pt 3:8], he did not overstep the thousand years, but died within them, thus bearing out the sentence of his sin [Against Heresies 5:23:2 (c. A.D 189)].
latin:
In ipsa itaque die mortui sunt, in qua et manducaverunt, et debitores facti sunt mortis, quoniam conditionis dies unus. «Factum est enim, inquit, vespere, et factum est mane dies unus.» [Genesis 1:5] In ipsa autem hac die manducaverunt; in ipsa autem et mortui sunt. Secundum autem circulum et cursum dierum, secundum quæ alia quidem prima, alia autem secunda, alia tertia vocatur, si quis velit diligenter discere, quæ die septem diebus mortuus est Adam, inveniet ex Domini dispositione. Recapitulas enim universum hominem in se ab initio usque ad finem, recapitulatus est et mortem ejus. Manifestum est itaque, quoniam in illa die mortem sustinuit Dominus, obediens Patri, in qua mortuus est Adam inobediens Deo. In qua autem mortuus est, in ipsa et manducavit. Dixit enim Deus: «In qua die manducabitis ex eo, morte moriemini.» [Genesis 2:17]

Hunc itaque diem recapitulans in semetipsum Dominus, venit ad passionem pridie ante sabbatum, quæ est sexta conditionis dies, in qua homo plasmatus est; secundam plasmatio-nem ei, eam quæ est a morte, per suam passionem donans. Quidam autem rursus in millesimum annum revocant mortem Adæ: quoniam enim «dies Domini, sicut mille anni» [Psalm 90:4]; non superposuit autem mille annos, sed intra eos mortuus est, transgressionis adimplens sententiam. Sive ergo secundum inobedientiam, quæ est mors; sive quod exinde traditi sint, et facti sint debitores mortis: sive secundum unum et eumdem diem, in quo manducaverunt, et mortui sunt, quoniam una conditionis dies: sive secundum hunc circulum dierum, quia in ipsa mortui sunt, in qua et manducaverunt, hæc est, Parasceve, quæ dicitur cœna pura, id est sexta feria, quam et Dominus ostendit passus in ea: sive secundum quod non sit supergressus mille annos, sed in ipsis mortuus sit: secundum omnia ergo quæ significantur, Deus quidem verax; mortui enim sunt, qui gustaverunt de ligno: serpens autem mendax ostensus est, homicida, sicut Dominus ait de eo: «Quoniam ab initio homicida est, et in veritate non stetit.» [John 8:44]

fr:
La tromperie, l'orgueil et le règne tyrannique de l'Antichrist, tels que les ont décrits Daniel et Paul.

Et cela est manifesté non seulement par ce qui a été dit, mais aussi par les événements qui surviendront sous l'Antichrist. En effet, lui qui est un apostat et un brigand, il veut être adoré comme Dieu ; et bien qu'il soit un esclave, il veut être proclamé roi. Car, recevant en lui toute la puissance du diable, il viendra non comme un roi juste, ni comme un souverain légitime soumis à Dieu, mais comme un être impie, injuste et sans loi ; en tant qu'apostat, criminel et meurtrier, il viendra comme un brigand, récapitulant en lui-même l'apostasie diabolique. D'une part, il mettra de côté les idoles pour persuader qu'il est lui-même Dieu ; d'autre part, il s'élèvera lui-même comme l'unique idole, portant en sa personne l'erreur multiforme de toutes les autres. De cette manière, ceux qui adorent le diable à travers de nombreuses abominations en viendront à le servir à travers cette idole unique. C'est à ce sujet que l'Apôtre dit, dans la seconde Épître aux Thessaloniciens : « Car il faut que vienne d'abord l'apostasie et que soit révélé l'homme du péché, le fils de la perdition, l'adversaire qui s'élève au-dessus de tout ce qu'on appelle Dieu ou de ce qu'on adore, jusqu'à s'asseoir dans le temple de Dieu et se montrer lui-même comme s'il était Dieu. » L'Apôtre montre donc manifestement son apostasie et le fait qu'il s'élève au-dessus de tout ce qu'on appelle Dieu ou de ce qu'on adore, c'est-à-dire au-dessus de toute idole (car ce sont elles que les hommes appellent dieux, bien qu'elles ne le soient pas), et qu'il tentera de se présenter comme Dieu à la manière d'un tyran.

En outre, il a aussi manifesté un point que nous avons nous-mêmes démontré de multiples manières : le temple de Jérusalem a été bâti selon le dessein du vrai Dieu. En effet, l'Apôtre lui-même, parlant en son propre nom, a appelé ce temple de façon catégorique « le temple de Dieu ». Or, nous avons montré dans le troisième livre que jamais les apôtres, parlant en leur propre nom, n'appellent « Dieu » quelqu'un d'autre que celui qui est véritablement Dieu, le Père de notre Seigneur. Et c'est son temple, celui de Jérusalem, qui a été bâti à juste titre pour les raisons que nous avons exposées. C'est dans ce temple que s'assiéra l'adversaire, en essayant de se faire passer pour le Christ, comme le dit aussi le Seigneur : « Quand donc vous verrez l'abomination de la désolation, annoncée par le prophète Daniel, établie dans le lieu saint – que celui qui lit comprenne ! –, alors, que ceux qui sont en Judée fuient dans les montagnes ; que celui qui est sur le toit ne descende pas pour prendre ce qui est dans sa maison. Car il y aura alors une grande détresse, telle qu'il n'y en a pas eu depuis le commencement du monde jusqu'à maintenant, et qu'il n'y en aura jamais plus. »
en: ST. IRENAEUS OF LYONS [Bly means of the events that shall occur in the time of Antichrist it is shown that he, being an apostate and a robber, is anxious to be adored as God; and that, although a mere slave, he wishes himself to be proclaimed as a king. For he [Antichrist] being imbued with the power of the devil, shall come, not as a righteous king, nor as a legitimate king, in subjection to God, but an impious, unjust, and lawless one setting aside idols to persuade [men] that he is God, raising himself up as the only idol. Moreover, [Paul] has also pointed out this that I have shown in many ways, that the temple in Jerusalem was made by the direction of the true God. For the apostle, speaking in his own person, distinctly called it the temple of God . . . in which the enemy shall sit, endeavoring to show himself as Christ [Against Heresies 5:25:1-2 (c. A.D. 189)].
latin:
CAPUT XXV.
Antichristi fraus, superbia, et tyrannicum regnum, prout a Daniele et Paulo descripta sunt.

Et non tantum autem per ea quæ dicta sunt, sed et per ea quæ erunt sub Antichristo, ostenditur; quoniam exsistens apostata et latro, quasi Deus vult adorari; et cum sit servus, regem se vult præonari. Hic enim omnem suscipiens diaboli virtutem, veniet non quasi rex justus, nec quasi in subjectione Dei legitimus; sed impius, et injustus, et sine lege, quasi apostata, et iniquus, et homicida, quasi latro, diabolicam apostasiam in se recapitulans: et idola quidem seponens, ad suadendum quod ipse sit Deus; se autem extollens unum idolum, habens in semetipso reliquorum idolorum varium errorem: ut hi qui per multas abominationes adorant diabolum, per hoc unum idolum serviant ipsi. Quo de Apostolus in Epistola ad Thessalonicenses secunda, sic ait: «Quoniam nisi venerit abscessio primum, et revelatus fuerit homo peccati, filius perditionis, qui adversatur et extollitur super omne quod dicitur Deus, aut colitur: ita ut in templo Dei sedeat, ostendens semetipsum tanquam sit Deus.» [2 Thessalonians 2:3-4] Manifeste igitur Apostolus ostendit apostasiam ejus, et quoniam extollitur super omne quod dicitur Deus, vel quod colitur, hoc est, super omne idolum (hi enim sunt qui dicuntur quidem ab hominibus, non sunt autem dii), et quoniam ipse tyrannico more conabitur ostendere Deum.

Super hæc autem manifestavit et illud, quod a nobis per multa ostensum est, quoniam in Hierosolymis templum dispositione veri Dei factum est. Ipse enim Apostolus ex sua persona diffinitive templum illud dixit Dei. Ostendimus autem in tertio libro, nullum ab apostolis ex sua persona Deum appellari, nisi eum qui vere sit Deus, Patrem Domini nostri: cujus justus hoc, quod est in Hierosolymis, factum est templum, ob eas causas quæ a nobis dictæ sunt: in quo adversarius sedebit, tentans semetipsum Christum ostendere, sicut et Dominus ait: «Cum autem videritis abominationem desolationis, quod dictum est per Danielem prophetam, stantem in loco sancto (qui legit, intelligat), tunc qui in Judæa sunt, fugiant in montes: et qui in tecto est, non descendat tollere quidquam de domo. Erit enim tunc pressura magna, qualis non est facta ab initio sæculi usque nunc, sed neque flet.» [Matthew 24:15-21]

fr:
Il faut donc que ces gens-là apprennent et s'en tiennent au véritable nombre du nom, pour ne pas être comptés au nombre des faux prophètes. Mais, connaissant le nombre certain qui est annoncé par l'Écriture, c'est-à-dire six cent soixante-six, qu'ils attendent d'abord la division du royaume en dix. Puis, ensuite, alors que les fils de ces rois règneront, commenceront à organiser leurs affaires et à étendre leur royaume, ils devront reconnaître que celui qui viendra à l’improviste pour s’arroger le pouvoir et qui anéantira les rois précités, celui-là même qui porte le nom contenant le fameux nombre, est véritablement l’abomination de la désolation. C'est aussi ce que dit l'Apôtre : « Quand les hommes diront : Paix et sécurité, alors une ruine soudaine fondra sur eux. » Jérémie, de son côté, a révélé non seulement la soudaineté de sa venue, mais aussi la tribu dont il sera issu, en disant : « De Dan on entend le bruit de ses chevaux rapides ; au son du hennissement de ses coursiers au galop, toute la terre est ébranlée. Il vient, il dévore la terre et ce qui la remplit, la cité et ceux qui l'habitent. » C'est pourquoi cette tribu n'est pas comptée dans l'Apocalypse parmi celles qui sont sauvées.

Il est donc plus sûr et moins risqué d'attendre l'accomplissement de la prophétie que de se livrer à des suppositions et à des conjectures sur des noms quelconques. En effet, on peut trouver de nombreux noms correspondant au nombre indiqué, et la question resterait de toute façon la même. Car s'il existe de nombreux noms qui totalisent ce nombre, la question demeure : lequel d'entre eux portera celui qui doit venir ? Or, si nous disons cela, ce n'est pas par manque de noms correspondant au nombre de son nom, mais par crainte de Dieu et par zèle pour la vérité. Le nom EUANTHAS, par exemple, correspond au nombre recherché, mais nous n'affirmons rien à son sujet. Le nom LATEINOS donne aussi le nombre six cent soixante-six, et il est très vraisemblable que ce soit le nom du dernier royaume. En effet, ce sont les Latins qui règnent actuellement. Mais nous ne nous en glorifierons pas. Il y a aussi le nom TEITAN – en écrivant la première syllabe avec les deux voyelles grecques *ei* – qui, de tous les noms que nous connaissons, est le plus digne de foi. En effet, non seulement il contient le nombre en question, mais il se compose de six lettres, chaque syllabe en comptant trois ; de plus, c'est un nom ancien et qui n'est pas d'usage courant. Car personne parmi nous ne s'est appelé Titan, et ce n'est pas non plus le nom d'une des idoles publiquement adorées chez les Grecs ou les barbares. Ce nom est même considéré comme divin par beaucoup de gens. Le soleil lui-même est appelé Titan par ceux qui détiennent le pouvoir. De plus, ce nom évoque une certaine idée de vengeance et de châtiment, car celui qui viendra prétendra venger ceux qui ont été maltraités. Par ailleurs, c'est un nom à la fois ancien, crédible, royal et, plus encore, tyrannique. Le nom de Titan réunit donc tant d'arguments en sa faveur qu'il est très vraisemblable – et c'est la conclusion que nous tirons de nombreux éléments – que celui qui doit venir s'appellera peut-être Titan.

Pour notre part, cependant, nous ne prendrons aucun risque à ce sujet et nous n'affirmerons pas avec certitude que tel sera son nom. Nous savons en effet que s'il avait fallu que son nom soit clairement proclamé à notre époque, il l'aurait été par celui-là même qui a eu la vision de l'Apocalypse. Car cette vision n'a pas eu lieu il y a très longtemps, mais presque à notre époque, vers la fin du règne de Domitien.
en: Moreover, another danger, by no means trifling, shall overtake those who falsely presume that they know the name of Antichrist. For if these men assume one name, when this [Antichrist] shall come having another name, they will be easily led away by him, as supposing him not to be the expected one. . . . It is therefore more certain, and less hazardous, to await the fulfillment of the prophecy, than to make surmises and cast about for any names that may present themselves, since many names can be found possessing the number mentioned; and the same question will, after all, remain unsolved [ibid., 5:30:2-3].
latin:
Oportet itaque tales discere, et ad verum recurrere nominum numerum; ut non in pseudoprophetarum loco deputentur. Sed scientes firmum numerum qui a Scriptura annuntiatus est, id est, sexcentorum sexaginta sex [Rev 13:18], sustineant primum quidem divisionem regni in decem: post deinde, filiis regnantibus, et incipientibus corrigere sua negotia, et augere suum regnum; qui de improviso advenerit regnum sibi vindicans et terebit prædictos, habens nomen continens prædictum numerum, hunc vere cognoscere esse abominationem desolationis [Matt 24:15]. Hoc et Apostolus ait: «Cum dixerint, pax et munitio, tunc subitaneus illis superveniet interitus.» [1 Thessalonians 5:3] Jeremias autem non solum subitaneum ejus adventum, sed et tribulum, ex qua veniet, manifestavit dicens: «Ex Dan aulietur vocem velocitatis equorum ejus; a voce binitus decursionis equorum ejus commovebitur tota terra; et veniet, et manducabit terram, et plenitudinem ejus, et civitatem, et qui habitant in ea.» [Jer 8:16] Et propter hoc non annumeratur tribus hæc in Apocalypsi cum his quæ salvantur.

Certius ergo et sine periculo est, sustinere adimplementum prophetiæ quam suspicari et divinare nomina quælibet: quando multa nomina inveniri possunt habentia prædictum numerum: et nihilominus quidem erit eadem quæstio. Si enim multa sunt quæ inveniuntur nomina, habentia numerum hunc: quod ex ipsis portabile, qui veniet, quæritur. Quoniam autem non propter inopiam nominum habentium numerum nominis ejus dicimus hæc, sed propter timorem erga Deum et zelum veritatis. EUANTHAS enim nomen habet numerum de quo quæritur: sed nihil de eo affirmamus. Sed et LATEINOS nomen habet sexcentorum sexaginta sex [Rev 13:18] numerum; et valde verisimile est, quoniam novissimum regnum hoc habet vocabulum. Latini enim sunt qui nunc regnant: sed nos in hoc non gloriabimur. Sed et TEITAN, prima syllaba per duas Græcas vocales est scripta, omnium nominum quæ apud nos inveniuntur, magis fide dignum est. Etenim prædictum numerum habet in se, et litterarum est sex, singulis syllabis ex ternis litteris constantibus, et vetus, et semotum; neque enim eorum qui, secundum nos sunt, aliquis vocatus est Titan; neque eorum qui quæ publice adorantur, idolorum apud Græcos et barbaros habet vocabulum: et divinum putatur apud multos esse hoc nomen, et etiam sol Titan vocetur ab his qui nunc tenent: et ostentationem quamdam continet ultionis, et vindictam inferentis, quod ille simulat se male tractatos vindicare. Et alias autem et antiquum, et fide dignum, et regale, magis autem et tyrannicum nomen. Cum igitur tantum suasionum haberet hoc nomen Titan, tamen habet verisimilitudinem, ut ex multis colligamus ne forte Titan vocatur, qui veniet.

Nos tamen non periclitabimur in eo, nec asseveranter pronunciabimus, hoc eum nomen habiturum: scientes, quoniam si oporteret manifeste præsenti tempore præconari nomen ejus, per ipsum utique editum fuisset, qui et Apocalypsim viderat. Neque enim ante multum temporis visum est, sed pene sub nostro sæculo ad finem Domitiani imperii.

fr:
Il a donc révélé le nombre de ce nom, pour que nous nous gardions de lui à sa venue, sachant qui il est. En revanche, il a passé son nom sous silence, car il n'est pas digne d'être proclamé par l'Esprit Saint. En effet, si ce nom avait été proclamé par lui, peut-être subsisterait-il même pour longtemps. Mais puisque, comme quelqu'un qui n'est pas, « il était, et il n'est plus ; il va monter de l'abîme et s'en aller à sa perte », son nom n'a pas non plus été proclamé. Car on ne proclame pas le nom de ce qui n'existe pas.

Lorsque cet Antichrist aura tout dévasté en ce monde, après avoir régné trois ans et six mois et s'être assis dans le temple à Jérusalem, alors le Seigneur viendra des cieux sur les nuées, dans la gloire du Père. Il le jettera, lui et ceux qui lui obéissent, dans l'étang de feu, mais il apportera aux justes les temps du royaume, c'est-à-dire le repos, le septième jour sanctifié, et il restituera à Abraham la promesse de l'héritage. C'est de ce royaume que le Seigneur a dit que beaucoup viendront d'Orient et d'Occident pour s'attabler avec Abraham, Isaac et Jacob.
en: But when this Antichrist shall have devastated all things in this world, he will reign for three years and six months, and sit in the temple at Jerusalem; and then the Lord will come from heaven in the clouds, in the glory of the Father, sending this man and those who follow him into the lake of fire [ibid., 5:30:4].
latin: Hunc autem numerum nominis ostendit, ut caveamus illum venientem, scientes quis est: nomen autem ejus tacuit, quoniam dignum non est præconari a Spiritu sancto. Si enim præconatum ab eo fuisset, fortassis et in multum permaneret. Nunc autem quoniam «fuit, et non est, et ascendet ab abysso, et in perditionem vadit» [Rev 17:8], quasi qui non sit; sic nec nomen ejus præconatum est: ejus enim quod non est, nomen non præconatur. Cum autem vastaverit Antichristus hic omnia in hoc mundo, regnans annis tribus et mensibus sex, et sederit in templo Hierosolymis; tunc veniet Dominus de cœlis in nubibus, in gloria Patris, illum quidem et obedientes ei in stagnum ignis mittens; adducens autem justis regni tempora, hoc est, requiestionem, septimam diem sanctificatam; et restituens Abrahæ promissionem hæreditatis: in quo regno ait Dominus, multos ab Oriente et Occidente venientes; recumbere cum Abraham, Isaac et Jacob. [Matthew 8:11]

fr:
CHAPITRE XXXV.
Il soutient que les témoignages précédents ne peuvent être interprétés de manière allégorique, comme ne concernant que les biens célestes, mais qu'ils doivent s'accomplir après la venue de l'Antichrist et la résurrection, dans la Jérusalem terrestre. Aux prophéties antérieures tirées d'Isaïe, de Jérémie et de l'Apocalypse de Jean, il en ajoute d'autres.

Si certains tentent d'allégoriser de telles prophéties, non seulement ils ne parviendront pas à être cohérents avec eux-mêmes sur tous les points, mais ils seront confondus par les termes mêmes des Écritures. Par exemple : « Quand les villes des nations seront dévastées au point de n’avoir plus d’habitants, et les maisons plus d’hommes, et que la terre sera laissée à l’abandon ». En effet, voici ce que dit Isaïe : « Le jour du Seigneur vient, implacable, plein de fureur et d'ardente colère, pour réduire le monde en désert et en exterminer les pécheurs. » Et il dit encore : « Qu'il soit enlevé, pour qu'il ne voie pas la gloire du Seigneur ». Et quand cela sera arrivé, dit-il, Dieu éloignera les hommes, et ceux qui auront été laissés se multiplieront sur la terre. Et ils bâtiront des maisons et les habiteront eux-mêmes, ils planteront des vignes et en mangeront eux-mêmes les fruits. Car toutes ces prophéties et les autres s'accompliront au temps de la résurrection, après la venue de l'Antichrist et la perdition de toutes les nations sous son emprise. C'est alors que les justes régneront sur la terre, en grandissant par la vision du Seigneur ; par lui, ils s'habitueront à recevoir la gloire de Dieu le Père, et ils obtiendront dans le Royaume la vie en société, la communion avec les saints anges et l'unité des êtres spirituels. Cela concernera aussi ceux que le Seigneur trouvera dans la chair, l'attendant depuis les cieux, eux qui auront subi la tribulation et échappé aux mains de l'inique. Ce sont eux que le prophète désigne quand il dit : « Et ceux qui auront été laissés se multiplieront sur la terre. »

Le prophète Jérémie a d'ailleurs montré que Dieu prépare un grand nombre de croyants à cela – à être de ceux qui, laissés sur la terre, s'y multiplieront, vivront sous le règne des saints, serviront cette Jérusalem et le royaume qui s'y trouvera. Il a dit : « Jérusalem, regarde vers l'orient et vois la joie qui te vient de Dieu lui-même. Voici, ils arrivent, les fils que tu avais envoyés au loin ; ils arrivent, rassemblés du levant au couchant par la parole du Saint, se réjouissant de la splendeur qui vient de ton Dieu. Quitte, Jérusalem, ta robe de deuil et d'affliction, et revêts pour l'éternité la magnificence de la gloire qui te vient de ton Dieu. Enveloppe-toi du double manteau de la justice qui vient de ton Dieu, pose sur ta tête le diadème de la gloire éternelle. Car Dieu montrera ta splendeur à tout ce qui vit sous le ciel. Et ton nom te sera donné par Dieu lui-même pour l'éternité : “Paix de la justice” et “Gloire de l'adoration de Dieu”. Lève-toi, Jérusalem, tiens-toi sur les hauteurs, regarde vers l'orient et vois tes fils, rassemblés depuis le lever du soleil jusqu'à son couchant par la parole du Saint, heureux du souvenir que Dieu a gardé d'eux. Car ils sont partis de chez toi à pied, emmenés par leurs ennemis ; mais Dieu te les ramène, portés avec gloire, comme sur un trône royal. Car Dieu a décrété que toute haute montagne et les collines éternelles seraient abaissées, et que les vallées seraient comblées pour aplanir la surface de la terre, afin qu'Israël marche en sécurité dans la gloire de Dieu. Les forêts et tout arbre odoriférant ont tissé pour Israël des ombrages, sur l'ordre de Dieu. Car Dieu lui-même précédera Israël, le conduisant dans la joie, à la lumière de sa splendeur, avec la miséricorde et la justice qui viennent de lui. »
en: Jeremiah the prophet has pointed out that as many believers as God has prepared to multiply those left on the earth should both be under the rule of the saints and minister to this [new] Jerusalem and that [his] kingdom shall be in it, saying, "Look around Jerusalem toward the east and behold the joy that comes to you from God himself. Behold, your sons whom you have sent forth shall come: They shall come in a band from the east to the west.. God shall go before you in the light of his splendor, with the mercy and righteousness which proceed from him" [Bar 4:36-5:9] [ibid., 5:35:1; Baruch was often considered part of Jeremiah, as it is here].
latin:
CAPUT XXXV.
Contendit superiora testimonia non posse per allegoriam de bonis tantum cœlestibus intelligi, sed implenda esse post adventum Antichristi, et resurrectionem in terræ Jerusalem; prioribusque prophetiis, ex Isaia, Jeremia et Joannis Apocalypsi alias subjungit.

Si autem quidam tentaverint allegorizare hæc, quæ ejusmodi sunt; neque de omnibus poterunt consonantes sibimetipsis inveniri, et convincantur ab ipsis dictionibus differenti-bus, quoniam «cum desolatæ fuerint civitates gentium, et quod non inhabitentur, et domus, eo quod non sint homines, et derelinquetur terra deserta» [Isaiah 6:11]: ecce enim, «Isaias ait, "dies Domini insanabilis venit, furore et ira plenus, ponere urbem terræ desertam, et peccatores perdere ex ea."» [Isaiah 13:9] Et iterum ait: «Tollatur, ut non videat gloriam Domini» [Isaiah 26:10]; et cum hæc facta fuerint, elongabit, inquit, Deus homines, et derelicti multiplicabuntur in terra [Isaiah 6:12]. Et ædificabunt domos, et ipsi inhabitabunt, et plantabunt vineas, et ipsi manducabunt [Isaiah 65:21]. Hæc enim alia universa in resurrectionem, post adventum Antichristi, et perditionem omnium gentium sub existentium, in qua regnabunt justi in terra, crescentes ex visione Domini, et per ipsum assuescent capere gloriam Dei Patris, et cum sanctis angelis conversationem et communionem, et unitatem spiritalium in regno capient; et illos quos Dominus in carne inveniet, exspectantes eum de cœlis, et per pessos tribulationem, qui et effugerint iniqui manus. Ipsam autem sunt de quibus ait propheta: «Et derelicti multiplicabuntur in terra.» [Isaiah 6:12]

Et quotquot ex credentibus ad hoc præparavit Deus, ad derelictos multiplicandos in terra, et sub regno sanctorum fieri, et ministrare huic Jerusalem, et regnum in ea, significavit Jeremias propheta, circa unum, dicens, ad orientem, Jerusalem, et vide lætitiam quæ adveniat tibi ab ipso Deo. Ecce, venient filii tui quos emisisti, venient collecti ab oriente usque ad occidentem verbo illius sancti, gaudentes ea quæ a Deo tuo est claritate. Exuere, Jerusalem, habitum luctus et afflictionis tuæ, et induere decorum ejus quæ a Deo tuo est claritatis in æternum: circumdare amictum duplicem ejus quæ a Deo tuo est justitiæ, impone mitram super caput tuum gloriæ æternæ. Deus enim demonstravit ei quæ sub cœlo est universæ unum fulgorem. Vocabitur namque nomen tuum ab ipso Deo in æternum, pax justitiæ et gloriæ colenti Deo. Surge, Jerusalem, et sta in excelso, et circumspice ad orientem, et vide collectos filios tuos a solis ortu usque ad occidentem verbo illius sancti, gaudentes ipsam Dei recordationem. Propfecti sunt enim a te pedites, dum adducerentur ab inimicis. Introducet illos Deus ad te portatus cum gloria tanquam thronus. Decrevit enim Deus ut humilieris omni menses excelsus, et congeries æternæ, et ut valles impleantur, ad redigendam planitiem terræ, ut ambulet Israel tute Dei gloria. Umbracula autem intexuerunt silvæ, et omne lignum boni odoris ipsi Israel præcipio Dei. Præibit enim Deus cum lætitia lumine claritatis suæ, cum misericordia et justitia, quæ ab ipso est. [Bar 4:36-5:9]

fr: Il se baptisa, est-il dit, sept fois dans le Jourdain. Et ce n’est pas en vain qu’autrefois Naaman le lépreux fut purifié par son baptême, mais c’était pour nous en être un signe : nous, en effet, qui sommes lépreux dans nos péchés, nous sommes purifiés de nos fautes anciennes par l’eau sainte et l’invocation du Seigneur, régénérés spirituellement comme des enfants nouveau-nés, selon la parole du Seigneur : « Si quelqu’un ne renaît pas de l’eau et de l’Esprit, il n’entrera pas dans le royaume des Cieux. »
en: ST. IRENAEUS OF LYONS And [Naaman] dipped himself . seven times in the Jordan [2 Kgs 5:14]. It was not for nothing that Naaman, when suffering from leprosy, was purified upon being baptized, but as an indication to us. For as we are lepers in sin, we are made clean of our old transgressions by means of the sacred water and the invocation of the Lord; we are spiritually regenerated as newborn babes, even as the Lord has declared: "Except a man be born again through water and the Spirit, he shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven" [Jn 3:5] [Fragments from the Lost Writings of Irenaeus 34 c. A.D. 190)].
latin: Atque baptizabat seipsum, ait, in Jordane septies. Neque frustra olim Naaman lepra laborans, cum baptizatus esset, in corporis puritatem restitutus est, sed ut viam salutis nobis ostenderet: qui quidem peccatis commissis leprosi facti, per aquam sacram et invocationem Domini a prioribus vitiis libertatem nanciscimur, sicuti infantes recens nati spiritualiter regenerati, ut Dominus dixit: «Nisi quis per aquam et spiritum denuo natus fuerit, in divinum regnum non est intraturus.» [John 3:5]
greek: Καὶ ἐβαπτίσατο, φησιν, ἐν τῷ Ἰορδάνῃ ἑπτάκις. Οὐ μάτην πάλαι Ναιμὰν λεπρὸς ὢν βαπτισθεὶς ἐκαθαίρετο, ἀλλ' εἰς ἔνδειξιν ἡμετέραν· οἱ λεπροὶ ὄντες ἐν ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις διὰ τοῦ ἁγίου ὕδατος καὶ τῆς τοῦ Κυρίου ἐπικλήσεως καθαριζόμεθα τῶν παλαιῶν παραπτωμάτων, ὡς παιδία νεόγονα πνευματικῶς ἀναγεννώμενοι, καθὼς καὶ ὁ Κύριος ἔφη· «Ἐὰν μή τις ἀναγεννηθῇ δι' ὕδατος καὶ πνεύματος, οὐ μὴ εἰσελεύσεται εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶν.» [John 3:5]
context: Hoc et proxime sequens fragmentum, ex ms. bibliothecæ Coislinianæ Catena in libros Regum exscripta, in editione D. Massueti leguntur inter Addenda et emendanda.

fr: Je m'étonne d'ailleurs qu'il nous ait proposé en exemple Juda et Thamar, à moins qu'il ne se délecte aussi des prostituées ; ou encore Onan, mis à mort pour avoir refusé sa semence à son frère, comme si nous approuvions n'importe quelle émission de semence en dehors de l'œuvre de procréation.
en: But I wonder why [Jovinianus] set Judah and Tamar before us for an example, unless perhaps even harlots give him pleasure; or Onan, who was slain because he grudged his brother seed [Gn 38:9]. Does he imagine that we approve of any sexual intercourse except for the procreation of children? [Against Jovinianus 1:20 (c. A.D. 393)].
latin: Miror autem cur Judam et Thamar nobis proposuerit in exemplum, nisi forte et meretricibus delectatur; aut occisum Onam, quod fratri semen inviderit: quasi nos qualemcumque seminis fluxum absque liberorum opere comprobemus.
context:
2. Additional Relevant Commentary (Based on the Surrounding Text)

The larger passage you found is a brilliant example of Jerome's polemical strategy. He is building an overwhelming case from the Old Testament to prove one central point: sexual activity, even within marriage, creates a state of ritual and spiritual impurity that is incompatible with sacred duties and direct encounters with God.

The quote about Onan is the lynchpin, but look at how he supports it with the surrounding examples:

    Moses at the Burning Bush: Jerome interprets the command for Moses to remove his sandals as a command to shed the "bonds of marriage" (vincula nuptiarum). To approach the holy, one must be free from marital (i.e., sexual) ties.

    The Israelites at Mount Sinai: Before the people can hear God's word directly, they are commanded to sanctify themselves by abstaining from their wives for three days. The clear implication is that sexual relations render one "unholy" or unprepared for a divine encounter.

    David and the Showbread: This is a crucial example for Jerome. David and his men can only eat the holy bread (which Jerome explicitly compares to the Body of Christ: quasi corpus Christi) if they are "clean from women." This directly links sexual abstinence with worthiness to receive what he sees as the Old Testament equivalent of the Eucharist.

    The Explicit Conclusion: Jerome then drops all subtlety and states his conclusion bluntly: videlicet quod ad munditias corporis Christi, omnis coitus immundus sit. This translates to: "Namely, that in relation to the purity of the Body of Christ, all intercourse is unclean." This is one of the most extreme statements on the matter in all of patristic literature.

    Priestly Laws: He reinforces his point with priestly laws. The high priest must marry a virgin, not a widow, establishing a clear hierarchy of purity (virginity > widowhood). A married sister of a priest is treated as an "outsider" (aliena).

How Your Quote Fits In:

The passage about Judah, Tamar, and Onan serves a specific function within this broader argument. Having established that all intercourse creates a state of "uncleanness," Jerome must now address its purpose. He argues that the only thing that can possibly justify this "unclean" act is the noble, God-ordained purpose of procreation.

    Onan's sin, in Jerome's view, was precisely that he engaged in the sexual act while deliberately frustrating its only valid purpose. He engaged in it for pleasure or out of spite, and for this, God killed him.

    Therefore, the Onan story becomes Jerome's ultimate proof-text that any sexual act that is not open to procreation is mortally sinful.

In summary, the text you found shows Jerome's two-pronged attack: First, all sexual intercourse makes one ritually impure for holy things. Second, the only justification for engaging in such an act is the intention to procreate. Any other use is condemned by the clear example of Onan.

fr: Mais tu objectes que l’Église est fondée sur Pierre. Or, bien qu’en un autre passage il en soit de même pour tous les Apôtres, qu’ils reçoivent tous les clés du royaume des cieux et que la force de l’Église s’affermisse sur eux à égalité, un seul a pourtant été choisi parmi les douze afin que, par l’institution d’un chef, soit écartée toute occasion de schisme.
en: But you say [Mt 16:18], the Church was founded upon Peter: although elsewhere the same is attributed to all the apostles, and they all receive the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and the strength of the Church depends upon them all, yet one among the Twelve is chosen so that when a head has been appointed, there may be no occasion for schism [Against Jovinianus 1:26 (c. A.D. 393)].
latin: At dicis, super Petrum fundatur Ecclesia: licet id ipsum in alio loco super omnes Apostolos fiat, et cuncti claves regni coelorum accipiant, et ex aequo super eos Ecclesiae fortitudo solidetur, tamen propterea inter duodecim unus eligitur, ut capite constituto, schismatis tollatur occasio.
context:
Additional Relevant Commentary

This passage is one of the most important and frequently cited patristic texts on the nature of the Church's structure and the role of Saint Peter. Understanding its context is crucial.

1. The Immediate Context: The Virginity Debate

The entire work, Against Jovinianus, is a polemic defending the superiority of consecrated virginity over marriage. The immediate context of this passage is a long comparison between St. Peter (who was married) and St. John the Apostle (whom Jerome, along with tradition, held to be a lifelong virgin). Jerome spends paragraphs elevating John as the "beloved disciple," the one who leaned on Jesus' breast, and the one entrusted with the care of the Virgin Mary.

Jerome then anticipates his opponent's powerful counter-argument: "If John the virgin is so superior, why did Jesus found the Church on Peter, the married man?" The quote you found is Jerome's direct answer to this anticipated objection.

2. The Theological Balancing Act

St. Jerome's answer is a masterful balancing act that holds two truths in tension:

    Shared Apostolic Authority: He immediately concedes that the Church's foundation is, in fact, shared by all the apostles. He uses the powerful phrase "ex aequo" (equally or on equal footing) to state that the Church's strength is solidified upon them all. They all receive the keys. This affirms the collegiate nature of the apostolic office.

    Peter's Unique Role as Head: Having established the equality of the apostles in their foundational role, Jerome then gives a specific, practical reason for Peter's primacy. Peter was chosen and made "head" (capite constituto) for a clear purpose: to be a visible, unifying principle to prevent division and schism (schismatis tollatur occasio).

3. The "Why" of the Primacy

For Jerome in this passage, Peter's primacy is not a primacy of greater power or a different apostolic rank, but a functional primacy of unity. He is the center of gravity, the rallying point appointed by Christ to keep the college of apostles (and the Church that follows) from splintering into factions.

4. Historical Significance

This passage has been central to ecumenical discussions for centuries, especially between Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant theologians.

    Catholic theology often points to this passage to affirm the ancient belief in a Petrine primacy instituted by Christ to safeguard Church unity. The phrase "ut capite constituto" is seen as a key patristic witness to the papacy's role.

    Orthodox and Protestant theologians often highlight Jerome's strong emphasis on the equal authority of all the apostles ("ex aequo") to argue against later, more expansive claims of papal jurisdiction and power.

In essence, St. Jerome provides a nuanced vision where the Church is built equally on the entire college of apostles, but with Peter designated as the focal point to preserve their unity.

fr:
Il y a des péchés légers et des péchés graves. C'est une chose de devoir dix mille talents, une autre un quart de sou. Certes, nous aurons à répondre aussi bien d'une parole oiseuse que d'un adultère ; mais ce n'est pas la même chose d'être couvert de confusion et d'être tourmenté, de rougir et de subir un long supplice.

... Tu vois bien que si nous prions pour des péchés moindres, nous en obtenons le pardon. S'il s'agit de péchés plus graves, il est difficile de l'obtenir ; et qu'entre un péché et un autre, la distance est grande.
en: Some offenses are light, some heavy. It is one thing to owe ten thousand talents, another to owe a farthing. We shall have to give account of the idle word no less than 01 adultery; but is not the same thing to be put to the blush and to be put upon the rack, to grow red in the face and to ensure lasting torment. . . . You observe that we entreat for smaller offenses. we obtain pardon: if for greater ones, it is difficult to obtain our request: and that there is a great difference between sins [ Against Jovinianus 2:30 (C. A.D. 393)].
latin:
Sunt peccata levia, sunt gravia. Aliud est decem millia talenta debere, aliud quadrantem. Et de otioso quidem verbo, et adulterio rei tenebimur; sed non est idem suffundi, et torqueri: erubescere, et longo tempore cruciari.

    ... Cernis quod si pro peccatis minoribus deprecemur, impetremus veniam. Si pro majoribus, difficilis impetratio sit: et inter peccata et peccata, magnam esse distantiam.
context:
Additional Relevant Commentary

This passage is not just a casual observation; it is a critical piece of St. Jerome's argument against the core teachings of a monk named Jovinianus. To understand its importance, you need to know what Jerome was fighting against.

1. The Opponent: Jovinianus's Radical Equality
Jovinianus taught a form of Christian stoicism that had been condemned as heretical. His key tenets were:

    Equal Merit: All baptized Christians who keep their faith have the same merit and reward in heaven, whether they are virgins, widows, or married.

    Equal Sins: All sins are equal. There is no difference in gravity between, for example, stealing a piece of bread and committing murder.

    Indefectibility: A person truly baptized with the Spirit cannot sin again.

2. Jerome's Counter-Argument: A World of Distinction
Jerome's entire treatise is a furious, learned, and often sarcastic refutation of this idea of radical equality. The larger block of text you provided shows his method perfectly:

    Analogy of the Body: Before your quote, Jerome points out that the Apostle Paul distinguishes between more and less "honorable" parts of the body (1 Cor. 12). He asks rhetorically, "Do you think the mouth and the bowels are of the same order and merit?" This is his way of saying that distinction and hierarchy are natural and God-ordained.

    Analogy of the Church: He also argues that the Church has different roles (mother, sister, spouse), implying different levels of relationship and merit.

3. The Specific Argument on Sin (Your Quote)
Your quote is the climax of this argument applied to morality. Jerome attacks Jovinianus's "all sins are equal" doctrine with a three-pronged argument:

    Appeal to Scripture & Reason: He alludes to Jesus's parable of the unforgiving servant (Matthew 18), contrasting a massive debt of ten thousand talents with a tiny debt of a farthing (quadrantem). This shows that Jesus Himself used the idea of differing degrees of obligation.

    Appeal to Justice: He argues that while we are accountable for all sins ("the idle word no less than of adultery"), the punishment must fit the crime. It is absurd to think that the penalty for a moment of shame (erubescere - to blush) should be the same as the penalty for a grave crime (longo tempore cruciari - to be tormented for a long time).

    Appeal to Apostolic Teaching: Immediately after the main part of your quote, Jerome cites 1 John 5:16 on the "sin that leads to death" versus the "sin that does not lead to death." This is his definitive scriptural proof that the Apostles themselves made a clear distinction between the gravity of sins.

Theological Significance:
This passage is a foundational text in the history of moral theology. St. Jerome's clear articulation of a distinction between "light sins" (peccata levia) and "heavy sins" (peccata gravia) became a cornerstone for the later, more systematic development of the concepts of venial sin and mortal sin in the Catholic tradition.

fr: C'est donc à nous qu'il appartient, en fonction de la diversité de nos vertus, de nous préparer des récompenses différentes. Si nous devons tous être égaux au ciel, c'est en vain que nous nous humilions ici-bas dans l'espoir d'y être plus grands. Pourquoi les vierges persévèrent-elles ? Pourquoi les veuves s’imposent-elles tant de peines ? Pourquoi les femmes mariées gardent-elles la continence ? Dans ce cas, péchons tous ! Et après la pénitence, nous serons les égaux des Apôtres.
en: Now our work is, according to our different virtues, to prepare for ourselves a different future. . . . If we are all to be equal in heaven, in vain do we humble ourselves here that we may be greater there. . . Why do virgins persevere? Widows toil? Why do married women practice continence? Let us all sin, and when once we have repented, we shall be on the same footing as the apostles [Against Jovinianus 2:32-34 (c. A.D. 393)].
latin: Jam nostri laboris est, pro diversitate virtutum, diversa nobis praemia praeparare. . . Si omnes in coelo aequales futuri sumus, frustra nos hic humiliamus, ut ibi possimus esse majores. . . Quid perseverant virgines? quid laborant viduae? cur maritatae se continent? Peccemus omnes, et post poenitentiam idem erimus quod Apostoli sunt.
context:
Commentary and Relevant Context

This passage is one of the most famous and fiery sections from St. Jerome's defense of asceticism. To understand its power, you need to know who he was arguing against.
The Opponent: Jovinianus

Jovinianus was a monk who began teaching in Rome around A.D. 390. His core theses were seen as a direct attack on the growing ascetic movement championed by figures like Jerome and Ambrose. Jovinianus argued:

    That virgins, widows, and married persons, once baptized, are of equal merit if they live according to their vows.

    That those who have kept their baptismal grace will receive the same reward in heaven.

    That fasting and feasting with thanksgiving are of equal value.

Jerome's Argument: A "Reductio ad Absurdum"

Jerome, a passionate and often abrasive advocate for virginity and self-denial, saw Jovinianus's teaching as a lazy, dangerous doctrine that would destroy Christian striving. The passage you've selected is a perfect example of his primary argumentative technique: the reductio ad absurdum (reduction to absurdity). He takes Jovinianus's premise and follows it to what he sees as its logical, catastrophic conclusion.

    The Core Principle (from Sec. 32): Jerome begins by stating the orthodox position: our efforts on earth matter. Different levels of virtue (diversitate virtutum) lead to different rewards (diversa praemia). This is a direct refutation of Jovinianus's idea of a single, equal reward for all.

    The Absurdity of Humility (from Sec. 33): He applies this to Christ's teaching. The Gospel says we should humble ourselves to be made greater (cf. Matt. 23:12). But if everyone's reward is equal, then this striving for "greatness" in heaven through humility on earth is pointless (frustra). Jerome's point is that Jovinianus's doctrine renders Christ's own words meaningless.

    The Rhetorical Climax (from Sec. 34): This is where Jerome unleashes his full sarcastic power. He applies the "equal reward" theory to the different states of Christian life:

        "Why do virgins persevere? Widows toil?...": If the state of virginity or chaste widowhood holds no higher heavenly reward than marriage, then why would anyone undertake these difficult and laborious paths? The incentive for heroic virtue is destroyed.

        "Let us all sin...": This is the final, shocking conclusion of his reductio ad absurdum. If a person who sins and then repents receives the exact same reward as the Apostles who gave their entire lives and blood for Christ, then the entire moral and spiritual economy of Christianity collapses. It becomes a system with no meaningful consequences for action, inviting laxity and sin.

In summary, Jerome's argument is that Jovinianus's teaching, while perhaps sounding egalitarian and comforting, is actually a destructive force that undermines Scripture, nullifies the value of heroic virtue, and makes a mockery of the sacrifices of the saints and apostles. This passage is a cornerstone of the Western Church's traditional teaching on merit and the degrees of glory in heaven.

fr:
Dans ton pamphlet, tu affirmes que, de notre vivant, nous pouvons prier les uns pour les autres ; mais qu'une fois morts, la prière de personne pour autrui n'est plus exaucée, d'autant que les martyrs, qui réclamaient vengeance pour leur sang, n'ont pu l'obtenir.

Or, si les apôtres et les martyrs, alors qu'ils étaient encore dans leur corps et devaient encore se soucier d'eux-mêmes, pouvaient prier pour les autres, à combien plus forte raison le peuvent-ils après les couronnes, les victoires et les triomphes ?
en: You say, in your pamphlet, that as long as we are alive we can pray for one another; but once we die, the prayer of no person for another can be heard, and all the more because the martyrs, though they [Rv 6:10] cry for the avenging of their blood, have never been able to obtain their request. apostles and martyrs while still in the body can pray for others, when they ought still to be anxious for themselves, how much more must they do SO when once they have won their crowns, overcome, and triumphed? [Against Vigilantius 6 (A.D. 406)].
latin: Dicis in libello tuo, quod dum vivimus, mutuo pro nobis orare possumus; postquam autem mortui fuerimus, nullius sit pro alio exaudienda oratio: praesertim cum martyres ultionem sui sanguinis obsecrantes, impetrare non quiverint.     Si apostoli et martyres adhuc in corpore constituti possunt orare pro caeteris, quando pro se adhuc debent esse solliciti: quanto magis post coronas, victorias et triumphos?
context:
Additional Relevant Commentary

The larger block of text you provided gives a fantastic window into St. Jerome's mind and the nature of this dispute. Here's what's happening:
1. The Opponent: Vigilantius

Vigilantius was a presbyter from Gaul who objected to several developing practices in the Church which he saw as superstitious or excessive. St. Jerome groups his errors together and attacks them with full force. Vigilantius was against:

    The veneration of martyrs' relics.

    All-night prayer vigils at the basilicas of the martyrs.

    The practice of lighting candles and lamps at their shrines.

    The value of monasticism and celibacy.

    Praying to the saints and asking for their intercession.

2. Jerome's Main Argument: A Fortiori ("From the Stronger")

Jerome's logic is powerful and simple. He argues a fortiori:

    Premise: Even on earth, when saints like Moses, Stephen, and Paul were still struggling with their own salvation, their prayers were incredibly powerful and effective for others (Jerome cites the examples of Moses saving Israel, Stephen forgiving his persecutors, and Paul saving the lives of those on his ship).

    Conclusion: Therefore, how much more powerful and effective must their prayers be now in heaven, after they have won their crowns, are perfected in glory, and follow the Lamb wherever He goes? To Jerome, it is absurd to think they would have less power or charity after death than before.

3. Jerome's Sarcastic and Dismissive Tone

This passage is classic Jerome. He doesn't just refute Vigilantius; he mocks him. Notice these elements from the larger text you provided:

    He refers to Vigilantius's work not as a book, but a "little book" or "pamphlet" (libello tuo).

    He later calls Vigilantius a "sleeping-while-awake" man who "writes while he's asleep" (Tu vigilans dormis, et dormiens scribis).

    He contrasts the "living dog" Vigilantius with the "dead lion" St. Paul, a direct and brutal insult.

4. The Context of the Apocryphal Book of Esdras

A crucial part of the text you found is Jerome's rant against an "apocryphal book... under the name of Esdras." Vigilantius was using a passage from a non-canonical book (likely 4 Esdras, or 2 Esdras in some traditions) which states that after death, no one can pray for another. Jerome's response is to dismiss the source entirely: "I have never read this book. For what need is there to take up in my hands what the Church does not receive?" This shows how central the established canon of Scripture was to settling doctrinal disputes.

In summary, you have found a foundational patristic text defending the Communion of Saints and the intercession of the saints in heaven. It perfectly showcases St. Jerome's method: grounding his argument in Scripture, employing sharp logic, and using powerful, often insulting, rhetoric to defend Church tradition.

fr: Il sait comment la Vierge a engendré Dieu ; et il ne sait pas comment lui-même est né.
en: As to how a virgin became the Mother of God, [Rufinus of Aquileia] has full knowledge; as to how he himself was born, he knows nothing [Apology Against Rufinus 2:10 (A.D. 401)].
latin: Scit quomodo Deum Virgo generarit; et nescit quomodo ipse sit natus.
context:
Additional Relevant Commentary

To understand the full force of this insult, you need to know the context of the bitter feud between Jerome and his former friend, Rufinus of Aquileia.

1. The Core Issue: The Origin of the Soul and Origenism

    The entire controversy revolved around the teachings of the 3rd-century theologian Origen. Some of Origen's ideas, especially the pre-existence of souls (the belief that souls were created long ago and are later put into bodies, often as a punishment), were being condemned as heretical.

    Rufinus had translated Origen's major work, On First Principles, into Latin. To protect himself, he claimed to have edited out the heretical parts.

    In his own Apology, Rufinus discussed the origin of the human soul. He laid out the three main theories of his day:

        Traducianism: The soul is generated by the parents along with the body.

        Creationism: God creates a new soul for each body at conception.

        Pre-existence: Origen's controversial view.

    Rufinus's crucial (and in Jerome's view, cowardly) move was to say, "I have read all these theories, but I confess I still do not know which one is true." He pleaded ignorance.

2. Jerome's Rhetorical Strategy: Accusation of Feigned Ignorance

Jerome did not believe Rufinus was genuinely ignorant. He saw this as a dishonest dodge. He believed Rufinus was secretly an Origenist and was only pretending not to know the answer so that he wouldn't have to explicitly condemn Origen's theory of pre-existence.

You can see this accusation directly in the Latin text you provided:

    Vide ne statim tibi objiciatur, idcirco te trium ignorantiam confiteri, ne unum damnare cogaris...
    ("See that it is not immediately objected against you, that you confess ignorance of the three, lest you be forced to condemn the one [Origen's view]...")

3. The Meaning of the Quote in Context

This is where your quote delivers the knockout blow. Jerome masterfully uses sarcasm to paint Rufinus as an absurd figure. The argument goes like this:

    The Unknowable Mystery: Jerome points to the most profound, supernatural mystery of the Christian faith: the Incarnation. How a finite, created virgin could give birth to the infinite, uncreated God is something beyond all human reason. It is accepted on faith alone.

    The Knowable Question: He then points to the origin of the soul. While a difficult theological question, it is a matter of created reality. It's about us.

    The Sarcastic Contrast: Jerome's jab is that Rufinus, the great theologian, speaks with audacious confidence about the ultimate divine mystery (Scit quomodo Deum Virgo generarit - "He knows how a Virgin gave birth to God!"). Yet, when it comes to the one controversial topic that could get him into trouble (the origin of his own soul), he suddenly becomes a humble agnostic (nescit quomodo ipse sit natus - "he doesn't know how he himself was born!").

The quote brilliantly exposes Rufinus's position as intellectually inconsistent and morally suspect. It implies that Rufinus is a proud theologian on "safe" topics but a cowardly fraud when his own heretical leanings are on the line. It remains one of the most famous and devastating insults in the history of Christian polemics.

fr:
En quoi ai-je donc péché, si j'ai suivi le jugement des églises ?

Quant au fait que je rapporte ce que les Hébreux ont coutume d'objecter contre l'histoire de Suzanne, le cantique des trois jeunes gens et les fables de Bel et du Dragon – récits qui ne se trouvent pas dans le canon hébraïque –, celui qui m'en accuse se révèle être un sot calomniateur.

En effet, je n'ai pas exposé ce que je pensais moi-même, mais bien ce qu'ils ont l'habitude de dire contre nous.

Et si, dans le prologue, je n'ai pas réfuté leur opinion, c'était par souci de brièveté, pour ne pas donner l'impression d'écrire un livre et non une préface. Je crois d'ailleurs avoir aussitôt enchaîné, car j'ai bien dit : « Ce n'est pas le moment d'en débattre. »
en: What sin have I committed if I follow the judgment of the churches? But he who brings charges against me for relating [in my preface to the book of Daniel] the objections that the Hebrews are wont to raise against the story of Susannah [Dn 13], the Song of the Three Children Dn 3:29-687, and the story of Bel and the Dragon [Dn 14], which are not found in the Hebrew volume, proves that he is just foolish sycophant. I was not relating my own personal views, but rather the remarks that they are wont to make against us. If did not reply to their views in my preface, in the interest of brevity, lest it seem that was composing not a preface, but a book, I believe added promptly the remark, for I said, "This is not the time to discuss such matters" [Apology Against Rufinus 2:33 (A.D 401)].
latin: Ego quid peccavi, si ecclesiarum judicium secutus sum? Quod autem refero, quid adversum Susannae historiam, et hymnum trium puerorum, et Belis, Draconisque fabulas, quae in volumine Hebraico non habentur, Hebraei soleant dicere, qui me criminatur, stultum se sycophantam probat. Non enim quid ipse sentirem, sed quid illi contra nos dicere soleant, explicavi. Quorum opinioni, si non respondi in Prologo, brevitati studens, ne non praefationem, sed librum viderer scribere, puto quod statim subjecerim; dixi enim, « De quo non est hujus temporis disserere. »
context:
Additional Relevant Commentary

This passage is far more than a simple academic defense; it's a key moment in a bitter and famous feud between two of the greatest scholars of the ancient Church, St. Jerome and his former friend, Tyrannius Rufinus.
1. The Context: The Jerome-Rufinus Controversy

    The Accusation: Rufinus had attacked Jerome's life's work—the translation of the Old Testament from Hebrew into Latin (the Vulgate). One of Rufinus's lines of attack was to claim that Jerome was undermining the authority of the Church's scriptures. By pointing out in his preface to Daniel that the stories of Susanna, Bel and the Dragon, etc., were not in the Hebrew text, Jerome appeared to be questioning their canonicity. Rufinus presented this as Jerome siding with the Jews against the Church.

    The Book: This quote comes from Jerome's brutal counter-attack, the Apology Against Rufinus. The tone is not one of gentle scholarly disagreement; it is one of outrage, personal insult, and a fierce defense of his life's work and his orthodoxy.

2. Jerome's Multi-Layered Defense

Jerome's argument here is brilliant and multifaceted:

    "I Follow the Churches!": He begins by turning the accusation on its head. He says, "What sin have I committed if I follow the judgment of the churches?" He points out that the churches of his day read the book of Daniel not from the old Greek Septuagint, but from a different Greek translation by a man named Theodotion. Why? Because the Church itself had judged the Septuagint version of Daniel to be flawed. With this single stroke, Jerome paints himself as the one who is truly faithful to the Church's practical judgment, while making Rufinus look ignorant.

    "I'm a Reporter, Not an Editor": His core defense regarding the Deuterocanonical additions (Susanna, etc.) is that he was not giving his own opinion. He was simply performing his scholarly duty by reporting what "the Hebrews" (the Jewish scholars he consulted) said about their own scriptures. He claims he was merely relating their objections, not endorsing them.

    The Insult (stultum se sycophantam probat): This is classic Jerome. He doesn't just refute Rufinus's argument; he attacks his character. He says anyone who can't distinguish between reporting an objection and holding it personally "proves that he is just a foolish sycophant." This raw, personal attack is characteristic of the entire work.

    "It Was a Preface, Not a Book": He defends his choice not to immediately refute the Jewish objections by pleading brevity. His goal was to write a short preface, and a full defense would have turned it into a book. He even quotes himself ("This is not the time to discuss such matters") to prove that he had intentionally deferred the discussion, not ignored it.

3. Lasting Significance: The Debate over the Canon

This passage is a landmark text in the history of the biblical canon. It perfectly encapsulates the tension Jerome lived with:

    On one hand, his scholarly principle of Hebraica veritas ("the Hebrew truth") led him to privilege the books found in the Hebrew Bible.

    On the other hand, as a churchman, he had to respect the longstanding tradition of the Church, which read and revered these additional texts (the Deuterocanon).

Here, we see him using both principles to defend himself. He uses his scholarly knowledge to explain why he mentioned the Hebrew objections, and he uses the Church's practical tradition to prove his own faithfulness. This very debate would continue for over a thousand years, culminating in the formal definitions of the canon at the Council of Trent.

fr: Ne t'étonne pas de cette nouveauté : qu'une Vierge enfante Dieu.
en: Do not marvel at the novelty of the thing, if a Virgin gives birth to God [Commentaries Isaiah 3:7:15 (c. A.D. 409)].
latin: non mireris ad rei novitatem, si Virgo Deum pariat
context:
Additional Relevant Commentary

This passage is a brilliant example of St. Jerome's mature Christology, where he masterfully holds together the full divinity and full humanity of Christ. Here is the context and significance of his argument in this section:

1. Immediate Context: Explaining Isaiah 7:15

Jerome is commenting on the verse, "He shall eat butter and honey, that he may know to refuse the evil and choose the good." He uses this verse to explain the mystery of the preceding verse (Isaiah 7:14), the prophecy of the Virgin birth.

2. Jerome's Argument (A Two-Pronged Defense of Orthodoxy)

Jerome's commentary here is designed to refute two opposing heresies at once:

    Against Arianism (which denied Christ's full divinity): The core of his argument is the astonishing phrase Virgo Deum pariat ("a Virgin gives birth to God"). This is not just a prophet or a super-human being; it is God Himself who is born. Jerome emphasizes this by stating that this child, though yet to be born, is so powerful that he can save the House of David now. He explicitly identifies this child with the pre-existent God who appeared to Abraham and Moses.

    Against Docetism/Gnosticism (which denied Christ's true humanity): Jerome then immediately addresses the "butter and honey." Why is this seemingly mundane detail included in the prophecy? For Jerome, it is crucial proof of Christ's true humanity (veritas humani corporis). He argues that Christ will eat the real food of an infant to show that he was not a phantom or a ghost, but a true human being.

3. The Union of Natures

The genius of Jerome's commentary is how he links these two points. He states that even while this child is a true infant, wrapped in swaddling clothes and eating infant food, he simultaneously possesses divine wisdom and judgment ("habebit boni malique judicium" - he will have judgment of good and evil). In other words, the limitations of his human infancy do not diminish his divine nature.

4. Significance for the Title Theotokos

Jerome's phrase Deum pariat ("gives birth to God") is a powerful Latin affirmation of the doctrine that would be dogmatically defined at the Council of Ephesus in 431 using the Greek term Theotokos ("God-bearer" or "Mother of God"). Jerome, writing two decades before the council, shows that this understanding of Mary's role and Christ's identity was already a firm part of orthodox teaching in the Western Church.

In summary, you have found a rich and concise passage where St. Jerome defends the orthodox faith in the Incarnation, affirming that the child born of the Virgin Mary is simultaneously true God and true man.

fr: Par conséquent, partout où il y a fornication, ou même soupçon de fornication, il est légitime de répudier son épouse. Et comme il pourrait arriver qu’un homme, en vue d’un second mariage, calomnie une innocente et impute une faute à sa première femme, il lui est ordonné de répudier celle-ci de telle manière qu’il ne puisse en prendre une seconde du vivant de la première.
en: Wherever there is fornication and a suspicion of fornication, a wife is freely dismissed. Because it is always possible that someone may calumniate the innocent and, for the sake of a second joining in marriage, act in criminal fashion against the first, it is commanded that when the first wife is dismissed, a second may not be taken while the first lives [ Commentaries on Matthew 3:19:9 (A.D. 398)].
latin: Ubicumque est igitur fornicatio, et fornicationis suspicio, libere uxor dimittitur. Et quia poterat accidere, ut aliquis calumniam faceret innocenti, et ob secundam copulam nuptiarum, veteri crimen impingeret, sic priorem dimittere jubetur uxorem, ut secundam, prima vivente, non habeat.
context:
This passage is a cornerstone of the Western patristic tradition on the indissolubility of marriage, arguing that even in cases of legitimate separation, the bond remains, precluding a second marriage. Additional Relevant Commentary from the Text

The rest of the text you provided is incredibly valuable. It reveals St. Jerome's complete line of thought.
1. The Justification for Dismissal (The text before your quote)

Jerome first explains why fornication is the sole exception that allows for separation.

    It Breaks the "One Flesh" Union: He states, "Only fornication is what conquers the affection for a wife." Why? Because when the wife "has divided the one flesh into another" (unam carnem in aliam diviserit), she has already, by her own action, "separated herself from her husband."

    It Places the Husband Under a Curse: He then provides a scriptural justification (from the Septuagint version of Proverbs 18:22), arguing that a man who knowingly keeps an adulterous wife is himself "foolish and impious" (stultus et impius). Therefore, dismissing her is not just a right, but a moral necessity to avoid sin.

2. The Pastoral Rationale Against Remarriage (The text after your quote)

After stating the rule, Jerome explains the pastoral wisdom behind prohibiting remarriage.

    A Test of Motives: He poses a rhetorical question to the husband who dismisses his wife: "If you are dismissing your wife not for the sake of lust but because of an injury, why, having experienced an unhappy first marriage, do you throw yourself into the danger of a new one?" He is saying that if the husband's motives are pure, he should be wary of entering another marriage, not eager for it.

    Symmetry: He immediately applies the same rule to a wife who might dismiss her husband, commanding that "she not take a second husband."

    Protecting the Dismissed Woman: He notes that a man who marries a dismissed woman is also an adulterer. He reasons that since a "harlot" or "adulteress" might not fear public shame, the command is placed on the second man to prevent the sin from occurring.

3. The Apostles' Shock and Jerome's Ascetic View (The second paragraph)

This section reveals Jerome's deeply ascetic view of marriage.

    The "Heavy Burden" of Marriage: He captures the apostles' shock: "The weight of a wife is heavy, if we are not permitted to dismiss her except for the cause of fornication!"

    A Litany of Flaws: He imagines their complaints, listing all the other reasons a man might want to leave his wife: she is a drunkard, wrathful, ill-mannered, lustful, a glutton, a wanderer, quarrelsome, or verbally abusive.

    The Stark Conclusion: Despite all these terrible flaws, the answer is unwavering: "Whether we want to or not, she must be endured" (Volumus nolumus, sustinenda est). He concludes with a classic statement of his ascetic worldview: "For when we were free, we voluntarily subjected ourselves to servitude" (voluntarie nos subjecimus servituti).

In summary, you have found a rich passage that shows Jerome's interpretation in its full context: fornication is the only grounds for separation, but even then, remarriage is forbidden. This prohibition serves as a crucial safeguard against the abuse of divorce and reflects a worldview where marriage is an unbreakable, though often difficult, "yoke of servitude."

fr:
Or, les hérétiques prononcent leur propre sentence en se retirant de l'église de leur propre chef : cette séparation est, en quelque sorte, la condamnation que prononce leur conscience.
On considère que la différence entre l'hérésie et le schisme tient à ceci : l'hérésie professe une doctrine déviante, tandis que le schisme, suite à une dissension épiscopale, se sépare de l'église. Une telle distinction peut, certes, se comprendre en partie à l'origine.
Cependant, il n'est pas de schisme qui ne se forge quelque hérésie, afin de donner l'impression d'avoir quitté l'église à juste titre.
en: Heretics bring sentence upon themselves since by their own choice they withdraw from the Church, a withdrawal that, since they are aware of it, constitutes damnation. Between heresy and schism there is this difference: heresy involves perverse doctrine, while schism separates one from the Church on account of disagreement with the bishop. Nevertheless, there is no schism that does not trump up a heresy to justify its departure from the Church [Commentaries on Titus 3:10-11 (C. A.D. 386)].
latin: Haeretici autem in semetipsos sententiam ferunt, suo arbitrio de Ecclesia recedentes: quae recessio propriae conscientiae videtur esse damnatio.   Inter haeresim et schisma hoc esse arbitrantur, quod haeresis perversum dogma habeat: schisma propter episcopalem dissensionem ab Ecclesia separetur: quod quidem in principio aliqua ex parte intelligi potest.   Caeterum nullum schisma non sibi aliquam confingit haeresim, ut recte ab Ecclesia recessisse videatur.
context:
Additional Relevant Commentary

This passage is foundational for the Western Church's understanding of heresy and schism. Jerome's analysis is both theologically profound and psychologically astute.

    Heresy as Self-Condemnation: Jerome is commenting on St. Paul's instruction to "reject" a heretic after two warnings (Titus 3:10), noting that such a person is "warped and sinful; he is self-condemned." Jerome's key insight is that the formal excommunication by the Church is not what primarily condemns the heretic. The heretic, by his own free choice (suo arbitrio) and against his own conscience (propriae conscientiae), has already separated himself from the body of truth. The Church's action is merely a formal recognition of a spiritual reality that the heretic has already created.

    The Classic Definition of Heresy vs. Schism: This is one of the clearest and most cited distinctions in early Christian literature.

        Heresy is a matter of content—it involves holding a "perverse doctrine" (perversum dogma) that corrupts the apostolic faith.

        Schism is a matter of communion—it is a separation from the Church's unity, specifically over a disagreement with the bishop (propter episcopalem dissensionem), who is the local center of that unity.

    The Inevitable Link (Jerome's Cynical Masterstroke): The final sentence is what makes this passage so brilliant and enduring. Jerome observes that a schism can rarely remain a "pure" schism for long. A group cannot justify the radical act of tearing the Body of Christ apart simply because they dislike a particular bishop. To legitimize their separation and attract followers, they must claim a higher moral or doctrinal ground. Therefore, they will inevitably "trump up a heresy" (sibi aliquam confingit haeresim) to make it seem that they left "rightly" (ut recte... recessisse videatur).

Historical Example: The Donatist movement in North Africa, which Jerome knew well, perfectly illustrates his point. It began as a schism over who was the legitimate Bishop of Carthage. However, to justify their separation, the Donatists developed a heretical ecclesiology, arguing that the true Church consisted only of the "pure" and that sacraments administered by "unworthy" (traditor) clergy were invalid. The schism thus gave birth to a heresy to sustain itself.

In summary, you have found a cornerstone text in which Jerome provides a lasting definition of terms and a profound insight into the dynamic relationship between doctrinal error and broken communion.
