fr: Autre interprétation : si le serpent diabolique a mordu quelqu'un en secret et, à l'insu de tous, l'a infecté du venin du péché ; si le blessé garde le silence, ne fait pas pénitence et refuse de confesser sa blessure à son frère et maître, ce maître et frère, qui a pourtant une langue pour guérir, ne pourra que difficilement lui être utile. Car si le malade a honte de confesser sa blessure au médecin, la médecine ne guérit pas ce qu'elle ignore.
en: If the serpent, the devil, bites someone secretly, he infects that person with the venom of sin. And if the one who has been bitten keeps silence and does not do penance, and does not want to confess his wound . then his brother and his master, who have the word [of absolution] that will cure him, cannot very well assist him [ Commentary on Ecclesiastes 10:11 (Cc. A.D. 388)].
latin: Aliter: Si quem serpens diabolus occulte momorderit, et nullo conscio, cum peccati veneno infecerit; si tacuerit qui percussus est, et non egerit poenitentiam, nec vulnus suum fratri et magistro voluerit confiteri, magister et frater, qui linguam habent ad curandum, facile ei prodesse non poterunt. Si enim erubescat aegrotus, vulnus medico confiteri, quod ignorat medicina non curat.
context:
Additional Commentary and Context

This is an extremely important passage in the history of the sacrament of Penance and Reconciliation.

    The Biblical Verse: St. Jerome is commenting on Ecclesiastes 10:11, which literally says, "If a serpent bites in silence, there is no advantage for the charmer." A charmer can't heal a secret bite he doesn't know about.

    Jerome's Two Interpretations: As was common in his exegesis, Jerome first gives a simple, moral interpretation and then a deeper, spiritual one.

        First Interpretation (Literal/Moral): He compares the serpent to a secret slanderer. Just as a serpent bites quietly, a slanderer secretly injects the poison of his words, and his tongue is no better than a serpent's.

        Second Interpretation (Allegorical/Spiritual): This is your quote. Here, Jerome moves to the spiritual realm:

            The Serpent: Is explicitly identified as the Devil.

            The Secret Bite: Is a secret sin, one not publicly known.

            The Venom: Is the spiritual poison of sin that infects the soul.

            The Silence: Is the sinner's refusal to confess, born out of shame (erubescat aegrotus - "if the sick man is ashamed").

    The "Brother and Master": The Role of the Priest: This is the most significant part of the passage. The "brother and master" (fratri et magistro) to whom one must confess is the priest or bishop.

        Master (magister): Signifies his teaching authority and his role as a spiritual guide appointed by the Church.

        Brother (frater): Signifies his role as a fellow Christian, a source of compassionate help.

        The "Tongue for Curing": The English "word of absolution" is an excellent interpretive translation of linguam ad curandum ("the tongue for curing"). This refers to the sacramental power given to the priest by Christ to forgive sins.

    The Medical Analogy: The final sentence is powerful: "Medicine does not cure what it does not know." This medical analogy for confession was very common among the Church Fathers. Sin is a wound or a disease of the soul; the sinner is the patient; the priest is the spiritual physician; and confession is the act of showing the wound to the doctor so he can apply the medicine of absolution.

In summary, this passage is a key patristic witness to the early Church's belief in and practice of private, auricular confession for secret sins, highlighting the essential role of the priest as the minister of God's forgiveness.

fr: En effet, puisque l'homme baptisé dans le Père, le Fils et le Saint-Esprit devient le temple du Seigneur, et qu'une fois l'ancienne demeure détruite, un nouveau sanctuaire de la Trinité est édifié, comment peux-tu affirmer que chez les Ariens les péchés peuvent être remis sans la venue de l'Esprit Saint ? Comment l'âme qui ne possède pas l'Esprit Saint est-elle purifiée de ses souillures anciennes ?
en: For seeing that a man baptized in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit becomes a temple of the Lord, and that while the old abode is destroyed a new shrine is built for the Trinity, how can you say that sins can be remitted among the Arians without the coming of the Holy Spirit? How is a soul purged from its former stains that does not have the Holy Spirit? [Dialogue Against the Luciferians 6 (C. A.D. 382)].
latin: Nam cum in Patre et Filio et Spiritu sancto baptizatus homo, templum Domini fiat, cum, veteri aede destructa, novum Trinitatis delubrum aedificetur, quomodo dicis, sine adventu Spiritus sancti apud Arianos peccata posse dimitti? Quomodo antiquis sordibus anima purgatur, quae sanctum non habet Spiritum?
context:
Additional Relevant Commentary

This quote is the central point of a powerful argument about the nature of baptism and the Holy Spirit.

1. The Speakers and the Debate:
The work is a dialogue between "Orthodoxus" (representing the mainstream Catholic position of St. Jerome) and "Luciferianus," a follower of the schismatic bishop Lucifer of Cagliari.

    The Luciferian Position: Luciferians were rigorists. They were willing to accept the validity of a baptism performed by an Arian heretic but insisted that the person baptized did not receive the Holy Spirit until they were later confirmed by a Catholic bishop through the laying on of hands.

    The Orthodox (Jerome's) Position: St. Jerome sees this as a fatal contradiction. You cannot separate the grace of baptism (forgiveness of sins) from the action of the Holy Spirit.

2. The Theological Argument (The "Gotcha" Moment):
The Luciferian has just said that he receives those baptized by Arians through the "imposition of hands and the invocation of the Holy Spirit," admitting that heretics cannot confer the Spirit.

The quote you found is Jerome's brilliant rebuttal. He is essentially saying:

    "Wait a minute. You accept their baptism, but say they don't give the Holy Spirit? Let's think about what baptism is."

    Baptism in the name of the Trinity makes a person a "temple of the Lord" and a "new shrine for the Trinity." This is a profound spiritual transformation.

    The Core Question: How can this incredible event—the remission of sins, the purging of the soul, the creation of a divine temple—possibly happen without the Holy Spirit, who is the agent of all sanctification? It's impossible. Water alone doesn't do it.

    The Logical Trap: Jerome forces the Luciferian into a corner. If Arian baptism is valid (as the Luciferian claims), then the Holy Spirit must have been present. If the Holy Spirit was not present (as the Luciferian also claims), then the baptism must be invalid, a mere washing with water that did nothing to the soul.

As Jerome concludes just after your quote: "Therefore, if an Arian cannot give the Holy Spirit, he cannot even baptize, because the baptism of the Church is not valid without the Holy Spirit."

You have chosen a passage that perfectly showcases St. Jerome's sharp logical mind and his profound understanding of sacramental theology. He masterfully demonstrates that the forgiveness of sins in baptism is inextricably linked to the indwelling of the Holy Spirit.

fr: ...il adressa sur cette affaire un synode africain à Étienne, alors évêque de la ville de Rome et vingt-deuxième successeur du bienheureux Pierre, mais sa tentative fut vaine.
en: [Pope] Stephen was the blessed Peter's twenty-second successor in the see of Rome [Dialogue Against the Luciferians 23 (c. A.D. 382)].
latin: ...ad Stephanum tunc Romanae urbis episcopum, qui a beato Petro vicesimus secundus fuit, super hac re Africanam synodum direxit, sed conatus ejus frustra fuit.
context:
Additional Relevant Commentary

This isn't just a historical footnote for Jerome; it's the core of a powerful argument. The context is crucial to understanding why he says this and why it's so significant.

1. The Broader Argument: Refuting Rigorism
Jerome is arguing against the Luciferian schismatics, who refused to accept the validity of sacraments administered by heretics and insisted on rebaptism. Jerome's position, representing the orthodox Catholic view, is that the ancient tradition of the Church is to accept the baptism of heretics if it was performed with the correct form and intention.

2. The Ultimate Test Case: Cyprian vs. Pope Stephen
To prove his point, Jerome brings up the most famous historical case on this very issue: the controversy between St. Cyprian of Carthage and Pope St. Stephen I in the mid-3rd century.

    St. Cyprian's Position: Cyprian, a revered martyr and bishop, along with a synod of African bishops, argued passionately that heretics were outside the Church and therefore could not confer valid sacraments. He insisted that those baptized by heretics must be rebaptized upon entering the Catholic Church.

    Pope St. Stephen's Position: Pope Stephen, representing the ancient and unbroken tradition of the Church of Rome, forcefully rejected Cyprian's view. He decreed that the universal custom was not to rebaptize, but to receive converts with the laying on of hands. His guiding principle was, "Let nothing new be introduced, but only what has been handed down" (Nihil innovetur nisi quod traditum est).

3. Jerome's Rhetorical Genius
By citing this case, Jerome does several things:

    He shows the Luciferians are not original: Their rigorist position is not new; it's the same error that a great saint, Cyprian, once fell into.

    He uses a Saint against them: He shows that even a holy and brilliant bishop like Cyprian could be wrong when he departed from the universal tradition.

    He highlights the authority of the Roman See: This is the key to your quote. By explicitly stating that Stephen "was the twenty-second from the blessed Peter," Jerome is underscoring the source of Stephen's authority. His teaching wasn't just his personal opinion; it was the tradition preserved and handed down through the unbroken succession of the bishops of Rome, beginning with Peter. This apostolic authority trumped the decision of a regional African synod, even one led by the great Cyprian.

    He points out that Stephen's position won: Jerome immediately adds, "but his effort was in vain" (sed conatus ejus frustra fuit), and that the very bishops who sided with Cyprian later "returned to the ancient custom" (ad antiquam consuetudinem revoluti). This proves to the Luciferians that they are clinging to a position that history has already judged and rejected in favor of the Roman tradition.

In summary, your quote is part of a masterfully constructed argument where St. Jerome uses a famous historical conflict to defend the Church's practice of mercy and to uphold the authority of the Roman See as the guardian of apostolic tradition.

fr: Loin de moi la pensée de dire du mal d'eux : succédant au rang des Apôtres, ils consacrent de leur bouche sainte le corps du Christ, et c'est par eux que nous sommes nous-mêmes chrétiens.
en: Far be it from me to censure the successors of the apostles, who with holy words consecrate the body of Christ, and who make us Christians Letters 14:8 (c. A.D. 376)].
latin: Absit ut de his quidquam sinistrum loquar, quia Apostolico gradui succedentes, CHRISTI CORPUS sacro ore conficiunt; per quos et nos Christiani sumus.
context:
Additional Commentary and Context

This quote is far more than just a simple statement of praise; its context and theological weight are immense.

1. Source and Context of the Letter:

    Work: Epistola XIV ad Heliodorum de laude vitae solitariae (Letter 14 to Heliodorus on the praise of the solitary life).

    Date: Written around A.D. 376.

    Purpose: St. Jerome writes this fiery and passionate letter to his friend Heliodorus, who had once committed to the ascetic life of a monk but was now wavering, perhaps considering the "softer" life of a secular cleric or even returning to worldly life. The entire letter is a powerful exhortation for Heliodorus to embrace the radical demands of the Cross and the desert.

2. The Rhetorical Purpose of the Quote:
This passage is a brilliant rhetorical move. Jerome is about to draw a very sharp contrast between the difficult, self-denying life of a true monk and the (in his view, often comfortable and worldly) life of the city clergy. To avoid being accused of attacking the priesthood itself, he prefaces his critique with this profound statement of reverence for the sacred office of the clergy.

His argument structure is: "I hold the office of the priesthood in the highest possible regard because of its sacred power... but the life of a monk is a different, and in some ways more demanding, calling." He is distinguishing the sacredness of the office from the potential failings of the men who hold it.

3. Key Theological Doctrines Affirmed:
This short sentence is a powerful patristic witness to several core Christian doctrines:

    Apostolic Succession: Jerome's phrase Apostolico gradui succedentes ("succeeding to the apostolic rank") is a clear affirmation of the belief that bishops and priests stand in a direct line of succession from the apostles, inheriting their authority.

    The Power of the Priesthood and the Eucharist: The phrase CHRISTI CORPUS sacro ore conficiunt ("they consecrate the Body of Christ with their sacred mouth") is a stunningly clear statement on the unique power of the ordained priest to celebrate the Eucharist. It points directly to the doctrine of the Real Presence and the priest acting in persona Christi. The words they speak are holy and effective.

    The Role of the Clergy in Initiation: The final clause, per quos et nos Christiani sumus ("through whom we also are Christians"), refers to the essential role of the clergy in administering the sacraments of initiation, primarily Baptism, which makes a person a Christian.

4. The Jerome Paradox:
This quote perfectly illustrates the "paradox" of St. Jerome. He could be the fiercest and most sarcastic critic of clerical corruption, worldliness, and laziness. Yet, he held the sacramental office of the priesthood in the utmost awe. He never attacked the office, only the men who failed to live up to its profound dignity. The rest of the text you provided, with its warnings about judgment (tradere me Satanae, spirituali mucrone truncatur), demonstrates this very tension.

fr: Puisque l'Orient, déchiré par la fureur ancestrale de ses peuples qui s'affrontent, met en lambeaux la tunique sans couture du Seigneur, celle qui fut tissée d'un seul tenant depuis le haut, j'ai donc jugé nécessaire de consulter la chaire de Pierre et la foi célébrée par une bouche apostolique. C'est de là que je viens aujourd'hui réclamer la nourriture pour mon âme, là même où j'ai reçu autrefois le vêtement du Christ. Le patrimoine a été dilapidé par une postérité indigne ; c'est auprès de vous seuls que se conserve, intact, l'héritage des pères.
en: Since the East. shattered as it is by the longstanding feuds, subsisting between its peoples, iS bit by bit tearing into shreds the seamless vest of the Lord. . . . I think it my duty to consult the chair of Peter, and to turn to a Church [Rome] whose faith has been praised by Paul [Rom 1:8]. I appeal for spiritual food to the Church whence have received the garb of Christ. Evil children have squandered their patrimony; you alone keep your heritage intact [Letters 15:1 (c. A.D. 376)].
latin: Quoniam vetusto Oriens inter se populorum furore collisus, indiscissam Domini tunicam, et desuper textam, minutatim per frusta discerpit... ideo mihi cathedram Petri et fidem Apostolico ore laudatam censui consulendam: inde nunc meae animae postulans cibum, unde olim Christi vestimenta suscepi. ... Profligato a sobole mala patrimonio, apud vos solos incorrupta patrum servatur haereditas.
context:
Additional Relevant Commentary
1. The Desperate Historical Context: The Meletian Schism

To understand this letter, you must understand Jerome's desperate situation around A.D. 376.

    Theological Chaos: The Arian controversy had fractured the Eastern Church. It wasn't a simple dispute between Arians and the Orthodox. In Antioch, where Jerome was, there was a schism with three men claiming to be the legitimate bishop:

        Meletius: Supported by many Eastern bishops, including the Cappadocian Fathers.

        Paulinus: Recognized as the legitimate bishop by Rome and Alexandria.

        Vitalis: A follower of the Apollinarian heresy.

    Theological Terminology: Jerome was being pressured by the followers of Meletius to affirm his orthodoxy by confessing "three hypostases" in the Trinity. To a native Latin speaker like Jerome, the Greek word hypostasis sounded dangerously similar to the Latin word substantia (substance). Confessing "three substances" would be tritheism (a belief in three gods). He was terrified of falling into heresy by using language he wasn't sure of.

    "A Fish Out of Water": Jerome felt lost in a sea of Greek theological subtleties and political factions. He saw the Eastern bishops as constantly feuding and changing their positions.

2. Theological Significance: The "Chair of Peter"

This letter is a classic and early witness to the role of the See of Rome as a final arbiter of doctrine.

    A Beacon in the Storm: Amidst the "fury of the peoples" and the theological chaos of the East, Jerome looks to Rome as the one stable and reliable source of orthodox faith.

    The Standard of Orthodoxy: He explicitly states his intention to "consult the chair of Peter" (cathedram Petri ... consulendam). He doesn't write to any other major see (like Alexandria or Constantinople) for this final word. For him, the authority of the Bishop of Rome is directly linked to St. Peter.

    Faith Praised by Paul: Jerome brilliantly links Rome's current authority to its ancient origins, reminding Pope Damasus that the faith of the Roman Church was famous even in the time of St. Paul (a reference to Romans 1:8). This gives Rome's claim a deep, apostolic foundation.

    Rome as the Uncorrupted Source: His powerful imagery contrasts the East, where "evil children have squandered their patrimony," with Rome, where "you alone keep your heritage intact." This highlights his view of Rome as the faithful guardian of apostolic tradition.

    Personal Connection: The phrase "whence I have received the garb of Christ" (unde olim Christi vestimenta suscepi) is a reference to his baptism. Since Jerome was baptized in Rome, he feels a personal, sacramental bond that justifies his appeal to the Roman See for spiritual nourishment.

In summary, this letter is a passionate, desperate plea from a brilliant scholar caught in a theological minefield. Feeling unable to trust the shifting factions of the East, he turns to the one authority he believes is stable, apostolic, and doctrinally pure: the Chair of Peter in Rome.

fr:
Hors de l'Église, point de salut.

Certes, votre grandeur m'intimide, mais votre bonté m'attire. Au prêtre, la victime que je suis demande le salut ; au pasteur, la brebis implore protection. Que la jalousie se retire, que s'efface l'ambition du siège de Rome, car c'est au successeur du Pêcheur et au disciple de la croix que je m'adresse. Moi, qui ne reconnais d'autre chef que le Christ, je m'unis par la communion à Votre Béatitude, c'est-à-dire à la chaire de Pierre. Je sais que l'Église est bâtie sur cette pierre. Quiconque mange l'agneau en dehors de cette maison est un profane. Celui qui ne se trouvera pas dans l'arche de Noé périra au milieu du déluge.

Et parce que mes péchés m'ont conduit à m'exiler dans ce désert qui marque la frontière de la Syrie avec les terres barbares, et que l'immense distance qui nous sépare ne me permet pas de recevoir constamment de Votre Sainteté le saint du Seigneur, c'est pourquoi, ici, je me joins à vos confrères, les confesseurs d'Égypte, et, telle une modeste barque, je m'abrite auprès des grands navires de charge. Je ne connais pas Vitalis, je rejette Mélèce, j'ignore Paulin. Quiconque n'amasse pas avec vous, disperse. Autrement dit : celui qui n'appartient pas au Christ appartient à l'Antichrist.
en: As follow no leader save Christ, so I communicate with none but your blessedness, that is, with the chair of Peter. For this, I know, is the rock on which the Church is built! [Mt 16:18]. This IS the only house where the Paschal Lamb can be rightly eaten [Ex 12:22]. This iS the Ark of Noah, and he who is not found in it shall perish when the flood prevails Letters 15:2 (A.D 376)].
latin: Extra Ecclesiam nulla salus.   --Quanquam igitur tui me terreat magnitudo, invitat tamen humanitas.   A Sacerdote victimae salutem, a Pastore praesidium ovis flagito.   Facessat invidia: Romani culminis recedat ambitio, 39 cum successore Piscatoris et discipulo crucis loquor.   Ego nullum primum, nisi Christum sequens, Beatitudini tuae, id est, cathedrae Petri, cummunione consocior.   Super illam Petram aedificatam Ecclesiam scio.   Quicumque extra hanc domum agnum comederit, profanus est.   Si quis in Noe Arca non fuerit, peribit regnante diluvio.   Et p. 0356 | quia pro facinoribus meis ad eam solitudinem commigravi, quae Syriam juncto Barbariae fine determinat; nec possum sanctum Domini tot interjacentibus spatiis a Sanctimonia tua semper expetere: ideo hic collegas tuos Aegyptios Confessores sequor; et sub onerariis navibus parva navicula delitesco.   Non novi Vitalem, Meletium respuo, ignoro Paulinum.   Quicumque tecum non colligit, spargit: hoc est, qui Christi non est, Antichristi est.
context:
Additional Relevant Commentary

This letter is one of the most important patristic texts regarding the authority of the See of Rome. To understand its full impact, we need to look at the historical context.
1. The Historical Crisis: The Meletian Schism

    Where is Jerome? When Jerome wrote this letter around A.D. 376, he was not in Rome. He was living as a monk in the desert of Chalcis, near the great city of Antioch in the East.

    What was the problem? The Church in Antioch was torn apart by a schism. There were three rival bishops all claiming to be the legitimate Patriarch of Antioch:

        Meletius: Supported by many Eastern bishops, including St. Basil the Great.

        Paulinus: Supported by Rome and Alexandria.

        Vitalis: A follower of the Apollinarian heresy.

    Jerome's Dilemma: As a Latin-speaking Westerner living in the East, Jerome was caught in the crossfire. The local monks were pressuring him intensely to declare his allegiance to one of these bishops. He felt isolated and confused, unsure of who represented the true faith. He writes to the Pope: "I do not know Vitalis, I reject Meletius, I am ignorant of Paulinus." (Non novi Vitalem, Meletium respuo, ignoro Paulinum.)

2. Jerome's Solution: Appealing to the Universal Standard

Frustrated by the local chaos, Jerome decides to cut through the noise by appealing to the one See he considers the unchanging standard of orthodoxy: Rome. This letter is his plea to Pope Damasus for a definitive ruling. He essentially says, "Tell me who you are in communion with, and that is who I will follow."
3. The Power of the Metaphors

Jerome uses three powerful biblical images to explain why he is appealing to the Chair of Peter. These are not just rhetorical flourishes; they are profound theological statements.

    The Rock of Peter: This is the foundational argument. By quoting Matthew 16:18, Jerome identifies the Church built on Peter with the one in communion with Peter's successor. For him, doctrinal truth and Church unity are anchored to this Petrine foundation.

    The House of the Paschal Lamb: This metaphor from Exodus raises the stakes from truth to salvation itself. Just as the Israelites had to be inside a marked house to be saved from the angel of death, Jerome argues that one must be inside the house of the Church—which he has just defined as the one built on Peter—to partake of the true Eucharist (the new Paschal Lamb) and be saved.

    The Ark of Noah: This is the most stark image of all. It directly connects to the doctrine of Extra Ecclesiam nulla salus ("Outside the Church, there is no salvation"). Just as everything outside the Ark was destroyed by the flood, anyone outside the Church (the one true Ark) will perish.

4. The Famous Conclusion

The final sentence of your Latin text drives the point home with absolute force:

    Quicumque tecum non colligit, spargit: hoc est, qui Christi non est, Antichristi est.
    "Whoever does not gather with you [Pope Damasus], scatters: that is, he who is not of Christ, is of Antichrist."

Here, Jerome makes communion with the See of Rome the very test of being with Christ. It is an astonishingly strong statement of papal authority from one of the greatest scholars of the ancient Church.

fr:
Pour ma part, ainsi que je l'ai déjà écrit, j'ai revêtu le vêtement du Christ à Rome ; me voici maintenant retenu aux confins barbares de la Syrie. Et pour que vous ne pensiez pas que ce jugement vienne d'un autre, c'est moi-même qui ai décidé de ce que je méritais. Mais, comme le dit le poète païen : « Celui qui franchit les mers change de ciel, non d'état d'âme. » C'est ainsi que l'ennemi implacable m'a poursuivi, si bien que je subis à présent dans le désert des combats plus grands encore. D'un côté, en effet, soutenue par les puissances de ce monde, la fureur arienne gronde. De l'autre, l'Église, déchirée en trois partis, s'empresse de m'attirer à elle. L'antique autorité des moines qui demeurent aux alentours se dresse contre moi.

Moi, pendant ce temps, je ne cesse de clamer : « Si quelqu'un est uni à la chaire de Pierre, celui-là est des miens. » Mélèce, Vitalis et Paulin affirment être en communion avec vous. Je pourrais le croire si un seul l'affirmait. Mais aujourd'hui, ou bien deux d'entre eux mentent, ou bien ce sont les trois.

C'est pourquoi j'en conjure Votre Béatitude, par la croix du Seigneur, par la Passion du Christ — gloire indispensable de notre foi —, vous qui succédez aux Apôtres en dignité, puissiez-vous leur succéder aussi en mérite ; puissiez-vous ainsi siéger sur le trône pour juger avec les Douze, puisse un autre ainsi vous ceindre dans votre vieillesse comme le fut Pierre, et puissiez-vous ainsi obtenir avec Paul le droit de cité des cieux : indiquez-moi par lettre avec qui, en Syrie, je dois être en communion. Ne méprisez pas une âme pour laquelle le Christ est mort.
en: The Church is rent into three factions. and each of these is eager to seize me for its own. The influence of the monks iS of long standing. and it is directed against me. I meantime keep crying: "He who clings to the chair of Peter IS accepted by me." Meletius, Vitalis, and Paulinus all profess to cleave to you, and I could believe the assertion it were made by one of them only. As it is, either two of them or else all three are guilty of falsehood. Therefore implore your blessedness, by our Lord's cross and Passion, those necessary glories of our faith, as you hold an apostolic office, to give an apostolic decision. Only tell me by letter with whom am to communicate in Syria [ibid., 16:2].
latin: Ego igitur, ut ante jam scripsi, Christi vestem in Romana urbe suscipiens, nunc barbaro Syriae limite teneor.   Et ne putes alterius hanc de me fuisse sententiam, quid mererer, ipse constitui.   Verum, ut ait Gentilis Poeta: Coelum non animum mutat, qui trans p. 0359 | mare currit * , ita me incessabilis inimicus post tergum sequutus est, ut majora in solitudine bella nunc patiar.   Hinc enim praesidiis fulta mundi Ariana 43 rabies fremit.   Hinc in tres partes scissa Ecclesia ad se rapere me festinat.   Monachorum circa manentium antiqua in me surgit auctoritas.   Ego interim clamito, si quis cathedrae Petri jungitur, meus est.   Meletius, Vitalis, atque Paulinus tibi haerere se dicunt, possem credere si hoc unus assereret.   Nunc aut duo mentiuntur, aut omnes.   Idcirco obtestor Beatitudinem tuam, per crucem Domini, per necessarium fidei nostrae decus, passionem Christi, ut qui Apostolos honore sequeris, sequaris et merito: ita in solio cum duodecim judicaturus sedeas: ita te alius senem cum Petro cingat: ita municipatum coeli cum Paulo consequaris, ut mihi litteris tuis, apud quem in Syria debeam communicare, significes.   Noli despicere animam, pro qua Christus mortuus est.
context:
Additional Relevant Commentary

1. The Historical Context: The Meletian Schism
Jerome was in the middle of a brutal Church crisis in Antioch. After the Arian controversies, the city had three rival bishops, all claiming to be the legitimate patriarch:

    Meletius: The most popular candidate, supported by many Eastern bishops like St. Basil the Great. However, his consecration was irregular, and he was seen with suspicion by the West. The monks pressuring Jerome were his followers.

    Paulinus: The candidate recognized by Rome (Pope Damasus) and Alexandria. He represented the staunchly anti-Arian "old guard" of the city.

    Vitalis: A follower of the heretic Apollinaris, who had broken away from Meletius's faction.

2. Jerome's Personal Crisis
As a Latin-speaking Westerner living in the Greek East, Jerome felt isolated. The local monks (Meletians) were pressuring him to accept their bishop, Meletius. They were even harassing him over his use of the Latin theological term tres personae ("three persons") for the Trinity, accusing it of being heretical. Overwhelmed and uncertain, he cut through all the local politics and appealed directly to the one authority he saw as stable and universal: the See of Rome.

3. Theological Significance: The "Chair of Peter"
Jerome's cry, "He who clings to the chair of Peter is accepted by me" (si quis cathedrae Petri jungitur, meus est), is one of the most powerful patristic testimonies to the role of the Pope as the touchstone of orthodoxy and the center of Catholic unity.

    A Clear Standard: In a world of confusing local schisms where all sides claimed to be "orthodox," Jerome identifies communion with the Bishop of Rome as the simple, clear test of true faith.

    Apostolic Authority: He explicitly asks for an "apostolic decision" from an "apostolic office." He sees Pope Damasus not just as the Bishop of Rome, but as the successor to St. Peter, inheriting his authority to bind and loose and to settle disputes for the universal Church.

This letter is a vivid snapshot of a church in turmoil and a powerful expression of one of its greatest scholars looking to the Papacy as the rock of stability and the final arbiter of truth.

fr:
J'ai honte de le dire : combien de vierges succombent chaque jour, combien l'Église, notre mère, en perd de son sein…

D'autres vont jusqu'à boire des breuvages de stérilité, et commettent ainsi le meurtre d'un être humain avant même sa conception. Certaines, lorsqu'elles se rendent compte qu'elles ont conçu dans le crime, ont recours à des poisons abortifs ; bien souvent, elles meurent elles-mêmes avec leur enfant et sont conduites aux enfers, coupables d'un triple crime : homicides d'elles-mêmes, adultères envers le Christ, et parricides de leur enfant qui n'était pas encore né.
en: I cannot bring myself to speak of the many virgins who fall every day and are lost to the bosom of the Church, their mother. . . . Some go SO far as to take potions, that they may ensure barrenness, and thus murder human beings almost before their conception. Some, when they find themselves with child through their sin, use drugs to procure abortion, and when (as often happens) they die with their offspring, they enter the lower world laden with the guilt not only of adultery against Christ but also of suicide and child murder [Letters 22:13 (A.D. 384)].
latin:
Pudet dicere, quot quotidie Virgines ruant, quantas de suo gremio mater perdat Ecclesia...

    Aliae vero sterilitatem praebibunt, et necdum sati hominis homicidium faciunt. Nonnullae cum se senserint concepisse de scelere, abortii venena meditantur, et frequenter etiam ipsae commortuae, trium criminum reae, ad inferos perducuntur, homicidae sui, Christi adulterae, necdum nati filii parricidae.
context:
Additional Relevant Commentary

This is one of the most powerful and frequently cited passages from the Church Fathers on the subjects of chastity, contraception, and abortion. To understand its full impact, here is some essential context:

    Context of the Letter (To Eustochium): Jerome is not writing a legal or philosophical treatise. He is writing an intense, passionate, and sometimes shocking spiritual exhortation to a young woman dedicating her life to Christ as a consecrated virgin. His goal is to show her both the sublime beauty of virginity and the horrific dangers of hypocrisy and sin. His language is intentionally extreme to make a powerful impression.

    The Target: Hypocrisy among Consecrated Virgins: The quote is part of a broader attack on women who have taken vows of virginity but live secretly immoral lives. Jerome is furious at the hypocrisy. He describes how they pretend to be chaste, dress modestly but flirtatiously, and then, when their sin results in pregnancy, they resort to the most extreme measures to hide it.

    Theological Framing of the Sins: Jerome's genius is in how he frames the sins, elevating them to the highest possible level of gravity:

        Adultery Against Christ: Because a consecrated virgin is a "bride of Christ," her sexual sin is not mere fornication but spiritual adultery (Christi adulterae). This was a common and powerful concept in early Christian asceticism.

        Homicide and Parricide: Jerome uses the strongest possible language for contraception and abortion. He calls the use of sterilizing potions homicidium (homicide) of a human being "not yet sown." He labels abortion as the work of a parricida—a term in Roman law for the murder of a close relative, which was considered the most heinous form of killing. He makes no distinction in moral gravity between contraception and abortion; both are seen as forms of murder.

        Suicide: By highlighting that the women often die from these dangerous potions, he adds the sin of suicide (homicidae sui) to the list, compounding the guilt.

    Historical Significance: This passage is a crucial piece of evidence for the early and consistent Christian condemnation of abortion and contraception. It shows that:

        These practices were known in the 4th-century Roman world.

        The Church unequivocally viewed them as gravely sinful.

        The condemnation was rooted in the belief that human life is sacred from its very earliest stages ("not yet sown") and that interfering with procreation was a form of homicide.

In summary, you have located a foundational text in Christian moral theology, delivered in St. Jerome's uniquely fiery, passionate, and unforgettable rhetorical style.

fr: Ne me parlez pas de la violence d'un rapt, de la persuasion d'une mère, de l'autorité d'un père, des pressions de la parenté, des complots et des outrages des serviteurs, ni de la perte du patrimoine. Tant que le mari est en vie, qu’il soit adultère, qu’il soit sodomite, qu’il soit couvert de toutes les infamies et même abandonné par sa femme en raison de ces crimes, il est considéré comme son époux, et elle n'a pas le droit d'en prendre un autre.
en: Do not tell me about the violence of the ravisher, about the persuasiveness of a mother, about the authority of a father, about the influence of relatives, about the intrigues and insolence of servants, or about household [financial] losses. So long as a husband lives, be he adulterer, be he sodomite, be he addicted to every kind of vice, if she left him on account of his crimes, he is her husband still and she may not take another Letters 55:3 (C. A.D. 393)].
latin: Noli mihi narrare raptus violentiam, matris persuasionem, patris auctoritatem, affinium catervas, servorum insidias et contumelias, rei familiaris damna. Quamdiu vivit vir, licet adulter sit, licet sodomita, licet flagitiis omnibus coopertus et ab uxore propter haec scelera derelictus, maritus ejus existimatur, cui alterum virum accipere non licet.
context:
Additional Relevant Commentary

    Context: A priest named Amandus wrote to Jerome with a pastoral problem. A woman in his community had been forced into a marriage she didn't want, left her husband, and was later baptized. She now considered herself "free" and wanted to marry a Christian man. Jerome is refuting her claim.

    Absolute Indissolubility: This passage is one of the most forceful and absolute statements on the indissolubility of marriage in all of Patristic literature. Jerome allows for no exceptions. Even the most extreme and vile behavior on the part of the husband does not sever the marital bond.

    Scriptural Foundation: Jerome doesn't invent this doctrine. Immediately before this famous quote, he grounds his argument firmly in the letters of St. Paul, citing Romans 7:2 ("A married woman is bound by law to her husband while he lives") and 1 Corinthians 7:27 ("Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek to be free"). His position is that apostolic authority has settled the matter.

    Rhetorical Power: Jerome's style is on full display. The opening list ("Do not tell me about...") is a rhetorical device called praeteritio. He is preemptively dismissing every possible excuse the woman could make for her situation, showing that in his view, none of them are relevant when faced with the permanence of the sacramental bond.

In summary, you found a powerful text from Jerome, but it was from his famous letter on virginity. The passage you were looking for, from his letter on marriage, is even more direct and has been a cornerstone of the Church's teaching on the permanence of the marital bond for centuries.

fr:
Elle partit, accompagnée de ses servantes et de ses eunuques. Son mari eut grand-peine à la persuader de faire route assise sur un ânon.
Arrivée auprès de lui, elle dit : « Je t’en prie, par Jésus notre Dieu infiniment bon, je t’adjure par sa croix et son sang, rends-moi mes trois fils ! Fais-le pour que le nom du Seigneur Sauveur soit glorifié dans la cité des païens, pour que son serviteur entre à Gaza et que l’idole de Marnas s’effondre ! »

Mais Hilarion refusait, disant qu’il ne quitterait jamais sa cellule et qu’il n’avait pas pour habitude d’entrer dans une ville. Elle se jeta alors à terre et se mit à crier sans relâche : « Hilarion, serviteur du Christ, rends-moi mes enfants ! Antoine a sauvé bien des gens en Égypte ; c’est à toi de sauver les miens en Syrie. »

Tous les assistants pleuraient ; et lui-même, tout en refusant, pleurait aussi. Bref, la femme ne partit pas avant qu’il ait promis d’entrer à Gaza après le coucher du soleil. Une fois sur place, il fit le signe de la croix sur la couche de chacun des enfants et sur leurs membres brûlants de fièvre, puis il invoqua le nom de Jésus. Et, ô puissance admirable ! une sueur jaillit de leurs trois corps en même temps, comme de trois sources. À l’heure même, ils acceptèrent de la nourriture. Reconnaissant leur mère en larmes et bénissant Dieu, ils baisèrent avec ferveur les mains du saint homme.
en: [S]he set out accompanied by her handmaids and eunuchs, and was hardly persuaded by her husband@ to take an ass to ride upon. On reaching the saint she said, pray you by Jesus our most merciful God, I beseech you by his cross and blood, to restore to me my three sons, so that the name of our Lord and Savior may be glorified in the city of the Gentiles. Then his servants shall enter Gaza and the idol Marnas fall to the ground." At first he refused and said that he never left his cell and was not accustomed to enter a house, much less the city; but she threw herself upon the ground and cried repeatedly, "Hilarion, servant of Christ. give me back my children: Antony kept them safe in Egypt, you save them in Syria." All present were weeping, and the saint himself wept as he denied her. But the woman did not leave him until he promised that he would enter Gaza after sunset. On coming there he made the sign of the cross over the bed and fevered limbs of each, and called upon the name of Jesus. Marvelous efficacy of the name! As if from three fountains the sweat burst forth at the same time. In that very hour they took food, recognized their mourning mother, and, with thanks to God, warmly kissed the saint's hands [Life of St. Hilarion 14 (A.D. 390)].
latin:
vadit comitata ancillulis et eunuchis: vixque a viro persuasum est, ut asello sedens pergeret. Ad quem cum pervenisset: Precor te, ait, per Jesum clementissimum Deum nostrum: obtestor per crucem ejus et sanguinem, ut reddas mihi tres filios; et glorificetur in urbe gentilium nomen Domini Salvatoris, et ingrediatur servus ejus Gazam, et idolum Marnes corruat.

    Renuente illo, et dicente, nunquam se egressurum de cella, nec habere consuetudinem, ut... civitatem... ingrederetur, prostravit se humi crebro clamitans: Hilarion, serve Christi, redde mihi liberos meos. Quos Antonius tenuit in Ægypto, a te servientur in Syria.

    Flebant cuncti qui aderant, sed et ipse negans flevit. Quid multa? non prius mulier recessit, quam ille pollicitus est se post solis occasum Gazam introïturum. Quo postquam venit, singulorum lectulos et ardentia membra consignans, invocavit Jesum. Et, o mira virtus! quasi de tribus fontibus sudor pariter erupit: eadem hora acceperunt cibos, lugentemque matrem cognoscentes, et benedicentes Deum, sancti manus deosculati sunt.
context:
Additional Relevant Commentary

This passage is a masterful example of hagiography (the writing of saints' lives) and reveals several important themes.

    Christ vs. Paganism: This is not just a healing story; it's a spiritual battle. The mother, Aristænete, explicitly frames the miracle as a victory for Christ over the chief pagan god of Gaza, Marnas. Her prayer is prophetic: if her sons are healed, Christ's name will be glorified, his servant (Hilarion) will enter the pagan stronghold of Gaza, and "the idol Marnas will fall." The miracle is a direct challenge to the demonic powers worshipped by the Gentiles.

    The Tenacious Faith of the Mother: Like the Syrophoenician woman in the Gospels (Matthew 15:21-28), Aristænete refuses to take no for an answer. She overcomes Hilarion's reluctance with her persistent, desperate, and powerful faith. She uses a brilliant rhetorical move by comparing Hilarion to his more famous predecessor, St. Antony the Great: "Antony kept them safe in Egypt, you save them in Syria." She is essentially challenging Hilarion to live up to the standard of his spiritual father.

    The Power of the Name of Jesus: Jerome makes it explicit that the power does not come from Hilarion himself, but from Christ. Hilarion's actions are simple: he makes the sign of the cross and "called upon the name of Jesus." Jerome exclaims, "O mira virtus!" (O marvelous efficacy/power!), attributing the miracle directly to the invocation of Jesus. This was a central tenet of early Christian belief—that the name of Jesus held power over sickness, demons, and death.

    The Reluctant Saint: Hilarion's initial refusal to leave his cell is a classic trope in the lives of desert fathers. The true holy man does not seek fame or worldly engagement. His reluctance serves to heighten the drama and emphasize that he acts not for his own glory, but only when compelled by desperate faith and charity.

    Jerome's Agenda: Promoting Monasticism: At the end of the full passage (which you provided), Jerome explicitly states his purpose: "For as yet there were no monasteries in Palestine, nor had anyone known a monk in Syria before Saint Hilarion. He was the founder and teacher of this way of life..." This miracle story serves as a powerful advertisement for the new monastic movement in Syria, demonstrating that its practitioners wield the same spiritual power as the famous monks of Egypt.

fr:
Simon Pierre, fils de Jean, de la province de Galilée, originaire du village de Bethsaïde, frère de l'apôtre André et prince des Apôtres. Après son épiscopat à l'église d'Antioche et sa prédication à la diaspora des croyants issus de la circoncision, dans le Pont, la Galatie, la Cappadoce, l'Asie et la Bithynie, il se rendit à Rome la deuxième année du règne de l'empereur Claude pour y combattre Simon le Magicien.

Là, il occupa la chaire épiscopale pendant vingt-cinq ans, jusqu'à la dernière année de Néron, c'est-à-dire la quatorzième. C'est sous le règne de ce dernier qu'il fut couronné du martyre, crucifié la tête tournée vers le sol et les pieds élevés en l'air, affirmant qu'il était indigne d'être crucifié de la même manière que son Seigneur.
en: Simon Peter, the son of John, from the village of Bethsaida in the province of Galilee, brother of Andrew the apostle, and himself chief of the apostles, after having been bishop of the church of Antioch and having preached to the dispersion pushed on to Rome in the second year of Claudius to overthrow Simon Magus, and held the sacerdotal chair there for twenty-five years until the last, the fourteenth, year of Nero. At his hands he received the crown of martyrdom, being nailed to the cross with his head towards the ground and his feet raised on high, asserting that he was unworthy to be crucified in the same manner as his Lord [Illustrious Men 1 (A.D. 392)].
latin: Simon Petrus, filius Joannis, provinciae Galileae, e vico Bethsaida, frater Andreae apostoli, et princeps Apostolorum, post episcopatum Antiochensis Ecclesiae, et praedicationem dispersionis... secundo Claudii imperatoris anno, ad expugnandum Simonem magum, Romam pergit, ibique viginti quinque annis Cathedram Sacerdotalem tenuit, usque ad ultimum annum Neronis, id est, decimum quartum. A quo et affixus cruci, martyrio coronatus est, capite ad terram verso, et in sublime pedibus elevatis: asserens se indignum qui sic crucifigeretur ut Dominus suus.
greek: Σίμων Πέτρος, ἀπόστολος, υἱὸς Ἰωνᾶ, ἐπαρχίας Γαλιλαίας, κώμης Βηθσαϊδὰ, ἀδελφὸς Ἀνδρέου Ἀποστόλου, καὶ ἀρχηγὸς τῶν Ἀποστόλων, μετὰ τὴν ἐπισκοπὴν τῆς Ἀντιοχέων ἐκκλησίας, καὶ τὸ κήρυγμα τῶν διασπαρέντων, καὶ ἐκ τῆς περιτομῆς πιστευσάντων, ἐν Πόντῳ, Γαλατίᾳ, Καππαδοκίᾳ, Ασίᾳ καὶ Βιθυνία, τῷ δευτέρῳ Κλαυδίου ἔτει εἰς τὸ ἐκπολεμῆσαι Σίμωνα τὸν μάγον τῇ Ῥώμῃ ἐφίσταται, ἔνθα εἴκοσι πέντε ἐνιαυτοὺς τὸν θρόνον τῆς ἱερωσύνης κατέσχεν, ἔως τοῦ τελευταίου ἐνιαυτοῦ Νέρωνος, τουτέστι τοῦ τεσσαρεσκαιδεκάτου, ἐφ' οὗ καὶ σταυρωθεὶς ἐμαρτύρησε, τὴν κεφαλὴν κατὰ γὴν ἔχων, τοὺς πόδας δὲ ἐν μετεώρῳ, φάσκων ἀνάξιον ἑαυτὸν εἶναι, τὸν ὅμοιον τρόπον σταυρωθῆναι τῷ πάντων Κυρίῳ.
context:
This short biographical entry by St. Jerome is one of the most important and influential historical summaries of St. Peter's life written in the early Church. Its significance lies in the way it consolidates several key traditions into a single, authoritative account.

1. The Source and Its Purpose:

    De Viris Illustribus (written in A.D. 392) was a groundbreaking work. It was the first Christian literary history, cataloging 135 important Christian authors from St. Peter to Jerome himself. By starting with Peter, Jerome firmly establishes the Apostles as the foundation of all subsequent Christian literature and teaching.

2. Key Historical Claims and Their Significance:

    "Princeps Apostolorum" (Chief of the Apostles): Jerome doesn't hesitate to give Peter this title. It is a powerful affirmation of Peter's primacy and leadership role among the apostles, a cornerstone of the argument for the authority of the Roman See.

    Episcopate in Antioch, then Rome: Jerome crystallizes the tradition that Peter founded the See of Antioch before traveling to Rome. This established a clear trajectory of Petrine authority moving from the East to its final seat in the capital of the Empire.

    The 25-Year Roman Episcopate: This is a crucial claim. Jerome, following the historian Eusebius, dates Peter's arrival in Rome to the 2nd year of Emperor Claudius (c. A.D. 42) and states he held the "sacerdotal chair" (Cathedram Sacerdotalem) for 25 years until his death under Nero (c. A.D. 67). While modern historians debate the historical precision of a continuous 25-year residency, Jerome's statement became the standard chronology for the Roman pontificate of Peter for over a millennium.

    The Inverted Crucifixion: This is one of the most famous parts of the account. While the tradition of Peter's inverted crucifixion first appears in the apocryphal Acts of Peter (late 2nd century) and is mentioned by Origen (as quoted by Eusebius), Jerome's clear, historical summary in Latin gave it immense weight and currency throughout the Western Church. It powerfully illustrates the apostle's humility.

    Burial in the Vatican: The final sentence (which you didn't include in your quote but is in the text block) is also vital: Sepultus Romae in Vaticano, juxta viam Triumphalem... ("He was buried in Rome at the Vatican, near the Triumphal Way..."). Jerome confirms the ancient and constant tradition that Peter was martyred and buried on Vatican Hill, a tradition later confirmed by the 20th-century archaeological excavations beneath St. Peter's Basilica.

In summary, this short paragraph is a historical and theological powerhouse. Writing as the most respected scholar of his age, St. Jerome consolidates and transmits to the Latin West the core traditions regarding Peter's primacy, his founding of the Roman Church, his 25-year pontificate, his martyrdom, and his burial site.

fr: Clément... quatrième évêque de Rome après Pierre : en effet, Linus fut le deuxième, Anaclet le troisième, bien que la plupart des Latins estiment que Clément fut le deuxième après l'Apôtre.
en: "Clement... [was] the fourth bishop of Rome after Peter, since Linus was the second and Anacletus was the third, although most of the Latins think that Clement was the second after the Apostle Peter."
latin: Clemens... quartus post Petrum Romae episcopus: siquidem secundus Linus fuit, tertius Anacletus, tametsi plerique Latinorum, secundum post Petrum Apostolum putent fuisse Clementem.
greek: Κλήμης... Τέταρτος μετὰ Πέτρον Ῥώμης Ἐπίσκοπος. Δεύτερος γὰρ Λῖνος ἐγένετο, τρίτος Ἀνέγκλητος, εἰ καὶ πολλοὶ τῶν Ῥωμαίων ὑπολαμβάνουσι, δεύτερον μετὰ τὸν Ἀπόστολον γεγενῆσθαι Κλήμεντα.
context:
Commentary and Significance

This short passage is packed with important information and provides a window into the historical understanding of the 4th century.

1. Affirmation of a Clear Line of Succession:
The primary importance of this quote is that St. Jerome, one of the most learned scholars of the ancient Church, affirms a clear, unbroken line of succession for the leadership of the Church in Rome, starting directly from the Apostle Peter. He presents the order accepted by most historians (following St. Irenaeus of Lyons):

    1st: Peter

    2nd: Linus

    3rd: Anacletus (also known as Cletus)

    4th: Clement

This list is not just a historical curiosity; for the early Church, it was proof of Apostolic Succession. It demonstrated that the authority and teaching of the Roman Church were directly traceable to the chief of the Apostles.

2. Scholarly Honesty and Historical Nuance:
Crucially, Jerome does not simply state the list as an unassailable fact. He immediately adds the phrase "although most of the Latins think that Clement was the second." This is a mark of a careful historian. Jerome is acknowledging that there was another tradition, particularly popular in the Latin-speaking West (citing figures like Tertullian), which placed Clement immediately after Peter.

    Why the discrepancy? One theory is that Peter may have ordained Clement as his successor before his death, but Clement, out of humility, allowed Linus and Anacletus to serve before him. Another is simply that early records were not perfectly uniform.

    What it means: Jerome's inclusion of this detail shows that the early Church was aware of these minor discrepancies in the lists but that they did not undermine the fundamental principle: the Bishop of Rome was the successor of Peter. Jerome is simply siding with the historical tradition he believes is most accurate (that of Irenaeus).

3. What This Quote Is (and Isn't):
This passage is a powerful historical statement about continuity. It establishes the who and the order of the succession.

However, it is not Jerome's most famous or theologically potent statement on the authority of Peter's successors. For that, one must turn to his Letter 15 to Pope St. Damasus I (written around A.D. 375). In that letter, Jerome writes:

    "I speak with the successor of the fisherman and a disciple of the cross. I, following no one as my chief but Christ, am united in communion with your beatitude, that is to say, with the Chair of Peter. I know that upon this rock the Church is built. Whosoever shall eat the Lamb outside this house is profane."

In summary: The passage you found in De Viris Illustribus is Jerome's scholarly, historical account of the Roman succession. His letter to Pope Damasus is his passionate, theological declaration of the Roman See's doctrinal authority as the "Chair of Peter." Both are essential for understanding his view.

fr:
Mais puisque mon discours a désormais échappé aux écueils et aux passages difficiles, il faut déployer les voiles et foncer sur la conclusion de mon adversaire, dans laquelle ce savant autoproclamé invoque le témoignage de Tertullien et cite les propos de Victorin, évêque de Poetovio.

Au sujet de Tertullien, je n'ai rien de plus à dire, sinon qu'il n'appartenait pas à l'Église. Quant à Victorin, j'affirme ce que j'ai déjà soutenu à propos des évangélistes : il a parlé des frères du Seigneur, et non des fils de Marie. Frères, donc, au sens que j'ai exposé plus haut : par les liens de la parenté, et non par le sang.

Mais nous perdons notre temps en futilités et, laissant de côté la source de la vérité, nous nous acharnons à suivre les ruisseaux des opinions. Ne pourrais-je pas mobiliser contre toi la cohorte entière des anciens auteurs : Ignace, Polycarpe, Irénée, Justin le Martyr et tant d'autres figures apostoliques et éloquentes qui, face à Ébion, Théodote de Byzance et Valentin – lesquels défendaient ces mêmes thèses – ont rédigé des ouvrages remplis de sagesse ? Si seulement tu les avais lus un jour, tu serais plus avisé.

Mais je crois préférable de répondre brièvement à chaque point, plutôt que de m'attarder davantage et d'allonger démesurément cet ouvrage.
en: Now that have cleared the rocks and shoals must spread sail and make all speed to reach his epilogue. Feeling himself to be a smatterer, he there produces Tertullian as a witness and quotes the words of Victorinus, bishop of Petavium. Of Tertullian I say no more than that he did not belong to the Church. But as regards Victorinus, assert what has already been proved from the Gospel-that he spoke of the brothers of the Lord not as being sons of Mary, but brethren in the sense I have explained, that is to say, in point of kinship, not by nature. We are, however, spending our strength on trifles, and, leaving the fountain of truth, are following tiny streams of opinion. Might I not array against you the whole series of ancient writers? Ignatius, Polycarp, Irenaeus, St. Justin Martyr, and many other apostolic and eloquent men, who against Ebion, Theodotus of Byzantium, and Valentinus, held these same views, and wrote volumes full of wisdom. If you read what they wrote, you would be a wiser man. But I think it better to reply briefly to each point than tO linger any longer and extend my book to an undue length [Perpetual Virginity of Blessed Mary 19 (A.D. 383)].
latin: Sed quoniam jam e cautibus et confragosis locis enavigavit oratio, pandenda sunt vela, et in epilogos illius irruendum, in quibus sciolus sibi visus, Tertullianum in testimonium vocat, et Victorini Petabionensis episcopi verba proponit. Et de Tertulliano quidem nihil amplius dico, quam Ecclesiae hominem non fuisse. De Victorino vero id assero, quod et de Evangelistis, fratres eum dixisse Domini, non filios Mariae. Fratres autem eo sensu, quem superius exposuimus, propinquitate, non natura. Verum nugas terimus, et fonte veritatis omisso, opinionum rivulos consectamur. Numquid non possum tibi totam veterum Scriptorum seriem commovere: Ignatium, Polycarpum, Irenaeum, Justinum Martyrem, multosque alios apostolicos et eloquentes viros, qui adversus Ebionem, et Theodotum, Byzantium, Valentinum, haec eadem sentientes, plena sapientiae volumina conscripserunt? Quae si legisses aliquando, plus saperes. Sed melius puto breviter ad singula respondere, quam diutius immorando, volumen extendere.
greek:
This passage is the concluding part of Jerome's direct refutation, where he dismisses Helvidius's authorities and appeals to the broader consensus of the early Church.
1. The Dismissal of Helvidius's Witnesses

    "De Tertulliano nihil amplius dico, quam Ecclesiae hominem non fuisse. De Victorino autem assero... fratres Domini, non filios Mariae, sed cognatos esse dixisse..."
    "Of Tertullian I say no more than that he did not belong to the Church. But as regards Victorinus, I assert... that he spoke of the brothers of the Lord not as being sons of Mary, but brethren in the sense I have explained, that is to say, in point of kinship..."

    Commentary: This is a classic example of Jerome's polemical style. He uses a two-pronged attack to neutralize Helvidius's sources:

        Tertullian: He is dismissed with a swift ad hominem argument. By the time he wrote some of his works, Tertullian had embraced the Montanist heresy. For Jerome, this makes him an unreliable witness ("he did not belong to the Church"), and he refuses to engage with his arguments further.

        Victorinus of Petavium: Jerome does not attack Victorinus's orthodoxy but instead reinterprets him. He claims that Victorinus must have meant "brothers" in the broader sense of "kinsmen," just as Jerome himself had argued earlier in the treatise. He co-opts his opponent's witness for his own side.

2. The Appeal to the "Cloud of Witnesses"

    "Quidni ego per ordinem tibi universam supellectilem proferam veterum scriptorum? Ignatium, Polycarpum, Irenaeum, Justinum martyrem, multosque alios Apostolicos et eloquentes viros..."
    "Might I not array against you the whole series of ancient writers? Ignatius, Polycarp, Irenaeus, St. Justin Martyr, and many other apostolic and eloquent men..."

    Commentary: This is Jerome's argument from Tradition. He is making a powerful claim that his position is not his own invention but is supported by the consensus of the earliest and most respected Christian writers, stretching back to the Apostolic Fathers (Ignatius and Polycarp). He lists these revered names to show that Helvidius's view is a novel and isolated opinion, while his own view stands in the mainstream of apostolic teaching.

3. The Rhetorical Conclusion

    "Sed hoc melius judico, ut singulis breviter respondeam, ne diutius evagantes, modum libri videamur excedere."
    "But I think it better to reply briefly to each point than to linger any longer and extend my book to an undue length."

    Commentary: This is a common rhetorical device. Jerome implies that he could provide overwhelming evidence by quoting from all these ancient writers, but for the sake of brevity, he will refrain. It allows him to claim the support of this "whole series" of Fathers without having to do the work of citing them all, while also appearing considerate of the reader's time.

In summary, you've found the section where Jerome wraps up his case by dismissing his opponent's sources, claiming the full weight of apostolic tradition for his own view, and concluding with a flourish of rhetorical confidence.
context:
Commentary on this Passage (Section 19)

This section is the rhetorical climax of Jerome's argument. He is refuting his opponent, Helvidius, who had cited two earlier writers to support his view that Mary had other children. Jerome's strategy is masterful:

    Dismiss the Opponent's Witnesses:

        Tertullian: Jerome dismisses him with a devastatingly simple attack: "he did not belong to the Church." By the late 4th century, Tertullian's association with the Montanist heresy made his testimony on certain Church matters suspect for Jerome.

        Victorinus: Jerome doesn't dismiss him but re-interprets him, claiming Victorinus meant "kinsmen" just as Jerome had argued earlier.

    Appeal to a Greater Tradition: This is the core of the passage. Jerome unleashes a "cloud of witnesses" against Helvidius's two meager sources. He invokes the names of some of the most revered figures of the 2nd century: Ignatius of Antioch, Polycarp of Smyrna, Irenaeus of Lyons, and Justin Martyr. This is a powerful rhetorical move, suggesting that the belief in Mary's perpetual virginity is not his own invention but is rooted in the ancient, apostolic tradition.

    The Insult: The line, "If you read what they wrote, you would be a wiser man" (Quae si legisses, aliquanto esses sapientior), is classic St. Jerome. He was famous for his sharp wit and devastatingly sarcastic takedowns of his theological opponents.

2. The Latin Passage You Found (from Section 21)

Now, let's look at the Latin text you actually found. This is a very famous and important passage in its own right, but it comes two sections later, in Section 21.
Migne Reference

    Patrologia Latina (PL), Volume 23, Columns 214-215

The Latin Text You Found (Section 21)

    Sed ut haec quae scripta sunt, non negamus, ita ea quae non sunt scripta, renuimus. Natum Deum esse de Virgine credimus, quia legimus. Mariam nupsisse post partum, non credimus, quia non legimus.

Commentary on this Passage (Section 21)

This passage contains Jerome's famous principle for this specific debate:

    "What is written, we do not deny; what is not written, we reject." This is a powerful statement about the role of Scripture.

    He applies it directly to the question at hand: "We believe God was born of the Virgin, because we read it. We do not believe Mary married after giving birth, because we do not read it."

    Jerome's argument here is that the burden of proof is on Helvidius. Since Scripture affirms the Virgin Birth but is silent on Mary having subsequent children, one should not affirm it. He sees the silence of Scripture as prohibitive in this case.

In summary, you found two distinct but crucial passages from Jerome's defense of Mary's perpetual virginity: one based on an appeal to Tradition (Section 19) and the other based on an appeal to the silence of Scripture (Section 21).

fr:
Mais de même que nous ne nions pas ce qui est écrit, de même nous rejetons ce qui ne l'est pas. Nous croyons que Dieu est né de la Vierge, parce que nous le lisons. Que Marie se soit mariée après l'enfantement, nous ne le croyons pas, car nous ne le lisons pas. Et nous ne disons pas cela pour condamner le mariage – la virginité elle-même est en effet le fruit du mariage –, mais parce qu'il ne nous est permis de rien conjecturer à la légère au sujet des saints personnages. Car, en se fondant sur ce genre de spéculations sur le possible, on pourrait tout aussi bien soutenir que Joseph eut plusieurs femmes – puisque Abraham en eut plusieurs, et Jacob de même – et que les frères du Seigneur sont issus de ces épouses ; une fiction que beaucoup forgent, non par piété, mais par une audacieuse témérité.

Tu affirmes que Marie n'est pas demeurée vierge ; moi, je vais plus loin : je soutiens que Joseph lui-même est resté vierge grâce à Marie, afin que d'un mariage virginal naisse un fils vierge. En effet, si la fornication ne peut convenir à un homme saint, et s'il n'est écrit nulle part qu'il ait eu une autre femme ; si, de plus, pour Marie, que l'on croyait être son épouse, il fut un gardien plutôt qu'un mari, il s'ensuit donc qu'il est demeuré vierge avec Marie, lui qui a mérité d'être appelé le père du Seigneur.
en: We believe that God was born of the Virgin, because we read it. That Mary was married after she brought forth, we do not believe, because we do not read it. Nor do we say this to condemn marriage, for virginity itself is the fruit of marriage; but because when we are dealing with saints we must not judge rashly. If we adopt possibility as the standard of judgment, we might maintain that Joseph had several wives because Abraham had, and so had Jacob, and that the Lord's brothers were the issue of those wives, an invention that some hold with a rashness that springs from audacity, not piety. You say that Mary did not continue a virgin: claim still more that Joseph himself, on account of Mary, was a virgin, SO that from a virgin wedlock : virgin son was born [ibid., 21].
latin: Sed ut haec quae scripta sunt, non negamus, ita ea quae non sunt scripta, renuimus. Natum Deum esse de Virgine credimus, quia legimus. Mariam nupsisse post partum, non credimus, quia non legimus. Nec hoc ideo dicimus, quo nuptias condemnemus, ipsa quippe virginitas fructus est nuptiarum: sed quod nobis de sanctis viris temere aestimare nihil liceat. Possumus enim hac aestimatione possibilitatis contendere, plures quoque uxores habuisse Joseph, quia plures habuerit Abraham, plures habuerit Jacob; et de his esse uxoribus fratres Domini, quod plerique non tam pia quam audaci temeritate confingunt. Tu dicis Mariam virginem non permansisse: ego mihi plus vindico, etiam ipsum Joseph virginem fuisse per Mariam, ut ex virginali conjugio virgo filius nasceretur. Si enim in virum sanctum fornicatio non cadit, et aliam eum uxorem habuisse non scribitur: Mariae autem, quam putatus est habuisse, custos potius fuit, quam maritus: relinquitur, virginem eum mansisse cum Maria, qui pater Domini meruit appellari.
greek:
Analysis and Relevant Commentary

This section is a masterclass in theological polemics and contains several of Jerome's most enduring arguments for the perpetual virginity of Mary.
1. The Principle of Scriptural Warrant

    "Natum Deum esse de Virgine credimus, quia legimus. Mariam nupsisse post partum, non credimus, quia non legimus."
    "We believe that God was born of the Virgin, because we read it. That Mary was married after she brought forth, we do not believe, because we do not read it."

    Commentary: This is the foundational argument of the passage. Jerome draws a sharp line between what is explicitly stated in Scripture (the Virgin Birth) and what is not (Mary having other children). He argues that silence on the latter point, combined with Church tradition, is grounds for rejection. It is a powerful rhetorical tool that puts the burden of proof entirely on his opponent, Helvidius.

2. The Rejection of Baseless Speculation

    "Possumus enim hac aestimatione possibilitatis contendere, plures quoque uxores habuisse Joseph... quod plerique non tam pia quam audaci temeritate confingunt."
    "If we adopt possibility as the standard of judgment, we might maintain that Joseph had several wives... an invention that some hold with a rashness that springs from audacity, not piety."

    Commentary: Here, Jerome attacks the "Joseph's previous marriage" theory for explaining the "brothers of the Lord." He dismisses it as an argument from mere possibility, not from evidence. By labeling it as stemming from "audacity, not piety," he frames the traditional view as the only truly pious one and alternative theories as rash and disrespectful to the Holy Family.

3. The Brilliant Counter-Argument

    "Tu dicis Mariam virginem non permansisse: ego mihi plus vindico, etiam ipsum Joseph virginem fuisse per Mariam, ut ex virginali conjugio virgo filius nasceretur."
    "You say that Mary did not continue a virgin: I claim still more that Joseph himself, on account of Mary, was a virgin, so that from a virgin wedlock a virgin son was born."

    Commentary: This is Jerome's famous rhetorical climax. He doesn't just defend the traditional position; he goes on the offensive. He essentially says, "You seek to lower our understanding of Mary's holiness? I will raise it even higher by proposing Joseph's perpetual virginity as well." This argument, that the marriage was a true but virginal union, became immensely influential in Western theology and art. It presents a vision of the Holy Family as consecrated entirely, in body and soul, to their divine mission.

Context from the Preceding Section (18)

Your image also includes Section 18. In that section, Helvidius is quoted as arguing that if people find the idea of Mary having marital relations "disgraceful," they should logically find the physical realities of the Virgin Birth (the nine-month pregnancy, the blood, the infant in cloths) even more disgraceful. Jerome brilliantly refutes this by embracing these "humiliations." He compares them to the ultimate "disgrace" of the Cross, which Christians do not hide but rather profess and glory in. This sets the stage for Section 19 by establishing that true piety does not shy away from the physical realities of the Incarnation but reveres them.

You have successfully found one of the most important and frequently quoted passages in the history of Marian theology. Congratulations on your persistent and successful search

fr:
Tu dis donc, hérétique — qui que tu sois, toi qui nies que Dieu est né de la Vierge —, que Marie, mère de notre Seigneur Jésus-Christ, ne peut être appelée *Théotokos*, c’est-à-dire Mère de Dieu, mais *Christotokos*, c’est-à-dire seulement mère du Christ, et non de Dieu ; car, dis-tu, personne ne met au monde quelqu’un de plus ancien que soi.

Quant à cet argument si insensé, qui te fait juger la naissance de Dieu avec une intelligence charnelle et soumettre le mystère de sa majesté aux raisonnements humains, nous en débattrons plus tard, s’il plaît à Dieu. Pour l’instant, contentons-nous de prouver par les témoignages divins que le Christ est Dieu et que Marie est Mère de Dieu.

Écoute donc l’ange de Dieu s’adresser aux bergers au sujet de la naissance de Dieu…
en: ST. JOHN CASSIAN And so you say, O heretic, whoever you may be. who deny that God was born of the Virgin, that Mary the Mother of our Lord Jesus Christ ought not to be called Theotokos, that is, Mother of God, but Christotokos, that is, only the Mother of Christ, not of God. For no one, you say, brings forth what is anterior in time. And of this utterly foolish argument by which you think that the birth of God can be understood by carnal minds, and fancy that the mystery of his majesty can be accounted for by human reasoning, we will, God permits, say something later on. In the meanwhile we will now prove by divine testimonies that Christ is God, and that Mary is the Mother of God. Hear then how the angel of God speaks to the shepherds of the birth of God [The Incarnation 2:2 c. A.D 429)].
latin: Dicis itaque, quisquis es ille haeretice, qui Deum ex Virgine natum negas, Mariam matrem Domini nostri Jesu Christi Θεοτόκον, id est, matrem Dei, appellari non posse, sed Χριστοτόκον, hoc est, Christi tantum matrem, non Dei: nemo enim, inquis, antiquiorem se parit. Ac de hoc quidem tam stulto argumento, quo nativitatem Dei carnali intelligentia aestimandam putas, et mysterium majestatis humanis credis censendum esse rationibus, postea, si Deus annuet, disputabimus; nunc interim et Christum Deum, et Mariam matrem Dei divinis testibus approbemus. Audi itaque loquentem ad pastores de Dei ortu angelum Dei...
context:
Commentary and Relevant Context

The Latin text you found is far richer than just the initial quote. It contains St. John Cassian's entire scriptural argument in this chapter. This work is historically and theologically crucial for several reasons:

1. Historical Context: The Nestorian Controversy
John Cassian wrote this treatise around A.D. 429-430 at the urgent request of a Roman deacon named Leo, who would later become Pope St. Leo the Great. The heresy of Nestorius, the Patriarch of Constantinople, was causing a massive crisis in the Church.

    Nestorius's Teaching: Nestorius taught that in Christ there were two distinct persons (a divine person and a human person) joined in a moral union. As a result, he claimed that Mary did not give birth to God, but only to the human person of Christ.

    Theotokos vs. Christotokos: This is the heart of the debate. The traditional title for Mary was Theotokos (Greek for "God-bearer" or "Mother of God"). Nestorius rejected this, arguing she should only be called Christotokos ("Christ-bearer" or "Mother of Christ"), to emphasize that she was only the mother of his human nature.

2. Cassian's Argument in This Chapter:
The full Latin text you provided shows Cassian's brilliant method for refuting Nestorius.

    He States the Heresy Clearly: He begins by directly quoting the heretical position: you can't call Mary Theotokos, you must call her Christotokos, because "no one gives birth to one who is older than herself." This is a rational, human-level argument.

    He Postpones the Philosophical Argument: Cassian dismisses this as a "foolish argument" based on "carnal understanding" and promises to deal with its flawed human reasoning later. This is a powerful rhetorical move.

    He Appeals to "Divine Testimonies" (Scripture): Instead of getting bogged down in philosophy, he immediately pivots to the ultimate authority: the Word of God. The rest of the chapter is a tour-de-force of biblical exegesis to prove his point.

    Witness of the Angels: He starts with the angelic announcements.

        To the Shepherds (Luke 2): The angel calls the newborn "Savior" and "Lord." Cassian argues that the power to save belongs to God alone, so these titles prove the divinity of the child.

        To Mary (Luke 1): The Archangel Gabriel explains that the Holy Spirit will come upon her and "the power of the Most High will overshadow" her. Cassian emphasizes the word "therefore" (ideo): because of this divine action, the child will be called the "Son of God." The divinity of the cause (the Holy Trinity's action) proves the divinity of the one conceived.

3. The Importance of the Text:
Cassian's work was one of the most important Western contributions to the Nestorian controversy. It provided a clear, biblically-grounded defense of the title Theotokos and the doctrine of the Incarnation. His arguments helped shape the theological understanding of the West just before the Council of Ephesus (A.D. 431), which formally condemned Nestorianism and solemnly affirmed that Mary is indeed the Theotokos, the Mother of God.

fr: Il est donc nécessaire que tu ne nies pas la grâce donnée par Dieu. C’est donc Dieu qui l’a donnée ; or, elle a été donnée par notre Seigneur Jésus-Christ ; par conséquent, le Seigneur Jésus-Christ est Dieu. Or, s'il est Dieu – et il l'est assurément –, alors celle qui a engendré Dieu est Theotokos, c’est-à-dire Mère de Dieu.
en: You cannot then help admitting that the grace comes from God. t is God then who has given it. But it has been given by our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore the Lord Jesus Christ is God. But if he be, as he certainly is, God, then she who bore God is Theotokos, that iS, the Mother of God [ibid., 2:5].
latin: A Deo ergo necesse est gratiam datam non neges. Deus ergo est qui dedit, data autem est per Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum; ergo Dominus Jesus Christus Deus. Si autem est ille, utique ut est, Deus, ergo illa quae Deum peperit, Theotocos, id est, genitrix Dei.
context:
Additional Relevant Commentary

This passage is a masterclass in theological reasoning and a crucial piece of writing from the Nestorian controversy.

1. The Author and His Purpose: St. John Cassian (c. 360 – c. 435) was a monk and theologian. He wrote this work, On the Incarnation, at the request of the Archdeacon of Rome (who would later become Pope St. Leo the Great). The purpose was to refute the teachings of Nestorius, the Patriarch of Constantinople.

2. The Heresy of Nestorius: Nestorius's central error was to over-separate the divine and human natures in Christ to the point where it seemed like there were two different persons—the man Jesus and the divine Son of God—loosely joined together. As a consequence of this, he famously rejected the traditional title for the Virgin Mary, Theotokos (Greek for "God-bearer" or "Mother of God"). He argued she only gave birth to the man Jesus, not to God.

3. Cassian's Brilliant "Soteriological" Argument: Cassian does not start his argument with Mary. He starts with the nature of salvation itself (soteriology). His logic is irrefutable:
* Premise 1: Saving grace is a divine gift. Only God can bestow the grace that leads to eternal life. A mere man, no matter how holy, cannot give what he does not possess by nature. Cassian establishes this by quoting Scripture (e.g., Titus 2:11, "the grace of God our Savior has appeared").
* Premise 2: Scripture explicitly states that this divine, saving grace comes to us through Jesus Christ (e.g., Acts 15:11, "we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus").
* Logical Conclusion (Christ's Divinity): If saving grace is from God, and it comes through Jesus Christ, then Jesus Christ must be God.
* The Inescapable Consequence (Mary as Theotokos): Once Christ's true divinity is established, the title for Mary follows as a simple matter of fact. If Christ is God, then the woman who bore Him in the flesh is, without any doubt, the Mother of God (Theotokos).

4. Significance: Cassian shows that the title Theotokos is not just about honoring Mary. It is a safeguard of correct Christology. To deny her the title is to deny the Incarnation itself—the truth that the baby in her arms was, in one person, truly God and truly man.

fr: Voyez combien sont nombreuses les largesses du Baptême : certains estiment que la grâce céleste ne consiste que dans la rémission des péchés, alors que nous, nous avons dénombré dix honneurs. C'est pourquoi nous baptisons aussi les petits enfants, bien qu'ils ne soient pas souillés par le péché, afin que leur soient ajoutés la sainteté, la justice, l'adoption, l'héritage, la fraternité avec le Christ, et qu'ils deviennent ses membres.
en: ST. JOHN CHRYSOSTOM You see the many benefits of baptism, and some think its heavenly grace consists only in the remission of sins, but we have enumerated ten honors [it bestows]! For this reason we baptize even infants, though they are not defiled by [personal] sin; so that there may be given to them holiness, righteousness, adoption, inheritance. brotherhood with Christ, and that they may be [Christ's] members [Baptismal Catecheses in St. Augustine, Against Julian 1:6:21 (C. A.D. 388)].
