Hac de causa etiam infantes baptizamus, cum non sint coinquinati peccato, ut eis addatur sanctitas, iustitia, adoptio, hereditas, fraternitas Christi, ut eius membra sint.
context:
Additional Relevant Commentary

This quote is at the heart of the Pelagian controversy and is a classic example of how the Church Fathers debated using proof-texts from other respected authorities.

1. The Source: A "Pseudo-Chrysostom" Mystery

The most critical piece of context is that this sermon, while attributed to St. John Chrysostom by both Augustine and his Pelagian opponent Julian of Eclanum, is not found anywhere in Chrysostom's surviving works. Modern scholars have been unable to locate it. This has led to several theories:

    It is from a genuine but now-lost homily of Chrysostom.

    It was misattributed to Chrysostom even in the 5th century. Some scholars suggest it might actually be from one of Chrysostom's rivals, like Severian of Gabala.

    It was a forgery created by one side of the debate. (This is less likely, as both sides seem to accept its authenticity).

For this reason, it is often referred to by scholars as a "Pseudo-Chrysostom" text. However, what matters historically is that in the 5th century, it was accepted by all parties as a genuine sermon of the great bishop of Constantinople.

2. The Center of a Debate: Augustine vs. Julian

This quote became a major weapon in the debate over original sin.

    Julian's Pelagian Interpretation: Julian of Eclanum triumphantly quoted this passage to Augustine. His argument was simple: "Look! The great St. John Chrysostom says infants are baptized 'though they are not defiled by sin' (cum non sint coinquinati peccato). This proves my point: there is no original sin transmitted at birth. Infants are baptized not for the remission of a sin they don't have, but only for the positive benefits—to be made holy, adopted, etc."

    Augustine's Catholic Interpretation: Augustine's response is brilliant. He accepts the text as authentic but provides a different interpretation. He argues that when "Chrysostom" says infants are not defiled by peccato (sin, singular), he means they are not defiled by personal, actual sin—the sins one commits through one's own will. This, Augustine argues, does not deny the existence of inherited original sin (peccatum originale). For Augustine, the ten positive benefits listed (holiness, adoption, etc.) are precisely the remedy for the negative state of original sin. Baptism doesn't just add gifts to a neutral soul; it transforms a soul from a state of alienation from God (due to original sin) into a state of communion and grace.

3. The Rich Theology of Baptism

Beyond the controversy, the quote itself is a beautiful and rich summary of the positive effects of Baptism. The author (whether Chrysostom or someone else) is pushing back against a minimalist view of the sacrament. Baptism is not just a "sin-eraser." It is a profound, transformative event that results in:

    Sanctification and Justification: Made holy and righteous.

    Divine Filiation: Adoption as sons and daughters of God.

    Heirship: Becoming heirs to the Kingdom of Heaven.

    Incorporation into Christ: Becoming brothers of Christ and members of his own Mystical Body.

You have found a quote that is a historical puzzle, a theological battleground, and a beautiful piece of sacramental teaching all in one.

fr: Tu as revêtu le Christ, tu es devenu membre du Seigneur, tu as été inscrit dans la cité d'en-haut, et tu rampes encore autour de la Loi ? Et comment pourrais-tu parvenir au Royaume ? Écoute ce que dit Paul : l'observance de la Loi renverse l'Évangile. Et, si tu le veux, apprends comment, frémis et fuis cet abîme. Car pourquoi observes-tu le sabbat et jeûnes-tu avec eux ?
en: You have put on Christ, you have become a member of the Lord, and been enrolled in the heavenly city, and you still grovel in the Law? How is it possible for you to obtain the kingdom? Listen to Paul's words, that the observance of the Law overthrows the gospel, and learn, if you will, how this comes to pass, and tremble, and shun this pitfall. Wherefore do you keep the Sabbath, and fast with the Jews? [Commentary on Galatians 2:17 c. A.D. 395)].
latin: Induisti Christum, membrum factus es Domini, in supernam civitatem adscriptus es, et adhuc circa legem serpis? et quomodo potes regnum illud consequi? Audi Paulum dicentem, Evangelium subverti per legis observationem. ... Cur enim observas sabbatum, ac jejunas cum illis?
greek: Τὸν Χριστὸν ἐνεδύσω, καὶ μέλος ἐγένου τοῦ Δεσπότου, καὶ εἰς τὴν ἄνω πόλιν ἐνεγράφης, καὶ ἔτι περὶ τὸν νόμον ἔρπεις; καὶ πῶς ἔνι σε τῆς βασιλείας ἐπιτυχεῖν; Ἄκουσον τοῦ Παύλου λέγοντος, ὅτι τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον ἀνατρέπεται διὰ τῆς παρατηρήσεως τοῦ νόμου. context:
The Full Context Provided by Your Image

What makes your find so excellent is that it includes the entire argument Chrysostom is making. He doesn't just state the warning; he builds a powerful case before and after it.
1. The Argument Before Your Quote:

Chrysostom points out that it was one thing for the very first Christians to continue some Jewish practices when the Temple in Jerusalem was still standing. But for the Christians of his day (late 4th century), long after the Temple's destruction and the scattering of the Jewish people, it is completely inexcusable.

    "...those men [the first Christians] did these things in the beginning, when the city and the temple and everything else still existed; but these men [in my day], who see the punishment the Jews have paid, and the utter destruction of their city, and yet observe even more—what excuse could they have, keeping the Law at a time when the Jews themselves, however much they may want to, are unable to keep it?"

He is saying that history itself has proven that the Old Covenant has been superseded, making a return to its practices an act of spiritual blindness.
2. The Argument After Your Quote:

After his passionate warning, Chrysostom uses a classic Pauline reductio ad absurdum argument to show the logical conclusion of "Judaizing":

    "For if you observe the Sabbath, why do you not also get circumcised? And if you get circumcised, why do you not also offer animal sacrifices? For if the Law must be kept, it must be kept in its entirety... If you are terrified of being condemned for breaking a part of it, you ought to be terrified about the whole of it... If the whole Law must be kept, then you must disobey Christ; or, if we obey Christ, we must become transgressors of the Law."

His point is devastating: you cannot pick and choose bits of the Law to add to your Christian faith. To take on one part is to place yourself under the obligation of the whole system, which would mean rejecting the sufficiency of Christ and, in fact, making Christ the "author of transgression" for having freed us from the Law.

You have found the complete, unabridged passage, which shows St. John Chrysostom at his pastoral best: passionately logical, historically aware, and deeply concerned for the salvation of his flock.

fr:
Qu'ils aillent donc jusqu'à se mutiler, ceux qui jettent le trouble parmi vous ! Voyez comme il est amer ici envers ceux qui les ont égarés. En effet, au commencement, c’est contre ceux qui avaient été trompés qu’il dirigeait son accusation, les traitant d’insensés à deux reprises. Mais après les avoir dûment instruits et corrigés, il se tourne désormais contre les trompeurs. Ce qu’il veut dire, c’est ceci : Je ne me soucie nullement d’eux. En effet, *l’homme hérétique, après un premier et un second avertissement, évite-le*. S’ils le veulent, qu’ils ne se contentent pas d’être circoncis : qu’ils se fassent entièrement mutiler !

Où sont-ils donc, ceux qui osent se mutiler eux-mêmes, attirant ainsi sur eux la malédiction, calomniant la création de Dieu et se faisant les complices des manichéens ? En effet, les premiers affirment que le corps est une source de pièges et qu’il provient de la matière mauvaise ; les seconds, par leurs actes, donnent du crédit à ces terribles doctrines, puisqu’ils amputent ce membre comme s’il était un ennemi, une source de dangers. Dans ce cas, ne faudrait-il pas bien davantage se crever les yeux ? Car c’est par les yeux que le désir pénètre dans l’âme. Mais ni l’œil ni aucun autre membre n’est en cause ; seule l’est la mauvaise disposition de la volonté. Et si tu n'arrives pas à te maîtriser, pourquoi ne pas aussi te couper la langue pour le blasphème, les mains pour le vol, et les pieds pour leur course vers le mal ? Pourquoi, en somme, ne pas mettre en pièces ton corps tout entier ? ... Mais tout cela relève de la plus extrême impiété et d’une folie satanique.
en: Observe how bitterly [Paul] speaks against their deceivers: would that they that unsettle you would even cut themselves off" [Gal 5:12]. On this account he curses them: and his meaning is as follows for them I have no concern, "A man that is heretical after the first and second admonition refuse" [Ti 3:10]. If they will, let them not only be circumcised, but mutilated. Where are those who dare to mutilate themselves, seeing that they draw down the apostolic curse, and accuse the workmanship of God, and take part with the Manicheans? [Commentary on Galatians 5:12 (c. A.D. 395)].
latin:
Utinam et concidantur qui vos conturbant. Vide quam hic est amarulentus in eos qui Galatas seduxerant. In initiò torquebat accusationen in seductos, semel atque iterum eos appellans stultos; verum ubi illos recte castigavit correxitque, deinceps in seductores fertur. Oportet autem nos et hanc Apostoli sapientiam perspicere, quomodo hos tamquam proprios filios, et tamquam correctionis capaces admonet, et ad mentem revocat: eos voro qui seduxerant, velut alienos et insanabili morbo laborantes resecat, partim cum ita dicit, Portabil judicium suum quisquis fuerit: partim cum imprecans ait, Utinam et abscindantur qui vos conturbant. Ac recte dixit conturbantes, hoc est, depellentes. Compulerant enim eos, ut propria patria, ut libertate, ut cælesti cognatione relicta, alienam ac peregrinam requirerent, ut jam ab illa superna liberaque Jerosolyma exsules, cogantur velut captivi, solumque vertere jussi, incertis vagari sedibus. Quapropter illis imprecatur.

    Quod autem dicit, hoc est: Nulla est mihi cura de illis: Hæreticum enim, inquit, hominem post unam et alteram admonitionem devita (Tit. 3. 10). Si volunt, non solum circumcidantur, verum etiam exsecentur.

    Contra eos qui virilia amputabant. — Ubi nunc sunt, qui seipsos audent evirare, simul et apostolicam imprecationem sibi accersentes, et Dei opificium accusantes, et cum Manichæis stantes? Nam illi quidem aiunt, corpus insidiosum esse malæque materiæ; hi vero factis suis, crudelibus illis opinionibus præbent ansam, dum membrum amputant velut insidiosum et inimicum. Itaque multo magis oportebat excœcare oculos; per oculos enim in animam descendit concupiscentia. Verum nec oculus, nec ullum aliud membrum est in culpa, sed sola prava animi affectio. Quod si non sustines, cur non et linguam ob blasphemias, cur non et manus ob rapinas, cur non et pedes ad malitiam currentes, denique cur non totum resecas corpus? ... Verum hæc extremæ sunt impietatis ac satanici furoris.

Ὄφελον καὶ ἀποκόψονται οἱ ἀναστατοῦντες ὑμᾶς. Ὅρα πῶς ἐστι πικρὸς ἐνταῦθα κατὰ τῶν ἠπατηκότων. Παρὰ μὲν γὰρ τὴν ἀρχὴν ἐπὶ τοὺς ἠπατημένους τὴν κατηγορίαν ἔτρεπεν, ἀνοήτους καλῶν, καὶ ἅπαξ καὶ δεύτερον· ἐπειδὴ δὲ καλῶς αὐτοὺς ἐπαίδευσε καὶ διώρθωσε, πρὸς τοὺς ἡπατηκότας τρέπεται λοιπόν. ...     Ποῦ τοίνυν εἰσὶν οἱ τολμῶντες ἀποκόπτειν ἑαυτοὺς, καὶ τὴν ἀρὰν ἐπισπώμενοι, καὶ τὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ δημιουργίαν διαβάλλοντες, καὶ τοῖς Μανιχαίοις συμπράττοντες; Ἐκεῖνοι μὲν γάρ φασι τὸ σῶμα ἐπίβουλον εἶναι καὶ ὕλης τῆς πονηρᾶς· οὗτοι δὲ διὰ τῶν ἔργων τοῖς χαλεποῖς δόγμασι τούτοις διδόασιν ἀφορμήν· ὡς γὰρ ἐχθρὸν καὶ ἐπίβουλον ἀποκόπτουσι τὸ μέλος. Οὐκοῦν πολλῷ μᾶλλον τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς πηρῶσαι ἐχρῆν· διὰ γὰρ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν εἰς τὴν ψυχὴν κάτεισιν ἡ ἐπιθυμία. Ἀλλὰ οὔτε ὀφθαλμὸς οὔτε τι ἄλλο μέλος αἴτιον, ἀλλ' ἡ πονηρὰ προαίρεσις μόνον. Εἰ δὲ οὐκ ἀνέχῃ, διὰ τί μὴ καὶ γλῶτταν διὰ τὴν βλασφημίαν, καὶ χεῖρας διὰ τὴν ἁρπαγὴν, καὶ πόδας διὰ τοὺς ἐπὶ πονηρίαν δρόμους, καὶ πᾶν, ὡς εἰπεῖν, τὸ σῶμα κατακόπτεις; ... Ἀλλ' ἐσχάτης ταῦτα παρανομίας, καὶ σατανικῆς παραπληξίας.
context:
Context and Analysis of the Passage

This passage comes from St. John Chrysostom's commentary on St. Paul's Letter to the Galatians, specifically on chapter 5, verse 12. The context is Paul's extreme frustration with the Judaizers, who were confusing the Galatian Christians by insisting they must be circumcised to be saved.

    Paul's Bitter Pun: Chrysostom highlights the sharp, sarcastic nature of Paul's words. Paul says, "I wish those who are unsettling you would not just circumcise, but go all the way and mutilate themselves" (ἀποκόψονται / abscindantur). Chrysostom explains that Paul, having rebuked the Galatians themselves, now turns his full fury on the false teachers. His curse is essentially, "If they are so obsessed with cutting off a piece of flesh, I wish they'd cut themselves off entirely," a clear and shocking reference to castration.

    Linking to Manichaeism: Chrysostom then makes a brilliant theological leap. He uses Paul's curse against self-mutilation to condemn the practice in his own day, explicitly connecting it to the heresy of the Manicheans. The Manicheans taught that the physical body was intrinsically evil, a creation of a lesser, malevolent god. Chrysostom argues that anyone who practices self-mutilation is, by their actions, siding with the Manicheans. They are treating God's good creation (Dei opificium / τοῦ Θεοῦ δημιουργίαν) as something evil and hostile that must be attacked.

    The True Source of Sin: To show the absurdity of this position, Chrysostom employs a reductio ad absurdum argument. If you cut off the part of the body associated with lust, then to be consistent, you should also blind your eyes for seeing temptation, cut out your tongue for blasphemy, and chop off your hands for theft. The logical end is the complete destruction of the body.

    The Core Christian Doctrine: He concludes by stating the true Christian understanding: the body and its parts are not the cause of sin. The fault lies not in the physical instrument but in the agent using it—the "wicked disposition of the soul" (prava animi affectio / ἡ πονηρὰ προαίρεσις). This is the classic distinction between the goodness of creation and the corruption introduced by a fallen will.

fr:
Voilà pour ce qui est de nos paroles. Quant à nous, manifestons par nos œuvres la droiture de notre vie, et allumons le feu généreux de la vertu. Car, est-il dit, « vous êtes des astres qui brillez au milieu du monde » ; et à chacun de nous, Dieu a confié une mission plus grande que celle du soleil, plus grande que celle du ciel, de la terre et de la mer ; une mission d’autant plus grande que les réalités spirituelles l’emportent sur les réalités sensibles. Ainsi, lorsque nous contemplons le disque solaire, lorsque nous admirons la beauté, la masse et l’éclat de cet astre, pensons alors que la lumière qui est en nous est plus grande et meilleure. De même, les ténèbres sont bien plus terribles si nous n’y prenons pas garde, car une nuit profonde s’est emparée du monde entier. Cette nuit, renversons-la donc et dissipons-la.

Cette nuit ne règne pas seulement chez les hérétiques ou chez les païens, mais aussi parmi beaucoup des nôtres, tant sur le plan des dogmes que sur celui de la vie. Beaucoup, en effet, doutent de la résurrection ; beaucoup se retranchent derrière l’astrologie ; beaucoup observent des superstitions, des présages, des augures et des symboles. D’autres encore ont recours aux amulettes et aux incantations. Mais nous parlerons contre eux plus tard, lorsque nous aurons achevé notre propos contre les païens. En attendant, retenez ce qui a été dit et rejoignez-moi dans le combat, en les attirant et en les amenant à nous par votre manière de vivre. Car, comme je le dis toujours, celui qui enseigne la philosophie doit d’abord l’enseigner par sa propre vie et se rendre désirable aux yeux de ses auditeurs.
en: ST. JOHN CHRYSOSTOM [jet us show forth by our actions all excellencies of conduct, and kindle the fire of virtue abundantly. For "you are lights," says he, "shining in the midst of the world" [Phil 2:15]. And God has given to each of us a greater function than he has to the sun: greater than heaven, and earth, and sea; as much greater, as spiritual things are more excellent than things sensible. When then we look unto the solar orb, and admire its beauty, and body and brightness, let us remember that greater and better is the light in us, as the darkness also is more dreadful unless we take heed, and a deep night oppresses the whole world. This is what we have to dispel and dissolve. It is night not among heretics and among Greeks only, but also in the multitude on our side, in respect to doctrines and to life. For many entirely disbelieve the Resurrection: many fortify themselves with their horoscope; many adhere to superstitious observances, and to omens, and auguries, and presages [Homilies on First Corinthians 4:11 (c. A.D. 392)].
latin:
Et nostra quidem hactenus. Nos autem operibus vitam recte geramus, et copiosum virtutis ignem accendamus. Luminaria enim estis, inquit, in medio mundi fulgentes (Philipp. 2. 15) : et singulis nostrum majorem Deus dedit usum, quam soli; majorem quam cælo et terræ et mari, et tanto majorem, quanto spiritualia sensibilibus præcellunt. Cum ergo solis circulum conspicimus et pulchritudinem, corpus et splendorem astri admiramur, cogitemus majorem et meliorem in nobis esse lucem; ut etiam graviores tenebras, nisi attendamus: nam nox profunda totum orbem occupat. Hanc igitur evertamus et solvamus.

    Nox non in hæreticis et Græcis tantum, sed etiam in multis qui nobiscum sunt, tam in dogmatibus, quam in vita. Multi enim resurrectioni non credunt, multi genethliaca sententia se muniunt; alii observationibus student, necnon vaticinationibus, auguriis et symbolis; alii ligaminibus et incantationibus utuntur. At adversus illos etiam postea dicturi sumus, postquam sermonem contra Græcos absolverimus: interim vero illa quæ dicta sunt retinete, et mecum ad pugnam accedite, per vitæ institutum illos ad nos attrahentes et transferentes. Etenim, quod semper dico, eum qui philosophiam docet, oportet primo per seipsum hoc docere, et auditoribus esse desiderabilem.
greek:
Καὶ τὰ παρ' ἡμῶν ὧδε. Παρεχώμεθα δὲ ἐπὶ τῶν ἔργων τὰ τοῦ βίου κατορθώματα, καὶ δαψιλὲς τὸ πῦρ ἀνάπτωμεν τῆς ἀρετῆς. Φωστῆρες γάρ ἐστε, φησὶν, ἐν μέσῳ τοῦ κόσμου λάμποντες· καὶ μείζονα ἡμῶν ἑκάστῳ χρείαν ἐνεχείρισεν ὁ Θεὸς, ἢ τῷ ἡλίῳ, μείζονα οὐρανοῦ καὶ γῆς καὶ θαλάττης, καὶ τοσούτῳ μείζονα, ὅσῳ τὰ πνευματικὰ τῶν αἰσθητῶν διενήνοχεν. Ὅταν οὖν πρὸς τὸν ἡλιακὸν ἴδωμεν κύκλον, καὶ θαυμάσωμεν τὸ κάλλος καὶ τὸ σῶμα καὶ τὴν φαιδρότητα τοῦ ἄστρου, λογιζώμεθα πάλιν, ὅτι μεῖζον καὶ ἄμεινον τὸ ἐν ἡμῖν φῶς, καθάπερ καὶ τὸ σκότος χαλεπώτερον, ἂν μὴ προσέχωμεν· καὶ γὰρ νὺξ βαθεῖα κατέχει τὴν οἰκουμένην ἅπασαν. Ταύτην τοίνυν ἀνατρέψωμεν καὶ λύσωμεν.

    Νὺξ οὐκ ἐν αἱρετικοῖς οὐδὲ ἐν Ἕλλησι μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ πολλοῖς τοῖς παρ' ἡμῖν δογμάτων ἕνεκεν καὶ βίου. Πολλοὶ γὰρ τῇ ἀναστάσει διαπιστοῦσι, πολλοὶ καὶ γένεσιν ἑαυτοῖς ἐπιτειχίζουσι, πολλοὶ καὶ παρατηρήσεις φυλάττουσι καὶ κληδωνισμοῖς καὶ οἰωνισμοῖς καὶ συμβόλοις· οἱ δὲ καὶ περιάπτοις καὶ ἐπῳδαῖς κέχρηνται. Ἀλλὰ καὶ πρὸς τούτους μὲν ὕστερον ἐροῦμεν, ὅταν τὰ πρὸς Ἕλληνας διανύσωμεν· τέως δὲ τὰ εἰρημένα κατέχετε, καὶ συλλάβεσθέ μοι τῆς μάχης, διὰ τοῦ βίου πρὸς ἡμᾶς ἕλκοντες αὐτοὺς καὶ μεθιστῶντες. Ὅπερ γὰρ ἀεὶ λέγω, τὸν περὶ φιλοσοφίας διδάσκοντα, πρότερον ἐν ἑαυτῷ τοῦτο διδάσκειν χρὴ καὶ ποθεινὸν εἶναι τοῖς ἀκούουσι.
context:
Context and Analysis

This passage provides a remarkable insight into the pastoral reality of a major city in the late Roman Empire (c. 392 AD), even after Christianity had become the state religion. St. John Chrysostom is not just fighting formal heresy but the deep-seated persistence of pagan beliefs and practices within his own congregation.

1. The Exhortation: Christians as a Greater Light
Chrysostom begins with a powerful call to action. Christians, he argues, have a greater function than the sun itself because spiritual light is superior to physical light. Their role is to dispel a profound darkness that has enveloped the world.

2. The "Darkness" is Not Just "Out There"
He explicitly states that this "night" exists not only among heretics and pagans ("Greeks") but also "in the multitude on our side" (ἐν τῷ πλήθει τῷ ἡμετέρῳ). He then lists the specific problems he sees among his own flock:

    Disbelief in the Resurrection: A fundamental rejection of core Christian doctrine.

    Astrology (Horoscopes): The phrase "fortify themselves with their horoscope" is a translation of the Greek γένεσιν ἑαυτοῖς ἐπιτειχίζουσι. The term γένεσις (genesis) was the technical term for the casting of a natal horoscope. This belief in fatalism was a primary target of the Church Fathers because it denied God's providence and human free will.

    Pagan Divination and Superstition: He lists several common practices:

        παρατηρήσεις (paratērēsesi): "Observations" of auspicious/inauspicious days or times.

        κληδωνισμοί (klēdōnismois): "Omens" taken from hearing random words or sounds.

        οἰωνισμοί (oiōnismois): "Auguries," often from observing the flight of birds.

        σύμβολα (symbolois): "Presages" or signs.

    Folk Magic: The full text adds another layer of common practice:

        περιάπτοις (periaptois): "Amulets" or protective charms worn on the body.

        ἐπῳδαῖς (epōdais): "Incantations" or magical chants.

3. The Pastoral Strategy: Attraction, Not Just Argument
Chrysostom’s proposed solution is not primarily intellectual debate. He tells his congregation to win over the pagans by the beauty and integrity of their own lives: "attracting them and transferring them to us through your way of life" (διὰ τοῦ βίου πρὸς ἡμᾶς ἕλκοντες αὐτοὺς καὶ μεθιστῶντες). The philosopher, he says, must first be a living example of his own philosophy.

fr:
La coupe de bénédiction que nous bénissons, n’est-elle pas communion au sang du Christ ? Quelle parole à la fois si vraie et si redoutable ! Car voici ce qu’il dit : ce qui est dans la coupe est cela même qui a coulé de son côté, et c’est à cela même que nous avons part.

Il l’a appelée « coupe de bénédiction » parce que, en la tenant dans nos mains, nous le louons, saisis d’admiration et de stupeur devant ce don ineffable, et nous le bénissons d’avoir versé ce sang même pour que nous ne demeurions pas dans l’erreur. Et non seulement il l’a versé, mais il nous en a tous fait don.

C’est pourquoi il dit : si tu as soif de sang, ne va pas rougir l’autel des idoles par le meurtre d’animaux privés de raison, mais rougis mon propre autel de mon propre sang. Qu’y a-t-il de plus redoutable ?
en: The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a communion of the blood of Christ? Very persuasively spoke he, and awfully. For what he says is this: "This that is in the cup is what flowed from his side, and of that do we partake. But he called it a cup of blessing, because holding it in our hands, we so exalt him in our hymn, wondering, astonished at his unspeakable gift, blessing him, among other things, for the pouring out of this self-same draught that we might not abide in error: and not only for the pouring it out, but also for imparting it to us all. "Wherefore if you desire blood," says he, "redden not the altar of idols with the slaughter of brute beasts, but my altar with my blood." Tell me, what can be more tremendous than this? [ Homilies on First Corinthians 24:3 (c. AD. 392)].
latin: «Calix benedictionis, cui benedicimus, nonne communicatio sanguinis Christi est?» Valde fideliter et horribiliter dixit. Quod enim dicit, hoc est: Illud quod est in calice, id est quod e latere fluxit, et illius participes sumus. Calicem autem benedictionis vocavit, quia cum ipsum in manibus tenemus, sic ipsum laudibus extollimus, admirantes et obstupescentes de ineffabili dono, benedicentes quod et ipsum hoc effudit, ne in errore maneremus: et non solum effudit, sed et nobis omnibus impertivit. Quare si sanguinem desideras, inquit, noli idolorum altare brutorum caede, sed meum altare meo cruentare sanguine. Quid hoc horrendius?
greek: Τὸ ποτήριον τῆς εὐλογίας, ὃ εὐλογοῦμεν, οὐχὶ κοινωνία τοῦ αἵματος τοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐστι; Σφόδρα πιστῶς καὶ φοβερῶς εἴρηκεν. Ὃ γὰρ λέγει, τοῦτό ἐστιν, ὅτι Τοῦτο τὸ ἐν τῷ ποτηρίῳ ὂν, ἐκεῖνό ἐστι τὸ ἀπὸ τῆς πλευρᾶς ῥεῦσαν, καὶ ἐκείνου μετέχομεν. Ποτήριον δὲ εὐλογίας ἐκάλεσεν, ἐπειδὴ αὐτὸ μετὰ χεῖρας ἔχοντες, οὕτως αὐτὸν ἀνυμνοῦμεν, θαυμάζοντες καὶ ἐκπληττόμενοι τῆς ἀφάτου δωρεᾶς, εὐλογοῦντες ὅτι καὶ αὐτὸ τοῦτο ἐξέχεεν, ἵνα μὴ μείνωμεν ἐν τῇ πλάνῃ: καὶ οὐ μόνον ἐξέχεεν, ἀλλὰ καὶ πᾶσιν ἡμῖν αὐτοῦ μετέδωκεν. Ὥστε εἰ αἵματος ἐπιθυμεῖς, φησὶ, μὴ τὸν τῶν εἰδώλων βωμὸν τῷ τῶν ἀλόγων φόνῳ, ἀλλὰ τὸ θυσιαστήριον τὸ ἐμὸν τῷ ἐμῷ φοίνισσε αἵματι. Τί τούτου φρικωδέστερον;
context:
You have located a powerful and famous passage on the Real Presence in the Eucharist.

    Source: St. John Chrysostom, Homily 24 on First Corinthians, Section 3 (sometimes numbered as Section 1 depending on the edition). The commentary is on 1 Corinthians 10:16.

    The Argument: St. Paul, and Chrysostom following him, is making a sharp contrast. The Corinthians were tempted to participate in pagan temple feasts, which involved eating meat sacrificed to idols. Chrysostom explains that this is incompatible with partaking of the Eucharist.

    "This that is in the cup is what flowed from his side": This is a direct and unambiguous statement of the Real Presence. Chrysostom identifies the contents of the Eucharistic cup with the literal blood that flowed from Christ's side on the cross.

    The "Cup of Blessing": He explains that it is called a "cup of blessing" because in receiving it, we bless and thank God for His "unspeakable gift"—not only for shedding His blood but for giving it to us personally.

    The Dramatic Contrast: The climax of the passage is the imagined speech from Christ: "Wherefore if you desire blood... redden not the altar of idols with the slaughter of brute beasts, but my altar with my blood." Chrysostom presents the Eucharist as the true, ultimate sacrifice that replaces and infinitely surpasses the animal sacrifices of both paganism and the Old Testament.

    "What can be more tremendous than this?": The Greek word is φρικωδέστερον (phrikōdesteron), which means awe-inspiring, fearsome, and tremendous. It conveys a sense of holy terror and wonder at the reality of the Eucharist.

fr: Portons-leur donc secours, et faisons mémoire d’eux. Car si le sacrifice du père purifiait les enfants de Job, pourquoi douterais-tu que nos offrandes pour les défunts leur apportent quelque consolation ? Telle est en effet la coutume de Dieu : faire grâce aux uns en faveur des autres.
en: Let us then give them aid and perform commemoration for them. For if the children of Job were purged by the sacrifice of their father, why do you doubt that when we too offer for the departed, some consolation arises to them, since God is wont to grant the petitions of those who ask for others? [ Homilies on First Corinthians 41:8 (c. A.D. 392)].
latin: Eis ergo opem feramus, et commemorationem eorum peragamus. Si enim Jobi filios expiabat patris sacrificium: quid dubitas, an nobis pro eis qui excesserunt offerentibus, ipsis detur aliqua consolatio? Solet enim Deus etiam aliis pro aliis gratificari.
greek: Βοηθῶμεν τοίνυν αὐτοῖς, καὶ μνείαν ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν ἐπιτελῶμεν. Εἰ γὰρ τοὺς παῖδας τοῦ Ἰὼβ ἐκάθαιρεν ἡ τοῦ πατρὸς θυσία, τί ἀμφιβάλλεις, εἰ καὶ ἡμῶν ὑπὲρ τῶν ἀπελθόντων προσφερόντων γίνεταί τις αὐτοῖς παραμυθία; Εἴωθε γὰρ ὁ Θεὸς καὶ ἑτέροις ὑπὲρ ἑτέρων χαρίζεσθαι.
context:
The texts you found are from St. John Chrysostom's Homily 41 on the First Epistle to the Corinthians. The passage is a magnificent example of his pastoral care and a foundational text for the Church's teaching on praying for the dead.

Here is the context:

    A Pastoral Sermon on Grief: Chrysostom is speaking to his congregation about how to handle the death of loved ones. He strongly rebukes excessive, pagan-style mourning (wailing, tearing clothes, despairing) as unworthy of Christians who believe in the resurrection.

    Action over Despair: He argues that instead of uselessly grieving for a loved one who was a sinner, Christians should take action to help them. This action consists of prayers, almsgiving, and, most importantly, offering the Eucharistic sacrifice on their behalf.

    The Power of the Eucharist: Chrysostom reminds his flock that the commemoration of the departed during the Divine Mysteries (the Eucharist) is not a mere human invention. He points to the priest who cries out, "For all who have fallen asleep in Christ," and argues that these practices were established by the Holy Spirit. The offering of the "Lamb who takes away the sin of the world" is a source of "consolation" and "pardon" for the departed.

    The Example of Job: The quote you selected is his key biblical proof for this practice. He argues from the lesser to the greater: if the simple sacrifice of a patriarch like Job in the Old Testament could have a cleansing effect on his children, how much more powerful must the prayers and sacrifices of the Church be for the faithful departed, offered in union with Christ's own sacrifice?

fr:
Alors ? N'offrons-nous pas le sacrifice chaque jour ?
Nous l'offrons, bien sûr, mais en faisant mémoire de sa mort. Et il s'agit d'un unique sacrifice, et non de plusieurs. Comment peut-il être unique, et non multiple ? Parce qu'il a été offert une fois pour toutes, comme le fut le sacrifice dans le Saint des saints. Le sacrifice du Temple est la figure de celui du Christ, et le nôtre l'est également. Car c'est toujours le même que nous offrons : non pas un agneau aujourd'hui et un autre demain, mais toujours le même. Voilà pourquoi le sacrifice est unique.
Sinon, en suivant ce raisonnement, du fait qu'il est offert en de nombreux lieux, y aurait-il plusieurs Christs ? Nullement. Il n'y a qu'un seul Christ partout, tout entier présent ici et tout entier là-bas, un unique corps. Par conséquent, de même que celui qui est offert en de nombreux lieux est un seul corps et non plusieurs, de même le sacrifice est unique.
Notre grand prêtre est celui-là même qui a offert le sacrifice qui nous purifie. C'est ce sacrifice que nous offrons aujourd'hui encore, celui qui fut offert alors, ce sacrifice inépuisable. Cela se fait en mémoire de l'événement d'alors, car il a dit : « Faites ceci en mémoire de moi. »
Nous n'offrons pas un autre sacrifice, comme le faisait le grand prêtre d'autrefois, mais nous accomplissons toujours le même. Ou plutôt, nous accomplissons le mémorial du sacrifice.
en: What then? Do not we offer every day? We offer indeed, but making remembrance of his death, and this [remembrance] is one and not many. How is one and not many? Because that [sacrifice] was once for all offered, [and] carried into the holy of holies. This is a figure of that [sacrifice] and a remembrance. For we always offer the same, not one sheep now and tomorrow another, but always the same thing: so that the sacrifice is one. And yet by this reasoning, since the offering is made in many places, are there many Christs? But Christ is one everywhere, being complete here and complete there also, one body. Even while offered in many places, he is one body and not many bodies; so also [he is] one sacrifice [Homilies on Hebrews 17:6 (C. A.D. 403)].
latin: Quid vero? annon nos quotidie offerimus? Offerimus quidem, sed ejus mortem revocamus in memoriam : et ipsa una est, non multæ. Quomodo una est, non multæ? Quoniam semel fuit oblata, sicut illa fuit in sancta sanctorum. Hoc est figura illius, et ipsa istius: eumdem enim semper offerimus, non nunc aliam, cras aliam ovem, sed semper eamdem. Quamobrem unum est sacrificium propter hanc rationem : alioquin hac ratione, quoniam multis in locis offertur, multine sunt Christi? Nequaquam, sed unus ubique Christus, qui et hic est plenus, et illic plenus, unum corpus. Ut ergo multis in locis oblatus unum est corpus, et non multa corpora: ita etiam unum est sacrificium. Pontifex noster ille est qui obtulit hostiam, quæ nos mundat. Illam nunc quoque offerimus, quæ tunc fuit oblata, quæ non potest consumi. Hoc fit in recordationem ejus quod tunc factum est : Hoc enim facite, inquit, in meam commemorationem (Luc. 22. 19). Non aliam hostiam, sicut pontifex, sed eandem semper facimus, vel potius sacrificii facimus commemorationem.
greek: Τί οὖν; ἡμεῖς καθ' ἑκάστην ἡμέραν οὐ προσφέρομεν; Προσφέρομεν μὲν, ἀλλ' ἀνάμνησιν ποιούμενοι τοῦ θανάτου αὐτοῦ: καὶ μία ἐστὶν αὕτη, καὶ οὐ πολλαί. Πῶς μία, καὶ οὐ πολλαί; Ἐπειδὴ ἅπαξ προσηνέχθη, ὥσπερ ἐκείνη ἡ εἰς τὰ Ἅγια τῶν ἁγίων. Τοῦτο ἐκείνης τύπος ἐστὶ, καὶ αὕτη ἐκείνης: τὸν γὰρ αὐτὸν ἀεὶ προσφέρομεν, οὐ νῦν μὲν ἕτερον πρόβατον, αὔριον δὲ ἕτερον, ἀλλ' ἀεὶ τὸ αὐτό: ὥστε μία ἐστὶν ἡ θυσία. Ἐπεὶ τῷ λόγῳ τούτῳ, ἐπειδὴ πολλαχοῦ προσφέρεται, καὶ πολλοὶ Χριστοί; ἀλλ' οὐδαμῶς, ἀλλ' εἷς πανταχοῦ ὁ Χριστὸς, καὶ ἐνταχοῦ πλήρης ὢν, καὶ ἐκεῖ πλήρης, ἓν σῶμα. Ὥσπερ οὖν πολλαχοῦ προσφερόμενος ἓν σῶμά ἐστι, καὶ οὐ πολλὰ σώματα, οὕτω καὶ μία θυσία. Ὁ ἀρχιερεὺς ἡμῶν ἐκεῖνός ἐστιν ὁ τὴν θυσίαν τὴν καθαίρουσαν ἡμᾶς προσενεγκών. Ἐκείνην προσφέρομεν καὶ νῦν, τὴν τότε προσενεχθεῖσαν, τὴν ἀνάλωτον. Τοῦτο εἰς ἀνάμνησιν γίνεται τοῦ τότε γενομένου: Τοῦτο γὰρ ποιεῖτε, φησὶν, εἰς τὴν ἐμὴν ἀνάμνησιν. Οὐκ ἄλλην θυσίαν, καθάπερ ὁ ἀρχιερεὺς τότε, ἀλλὰ τὴν αὐτὴν ἀεὶ ποιοῦμεν: μᾶλλον δὲ ἀνάμνησιν ἐργαζόμεθα θυσίας.
context:
St. John Chrysostom is preaching on the Epistle to the Hebrews, which contrasts the single, perfect, and eternal sacrifice of Christ with the multiple, imperfect, and repeated sacrifices of the Old Testament priests.

    The Central Problem: He anticipates a question from his listeners: "If the sacrifice of Jesus on the Cross was 'once for all' (Heb. 9:28), why do we in the Church offer a sacrifice every single day in the Divine Liturgy?" This seems like a contradiction.

    The Solution: Remembrance (Anamnesis): Chrysostom's brilliant answer is that the daily Eucharistic offering is not a new or different sacrifice. It is a remembrance (ἀνάμνησις/anamnesis) of the one, eternal sacrifice on Calvary. When the Church celebrates the Eucharist, she is making that one sacrifice present again in an unbloody manner.

    The Core Logic: His argument rests on two points:

        The Victim is the Same: We don't offer a new lamb each day. We always offer the same Christ. Because the victim is one, the sacrifice is one.

        The "Many Christs?" Analogy: He uses a powerful analogy. Just as Christ is fully present on thousands of altars around the world yet remains one Christ and one Body, so the one sacrifice of Christ is made present on those thousands of altars without being multiplied into thousands of different sacrifices.

This passage is a cornerstone of Catholic and Orthodox theology of the Eucharist, explaining how the Mass/Divine Liturgy is a true sacrifice that does not add to or repeat the one perfect sacrifice of Christ on the Cross, but rather makes it present in time for the faithful of every generation.

fr: Quant à leurs doctrines sur l'âme, ils ont atteint le comble de l'ignominie, prétendant que les âmes humaines deviennent des mouches, des moustiques et des buissons, affirmant que Dieu lui-même est une âme, et débitant d'autres infamies de ce genre... Tantôt, en effet, il dit qu'elle est de la substance de Dieu ; tantôt, après l'avoir élevée de façon si démesurée et impie, il la dégrade à nouveau par l'excès contraire, en la faisant entrer dans des porcs, des ânes, et dans des bêtes plus viles encore.
en: ST. JOHN CHRYSOSTOM As for doctrines on the soul, there is nothing very shameful that the disciples of Plato and Pythagoras] have left unsaid, asserting that the souls of men become flies and gnats and bushes and that God himself is a [similar] soul, with similar indecencies. . . . At one time he says that the soul is of the substance of God; at another, after having exalted it thus, immoderately and impiously, he exceeds again in different way, and treats it with insult, making it pass into swine and asses and other animals of less esteem than these [Homilies on John 2:3, 6 (c. A.D. 391)].
latin: De anima vero doctrinam omnium turpissimam statuerunt, dum animas hominum, muscas, culices, frutices fieri, Deumque ipsum animam esse dicerent; et alia quædam turpissima assererent. . .     Nunc enim illam ex Dei substantia esse dicit; nunc illam præter modum et impie elatam, per alteram hyperbolen deturpat, dum illam in porcos, asinos, inque viliora animantia inducit.
greek: Δογμάτων δὲ ἕνεκεν τῶν περὶ ψυχῆς, οὐδὲ ὑπερβολήν τινα κατέλιπον αἰσχύνης λοιπὸν, μυίας, καὶ κώνωπας, καὶ θάμνους τὰς τῶν ἀνθρώπων λέγοντες γίνεσθαι ψυχὰς, καὶ τὸν Θεὸν αὐτὸν ψυχὴν εἶναι φάσκοντες, καὶ ἕτερα ἄττα τινὰ τοιαῦta ἀσχημονοῦντες. . . Νῦν μὲν γὰρ αὐτὴν τῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ φησιν οὐσίας εἶναι: νῦν δὲ αὐτὴν οὕτως ἀμέτρως καὶ ἀσεβῶς ἐπάρας, μεθ' ἑτέρας καθυβρίζει πάλιν ὑπερβολῆς, εἰς χοίρους καὶ ὄνους εἰσάγων, καὶ τὰ ἔτι τούτων ἀτιμότερα ζῶα.
context:
This passage comes from Homily 2 on John's Gospel. St. John Chrysostom's goal here is to establish the absolute superiority and divine authority of the Evangelist's teaching.

His method is one of stark contrast:

    On one side: He presents the most celebrated Greek philosophers, Plato and Pythagoras. He describes them as confused, contradictory, and ultimately ridiculous. He uses their own teachings—specifically the doctrine of metempsychosis (the transmigration of souls)—to show how their "wisdom" leads to absurdities like human souls becoming insects or pigs. He points out that they are constantly changing their minds ("like a Euripus," a notoriously shifting channel of water).

    On the other side: He presents St. John the Evangelist, whom he calls the "unlearned fisherman from Bethsaida." Despite this humble origin, John's teaching is clear, consistent, firm as a rock, and divinely inspired.

The purpose of this attack on pagan philosophy is rhetorical. By showing the "best" of human wisdom to be foolish and shameful, Chrysostom elevates the "foolishness" of the Gospel as the true, unshakable wisdom of God. He is preparing his audience to listen to the sublime theology of John's prologue with the reverence it deserves, having dismissed all worldly alternatives as nonsense.

fr:
En effet, à notre propre époque, sous le règne de Julien qui surpassa tous les hommes en impiété, de nombreux prodiges se sont produits. Ainsi, alors que les Juifs tentaient de relever le temple de Jérusalem, un feu jaillit des fondations et les en empêcha tous. De même, quand le trésorier de l’empereur, ainsi que son oncle et homonyme, manifestèrent la fureur sacrilège de celui-ci contre les vases sacrés, le premier, dévoré par les vers, rendit l’âme, tandis que le second éclata par le milieu.

De plus, le tarissement des sources après qu’on y eut offert des sacrifices, et la famine qui s’abattit sur les cités sous son règne, furent un signe éclatant.

Car c’est la coutume de Dieu d’agir ainsi : lorsque les maux s’aggravent, qu’il voit les siens maltraités et leurs adversaires complètement ivres de la tyrannie qu’ils exercent contre eux, c’est alors qu’il manifeste sa propre puissance.
en: ST. JOHN CHRYSOSTOM For even in our generation, in the instance of Julian, who surpassed all in ungodliness, many strange things happened. When the Jews were attempting to raise up the temple at Jerusalem, fire burst out from the foundations and utterly hindered them; and when both his treasurer, and his uncle and namesake, made the sacred vessels the subject of insolence, the one was "eaten with worms, and gave up the ghost," the other "burst asunder." Moreover, the fountains failed when sacrifices were made there, and the entrance of famine in the cities where the emperor went was a very great sign. For it is usual with God to do such things when evils are multiplied [ Homilies on Matthew 4:2 (c. A.D. 370)].
latin: Signa quoque apud nos facta videre licuit : nam ætate nostra sub Juliano, qui omnes impletate superavit, multa mirabiliaque facta sunt. Cum enin Judæi templum Jerosolymitanum reædificare tentarent, ignis e fundamentis erumpens omnes deterruit; et cum Julianus furorem suum in vasa sacra exerceret, quæstor et Juliani avunculus ipsi cognominis plexi sunt : prior enim a vermibus corrosus interiit, alter vero medius diruptus est; peractisque ibidem sacrificiis fontes defecerunt, et fames quæ eodem imperante civitates invasit, maximum erat miraculum.
greek:
Καὶ γὰρ καὶ ἐν τῇ γενεᾷ τῇ ἡμετέρᾳ, ἐπὶ τοῦ πάντας ἀσεβείᾳ νικήσαντος Ἰουλιανοῦ, πολλὰ καὶ παράδοξα συνέβη. Καὶ γὰρ τῶν Ἰουδαίων τὸν ἐν Ἱεροσολύμοις ναὸν ἀναστῆσαι ἐπιχειρούντων, πῦρ τῶν θεμελίων ἐκπηδῆσαν ἅπαντας διεκώλυσε· καὶ ὅτε ἐπὶ τὰ σκεύη τὰ ἱερὰ τὴν αὑτοῦ παροινίαν ἐπεδείξατο ὅ τε ταμίας, ὅ τε θεῖος καὶ ὁμώνυμος ἐκείνου, ὁ μὲν σκοληκόβρωτος γενόμενος ἐξέψυξεν, ὁ δὲ ἐλάκισε μέσος.

    καὶ τὸ τὰς πηγὰς δὲ ἐπιλιπεῖν, θυσιῶν ἐκεῖ γενομένων, καὶ μετ' αὐτοῦ τοῦ βασιλέως τὸν λιμὸν εἰς τὰς πόλεις συνεμπεσεῖν, σημεῖον μέγιστον ἦν.

    Ἔθος γὰρ τοιαῦτα ποιεῖν τῷ Θεῷ· ὅταν αὐξηθῇ τὰ κακὰ, καὶ τοὺς μὲν αὐτοῦ κακουμένους ἴδῃ, τοὺς δὲ ἐναντίους σφόδρα τῇ κατ' αὐτῶν τυραννίδι μεθύοντας, τότε τὴν οἰκείαν ἐπιδείκνυσθαι δυναστείαν.
context:
The Occasion: Chrysostom is commenting on the genealogy of Christ in Matthew 1. He is explaining that God allows His people to endure periods of hardship (like the Babylonian Captivity) before intervening.

    The Contemporary Example: To prove this point is still relevant, he uses the recent and traumatic reign of the Emperor Julian the Apostate (reigned 361-363 AD) as a powerful example his audience would remember well. Julian had attempted to reverse the Christianization of the Roman Empire and restore paganism.

    Historical Events Mentioned:

        Rebuilding the Temple: Julian famously gave the Jews permission to rebuild their Temple in Jerusalem, partly to undermine Christian prophecies. Chrysostom, along with other contemporary Christian historians (like Ammianus Marcellinus, a pagan historian who also reports the event), records that the project was halted by "terrible balls of fire" that burst from the foundations.

        Desecration of Vessels: He refers to Julian's uncle (also named Julian) and a treasurer (likely named Felix) who profaned sacred church vessels. Christian historians record their gruesome deaths as divine punishment, explicitly comparing them to the biblical accounts of Herod Agrippa (Acts 12:23 - "eaten by worms") and Judas Iscariot ("burst asunder").

    Theological Point: Chrysostom's main goal is pastoral. He is reminding his congregation that even when a powerful, anti-Christian ruler like Julian is in power and evil seems to be winning, God will eventually intervene to demonstrate His power and protect His people. The memory of Julian's ultimate failure was a source of great encouragement for the Church.

fr: En effet, chacun sait bien que ceux qui sont possédés par ce mal trouvent pesante la vieillesse de leur père et considèrent comme une charge lourde et pénible ce qui est doux et désirable pour tous : avoir des enfants. C’est ainsi que beaucoup, pour cette raison, ont préféré la stérilité et ont mutilé la nature ; non pas en faisant périr leurs enfants une fois nés, mais en ne leur permettant même pas de voir le jour.
en: ST. JOHN CHRYSOSTOM [Un truth all men know that they who are under the power of this disease are wearied even of their father's old age; and what is sweet, and universally desirable, the having children, they esteem grievous and unwelcome. Many with this view have even paid money to be childless, and have maimed their nature, not only by slaying their children after birth, but by not suffering them to be born at all [Homilies on Matthew 28:5 (c. A.D. 370)]
latin: Imo vero nulla interrogandi necessitas, cum nemo nesciat eos, qui hoc tenentur morbo, senectutem patris sui ægre ferre, et quod aliis dulce optabileque est, nempe filios habere, onerosum existimare. Multi enim hac de causa orbitatem sunt adepti, naturamque sterilem reddiderunt, non modo natos occidentes, sed etiam ne nascerentur efficientes.
greek: Καὶ γὰρ πάντες ἴσασιν ὡς οἱ τούτῳ κατεχόμενοι τῷ νοσήματι, καὶ γῆρας βαρύνονται πατρὸς, τό τε γλυκὺ καὶ πᾶσιν ἐπέραστον, τὸ παῖδας ἔχειν, βαρὺ καὶ ἐπαχθὲς εἶναι νομίζουσι. Πολλοὶ γοῦν καὶ ἀτοκίαν διὰ τοῦτο ὠνήσαντο, καὶ τὴν φύσιν ἐπήρωσαν, οὐκ ἀνελόντες τεχθέντας τοὺς παῖδας, ἀλλὰ μηδὲ φῦναι τὴν ἀρχὴν συγχωρήσαντες.
context:
Overall Theme: This entire section of the homily is a fiery condemnation of the sin of avarice (greed). St. John Chrysostom personifies greed as a demonic force that is even worse and more destructive than actual demonic possession.

    The Preceding Argument: Before your specific quote, Chrysostom paints a horrifying, monstrous picture of the greedy man. He compares him to a wild beast with swords for teeth and poison for a tongue, a creature who would kill everyone—friend, brother, even his own father—if the law did not restrain him.

    The Role of Your Quote: Your quote serves as the climax and the most shocking proof of his argument. Chrysostom's point is that greed is so profoundly dehumanizing that it inverts the most fundamental and sacred laws of nature. He provides two ultimate examples:

        A son who is so greedy for his inheritance that he finds his own father's old age to be a burden (γῆρας βαρύνονται πατρὸς | aetate patris gravari).

        People who find the universal joy of having children to be "grievous and unwelcome" (βαρὺ καὶ ἐπαχθὲς).

    Historical Condemnation: The final sentence is a direct condemnation of contraceptive and abortifacient practices. When he says they "paid money to be childless" (ἀτοκίαν ὠνήσαντο | sterilitatem emerunt) and "maimed their nature... not suffering them to be born at all," he is referring to the use of potions and other methods prevalent in the Greco-Roman world to prevent or terminate pregnancy, all driven, in his view, by the monstrous vice of greed.

fr:
Quand il dit : « Ils se sont faits eunuques », il ne parle pas de la mutilation des membres — loin de là ! — mais de la destruction des pensées mauvaises. Celui qui se mutile un membre tombe en effet sous le coup d'une malédiction, comme le dit Paul : « Puissent-ils aller jusqu'à se mutiler, ceux qui sèment le trouble parmi vous ! » Et à juste titre. En effet, un tel homme commet un acte digne d'un meurtrier, il fournit un prétexte à ceux qui calomnient la création de Dieu, il ouvre la bouche aux manichéens et viole la loi tout comme ceux qui, chez les Grecs, se mutilent.

Car se couper les membres est depuis l'origine une œuvre de l'activité démoniaque et de la ruse satanique. Le but est de calomnier l'œuvre de Dieu, de défigurer cet être vivant, et de faire en sorte que la plupart des hommes pèchent sans crainte en attribuant toute la question non pas au libre arbitre mais à la nature de leurs membres, se croyant alors irresponsables. Ils causent ainsi un double tort à cet être vivant, à la fois en estropiant ses membres et en paralysant l'élan de son libre arbitre vers le bien.
en: Since the man who has mutilated himself, in fact, IS subject to a curse. as Paul says, would they were even cut off which trouble you." And very reasonably. For such a one is venturing on the deeds of murderers, and giving occasion to those who slander God's creation, and opens the mouths of the Manicheans, and is guilty of the same unlawful acts as those Greeks who mutilate themselves. For to cut off our members is a work of demoniacal agency, and satanic device, that they may bring up a bad report on the work of God, that they may mar this living creature, that imputing all not to the choice but to the nature of our members, the more part of them may sin in security, as being irresponsible; and doubly harm this living creature, both by mutilating the members, and by impeding the free choice on behalf of good deeds [ibid., 62:3].
greek: Ὅταν δὲ λέγῃ, ὅτι Εὐνούχισαν ἑαυτοὺς, οὐ τῶν μελῶν λέγει τὴν ἐκτομήν: ἄπαγε: ἀλλὰ τῶν πονηρῶν λογισμῶν τὴν ἀναίρεσιν. Ὡς ὅ γε τὸ μέλος ἐκτεμὼν, καὶ ἀρᾷ ἐστιν ὑπεύθυνος, καθὼς ὁ Παῦλός φησιν: Ὄφελον καὶ ἀποκόψονται οἱ ἀναστατοῦντες ὑμᾶς. Καὶ μάλα εἰκότως. Καὶ γὰρ τὰ τῶν ἀνδροφόνων ὁ τοιοῦτος τολμᾷ, καὶ τοῖς τοῦ Θεοῦ διαβάλλουσι τὴν δημιουργίαν δίδωσιν ἀφορμὴν, καὶ τῶν Μανιχαίων ἀνοίγει τὰ στόματα, καὶ τοῖς παρ' Ἕλλησιν ἀκρωτηριαζομένοις τὰ αὐτὰ παρανομεῖ. Τὸ γὰρ ἀποκόπτειν τὰ μέλη, δαιμονικῆς ἐνεργείας καὶ σατανικῆς ἐπιβουλῆς ἐξ ἀρχῆς γέγονεν ἔργον: ἵνα τοῦ Θεοῦ τὸ ἔργον διαβάλλωσιν: ἵνα τὸ ζῶον τοῦτο λυμήνωνται: ἵνα μὴ τῇ προαιρέσει, ἀλλὰ τῇ τῶν μελῶν φύσει τὸ πᾶν λογισάμενοι, οὕτως ἀδεῶς ἁμαρτάνωσιν αὐτῶν οἱ πολλοὶ, ἅτε ἀνεύθυνοι ὄντες: καὶ διπλῇ παραβλάψωσι τὸ ζῶον τοῦτο, καὶ τῷ τὰ μέλη πηροῦν, καὶ τῷ τῆς προαιρέσεως τὴν ὑπὲρ τῶν ἀγαθῶν προθυμίαν κωλύειν.
context:
Context and Analysis

    Biblical Context: St. John is preaching on Matthew 19, specifically Jesus's statement about those who have "made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven" (Matt. 19:12). This was a controversial passage, and some, most famously the theologian Origen, had taken it literally and castrated themselves. Chrysostom is forcefully refuting this literal interpretation.

    Chrysostom's Argument:

        Spiritual, Not Physical: He begins by stating unequivocally that Jesus is referring to the "destruction of wicked thoughts," not the cutting off of body parts.

        A Cursed Act: He quotes St. Paul's angry curse against the Judaizers in Galatians 5:12 ("I wish they would go the whole way and emasculate themselves!"). He uses this to show that the apostolic tradition sees such physical mutilation as a cursed act.

        Theological Horrors: He then lists the grave sins and errors that this act entails:

            It is an act of murder (self-murder).

            It slanders God's creation, implying that God made the body evil.

            It gives ammunition to heretics like the Manicheans, who taught that the material world was evil.

            It is a pagan practice, not a Christian one.

        Demonic Origin: Chrysostom attributes the entire impulse to demonic and satanic influence. The devil's goal, he argues, is to defame God's creation and to promote a fatalistic worldview where sin is blamed on the body's nature rather than on personal free choice (προαίρεσις). This, he says, is a twofold harm: it mutilates the body and cripples the will to do good.

In summary, you have located Chrysostom's classic and definitive rejection of a literalist interpretation of Matt. 19:12, arguing instead for a spiritual understanding centered on the inner battle against sinful thoughts.

fr: Quelle est donc cette fumée infecte ? Beaucoup entrent ici en promenant leurs regards sur la beauté des femmes ; d’autres, en convoitant la fraîcheur des jeunes gens. Et après cela, ne t’étonnes-tu pas que la foudre ne tombe pas et que tout ne soit pas arraché jusqu’aux fondations ? En effet, de tels agissements sont dignes de la foudre et de la géhenne. Mais Dieu, patient et plein de miséricorde, retient pour l’instant sa colère, pour t’appeler au repentir et à la conversion.
en: ST. JOHN CHRYSOSTOM [Certain men in church] come in gazing about at the beauty of women; others curious about the blooming youth of boys. After this. do you not marvel that [lightning] bolts are not launched from heaven], and all these things are not plucked up from their foundations? For the things that are done are worthy of thunderbolts and hell; but God, who is long suffering, and of great mercy, forbears his wrath, calling you to repentance and amendment [Homilies on Matthew 73:3 (c. A.D. 370)].
greek: Τίς οὖν ὁ καπνὸς ὁ δυσώδης; Πολλοὶ εἰσίασι κάλλη γυναικῶν περιβλέποντες· ἄλλοι παίδων ὥρας περιεργαζόμενοι. Εἶτα οὐ θαυμάζεις, πῶς οὐ σκηπτοὶ φέρονται, καὶ πάντα ἐκ βάθρων ἀνασπᾶται; Καὶ γὰρ ἄξια μὲν σκηπτῶν καὶ γεέννης τὰ γινόμενα· ἀλλ' ὁ Θεὸς, μακρόθυμος ὢν καὶ πολυέλεος, ἀνέχει τέως τὴν ὀργὴν, εἰς μετάνοιάν σε καλῶν καὶ διόρθωσιν.
context:
Part 2: The Powerful Broader Context

The full text you provided is even more valuable because it shows the incredible rhetorical buildup to this fiery denunciation. Here is the context of St. John's argument:

    The Whited Sepulchre Metaphor: He begins by comparing people in the congregation to "whited sepulchres"—beautiful on the outside, but full of worms, pus, and an unspeakable stench on the inside (πολλοὺς τοὺς σκώληκας καὶ τὸν ἰχῶρα εὑρήσει, καὶ δυσωδίαν ἄφατον). He says these are their "improper desires and wickednesses" (ἐπιθυμίας ἀτόπους λέγω καὶ πονηρίας).

    Desecrating the Temple of God: He expresses his horror that the members of Christ, the temples of the Holy Spirit, have become stinking tombs. He asks, "How do you dare to enter the churches of God... reeking of such abomination within?" (Πῶς δὲ καὶ τολμᾷς ἐκκλησίαις ἐπιβαίνειν Θεοῦ... ἔνδον τοσαύτης βδελυγμίας ὄζων;)

    From Foul Smell to Foul Smoke: He then transitions metaphors. The prayer of the faithful should rise like sweet-smelling incense (θυμίαμα). But from these people, a foul-smelling smoke (καπνὸς δυσώδης) rises up. He asks, "What then is this foul-smelling smoke?"

    The Climax (Your Quote): This leads directly into your quote. The "foul smoke" is the lustful gazing at women and boys inside the church itself. This is the ultimate desecration that he believes is worthy of immediate, fiery destruction from heaven.

    The Aftermath: Following the quote, Chrysostom blames the moral corruption of the theaters (θέατρα) for teaching this licentiousness. He laments that the church fathers had to install physical barriers between men and women, something that wasn't needed in the holier, more self-controlled age of the Apostles.

You have found a classic example of Chrysostom's "golden-mouthed" oratory: a masterful build-up of vivid imagery leading to a powerful, thundering denunciation of sin, followed by a call to repentance. Excellent find

fr:
Comment cela ? Y avait-il plusieurs évêques dans une seule ville ? Nullement ; mais c’est ainsi qu’il appelait les presbytres. En effet, à cette époque, les termes étaient encore interchangeables, et l’évêque lui-même était appelé diacre.

C’est pourquoi, en écrivant à Timothée, il lui disait : « Accomplis pleinement ton ministère », alors que celui-ci était évêque. Car la preuve qu’il était évêque, c’est que Paul lui dit : « N’impose les mains à personne avec précipitation ». Et encore : « le don qui t’a été accordé par l’imposition des mains du collège des presbytres ». Or, des presbytres n’auraient pas ordonné un évêque.
en: ST. JOHN CHRYSOSTOM [in Philippians 1:1 Paul says] "Paul and Timothy, servants of Christ Jesus, to all the saints in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi, fellow bishops and deacons: Grace to you, and peace, from God our Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ." Here, as writing to those of equal honor, he does not set down his rank of teacher, but another, and that great one. And what is that? He calls himself a "servant,' and not an apostle. For great truly is this rank too, and the sum of all good things. to be a servant of Christ, and not merely to be called so. 'The servant of Christ" is truly a free man in respect to sin, and being a genuine servant, he IS not a servant to any other, since then he would not be Christ's servant, but by halves. And in again writing to the Romans also, he says, "Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ" [Rom 1:1]. But writing to the Corinthians and to Timothy ne calls himself an "apostle.' Why is this? Not because they were superior to Timothy. Far from it. But rather he honors them, and shows them attention, beyond all others to whom he wrote. For he also bears witness to great virtue in them. For besides, there indeed he was about to order many things, and therefore assumed his rank as an apostle. But here he gives them no injunctions but such as they could perceive of themselves. "To the saints in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi." Since it was likely that the Jews too would call themselves "saints* from the first oracle, when they were called a "holy people, a people for God's own possession" [Ex 19:6; Dt 7:6, etc.]; for this reason he added, "to the saints in Christ Jesus." For these alone are holy, and those henceforward profane. "To the fellow bishops and deacons." What is this? Were there several bishops of one city? Certainly not; but he called the presbyters so. For then they still interchanged the titles, and the bishop was called a deacon. For this reason in writing to Timothy, he said, "Fulfill your ministry," when he was a bishop. For that he was a bishop appears by his saying to him, "Lay hands hastily on no man" [1 Im 5:22]. And again, "Which was given you with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery" [1 Im 4:14]. Yet presbyters would not have laid hands on bishop [Homilies on Philippians (c. A.D. 402)].
greek:
Τί τοῦτο; μιᾶς πόλεως πολλοὶ ἐπίσκοποι ἦσαν; Οὐδαμῶς· ἀλλὰ τοὺς πρεσβυτέρους οὕτως ἐκάλεσε. Τότε γὰρ τέως ἐκοινώνουν τοῖς ὀνόμασι, καὶ διάκονος ὁ ἐπίσκοπος ἐλέγετο.

    ∆ιὰ τοῦτο γράφων καὶ Τιμοθέῳ ἔλεγε· Τὴν διακονίαν σου πληροφόρησον· ἐπισκόπῳ ὄντι. Ὅτι γὰρ ἐπίσκοπος ἦν, φησὶ πρὸς αὐτὸν, Χεῖρας ταχέως μηδενὶ ἐπιτίθει· καὶ πάλιν· Ὃ ἐδόθη σοι μετὰ ἐπιθέσεως τῶν χειρῶν τοῦ πρεσβυτερίου· οὐκ ἂν δὲ πρεσβύτεροι ἐπίσκοπον ἐχειροτόνησαν.
context:
This passage is one of the most frequently cited patristic texts in discussions about the development of the threefold ministry (bishop, presbyter/priest, deacon) in the early Church. Here is why it is so significant:

    Acknowledgment of Interchangeable Titles: Chrysostom, writing around A.D. 400 when the threefold hierarchy was universally established, explicitly acknowledges that in the Apostolic era (when Philippians was written), the titles ἐπίσκοπος (episkopos - overseer/bishop) and πρεσβύτερος (presbyteros - elder/priest) were used interchangeably. He correctly recognizes that a single city like Philippi would not have had a college of bishops in the later sense of the term.

    Harmonizing Scripture with Church Practice: The core of Chrysostom's argument is an attempt to harmonize the biblical text with the established Church structure of his own day. He sees an apparent contradiction: Philippi has multiple "bishops," but his own Church experience tells him a city has only one. His solution is to say that in this case, "bishops" really means "presbyters."

    The Exegesis of 1 Timothy: His "proof" is fascinating. To show Timothy was a bishop, he quotes 1 Timothy 5:22 ("Lay hands hastily on no man"), correctly identifying the power to ordain as a key episcopal function. However, he then has to deal with 1 Timothy 4:14, which says Timothy received his gift through the "laying on of the hands of the presbytery." This seems to suggest presbyters could ordain.

    Chrysostom's Hierarchical Interpretation: Chrysostom resolves this by making a definitive statement based on the practice of his own time: "Yet presbyters would not have laid hands on a bishop" (οὐκ ἂν δὲ πρεσβύτεροι ἐπίσκοπον ἐχειροτόνησαν). By this, he implies that the "presbytery" mentioned in 1 Timothy must have included apostles or bishops (like Paul himself) who were leading the ordination, and that the presbyters present were merely concurring. He interprets the earlier, less defined text through the lens of the later, more structured hierarchy.

In summary, this passage is a historical treasure. It shows a brilliant 4th-century mind acknowledging the fluidity of titles in the 1st-century Church while simultaneously interpreting those early texts in a way that upholds the established hierarchical and sacramental order of his own time.

fr:
Pleurons ceux qui sont morts dans la richesse, sans avoir conçu de leur fortune la moindre consolation pour leur âme ; eux qui avaient reçu le pouvoir de laver leurs péchés, mais ne l’ont pas voulu.

Pleurons-les, tous, en privé comme en public, mais avec retenue, avec dignité, et sans nous donner en spectacle. Pleurons-les, non pas un jour ou deux, mais toute notre vie. Ces pleurs ne sont pas le fruit d’une passion désordonnée, mais d’une tendre affection ; les autres, au contraire, naissent de la passion, et voilà pourquoi ils s’éteignent si vite. Car lorsque les pleurs naissent de la crainte de Dieu, ils demeurent éternellement.

Pleurons donc pour eux, aidons-les selon nos moyens, imaginons pour eux une aide, si modeste soit-elle, mais qui puisse néanmoins les secourir. Comment et de quelle manière ? En priant nous-mêmes, en invitant les autres à faire des prières pour eux, et en faisant continuellement l’aumône en leur faveur.
en: Mourn for those who have died in wealth, and did not from their wealth think of any solace for their soul, those who had power to wash away their sins and would not. Let us all weep for these in private and in public, but with propriety, with gravity, not so as to make exhibitions of ourselves; let us weep for these, not one day, or two. but all our life. Such tears spring not from senseless passion, but from true affection. The other sort are of senseless passion. For this reason they are quickly quenched, but if they spring from the fear of God, they always abide with us. Let us weep for these; let us assist them according to our power; let us think of some assistance for them, small though it be, yet still let us assist them. In what way? By praying and entreating others to make prayers for them, by continually giving to the poor on their behalf [Homilies on Philippians (c. A.D. 402)].
greek:
Κλαῦσον τοὺς ἐν πλούτῳ τετελευτηκότας, καὶ μηδεμίαν ἀπὸ τοῦ πλούτου παραμυθίαν ταῖς ἑαυτῶν ψυχαῖς ἐπινοήσαντας, τοὺς λαβόντας ἐξουσίαν ἀπολούσασθαι αὑτῶν τὰ ἁμαρτήματα, καὶ μὴ βουληθέντας.

    Τούτους κλαίωμεν καὶ ἰδίᾳ καὶ κοινῇ πάντες, ἀλλὰ μετὰ κοσμιότητος, ἀλλὰ μετὰ σεμνότητος, ἀλλὰ μὴ ὥστε παραδειγματίζειν ἑαυτούς. Τούτους κλαίωμεν μὴ μίαν ἡμέραν, μηδὲ δευτέραν, ἀλλὰ τὸν πάντα βίον ἡμῶν. Τοῦτο οὐκ ἔστι πάθους ἀλόγου τὸ δάκρυον, ἀλλὰ φιλοστοργίας· ἐκεῖνο δὲ πάθους ἀλόγου· διὰ τοῦτο καὶ ταχέως σβέννυται. Ὅταν γὰρ διὰ τὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ φόβον γίνηται, ἀεὶ παραμένει.

    Κλαίωμεν οὖν τούτους, βοηθῶμεν αὐτοῖς κατὰ δύναμιν, ἐπινοήσωμεν αὐτοῖς τινα βοήθειαν, μικρὰν μὲν, βοηθεῖν δὲ ὅμως δυναμένην. Πῶς καὶ τίνι τρόπῳ; Αὐτοί τε εὐχόμενοι, καὶ ἑτέρους παρακαλοῦντες εὐχὰs ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν ποιεῖσθαι, πένησιν ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν διδόντες συνεχῶς.
context:
Additional Relevant Context

You have provided the full text of the homily, which gives us a rich context for this passage. St. Chrysostom, a master preacher, builds his sermon in a clear, logical flow:

1. Exegesis of Philippians 1:18-21: The homily begins with a direct commentary on St. Paul's words: "I know that this will turn out for my salvation... for to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain." Chrysostom explores Paul's incredible spiritual state, where he has no fear of death and sees both life and death as ways to glorify Christ.

2. Transition to a General Moral Teaching: Using Paul's attitude toward death as a starting point, Chrysostom pivots to a broader pastoral lesson for his congregation. He asks: If this is how a great saint views death, how should we, as ordinary Christians, approach the death of our loved ones?

3. Correcting Improper Mourning: This is where your quote is situated. Chrysostom instructs his flock to redirect their grief.

    Don't mourn the righteous dead: He argues that we should rejoice for those who die in faith, because they have gone to be "with Christ, which is far better."

    Mourn for the unrepentant dead: The true tragedy, he preaches, is dying in sin. He specifically singles out the wealthy who used their resources for themselves instead of for their salvation through charity. These are the ones who are truly worthy of our tears.

4. The Practical "How-To" of Christian Mourning: Chrysostom then gives concrete, practical actions. Grief should not be a theatrical, public display of despair (pulling hair, wailing loudly). Instead, it should be channeled into spiritually productive acts for the soul of the deceased. This is the heart of your quote:

    Pray for them.

    Ask others to pray for them.

    Give alms to the poor in their name.

5. The Apostolic Foundation for the Practice: Immediately after your quote, Chrysostom provides the theological basis for this practice, stating that it is not his own invention:

    "These things were not instituted by the Apostles in vain: that a memorial of the departed should be made at the awesome mysteries. They knew that great gain and much benefit would accrue to them."
    (Οὐκ εἰκῆ ταῦτα ἐνομοθετήθη ὑπὸ τῶν ἀποστόλων, τὸ ἐπὶ τῶν φρικτῶν μυστηρίων μνήμην γίνεσθαι τῶν ἀπελθόντων.)

This shows that the practice of praying for the dead during the Divine Liturgy (the "awesome mysteries" of the Eucharist) was considered an ancient, apostolic tradition.

You have found a classic and powerful passage where St. John Chrysostom outlines the Church's ancient practice of praying for the dead, grounding it in both pastoral compassion and apostolic tradition.

fr: Chez les Juifs, la circoncision était une chose vénérable, au point que la Loi elle-même s'effaçait devant elle, et que le sabbat lui était inférieur. En effet, pour qu'une circoncision ait lieu, le sabbat était transgressé ; mais pour que le sabbat soit observé, la circoncision ne l'était jamais. Et considérez l'économie de Dieu : cette pratique, plus vénérable que le sabbat, se trouve pourtant avoir été omise à certaines époques. Si donc elle-même est transgressée, à bien plus forte raison le sabbat.
en: The rite of circumcision was venerable in the Jews' account, because the Law itself gave way to it, and the Sabbath was less esteemed than circumcision. The Sabbath was broken so that circumcision might be performed; but so the Sabbath might be kept, circumcision was never broken; and mark, I pray, the dispensation of God. This is found to be even more solemn than the Sabbath, as not being omitted at certain times. When it iS done away, much more is the Sabbath [Homilies on Philippians 10 (c. A.D. 402)].
greek: Σεμνὸν ἦν παρὰ Ἰουδαίοις τὸ τῆς περιτομῆς, ὅπου γε καὶ ὁ νόμος αὐτῇ ὑπεξίστατο, καὶ τὸ σάββατον ἦν εὐτελέστερον αὐτῆς. Ἵνα μὲν γὰρ περιτομὴ γένηται, ἐλύετο σάββατον· ἵνα δὲ σάββατον φυλαχθῇ, οὐδέποτε ἐλύετο ἡ περιτομή. Καὶ θέα μοι τὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ οἰκονομίαν· αὕτη ἡ τοῦ σαββάτου αἰδεσιμωτέρα, εὑρίσκεται ἔν τισι χρόνοις [μὴ] παραλειφθεῖσα. Ὅταν οὖν αὐτὴ λύηται, πολλῷ μᾶλλον τὸ σάββατον.
context:
Additional Relevant Context

To understand why Chrysostom makes this point, we need to look at the flow of his sermon.

    The Problem: St. Paul warns the Philippians to "beware of the dogs, beware of the evil workers, beware of the mutilation (κατατομή)." Chrysostom identifies these people as Judaizers—insincere teachers who were trying to force Gentile Christians to be circumcised and follow Jewish law, thereby corrupting the Gospel.

    The Insult: St. Paul deliberately uses the insulting word "mutilation" (κατατομή) instead of the honored word "circumcision" (περιτομή). This is a powerful rhetorical move.

    Building Up the Argument (This is where your quote fits): To show his congregation just how radical Paul's insult is, Chrysostom first explains the immense honor and importance that circumcision held under the Old Law. He does this by proving that circumcision was superior to the Sabbath.

        On the eighth day, a male child had to be circumcised, even if that day was the Sabbath. The work of circumcision "broke" the Sabbath rest.

        However, the reverse was never true. Circumcision was never postponed to keep the Sabbath.

        Therefore, in the hierarchy of the Old Law, Circumcision > Sabbath.

    The Knockout Punch: After establishing this hierarchy, Chrysostom delivers the main point: If this greater and more venerable rite of circumcision is now abolished in Christ—so much so that Paul calls it mere "mutilation"—then the lesser rite of the Sabbath is even more certainly and completely done away with for Christians.

The rest of the very long homily you posted then pivots, in Chrysostom's typical style, from this theological point to a broad moral exhortation against worldly attachments (like wealth, fine clothes, and luxury), urging his listeners to find their "profit" in Christ alone, just as Paul did.

fr: Toutes les passions sont donc infâmes, mais par-dessus tout la passion furieuse envers les hommes. En effet, l’âme, dans les péchés, souffre et se déshonore bien plus que le corps dans les maladies.
en: All of these affections [in Rom 1:26-27 . . . were vile, but chiefly the mad lust after males; for the soul is more the sufferer in sins, and more dishonored than the body in diseases [Homilies on Romans (C. A.D. 391)].
greek: Πάντα μὲν οὖν ἄτιμα τὰ πάθη, μάλιστα δὲ ἡ κατὰ τῶν ἀῤῥένων μανία· καὶ γὰρ πάσχει ἐν τοῖς ἁμαρτήμασιν ἡ ψυχὴ μᾶλλον καὶ καταισχύνεται, ἢ τὸ σῶμα ἐν τοῖς νοσήμασι.
context:
Additional Relevant Context (from the rest of your text)

The rest of the homily you provided is a powerful and detailed expansion on this opening statement. St. John Chrysostom builds a multi-layered argument to explain why he considers this behavior to be so grave. Here are the key points he makes in the text you posted:

    A Sin Without Excuse: Chrysostom's central argument is that these acts are inexcusable because they involve abandoning what is natural. He focuses on Paul’s phrases "exchanged the natural use" (μετήλλαξαν τὴν φυσικὴν χρῆσιν) and "left the natural use" (ἀφέντες τὴν φυσικὴν χρῆσιν). He argues that because a natural and lawful pleasure was available to them, choosing to abandon it for an "unnatural" one removes any possible defense or apology.

    A Corruption of Nature Itself: He argues that this sin is worse than fornication. While fornication is unlawful, he considers the act itself to be "according to nature" (κατὰ φύσιν). This, however, is both unlawful and "contrary to nature" (παρὰ φύσιν). He sees it as an insult to nature itself, turning God's created order "upside down" (ἄνω καὶ κάτω).

    The Punishment is Inherent in the Sin: Chrysostom interprets Paul's phrase "receiving in themselves the due penalty for their error" as meaning the punishment is not just a future event (hell), but is present in the act itself. The dishonor, the degradation of the soul, and the corruption of one's own being is the penalty. He compares those who enjoy it to madmen who laugh while harming themselves, stating their lack of awareness makes their condition even more pitiable.

    A Betrayal of One's Own Identity: He makes a powerful argument that in this act, a man has "destroyed his own manhood" (ἀπώλεσας καὶ τὸ εἶναι ἀνὴρ) without becoming a woman, thus becoming a "traitor to both natures" (κοινὸς ἑκατέρας ἐγένου προδότης), worthy of being driven out by both men and women.

    A Prefigurement of Hell: To those who might doubt the reality of hellfire, Chrysostom points to the destruction of Sodom as a real, historical "image of hell" (γεέννης εἰκόνα). He argues God showed this judgment on earth precisely to warn humanity about the reality of the punishment to come.

    The Root Cause: He identifies the root cause of this moral decay as luxury (τρυφή) and, most importantly, a turning away from the knowledge and fear of God (ἀπὸ τοῦ μὴ εἰδέναι Θεόν). When the fear of God is abandoned, he argues, all good things are lost.

In summary, the quote you identified is St. John Chrysostom's opening thesis statement for a long and powerful sermon where he argues that same-sex acts are a uniquely grave sin because they are an inexcusable corruption of nature, a punishment for idolatry, and a betrayal of one's own created identity.

fr: Révérez donc, révérez cette table à laquelle nous communions tous, le Christ immolé pour nous, la victime qui repose sur elle.
en: Reverence now, oh reverence, this table of which we all are partakers! [1 Cor 10:16-18.] Christ, who was slain for us, the victim who is placed thereon! [ Homilies on Romans 8 (c. A.D. 391)].
greek: Αἰδέσθητε τοίνυν, αἰδέσθητε τὴν τράπεζαν ταύτην, ἧς κοινωνοῦμεν ἅπαντες, τὸν δι' ἡμᾶς σφαγέντα Χριστὸnν, τὸ θῦμα τὸ ἐπ' αὐτῆς κείμενον.
context:
Additional Relevant Context (from the text you provided)

The passage is even more powerful when you understand what St. John is talking about immediately before and after. Your Greek text provides this perfectly.

1. The Problem: Internal Warfare in the Church

Before the quote, Chrysostom is weeping over the state of his community. He compares himself to the prophet Jeremiah, but says his situation is even worse. Jeremiah saw foreign enemies attacking, but Chrysostom sees Christians, who serve under one general (Christ), making war on each other.

    He laments seeing them "standing against one another, and biting and tearing one another's limbs apart" (κατ' ἀλλήλων ἱσταμένους καὶ δάκνοντας καὶ σπαράττοντας τὰ ἀλλήλων μέλη).

    He says the name "brother" has become an empty word (τὸ τῶν ἀδελφῶν ὄνομα ψιλὸν μόνον λοιπὸnν ὂν).

    The specific weapons in this war are not swords, but words: slander, gossip, and evil speech. He calls them "arrows from the tongue and mouth" (Τὰ ἀπὸ γλώττης καὶ στόματος).

2. The Eucharistic Rebuke (Your Quote)

It is in the middle of this passionate sermon against slander and disunity that he points to the Altar. The command to "reverence this table" is his ultimate argument. His point is:

How can you tear each other apart with your words and then dare to approach this Holy Table? This Table is the very symbol and source of your unity. On it lies the one Christ, slain for all of you, to make you one body. Your slanderous behavior is a sacrilegious contradiction to the Eucharist you are about to receive.

3. The Analogy of the Bandits (Immediately After Your Quote)

To shame his congregation, Chrysostom uses a brilliant analogy:

    "Bandits who share salt are no longer bandits to those with whom they have shared it... the table changes their character... But we, partaking of such a Table, partaking of such food, take up arms against one another!" (Λῃσταὶ κοινωνοῦντες ἁλῶν, οὐκέτι εἰσὶ λῃσταὶ... ἡμεῖς δὲ τοιαύτης τραπέζης μετέχοντες... ὁπλιζόμεθα κατ' ἀλλήλων).

His point is that even criminals have a code of honor established by sharing a meal, yet Christians, who share the very Body and Blood of Christ, continue to betray and attack one another with their words.

fr:
Que vous mangiez, dit l'Apôtre, que vous buviez, ou quoi que vous fassiez, faites tout pour la gloire de Dieu. Car c'est de ces festins que naissent en vous les désirs pervers ; de là vient la débauche ; de là vient que les épouses sont méprisées parmi vous, tandis que les prostituées sont honorées...

C'est pourquoi, je vous en supplie, fuyez la fornication et l'ivresse, qui en est la mère. Pourquoi sèmes-tu là où l'on ne peut moissonner ? Ou plutôt, même si tu moissonnes, le fruit ne t'apporte qu'une immense honte. En effet, même si un enfant naît, non seulement il te couvre de honte, mais lui-même subit une injustice par ta faute, en devenant un bâtard, un enfant illégitime.

...Pourquoi donc tout déshonorer ?

Pourquoi sèmes-tu là où la terre elle-même s'empresse de détruire le fruit, là où abondent les pratiques abortives, là où le meurtre précède la naissance ? Car tu ne te contentes pas de laisser la prostituée être une prostituée : tu en fais une meurtrière. Vois-tu la chaîne ? De l'ivresse vient la fornication, de la fornication l'adultère, de l'adultère le meurtre. Ou plutôt, quelque chose de pire encore que le meurtre – car je ne sais même pas comment nommer cela : ce n'est pas tuer un être déjà né, c'est l'empêcher de naître.

Eh quoi ? Tu outrages le don de Dieu, tu combats ses propres lois, tu recherches comme une bénédiction ce qui est une malédiction, tu fais du sanctuaire de la procréation un lieu de massacre, et tu pousses au meurtre la femme qui a été donnée pour enfanter ? Car pour rester toujours disponible et désirable pour ses amants, et pour attirer plus d'argent, elle ne recule pas devant cet acte, amassant par là sur ta propre tête un feu dévorant. Car si le crime vient d'elle, c'est sur toi qu'en retombe la responsabilité.
en: ST. JOHN CHRYSOSTOM I beseech you, flee fornication. . . Why sow where the ground makes it its job to destroy the fruit? Where there are many efforts at abortion? Where there is murder before the birth? For even the harlot you do not let continue a mere harlot, but make her a murderess also. You see how drunkenness leads to whoredom, whoredom to adultery, adultery to murder, or rather to something even worse than murder. For I have no name to give it, since it does not take away the thing born, but prevents its being born. Why then do you abuse the gift o1 God, and fight with his laws, and follow after what is a curse as if it were a blessing, and make the chamber of procreation a chamber for murder, and arm the woman that was given for childbearing into slaughter? For with a view to drawing more money by being agreeable and an object of longing to her lovers, even this she will do, heaping upon your head a great pile of fire. For even if the daring deed be hers, yet the cause of it is yours [ Homilies on Romans 24 (C. A.D. 391)].
greek:
Εἴτε γὰρ ἐσθίετε, φησὶν, εἴτε πίνετε, εἴτε τι ποιεῖτε, πάντα εἰς δόξαν Θεοῦ ποιεῖτε. Καὶ γὰρ ἀπὸ τῶν τοιούτων τραπεζῶν ὑμῖν αἱ πονηραὶ ἐπιθυμίαι, ἐντεῦθεν αἱ ἀσέλγειαι, ἐντεῦθεν αἱ γυναῖκες μὲν ἐν καταφρονήσει, αἱ δὲ πόρναι ἐν τιμῇ παρ' ὑμῖν...

    Διὸ, παρακαλῶ, φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν καὶ τὴν ταύτης μητέρα τὴν μέθην: Τί σπείρεις ὅπου θερίσαι οὐκ ἔνι, μᾶλλον δὲ, κἂν θερίσῃς, πολλήν σοι φέρει τὴν αἰσχύνην ὁ καρπός; Κἂν γὰρ τεχθῇ παιδίον, καὶ σὲ ᾔσχυνε, καὶ αὐτὸ ἠδίκηται διὰ σὲ νόθον καὶ δυσγενὲς γενόμενον.

    ...Τί τοίνυν ἅπαντα καταισχύνεις;

    Τί σπείρεις ἔνθα ἡ ἄρουρα σπουδάζει διαφθεῖραι τὸν καρπόν; ἔνθα πολλὰ τὰ ἀτόκια; ἔνθα πρὸ τῆς γενέσεως φόνος; καὶ γὰρ καὶ τὴν πόρνην οὐκ ἀφίης μεῖναι πόρνην μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀνδροφόνον ποιεῖς. Εἶδες ἀπὸ μέθης πορνείαν, ἀπὸ πορνείας μοιχείαν, ἀπὸ μοιχείας φόνον; μᾶλλον δὲ καὶ φόνου τι χεῖρον: οὐδὲ γὰρ ἔχω πῶς αὐτὸ καλέσω: οὐ γὰρ τεχθέντα ἀναιρεῖ, ἀλλὰ καὶ τεχθῆναι κωλύει.

    Τί τοίνυν; Καὶ τοῦ Θεοῦ τὴν δωρεὰν ὑβρίζεις, καὶ τοῖς αὐτοῦ μάχῃ νόμοις, καὶ ὅπερ ἐστὶ κατάρα, τοῦτο ὡς εὐλογίαν μεταδιώκεις, καὶ τὸ ταμιεῖον τῆς γενέσεως ταμιεῖον ποιεῖς σφαγῆς, καὶ τὴν πρὸς παιδοποιίαν δοθεῖσαν γυναῖκα πρὸς φόνον παρασκευάζεις; Ἵνα γὰρ ἀεὶ τοῖς ἐρασταῖς εὔχρηστος ᾖ καὶ ποθεινὴ καὶ πλέον ἀργύριον ἕλκῃ, οὐδὲ τοῦτο παραιτεῖται ποιῆσαι, μέγα ἐπὶ τὴν σὴν κεφαλὴν τὸ πῦρ ἐντεῦθεν σωρεύουσα: εἰ γὰρ καὶ ἐκείνης τὸ τόλμημα, ἀλλὰ σὴ ἡ αἰτία γίνεται.
context:
Analysis and Relevant Context

You've asked for additional context, which is crucial for understanding the full force of this passage.

    Scriptural Context: Chrysostom is preaching on Romans 13:13: "Let us walk honestly, as in the day; not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness..." This verse is a direct condemnation of the lifestyle that Chrysostom sees as the root cause of the sins he describes. His sermon is a practical application of St. Paul's command.

    The "Cascade of Sin": Chrysostom is a master of rhetoric. He shows his congregation how one seemingly "lesser" sin leads to a cascade of ever-worsening evils:

        Drunkenness (μέθη) leads to...

        Fornication/Whoredom (πορνεία) which can lead to...

        Adultery (μοιχεία) which then leads to...
