        Murder (φόνος).

    "Worse Than Murder": Chrysostom's argument reaches its rhetorical and theological peak when he describes abortion. He struggles to even find a name for it (οὐδὲ γὰρ ἔχω πῶς αὐτὸ καλέσω), calling it "something even worse than murder." His reasoning is profound: it's not just the destruction of a life that has been born, but an attack on life itself, an act that "prevents it from being born" (τεχθῆναι κωλύει). He sees it as a direct frustration of God's creative will.

    Historical Practice: The term Chrysostom uses, ἀτόκια (atokia), is very specific. It doesn't just mean "abortion"; it refers to contraceptive or abortifacient drugs and potions. This shows that Chrysostom is not speaking abstractly; he is addressing a common and known practice in the late Roman Empire, particularly in a bustling city like Antioch or Constantinople where he preached.

    Shared Culpability (The Man's Responsibility): One of the most powerful pastoral points in the passage is his direct address to the man who solicits the prostitute. He refuses to let the man off the hook. While the woman may perform the "daring deed" (τόλμημα), Chrysostom declares that the ultimate cause (αἰτία) is the man's. He makes the man complicit in turning the prostitute from a "harlot" into a "murderess" (ἀνδροφόνον). This is a searing indictment of the male user's responsibility.

    Abuse of a Divine Gift: Chrysostom frames the entire issue in theological terms. Sex, procreation, and the human body are gifts from God. He accuses the man of abusing this gift, fighting God's laws, and turning the "chamber of procreation" (ταμιεῖον τῆς γενέσεως) into a "chamber for murder" (ταμιεῖον σφαγῆς).

You have found a classic and powerful example of St. John Chrysostom's "Golden Mouth"—his ability to combine fiery rhetoric, sharp social critique, and profound theological reasoning to confront the sins of his time.

fr: Car celui-là même qui est vêtu de pourpre s’en va embrasser ces tombeaux ; déposant tout son faste, il se tient là, suppliant les saints d’intercéder pour lui auprès de Dieu. Et celui qui porte le diadème implore le fabricant de tentes et le pêcheur, pourtant morts, pour qu'ils soient ses protecteurs.
en: ST. JOHN CHRYSOSTOM For he who wears the purple himself goes to embrace those tombs. and, laying aside his pride, stands begging the saints to be his advocates with God. and he that wears the crown implores the tentmaker and the fisherman, though dead, to be his patrons [Homilies on Second Corinthians 26:2:5 (c. A.D. 392)].
greek: Καὶ γὰρ αὐτὸς ὁ τὴν ἁλουργίδα περικείμενος ἀπέρχεται τὰ σήματα ἐκεῖνα περιπτυξόμενος, καὶ τὸν τῦφον ἀποθέμενος ἕστηκε δεόμενος τῶν ἁγίων, ὥστε αὐτοῦ προστῆναι παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ, καὶ τοῦ σκηνοποιοῦ καὶ τοῦ ἁλιέως προστατῶν καὶ τετελευτηκότων δεῖται ὁ τὸ διάδημα ἔχων.
context:
The Broader Context (What Chrysostom is Arguing)

The full passage you provided is a masterpiece of Christian rhetoric. St. John Chrysostom's goal is to prove the immense power and glory of Christ by showing the even greater glory of His dead servants compared to the most powerful earthly rulers.

Here is the flow of his argument:

    The Failure of Worldly Power (Alexander the Great): He begins by challenging his audience: "Where is the tomb of Alexander the Great? Show it to me! Tell me the day he died!" No one knows. His memory and physical resting place are lost.

    The Triumph of the Saints: In stark contrast, he says, the tombs of Christ's servants (like Peter and Paul) are famous throughout the world. They are located in the most imperial city (Rome), and the days of their deaths are celebrated as universal feasts.

    The Role Reversal (The Emperor and the Saints): This leads directly to your quote. The tombs of the saints are more glorious than the emperor's palace, not because of their architecture, but because of the crowds who visit them.

        Your quote is the ultimate proof: The Emperor himself—the most powerful man in the world, clothed in purple and wearing the crown—comes to the tombs of a fisherman and a tentmaker. He sheds his pride and begs these dead men to be his protectors and advocates before God. This is a stunning reversal of worldly power.

    The Example of Constantine: Chrysostom drives the point home with an example from his own city, Constantinople. He says that the son of Constantine the Great (Constantius II) believed he was giving his father the highest honor by burying him at the threshold of the Church of the Holy Apostles.

        The Emperors as Gatekeepers for Fishermen: "What gatekeepers are to emperors in their palaces, the emperors are to the fishermen at their tomb." The emperors guard the door, while the saints possess the glorious interior.

Conclusion: Chrysostom's point is clear and devastating to any pagan notion of glory. If the dead servants of Christ are more powerful and honored than living emperors, how can anyone dare to call their Master, the crucified Christ, "dead"? His power is proven by the incredible post-mortem glory of his followers.

fr:
Ainsi donc, frères, demeurez fermes et retenez les traditions qui vous ont été enseignées, soit de vive voix, soit par notre lettre.

Il est donc clair qu’ils n’ont pas tout transmis par lettre, mais aussi beaucoup de choses oralement ; or, les unes comme les autres sont également dignes de foi. C'est pourquoi nous devons aussi considérer la tradition de l'église comme digne de foi. C’est une tradition : ne cherche rien de plus.
en: ST. JOHN CHRYSOSTOM "So then. brethren, stand fast, and hold the traditions that you were taught, whether by word, or by letter of ours." From this it is manifest that they did not deliver all things by letter, but many things also unwritten, and in like manner both the one and the other are worthy of credit. Therefore let us think the Tradition of the Church also worthy of credit. It is a Tradition, seek no farther [Homilies on Second Thessalonians 4:15 (c A.D. 402)].
greek:
Ἄρα οὖν, ἀδελφοὶ, στήκετε, καὶ κρατεῖτε τὰς παραδόσεις, ἃς ἐδιδάχθητε εἴτε διὰ λόγου εἴτε δι' ἐπιστολῆς ἡμῶν.

    Ἐντεῦθεν δῆλον ὅτι οὐ πάντα δι' ἐπιστολῆς παρεδίδοσαν, ἀλλὰ πολλὰ καὶ ἀγράφως· ὁμοίως δὲ κἀκεῖνα καὶ ταῦτά ἐστιν ἀξιόπιστα. Ὥστε καὶ τὴν παράδοσιν τῆς Ἐκκλησίας ἀξιόπιστον ἡγώμεθα. Παράδοσίς ἐστι, μηδὲν πλέον ζήτει.
context:
Additional Relevant Context

The context you've provided is excellent because it shows how this famous declaration is embedded within St. John's pastoral and theological exhortation. Let's break it down:

1. The Context Immediately Before Your Quote:

    Chrysostom has just been talking about how our salvation is a source of glory for Christ and how the Holy Spirit works to sanctify us. He is building up his listeners' confidence in God's work in their lives.

    This leads directly to his command, which is a quotation of St. Paul: "Therefore (Ἄρα οὖν), brethren, stand fast and hold to the traditions..." The command to hold fast to Tradition is the logical consequence of God's saving action.

2. The Core Argument (Your Quote):

    Chrysostom reads St. Paul's words—"by word or by our letter"—and immediately draws a clear and forceful conclusion.

    "From this it is manifest (Ἐντεῦθεν δῆλον)...": He presents his interpretation not as a guess, but as an obvious and undeniable fact flowing from the text.

    "...they did not deliver all things by letter, but many things also unwritten (ἀγράφως).": This is the central claim. The Apostles' teaching was not confined to their written epistles.

    "...in like manner both the one and the other are worthy of credit (ὁμοίως δὲ κἀκεῖνα καὶ ταῦτά ἐστιν ἀξιόπιστα).": This is the crucial statement on authority. He places the unwritten, oral apostolic teaching on the same level of trustworthiness as the written apostolic teaching (Scripture).

    "Therefore let us think the Tradition of the Church also worthy of credit.": He broadens the principle from the specific "unwritten" apostolic teachings to the ongoing "Tradition of the Church" which preserves them.

    "It is a Tradition, seek no farther (Παράδοσίς ἐστι, μηδὲν πλέον ζήτει).": This famous, punchy conclusion is not an argument against thinking or questioning. It is an argument about the source of authority. Once something is identified as being part of the authentic, received Tradition of the Church, its authority is established. For Chrysostom, to question it at that point would be to question the Apostles and the Church itself.

3. The Context Immediately After Your Quote:

    As soon as he delivers this powerful command, Chrysostom immediately pivots to prayer: "May our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father..."

    This shows that for him, theology and pastoral care are inseparable. The command to hold the Tradition is not a burden but is made possible by the grace of God, which he immediately prays for.

    He also slips in a quick anti-Arian point by noting that St. Paul names Jesus before the Father in this prayer, demonstrating their equality.

In summary, you have found a cornerstone text for the Catholic and Orthodox understanding of Divine Revelation, where Sacred Scripture and Sacred Tradition are seen as two complementary and equally authoritative modes of transmitting the one Apostolic faith.

fr:
Et pour que tu comprennes que nous savons cela depuis l'origine, le législateur, en donnant plus tard ses lois et en disant : « Tu ne tueras pas », n’a pas ajouté : « Car le meurtre est un mal ». Il a dit simplement : « Tu ne tueras pas » ; en effet, il s'est contenté d'interdire le péché, il n'a pas cherché à l'expliquer.

Pourquoi donc, après avoir dit : « Tu ne tueras pas », n’a-t-il pas ajouté : « Parce que le meurtre est un mal » ? Parce que la conscience nous l'avait enseigné au préalable, et c'est à des gens qui savent et qui comprennent qu'il s'adresse ainsi. C'est pourquoi, lorsqu'il parle d'un autre commandement, qui ne nous est pas connu par notre conscience, il ne se contente pas d’interdire, mais il en ajoute aussi la raison. Par exemple, en légiférant sur le sabbat et en disant : « Le septième jour, tu ne feras aucun travail », il a aussi ajouté la raison de ce repos. Et quelle est-elle ? « Car le septième jour, Dieu s’est reposé de toutes les œuvres qu’il avait commencé à faire » ; et encore : « Car tu as été esclave au pays d’Égypte. »

Pourquoi donc, dis-moi, a-t-il ajouté la raison pour le sabbat, mais n’a-t-il rien fait de tel pour le meurtre ? Parce que ce commandement-là ne faisait pas partie des commandements fondamentaux, ni de ceux que la conscience nous a enseignés avec certitude ; c'était au contraire un précepte particulier et temporaire, et c’est pourquoi il a été aboli par la suite. En revanche, les commandements nécessaires, qui sont le fondement de notre vie, sont ceux-ci : « Tu ne tueras pas », « Tu ne commettras pas d’adultère », « Tu ne voleras pas ». C'est pourquoi, pour ceux-là, il ne donne nulle part de raison ni n’introduit d’enseignement, mais se contente de la simple interdiction.
en: ST. JOHN CHRYSOSTOM And that you may learn that we know this from the first, the lawgiver, when he afterwards gave laws, and said, "You shall not kill" [Ex 20:137. did not add, "since murder is an evil thing," but simply said, "You shall not kill"; for he merely prohibited the sin, without teaching. How was it then when he said, You shall not kill," that he did not add, "because murder is a wicked thing." The reason was that conscience had taught this beforehand; and he speaks thus to those who know and understand the point. This is why when he speaks to us of another commandment, not known to us by the dictates of conscience, he not only prohibits, but adds the reason. When, for instance, he gave the commandment respecting the Sabbath, "On the seventh day you shall do no work ; he gave the reason for this cessation. "Because on the seventh day God rested from all his works which he had begun to make" [Ex 20:10]. And again; "Because thou were a servant in the land of Egypt" [Dt 21:18]. For what purpose, then, did he add a reason respecting the Sabbath, but did no such thing in regard to murder? Because this commandment was not one of the leading ones. It was not one of those that were accurately defined by our conscience, but a kind of partial and temporary one; and for this reason it was abolished afterwards. But those that are necessary and uphold our life are the following: "You shall not kill. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not steal." On this account he adds no reason in this case. nor enters into any instruction on the matter, but is content with the bare prohibition [ Homilies on the Statues 12:9 (A.D. 387)].
latin: Et ut discas nos ab initio hoc scire, legislator leges postea ferens, et dicens: Non occides: non intulit, Malum enim cædes: sed simpliciter: Non occides, inquit: prohibuit enim peccatum dumtaxat, non docuit. Quare igitur qui dixit, Non occides, non addidit, Quia malum cædes? Quoniam prius conscientia nos hoc docuit, et tamquam scientibus et intelligentibus ita loquitur. Cum igitur de alio loquitur mandato, non nobis per conscientiam noto, non tantum prohibet, sed et causam apponit. De sabbato itaque legem ferens, et dicens: Septima die non facies opus: subjunxit causam quoque cessationis: qualem vero? Quia in die septima requievit Deus ab omnibus operibus suis quæ cœperat facere: et rursum: Quoniam servus fuisti in terra Ægypti. Quare igitur, dic mihi, in sabbato quidem causam adjecit, in cæde vero nihil tale fecit? Quoniam hoc quidem mandatum non de primariis erat, nec per conscientiam nobis exquisitis, sed particulare quoddam et temporaneum: propterea post hæc solutum est: necessaria vero, et vitam nostram continentia, illa sunt: Non occides, non furaberis, non mœchaberis: et ideo nullatenus hic causam ponit, nec doctrinam adducit, sed sola opus esse putat prohibitione.
greek: Καὶ ἵνα μάθῃς ὅτι τοῦτο ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἴσμεν, ὁ νομοθέτης νόμους διδοὺς ὕστερον, καὶ εἰπών, Οὐ φονεύσεις, οὐκ ἐπήγαγε, Κακὸν γὰρ ὁ φόνος, ἀλλ᾽ ἁπλῶς. Οὐ φονεύσεις, εἶπεν· ἀπηγόρευσε γὰρ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν μόνον, οὐκ ἐδίδαξε. Τίνος οὖν ἕνεκεν εἰπὼν, Οὐ φονεύσεις, οὐ προσέθηκεν, Ὅτι κακὸν ὁ φόνος; Ἐπειδὴ προλαβὸν τὸ συνειδὸς ἡμᾶς ἐπαίδευσε τοῦτο, καὶ ὡς εἰδόσι καὶ ἐπισταμένοις οὕτω διαλέγεται. Ὅταν γοῦν περὶ ἑτέρας ἐντολῆς λέγῃ τῆς οὐ γνωρίμης ἡμῖν ἀπὸ τοῦ συνειδότος γενομένης, οὐκ ἀπαγορεύει μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὴν αἰτίαν προστίθησι. Περὶ σαββάτου γοῦν νομοθετῶν καὶ λέγων, Τῇ δὲ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ ἑβδόμῃ οὐ ποιήσεις ἔργον, καὶ τὴν αἰτίαν ἐπήγαγε τῆς ἀργίας· ποίαν δὴ ταύτην; Ὅτι ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ ἑβδόμῃ κατέπαυσεν ὁ Θεὸς ἀπὸ πάντων τῶν ἔργων αὐτοῦ ὧν ἤρξατο ποιῆσαι· καὶ πάλιν, Ὅτι οἰκέτης ἦσθα ἐν γῇ Αἰγύπτῳ. Τίνος οὖν ἕνεκεν, εἰπέ μοι, ἐπὶ μὲν τοῦ σαββάτου τὴν αἰτίαν προσέθηκεν, ἐπὶ δὲ τοῦ φόνου οὐδὲν τοιοῦτον ἐποίησεν; Ἐπειδὴ αὕτη μὲν ἡ ἐντολὴ οὐ τῶν προηγουμένων ἦν, οὐδὲ τῶν ἐκ τοῦ συνειδότος ἡμῖν ἠκριβωμένων, ἀλλὰ μερική τις καὶ πρόσκαιρος, διὰ τοῦτο καὶ κατελύθη μετὰ ταῦτα· αἱ δὲ ἀναγκαῖαι καὶ συνέχουσαι τὴν ζωὴν τὴν ἡμετέραν, ἐκεῖναί εἰσιν· Οὐ φονεύσεις, Οὐ μοιχεύσεις, Οὐ κλέψεις. Διόπερ οὐδαμοῦ αἰτίαν ἐνταῦθα τίθησιν, οὐδὲ διδασκαλίαν εἰσάγει, ἀλλ' ἀρκεῖται ψιλῇ τῇ ἀπαγορεύσει.
context:
Additional Relevant Context

You have not only found the quote but the entire section where St. John develops his argument. This provides incredibly rich context:

1. The Historical Setting (The "Statues"): These 21 homilies were delivered in Antioch in A.D. 387 during a city-wide crisis. The citizens had rioted over a new tax and, in their anger, had pulled down and desecrated the statues of the Emperor Theodosius and his family. This was an act of high treason, and the entire city was terrified of the Emperor's brutal retribution. Chrysostom preached these sermons to calm the panicked populace, call them to repentance, and strengthen their faith.

2. The Theological Theme (The Natural Law): The core of this homily is the doctrine of the Natural Law (νόμος φυσικός). Chrysostom's central point is that God did not leave humanity without a moral compass before the time of Moses and the Ten Commandments. From the very beginning of creation, He implanted a moral law within the human heart.

3. The Role of Conscience: Chrysostom identifies the faculty that perceives this law as conscience (τὸ συνειδὸς). Conscience is the "self-teaching" faculty (αὐτοδίδακτος) that gives us innate knowledge of foundational good and evil.

4. The Argument in the Broader Text: The text you provided shows how Chrysostom proves this point:
* Pre-Mosaic Examples: Before he even gets to the Ten Commandments, he points to Adam and Cain. Adam knew he had sinned because he hid from God before any written law existed. Cain knew his murderous intent was evil because he tried to hide it with deceit ("Let us go out to the field"). This proves, Chrysostom argues, that conscience was active from the dawn of humanity.
* The Contrast in the Mosaic Law: This is your specific quote. He brilliantly argues that the form of the Ten Commandments itself proves the existence of a prior Natural Law.
* Laws aligned with Conscience (Murder, Adultery, Theft): God simply states the prohibition ("You shall not kill") without giving a reason, because He is speaking to people whose consciences already know this is wrong.
* Laws NOT known by Conscience (The Sabbath): The obligation to rest on the seventh day is not self-evident to human reason. It is a positive divine command. Therefore, God provides the reasons for it ("because God rested," "because you were a slave in Egypt") to teach the people why they must obey.

In summary, you have found a masterful piece of pastoral theology where St. John Chrysostom uses scriptural analysis to teach his terrified congregation about the unshakable moral foundation God has placed within every human being.

fr:
Ils s'adonnaient à la pédérastie. L'un de leurs philosophes a même légiféré pour interdire aux esclaves de la pratiquer..., comme si cet acte était vertueux et digne d'un grand honneur. C'est pourquoi ils s'affichaient et le pratiquaient ouvertement dans des maisons de débauche.

Et si l'on examinait l'ensemble de leurs coutumes, on verrait clairement qu'ils en venaient à outrager la nature elle-même, et que personne ne les en empêchait...

Quant à leurs passions pour les jeunes garçons, qu'ils ont coutume d'appeler leurs « mignons », il n'est même pas possible d'en parler.
en: [The pagans] were addicted to the love of boys, and one of their wise men made a law that pederasty should not be allowed to slaves, as if it were an honorable thing; and they had houses for this purpose, in which it was openly practiced. And if all that were done among them was related, it would be seen that they openly outraged nature, and no one restrained them. . . . As for their passion for boys, whom they called their paedica, it is not fit to be named [Homilies on Titus 5:6 (c. A.D. 390)].
greek:
Ἐπαιδεράστουν· καὶ παρ' αὐτοῖς φιλόσοφός τις ἐνομοθέτει, δούλῳ ἐξεῖναι μήτε παιδεραστεῖν... ὡς ἐναρέτου τοῦ πράγματος ὄντος καὶ πολλὴν ἔχοντος τιμήν. Διὰ τοῦτο καὶ ἐπ' οἰκήματος εἱστήκεισαν φανερῶς τοῦτο ποιοῦντες.

    Καὶ εἰ πάντα τις ἐπέλθοι τὰ κατ' αὐτοὺς, εὑρήσει φανερῶς ὅτι καὶ εἰς τὴν φύσιν αὐτὴν ἐνύβριζον, καὶ οὐδεὶs ὁ κωλύων ἦν...

    Τοὺς γὰρ τῶν παίδων ἔρωτας, οὕσπερ αὐτοῖς παιδικὰ καλεῖν ἔθος ἐστὶν, οὐδὲ εἰπεῖν ἔνι.
context:
Additional Relevant Context: A Portrait of Pagan Depravity

The quote you've isolated is part of a much larger rhetorical argument. St. John Chrysostom is giving this homily on Titus 3:3: "For we ourselves were once foolish, disobedient, led astray, slaves to various passions and pleasures..."

To illustrate the depths of the depravity from which Christ saved them, Chrysostom paints a vivid and horrifying picture of the pre-Christian pagan world. The passage on pederasty is just one example in a long list of moral chaos. Here is the context from the full text you provided:

    Familial Breakdown: He begins by stating that before Christ, fathers slaughtered their own children (τοὺς παῖδας ἔσφαζον τοὺς ἑαυτῶν πατέρες), and mothers were crazed for their sons. All natural and written laws were overturned.

    Constant Violence & Immorality: He speaks of perpetual adultery, murder, and theft, noting that some pagans even considered theft a virtue. He mentions oracles that commanded murders.

    Mythological Cruelty: He re-tells the myth of Androgeos and the Minotaur (the sacrifice of fourteen Athenian youths) not as a myth, but as an example of demonic, tyrannical cruelty commanded by the god Apollo.

    Brutal Entertainment: They worshipped boxers and wrestlers.

    Pervasive Warfare: There were constant wars between cities, villages, and even houses.

    Pederasty (Your Quote): He then launches into the section you found, presenting pederasty as a celebrated practice, even codified in law by a philosopher, and practiced openly.

    Public Debauchery: He describes lewd plays full of adultery and corruption, and all-night festivals (Παννυχίδες) where young virgins sat among drunk and crazed men in the dark.

    Incest and Mythological Sins: He explicitly mentions incest (μητρογαμίας, a reference to Oedipus), noting that their gods did nothing to prevent nature from being outraged. He alludes to other myths involving adultery, murder, and revenge (likely the story of Clytemnestra, Agamemnon, and Orestes).

The Theological Point: Chrysostom's goal is not just to condemn paganism. His primary aim is to inspire gratitude in his Christian audience. He is saying, "Look at the horrifying pit of moral chaos you were born into! This is the world without Christ. Now look at the grace, order, and salvation you have received. Never forget the darkness from which you have been rescued."

fr: Mais lorsqu'il s'agit de gouverner une église et de se voir confier le soin d'un si grand nombre d'âmes, que toute la nature féminine recule devant l'ampleur de cette charge, et la plupart des hommes également. Que l'on mette alors en avant ceux qui surpassent de loin tous les autres, et qui s'élèvent par la vertu de leur âme aussi haut au-dessus du reste des hommes que Saül dominait de sa taille tout le peuple hébreu — ou plutôt, bien plus encore.
en: ST. JOHN CHRYSOSTOM [W]hen one is required to preside over the Church and to be entrusted with the care of so many souls, the whole female sex must retire before the magnitude of the task, and the majority of men also, and we must bring forward those who to large extent surpass all others and soar as much above them in excellence of spirit as Saul overtopped the whole Hebrew nation in bodily stature [Priesthood 2:2 (c. A.D. 388)].
greek: ὅταν δὲ Ἐκκλησίας προστῆναι δέῃ καὶ ψυχῶν ἐπιμέλειαν πιστευθῆναι τοσούτων, πᾶσα μὲν ἡ γυναικεία φύσις παραχωρείτω τῷ μεγέθει τοῦ πράγματος, καὶ ἀνδρῶν δὲ τὸ πλέον. Ἀγέσθωσαν δὲ εἰς μέσον οἱ πολλῷ τῷ μέτρῳ πλεονεκτοῦντες ἁπάντων, καὶ τοσοῦτον ὑψηλότεροι τῶν ἄλλων κατὰ τὴν τῆς ψυχῆς ὄντες ἀρετὴν ὅσον τοῦ παντὸς ἔθνους Ἑβραίων κατὰ τὸ τοῦ σώματος μέγεθος ὁ Σαούλ, μᾶλλον δὲ καὶ πολλῷ πλέον.
context:
Additional Relevant Context

Your block of text provides the full argument St. John is making. Here is the context from immediately before and after your quote, which makes its meaning even clearer.
Context: What Comes Immediately Before

St. John establishes the supreme importance of the priesthood by citing Jesus's final command to Peter, arguing that the care of souls ("Feed my sheep") surpasses all other ascetic practices.

Greek Text:

    ...Νῦν δὲ πάντα ταῦτα ἀφεὶς τί φησι; »Ποίμαινε τὰ πρόβατά μου.« Ἐκεῖνα μὲν γὰρ ἃ προεῖπον καὶ τῶν ἀρχομένων πολλοὶ δύναιντ' ἂν ἐπιτελεῖν ῥᾳδίως, οὐκ ἄνδρες μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ γυναῖκες...

English Translation:

    "...But now, setting all these things aside, what does He say? 'Feed my sheep.' For the things I mentioned before [fasting, vigils, etc.], many of those under authority could easily perform, not only men, but women also..."

Explanation: Chrysostom argues that while many people (men and women) can perform acts of personal piety, the specific task of pastoral governance ("feeding the sheep") is a unique and far greater responsibility. This leads directly into your quote.
Context: What Comes Immediately After

After using the powerful image of Saul's stature to describe the necessary spiritual greatness of a priest, Chrysostom immediately raises the stakes by contrasting the earthly work of a literal shepherd with the eternal work of a spiritual one.

Greek Text:

    Ὁ μὲν γὰρ πρόβατα ἀπολλὺς... τύχοι μὲν ἄν τινος καὶ συγγνώμης παρὰ τοῦ κυρίου τῆς ποίμνης: εἰ δὲ καὶ δίκην ἀπαιτοῖτο, μέχρι τῶν χρημάτων ἡ ζημία. Ὁ δὲ ἀνθρώπους πιστευθείς, τὸ λογικὸν τοῦ Χριστοῦ ποίμνιον, πρῶτον μὲν οὐκ εἰς χρήματα, ἀλλ' εἰς τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ψυχὴν τὴν ζημίαν ὑφίσταται ὑπὲρ τῆς τῶν προβάτων ἀπωλείας.

English Translation:

    "For a man who loses sheep... might obtain some forgiveness from the owner of the flock; and even if he were required to pay, the penalty is only a matter of money. But the one entrusted with human beings, the rational flock of Christ, suffers the penalty for the loss of the sheep not in his money, but in his own soul."

Explanation: Chrysostom's point is that the standard for the priesthood must be astronomically high because the consequences of failure are eternal. The loss of a sheep is a financial matter; the loss of a soul is a matter of eternal salvation or damnation, for which the priest himself is held accountable.

You have successfully found a key passage where St. John Chrysostom builds his powerful and intimidating case for the immense dignity and overwhelming responsibility of the priestly office.

fr: Car lorsque tu vois le Seigneur immolé et étendu là, le prêtre penché sur la victime et en prière, et tous les fidèles empourprés de ce sang précieux, crois-tu encore être parmi les hommes et te tenir sur la terre ? N’es-tu pas plutôt, à l’instant même, transporté dans les cieux ?
en: ST. JOHN CHRYSOSTOM For when you see the Lord sacrificed, and laid upon the altar, and the priest standing and praying over the victim, and all the worshippers empurpled with that precious blood. can you then think that you are still among men, and standing upon the earth? Are you not, on the contrary, immediately translated to heaven? [The Priesthood 3:4 (c. A.D. 388)].
greek: Ὅταν γὰρ ἴδῃς τὸν Κύριον τεθυμένον καὶ κείμενον, καὶ τὸν ἱερέα ἐφεστῶτα τῷ θύματι καὶ ἐπευχόμενον, καὶ πάντας ἐκείνῳ τῷ τιμίῳ φοινισσομένους αἵματι, ἆρα ἔτι μετὰ ἀνθρώπων εἶναι νομίζεις καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς ἑστάναι, ἀλλ' οὐκ εὐθέως ἐπὶ τοὺς οὐρανοὺς μετανίστασαι;
context:
Additional Relevant Context

The full text you provided gives the entire magnificent argument of this chapter. Here is the context that surrounds your quote:

1. Context Before: The New Priesthood is More Awesome than the Old

St. Chrysostom begins the chapter by arguing that the New Covenant priesthood, while exercised on earth, has the "rank of heavenly things." It was not established by a man or an angel, but by the Holy Spirit Himself. He makes two key points to build his case:

    Purity: The priest must be as pure as an angel, as if he were "standing in the heavens themselves."

    Superiority to the Old Covenant: He lists the "fearful and awesome" elements of the Old Testament temple worship (the bells, the pomegranates, the precious stones, the high priest's garments, the Holy of Holies). But he says these all seem small when compared to the realities of the New Covenant, quoting 2 Corinthians 3:10: "that which was made glorious has no glory in this respect, by reason of the glory that excels."

This build-up is designed to prepare the reader for the awe-inspiring reality he is about to describe. Your specific quote is the climax of this comparison—it is the ultimate proof of why the New Liturgy is so much more "awesome."

2. Context After: The Miracle of the Eucharist Surpasses Old Testament Miracles

After describing the heavenly scene of the Liturgy, Chrysostom provides two more stunning images to amplify his point:

    Divine Condescension: He exclaims, "O, the wonder! O, the love of God for man! He who is seated on high with the Father is at that hour held in the hands of all, and gives Himself to those who wish to embrace and receive Him." This highlights the incredible intimacy and humility of Christ in the Eucharist.

    The Superiority to Elijah: He draws a powerful comparison between the priest and the Prophet Elijah on Mount Carmel.

        Elijah stood before the sacrifice, and a visible fire came down from heaven to consume it. This was an awesome miracle.

        The Priest, Chrysostom says, stands at the altar and calls down not fire, but the Holy Spirit. The Spirit does not consume the sacrifice but consecrates it, inflaming the souls of the faithful and making them "brighter than silver refined by fire."

This comparison brilliantly argues that the priest's action during the Liturgy is an even greater and more profound miracle than one of the most famous wonders of the Old Testament. You have located the heart of Chrysostom's theology of the priesthood and the Eucharist.

fr:
Car ceux qui habitent la terre et y mènent leur existence se sont vu confier l’administration des choses du ciel, et ils ont reçu un pouvoir que Dieu n’a donné ni aux anges ni aux archanges. Car ce n’est pas à eux qu’il a été dit : « Tout ce que vous lierez sur la terre sera lié dans le ciel, et tout ce que vous délierez sur la terre sera délié dans le ciel. »

Certes, les puissants de ce monde possèdent aussi le pouvoir de lier, mais uniquement les corps. Ce lien, en revanche, atteint l’âme elle-même et traverse les cieux ; et ce que les prêtres accomplissent ici-bas, Dieu le ratifie là-haut, et le Maître confirme la sentence de ses serviteurs.

Car en vérité, ne leur a-t-il pas donné toute l'autorité céleste ? « Les péchés seront remis à ceux à qui vous les remettrez, dit-il, et ils seront retenus à ceux à qui vous les retiendrez. » Quelle autorité pourrait être plus grande que celle-ci ? « Le Père a remis tout jugement au Fils. » Or, je vois que le Fils leur a confié entièrement ce jugement. C’est comme si, déjà transportés dans les cieux, ayant dépassé la nature humaine et s’étant affranchis de nos passions, ils avaient été ainsi élevés à une si haute charge.
en: ST. JOHN CHRYSOSTOM For they who inhabit the earth and make their abode are entrusted with the administration of things that are in heaven, and have received an authority that God has not given to angels or archangels. For it has not been said to them, "Whatsoever you shall bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatsoever you shall loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven" [Mt 18:18]. They who rule on earth have authority to bind, but only the body: whereas this binding lays hold of the soul and penetrates the heavens; and what priests do here below God ratifies above, and the master confirms the sentence of his servants. For indeed what is it but all manner of heavenly authority has he given them when he says, "Whose sins you remit they are remitted, and whose sins you retain they are retained?" [Jn 20:23]. What authority could be greater than this? "The Father has committed all judgment to the Son?" [Jn 5:22]. But I see it all put into the hands of these men by the Son. For they have been conducted to this dignity as they were already translated to heaven [The Priesthood 3:5 (c. A.D. 388)].
greek:
Οἱ γὰρ τὴν γῆν οἰκοῦντες καὶ ἐν ταύτῃ ποιούμενοι τὴν διατριβὴν τὰ ἐν οὐρανοῖς διοικεῖν ἐπετράπησαν καὶ ἐξουσίαν ἔλαβον ἣν οὔτε ἀγγέλοις οὔτε ἀρχαγγέλοις ἔδωκεν ὁ Θεός· οὐ γὰρ πρὸς ἐκείνους εἴρηται· »Ὅσα ἂν δήσητε ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς ἔσται δεδεμένα καὶ ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ, καὶ ὅσα ἂν λύσητε ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς ἔσται λελυμένα ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ.«

    Ἔχουσι μὲν γὰρ καὶ οἱ κρατοῦντες ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς τὴν τοῦ δεσμεῖν ἐξουσίαν, ἀλλὰ σωμάτων μόνων· οὗτος δὲ ὁ δεσμὸς αὐτῆς ἅπτεται τῆς ψυχῆς καὶ διαβαίνει τοὺς οὐρανούς, καὶ ἅπερ ἂν ἐργάσωνται κάτω οἱ ἱερεῖς, ταῦτα ὁ Θεὸς ἄνω κυροῖ καὶ τὴν τῶν δούλων γνώμην ὁ δεσπότης βεβαιοῖ.

    Καὶ τί γὰρ ἀλλ' ἢ πᾶσαν αὐτοῖς τὴν οὐράνιον ἔδωκεν ἐξουσίαν; »Ὧν γὰρ ἄν,« φησίν, »ἀφῆτε τὰς ἁμαρτίας, ἀφέωνται, καὶ ὧν ἂν κρατῆτε, κεκράτηνται.« Τίς ἂν γένοιτο ταύτης ἐξουσία μείζων; »Πᾶσαν τὴν κρίσιν ἔδωκεν ὁ πατὴρ τῷ υἱῷ.« Ὁρῶ δὲ πᾶσαν αὐτὴν τούτους ἐγχειρισθέντας ὑπὸ τοῦ υἱοῦ· ὥσπερ γὰρ εἰς οὐρανοὺς ἤδη μετατεθέντες καὶ τὴν ἀνθρωπείαν ὑπερβάντες φύσιν καὶ τῶν ἡμετέρων ἀπαλλαγέντες παθῶν, οὕτως εἰς τοσαύτην ἤχθησαν τὴν ἀρχήν.
context:
Additional Relevant Context
Immediate Context (Within the Chapter)

Your Greek text actually contains a little more than the English translation you cited. Immediately after the final sentence ("...already translated to heaven"), Chrysostom draws a powerful comparison:

    "Then if a king should bestow on one of his subjects this honor, so that he could cast into prison whom he wished and release them again, he is envied and looked upon by all. But he who has received from God an authority as much greater as heaven is more precious than earth, and souls than bodies—does it seem to some that he has received so small an honor that they could even imagine that one entrusted with these things would despise the gift? Away with such madness! For it is manifest madness to despise so great an office, without which it is not possible for us to obtain salvation or the promised good things."

Chrysostom's point is that people are impressed by the earthly authority of kings to imprison bodies, yet some fail to grasp the infinitely greater heavenly authority of the priest to bind and loose souls. He calls it "madness" to belittle such a divine gift.
Broader Context (Within the Book)

On the Priesthood is a dialogue written by St. John in his youth. He is explaining to his friend Basil why he tricked Basil into being ordained a bishop while he himself fled from the office. The entire book is an extended reflection on the awesome, almost terrifying, dignity and responsibility of the priesthood. Chrysostom argues that the office is so sublime and its duties so weighty (especially the care of souls) that he felt utterly unworthy to take it on.
Theological Significance

This passage is foundational for the Catholic and Orthodox understanding of the Sacrament of Holy Orders for several reasons:

    A Heavenly Authority on Earth: It powerfully articulates that the priest, though a mere man, acts as an administrator of heavenly realities.

    Superiority to Angels: The contrast is stark. Angels are glorious celestial beings, but they were not given the sacramental power to forgive sins. This power was given to the apostles and their successors.

    Real, Not Symbolic, Power: Chrysostom insists that the priest's act of binding or loosing is not merely symbolic. It has a real, binding effect in heaven. "What priests do here below God ratifies above."

    Participation in Christ's Judgment: The most profound claim is that the priest participates in the authority of Christ the Judge. The Father gave all judgment to the Son (John 5:22), and Chrysostom sees the Son entrusting this very authority (specifically regarding sins) into the hands of his priests.

fr:
Car si personne ne peut entrer dans le royaume des Cieux sans renaître de l'eau et de l'Esprit, et si celui qui ne mange pas la chair du Seigneur et ne boit pas son sang est privé de la vie éternelle, et que tout cela ne s'accomplit par nul autre, mais seulement par ces mains saintes — je parle de celles du prêtre —, comment pourrait-on, sans elles, échapper au feu de la géhenne ou obtenir les couronnes qui nous sont promises ?

Ce sont eux, en effet, à qui ont été confiées les douleurs de l'enfantement spirituel et la naissance qui s'opère par le baptême. C'est par eux que nous revêtons le Christ, que nous sommes ensevelis avec le Fils de Dieu et que nous devenons membres de cette tête bienheureuse.
en: ST. JOHN CHRYSOSTOM [Njo one can enter into the kingdom of heaven except he be regenerated through water and the Spirit, and he who does not eal the flesh of the Lord and drink his blood is excluded from eternal life, and if all these things are accomplished only by means of the holy hands of the priest, how will anyone, without them, be able to escape the fire of hell, or attain those crowns reserved for the victorious? These [priests] truly are entrusted with the pangs of spiritual travail and the birth that comes through baptism: by their means we put on Christ, and are buried with the Son of God, and become members 01 that blessed head [the Mystical Body of Christ][ The Priesthood 3:5-6 (C. A.D. 388)].
greek:
Εἰ γὰρ οὐ δύναταί τις εἰσελθεῖν εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶν, ἐὰν μὴ δι' ὕδατος καὶ πνεύματος ἀναγεννηθῇ, καὶ ὁ μὴ τρώγων τὴν σάρκα τοῦ Κυρίου καὶ τὸ αἷμα αὐτοῦ πίνων ἐκβέβληται τῆς αἰωνίου ζωῆς, πάντα δὲ ταῦτα δι' ἑτέρου μὲν οὐδενός, μόνον δὲ διὰ τῶν ἁγίων ἐκείνων ἐπιτελεῖται χειρῶν, τῶν τοῦ ἱερέως λέγω, πῶς ἄν τις τούτων ἐκτὸς ἢ τὸ τῆς γεέννης ἐκφυγεῖν δυνήσεται πῦρ ἢ τῶν ἀποκειμένων στεφάνων τυχεῖν;

    Οὗτοι γάρ εἰσιν, οὗτοι οἱ τὰς πνευματικὰς πιστευθέντες ὠδῖνας καὶ τὸν διὰ τοῦ βαπτίσματος ἐπιτραπέντες τόκον· διὰ τούτων ἐνδυόμεθα τὸν Χριστὸν καὶ συνθαπτόμεθα τῷ υἱῷ τοῦ Θεοῦ, μέλη γινόμεθα τῆς μακαρίας ἐκείνης κεφαλῆς.
context:
Additional Relevant Context (From the Greek Text You Provided)

The Greek text you posted is even better than the quote alone because it gives the full force of Chrysostom's argument. He builds his case in two main stages:

1. The Priest's Judicial Power (Chapter 5, marked εʹ)

Before he even gets to the sacraments of initiation, Chrysostom establishes the priest's awesome judicial authority, which he says surpasses that of angels and earthly kings:

    Binding and Loosing: He quotes Matthew 18:18 ("Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven..."). He notes that while earthly rulers can only bind a person's body, the priest's binding "touches the soul itself and passes through the heavens."

    Forgiving Sins: He quotes John 20:23 ("Whose sins you forgive are forgiven..."). He marvels that the Father gave all judgment to the Son, and the Son has now entrusted this very power to priests.

    A Power Beyond Kings: A king can throw a man in prison, but a priest's authority is as much greater than a king's as heaven is to earth and souls are to bodies. To scorn this authority, he says, is "manifest madness."

2. The Priest's Sacramental Power (Chapter 6, marked Ϛʹ)

This is where your quote comes in. After establishing the priest's authority over sin, he moves to their role in conferring new life itself:

    The Gateway to Life (Your Quote): Priests are the indispensable ministers of Baptism ("water and Spirit") and the Eucharist ("flesh... and blood"), without which salvation is impossible. They are the instruments of our spiritual birth.

    Greater than Parents: Immediately after your quote, Chrysostom makes a stunning comparison. Priests are more to be honored than our own fathers, because our parents gave us biological life ("from blood and the will of the flesh"), but priests are the cause of our divine birth ("the birth from God"), which leads to true freedom and adoption as sons of God.

    Greater than the Old Testament Priesthood: He then contrasts the new priesthood with the old. The Jewish priests could only inspect a leper and declare him clean; the priests of Christ have the power not just to declare a soul clean from the leprosy of sin, but to actually cleanse it.

In summary, your quote is the heart of Chrysostom's argument about the priest's role as the agent of sacramental regeneration. It is powerfully framed by his discussion of the priest's judicial power over sin (before) and his dignity above parents and the old priesthood (after). Excellent find

fr:
Voici comment nous reconnaîtrons qu'il est impossible que vos deux principes soient sans commencement dans le temps. Ce qui n'a pas de commencement est immuable ; car si cela changeait, ce ne serait pas absolument sans commencement. En effet, une chose qui change — qu'elle passe de l'incorporel au corporel, de l'informe à la forme, de l'immobilité au mouvement, ou encore du calme et de la quiétude au conflit — commence à devenir ce qu'elle n'était pas auparavant. Et ce qui passe d'un état sans commencement à un état qui en a un n'est pas sans commencement. Car ce qui reçoit un commencement, ce qui a commencé d'être, n'est pas sans commencement.

Le Manichéen : Qu'en est-il donc ? Votre Dieu n'a-t-il pas changé en engendrant le Fils et en faisant procéder l'Esprit ?

L'Orthodoxe : Nullement. Car je ne dis pas que, n'étant pas Père auparavant, il le serait devenu par la suite. Je dis au contraire qu'il a toujours été, possédant de lui-même son propre Verbe, et que de lui-même, par son Verbe, son Esprit procédait.
en: ST. JOHN OF DAMASCUSI say that God IS always Father since he has always his Word [the Son] coming from himself and, through his Word, the Spirit issuing from him [Dialogue Against the Manicheans (c. A.D. 728)].
greek: Ὅτι δὲ οὐ κατὰ χρόνον ἀνάρχους εἶναι δυνατὸν τὰς καθ' ὑμᾶς δύο ἀρχάς, οὕτω γνωσόμεθα. Τὸ μὴ ἀρξάμενον τοῦ εἶναι ἄτρεπτόν ἐστιν· εἰ γὰρ ἐτράπη, οὐ παντελῶς ἐστιν ἄναρχον. Τρεπόμενον γὰρ ἐξ ἀσωμάτου εἰς σῶμα ἢ ἐξ ἀνειδέου εἰς εἶδος ἢ ἐξ ἀκινήτου εἰς κίνησιν ἢ ἐξ ἡσυχίας καὶ ἠρεμίας εἰς στάσιν ἄρχεται τοῦ γίνεσθαι, ὅπερ οὐκ ἦν πρότερον. Καὶ οὐκ ἔστιν ἄναρχον τρεπόμενον ἐξ ἀνάρχου εἰς ἀρχόμενον· τὸ γὰρ ἀρχὴν λαμβάνον καὶ ἠργμένον οὐκ ἄναρχον. Μανιχαῖος· Τί οὖν; Ὁ κατὰ σὲ θεὸς οὐκ ἐτράπη γεννήσας υἱὸν καὶ προαγαγὼν πνεῦμα; Ὀρθόδοξος· Οὐδαμῶς· οὐ γὰρ λέγω· Μὴ ὢν πρότερον πατὴρ ὕστερον γέγονε πατήρ, ἀλλὰ ἀεὶ ἦν ἔχων ἐξ αὑτοῦ τὸν αὐτοῦ λόγον καὶ διὰ τοῦ λόγου αὐτοῦ ἐξ αὑτοῦ τὸ πνεῦμα αὐτοῦ ἐκπορευόμενον.
context:
Additional Relevant Context

This passage is a brilliant defense of a core Christian doctrine—divine immutability (that God is unchanging)—within the context of the Trinity.
1. The Work Itself: The Dialogue

St. John of Damascus (c. 675–749) was a great synthesizer of patristic theology. This work is a polemical dialogue written to refute Manichaeism. The Manicheans were dualists; they believed in two co-eternal, uncreated first principles: a good God of light and spirit, and an evil god of darkness and matter. For them, the material world was the creation of the evil principle.
2. The Immediate Argument in the Dialogue

The full text you provided shows the Manichean character setting a logical trap for the Orthodox Christian:

    The Manichean's Premise: An eternal, uncreated being must be unchangeable (ἄτρεπτον). If it changes, it means it began to be something it wasn't before, which would mean it isn't truly eternal.

    The Manichean's "Gotcha" Question: "So what about your God? Didn't He change when He begot a Son and brought forth a Spirit? Wasn't there a time He wasn't a Father, and then He became a Father? If so, your God changed and is not truly eternal and unchangeable."

        This is a classic Arian-style argument, repurposed by the Manichean character to attack the Christian God.

3. The Theological Importance of the Orthodox Response (Your Quote)

St. John's response is the classic orthodox refutation of this error, and it is the heart of your quote:

    Denial of Change: The Orthodox speaker starts with an emphatic "By no means!" (Οὐδαμῶς).

    Rejection of a Temporal "Becoming": He clarifies, "I do not say, 'Not being a Father previously, He later became a Father.'" This rejects the idea that God's Fatherhood is an event in time.

    The Eternal Relations: The core of the answer is that the Trinity does not involve change because the relationships are eternal.

        ἀεὶ ἦν πατὴρ ("He was always Father"). God's Fatherhood is not something He acquires. It is part of His eternal nature.

        ἔχων ἐξ αὑτοῦ τὸν αὐτοῦ λόγον ("having from Himself His Word"). The Son (the Word) is not created in time but is eternally generated from the Father.

        διὰ τοῦ λόγου αὐτοῦ ... τὸ πνεῦμα αὐτοῦ ἐκπορευόμενον ("through His Word... His Spirit issuing forth"). The Holy Spirit is not created in time but eternally proceeds from the Father through the Son.

In summary, you have found a masterful passage where St. John of Damascus defends the Trinity by explaining that the generation of the Son and the procession of the Spirit are not temporal events that imply change in God. Rather, they are the eternal, unchanging, and internal relations that constitute the very being of the one, immutable God.

fr: Nous croyons de même en un seul Esprit Saint, le Seigneur qui donne la vie, qui procède du Père et qui repose dans le Fils ; adoré et glorifié avec le Père et le Fils comme consubstantiel et coéternel ; l’Esprit de Dieu, l’Esprit droit, l’Esprit souverain, source de la vie et de la sanctification ; Dieu, existant et proclamé tel avec le Père et le Fils ; incréé, plénier, créateur, maître de l’univers, artisan de tout, tout-puissant, d’une puissance infinie ; maître de toute la création et lui-même sans maître ; remplissant tout sans être rempli ; auquel on participe sans qu’il participe ; sanctifiant sans être sanctifié ; Paraclet, car il accueille les supplications de tous ; en toutes choses semblable au Père et au Fils ; procédant du Père, communiqué par le Fils et reçu par toute la création...
en: Likewise we believe also in one Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life God existing and addressed along with Father and Son: uncreated, full, creative, all-ruling, all-effecting, all-powerful, of infinite power, Lord of all creation and not under any Lord; deifying, not deified; filling, not filled; shared in, not sharing in; sanctifying, not sanctified; the intercessor, receiving the supplications of all; in all things like the Father and Son, proceeding from the Father and communicated through the Son [Exposition of the Orthodox Faith 1:8 (c. A.D. 746)].
greek: Ὁμοίως πιστεύομεν καὶ εἰς ἓν πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον, τὸ κύριον καὶ ζωοποιόν, τὸ ἐκ τοῦ πατρὸς ἐκπορευόμενον καὶ ἐν υἱῷ ἀναπαυόμενον, τὸ τῷ πατρὶ καὶ υἱῷ συμπροσκυνούμενον καὶ συνδοξαζόμενον ὡς ὁμοούσιόν τε καὶ συναΐδιον, τὸ τοῦ θεοῦ πνεῦμα, τὸ εὐθές, τὸ ἡγεμονικόν, τὴν πηγὴν τῆς ζωῆς καὶ τοῦ ἁγιασμοῦ, θεὸν σὺν πατρὶ καὶ υἱῷ ὑπάρχον καὶ προσαγορευόμενον, ἄκτιστον, πλῆρες, δημιουργόν, παντοκρατορικόν, παντουργόν, παντοδύναμον, ἀπειροδύναμον, δεσπόζον πάσης τῆς κτίσεως οὐ δεσποζόμενον, πληροῦν οὐ πληρούμενον, μετεχόμενον οὐ μετέχον, ἁγιάζον οὐχ ἁγιαζόμενον, παράκλητον ὡς τὰς τῶν ὅλων παρακλήσεις δεχόμενον, κατὰ πάντα ὅμοιον τῷ πατρὶ καὶ τῷ υἱῷ, ἐκ τοῦ πατρὸς ἐκπορευόμενον καὶ δι' υἱοῦ μεταδιδόμενον καὶ μεταλαμβανόμενον ὑπὸ πάσης τῆς κτίσεως...
context:
Additional Relevant Context

    The Work: St. John of Damascus's Exposition of the Orthodox Faith is not a polemical work written against a specific heresy (like St. Gregory's Against Eunomius). Instead, it is the first great systematic theology or summa of the Greek Fathers. St. John masterfully gathers and synthesizes centuries of Orthodox teaching into a single, coherent whole.

    The Chapter (Book 1, Chapter 8): The massive text you posted is the entire chapter. This chapter is famous for being one of the most comprehensive and concise explanations of the Holy Trinity ever written. It is structured like the Creed:

        It begins by defining the one God.

        It then discusses God the Father as the sole source.

        It moves to a long and detailed explanation of God the Son and His eternal generation.

        Finally, it culminates in the paragraph you were looking for—a rich and powerful summary of the person and work of the Holy Spirit.

    Theological Importance: This passage is a cornerstone of Eastern Orthodox pneumatology (theology of the Holy Spirit). Note the precise language:

        "Proceeding from the Father" (ἐκ τοῦ πατρὸς ἐκπορευόμενον): This is the classic formula based on John 15:26, affirming the Father as the sole eternal source or cause of the Spirit's personhood.

        "Communicated through the Son" (δι' υἱοῦ μεταδιδόμενον): This is the classic Eastern understanding of the Son's role in the Spirit's mission. The Spirit proceeds eternally from the Father alone but is revealed, sent, and given to creation through the Son. This formula preserves the Father's monarchy while affirming the intimate and inseparable relationship of the Son and Spirit.

You have located a foundational text from the last of the great Greek Church Fathers, a passage that summarizes the Trinitarian faith of the ecumenical councils.

fr: L'Esprit Saint est la puissance du Père qui révèle le secret de la divinité, procédant du Père par le Fils — d'une manière que Lui seul connaît — et non par mode de génération...
en: And the Holy Spirit is the power of the Father revealing the hidden mysteries of his divinity, proceeding from the Father through the Son in a manner known to himself, but different from that of generation [ibid., 12].
greek: Τὸ δὲ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον ἐκφαντορικὴ τοῦ κρυφίου τῆς θεότητος δύναμις τοῦ πατρός, ἐκ πατρὸς μὲν δι' υἱοῦ ἐκπορευομένη, ὡς οἶδεν, οὐ γεννητῶς...
context:
Additional Relevant Context

The full text you provided is even more valuable because it shows exactly what St. John is doing in this chapter. He is systematically outlining the distinctive properties (idiomata) of each of the three divine Persons to show how they are distinct from one another, yet united in a single divine essence.

Here is the context based on the full passage you found:

    The Father as Sole Cause: St. John begins by defining the Father as the "super-essential sun," the "fountain of goodness," and the "abyss of essence." Critically, he calls the Father the source who is a "begetter of the Word (the Son)" and, "through the Word, the producer of the revealing Spirit." For St. John, and for Orthodox theology as a whole, the Father is the sole source, principle, and cause (αἰτία) within the Godhead.

    The Son as Begotten: The Son is defined by His relationship to the Father. He is the "begotten" Word, Wisdom, and Power of the Father. He is from the Father.

    The Holy Spirit as Proceeding (Your Quote): Your quote fits in here. The Holy Spirit is defined by His unique relationship to the Father.

        He is the "revealing power" (ἐκφαντορικὴ... δύναμις), manifesting the hidden things of God.

        His mode of origin is "procession" (ἐκπορευομένη), which is explicitly stated to be "not by way of generation" (οὐ γεννητῶς). This preserves the unique status of the Son as the only-begotten.

        His procession is "from the Father through the Son" (ἐκ πατρὸς... δι' υἱοῦ). This is the classic Orthodox formula. It means the Father is the sole ultimate source of the Spirit's being, but the Son is intimately involved in that eternal procession. This is distinct from the Western Filioque clause, which states the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son as from a single principle. St. John clarifies this later in the paragraph: the Spirit is called the "Spirit of the Son," not because He proceeds from the Son, but because He proceeds through Him from the Father, for "the Father alone is cause" (μόνος γὰρ αἴτιος ὁ πατήρ).

In essence, you have found a perfect, concise summary of the Cappadocian Fathers' Trinitarian theology, brilliantly synthesized and systematized by St. John of Damascus. This passage clearly defines the Father as the sole Cause, the Son as the eternally Begotten, and the Spirit as the eternally Proceeding.

fr:
...il aurait fallu que le jugement soit rendu selon le canon ecclésiastique, et non de cette manière.

Ignorez-vous que la coutume est de nous écrire en premier, afin que ce soit d’ici que soit défini ce qui est juste ? Par conséquent, si une telle suspicion venait à peser sur l’évêque de cette ville, il fallait en écrire à cette église.

Or, maintenant, après nous avoir laissés dans l’ignorance et avoir agi comme ils l’entendaient, ils voudraient que nous, qui n’avons pas examiné leur cause, nous donnions notre suffrage à leur décision. Telles ne sont pas les ordonnances de Paul, telle n’est pas la tradition que les pères nous ont transmise. Voilà une tout autre règle, une pratique nouvelle.

Car ce que nous avons reçu du bienheureux apôtre Pierre, c’est ce que je vous signifie.
en: POPE ST. JULIUS I [The] judgment [against Athanasius] ought to have been made, not as it was, but according to the ecclesiastical canon. Are you ignorant that the custom has been for word to be written first to us. and then for a just decision to be passed from this place [Rome]? If any suspicion rested upon the bishop there, notice of it ought to have been sent to the church here; but, after neglecting to inform us, and proceeding on their own authority as they pleased, they now desire to obtain our agreement with their decisions, though we never condemned him. Not so have the constitutions of Paul. or the traditions of the Fathers directed; this is another form of procedure, a novel practice . . [W]hat I write is for the common good. For what we have received from the blessed apostle Peter is what I signify to you [Letter on Behalf of Athanasius (A.D. 341), contained in St. Athanasius, Apology Against the Arians 1:2:35].
latin:
Oportuit juxta ecclesiasticum canonem, et non eo pacto, rem juditari.

    An ignoratis hanc esse consuetudinem, ut primum nobis scribatur, et hinc, quod justum est, decernatur? Sane si qua hujusmodi suspicio in illius urbis episcopum cadebat, ad hanc Ecclesiam illud rescribendum fuit.

    Nunc autem illi, re nobis non indicata, posteaquam quod libuit egere, nos quibus ea crimina explorata non sunt, sibi suffragatores esse volunt. Nequaquam talia sunt Pauli statuta, non hæc Patres tradiderunt: sed aliena est ista forma, novum hoc institutum.

    Nam quæ accepimus a beato Petro apostolo, ea vobis significo.
greek:
...ἔδει κατὰ τὸν ἐκκλησιαστικὸν κανόνα, καὶ μὴ οὕτως γεγενῆσθαι τὴν κρίσιν.

    Η ἀγνοεῖτε, ὅτι τοῦτο ἔθος ἦν, πρότερον γράφεσθαι ἡμῖν, καὶ οὕτως ἔνθεν ὁρίζεσθαι τὰ δίκαια; Εἰ μὲν οὖν τι τοιοῦτον ἦν ὑποπτευθὲν εἰς τὸν ἐπίσκοπον τὸν ἐκεῖ, ἔδει πρὸς τὴν ἐνταῦθα Ἐκκλησίαν γραφῆναι.

    νῦν δὲ οἱ ἡμᾶς μὴ πληροφορήσαντες, πράξαντες δὲ αὐτοὶ ὡς ἠθέλησαν, λοιπὸn καὶ ἡμᾶς οὐ καταγνόντας βούλονται συμψήφους εἶναι. Οὐχ οὕτως αἱ Παύλου διατάξεις, οὐχ οὕτως οἱ πατέρες παραδεδώκασιν· ἄλλος τύπος ἐστὶν οὗτος, καὶ καινὸν τὸ ἐπιτήδευμα.
   
    ἃ γὰρ παρειλήφαμεν παρὰ τοῦ μακαρίου Πέτρου τοῦ ἀποστόλου, ταῦτα καὶ ὑμῖν δηλῶ.
context:
Historical and Theological Context

This letter is one of the most important documents of the 4th century regarding the authority of the Bishop of Rome.

    The Situation: St. Athanasius, the great defender of the divinity of Christ against the Arian heresy, had been unjustly condemned and deposed by a synod of his enemies (mostly Arian and pro-Arian bishops) at Tyre in A.D. 335. He and other orthodox bishops appealed to Pope Julius I in Rome for justice.

    The Pope's Action: Pope Julius called for a council in Rome where both sides could be heard fairly. The accusers (the Eusebian party from the East) refused to attend and instead sent a disrespectful letter to Julius, challenging his right to interfere.

    This Letter's Purpose: The text you have found is from Pope Julius's firm, authoritative reply to the Eusebian bishops in A.D. 341. He is rebuking them for their uncanonical actions and explaining the proper procedure.

    Key Points of Authority:

        Violation of Canon Law: He first faults them for not following established Church law ("the ecclesiastical canon").

        The Roman Custom (consuetudo / ἔθος): He then asserts that there is a long-standing custom that major cases concerning bishops, especially from a major See like Alexandria, must be referred to Rome for a final judgment. This is a powerful claim to universal appellate jurisdiction.

        Petrine Authority: Crucially, he grounds this entire procedure not merely in custom but in the authority he has received directly from St. Peter the Apostle. He is not inventing a new rule; he is communicating the tradition passed down from the Prince of the Apostles.

This passage is therefore a cornerstone for understanding the early development and self-awareness of the Papacy's role as the final arbiter of doctrine and discipline in the universal Church.

fr: Il n'y aura jamais d'autre dieu, ô Tryphon, et il n'y en a jamais eu de toute éternité, hormis celui qui a créé et ordonné cet univers. Nous ne considérons pas non plus que nous ayons un dieu et vous un autre, mais qu'il s'agit de celui-là même qui a fait sortir vos pères de la terre d’Égypte d’une main forte et d’un bras étendu. Nous n'avons mis notre espérance en aucun autre — car il n'en existe pas — mais en celui-là même en qui vous aussi vous espérez, le Dieu d'Abraham, d'Isaac et de Jacob.
en: ST. JUSTIN MARTYR There will be no other God, Trypho, nor was there from eternity any other. but he who made this universe. Nor do we think that there is one God for us and another for you, but that he alone is God who led your fathers out of Egypt with a strong hand and a high arm. Nor have we trusted in any other, for there IS no other, but him, in whom you also have trusted, the God of Abraham, and of Isaac, and of Jacob [Dialogue with Trypho 11 C. A.D. 155)].
greek: Οὔτε ἔσται ποτὲ ἄλλος θεός, ὦ Τρύφων, οὔτε ἦν ἀπ' αἰῶνος ... πλὴν τοῦ ποιήσαντος καὶ διατάξαντος τόδε τὸ πᾶν. οὐδὲ ἄλλον μὲν ἡμῶν, ἄλλον δὲ ὑμῶν ἡγούμεθα θεόν, ἀλλ' αὐτὸν ἐκεῖνον τὸν ἐξαγαγόντα τοὺς πατέρας ὑμῶν ἐκ γῆς Αἰγύπτου ἐν χειρὶ κραταιᾷ καὶ βραχίονι ὑψηλῷ: οὐδ' εἰς ἄλλον τινὰ ἠλπίκαμεν, οὐ γὰρ ἔστιν, ἀλλ' εἰς τοῦτον εἰς ὃν καὶ ὑμεῖς, τὸν θεὸν τοῦ Ἀβραὰμ καὶ Ἰσαὰκ καὶ Ἰακώβ.
context:
Additional Relevant Context

The rest of the Greek text you provided is absolutely crucial. Immediately after establishing this common ground—that Christians and Jews worship the same one God—St. Justin makes a dramatic pivot to explain the fundamental difference.

The argument unfolds in these steps:

1. The Point of Departure: The Law of Moses is Not the Way

Justin immediately follows the quote by saying:

    "But we have not hoped through Moses or through the Law; for then we would have done the same thing as you."

    (ἠλπίσαμεν δὲ οὐ διὰ Μωυσέως οὐδὲ διὰ τοῦ νόμου: ἦ γὰρ ἂν τὸ αὐτὸ ὑμῖν ἐποιοῦμεν.)

This is the core of his argument. He agrees on who God is but disagrees on how humanity is to be saved and united with Him.

2. The New Law and the New Covenant

Justin then argues that the Law of Moses was temporary and particular, whereas Christ has established a universal and eternal covenant.

    "For I have read, O Trypho, that there would be a final law and a covenant more sovereign than all, which now all men must keep who seek the inheritance of God. For the law given at Horeb is already old and for you alone, but this one is for all, absolutely."

He is declaring that the Mosaic Covenant has been superseded by the New Covenant in Christ.

3. Proof from the Jewish Prophets

To prove his point from Scripture that Trypho would accept, Justin quotes two key passages:

    Isaiah 51:4-5: "...for a law will go forth from me, and my judgment for a light to the nations... the nations will hope in my arm."

    Jeremiah 31:31-32: "Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, not like the covenant which I made with their fathers..."

By using these prophets, Justin argues that the Jewish scriptures themselves predicted the obsolescence of the Mosaic Law and the coming of a new, universal covenant for all nations.

4. The Climax: The Church is the New Israel

Finally, Justin makes his most radical claim: the Christians, gathered from all nations through the crucified Christ, are the true fulfillment of God's promises.

    "For the true, spiritual Israel, and the descendants of Judah, Jacob, Isaac, and Abraham... are we, who have been led to God through this crucified Christ."

He redefines what it means to be "Israel," shifting the identity from ethnic lineage to faith in Christ, just as Abraham himself was justified by faith.

In Summary: The full passage you provided is a perfect example of early Christian apologetics. Justin begins by building a bridge of common ground (monotheism), then walks across it to deliver his main point: that Christ is the fulfillment of the prophecies, the bringer of the New Covenant, and the founder of the true, spiritual Israel.

fr:
Quant à nous, nous observerions même cette circoncision de la chair, ainsi que les sabbats et absolument toutes les fêtes, si nous n’avions pas su la raison pour laquelle cela vous a été prescrit, à savoir : à cause de vos iniquités et de la dureté de votre cœur. . . . Et c’est en signe, comme je l’ai déjà dit, et à cause de vos injustices et de celles de vos pères, que Dieu vous a ordonné d’observer le sabbat et qu’il a ajouté les autres préceptes...

...comment se fait-il, Tryphon, que nous n’observions pas même ce qui ne nous cause aucun tort, je veux parler de la circoncision charnelle, des sabbats et des fêtes ?
en: [WJe too would observe the fleshly circumcision, and the Sabbaths, and in short all the feasts, if we did not know for what reason they were enjoined [on] you-namely, on account of your transgressions and the hardness of your heart. . . . [H]ow is it, Trypho, that we would not observe those rites that do not harm us-I speak of fleshly circumcision and Sabbaths and feasts? . . . God enjoined you to keep the Sabbath, and imposed on you other precepts for a sign, as I have already said, on account of your unrighteousness and that of your fathers [Dialogue with Trypho 18, 21 (c. A.D. 155)].
greek:
ἡμεῖς γὰρ καὶ ταύτην ἂν τὴν περιτομὴν τὴν κατὰ σάρκα καὶ τὰ σάββατα καὶ τὰς ἑορτὰς πάσας ἁπλῶς ἐφυλάσσομεν, εἰ μὴ ἔγνωμεν δι' ἣν αἰτίαν καὶ ὑμῖν προσετάγη, τοῦτ' ἔστι διὰ τὰς ἀνομίας ὑμῶν καὶ τὴν σκληροκαρδίαν. . . .     Καὶ ὅτι διὰ τὰς ἀδικίας ὑμῶν καὶ τῶν πατέρων ὑμῶν εἰς σημεῖον, ὡς προέφην, καὶ τὸ σάββατον ἐντέταλται ὁ θεὸς φυλάσσειν ὑμᾶς καὶ τὰ ἄλλα προστάγματα προσετετάχει...

    ...πῶς οὐχὶ καὶ τὰ μηδὲ βλάπτοντα ἡμᾶς, περιτομὴν δὲ σαρκικὴν λέγω καὶ σάββατα καὶ τὰς ἑορτάς, ἐφυλάσσομεν, ὦ Τρύφων;
context:
Additional Relevant Context

The block of text you provided (Chapters 18-21) contains the core of St. Justin's argument for why Christians do not observe the ceremonial precepts of the Mosaic Law. The context is a debate with Trypho, a learned Jew, who has challenged the Christians on this very point.

Here is the flow of Justin's argument across these chapters:

1. Chapter 18: The Law as a Remedial Measure for Israel.
Justin lays out his central thesis: The ceremonial laws (circumcision, Sabbath, feasts, dietary rules) were not given as universal and eternal requirements for righteousness. They were given specifically to the Jewish people for a remedial reason: "on account of your transgressions and the hardness of your heart." He makes a powerful rhetorical point: Christians are willing to suffer martyrdom for their faith. Why would they refuse to observe something as simple as the Sabbath if they believed it was God's universal will? The fact that they don't shows that they understand its purpose was temporary and specific to Israel.

2. Chapter 19: The Witness of the Righteous before Moses.
This is a classic argument used by the early Church Fathers. To prove that the Mosaic Law was not the only path to righteousness, Justin lists numerous figures who were considered righteous by God before the Law was given at Sinai. These include:

    Adam, Abel, Enoch, Lot, and Noah: All were uncircumcised and did not keep the Sabbath, yet they were pleasing to God.

    Melchizedek: He was an uncircumcised priest to whom Abraham himself, the father of circumcision, paid tithes.
    This proves that God's favor is not dependent on these physical rites.

3. Chapter 20: The Purpose of the Dietary Laws.
Justin applies the same logic to the dietary restrictions. He argues they were not given because certain animals are inherently "unclean," but to constantly remind the Israelites of God, since they were "prone and quick to depart from the knowledge of Him." He explicitly links this to their apostasy with the golden calf in the desert. The laws were a pedagogical tool for a people prone to idolatry.

4. Chapter 21: The Prophetic Proof from Ezekiel.
Justin concludes his argument by bringing in the testimony of the prophet Ezekiel. He quotes Ezekiel 20, which explicitly states that the Sabbath was given as a "sign" (σημεῖον) between God and Israel. This reinforces his point that it was a specific marker for a particular covenant, not a universal moral law. He then delivers his most powerful scriptural proof by quoting a shocking verse from Ezekiel 20:25:

    "And I gave them precepts that were not good, and ordinances in which they shall not live."

Justin uses this to argue that God, dealing with a rebellious people, gave them a harsh law that, while holy, was a law of discipline rather than the ultimate law of life and grace that would come through Christ.

In essence, Justin's entire argument is that the ceremonial law was a temporary and pedagogical covenant for Israel, made necessary by their sinfulness. With the coming of Christ and the establishment of the New Covenant, the "signs" of the old one have been fulfilled and are no longer necessary for the People of God.

fr: C'est pourquoi, au sujet des sacrifices que vous offriez en ce temps-là, Dieu déclare, comme je l'ai dit précédemment, par Malachie, l'un des douze : « Je n'ai nulle complaisance en vous, dit le Seigneur, et je n'accepterai pas les sacrifices de vos mains ; car du lever du soleil jusqu'à son couchant, mon nom est glorifié parmi les nations. En tout lieu, un encens est offert à mon nom, ainsi qu'un sacrifice pur, car mon nom est grand parmi les nations, dit le Seigneur. Vous, au contraire, vous le profanez. » S'agissant des sacrifices qui sont offerts en tout lieu par nous, les nations – à savoir le pain de l'eucharistie et, de même, la coupe de l'eucharistie –, il prophétise alors à leur sujet...
en: ST. JUSTIN MARTYR Hence God speaks by the mouth of Malachi, one of the twelve [prophets ], as I said before, about the sacrifices at that time presented by you: I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord; and I will not accept your sacrifices at your hands: for, from the rising of the sun unto the going down of the same, my name has been glorified among the Gentiles, and in every place incense is offered to my name, and a pure offering: for my name is great among the Gentiles, says the Lord: but you profane it" [Mal 1:10-12]. [So] he then speaks of those Gentiles, namely us, who in every place offer sacrifices to him, that iS, the bread of the Eucharist, and also the cup of the Eucharist [Dialogue with Trypho 41 (C. A.D. 155)7.
greek: ...ὅθεν περὶ μὲν τῶν ὑφ' ὑμῶν τότε προσφερομένων θυσιῶν λέγει ὁ θεός, ὡς προέφην, διὰ Μαλαχίου, ἑνὸς τῶν δώδεκα: Οὐκ ἔστι θέλημά μου ἐν ὑμῖν, λέγει κύριος, καὶ τὰς θυσίας ὑμῶν οὐ προσδέξομαι ἐκ τῶν χειρῶν ὑμῶν: διότι ἀπὸ ἀνατολῆς ἡλίου ἕως δυσμῶν τὸ ὄνομά μου δεδόξασται ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσι, καὶ ἐν παντὶ τόπῳ θυμίαμα προσφέρεται τῷ ὀνόματί μου καὶ θυσία καθαρά, ὅτι μέγα τὸ ὄνομά μου ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσι, λέγει κύριος, ὑμεῖς δὲ βεβηλοῦτε αὐτό. περὶ δὲ τῶν ἐν παντὶ τόπῳ ὑφ' ἡμῶν τῶν ἐθνῶν προσφερομένων αὐτῷ θυσιῶν, τοῦτ' ἔστι τοῦ ἄρτου τῆς εὐχαριστίας καὶ τοῦ ποτηρίου ὁμοίως τῆς εὐχαριστίας, προλέγει τότε...
context:
Additional Relevant Content and Context

The rest of the Greek text you provided is crucial for understanding St. Justin's full argument. He is using a method called typology, where people, events, and rituals in the Old Testament are seen as prefiguring the realities of the New Covenant.
1. Context from the Beginning of the Passage (Before the Malachi Quote)

    Καὶ ἡ τῆς σεμιδάλεως δὲ προσφορά... τύπος ἦν τοῦ ἄρτου τῆς εὐχαριστίας...

    "And the offering of fine flour... which was prescribed to be offered for those cleansed of leprosy, was a type (τύπος) of the bread of the Eucharist..."

Relevance: St. Justin doesn't just pull the Malachi prophecy out of thin air. He first establishes his method by pointing to an Old Testament ritual—the flour offering for a cleansed leper (Leviticus 14:10)—and explicitly states that it was a type, or prefigurement, of the Eucharistic bread. This sets the stage for his argument that Old Testament prophecies also point to the Eucharist.
2. Context from the End of the Passage (After the Malachi Quote)

    ἡ δὲ ἐντολὴ τῆς περιτομῆς, κελεύουσα τῇ ὀγδόῃ ἡμέρᾳ... τύπος ἦν τῆς ἀληθινῆς περιτομῆς, ἣν περιετμήθημεν... διὰ τοῦ ἀπὸ νεκρῶν ἀναστάντος τῇ μιᾷ τῶν σαββάτων ἡμέρᾳ...

    "And the commandment of circumcision, which commanded that infants be circumcised on the eighth day, was a type (τύπος) of the true circumcision by which we are circumcised from error and wickedness through Jesus Christ our Lord, who rose from the dead on the first day of the week..."

Relevance: After interpreting Malachi, Justin immediately provides another example of typology. He argues that circumcision on the eighth day prefigured Christian baptism and the new life received through Christ's resurrection on Sunday (which he refers to as the "eighth day," following the seven-day week). This reinforces that his interpretation of Malachi is part of a consistent interpretive framework for the entire Old Testament.
3. Theological Significance of the Passage

    The Eucharist as a Sacrifice: This is one of the earliest and most explicit non-biblical texts that identifies the Eucharist as a sacrifice (θυσία). This became a foundational doctrine for the Catholic and Orthodox Churches.

    Fulfillment of Prophecy: Justin's primary goal is to convince Trypho the Jew that Christianity is the true fulfillment of the Jewish scriptures. He uses the prophecy of Malachi to argue that God Himself foretold the rejection of the Temple sacrifices and their replacement by a new, universal, and "pure" sacrifice.

    Universality of the Church: The prophecy's reference to offerings "in every place" and "among the Gentiles" is key for Justin. It proves that the new covenant is not limited to Jerusalem or the Jewish people, but is global, celebrated by Christians everywhere.

fr:
...Je vais de nouveau rapporter les paroles prononcées par Moïse lui-même, à partir desquelles nous pouvons reconnaître sans le moindre doute qu'il s'est entretenu avec quelqu'un, un être distinct par le nombre et doué de raison. ...

...Mais cet Engendré, véritablement issu du Père avant toutes les créatures, était auprès du Père, et c'est avec lui que le Père s'entretient...
en: ST. JUSTIN MARTYR God speaks in the creation of man with the very same design, in the following words: "Let us make man after our image and likeness.' I shall quote again the words narrated by Moses himself, from which we can indisputably learn that [God] conversed with someone distinct from himself and also rational being. But this offspring who was truly brought forth from the Father, was with the Father before all the creatures, and the Father communed with him [Dialogue with Trypho 62 (c. A.D. 155)].
greek:
...λόγους τοὺς εἰρημένους ὑπ' αὐτοῦ τοῦ Μωυσέως πάλιν ἱστορήσω, ἐξ ὧν ἀναμφιλέκτως πρός τινα, καὶ ἀριθμῷ ὄντα ἕτερον καὶ λογικὸν ὑπάρχοντα, ὡμιληκέναι αὐτὸν ἐπιγνῶναι ἔχομεν. ...

    ...ἀλλὰ τοῦτο τὸ τῷ ὄντι ἀπὸ τοῦ πατρὸς προβληθὲν γέννημα πρὸ πάντων τῶν ποιημάτων συνῆν τῷ πατρί, καὶ τούτῳ ὁ πατὴρ προσομιλεῖ...
context:
Additional Relevant Content and Context

In this chapter, St. Justin Martyr is making a sophisticated argument to his Jewish dialogue partner, Trypho. His primary goal is to prove from the Hebrew Scriptures that the God who created the world is not a solitary monad, but that He had a divine companion with whom He spoke. This companion, Justin argues, is the Son or Logos of God.

Here is a step-by-step breakdown of Justin's argument in the full text you provided:

1. The Primary Proof-Text: Genesis 1:26
Justin begins by quoting the creation of man: "Let us make man in our image and likeness." He emphasizes the plural pronouns ("us," "our") as evidence that God the Father was speaking to another person.

2. Anticipating and Refuting Jewish Interpretations
Justin is a skilled debater. He knows what Trypho will say, so he addresses the common Jewish interpretations of this verse first:

    Objection 1: God was speaking to Himself. Justin dismisses this as illogical.

    Objection 2: God was speaking to the elements (earth, water, etc.). Justin also finds this absurd.

    Objection 3 (The most common one): God was speaking to the angels. This is the main argument he needs to defeat.

3. The Knock-Down Argument: Genesis 3:22
To demolish the "God spoke to angels" theory, Justin introduces a second, even more powerful proof-text. After the Fall, God says, "Behold, Adam has become like one of us."

    Justin's Logic: God would never say this to angels. To say "one of us" implies that the speaker and the one spoken to are of the same kind or class. It would be blasphemous for God to group Himself with created angels in this way.

    His Conclusion: Therefore, the Person God was speaking to must also be divine. This proves He was speaking to "someone who was numerically distinct from himself and also a rational being" of a divine nature.

4. The Theological Climax: Identifying the Divine Companion
Having proven that God spoke to another divine being, Justin then identifies who this being is:

    "But this offspring who was truly brought forth from the Father, was with the Father before all the creatures, and the Father communed with him."

Here, Justin identifies this divine companion as the Logos (Word/Reason) of God, whom he calls an "offspring" (γέννημα) "brought forth" (προβληθὲν) from the Father before all creation. This is a cornerstone of Logos-Christology. He explicitly connects this figure to "Wisdom" from the book of Proverbs.

5. Further Corroboration: Joshua 5
As a final piece of evidence, Justin brings up the account of Joshua meeting the "Commander of the army of the LORD." He points out that this figure accepted worship from Joshua and that the ground He stood on was holy—actions and attributes appropriate only for God. Justin identifies this Commander as another appearance of the pre-incarnate Son.

In summary, this chapter is a masterclass in early Christian apologetics, demonstrating how the first Christian thinkers used the Hebrew Scriptures to argue for the plurality of Persons within the one Godhead, long before the formal language of the Trinity was developed at Nicaea.

fr: Car, comme il a été dit à Adam que le jour où il mangerait de l’arbre, ce jour-là il mourrait, nous avons reconnu qu’il n’a pas accompli mille ans. Nous avons aussi compris que la parole : « Un jour du Seigneur est comme mille ans », se rapporte à ce fait.
en: ST. JUSTIN MARTYR For as Adam was told that on the day he ate of the tree he would die. we know that he did not complete a thousand years. We have perceived, moreover, that the expression "The day of the Lord is as thousand years" is connected with this subject [Dialogue with Trypho 81 (c. A.D. 155)].
greek: ὡς γὰρ τῷ Ἀδὰμ εἴρητο, ὅτι ᾗ δ' ἂν ἡμέρᾳ φάγῃ ἀπὸ τοῦ ξύλου, ἐν ἐκείνῃ ἀποθανεῖται, ἔγνωμεν αὐτὸν μὴ ἀναπληρώσαντα χίλια ἔτη. συνήκαμεν καὶ τὸ εἰρημένον, ὅτι Ἡμέρα κυρίου ὡς χίλια ἔτη, εἰς τοῦτο συνάγειν.
context:
2. Additional Relevant Context

The passage you quoted is the interpretive key to the entire chapter. Justin Martyr is making a sophisticated argument for a literal 1000-year reign of Christ on earth (a belief known as premillennialism or chiliasm). Here is the flow of his logic in Chapter 81:

    Prophetic Basis (Isaiah): He begins by quoting a long passage from Isaiah 65, which describes a new heaven and a new earth where people will live long, peaceful lives in a renewed Jerusalem. This is his Old Testament foundation for a future, earthly kingdom.

    The "Tree of Life" and the 1000 Years: Justin focuses on a specific phrase from the Isaiah prophecy: "For as the days of the tree of life, so shall be the days of my people." He sees this as a mystical reference pointing back to Genesis and signifying a 1000-year period.

    The Adam Typology (Your Quote): This is where your quote comes in. Justin uses a typological argument to prove that a "divine day" equals 1000 years.

        The Problem: God told Adam, "in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die" (Gen 2:17). But Adam lived to be 930 years old. How could he die "on that day"?

        Justin's Solution: He connects this with Psalm 90:4 (and 2 Peter 3:8), "a day of the Lord is as a thousand years." Therefore, the "day" on which Adam was sentenced to die was a 1000-year period. Since Adam died at 930, he did indeed die within that first divine day, thus fulfilling the prophecy in a mystical sense.

    New Testament Confirmation (St. John): Having established his interpretive principle, Justin provides New Testament proof. He explicitly refers to the Book of Revelation:

        "And further, a certain man among us, whose name was John, one of the apostles of Christ, in a revelation made to him, prophesied that those who have believed in our Christ would spend a thousand years in Jerusalem."

    Distinction from the Final State: Justin is careful to distinguish this 1000-year earthly kingdom from the final, eternal state. He concludes the chapter by noting that after the millennium, the universal and eternal resurrection will occur, at which point believers will be "like the angels," no longer marrying or giving in marriage (quoting Jesus from Luke 20:35-36).

In summary, your quote is the central pillar of Justin's argument, using Adam's lifespan to prove the "day = 1000 years" principle, which he then applies to prophecies about the Millennial Kingdom.

fr: Car il existe parmi nous, jusqu'à ce jour encore, des dons prophétiques. Par là, vous devriez comprendre vous-mêmes que les dons qui se trouvaient autrefois au sein de votre peuple nous ont été transférés.
en: ST. JUSTIN MARTYR For the prophetical gifts remain with us [Christians], even to the present time. And hence you [Jews] ought to understand that [the gifts] formerly among your nation have been transferred to us [Dialogue with Trypho 82 (c. A.D. 155)].
greek: Παρὰ γὰρ ἡμῖν καὶ μέχρι νῦν προφητικὰ χαρίσματά ἐστιν, ἐξ οὗ καὶ αὐτοὶ συνιέναι ὀφείλετε, ὅτι τὰ πάλαι ἐν τῷ γένει ὑμῶν ὄντα εἰς ἡμᾶς μετετέθη.
context:
Additional Relevant Context

This single sentence is packed with theological and historical importance. Here's what makes it so significant, based on the rest of the chapter you provided and the broader context of Justin's work.
Immediate Context (What Justin says next)

Immediately after making this bold claim, Justin anticipates Trypho's objection by qualifying his statement. He shows that the transfer of gifts is not perfect or without problems:

    The Parallel of False Prophets: Justin immediately adds, "Just as there were false prophets among the holy prophets who were with you, so now there are also many false teachers among us." This is a crucial admission. He isn't claiming the Christian community is perfect, but that it mirrors the experience of ancient Israel, which had both true and false prophets.

    Christ's Prophecy as Proof: He argues that the existence of these false teachers was actually prophesied by Christ himself. This turns a potential weakness (heresy and division) into a strength, framing it as yet another fulfillment of prophecy and a sign of Christ's divine foreknowledge.

    The Moral Obligation to Speak: Justin explains why he is engaging in this debate. He cites the prophet Ezekiel's duty as a "watchman" for the house of Israel.
