Θεὸς γὰρ ὢν ὁμοῦ τε καὶ ἄνθρωπος τέλειος ὁ αὐτὸς, τὰς δύο αὐτοῦ οὐσίας ἐπιστώσατο ἡμῖν· τὴν μὲν θεότητα αὐτοῦ, διὰ τῶν σημείων ἐν τῇ τριετίᾳ τῇ μετὰ τὸ βάπτισμα· τὴν δὲ ἀνθρωπότητα αὐτοῦ, ἐν τοῖς τριάκοντα χρόνοις τοῖς πρὸ τοῦ βαπτίσματος. Ἐν οἷς διὰ τὸ ἀτελὲς, τὸ κατὰ σάρκα ἀπέκρυβε τὰ σημεῖα τῆς αὐτοῦ θεότητος, καίπερ Θεὸς ἀληθὴς προαιώνιος ὑπάρχων.
context:
Context and Theological Significance

This fragment is treasured by theologians for several reasons:

    Extreme Antiquity: Written around 170 A.D., this is one of the earliest and clearest non-scriptural affirmations of Christ's two natures. It predates the Council of Nicaea by 150 years and the Council of Chalcedon by nearly 300 years.

    Proto-Chalcedonian Language: Melito's use of the phrase "two natures" (δύο οὐσίας) is remarkably precise for such an early period. He clearly distinguishes between the divinity and the humanity, assigning different periods of Christ's life as primary proofs for each, while insisting they belong to the one and same person (ὁ αὐτός - "the same").

    Anti-Docetic: His insistence that Christ's human nature was "real and not phantasmal" (ἀληθῆ καὶ οὐ φαντασιώδη) is a direct refutation of Docetism, an early heresy that claimed Christ only appeared to be human.

You've identified a foundational text in the development of orthodox Christology.

fr: Si… l’homme est créé à partir du néant, comment, à plus forte raison, ne redeviendra-t-il pas homme à partir de l’homme qui a déjà existé ? En effet, il est moins difficile de reconstituer ce qui a déjà existé et a été dissous, que de produire à partir du néant ce qui n’a encore jamais été.
en: ST. METHODIUS OF PHILIPPI [In fact out of nothing, man is brought into being, [so] how much rather shall man spring into being again out of a previously existing man? For it is not so difficult to make anything anew after it has once existed and fallen into decay, as to produce out of nothing what has never existed [Discourse on the Resurrection 1:14 (c. A.D. 300)].
latin: ...denique ex nihilo, homo fit : qui non potius ex homine qui fuit, fuerit rursus resurrectione homo? Minus quippe videtur difficile, ut quod fuit et est dissolutum, denuo componatur et reparatum fiat, quam ut quod nondum fuit, ex nihilo prodeat.
greek: Εἰ... ἐκ τοῦ μηδενὸς ἄνθρωπος γίνεται, πῶς οὐχὶ μᾶλλον ἐκ τοῦ ἤδη ὑπάρξαντος ἀνθρώπου ἄνθρωπος ἔσται αὖθις ὁ ἄνθρωπος; Οὐ γὰρ οὕτω [χαλεπὸν] μετὰ τὸ ἤδη γεγενημένον καὶ διαλυθὲν ποιῆσαι πάλιν, ὡς μηδέπω γεγενημένον ἐκ τοῦ μὴ ὄντος κατασκευάσαι.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Author and Work: The quote is from St. Methodius of Philippi (often called Methodius of Olympus), an early 3rd-century bishop and martyr. The work is his Discourse on the Resurrection (Greek: Aglaophon, sive De Resurrectione). He was a significant theologian known for opposing the teachings of Origen on certain points, especially regarding the nature of the resurrected body.

    The Core Argument (A Fortiori): St. Methodius's logic is powerful and intuitive. He argues:

        The Greater Miracle (Creation): God creates a complex human being ex nihilo ("out of nothing"). In context, he means from a tiny drop of seed (σταγόνος βραχείας), which for all practical purposes is "nothing" compared to the final result. This is the harder, more astonishing act.

        The Lesser Miracle (Re-creation): The resurrection involves re-creating a human from matter that has already existed and possessed human form (a corpse).

        Conclusion: If God can perform the greater miracle of initial creation, He can certainly perform the lesser miracle of resurrection.

    Immediate Context in the Chapter: As your provided text shows, Methodius immediately follows this logical point with a vivid illustration. He asks his audience to imagine two things placed side-by-side: a drop of seed and a dead body. He asks, which one would you believe is more likely to become a living human being? The obvious answer is the body, which already has shape, size, and substance (σχῆμα καὶ μέγεθος καὶ ὑπόστασιν). Yet, God brings forth a human from the seed. Therefore, it is even more plausible that He will raise the body.

    Source of Your Text: The parallel Greek and Latin columns, along with the scholarly footnotes, are characteristic of Jacques-Paul Migne's Patrologia Graeca (PG). This passage is found in PG Volume 18, columns 285-288.

fr: Car unique est le règne du Père, du Fils et du Saint-Esprit, de même que sont uniques leur substance et leur souveraineté. C'est pourquoi, d'une seule adoration, nous adorons l'unique Divinité en trois hypostases, sans principe, incréée, infinie et sans successeur. En effet, jamais le Père ne cessera d'être Père, ni le Fils d'être Fils et roi, ni l'Esprit Saint d'être ce qu'il est dans son hypostase. Car rien de la Trinité ne sera jamais diminué, ni dans son éternité, ni dans sa communion et son règne.
en: ST. METHODIUS OF PHILIPPI For the kingdom of the Father, of the Son. and of the Holy Spirit is one, even as their substance iS one and their dominion one. Therefore with one and the same adoration we worship the one Deity in three Persons, subsisting without beginning, uncreated, without end, and to which there is no successor. For neither will the Father ever cease to be the Father, nor the Son to be the Son and king, nor the Holy Spirit to be what in substance and personality he is. For nothing of the Trinity will be diminished, either in respect of eternity, communion, or sovereignty [ Oration on the Psalms 5 (c. A.D. 300)].
latin: Unum quippe regnum est Patris, et Filii, et Spiritus sancti, quemadmodum etiam est una substantia unaque dominatio. Unde et una adoratione unam trine subsistentem Deitatem colimus, principii expertem, increatam, interminabilem et cui successor minime sit. Nam neque Pater unquam desierit esse Pater, neque Filius esse Filius et rex, neque Spiritus sanctus esse quod subsistentia et sua ipse persona est. Nihil enim Trinitatis aut æternitate, aut communione et regno minuendum est.
greek: Μία γὰρ ἡ βασιλεία Πατρὸς καὶ Υἱοῦ καὶ ἁγίου Πνεύματος· ὥσπερ καὶ μία οὐσία, καὶ μία κυριότης. Ὅθεν καὶ μίᾳ προσκυνήσει λατρεύομεν μίαν τρισυπόστατον Θεότητα, ἄναρχον, ἄκτιστον, ἀπέραντον καὶ ἀδιάδοχον. Οὔτε γὰρ ὁ Πατὴρ παύσηταί ποτε τοῦ εἶναι Πατήρ· οὔτε ὁ Υἱὸς τοῦ εἶναι Υἱὸς καὶ βασιλεύς· οὔτε δὲ τὸ Πνεῦμα τὸ Ἅγιον τοῦ εἶναι τοῦτο ὅπερ ἐστὶ τῇ ὑποστάσει. Οὐδὲν γὰρ τῆς Τριάδος ἐλαττωθήσεται, ἢ τῆς ἀϊδιότητος, ἢ τῆς κοινότητος καὶ βασιλείας.
context:
Context from the Surrounding Text (What You Found)

The full page you provided is magnificent because it shows how this dense theological statement functions within a sermon.

    Before Your Quote (The Sermon): The author is delivering a homily on Palm Sunday. He contrasts the welcome Jesus received from the children with the rejection from the elders. He builds up a series of acclamations: "Blessed is he who comes as God, the King of glory... Blessed is he who comes in humility, and will come again in glory." He is establishing the divine kingship of Christ.

    Leading into Your Quote (The Anti-Heretical Point): Right before your passage, the author makes a crucial point against Arianism (or similar heresies). He insists that Christ's kingdom is "co-eternal and pre-eternal" (συναΐδιον καὶ προαιώνιον) with the Father's. He states that Christ's kingship is not something that began or was added to him; it is his by nature (φυσικὴν καὶ ἰδιόκτητον).

    Your Quote (The Theological Foundation): To prove this point, he then delivers the dense Trinitarian statement you were looking for. This passage functions as the dogmatic bedrock for his entire sermon. Christ is an eternal king because the kingdom, substance, and dominion of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one and the same, eternal and undiminished.

    After Your Quote (The Direct Confrontation): Immediately after the creed-like statement, the author turns directly to his opponent: "Do not blaspheme the kingdom of Christ, O heretic (αἱρετικὲ), lest you dishonor the One who begot him." He quotes Scripture ("He who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father") to seal his argument.

In short, you have found a perfect example of how a 4th-century preacher would weave a high-level, precise Trinitarian formula directly into a sermon to both edify the faithful and refute heretics. Excellent find

fr: Car tout t’est soumis comme à son principe et à son auteur : comme à celui qui a fait passer l’univers du néant à l’être et a donné une constitution solide aux réalités instables ; comme à la force qui assure la cohésion et la protection de la création ; comme à l’artisan des natures diverses ; comme à celui qui gouverne le monde d’une main toute-puissante et infiniment sage ; comme au rythme de tout ordre harmonieux ; comme au lien indissoluble de la concorde et de la paix.
en: ST. METHODIUS OF PHILIPPI [A]lI things are placed under you as their cause and author, as he who brought all things into being out of nothing, and gave coherence to what was unstable: as the connecting band and preserver of what has been brought into being; as the framer of things by nature different; as he who, with wise and steady hand, holds the helm of the universe; as the very principle of all good order: as the unbreakable bond of concord and peace [Oration on Simeon and Anna 6 (c. A.D. 300)]
latin: Tibi enim substrata sunt omnia ut causæ et auctori, ut ei qui universa ex nihilo ad esse deduxit, rebusque instabilibus firmam constitutionem tribuit: tanquam rerum in esse deductarum nexui commissuræque, atque præsidio: tanquam natura diversorum opifici: velut ei, qui manu prorsus fortissima sapientissimaque moderatur universa: velut compositi cujuscunque ordinis rhythmo et concinnitati: ut concordiæ pacisque indissolubili vinculo.
greek: Ὑποβέβληται γάρ σοι τὰ πάντα ὡς αἰτίῳ· ὡς παραγαγόντι τὰ ὅλα ἐκ μὴ ὄντων εἰς τὸ εἶναι, καὶ σύστασιν εὐπαγῆ τοῖς ἀστάτοις παρασχόντι· ὡς συνοχῇ καὶ φρουρᾷ τῶν παρενηνεγμένων· ὡς φύσεων διαφόρων δημιουργῷ· ὡς οἰακίζοντι παλάμῃ παναλκεστάτῃ καὶ πανσοφωτάτῃ τὰ σύμπαντα· ὡς εὐταξίας ἁπάσης ῥυθμῷ· ὡς συμφωνίας καὶ εἰρήνης ἀῤῥαγεῖ συνδέσμῳ.
context:
Author and Work: St. Methodius of Philippi (also known as Methodius of Olympus, d. c. 311 AD) was a bishop, theologian, and martyr. He is known for his sophisticated Greek prose and for being one of the first major theological opponents of Origen's more speculative ideas. The work, Oration on Simeon and Anna, is a homily celebrating the Feast of the Presentation of the Lord (also called the Meeting of the Lord, or Hypapante).

Theological Context: The passage is part of a long, poetic prayer or hymn placed on the lips of Simeon as he holds the infant Christ in the Temple. Methodius uses this moment to articulate a very high Christology, identifying the baby Jesus as the divine Logos, the eternal Son of God through whom the entire universe was created and is sustained.

Content and Significance: The quote is a chain of titles for Christ that describe His role as the Creator and Governor of the cosmos. It identifies Him as:

    The Cause and Author: The ultimate reason for all existence.

    The Creator ex nihilo: The one who brought everything into being from nothingness.

    The Sustainer: The one who gives stability and coherence to an otherwise unstable reality.

    The Unifier of Opposites: The "framer of things by nature different," who holds the diverse elements of creation together.

    The Divine Helmsman: The one who governs the universe with a "wise and steady hand" (literally, "all-strongest and all-wisest hand").

    The Principle of Order: The "rhythm" and harmony underlying all of creation's good order.

    The Bond of Peace: The unbreakable link that ensures concord and peace in the created order.

fr: Tandis donc que le vieillard exultait ainsi, rayonnant d'une allégresse divine, la sainte Mère de Dieu accomplissait de manière éclatante ce que le prophète Isaïe avait annoncé en figure.
en: While [Simeon] was thus exultant, and rejoicing with exceeding great and holy joy, what had before been spoken of in figure by the prophet Isaiah, the holy Mother of God now manifestly fulfilled [ Oration on Simeon and Anna 7 (c. A.D. 300)].
latin: Sic vero saliente sene, divinoque gaudio impensius exsultante; quod antea per figuram propheta Isaias fuerat vaticinatus, sacra Dei Mater perspicue re ipsa fecit.
greek: Χορεύοντος δὲ οὕτω τοῦ πρεσβύτου, καὶ γανυμένου τῇ θείᾳ εὐφρασίᾳ, τὰ κεχρηματισμένα τυπικῶς τῷ προφήτῃ Ἠσαΐᾳ, περιφανῶς ἡ ἱερὰ Θεομήτωρ ἐξετέλει.
context:
Additional Details and Context

This single sentence serves as the introduction to one of the most beautiful and theologically rich typological interpretations in early patristic literature.

    The Author and Work: St. Methodius (died c. 311 AD) was a bishop and martyr known for his sophisticated literary style and deep use of Scripture. This oration is a sermon on the Presentation of Jesus in the Temple, as described in Luke 2:25-35.

    The Central Typology (Isaiah 6): The "figure" from the prophet Isaiah that Methodius refers to is from Isaiah 6:6-7. In this passage, Isaiah sees the glory of the Lord, and a seraph takes a burning coal from the altar with a pair of tongs and touches it to Isaiah's lips to purify him from sin.

    The Unfolding of the Typology: The rest of the text you provided explains this typology in magnificent detail:

        Christ is the Divine Coal: Mary takes "that life-giving and ineffable coal, clothed in flesh" (ζωοποιὸν καὶ ἀνέκφραστον ἄνθρακα, σαρκωθέντα). Christ, in His divine nature, is like the purifying fire.

        Mary is the Altar: Christ the coal is taken "from her pure and all-blameless altar" (ἐκ τοῦ ἀχράντου καὶ παναμώμου αὐτῆς θυσιαστηρίου), referring to Mary's womb.

        Mary's Hands are the Tongs: She holds this divine "coal" and presents him to Simeon "as with tongs, by the clasp of her holy hands" (ὡς λαβίδι τῇ συζεύξει τῶν ἁγίων αὐτῆς χειρῶν).

    Significance for Marian Theology: This is an exceptionally early and powerful example of Marian theology. Mary is not merely a passive instrument but is identified with the holy altar of the temple. She is explicitly called Θεομήτωρ (Theomētōr), "Mother of God," a title that would be dogmatically affirmed over a century later at the Council of Ephesus.

    Literary Style: The long, beautiful speech that follows is a rhetorical device where Methodius imagines what the Mother of God would say to Simeon as she presents the Christ child. It is a profound meditation on the mystery of the Incarnation, not a historical account

fr:
Réjouis-toi pour toujours, toi, notre joie qui ne cesse jamais ; car c’est vers toi que je me tourne à nouveau. … Réjouis-toi, source de l’amour du Fils pour les hommes ; …

C’est pourquoi nous t’implorons, toi la plus excellente de toutes, qui tires ta gloire et ton assurance de tes honneurs de mère, de te souvenir de nous sans cesse, ô Toute-Sainte Mère de Dieu ; de nous qui tirons notre gloire de toi et qui, par des hymnes dignes de Dieu, célébrons ta mémoire toujours vivante et ineffaçable.
en: Hail to you forever, you Virgin Mother of God, our unceasing joy, for unto you do I again return. . . . Hail, you fount of the Son's love for man. Therefore we pray you, the most excellent among women, who boast in the confidence of your maternal honors, unceasingly to keep us in remembrance. O holy Mother of God, remember us, I say, who make our boast in you, and who in august hymns celebrate your memory, which will ever live, and never fade away [ibid., 14].
latin:
Salve in æternum, indesinens nostra laetitia [Dei Genitrix Virgo] : ad te enim rursus accurro. ...

    Salve, Filii in genus humanum, propensionis illius ac ejus humanitatis fons: ...

    Propterea te deprecamur omnium præstantissimam, maternisque honoribus fiducia gloriantem, ut indesinentem nostri memoriam, Dei Mater sanctissima, habeas : nostri, inquam, qui in te gloriamur, augustioribusque canticis perpetuo victuram et nullis desituram temporibus tui memoriam celebramus.
greek:
Χαίροις εἰς ἀεὶ ἡ ἄληκτος ἡμῶν χαρά· ἐπὶ σὲ γὰρ πάλιν ἀνατρέχομαι. ... Χαίροις, φιλανθρωπίας Υἱοῦ πηγή· ...

    Διὰ τοῦτο ἐκλιπαροῦμέν σε τὴν ἀμείνω πάντων, καὶ μητρῴαις ἐπαυχοῦσαν τιμαῖς καὶ παῤῥησίαις, μνήμην ἀδιάλειπτον ἡμῶν ποιοῦ, παναγία Θεοτόκε, καὶ εἰς σὲ κατακαλλυνομένων, καὶ ὕμνοις θεοπρεπέσι γεραιρόντων σου τὴν ἀείζωον καὶ ἀνεξάλειπτον μνήμην.
context:
Author & Work: The passage is from the Oratio de Simeone et Anna in diem occursus Domini et de sancta Deipara (Oration concerning Simeon and Anna on the Day of the Presentation of the Lord, and concerning the holy Mother of God).

    Citation: The standard citation for this work is Migne, Patrologia Graeca (PG) 18:381. Your reference, "[ibid., 14]," correctly points to Section 14 of this oration.

    Context: This homily was written for the feast of the Presentation of the Lord in the Temple (also known as the Meeting of the Lord, or Candlemas). The text is a beautiful example of early, highly developed Marian devotion. The author praises Mary with rich titles and confidently asks for her powerful intercession. The mention of Simeon in the text immediately following your quote confirms the homily's focus on this feast day.

    Note on Authorship: While this work is traditionally attributed to St. Methodius of Philippi (died c. 311 AD), many modern scholars believe it is from a later period, possibly the 5th to 8th centuries. The highly developed Marian theology and rhetorical style are often seen as more characteristic of a post-Ephesian (after 431 AD) author. Regardless of the exact author, it remains a significant and beautiful text within the patristic tradition.

    Theological Significance:

        Theotokos (Mother of God): The use of the title Παναγία Θεοτόκε (Panagia Theotoke / All-Holy Mother of God) is explicit and central.

        Intercession: The passage is a direct prayer for Mary's unceasing remembrance and intercession, highlighting a belief in her powerful role as an advocate for the faithful.

        Maternal Confidence: The phrase "who boast in the confidence of your maternal honors" (maternìsque honoribus fiducia gloriantem / μητρῴαις ἐπαυχοῦσαν τιμαῖς) beautifully captures the idea that Mary's power to intercede is directly linked to her unique status as the Mother of Christ.

fr: Réjouis-toi à jamais, notre joie qui ne finit pas ; c’est vers toi que je me tourne à nouveau. Tu es le commencement de notre fête ; tu en es le cœur ; tu en es l’achèvement. Tu es la perle de grand prix du Royaume, la source nourricière de toute sainteté, l’autel vivant du pain de vie. Réjouis-toi, trésor de l’amour de Dieu ; réjouis-toi, source de l’amour du Fils pour l’humanité. Tu as resplendi... par les flammes insoutenables d’un amour bouillonnant, en enfantant à la fin des temps celui qui fut conçu avant le commencement, et en manifestant le mystère caché et indicible : le Fils du Père invisible, l’arbitre de la paix, lui qui, paradoxalement, s’est fait plus petit que toute petitesse.
en: ST. METHODIUS OF PHILIPPI Hail to you forever, you Virgin Mother of God, our unceasing joy, for to you do I again return. You are the beginning of our feast; you are its middle and end; the pearl of great price that belongs to the kingdom; the fat of every victim, the living altar of the bread of life. Hail, you treasure of the love of God. Hail, you fount of the Son's love for man. You gleamed with the insupportable fires of a most fervent charity, bringing forth in the end what was conceived of you making manifest the mystery hidden and unspeakable, the invisible Son of the Father-the Prince of Peace, who in a marvelous manner showed himself as less than all littleness [ Oration on Simeon and Anna 14 (c. A.D. 300)].
latin: Salve in æternum, indesinens nostra laetitia [Dei Genitrix Virgo]: ad te enim rursus accurro. Τu nobis festæ lucis initium; tu medium, tu finis: pretiosissima regni margarita; vere totius victimæ adeps; animatum panis illius vitæ altare. Salve, dilectionis Dei thesaure: salve, Filii in genus humanum, propensionis illius ac ejus bumanitatis fons. ... Fulgurasti... importabilibus charitatis præferventis ignibus, eo in fine partu edito quod ante principium conceptum erat: palam exhibito, quod erat absconditum et inenarrabile sacramentum; invisibili illo Patris Filio, sequestro pacis, quippe admirabili quadam ratione, omni se parvitate minorem exhibuit.
greek: Χαίροις εἰς ἀεὶ ἡ ἄληκτος ἡμῶν χαρά· ἐπὶ σὲ γὰρ πάλιν ἀνατρέχομαι. Σὺ τῆς ἑορτῆς ἡμῶν ἀρχή· σὺ μεσότης· σὺ τέλος· ὁ πολύτιμος μαργαρίτης τῆς βασιλείας· τὸ ὄντως οὖθαρ πάσης ἁγιστείας· τὸ ἔμψυχον θυσιαστήριον τοῦ ἄρτου τῆς ζωῆς. Χαίροις, ἀγάπης Θεοῦ θησαυρέ· χαίροις, φιλανθρωπίας Υἱοῦ πηγή. Ήστραψας... πυρσοῖς ἀκαρτερήτοις ἀγάπης ὑπερζεούσης, τὸ πρὸ ἀρχῆς συλληφθὲν ἐν τῷ τέλει τεκοῦσα, φανερώσασα τὸ κρυπτὸν μυστήριον καὶ ἀλάλητον, τὸν ἀοράτου Πατρός Υἱόν, εἰρήνης βραβευτήν, πάσης γενόμενον ἥττονα βραχύτητος παραδόξως.
context:
2. Theological and Historical Significance

This passage is extremely important for several reasons, primarily for its advanced Marian theology at such an early date (around the year 300 AD, well over a century before the Council of Ephesus).

    Rich Marian Titles: The homily bestows a series of profound and poetic titles upon the Virgin Mary, demonstrating a well-developed sense of her unique role in salvation history. Key titles in your quote include:

        "Our unceasing joy" (ἡ ἄληκτος ἡμῶν χαρά): Highlighting her role as the source of the joy of the Gospel.

        "The living altar of the bread of life" (τὸ ἔμψυχον θυσιαστήριον τοῦ ἄρτου τῆς ζωῆς): A stunning Eucharistic image. Just as a stone altar holds the Eucharist, Mary's body held the living Bread from Heaven. She is a living, breathing altar.

        "Treasure of the love of God" (ἀγάπης Θεοῦ θησαυρέ): She contains and reveals God's love.

        "Fount of the Son's love for man" (φιλανθρωπίας Υἱοῦ πηγή): She is the source through which Christ's love for humanity entered the world.

    Early Use of Theotokos: While your specific quoted section does not contain the word, the full paragraph in the image does. A few lines later, Methodius prays: "Keep unceasing memory of us, O most holy Mother of God (παναγία Θεοτόκε)". This is one of the earliest surviving attestations of the title Theotokos ("God-bearer" or "Mother of God") in patristic literature, a title that would become the central point of contention at the Council of Ephesus in 431.

    Christological Paradox: The final lines beautifully capture the mystery of the Incarnation: "...the invisible Son of the Father—the Prince of Peace, who in a marvelous manner showed himself as less than all littleness." This expresses the core Christian belief in a God who is both infinitely great and infinitesimally small, a Prince who becomes a helpless infant.

fr:
Certaines femmes, au moyen de drogues et de breuvages, anéantissent jusque dans leurs entrailles la vie naissante, et commettent un parricide avant même d’enfanter. Et de telles pratiques, bien entendu, découlent des enseignements de vos dieux.

Pour nous, il n’est permis ni de voir un homicide, ni d’en entendre parler ; et nous avons le sang humain en une telle horreur que nous nous abstenons même du sang des animaux de boucherie dans nos aliments.
en: MINUCIUS FELIX There are some women who, by drinking medical preparations, extinguish the source of the future man in their bowels, and thus commit a parricide before they bring forth. And these things assuredly come down from the teaching of your gods. . . . To us it is not lawful either to see or to hear of homicide [Octavius 30 (c. A.D. 226)].
latin:
"Sunt quae in ipsis visceribus, medicaminibus et potis, originem futuri hominis exstinguant, et parricidium faciant antequam pariant. Et haec utique de deorum vestrorum disciplina descendunt. ...

    Nobis homicidium nec videre fas, nec audire; tantumque ab humano sanguine cavemus, ut nec edulium pecorum in cibis sanguinem noverimus."
context:
Additional Relevant Details
The Source

    Author: Minucius Felix (c. late 2nd – early 3rd century AD). He was an early Latin Christian apologist, likely a lawyer in Rome.

    Work: The Octavius. This work is one of the earliest and finest examples of Christian apologetics in Latin. It is written in the style of a Ciceronian dialogue between three friends:

        Caecilius Natalis: A pagan who voices the common accusations against Christians.

        Octavius Januarius: A Christian who refutes the pagan arguments and defends the Christian faith.

        Minucius Felix: The author himself, who acts as the judge of the debate.

    Citation: The passage is from Chapter 30 (Caput XXX). The column numbers (0333A, etc.) indicate your source is likely a printing of Migne's Patrologia Latina (PL), Volume 3.

The Context: Apologetic Reversal (Tu Quoque)

This passage is a prime example of a powerful rhetorical strategy used by early Christian apologists known as tu quoque (meaning "you, too"). The context is crucial:

    The Pagan Accusation: The chapter begins with Octavius addressing the most vile pagan slander: that Christians practiced ritual infanticide and cannibalism, supposedly killing an infant and drinking its blood as part of an initiation rite.

    The Denial and Reversal: Octavius doesn't just deny this horrific charge. He immediately turns the accusation of cruelty to children back onto the pagans themselves.

    Pagan Practices: He lists two common pagan practices:

        Infant Exposure: "You, I see, now expose your own sons to wild beasts and birds..." This refers to the widespread Roman practice of abandoning unwanted newborns to die of exposure.

        Abortion: This is your quoted passage, where he condemns abortion via potions and drugs (medicaminibus et potis).

    Blaming Pagan Religion: Critically, he blames these immoral acts on the pagans' own religion: "And these things assuredly come down from the teaching of your gods." He then cites the myth of Saturn devouring his own children and the historical reality of human sacrifice in Roman and other pagan cults.

Theological and Historical Significance

    Early Christian Condemnation of Abortion: This is one of the earliest and most forceful condemnations of abortion in Latin Christian literature. The language used is incredibly strong. Calling it parricidium (parricide—the murder of a close relative) elevates it to the level of the most heinous crimes imaginable in Roman society.

    A Comprehensive Pro-Life Ethic: The passage demonstrates that the early Christian respect for life was comprehensive. Octavius links the prohibition of abortion directly to a total rejection of bloodshed (homicidium), which also explains the early Christian refusal to attend gladiatorial games or eat food containing animal blood (a practice rooted in the Apostolic decree in Acts 15). The Christian ethic is presented as one that cherishes life from its very beginning.

fr:
Voyez donc comment, pour notre réconfort, la nature tout entière préfigure la résurrection future ! Le soleil se couche et renaît, les astres déclinent et reviennent, les fleurs meurent et reprennent vie, les arbustes après leur vieillesse se couvrent de feuilles, les semences ne germent qu'après s'être décomposées. Ainsi le corps en ce monde, comme les arbres en hiver, cache sa vitalité sous une aridité trompeuse. Pourquoi se hâter de le voir revivre et revenir, alors que l'hiver est encore dans sa rigueur ? Il nous faut attendre, à nous aussi, le printemps du corps.

Et je n'ignore pas que la plupart des gens, sous le poids de leur conscience, souhaitent le néant après la mort bien plus qu'ils n'y croient : ils préfèrent en effet être totalement anéantis plutôt que de renaître pour le châtiment.
en: MINUCIUS FELIX See, therefore, how for our consolation all nature suggests a future resurrection. The sun sinks down and arises, the stars pass away and return, the flowers die and revive again, after their wintry decay the shrubs resume their leaves, and seeds do not flourish unless they are rotted. Thus the body in the sepulchre is like the trees that in winter hide their verdure with a deceptive dryness. Why are you in haste for it to revive and return, while the winter is still raw? We must wait also for the springtime of the body. And I know that many, conscious of what they deserve, desire rather than believe that they shall be nothing after death; for they would prefer to be altogether extinguished, rather than to be restored for the purpose of punishment [Octavius 34 c. AD. 226)].
latin:
Vide adeo quam, in solatium nostri, resurrectionem futuram omnis natura meditetur! Sol demergit et nascitur, astra labuntur et redeunt, flores occidunt et reviviscunt, post senium arbusta frondescunt, semina non nisi corrupta revirescunt. Ita corpus in saeculo, ut arbores in hyberno, occultant virorem ariditate mentita. Quid festinas, ut cruda adhuc hyeme reviviscat et redeat? Expectandum nobis etiam corporis ver est.

    Et ignoro plerosque, conscientia meritorum, nihil se esse post mortem magis optare quam credere: malunt enim exstingui penitus, quam ad supplicia reparari.
context:
Additional Relevant Details
About the Author and the Work

    Author: Minucius Felix was a Roman lawyer and Christian apologist who likely wrote in the late 2nd or early 3rd century (the date c. A.D. 226 is a possible but not universally agreed-upon estimate).

    Work: The Octavius is a philosophical dialogue modeled on Cicero's De Natura Deorum. It is not a sermon or a theological treatise but a refined, literary conversation between three friends.

    Characters:

        Caecilius Natalis: A pagan who voices the common philosophical and popular objections to Christianity.

        Octavius Januarius: A Christian who eloquently refutes Caecilius's arguments and presents the Christian faith in a way that would appeal to a cultured Roman audience.

        Minucius Felix: The narrator and judge of the debate.

Context of the Passage (Chapter 34)

In the preceding chapters, Caecilius had mocked the Christian belief in the resurrection of the body as absurd and impossible. In Chapter 34, Octavius is giving his systematic rebuttal. His argument unfolds in three stages:

    Philosophical Precedent: He points out that even respected pagan philosophers like the Stoics and Plato taught about the world's eventual destruction by fire and its renewal.

    Argument from Divine Power: He argues that it is logically easier for God to re-create a body from existing elements than it was to create it from nothing in the first place.

    Argument from Natural Analogy: This is where your quote comes in. Octavius moves from abstract logic to the observable world, arguing that nature itself is a constant sermon on the theme of death and rebirth.

Analysis of the Quote's Argument

This passage is famous for its beautiful rhetoric and powerful logic.

    The Book of Nature: Octavius uses a series of powerful analogies from the natural world to make the resurrection seem not just possible, but natural and expected. The daily cycle of the sun, the return of the stars, the seasonal rebirth of flowers and trees, and the germination of seeds after they "rot" are all presented as divine lessons (omnis natura meditetur - "all nature suggests/meditates upon").

    "The Springtime of the Body": The most beautiful metaphor is corporis ver ("the springtime of the body"). Death is reframed as a temporary, necessary winter. Just as one would not expect a tree to bud in the middle of a harsh winter, one should not be impatient for the resurrection before its appointed time, the "springtime" appointed by God. The body in the tomb only has a "deceptive dryness" (ariditate mentita), hiding its life within.

    A Brilliant Psychological Insight: The final paragraph is a masterful rhetorical turn. Octavius argues that the true obstacle to belief in the resurrection is not intellectual but moral. He claims that many pagans desire annihilation (exstingui penitus) because their guilty conscience (conscientia meritorum) makes them fear a future judgment. They would rather cease to exist than be "restored for the purpose of punishment" (ad supplicia reparari). This cleverly shifts the burden of proof from the Christian defender to the conscience of the pagan objector.

fr:
Je n’ignore pas que nombreux sont ceux qui, ayant conscience de leurs fautes, préfèrent souhaiter n’être plus rien après la mort plutôt que de le croire : ils aiment mieux en effet être totalement anéantis que ramenés à la vie pour les supplices.

... Et ces tourments n’ont ni mesure, ni fin. Là, un feu savant brûle les membres et les restaure ; il les consume et les nourrit, de même que la foudre qui frappe les corps sans les anéantir...
en: MINUCIUS FELIX And I am not ignorant that many, conscious of what they deserve. desire rather than believe that they shall be nothing after death: for they would prefer to be altogether extinguished than to be restored for the purpose of punishment. There is no measure or termination to these torments. The intelligent fire burns the limbs and restores them, feeds on them and nourishes them, as the fires of the thunderbolts strike the bodies, and do not consume them [Octavius 34-35 (c. A.D. 226)].
latin:
Nec ignoro plerosque, conscientia meritorum, nihil se esse post mortem magis optare quam credere: malunt enim exstingui penitus, quam ad supplicia reparari.

    ... Nec tormentis aut modus ullus, aut terminus. Illic sapiens ignis membra urit et reficit; carpit et nutrit, sicut ignes fulminum corpora tangunt, nec absumunt...
context:
Additional Relevant Details
About the Author and Work

    Author: Minucius Felix was one of the earliest Latin Christian apologists, likely writing in the late 2nd or early 3rd century.

    Work: The Octavius is a Christian apology written in the form of a Ciceronian dialogue. The conversation takes place between three friends walking on the beach at Ostia: the pagan Caecilius Natalis, the Christian Octavius Januarius, and Minucius Felix himself, who acts as the judge. The text you have provided is part of Octavius's powerful defense of Christianity against Caecilius's attacks.

Context and Theological Significance of the Quote

This passage is a brilliant piece of apologetics concerning Christian eschatology (the theology of the end times, judgment, and the afterlife).

    A Psychological Argument for the Afterlife: The first part of the quote offers a sharp psychological insight. Octavius argues that the denial of an afterlife is not an intellectual position but a moral one. The wicked, burdened by a guilty conscience (conscientia meritorum), wish for annihilation because they fear judgment. They would rather cease to exist than be held accountable. This is a powerful rhetorical move that reframes atheism or materialism as a form of wishful thinking driven by fear.

    The Nature of Eternal Punishment: The second part provides one of the most vivid and paradoxical descriptions of hellfire in early Christian literature.

        sapiens ignis ("intelligent fire"): This is a striking and memorable phrase. The fire of hell is not a blind, consuming element like earthly fire. It is an instrument of divine justice that acts with purpose and intelligence.

        urit et reficit ("burns and restores"): This is the core paradox of eternal punishment. The fire punishes the resurrected body but does not annihilate it; instead, it perpetually restores the body so that the punishment can continue. This answers the logical objection of how a body could burn forever.

        carpit et nutrit ("feeds on and nourishes"): This poetic phrase powerfully reinforces the previous one. The fire is simultaneously destructive and sustaining, a torment that feeds itself by nourishing that which it torments.

        The Analogy of Lightning: The comparison to lightning (ignes fulminum) is clever. It uses a known natural phenomenon—where a lightning strike can kill or injure a person without necessarily incinerating the body—as an analogy to make the supernatural reality of eternal punishment more conceivable to his audience.

fr: ... cependant, il y a une lettre à Philémon, une à Tite et deux à Timothée, écrites par affection et par amour ; elles sont néanmoins tenues pour sacrées en l’honneur de l’église catholique, pour l’organisation de la discipline ecclésiastique. On fait aussi circuler une lettre aux Laodicéens et une autre aux Alexandrins, forgées au nom de Paul pour soutenir l’hérésie de Marcion, ainsi que plusieurs autres écrits qui ne peuvent être reçus dans l’église catholique ; car il ne convient pas de mélanger le fiel au miel. Par ailleurs, l’épître de Jude et les deux lettres sous le nom de Jean sont admises dans l’église catholique, de même que la Sagesse, écrite par les amis de Salomon en son honneur.
en: MURATORIAN FRAGMENT [Paul also wrote] out of affection and love one to Philemon, one to Titus, and two to Timothy; and these are held sacred in the esteem 01 the Catholic Church for the regulation of ecclesiastical discipline. There is current also [ a letter] to the Laodiceans, [and] another to the Alexandrians, [both] forged in Paul's name to [further] the heresy of Marcion, and several others that cannot be received into the Catholic Church-for it is not fitting that gall be mixed with honey. Moreover, the letter of Jude and two of the above-mentioned (or, bearing the name of) John are counted (or, used) in the Catholic [Church]; and [the book of] Wisdom, written by the friends of Solomon in his honor [Muratorian Fragment (C. A.D. 178)].
latin: ...verum ad filemonem una et at titu una et ad tymotheu duas pro affecto et dilectione; in honore tamen eclesiae catholice in ordinatione eclesiastice discepline scificate sunt. fertur etiam ad laudecenses, alia ad alexandrinos, pauli nomine fincte ad heresem marcionis, et alia plura que in catholicam eclesiam recepi non potest; fel enim cum melle misceri non congruit. epistola sane iude et superscrictio iohannis duas in catholica habentur; et sapientia ab amicis salomonis in honore ipsius scripta.
context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. About the Muratorian Fragment

    Significance: This document is the earliest known canonical list of New Testament books. Dated to approximately A.D. 170-180, it provides an unparalleled snapshot of which books were considered authoritative in the Church of Rome at that very early date.

    Language: The Latin is famously "barbarous" or rustic. It is full of grammatical errors and misspellings (e.g., scificate for sanctificatae, recepi for recipi). Most scholars believe it is a clumsy translation of a lost Greek original.

2. Analysis of the Extracted Passage

    The Pastoral Epistles: This is one of the earliest and most important witnesses to the acceptance of the Pastoral Epistles (1 & 2 Timothy, Titus) and Philemon. The author notes they were written for personal reasons ("out of affection and love") but are nevertheless held as authoritative for the whole Church's "ecclesiastical discipline." This counters early arguments that they were merely private letters.

    Fighting Heresy (Marcion): The explicit mention of forged letters to the Laodiceans and Alexandrians is incredibly valuable. It shows that the early Church was not just passively receiving books; it was actively discerning and rejecting forgeries, especially those created to promote heresy. Marcion, a major 2nd-century heretic, created his own canon by editing Luke and ten of Paul's letters, so a forgery in Paul's name supporting his views was a serious threat.

    "Gall Mixed with Honey": This metaphor (fel enim cum melle misceri non congruit) is a powerful patristic expression for maintaining doctrinal purity. The "honey" is the pure apostolic teaching, and the "gall" represents heretical falsehoods. The Church cannot allow the two to be mixed in its collection of sacred Scripture.

    Jude and the Johannine Epistles: The fragment clearly accepts the Epistle of Jude. The phrase superscrictio iohannis duas in catholica habentur ("two of the superscription/title of John are held in the Catholic [Church]") is usually understood to mean 1 John and 2 John. The ambiguity might suggest that 3 John was less known or still disputed in the Roman community at this time, which aligns with other historical evidence.

    Wisdom of Solomon: The inclusion of the Wisdom of Solomon is fascinating. It shows that the Old Testament canon was still somewhat fluid in the West, and certain deuterocanonical books were held in very high esteem, even if their authorship was understood differently than it is today (here attributed to "friends of Solomon"). This demonstrates the gradual process by which the final, fixed biblical canons were formed.

fr:
En effet, si les poissons pourvus d'écailles rugueuses sont considérés comme purs, c’est que sont approuvés les caractères rudes, âpres, fermes et graves. En revanche, ceux qui en sont dépourvus sont impurs, car sont réprouvés les caractères légers, fuyants, perfides et efféminés. ...

Ou encore, lorsqu’il interdit de consommer le porc ? Il condamne sans aucun doute une vie souillée, boueuse, qui se complaît dans la fange des vices... Ou encore, le lièvre ? Il dénonce les hommes dénaturés en femmes.
en: NOVATIAN OF ROME [God forbade the Jews to eat certain foods for symbolic reasons:] For in fishes the roughness of scales is regarded as a sign of their cleanness; rough, and rugged, and unpolished, and substantial, and grave manners are approved in men; while those that are without scales are unclean, because trifling, and fickle, and faithless, and effeminate manners are disapproved. Moreover, what does the law mean when it . . . forbids the swine to be taken for food? It assuredly reproves a life filthy and dirty, and delighting in the garbage of vice.. Or when it forbids the hare? It rebukes men deformed into women [Jewish Foods 3 (c. A.D. 253)].
latin:
Nam quod in piscibus squamis aspera pro mundis habentur; asperi et hispidi et hirti et firmi et graves mores hominum probantur: quae autem sine his sunt, immunda; quia leves et lubrici et infidi et effeminati mores improbantur. ...

    Aut cum (Ibid. 7) suem cibo prohibet assumi? Reprehendit utique coenosam et luteam et gaudentem vitiorum sordibus vitam... Aut cum (Ibid. 6) leporem? Accusat deformatos in feminam viros.
context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. Source and Citation

    Author: Novatian of Rome (c. 200–258 AD)

    Work: De Cibis Judaicis (On Jewish Foods)

    Chapter: 3

    Migne Citation: The text you provided is from Patrologia Latina (PL), Volume 3, columns 956-959. Your specific quote is found in column 958.

2. Theological Context: Allegory vs. Literalism

Novatian's main goal in this treatise is to explain why Christians are not bound by the Old Testament dietary laws. He does this by employing a standard early Christian interpretive method: typology or allegory.

    Against Judaizing: He argues against a literal, physical observance of these laws, which would be to revert to the Old Covenant. The law is "spiritual" and must be understood spiritually.

    Against Marcionism: At the same time, he defends the Old Testament and its divine author against Gnostics and Marcionites who claimed the Creator God was flawed for making "unclean" animals. Novatian insists that nothing God created is inherently evil or unclean (quidquid est a Deo institutum, mundum esse).

    The "Mirror of Human Life": Novatian's solution is that the "uncleanness" is not in the animal itself, but is a symbol or type of human sin and vice. The dietary code is a "mirror of human life" (humanae vitae speculum) intended to teach moral lessons. The animals' natural characteristics correspond to human virtues and vices.

3. Symbolism in Your Quote

    Fish: The scales represent moral fortitude, gravity, and roughness—a "thick skin" against temptation. Fish without scales are "slippery" and represent morally weak, effeminate, and untrustworthy characters.

    Swine (Pig): This is a classic symbol. The pig's nature of wallowing in mud (coenosam et luteam) represents a person who delights in filth, sin, and the "garbage of vice."

    Hare: This is based on an ancient biological error. Pliny the Elder and others believed that hares were hermaphrodites and could change their sex annually. For Novatian, this natural "abnormality" became a powerful symbol for men who unnaturally "deform themselves into women," which was understood as a reference to effeminacy and homosexual practices.

Novatian's work is a fascinating window into how early Christian thinkers read the Old Testament, finding deep moral and spiritual meaning in passages that might otherwise seem obscure or irrelevant to the New Covenant.

fr:
Car l’Écriture proclame le Christ Dieu tout autant qu’elle proclame Dieu cet homme même ; elle a dépeint Jésus-Christ comme homme tout comme elle a aussi dépeint le Christ Seigneur comme Dieu. En effet, elle ne le présente pas seulement comme Fils de Dieu, mais aussi de l’homme ; elle ne le dit pas seulement fils de l’homme, mais a aussi coutume de le présenter comme Fils de Dieu, de sorte que, puisqu'il est issu des deux, il soit l’un et l’autre, afin que s’il n’était que l’un, il ne puisse être l’autre.

Car de même que la nature elle-même impose de croire qu’est homme celui qui est issu de l’homme, de même cette même nature impose de croire qu’est Dieu celui qui est issu de Dieu, de peur que, s’il n’est pas aussi Dieu tout en étant issu de Dieu, il ne soit même plus homme, bien qu’issu de l’homme. Et ainsi, le sort de l’une et l'autre nature est en péril, dès lors qu’il est démontré que l’une fait perdre sa crédibilité à l’autre.

Par conséquent, que ceux qui lisent que le Christ Jésus est l’homme, fils de l’homme, lisent également que ce même Christ est proclamé Dieu et Fils de Dieu.
en: NOVATIAN OF ROME For Scripture announces Christ as God, as it announces God himself as man. It has described Jesus Christ as man, as it has described Christ the Lord as God. It does not set him forth as the Son of God only, but also the Son of man: nor only as the Son of man, but it has been accustomed to speak of him as the Son of God. Being of both, he is both, lest if he should be only one, he could not be the other. For as nature has prescribed that he must be believed to be a man who iS of man, so nature prescribes that her must be believed to be God who is of God: but if he should not also be God when he is of God, then he should not be man although he is of man. And thus both doctrines would be endangered in one or the other way, by one being convicted to have lost belief in the other. Let them, thereforewho read that Jesus Christ the Son of man is man read also that this same Jesus is also called God and the Son of God [ The Trinity 11 (c. A.D. 235)].
latin: Tam enim Scriptura etiam Deum annuntiat Christum, quam etiam hominem ipsum annuntiat Deum; tam hominem descripsit Jesum Christum, quam etiam Deum quoque descripsit Christum Dominum. Quoniam nec Dei tantum illum Filium esse proponit, sed et hominis; nec hominis tantum dicit, sed et Dei referre consuevit: ut dum ex utroque est, utrumque sit; ne si alterum tantum sit, alterum esse non possit. Ut enim praescripsit ipsa natura hominem credendum esse, qui ex homine sit; ita eadem natura praescribit et Deum credendum esse, qui ex Deo sit: ne si non et Deus fuerit, cum ex Deo sit; jam nec homo sit, licet ex homine fuerit. Et sic in alterutro utrumque periclitetur, dum alterum altero fidem perdidisse convincitur. Qui legunt ergo hominis filium hominem Christum Jesum, legant hunc eumdem et Deum et Dei Filium nuncupatum.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Author and Work: Novatian (c. 200–258 AD) was a brilliant Roman priest and theologian. His treatise De Trinitate is a landmark achievement, considered the first major theological work written in Latin in the city of Rome. It is a systematic and scripturally-grounded defense of orthodox doctrine against various heresies.

    Historical Context (The Novatian Schism): Despite his theological orthodoxy, Novatian is not called a "Saint." After the election of Pope Cornelius in 251 AD, Novatian set himself up as a rival pope (an antipope), creating a major schism. The controversy was over pastoral discipline: Novatian was a rigorist who believed that those who had renounced the faith during persecution (the lapsi) could not be readmitted to communion, a position the Church rejected. Because of this schism, his writings were not as widely influential in the ancient Church as they might have been otherwise.

    Theological Significance of the Passage:

        Extremely Early Date: Written around A.D. 235, this is an incredibly early and clear articulation of Christ's two natures. It predates the great Christological councils (like Nicaea, Ephesus, and Chalcedon) by a century or more.

        Rule of Faith (Regula Fidei): Novatian's argument demonstrates the established "Rule of Faith" in the Roman Church. He insists that to have true faith, one must hold both truths about Christ simultaneously. To deny one is to lose the other.

        Balanced Argumentation: His style is marked by beautiful, balanced clauses (antithesis). The whole chapter is built on this structure: "If His weaknesses prove He is man, His powers prove He is God." This rhetorical strategy makes his argument powerful and memorable.

        Communicatio Idiomatum: This passage is a classic early example of the theological principle known as the communicatio idiomatum (the communication of properties). This doctrine states that because Jesus Christ is one person, the properties of his divine nature can be attributed to the man, and the properties of his human nature can be attributed to God the Son. Novatian's entire argument hinges on this concept.

fr: Il faut donc croire, selon la règle prescrite, au Seigneur, unique vrai Dieu, et ensuite en celui qu’il a envoyé, Jésus Christ. Celui-ci ne se serait nullement uni au Père, comme nous l’avons dit, s’il n’avait pas voulu être également compris comme Dieu. Car il se serait séparé de lui, s’il n’avait pas voulu être compris comme Dieu.
en: NOVATIAN OF ROME We must therefore believe, according to the rule prescribed, in the Lord, the one true God, and consequently in him whom he has sent, Jesus Christ, who would not have linked himself to the Father if he did not wish to be understood to be God also, for he would have separated himself from him he did not wish to be understood to be God [ The Trinity 16 (c. A.D. 235)].
latin: Est ergo credendum, secundum praescriptam regulam, in Dominum, unum verum Deum, et in eum quem misit Jesum Christum consequenter, qui se nequaquam Patri, ut diximus, junxisset, nisi Deum quoque intelligi vellet; separasset enim ab eo, si Deum intelligi se noluisset.
context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. Author and Work

    Author: Novatian (c. 200–258 AD) was a highly educated Christian theologian and writer in Rome. He was a presbyter of the Roman Church but broke away after the election of Pope Cornelius, founding a rival schismatic church known for its rigorist stance on readmitting those who had lapsed during persecution.

    Work: De Trinitate (On the Trinity) is Novatian's most important work and one of the earliest major theological treatises written in Latin. Written around A.D. 235, it predates the First Council of Nicaea by nearly a century and shows a sophisticated, orthodox understanding of the relationship between the Father and the Son, strongly defending Christ's divinity against various heresies.

2. Immediate Context of the Argument (Chapter 16)

The chapter you provided, "CAPUT XVI. Iterum ex Evangelio Christum Deum comprobat" ("Chapter 16. He proves again from the Gospel that Christ is God"), is a series of short arguments based on the words of Jesus in the Gospel of John. Your specific quote is the climax of one of these arguments:

    Lead-in Scripture: Novatian has just quoted John 17:3: "This is eternal life, that they may know you, the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent."

    The Problem: A heretic might use this verse to argue that only the Father is the "one true God," and Jesus is someone separate and lesser.

    Novatian's Logic: Novatian seizes on the fact that Jesus links his own name directly with the Father's in this "rule of faith." He argues:

        If Jesus had wanted to be understood as only a man, he would have been careful to distinguish himself. He might have added, "...and the man Jesus Christ whom you have sent."

        By not adding this clarification and instead joining (junxit) his name to the Father's, Jesus intentionally placed himself on the divine side of the equation.

        To be understood as merely human would have required an act of separation (separasset). The fact that he did not separate himself is, for Novatian, a powerful, implicit claim to divinity.

3. The Core Theological Point

The core of Novatian's argument is a principle of conjunction and disjunction. In the context of monotheistic worship, to join any created being to the "one true God" as an object of saving faith would be blasphemy. Therefore, Christ's act of linking himself to the Father in this foundational statement of belief is itself a proof of his divinity. He is not a third party between God and humanity; he is on the side of God, presented alongside the Father for belief.

fr:
Si le Christ n’était qu’un homme, pourquoi nous a-t-il prescrit une telle règle de foi en disant : « Or, la vie éternelle, c’est qu’ils te connaissent, toi, le seul vrai Dieu, et celui que tu as envoyé, Jésus Christ » ? S’il n’avait pas voulu être également compris comme Dieu, pourquoi aurait-il ajouté : « et celui que tu as envoyé, Jésus Christ », si ce n’est parce qu’il voulait aussi être reconnu comme Dieu ?

Car s’il n’avait pas voulu être compris comme Dieu, il aurait ajouté : « et l’homme Jésus Christ ». Or, non seulement il n’a rien ajouté de tel, mais le Christ ne s’est pas présenté à nous comme un simple homme ; au contraire, il s’est uni à Dieu pour être, par cette union, compris aussi comme Dieu, tel qu’il est.

Il faut donc croire, selon la règle établie, dans le Seigneur, unique vrai Dieu, et par conséquent en celui qu’il a envoyé, Jésus Christ. Jamais il ne se serait uni au Père, comme nous l’avons dit, s’il n’avait pas voulu être également compris comme Dieu ; en effet, il se serait séparé de lui s’il n’avait pas voulu être compris comme Dieu.
en: NOVATIAN OF ROME If Christ was only man, why did he lay down for uS this rule of believing, "And this is life eternal, that they should know you, the only and true God, and Jesus Christ, whom you have sent"? If he did not wish to be understood to be God, why did he add, "And Jesus Christ. whom you have sent, unless he wished to be received as God? Because if he did not wish to be understood to be God, he would have added. "And the man Jesus Christ, whom you have sent"; but, in fact, he did not, nor did Christ deliver himself to us as Christ only, but associated himself with God, as he wished to be understood by this to be God also, as he is. We must therefore believe, according to the rule prescribed, in the Lord, the one true God. and consequently in him whom he has sent, Jesus Christ, who would not have linked himself to the Father if he had not wished to be understood to be God also: for he would have separated himself from him if he did not wish to be understood to be God [The Trinity 16 (c. A.D. 235)].
greek: Si homo tantummodo Christus; quare credendi nobis talem regulam posuit quo diceret: Haec est autem vita aeterna ut sciant te unum et verum Deum, et quem misisti Jesum Christum? Si noluisset se etiam Deum intelligi, cur addidit: Et quem misisti Jesum Christum, nisi quoniam et Deum accipi voluit? Quoniam si se Deum nollet intelligi, addidisset: Et quem misisti hominem Jesum Christum: nunc autem neque addidit, nec se hominem nobis tantummodo Christus tradidit, sed Deo junxit, ut et Deum per hanc conjunctionem, sicut est, intelligi vellet. Est ergo credendum, secundum praescriptam regulam, in Dominum, unum verum Deum, et in eum quem misit Jesum Christum consequenter, qui se nequaquam Patri, ut diximus, junxisset, nisi Deum quoque intelligi vellet; separasset enim ab eo, si Deum intelligi se noluisset.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Author and Work: Novatian of Rome, a prominent and learned Roman presbyter. The work is De Trinitate (On the Trinity), written around A.D. 235-250. This makes it one of the very first major theological treatises written in Latin.

    Historical Context: Novatian was writing before the Council of Nicaea (A.D. 325). His primary opponents were not Arians, but earlier heresies that undermined the Trinity:

        Adoptionism: The belief that Jesus was a mere man who was "adopted" as God's Son.

        Modalistic Monarchianism (or Sabellianism): The belief that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not distinct persons, but merely different "modes" or manifestations of one divine person.
        Novatian's entire book is a careful, scripturally-based argument proving that the Son is a distinct divine Person, truly God from God, and not a mere man or a temporary mode of the Father.

    Analysis of the Argument: This specific passage is a brilliant piece of logical and scriptural reasoning based on John 17:3. Novatian's argument unfolds in several steps:

        The "Rule of Believing": He calls Jesus's prayer a regula credendi, a formal rule or standard for our faith.

        The Logic of Association: His core point is that a mere man would never "link" or "join" (junxit) his own name to that of the "one true God" in a statement defining eternal life. To do so would be blasphemous.

        The Argument from Omission: He points out what Jesus didn't say. Jesus did not specify "the man Jesus Christ," which he would have done if he wanted to clarify he was only human.

        Separation vs. Conjunction: The conclusion is powerful. If Christ were not God, he would have separated himself from the Father in this declaration. Instead, he associated himself with the Father, intending for us to understand his own divinity through this conjunction.

    Significance: This passage is a crucial witness to the high Christology of the Roman Church in the early 3rd century, nearly a century before the Arian crisis and the Council of Nicaea. It demonstrates a sophisticated use of Scripture to defend the full divinity of Jesus Christ.

fr:
Qui, en effet, ne reconnaîtrait la seconde personne du Fils, après le Père, lorsqu'il lit cette parole adressée par le Père au Fils : « Faisons l'homme à notre image et à notre ressemblance » ; et qu’il est rapporté ensuite : « Et Dieu fit l'homme ; il le fit à l'image de Dieu » ?

Ou lorsqu'il tient entre les mains ce passage : « Le Seigneur fit pleuvoir sur Sodome et Gomorrhe du soufre et du feu, de la part du Seigneur, du haut du ciel » ?

Ou lorsqu'il lit ces paroles adressées au Christ : « Tu es mon Fils, moi, aujourd'hui, je t'ai engendré. Demande, et je te donnerai les nations en héritage, et en possession les extrémités de la terre » ?

Ou encore, lorsque cet illustre scribe déclare : « Le Seigneur a dit à mon Seigneur : Siège à ma droite, jusqu’à ce que je fasse de tes ennemis l’escabeau de tes pieds » ?

Ou lorsque, parcourant les prophéties d'Isaïe, il trouve écrit ceci : « Voici ce que dit le Seigneur à mon Christ, le Seigneur » ?

Ou lorsqu'il lit : « Je ne suis pas descendu du ciel pour faire ma volonté, mais la volonté de celui qui m'a envoyé » ?

Ou quand il trouve écrit : « Car celui qui m'a envoyé est plus grand que moi » ?

Ou lorsqu'il considère ce qui est écrit : « Je monte vers mon Père et votre Père, vers mon Dieu et votre Dieu » ?

Ou enfin, quand il lit, parmi tant d’autres, ce passage : « Il est écrit dans votre loi que le témoignage de deux personnes est vrai. Moi, je témoigne de moi-même, et le Père qui m’a envoyé témoigne de moi » ?
en: NOVATIAN OF ROME For who does not acknowledge that the person of the Son is second after the Father, when he reads that it was said by the Father, thus to the Son, "Let us make man in our image and our likeness"; and that after this it was said, "And God made man, in the image of God made he him"? Or when he holds in his hands: "The Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah fire and brimstone from the Lord from heaven"? Or when he reads what was said to Christ: "You are my Son, this day have I begotten You. Ask of me, and I will give you the heathens for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession"? Or when that beloved writer says: The Lord said unto my Lord, Sit on my right hand, until shall make your enemies the stool of your feet"? Or when, unfolding the prophecies of Isaiah, he finds this written: "Thus says the Lord to Christ my Lord"? Or when he reads: came not down from heaven to do my own will, but the will 01 him that sent me"? Or: "Because he who sent me is greater than I'? Or when he considers the passage: go to my Father, and your Father; to my God, and your God"? Or when he finds it compared with others: "Moreover, in your law it is written that the witness of two is true. I bear witness of myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness of me"? [The Trinity 26 (c. A.D. 235)].
greek:
Quis enim non secundam Filii post Patrem agnoscat esse personam, cum legat dictum a Patre consequenter ad Filium: Faciamus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram; et post haec relatum, et fecit Deus hominem, ad imaginem Dei fecit illum?

    Aut cum inter manus teneat: Pluit Dominus super Sodomam et Gomorrham ignem et sulphur a Domino de coelo?

    Aut cum ad Christum : Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te; postula a me, et dabo tibi gentes haereditatem tuam, et possessionem tuam terminos terrae?

    Aut cum etiam ille desideratus scriba ait: Dixit Dominus Domino meo: Sede a dextris meis, donec ponam inimicos tuos, scabellum pedum tuorum?

    Aut cum Isaiae prophetias explicans, invenit positum sic: Haec dicit Dominus Christo meo Domino?

    Aut cum legit: Non descendi de coelo ut faciam voluntatem meam, sed voluntatem ejus qui misit me?

    Aut dum invenit positum: Quoniam qui me misit, major me est?

    Aut cum considerat scriptum: Eo ad patrem meum et Patrem vestrum, Deum meum et Deum vestrum?

    Aut quando habet cum caeteris collocatum: Sed in lege vestra scriptum est, quia duorum testimonium verum est; ego de me testificor, et testificatus est de me qui me misit Pater?
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Author and Work: Novatian (c. 200–258 AD) was a highly educated Roman presbyter and theologian. Although he became the leader of a schismatic group (the Novatianists) over issues of church discipline, his major theological work, De Trinitate, was largely orthodox and became one of the first great theological treatises written in Latin. It was foundational for the development of Latin Trinitarian vocabulary before the Arian controversy.

    The Heresy Being Refuted: The chapter heading in your Latin text, "Adversus autem Sabellianos..." ("But against the Sabellians..."), is key. Sabellianism (also called Modalism or Patripassianism) was a heresy that denied the real distinction of persons in the Godhead. It taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were just three different "modes" or "masks" of a single divine person. This led to the conclusion that the Father himself suffered on the cross (hence Patri-passianism, "Father-suffering").

    Novatian's Argumentative Strategy: Novatian's method is overwhelmingly scriptural. His argument is that the Bible consistently portrays the Father and the Son as two distinct persons in dialogue and relationship with each other:

        One speaking to another ("Let us make man...", "You are my Son...").

        One acting distinctly from another ("The Lord... from the Lord...").

        One sending, the other being sent ("...the will of him that sent me.").

        One being "greater" in role/origin ("...greater than I.").

        Two distinct witnesses ("...the witness of two is true.").
        This constant distinction of persons makes the Sabellian idea of a single person wearing different "masks" biblically untenable.

    Significance of the Full Chapter: The Latin text you provided contains the entire chapter. The section you quoted is just the beginning of Novatian's scriptural proof. He goes on to list many more examples, including Peter's confession ("You are the Son of the living God"), Christ's prayers to the Father, and the definition of eternal life in John 17, creating an overwhelming cascade of evidence for his case.

fr:
Dieu le Père est donc le fondateur et le créateur de toutes choses. Lui seul est sans origine, invisible, immense, immortel, éternel, l'unique Dieu. À sa grandeur, à sa majesté, à sa puissance, rien ne peut, je ne dis pas être préféré, mais ne serait-ce qu'être comparé. De lui, quand il l'a voulu, est né le Verbe, le Fils.

Lui donc, bien qu'engendré par le Père, est toujours dans le Père. Or, quand je dis « toujours », c'est pour établir qu'il est engendré, et non pas inengendré. Mais lui qui existe avant tous les temps, on doit dire qu'il a toujours été dans le Père, car on ne peut assigner de commencement dans le temps à celui qui est avant le temps. Il est en effet toujours dans le Père, sans quoi le Père ne serait pas toujours Père. Bien plus, le Père le précède en un certain sens, car il faut bien, d'une certaine manière, qu'il soit antérieur en tant qu'il est le Père.
en: Thus God the Father, the founder and Creator of all things, who knows no beginning, invisible, infinite, immortal, eternal, is one God; to whose greatness, or majesty, or power nothing can be compared; of whom, when he willed it, the Son, the Word, was born. [H]e then, since he was begotten of the Father, is always in the Father. And I thus say that I may show him not to be unborn, but born. But he who is before all time must be said to have been always in the Father; for no time can be assigned to him who is before all time %. And he is always in the Father, unless the Father be not always Father, only that the Father also precedes him, in a certain sense, since it iS necessary - in some degree-that he should be before he is Father [ibid., 31].
greek:
Est ergo Deus Pater omnium institutor et creator, solus originem nesciens, invisibilis, immensus, immortalis, aeternus, unus Deus; cujus neque magnitudini, neque majestati, neque virtuti quidquam non dixerim praeferri, sed nec comparari potest. Ex quo, quando ipse voluit, Sermo Filius natus est.

    Hic ergo, cum sit genitus a Patre, semper est in Patre. Semper autem sic dico, ut non innatum, sed natum probem. Sed qui ante omne tempus est, semper in Patre fuisse dicendus est: nec enim tempus illi assignari potest, qui ante tempus est. Semper enim in Patre; ne Pater non semper sit Pater: quin et Pater illum etiam (quadam ratione) praecedit, quod necesse est (quodammodo) prior sit qua Pater sit.
context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. Author and Work

    Author: Novatian of Rome (c. 200–258 A.D.)

    Work: De Trinitate (On the Trinity)

    Date: Written around A.D. 257. This is a critically important date because it is pre-Nicene. Novatian is writing over 60 years before the Arian controversy exploded and the Council of Nicaea (325) defined the term homoousios (consubstantial). His work is one of the first complete Latin treatises dedicated to the Trinity.

2. Theological Context and Significance

This passage is a masterclass in pre-Nicene Trinitarian theology, as Novatian carefully navigates between two major heresies without the benefit of later conciliar language:

    Against Modalism (Sabellianism): Novatian insists that the Son is truly born (natus) from the Father, not just a different mode or mask of the same person. The Father is always Father, and the Son is always Son.

    Against Ditheism (Belief in Two Gods): The rest of Chapter 31, which you provided in full, is a brilliant logical argument for why confessing the Son as a distinct, divine person does not create two Gods. His core argument is that since the Son derives his entire being and origin from the Father, He cannot be a rival principle. The Father is the sole source (solus originem nesciens), and this preserves the monarchy (sole rule) of God.

3. The "Subordinationist" Language

The most debated part of your quote is this line:

    "...the Father also precedes him, in a certain sense (quadam ratione), since it is necessary - in some degree (quodammodo) - that he should be before he is Father."

This is a classic example of what is often called "subordination of origin" in orthodox theology.

    It is NOT Arianism: Arius would later teach that the Son was a creature, made from nothing, and of a different substance than the Father. Novatian firmly rejects this, stating the Son is born from the Father's own substance ("Deus ex Deo" - God from God).

    What Novatian Means: He is making a logical, not a temporal, point. For the Father to be the Father, He must logically "precede" the Son, as a cause precedes its effect or a source precedes what flows from it. The Father is the unoriginated origin; the Son is the originated origin. Novatian qualifies his statement heavily with phrases like "in a certain sense" and "in some degree" to show he isn't talking about a gap in time or a difference in nature.

4. Historical Context of Novatian

Novatian was a brilliant Roman presbyter who, in 251, became a rival bishop of Rome (an antipope) in opposition to the elected Pope Cornelius. The dispute was not primarily about the Trinity but about Church discipline: Novatian was a rigorist who believed that those who had renounced the faith during persecution (the lapsi) could not be forgiven and readmitted to the Church. This led to the Novatianist schism, a movement that persisted for several centuries. Despite his schismatic status, his work De Trinitate was highly regarded for its orthodoxy and was a major influence on later Latin theology.

context:
Additional Context from Your Images

Your images provide the entire context of Ode 19, which is a beautiful, mystical poem about the Incarnation. The verses leading up to your quote describe the divine action that brings about the virgin birth:

    Verse 1: "A cup of milk was offered to me, and I drank it in the sweetness of the Lord's kindness." (A metaphor for divine grace).

    Verse 2-3: The Son is the cup, the Father is he who was milked, and the Holy Spirit is she who milked him. (A highly symbolic Trinitarian description).

    Verse 4-5: The Holy Spirit opened the Virgin's womb and she received the conception and gave birth.

    Verse 6: The "I" of the Ode (often identified as Christ) speaks of fashioning the members of this new creation.

This leads directly into your passage (verses 7-9), which describes the result of this divine action: a miraculous, painless, and divinely-assisted birth.

You have successfully located the ancient Syriac text for this beautiful and historically important passage. The edition you are using is clearly a scholarly one, as shown by the footnotes indicating manuscript variations. Excellent work
