context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. Author and Work: Pseudo-Hippolytus

It is crucial to understand that while this work is traditionally attributed to St. Hippolytus of Rome (d. c. 235 AD), modern scholarship identifies the author as Pseudo-Hippolytus. The style, theological content, and historical context suggest it was written at a later date, possibly in the 4th century or even later, and then attached to the famous name of Hippolytus.

The authentic work of St. Hippolytus on this topic is titled On Christ and Antichrist. The text you are citing, On the End of the World, is a separate, later work.
2. Source Citation

The parallel Greek and Latin column format is characteristic of J.-P. Migne's patristic collections. This text is found in:

    Migne, Patrologia Graeca (PG), Volume 10, columns 925-930.

3. Narrative Context: The Antichrist's Strategy

The sections you provided (XXIII-XXV) lay out a classic three-act strategy for the Antichrist's rise to power:

    Act I - The Virtuous Ascetic (Section XXIII): The Antichrist begins his career by appearing as a perfect, holy man. He is gentle, pious, peaceful, a lover of the poor, a miracle worker, and shows great respect for the Jewish people and their Scriptures. This is a campaign of deception to win the hearts of the people.

    Act II - The People's King (Section XXIV): Fooled by his false virtues and miracles, the people of the world—and especially, the text emphasizes, the Jewish people—acclaim him as a just and righteous ruler. They see him as their long-awaited savior and king and willingly submit to his authority.

    Act III - The Tyrant Revealed (Section XXV): As soon as he is crowned king, his true nature emerges. He becomes arrogant, merciless, and inhuman. He persecutes the righteous and launches wars. It is at this point, having consolidated his power, that he undertakes the rebuilding of the temple.

4. Theological Significance of Rebuilding the Temple

In Christian eschatology, the Antichrist rebuilding the temple in Jerusalem is a profoundly significant act:

    Appeal to Messianic Hope: It is a direct and powerful appeal to Jewish messianic expectations. By restoring the temple, he presents himself as the fulfillment of prophecy and solidifies his claim as a messianic figure in the eyes of those who accept him.

    Setting for the Abomination: The rebuilt temple becomes the stage for his ultimate act of blasphemy. Many Christian interpreters see this as the necessary precursor to the "abomination of desolation" spoken of by the prophet Daniel and by Jesus in the Gospels (Matthew 24:15), where the Antichrist will set himself up in the temple to be worshipped as God.

fr:
Alors les justes répondront, saisis d’étonnement par la grandeur du prodige, car celui que les armées d’anges ne peuvent contempler clairement, il les appelle comme des amis. Et ils s’écrieront en s’adressant à lui :
« Seigneur, quand t’avons-nous vu avoir faim, et t’avons-nous nourri ? Maître, quand t’avons-nous vu avoir soif, et t’avons-nous donné à boire ? Ô Redoutable, quand t’avons-nous vu nu, et t’avons-nous vêtu ? Ô Immortel, quand t’avons-nous vu étranger, et t’avons-nous accueilli ? Ami des hommes, quand t’avons-nous vu malade ou en prison, et sommes-nous venus jusqu’à toi ?
Tu es celui qui est de toute éternité. Tu es sans commencement avec le Père et coéternel à l’Esprit Saint. C’est toi qui as tout créé à partir du néant. »
en: ON THE END OF THE WORLD Then shall the righteous answer, astonished at the mighty and wondrous fact that he, who the hosts of angels cannot look upon openly, addresses them as friends, and they shall cry out to him, "Lord, when saw we you hungry, and fed you? Master, when saw we you thirsty, and gave you drink? You terrible one, when saw we you naked, and clothed you? Immortal, when saw we you a stranger, and took you in? You friend of man, when saw we you sick or in prison, and came to you? You are the ever-living one. You are without beginning, like the Father, and co-eternal with the Spirit. You are he who made all things out of nothing" [On the End of the World 43 (c. A.D. 267)].
latin: Tunc respondebunt justi, attoniti magnitudine miraculi, quod is quem ordines angelorum intueri clare ac vere non possunt, consolatur eos velut amicos, clamabuntque ad illum : Domine, quando te vidimus esurientem, et pavimus? Domine, quando te vidimus sitientem, et præbuimus potum? Tremende, quando te vidimus nudum, et operuimus? Immortalis, quando te vidimus peregrinum, et collegimus? Amator hominum, quando te vidimus infirmum, aut in carcere, et venimus ad te? Tu es, qui semper est. Tu una cum Patre cares principio, et coæternus es Spiritui sancto. Tu es, qui ex nihilo omnia creasti. (Note: The text you provided has "præbuimus polum," which is a common transcription error. "Polum" means "pole/heaven." The correct reading, matching the Greek and the context, is "præbuimus potum," meaning "we provided a drink.")
greek: Τότε ἀποκριθήσονται οἱ δίκαιοι ἐκπληττόμενοι τῷ μεγέθει τοῦ θαύματος, ὅτι ἐν οὐ δύνανται βλέπειν τρανῶς ἀγγέλων τὰ τάγματα, ὡς φίλους αὐτοὺς προσκαλεῖται, καὶ βοήσουσι πρὸς αὐτόν· Κύριε, πότε σε ίδομεν πεινώντα, καὶ ἐθρέψαμεν; Δέσποτα, πότε σε ίδομεν διψῶντα, καὶ ἐποτίσαμεν; Φοβερέ, πότε σε ίδομεν γυμνὸν, καὶ περιελάβομεν; 'Αθάνατε, πότε σε ίδομεν ξένον, καὶ συνηγάγομεν; Φιλάνθρωπε, πότε σε ίδομεν ἀσθενῆ ἡ ἐν φυλακῇ, καὶ ἤλθομεν πρὸς σέ; Σὺ εἶ ὁ ἀεὶ ὤν. Σὺ εἶ ὁ συνάναρχος τῷ Πατρὶ καὶ συναΐδιος τῷ Πνεύματι. Σὺ εἶ ὁ ἐκ μὴ ὄντων τὰ πάντα ποιήσας.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Author and Authenticity: The work, On the End of the World (De consummatione mundi), is traditionally attributed to St. Hippolytus of Rome (c. 170 – c. 235 AD). However, modern scholarly consensus is that this work is Pseudo-Hippolytan. The theological language and style are considered too advanced for the early 3rd century and more characteristic of the 4th or even 5th century. The date you cited (c. 267) is likely a historical attempt to place it after Hippolytus's death but is also not considered accurate by modern scholars.

    Theological Significance of the Hymn: This passage is a remarkable piece of early Christian theology, blending the Gospel narrative with a highly developed Christological and Trinitarian confession.

        Christology: It beautifully juxtaposes the humble, hidden Christ of Matthew 25 (the hungry, thirsty, naked stranger) with the transcendent, divine Christ who is co-eternal with the Father and Spirit and the Creator of all things.

        Divine Titles: The series of titles used for Jesus—Lord (Κύριε), Master (Δέσποτα), Terrible One (Φοβερέ), Immortal (Ἀθάνατε), Friend of Man (Φιλάνθρωπε)—reflects a rich liturgical and devotional tradition.

        Trinitarian Language: The phrase "You are without beginning, like the Father, and co-eternal with the Spirit" (Σὺ εἶ ὁ συνάναρχος τῷ Πατρὶ καὶ συναΐδιος τῷ Πνεύματι) is particularly significant. The Greek terms συνάναρχος (synanarchos, co-unoriginate or co-beginningless) and συναΐδιος (synaïdios, co-eternal) are theologically precise terms that became central to post-Nicaean orthodoxy. Their presence is one of the strongest arguments that this work was written much later than the time of the historical Hippolytus.

        Creation ex nihilo: The line "You are he who made all things out of nothing" (Σὺ εἶ ὁ ἐκ μὴ ὄντων τὰ πάντα ποιήσας) is a clear affirmation of the core Christian doctrine of creation from nothing, distinguishing it from pagan philosophies that posited creation from pre-existing matter.

fr: Tu ne peux donc nier savoir que la chaire épiscopale a été conférée en premier à Pierre dans la ville de Rome, sur laquelle a siégé le chef de tous les Apôtres, Pierre — qui pour cette raison fut aussi appelé Céphas. C’est dans cette chaire unique que l’unité devait être gardée par tous, afin que les autres Apôtres ne revendiquent pas chacun la leur ; de sorte que soit désormais schismatique et pécheur celui qui, contre cette chaire unique, en établirait une autre.
en: ST. OPTATUS OF MILEVIS You cannot then deny that you do know that upon Peter first in the city of Rome was bestowed the episcopal cathedra, on which sat Peter, the head of all the apostles (for which reason he was called Cephas), that, in this one cathedra, unity should be preserved by all [Schism of the Donatists 2:2 (c. A.D. 367)].
latin: Igitur negare non potes scire te in urbe Roma Petro primo Cathedram episcopalem esse collatam, in qua sederit omnium Apostolorum caput Petrus; unde et Cephas appellatus est: in qua una cathedra unitas ab omnibus servaretur, ne caeteri Apostoli singulas sibi quisque defenderent, ut jam schismaticus et peccator esset, qui contra singularem cathedram alteram collocaret.
context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. Author and Context

    Author: St. Optatus, Bishop of Milevis in North Africa (modern-day Algeria) in the mid-4th century. He was a contemporary of St. Augustine and one of the earliest Latin Fathers to write extensively on the nature of the Church.

    Work: De Schismate Donatistarum (On the Schism of the Donatists), written around A.D. 367.

    The Donatist Schism: This was a major crisis that tore the North African Church apart. The Donatists were a rigorist group who broke away from the Catholic Church, claiming that sacraments administered by bishops or priests who had been "traitors" (traditores) during the Diocletian persecution were invalid. They set up their own rival bishops in nearly every city, creating a parallel church. St. Optatus's entire work is an argument against this schism and in defense of the one, universal (Catholic) Church.

2. The Argument of the Surrounding Text

The text you provided before the quote is Optatus's setup for his knockout punch.

    He argues that the true Church has certain "gifts" or "endowments" (dotes).

    He identifies the first and most important of these gifts as the cathedra—the episcopal chair of authority.

    He then directly challenges his Donatist opponent (tu): "If you don't know, learn; if you know, be ashamed... You cannot deny that you know..." This is a powerful rhetorical move, accusing the Donatist bishop of acting in bad faith against what he knows to be true.

3. Theological Significance and Key Terms

This passage is famous for its clear, early articulation of the role of the See of Rome as the center of Christian unity.

    Cathedra Petri (Chair of Peter): For Optatus, this is not just a historical fact but a theological principle. The cathedra is the singular, authoritative teaching office established by Christ in Peter. Optatus unequivocally locates this chair "in the city of Rome."

    Caput omnium Apostolorum (Head of all the Apostles): Peter is not just one among equals; he is the "head." This term implies leadership, primacy, and a unifying role among the college of apostles.

    Unde et Cephas appellatus est (For which reason he was called Cephas): This is a fascinating bit of patristic etymology. While "Cephas" (from Aramaic Kēphā) means "Rock," St. Optatus links it rhetorically to the Greek word for "head" (kephalē). He is making a theological connection: Peter's role as the foundational Rock (Matthew 16:18) is inseparable from his role as the unifying Head of the Church.

    In qua una cathedra unitas... servaretur (In this one chair, unity should be preserved): This is the core of Optatus's argument. The very purpose of Peter's unique chair is to be the visible, tangible source and guarantee of unity for the entire Church. By setting up their own rival chairs in Africa, the Donatists have sinned against this principle and have therefore cut themselves off from the one true Church.

fr:
Tu ne peux donc nier savoir que c'est à Pierre, le premier, qu'a été conférée la chaire épiscopale dans la ville de Rome, où a siégé le chef de tous les Apôtres, Pierre — ce qui lui valut d'être aussi appelé Céphas. C'est dans cette chaire unique que l'unité devait être gardée par tous, afin que les autres Apôtres ne revendiquent pas chacun la leur ; ainsi, se comporterait déjà en schismatique et en pécheur celui qui établirait une autre chaire face à cette chaire unique.

C'est donc sur la chaire unique, qui est la première des prérogatives, que Pierre a siégé le premier...
en: ST. OPTATUS OF MILEVIS You cannot then deny that you know that upon Peter first in the city of Rome was bestowed the episcopal cathedra, on which he sat, the head of all the apostles (for which reason he was called Cephas), that, in this one cathedra, unity should be preserved by all, lest the other Apostles might claim-each for himself -separate cathedras, so that he who should set up a second Cathedra against the unique cathedra would already be a schismatic and a sinner. Well then, on the one cathedra, which is the first of the endowments, Peter was the first to sit [Schism of the Donatists 2:2 (c. A.D 367)].
latin:
Igitur negare non potes scire te in urbe Roma Petro primo Cathedram episcopalem esse collatam, in qua sederit omnium Apostolorum caput Petrus; unde et Cephas appellatus est: in qua una cathedra unitas ab omnibus servaretur, ne caeteri Apostoli singulas sibi quisque defenderent, ut jam schismaticus et peccator esset, qui contra singularem cathedram alteram collocaret.

    Ergo in una cathedra, quae prima est de dotibus, sedit prior Petrus...
context:
The Argument of the "Dotes": In this part of his book, Optatus argues that the true Church possesses five "endowments" or "marks" (quinque dotes). The very first and most important endowment he lists is the Cathedra—the episcopal chair, a symbol of legitimate apostolic authority.

Key Theological Concepts in this Passage:

    Cathedra Petri (The Chair of Peter): Optatus makes a clear, historical, and theological argument that the primary Cathedra was given first to Peter.

    Location in Rome: He explicitly locates this Petrine Cathedra in the city of Rome. This is one of the earliest and clearest patristic testimonies to the unique apostolic foundation of the Roman See.

    Source of Unity: The purpose of this single, primary chair is to be a visible principle and safeguard of unity for the entire Church (unitas ab omnibus servaretur). All other apostles (and by extension, all other bishops) are to be in communion with this one chair.

    Definition of a Schismatic: Optatus provides a powerful and precise definition of a schismatic: one who sets up a second chair against the unique chair (qui contra singularem cathedram alteram collocaret). This was a direct attack on the Donatist bishop in Rome, Macrobius, who represented a rival and schismatic line of succession.

fr: Par conséquent, vous ne pouvez nier savoir qu’à Rome la chaire épiscopale a été conférée en premier à Pierre, sur laquelle a siégé le chef de tous les Apôtres, Pierre, d’où le nom de Céphas qui lui fut donné ; c’est dans cette chaire unique que l’unité devait être gardée par tous, afin que les autres Apôtres ne revendiquent pas chacun la leur, de sorte que soit désormais schismatique et pécheur celui qui, contre cette chaire unique, en établirait une autre.
en: ST. OPTATUS OF MILEVIS You cannot then deny that you know that upon Peter first in the city of Rome was bestowed the episcopal cathedra, on which he sat, the head of all the apostles (for which reason he was called Cephas), that, in this one cathedra, unity should be preserved by all. Neither do the apostles proceed individually on their own, and anyone who would presume to] set up another chair in opposition to that single chair would. by that very fact, be a schismatic and a sinner. Recall, then, the origins of your chair, those of you who wish to claim for yourselves the title of holy Church [Schism of the Donatists 2:2 (C. A.D. 367)].
latin: Igitur negare non potes scire te in urbe Roma Petro primo Cathedram episcopalem esse collatam, in qua sederit omnium Apostolorum caput Petrus; unde et Cephas appellatus est: in qua una cathedra unitas ab omnibus servaretur, ne caeteri Apostoli singulas sibi quisque defenderent, ut iam schismaticus et peccator esset, qui contra singularem cathedram alteram collocaret.
context:
Theological Argument: The Cathedra Petri as the Principle of Unity

St. Optatus's argument is a masterstroke of polemics:

    He establishes that Christ gave a unique "chair" (cathedra) to Peter.

    He identifies this chair historically with the episcopal see of Rome.

    He defines the purpose of this single chair: to be the visible source and guarantee of unity for the entire Church ("in qua una cathedra unitas ab omnibus servaretur").

    By this logic, anyone who sets up a competing chair against this one, singular chair is, by definition, a schismatic.

    Since the Donatists had done exactly that by installing their own bishop in Rome, Optatus proves that they—the very people claiming to be the only true Church—are in fact the schismatics and sinners.

4. Key Phrases Explained

    "...unde et Cephas appellatus est" (...for which reason he was called Cephas): This is a fascinating piece of patristic etymology. St. Optatus makes a linguistic connection between the Greek word Κεφαλἠ (Kephalē, meaning "head") and Peter's Aramaic name Cephas (meaning "Rock"). While not linguistically accurate, he uses this wordplay to reinforce his theological point that Peter is the "head" (caput) of the apostles.

    "...contra singularem cathedram..." (...against that single chair...): The word singularem is crucial. It emphasizes the uniqueness and exclusivity of Peter's chair as the center of unity. There cannot be two.

fr: Il n'y a pas un moment où Dieu n'ait voulu rendre juste la vie des hommes ; il en a toujours pris soin, donnant à la créature raisonnable des occasions de pratiquer la vertu pour se corriger. En effet, à chaque génération, la sagesse de Dieu, descendant dans les âmes qu'elle trouve saintes, en fait des amis de Dieu et des prophètes.
en: ORIGEN OF ALEXANDRIA [T]here was never a time when God did not wish to make men live righteous lives; but he continually showed his care for the improvement of the rational animal by affording him occasions for the exercise of virtue. For in every generation the wisdom of God, passing into those souls it ascertains to be holy, converts them into friends and prophets of God [Against Celsus 4:7 (C. A.D. 248)].
latin: Respondco Deum nunquam non voluisse ut homines justi fierent; id semper cordi habuisse; quippe qui animali rationis compoti et consectandæ virtutis et recte faciendi occasiones præbuerit. Per singulas enim generationes Dei sapientia in animas, quas sanctas invenit, descendens amicos Dei prophetasque facit.
greek: ...οὐκ ἔστιν ὅτ' οὐκ ἐβουλήθη δικαιῶσαι τὸν ἀνθρώπων βίον ὁ Θεός· ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀεὶ ἐπεμελήθη, διδοὺς ἀρετῆς ἀφορμὰς τοῦ ἐπανορθοῦσθαι τὸ λογικὸν ζῶον. Κατὰ γὰρ ἑκάστην γενεὰν ἡ σοφία τοῦ Θεοῦ εἰς ψυχάς, ἃς εὑρίσκει ὁσίας, μεταβαίνουσα, φίλους Θεοῦ καὶ προφήτας κατασκευάζει.
context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. The Immediate Context: Refuting Celsus's Challenge

The quote is Origen's direct response to a classic pagan criticism of Christianity, which you can see in the text surrounding the quote. Celsus asks:

    "What? After so many ages, has it only now at last come into God's mind to make the life of men righteous; but before this, he did not care?"

This was a powerful challenge. To a Greco-Roman mindset, a true God should be eternal and unchanging. A God who suddenly "wakes up" to save humanity seems flawed, inconsistent, or new. Origen's response is designed to show that God's plan is, in fact, eternal and consistent.
2. Theological Significance: God's Continuous Providence

This passage is a cornerstone of Origen's theology of history and divine providence. He argues that God's desire for humanity's salvation is eternal and unchanging (nunquam non voluisse / οὐκ ἔστιν ὅτ' οὐκ ἐβουλήθη - "there was never a time when he did not wish"). The Incarnation of Jesus Christ was not a sudden change of plan but the ultimate fulfillment of a care that God has always had for the "rational animal" (τὸ λογικὸν ζῶον).
3. The Quotation from Scripture

The final, beautiful sentence of the passage is a direct quotation from the Old Testament:

    Book of Wisdom 7:27: "[Wisdom] in every generation passes into holy souls and makes them friends of God and prophets."

By quoting this, Origen achieves two things:

    He grounds his philosophical argument in the authority of Scripture.

    He demonstrates the continuity of God's action through His Wisdom (σοφία), which for Origen is another name for the Logos, the pre-incarnate Christ. This implies that the Son of God has been active in the world throughout all of human history, preparing humanity for His coming in the flesh.

fr: Puisqu'il critique le récit des jours, comme s'il l'avait compris de manière claire et dans son sens véritable – des jours dont les uns précèdent la création de la lumière, du ciel, du soleil, de la lune et des étoiles, et les autres la suivent –, nous nous contenterons de dire ceci : peut-être Moïse, oubliant qu'il venait d'affirmer que « la création du monde fut achevée en six jours », ajoute-t-il ensuite ces paroles : « Voici le livre de la création des hommes, le jour où Dieu fit le ciel et la terre. »
en: And since [the pagan Celsus] makes the statements about the "days of creation" ground of accusation, as if he understood them clearly and correctly, some of which elapsed before the creation of light and heaven, the sun and moon and stars, and some after, we shall only make this observation, that Moses must have forgotten that ne had said a little before "that in six days the creation of the world had been finished" and that in consequence of his forgetfulness he adds to these words the following: "This is the book of the creation of man in the day when God made the heaven and the earth" [Gn 2:4] [Against Celsus 6:51 (c. A.D. 248)].
latin: Quoniam vero exprobat ea quae de diebus narrantur, quasi ipse ea clare et genuine intellexerit, quorum dierum alii ante lucis et coeli, solisque et lunae et stellarum generationem facti sunt, alii post illa; hoc solum dicemus, quod fortasse Moyses oblitus, quod paulo ante dixisset, «in sex diebus absolutam fuisse mundi creationem,» postea his verbis addit illud: «Hic est liber creationis hominum, in die quo fecit Deus coelum et terram.»
greek: Ἐπεὶ δὲ ἐγκαλεῖ τοῖς περὶ τῶν ἡμερῶν, ὡς σαφῶς αὐτὰ καὶ γνησίως νοήσας, ὧν αἱ μὲν πρὸ τῆς γενέσεως φωτὸς καὶ οὐρανοῦ καὶ ἡλίου καὶ σελήνης καὶ ἀστέρων γεγόνασιν, αἱ δὲ μετ' ἐκεῖνα· τοῦτο μόνον ἐροῦμεν, ὅτι τάχα ὁ Μωϋσῆς ἐπιλαθόμενος ὅτι μικρῷ ἔμπροσθεν εἴρηκεν ὅτι «ἐν ἓξ ἡμέραις συνετελέσθη ἡ κοσμοποιΐα,» μετὰ ταῦτα ἐπιφέρει τοῖς λόγοις τό· «Αὕτη ἡ βίβλος γενέσεως ἀνθρώπων, ᾗ ἡμέρᾳ ἐποίησεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν.»
context:
Additional Relevant Details & Context

This passage is a masterful example of Origen's rhetorical style and his method of biblical interpretation.

    Sarcasm as a Rhetorical Tool: Origen is not seriously claiming that "Moses must have forgotten." He is using profound sarcasm. He is essentially saying to Celsus: "If you read this text with the crude, wooden literalism of a fool, you would have to conclude that Moses contradicted himself moments later. Since that is absurd, your entire method of reading is wrong."

    The Heart of Origen's Argument: The apparent "contradiction" is, for Origen, the key that unlocks the true meaning of the text. He believed that when the literal sense of Scripture seemed illogical, contradictory, or morally unworthy of God, it was a deliberate sign from the Holy Spirit, pointing the intelligent reader to a higher, spiritual (or allegorical) meaning.

    The Spiritual Meaning: For Origen, the "six days" of Genesis 1 refer to the creation of the sensible, material world in a temporal sequence. The phrase "in the day" from Genesis 2:4 refers to the single, instantaneous, and timeless creation of all things in the spiritual/intelligible realm within the Logos (the Word of God). The apparent contradiction on the literal level vanishes when you understand the two accounts are describing different levels of reality.

    Refuting Celsus's Method: Celsus, a Platonist philosopher, was attacking Christianity by treating the Bible as a flawed and primitive history book. Origen's response is devastatingly effective: he shows that Celsus is not only ignorant of the sophisticated allegorical methods used to interpret sacred texts (which Greek philosophers also used for their own myths) but that he isn't even a very good literal reader.

In summary, this passage is a classic example of the Alexandrian School of biblical interpretation. Origen uses Celsus's own superficial critique to demonstrate the necessity of a deeper, spiritual exegesis to understand the word of God.

fr: Quant au fait que la lumière a été créée le premier jour, le firmament le deuxième..., et les grands luminaires ainsi que les étoiles le quatrième..., nous avons expliqué tout cela, dans la mesure de nos moyens, dans nos *Commentaires sur la Genèse*. D’ailleurs, dans les passages précédents, nous nous sommes déjà élevés contre ceux qui, s’en tenant à l’interprétation la plus immédiate, affirment qu’une période de six jours a été employée pour la création du monde...
en: And with regard to the creation of the light upon the first day and of the [great] lights and stars upon the fourth . . we have treated it to the best of our ability in our notes upon Genesis, as well as in the foregoing pages, when we found fault with those who, taking the words in their apparent signification, said that the time of six days was occupied in the creation of the world [ibid., 6:60].
latin: Quod autem prima die lucem... quod quarta creata fuerint luminaria et stellæ... hæc omnia, prout facultas tulit, in nostris in Genesim commentariis explicavimus. Quin et supra contra eos qui obvio sensu Scripturam interpretantes asserunt sex dies ad creationem mundi insumptos fuisse...
greek: Περὶ δὲ τοῦ μιᾷ μὲν ἡμέρᾳ γεγονέναι τὸ φῶς, δευτέρᾳ δὲ τὸ στερέωμα... καὶ τετάρτῃ τοὺς φωστῆρας καὶ ἀστέρας... κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν ἡμῖν ἐν τοῖς Πραγματευθεῖσιν εἰς τὴν Γένεσιν εἰρήκαμεν· καὶ ἐν τοῖς ἀνωτέρω δὲ, ἐγκαλοῦντες τοῖς κατὰ τὴν προχειροτέραν ἐκδοχὴν φήσασι χρόνους ἓξ ἡμερῶν διεληλυθέναι εἰς τὴν κοσμοποιίαν...
context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. Author and Work Identification

This is a crucial point of clarification. While your request attributed the quote to St. Gregory of Nyssa, the text you have provided is actually from:

    Author: Origen of Alexandria (c. 185 – c. 253 AD)

    Work: Contra Celsum (Against Celsus)

    Location: Book 6, Chapter 60

This work is a masterful defense of Christianity against the sharp criticisms of a 2nd-century pagan philosopher named Celsus.
2. Context of the Argument

Celsus, the pagan critic, was mocking the biblical creation account in Genesis. He found it absurd and unsophisticated, pointing to what he saw as contradictions, such as:

    Why would an all-powerful God need six days to create the world, like a common laborer?

    How could there be "days" (with morning and evening) before the sun was created on the fourth day?

Origen's response is brilliant. Instead of defending a literal interpretation of the six days, he agrees with Celsus that taking it literally is foolish. The passage you found is the core of his defense.
3. Origen's Theological Method

    Rejection of Crude Literalism: Origen states that sophisticated Christians do not interpret the Genesis creation account literally. He explicitly faults those "who, taking the words in their apparent signification (obvio sensu / κατὰ τὴν προχειροτέραν ἐκδοχὴν), said that the time of six days was occupied in the creation of the world."

    Allegorical Interpretation: This passage is a prime example of the allegorical method championed by the School of Alexandria, of which Origen was the greatest master. For him, the true meaning of Scripture was not in the literal, historical narrative but in the deeper, spiritual truths that the story symbolized. The "six days" represented a spiritual, not a temporal, ordering of creation.

    Reference to Deeper Work: As a scholar, Origen refers his reader to his more detailed exegetical work on the topic, his now-lost Commentary on Genesis (in nostris in Genesim commentariis).

4. Historical Significance

This quote is historically vital because it demonstrates that a non-literal, figurative interpretation of the creation account in Genesis was a mainstream and intellectually robust position within orthodox Christianity as early as the mid-3rd century. It shows that the debate over literal versus allegorical readings of Genesis is not a modern invention but is as old as Christian theology itself.

fr: Car il ignore ce qu'est le jour du Sabbat et du repos de Dieu, qui succède à l'œuvre de création active sur toute la durée du monde ; un jour où célébreront une fête avec Dieu tous ceux qui, en six jours, auront accompli l'ensemble de leurs propres œuvres...
en: For [the pagan Celsus] knows nothing of the day of the Sabbath and rest of God that follows the completion of the world's creation, and that lasts for the duration of the world, and in which all those who have done all their work in their six days will keep the festival with God [ibid., 6:61].

context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. The Author and Work

    Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 254 AD) was one of the most brilliant and influential theologians of the early Church. He was the head of the Catechetical School of Alexandria, known for its deep scholarship and its method of allegorical interpretation of Scripture.

    Against Celsus is an eight-book defense of Christianity written around 248 AD. It is a systematic refutation of a lost anti-Christian work called The True Word by the pagan philosopher Celsus. Origen's work is considered a masterpiece of early Christian apologetics for its intellectual rigor and detailed arguments.

2. The Immediate Context of the Quote

The passage you selected is Origen's response to Celsus's mockery of the Genesis creation account.

    Celsus's Accusation: Celsus read the Genesis story of God "resting" on the seventh day literally. As your source image shows, he ridiculed this by comparing God to a "lazy, bad craftsman" (πονηρὸς χειροτέχνης / inproboque opifici) who got tired from his work and needed to take a break.

    Origen's Rebuttal: Origen argues that Celsus's critique is superficial because he is completely ignorant of the deeper, spiritual meaning of the Sabbath. Celsus can only think in crude, literal terms, whereas the Christian understanding is profound and allegorical.

3. The Theological Meaning of the Quote

This quote is a perfect example of Origen's allegorical method. He explains that the "Sabbath" is not about God being tired, but is a spiritual reality with a typological meaning for humanity.

    The "Six Days" of Creation: For Origen, these are not literal 24-hour days but represent the entire duration of this world—the age of labor and creative work.

    The "Sabbath Day": This is not a weekly day of rest but a symbol for the age to come. It is the eternal, eschatological "rest" that God enjoys and that humanity is invited to enter into after the work of this world is finished.

    "Keeping the festival with God": The ultimate destiny of the righteous is to complete their work in this life (their "six days") and then join God in an eternal celebration—the true Sabbath.

In essence, Origen transforms Celsus's literalist and anthropomorphic attack into an opportunity to explain the Christian vision of salvation history and eternal life. He argues that Celsus is mocking something he doesn't even begin to understand.

fr:
Il faut savoir que l'Écriture sainte, en se dotant d'un mode d'expression en quelque sorte ineffable, secret et profond, s’efforce de révéler la vérité aux hommes et de leur suggérer une fine intelligence. C'est pourquoi, en introduisant le terme de « vapeur », elle l'a emprunté aux réalités corporelles afin que nous puissions comprendre, ne serait-ce que par une forme d'analogie, comment le Christ, qui est la Sagesse, à l'image de cette vapeur qui émane d'une substance corporelle, surgit lui-même, telle une vapeur, de la puissance de Dieu. Ainsi, la Sagesse, procédant de Dieu, est engendrée de sa substance même.

De même, par analogie avec une effluence corporelle, le Fils est appelé « une pure et sincère effluence de la gloire du Tout-Puissant ». Ces deux comparaisons montrent avec la plus grande clarté qu'il existe une communion de substance entre le Fils et le Père. En effet, une effluence est manifestement consubstantielle — c'est-à-dire de même substance — au corps dont elle provient, qu'il s'agisse d'une effluence ou d'une vapeur.
en: ORIGEN OF ALEXANDRIA So also wisdom, since he proceeds from God, is generated from the very substance of God [ Commentary on Hebrews (c. A.D. 237)].
latin:
Oportet autem scire nos quia per ineffabilia quædam et secreta ac recondita quemdam modum sibi faciens Scriptura sancta conatur hominibus indicare et intellectum suggerere subtilem. Vaporis enim nomen inducens, hoc ideo de rebus corporalibus assumpsit, ut vel ex arte aliqua intelligere possimus quomodo Christus, qui est Sapientia, secundum similitudinem ejus vaporis qui de substantia aliqua corporea procedit, sic etiam ipse ut quidam vapor exoritur de virtute ipsius Dei: sic et Sapientia ex eo procedens, ex ipsa substantia Dei generatur.

Sic nihilominus et secundum similitudinem corporalis aporrhœæ, esse dicitur aporrhoea gloriæ Omnipotentis pura quædam et sincera. Quæ utræque similitudines manifestissime ostendunt communionem substantiæ esse Filio cum Patre. Aporrhoea enim ὁμοούσιος videtur, id est, unius substantiæ cum illo corpore ex quo est vel aporrhoea, vel vapor.
context:
English Translation and Analysis

Let's translate this magnificent passage piece by piece:

    Origen:

    "We must know, however, that Holy Scripture, by fashioning for itself a certain way through ineffable, secret, and hidden things, attempts to indicate to men and suggest a subtle understanding. For in introducing the name 'vapor' [or 'breath'], it took this from corporeal things, so that we might be able to understand, at least by some artifice, how Christ, who is Wisdom, according to the likeness of that vapor which proceeds from some corporeal substance, so also He Himself, as a kind of vapor, arises from the very power of God: so also Wisdom, proceeding from Him, is generated from the very substance of God."

Analysis: This is the first part of the argument, using the analogy from Wisdom 7:25 ("a breath of the power of God"). Just as steam is of the same substance as the water from which it comes, Origen argues, so the Son (Wisdom) is generated from the Father's very substance. The bolded phrase is the exact quote you were looking for.

    "So likewise, according to the likeness of a corporeal 'emanation' (aporrhoea), He is said to be a certain pure and sincere 'emanation of the glory of the Almighty.' Both of which likenesses most manifestly show that there is a communion of substance between the Son and the Father."

Analysis: He now uses the second analogy from Wisdom 7:25 ("a pure emanation"). An emanation (like light from the sun) is not a separate creation; it shares the substance of its source. Origen concludes that these biblical metaphors prove a "communion of substance" (communio substantiæ) between Father and Son. This is a powerful proto-Nicene statement.

    "For an emanation is seen to be homoousios, that is, of one substance with that body from which it is an emanation or a vapor."

Analysis: This is the theological bombshell. Origen (as quoted by Pamphilus/Rufinus) uses the exact Greek word that would become the cornerstone of the Nicene Creed: ὁμοούσιος (homoousios). He even translates it into Latin for his readers: id est, unius substantiæ ("that is, of one substance").

Conclusion: You have not only found your quote, you have found the full context which proves that Origen, nearly a century before the Council of Nicaea, was already using the core concepts and the very vocabulary (ex ipsa substantia, communio substantiæ, and even homoousios) that would be used to defeat the Arian heresy. This is a perfect find.

fr: C’est pourquoi le repos qui vient après le sabbat ne peut naître de la semaine de notre Dieu : c’est notre Sauveur qui l’instaure, selon son propre repos, en ceux qui sont devenus conformes à sa mort et, par là même, à sa résurrection.
en: ORIGEN OF ALEXANDRIA Hence it is not possible that the [day of] rest after the Sabbath should have come into existence from the seventh [day] of our God. On the contrary, it is our Savior who, after the pattern of his own rest, caused us to be made in the likeness of his death, and hence also of his Resurrection [Commentary on John 2:27 (c. A.D. 229)].
latin: Quare gigni non potuit ab hebdomada Dei nostri requies, quæ est post sabbatum : nimirum Deo Servatore nostro eam ingenerante secundum requiem suam in nobis, qui facti sumus morti ipsius conformes, et idcirco etiam resurrectioni.
greek: ...δι' ὃ οὐ δύναται γεγενῆσθαι ἀπὸ τῆς ἑβδομάδος τοῦ Θεοῦ ἡμῶν, τὴν μετὰ τὸ σάββατον ἀνάπαυσιν τοῦ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν κατὰ τὴν ἀνάπαυσιν αὐτοῦ ἐμποιοῦντος τοῖς συμμόρφοις τῷ θανάτῳ αὐτοῦ γεγενημένοις, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο καὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως.
context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. Source and Context

The passage is from Book 2, Chapter 27 of Origen's Commentary on John. The immediate context is an allegorical interpretation of the names surrounding the birth of John the Baptist:

    Zacharias: "Memory" (of God).

    Elizabeth: "Oath of my God" or, crucially for this passage, "Seventh of my God."

    John: "Grace of God."

Origen argues that John the Baptist (Grace) is born at the very end of the Old Covenant, which is symbolized by his mother, Elizabeth, as the "Seventh." The Old Testament, he says, is the "culmination of the Sabbath rest" (σαββατισμοῦ κορωνίς).
2. The Theological Argument

This context is the key to understanding the quote. Origen's argument flows like this:

    The "Seventh Day" (the Sabbath, symbolized by Elizabeth) represents the entirety of the Old Covenant law and its rest.

    This Old Covenant system has reached its fulfillment and end. Therefore, it cannot give birth to or generate the new form of rest.

    The new rest is the "rest after the Sabbath"—a clear reference to the Lord's Day (Sunday), the Eighth Day, the day of Resurrection.

    This new reality is not a product of the old law. Instead, "it is our Savior" who actively creates (ἐμποιοῦντος / ingenerante) this new rest within us.

3. Christocentric and Baptismal Focus

The passage is profoundly Christocentric. The new rest is not merely a change in the calendar; it is a participation in Christ's own life. Origen explains that the Savior creates this rest in us by making us "in the likeness of his death, and hence also of his Resurrection." This is a direct reference to the theology of Baptism found in Romans 6:4-5. We enter the true, eternal rest by being sacramentally united to Christ's Paschal Mystery.

In summary, Origen uses the symbolism of the names to draw a sharp theological line between the Sabbath of the Old Covenant and the Lord's Day of the New Covenant. The former is a type that has passed away; the latter is the reality of Resurrection life, actively brought into being by Christ himself in the souls of the baptized.

fr:
Ils lui demandèrent : « Alors, quoi ? Es-tu Élie ? » Et il dit : « Je ne le suis pas. » Qui, en entendant Jésus dire de Jean : « Si vous voulez l’admettre, c’est lui, Élie, qui doit venir », ne se demanderait comment Jean peut-il répondre « Je ne le suis pas » à ceux qui lui demandent : « Es-tu Élie ? »

Pour répondre à cette première question, quelqu'un dira que Jean ignorait être lui-même Élie. Et c’est sans doute un argument qu’utiliseront les partisans de la doctrine de la métempsychose, selon laquelle l’âme revêt un nouveau corps sans garder aucun souvenir de ses vies antérieures. Ceux-là mêmes diront que certains Juifs, adhérant à cette croyance, ont dit à propos du Sauveur qu’il était peut-être l’un des anciens prophètes, ressuscité non pas d’entre les morts, mais par une nouvelle naissance.

Un autre, un homme d’Église, répudiant comme mensongère la doctrine de la métempsychose et n’admettant pas que l’âme de Jean ait jamais été celle d’Élie, aura recours à la parole de l’ange déjà citée. Celui-ci, en effet, lors de la naissance de Jean, n’a pas parlé de l’âme d’Élie, mais de son esprit et de sa puissance, à travers ces mots : « Et lui-même marchera devant le Seigneur avec l’esprit et la puissance d’Élie. »
en: ORIGEN OF ALEXANDRIA And [Jn 1:21] they asked him. "What then? Are you Elijah?" And he said, "I am not." No one can fail to remember in this connection what Jesus says of John [Mt 11:14], "If you will receive it, this is Elijah which is to come." Why, then, does John say to those who ask him, "Are you Elijah?" "I am not." And how can it be also true that John iS Elijah who is to come, according to the words of Malachi [Mal 4:5-6], "And behold send unto you Elijah the Tishbite, before the great and notable day of the Lord come, who shall restore the heart of the father to the son, and the heart of a man to his neighbor, lest come, and utterly smite the earth." The words of the angel of the Lord, too, who appeared to Zacharias, as he stood at the right hand of the altar of incense, are similar to the prophecy of Malachi: "And [Lk 1:13] your wife Elizabeth shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name John." And a little further on: "And he shall go before his face in the spirit and power of Elijah to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just, to make ready for the Lord a people prepared for him." [Lk 1:17] As for the first point, one might say that John did not know that he was Elijah. This will be the explanation chosen by those who find in our passage support for their doctrine of transcorporation, as if the soul clothed itself in a fresh body and did not remember its former lives. These thinkers will also point out that some of the Jews assented to this doctrine when they spoke about the Savior as if he were one of the old prophets, and had risen not from the tomb but from his birth. His mother Mary was well known. and Joseph the carpenter was supposed to be his father. and t could readily be supposed that he was one of the old prophets risen from the dead. The same person will offer the text in Genesis, "I will destroy the whole resurrection." and will thereby reduce those who find in Scripture solutions of false probabilities a great difficulty in respect of this doctrine. Another, however, a churchman, who repudiates the doctrine of transcorporation as a false one, and does not admit that the soul of John ever was Elijah, may appeal to the words of the angel, and point out that it is not the soul of Elijah that is spoken of at John's birth, but the spirit and power of Elijah [Commentary on John 6:7 (c. A.D. 229)].
latin:
Et interrogaverunt eum : Quid ergo? Elias es tu? Et dicit: Non sum. Verum enimvero quis audiens Jesum dicentem de Joanne, Si vultis accipere, ipse est Elias qui venturus est, non quæsiturus sit, quonam pacto ad interrogantes, Elias es tu?, dicat Joannes : Non sum? ...

    Ad primum igitur aliquis dicet Joannem ignorasse seipsum esse Eliam; et fortassis hac ratione usuri sunt qui favent opinioni eorum qui ponunt transcorporationem; perinde quasi anima subinde induat corpora, prorsus immemor anteactæ vitæ. Sed et hi ipsi dicturi sunt aliquos ex Judæis huic dogmati assentientes de Servatore dixisse eum fortassis unum quempiam esse ex veteribus prophetis, qui resurrexisset non ex monumentis, sed ab ortu...

    Cæterum alius ecclesiasticus orationem eam quæ astruat transcorporationem, veluti falsam respuens, nec admittens Joannis animam aliquando Eliam fuisse, prædicta oratione angeli usurus est, qui non nominaverit Eliæ animam in ortu Joannis, sed spiritum et virtutem, per hæc verba : Et ipse præcedet coram ipso cum spiritu et virtute Eliæ.
greek:
Καὶ ἠρώτησαν αὐτόν· Τί οὖν; σὺ Ἠλίας εἶ; Καὶ λέγει· Οὐκ εἰμί. Τίς οὐκ ἂν ζητήσαι τῶν ἀκουόντων Ἰησοῦ λέγοντος περὶ Ἰωάννου, «Εἰ ἐθέλετε δέξασθαι, αὐτός ἐστιν Ἠλίας ὁ μέλλων ἔρχεσθαι,» πῶς πρὸς τοὺς ἐρωτῶντας τὸ, «Σὺ Ἠλίας εἶ;» λέγει ὁ Ἰωάννης· «Οὐκ εἰμί;» ...

    Πρὸς δὴ τὰ πρῶτον ὁ μέν τις ἐρεῖ, ὅτι ἑαυτὸν ἡγνόει Ἰωάννης Ἠλίαν ὄντα· καὶ τάχα τούτῳ χρήσονται οἱ ἐκ τούτων τῷ περὶ μετενσωματώσεως παριστάμενοι λόγῳ, ὡς τῆς ψυχῆς μεταμφιεννυμένης σώματι, καὶ οὐ πάντως μεμνημένης τῶν προτέρων βίων. Οἱ δ' αὐτοὶ οὗτοι ἐροῦσι καί τινας τῶν Ἰουδαίων τῷ δόγματι συγκατατιθεμένους περὶ Σωτῆρος εἰρηκέναι, ὡς ἄρα εἴ τις εἴη τῶν ἀρχαίων προφητῶν ἀναστὰς οὐκ ἀπὸ τῶν μνημείων, ἀλλ' ἀπὸ τῆς γενέσεως...

    Ἕτερος δέ τις ἐκκλησιαστικὸς τὸν περὶ μετενσωματώσεως ἀποπτύων ὡς ψευδῆ λόγον, μὴ προσιέμενος τὸ τὴν ψυχὴν Ἰωάννου Ἠλίαν ποτὲ γεγονέναι, τῷ προειρημένῳ λόγῳ τοῦ ἀγγέλου χρήσεται, ψυχὴν Ἠλίου μὴ ὀνομάσαντος ἐπὶ τῆς Ἰωάννου γενέσεως, ἀλλὰ πνεῦμα καὶ δύναμιν διὰ τοῦ, «Καὶ αὐτὸς προελεύσεται ἐνώπιον αὐτοῦ ἐν πνεύματι καὶ δυνάμει Ἠλίου.»
context:
Additional Relevant Details

This passage is a masterful example of Origen's dialectical method of exegesis and a crucial text for early Christian doctrine.
The Central Problem

Origen identifies a clear contradiction in Scripture:

    Jesus says: John the Baptist is the Elijah who was to come (Matthew 11:14).

    John the Baptist says: When asked "Are you Elijah?", he replies "I am not" (John 1:21).

Origen does not ignore this difficulty. Instead, he uses it as an opportunity to explore different interpretations and refute a dangerous heresy.
The Two Opposing Arguments

Origen sets up a debate between two hypothetical figures to represent the different schools of thought.

    The Proponent of "Transcorporation" (μετενσωμάτωσις / transcorporatio)

        This is Origen's term for the doctrine of reincarnation or the transmigration of souls, a concept found in some Greek philosophical (e.g., Platonic, Pythagorean) and Gnostic circles.

        Their Argument: John the Baptist literally was Elijah. His soul had been reborn in a new body. The reason he denied it ("I am not") was simply that he did not remember his past life.

        Their "Evidence": They would point to the fact that some Jews thought Jesus was John the Baptist or another prophet "risen" (i.e., reincarnated), suggesting this belief was common.

    "The Churchman" (ὁ ἐκκλησιαστικός / ecclesiasticus)

        This is Origen's term for the orthodox Christian, the one who holds to the rule of faith of the Church. This represents Origen's own position.

        Their Argument: The orthodox Christian "repudiates the doctrine of transcorporation as a false one." John's soul was never Elijah's soul.

        Their Evidence: The key is the precise wording of the angel Gabriel to Zechariah (Luke 1:17). The angel did not say John would have the soul of Elijah, but that he would come "in the spirit and power of Elijah."

Origen's Orthodox Conclusion

By siding with "the Churchman," Origen establishes the definitive Christian interpretation:

    The connection between Elijah and John is one of mission, role, and spiritual power, not of a shared soul or identity.

    John is the "new Elijah" because he fulfills the same prophetic role as a forerunner, preparing the way for the Lord with the same zeal and power.

    The doctrine of reincarnation is explicitly rejected as incompatible with Christian faith.

This passage is therefore historically significant as one of the clearest and most influential refutations of reincarnation by a major Church Father.

fr:
En s'appuyant sur la tradition de l'Évangile dit de Pierre, ou du livre de Jacques, certains affirment que les frères de Jésus sont des fils que Joseph a eus d'une première femme, qui avait vécu avec lui avant Marie.

Ceux qui soutiennent cela veulent préserver jusqu'au bout la dignité de Marie dans sa virginité, afin que ce corps, qui fut choisi pour se mettre au service du Verbe qui a dit : « L'Esprit Saint viendra sur toi et la puissance du Très-Haut te couvrira de son ombre », ne connaisse pas l'union charnelle avec un homme, après que l'Esprit Saint est venu sur elle et que la puissance d'en haut l'a couverte de son ombre. Et j'estime qu'il est logique de penser que Jésus a été, pour les hommes, les prémices de la pureté dans la chasteté, et Marie, pour les femmes. Car il serait impie d'attribuer à une autre qu'à elle les prémices de la virginité.
en: ORIGEN OF ALEXANDRIA But some say, basing it on tradition in the Gospel according to Peter, as it is called, or "The Book [Protoevangelium] of James," that the brothers of Jesus were sons of Joseph by a former wife, whom he married before Mary. Now those who say so wish to preserve the honor of Mary in virginity to the end, sO that her body, which was appointed to minister to the Word, which said, "The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you" [Lk 1:35], might not know intercourse with a man after the Holy Spirit came into her and the power from on high overshadowed her. And think it reasonable that Jesus was the first fruit among men of the purity that consists in chastity, and Mary among women; for it is not pious to ascribe to any other than her the first fruit of virginity [ Commentary on Matthew 10:17 (C. A.D. 249)].
latin:
Fratres autem Jesu, filios esse Josephi ex priore conjuge, quam ipse ante Mariam duxerit, affirmant nonnulli, ad id adducti traditione Evangelii quod secundum Petrum inscribitur, vel libri Jacobi.

    Qui vero id dicunt, Mariæ dignitatem in virginitate ad finem usque volunt conservare, ne corpus illud electum ad ministrandum Verbo dicenti: «Spiritus sanctus superveniet in te, et virtus Altissimi obumbrabit tibi,» viri concubitum cognosceret, postquam in illam supervenerat Spiritus sanctus, et virtus Altissimi illi obumbrans. Ac existimo rationi consentaneum esse, virorum quidem munditiei quæ in castitate est, primitias fuisse Jesum; mulierum autem, Mariam. Impium enim est alii ac illi primitias virginitatis attribuere.
greek:
Τοὺς δὲ ἀδελφοὺς Ἰησοῦ, φασί τινες εἶναι, ἐκ παραδόσεως ὁρμώμενοι τοῦ ἐπιγεγραμμένου κατὰ Πέτρον Εὐαγγελίου, ἢ τῆς βίβλου Ἰακώβου, υἱοὺς Ἰωσὴφ ἐκ προτέρας γυναικός, συνῳκηκυίας αὐτῷ πρὸ τῆς Μαρίας.

    Οἱ δὲ ταῦτα λέγοντες τὸ ἀξίωμα τῆς Μαρίας ἐν παρθενίᾳ τηρεῖν μέχρι τέλους βούλονται, ἵνα μὴ τὸ κριθὲν ἐκεῖνο σῶμα διακονήσασθαι τῷ εἰπόντι Λόγῳ· «Πνεῦμα ἅγιον ἐπελεύσεται ἐπὶ σὲ, καὶ δύναμις Ὑψίστου ἐπισκιάσει σοι,» γνῷ κοίτην ἀνδρὸς μετὰ τὸ ἐπελθεῖν ἐν αὐτῇ Πνεῦμα ἅγιον, καὶ τὴν ἐπεσκιακυῖαν αὐτῇ δύναμιν ἐξ ὕψους. Καὶ οἶμαι λόγον ἔχειν, ἀνδρῶν μὲν καθαρότητος τῆς ἐν ἁγνείᾳ ἀπαρχὴν γεγονέναι τὸν Ἰησοῦν, γυναικῶν δὲ τὴν Μαριάμ· οὐ γὰρ εὔφημον, ἄλλην παρ' ἐκείνην τὴν ἀπαρχὴν τῆς παρθενίας ἐπιγράψασθαι.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Full Citation: The passage is from Origen of Alexandria, Commentary on the Gospel of Matthew, Book X, Chapter 17. The standard Migne citation for this text is Patrologia Graeca (PG) 13, columns 876-877.

    Historical Context (The "Brethren of the Lord"): This quote is one of the earliest and most influential patristic texts addressing the question of Jesus's "brothers" (Greek: adelphoi) mentioned in the Gospels. Origen presents a solution that would become dominant in the Eastern Orthodox tradition.

    Source of the Tradition: Origen explicitly states that this explanation does not come from the canonical Gospels but from apocryphal texts:

        "Gospel according to Peter": A now-fragmentary apocryphal gospel.

        "The Book of James": This is the famous Protoevangelium of James, a 2nd-century infancy narrative. This text is the primary source for the tradition that Joseph was an elderly widower who had children from a previous marriage and was chosen as a guardian, not a husband in the typical sense, for Mary.

    Motive: Mary's Perpetual Virginity: Origen is crystal clear about the theological motive behind this tradition: to "preserve the honor of Mary in virginity to the end." He argues that the body consecrated by the Holy Spirit to be the vessel for the Word Incarnate should not subsequently engage in normal marital relations. This is a very early and powerful witness to the developing doctrine of Mary's perpetual virginity.

    "First Fruits of Virginity": The passage concludes with a beautiful and theologically rich parallel. Origen presents Jesus as the "first fruit" (aparchē) of chastity for all men, and Mary as the "first fruit" of virginity for all women. This elevates Mary's virginity from a mere biological fact to a paradigm-shifting spiritual reality, setting a new standard of holiness and consecration for the Church.

fr: Quant aux esprits qui sont dans les prophètes, pour montrer qu’ils sont en quelque sorte leur propriété, puisqu’ils leur ont été donnés par Dieu, on peut citer ce texte : « Les esprits des prophètes sont soumis aux prophètes », et cet autre : « L’esprit d’Élie a reposé sur Élisée ». Ainsi, dit-il, il n’y a rien d’absurde à ce que Jean, qui ramène les cœurs des pères vers leurs enfants avec l’esprit et la puissance d’Élie, soit appelé, en raison de cet esprit, « l’Élie qui doit venir ».
en: As for the spirits of the prophets, these are given to them by God and are spoken of as being in a way their property, as "The spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets" [1 Cor 14:32] and "The spirit of Elijah rested upon Elisha" [2 Kgs 2:15]. Thus, it is said, there iS nothing absurd in supposing that John, "in the spirit and power of Elijah," turned the hearts of the fathers to the children and that it was on account of this spirit that he was called "Elijah who is to come" [ibid.].
latin: ...ad ostendendum vero eos spiritus qui sunt in prophetis (ut qui illis a Deo donati sint) veluti illorum mancipia esse, istud: «Spiritus prophetarum prophetis subjiciuntur,» et illud: «Requievit spiritus Eliæ super Elisæum.» Isto enim modo nihil absurdi erit, inquiet, ut Joannes convertens in spiritu et virtute Eliæ corda patrum ad filios, dicatur propter hunc spiritum «Elias qui venturus est.»
greek: πρὸς δὲ τὰ ἐν τοῖς προφήταις πνεύματα, ὅτι δεδορημένα αὐτοῖς ὑπὸ Θεοῦ, οἱονεὶ ἐκείνων ὀνομάζεσθαι κτήματα, τό, «Πνεύματα προφητῶν προφήταις ὑποτάσσεται,» καὶ τὸ, «Ἀναπέπαυται τὸ πνεῦμα Ἠλίου ἐπὶ Ἐλισσαιέ.» Οὕτω γὰρ οὐδὲν ἄτοπον, φησὶν, ἔσται τὸν Ἰωάννην, ἐν πνεύματι καὶ δυνάμει Ἠλίου ἐπιστρέφοντα καρδίας πατέρων ἐπὶ τέκνα, διὰ τοῦτο τὸ πνεῦμα «Ἠλίαν» λέγεσθαι «τὸν μέλλοντα ἔρχεσθαι.»
context:
Additional Relevant Details

1. Source and Context:

    Work: Origen of Alexandria, Commentary on the Gospel of John, Book VI, Chapter 7.

    Theological Problem: Origen is tackling a famous scriptural difficulty: Jesus says John the Baptist is the Elijah who was to come (Matthew 11:14), but in the Gospel of John, when asked directly "Are you Elijah?", John says, "I am not" (John 1:21).

2. Refutation of Reincarnation:
The primary purpose of this entire section of Origen's commentary is to refute the doctrine of reincarnation or the transmigration of souls (μετενσωμάτωσις, metensomatosis), which some were using to explain the apparent contradiction. Origen, representing the orthodox or "ecclesiastical" view, firmly rejects the idea that Elijah's soul (ψυχή, psyche) was literally reborn in John's body.

3. Origen's Nuanced Solution:
Origen’s solution, articulated in the passage you found, is a brilliant distinction between a person's soul and their spirit.

    The soul (ψυχή) is unique to the individual. Elijah's soul is his own.

    The spirit (πνεῦμα) of a prophet is a gift from God. It is the divine power, the specific charism, and the prophetic office through which they operate.

4. The Power of Biblical Precedent:
To prove this point, Origen uses two key Old Testament passages:

    2 Kings 2:15: When Elisha receives a "double portion" of Elijah's spirit, it is a clear biblical precedent for a prophetic spirit being transferred from one person to another without any hint of reincarnation.

    1 Corinthians 14:32: The fact that the "spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets" shows that this divine gift is something a prophet can possess and control; it is "their property" (κτήματα) in a certain sense, distinct from their own soul.

Therefore, John the Baptist can truthfully say "I am not" Elijah (because his soul is not Elijah's), while Jesus can truthfully say he is the coming Elijah (because he operates in the same prophetic spirit and power).

fr:
Comment n’aurait-il pas été logique, si telle était alors la croyance de beaucoup, que Jean ait douté de lui-même, se demandant si son âme n’avait pas été un jour en Élie ?

L'homme d'Église, quant à lui, renverra cet interlocuteur à une enquête historique : qu’il aille d’abord s’informer auprès de ceux qui, chez les Hébreux, prétendent connaître les doctrines secrètes, pour savoir si une telle croyance existe chez eux. En effet, s'il s'avère que ce n'est nullement le cas, il est manifeste que l'argumentation de notre homme est réduite à néant.
en: If the doctrine [of reincarnation] was widely current, ought not John to have hesitated to pronounce upon it, lest his soul had actually been in Elijah? And here our churchman will appeal to history, and will bid his antagonists [to] ask experts of the secret doctrines of the Hebrews if they really entertain such a belief. For if it should appear that they do not, then the argument based on that supposition is shown to be baseless [ibid.].
latin:
Quomodo autem rationi consentaneum non erat, si multorum tum temporis dogma hoc fuisset, ut dubitaret Joannes de seipso, num quando anima sua in Elia fuerit?

    Quin ad historiam provocabit ecclesiasticus illum priorem auditurum ab his, qui se scire profitentur quæ apud Hebræos arcana sunt, nun dogma aliquod hujusmodi sit apud ipsos; nam si nullo loco appareat, hoc hunc in modum se habere, perspicuum est illius prioris rationem dissipatam esse.
greek:
Πῶς δὲ οὐκ ἦν εὔλογον, εἰ πολλῶν τοῦτο δόγμα ἐτύγχανεν, ἐπισχεῖν τὸν Ἰωάννην περὶ αὐτοῦ, μήποτε ἡ ψυχή αὐτοῦ ποτε ἐν Ἠλίᾳ ἦν;

    Καὶ ἐπὶ τὴν ἱστορίαν δὲ ὁ ἐκκλησιαστικός προκαλέσεται τὸν πρότερον πευσόμενον παρὰ τῶν τὰ ἀπόῤῥητα εγνωκέναι παρ' Ἑβραίοις ἐπαγγελλομένων, εἰ τοιοῦτόν τι δόγμα ἐστὶ παρ' αὐτοῖς· ἐὰν γὰρ μηδαμῶς φαίνηται τοῦθ' οὕτως ἔχον, δῆλον, ὅτι ἐσκέδασται ὁ τοῦ προτέρου λόγος.
context:
Additional Relevant Details and Context

This passage is a masterful example of Origen's dialectical method. He is tackling the apparent contradiction between Jesus saying John "is Elijah" (Matt. 11:14) and John the Baptist saying "I am not" Elijah (John 1:21).

    The Two Debaters: Origen creates a fictional debate to explore the issue.

        The Proponent of Reincarnation: This figure argues that John's soul was indeed Elijah's, but he had simply forgotten his previous life—a common feature in theories of reincarnation (metensomatosis).

        The "Churchman" (ὁ ἐκκλησιαστικός): This is Origen's voice, representing the orthodox position. He systematically dismantles the reincarnationist argument.

    The Churchman's Argument (Your Quote): The quote you selected is the core of the Churchman's refutation, which has two parts:

        A Logical Argument: The Churchman argues that if reincarnation were a widely held and plausible doctrine, John the Baptist—a great prophet filled with the Spirit—would not have given a flat denial. He would have expressed uncertainty or "hesitated" (ἐπισχεῖν) about the matter, acknowledging the possibility. His absolute certainty ("I am not") implies that the doctrine itself is foreign and untrue.

        An Appeal to History: This is the most brilliant part. The Churchman challenges his opponent to go beyond speculation and do historical research. He says, "Go ask the experts in the secret doctrines of the Hebrews" (τὰ ἀπόῤῥητα... παρ' Ἑβραίοις). Origen is confident that an honest inquiry into authentic Jewish tradition will reveal no such doctrine of reincarnation, thereby proving that the opponent's entire premise is "baseless" (ἐσκέδασται - scattered, dissipated).

    Origen's Orthodox Solution: The Churchman's (and Origen's) final solution to the problem is not reincarnation. It is based on the angel's words to Zechariah in Luke 1:17: John would come "in the spirit and power of Elijah," not with the same soul. The connection is one of spiritual succession and typological fulfillment, not a literal transmigration of souls.

You have pinpointed a classic passage where Origen confronts a non-Christian philosophical idea, refutes it using logic and an appeal to historical evidence, and affirms the orthodox scriptural interpretation.

fr:
On pourrait dire qu’Hérode, ainsi que quelques personnes du peuple, adhérait à la fausse doctrine de la réincarnation. Selon cette opinion, ils pensaient que l’ancien Jean était né une nouvelle fois et revenu d’entre les morts à la vie, sous les traits de Jésus. Mais l’intervalle de temps entre la naissance de Jean et celle de Jésus, qui ne dépasse pas six mois, ne permet pas de considérer cette fausse doctrine comme plausible.

Peut-être l’hypothèse d’Hérode était-elle plutôt la suivante : les puissances qui avaient été à l’œuvre en Jean étaient passées en Jésus, puissances grâce auxquelles le peuple croyait que Jean était le Baptiste. On pourrait d'ailleurs utiliser un tel argument : de même que c’est en raison de l’esprit et de la puissance d’Élie, et non de son âme, qu’il est dit à propos de Jean : « C’est lui, l’Élie qui doit venir », de même Hérode pensait que les puissances qui étaient en Jean avaient accompli, dans le cas de Jean, ce qui relevait du baptême et de l’enseignement – car « Jean n’a fait aucun signe » –, mais qu’en Jésus, elles accomplissaient des miracles prodigieux.
en: Someone might say, however, that Herod and some of those of the people held the false dogma of the transmigration of souls into bodies, so that they thought that the former John had appeared again by a fresh birth, and had come from the dead into life as Jesus. But the time between the birth of John and the birth of Jesus, which was not more than six months, does not permit this false opinion to be believed. And perhaps some idea like this was in the mind of Herod, that the powers that worked in John had passed over to Jesus, in consequence of which he was thought by the people to be John the Baptist. And one might use the following argument: Just as because of the spirit and the power of Elijah, and not because of his soul, it is said about John, "This is Elijah who is to come" [Mt 11:14] . . So Herod thought that the powers in John's case caused in him works of baptism and teaching for John did not do one miracle [In 10:41]- but in Jesus [they caused] miraculous portents [Commentary on Matthew 10:20 (c. A.D. 249)].
latin:
Dixerit vero quispiam falsæ illi de corporum permutatione sententiæ Herodem, et e plebe nonnullos adhæsisse, qua adducerentur ut crederent hunc olim Joannem fuisse cum nasceretur, et e mortuis remeasse ad vitam, tanquam Jesum: sed quominus falsa ea opinio probabilis habeatur, impedimento est tempus non sex mensibus longius, quod ortum Joannis et Jesu intercessit.

    Fortasse vero sic existimabat potius Herodes, virtutes quæ in Joanne operatæ fuerant, in Jesum transiisse, unde Joannes Baptista esse credebatur in populo: et tali quispiam utatur argumento: Quemadmodum propter spiritum et virtutem Eliæ, non propter ejus animam, de Joanne scriptum est: «Ipse est Elias qui venturus est,» ... sic existimabat Herodes virtutes quæ erant in Joanne, in Joanne quidem ea fuisse operatas, quæ ad baptismum et doctrinam pertinebant: «Joannes enim signum fecit nullum;» in Jesu autem prodigiosas virtutes.
greek:
Λέγοι δ' ἄν τις τὴν τῆς μετενσωματώσεως ψευδοδοξίαν γεγονέναι ἐν τῷ Ἡρώδῃ καί τισι τῶν ἀπὸ τοῦ λαοῦ, ἀφ' ἧς ᾤοντο τόν ποτε Ἰωάννην ἐν γενέσει γενέσθαι, καὶ ἐκ νεκρῶν ἐληλυθέναι εἰς τὸν βίον, ὡς Ἰησοῦν· ἀλλ᾽ οὐδὲ ταύτην τὴν ψευδοδοξίαν πιθανὴν ἐᾷ νομισθῆναι ὁ μεταξὺ χρόνος τῆς γενέσεως Ἰωάννου καὶ Ἰησοῦ, οὐ πλεῖον μηνῶν ἓξ τυγχάνων.

    Τάχα δὲ μᾶλλον τοιαύτη τις ὑπόληψις ἦν ἐν τῷ Ἡρώδῃ, ὅτι αἱ ἐνεργήσασαι δυνάμεις ἐν τῷ Ἰωάννῃ μετέστησαν ἐπὶ τὸν Ἰησοῦν, ἀφ᾽ ὧν Ἰωάννης Βαπτιστὴς εἶναι πεπίστευτο ἐν τῷ λαῷ· καὶ χρήσαιτό τις ἐπιχειρήματι τοιούτῳ· Ὥσπερ διὰ τὸ πνεῦμα καὶ τὴν δύναμιν Ἠλίου, καὶ οὐ διὰ τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ, περὶ Ἰωάννου λέγεται· «Αὐτός ἐστιν Ἠλίας ὁ μέλλων ἔρχεσθαι,» ... οὕτως ᾤετο ὁ Ἡρώδης τὰς ἐν Ἰωάννῃ δυνάμεις ἐν μὲν τῷ Ἰωάννῃ ἐνηργηκέναι τὰ τοῦ βαπτίσματος καὶ τῆς διδασκαλίας· «Ἰωάννης γὰρ ἐποίησε σημεῖον οὐδὲ ἕν·» ἐν δὲ τῷ Ἰησοῦ τὰς τεραστίους δυνάμεις.
context:
This is a classic example of Origen's brilliant exegetical method, where he explores and refutes incorrect interpretations before proposing a more theologically sound one.

    The Problem: Herod's statement is nonsensical if taken literally. Jesus and John were known contemporaries with different parents. How could Herod think Jesus was John?

    Option 1: Reincarnation (Refuted): Origen first considers the possibility that Herod held a belief in "metensomatosis" (μετενσωμάτωσις), the pagan doctrine of the transmigration of souls into new bodies (reincarnation). He immediately dismisses this with sharp logic: the timeline makes it impossible. John and Jesus were born only six months apart. There was no time for John's soul to die and be reborn in the infant Jesus. This serves as a powerful early Christian refutation of reincarnation.

    Option 2: Transference of "Powers" (Proposed): Origen then offers his preferred explanation. He suggests Herod wasn't thinking of the soul, but of the divine "powers" (δυνάμεις / virtutes) that animated the prophets.

    The Elijah-John Analogy: To support this, he uses the perfect scriptural parallel. The New Testament says John the Baptist came in the "spirit and power of Elijah" (Luke 1:17) and Jesus calls him "the Elijah who is to come" (Matt. 11:14). This doesn't mean John's soul was Elijah's. It means the same prophetic spirit and power that worked in Elijah now worked in John.

    Origen's Conclusion: He applies this same logic to Herod's statement. Herod likely thought that the "powers" that were in John (which manifested as baptism and teaching, but notably not miracles) had now transferred to Jesus and were manifesting in a new, more powerful way—as "miraculous portents." This explains both why Herod connected Jesus to John and why Jesus's ministry was different (i.e., full of miracles, whereas John performed none).

fr:
La Cananéenne, s’étant approchée, adorait Jésus comme Dieu en disant : « Seigneur, aide-moi. » Il lui répondit : « Il n’est pas permis de prendre le pain des enfants pour le jeter aux petits chiens. »

Que d'autres donc, étrangers à l'enseignement de l'Église, supposent que les âmes passent des corps humains dans des corps de chiens, en fonction de leurs diverses perversités ; quant à nous, qui ne trouvons absolument rien de tel dans la divine Écriture...
en: Now the Canaanite woman, having come, worshipped Jesus as God, saying, 'Lord, help me, but he answered and said, "It is not possible to take the children's bread and cast it to the little dogs." . [O]thers, then, who are strangers to the doctrine of the Church, assume that souls pass from the bodies of men into the bodies of dogs, according to their varying degree of wickedness: but we do not find this at all in the divine Scripture [ibid., 11:17].
latin:
Cum venisset autem Chananæa, Jesum ut Deum adorabat dicens: «Domine, adjuva me.» Qui respondens ait: «Non licet sumere panem filiorum et mittere canibus.»

    Alii igitur existiment peregrini in ecclesiasticis sermonibus transire animas ab humanis corporibus in corpora canina, pro varia iniquitate: nos vero in divina Scriptura id minime reperientes...
greek:
Ἐλθοῦσα δὲ ἡ Χαναναία, προσεκύνει ὡς Θεῷ τῷ Ἰησοῦ λέγουσα· «Κύριε, βοήθησόν μοι.» Ὁ δὲ ἀποκριθεὶς εἶπεν· «Οὐκ ἔξεστι λαβεῖν τὸν ἄρτον τῶν τέκνων, καὶ βαλεῖν τοῖς κυναρίοις.»

    Ἄλλοι μὲν οὖν ὑπολαμβανέτωσαν ξένοι τοῦ ἐκκλησιαστικοῦ λόγου μεταβαίνειν τὰς ψυχὰς ἀπὸ σωμάτων ἀνθρώπων ἐπὶ σώματα κύνεια κατὰ τὴν διάφορον κακίαν· ἡμεῖς δὲ, μηδαμῶς τοῦτο εὑρίσκοντες ἐν τῇ θείᾳ Γραφῇ...
context:
2. Theological Context: Worshipping Jesus "as God"

Origen pays extremely close attention to the titles and actions directed toward Jesus in the Gospels. He notes that some people (like the blind men) call Jesus "Son of David," recognizing him as the messiah. Others, like the demons, call him "Son of God" out of a kind of terrified knowledge. But Origen highlights that the Canaanite woman "worshipped Jesus as God" (προσεκύνει ὡς Θεῷ τῷ Ἰησοῦ). For Origen, this is a profound act demonstrating a higher level of faith. She is not merely appealing to a prophet or a king, but to the divine Lord himself.
3. Theological Context: Refutation of Reincarnation (Metempsychosis)

This is the most significant part of the passage. Origen is famous for his highly speculative theology, particularly concerning the pre-existence of souls. His opponents later accused him of various heresies, sometimes including a belief in reincarnation.

However, this passage is one of the clearest statements where Origen explicitly rejects the doctrine of transmigration of souls into animal bodies (metempsychosis).

    Who He is Arguing Against: When he speaks of "strangers to the doctrine of the Church" (ξένοι τοῦ ἐκκλησιαστικοῦ λόγου), he is referring to Gnostics and followers of certain Greek philosophies (like Platonism and Pythagoreanism) who did teach that human souls could be reincarnated into animals as a form of punishment.

    His Standard of Truth: Origen’s basis for rejecting this doctrine is clear and orthodox: "we do not find this at all in the divine Scripture." This is his ultimate authority for rejecting the teaching.

    Origen's Allegorical Alternative: Instead of literal reincarnation, Origen argues that a "dog" in Scripture is a symbol for a soul that, through sin, shamelessness, and vice, has become irrational like a dog. The change is moral and spiritual, not a physical transmigration of the soul into an animal's body. He writes that a "more rational constitution" can change into a "more irrational one" through vice, and vice-versa through virtue.

This passage is therefore crucial for understanding Origen's actual teaching and defending him against the later accusation that he believed in the transmigration of souls into animals. He firmly rejects it as unscriptural and foreign to the Church.

fr: Dans ce passage, il me semble que par « Élie » il ne faut pas entendre l'âme, afin de ne pas tomber dans ce dogme de la métempsomatose, étranger à l'église de Dieu, qui n'a été ni transmis par les apôtres, ni ne se manifeste nulle part dans les Écritures.
en: In this place when Jesus said Elijah had come and referred to John the Baptist] it does not appear to me that by Elijah the soul is spoken of, lest fall into the doctrine of transmigration, which is foreign to the Church of God, and not handed down by the apostles, nor anywhere set forth in the Scriptures [ibid., 13:1].
latin: In his quidem per Eliam non mihi videtur anima significari, ne forte in alienam ab Ecclesia Dei de migratione e corpore in corpus sententiam, neque ab apostolis traditam, neque uspiam in Scripturis prolatam incidam.
greek: Ἐν τούτοις Ἠλίας οὐχ ἡ ψυχὴ δοκεῖ μοι λέγεσθαι, ἵνα μὴ ἐμπίπτω εἰς τὸ ἀλλότριον τῆς Ἐκκλησίας τοῦ Θεοῦ περὶ τῆς μετενσωματώσεως δόγμα, οὔτε παραδιδόμενον ὑπὸ τῶν ἀποστόλων, οὔτε ἐμφαινόμενόν που τῶν Γραφῶν.
context:
Theological and Historical Context

This passage is profoundly significant for several reasons:

    The Exegetical Problem: Jesus's statement that Elijah had already come (referring to John the Baptist) created a potential theological problem. Some could interpret this to mean that the literal soul of Elijah had been reincarnated in the body of John.

    Origen's Orthodox Stance: Origen confronts this potential misinterpretation head-on. He explicitly states that Jesus is not talking about Elijah's soul. He then gives three powerful reasons for rejecting the doctrine of transmigration of souls (Greek: μετενσωμάτωσις, metensomatosis):

        It is "foreign to the Church of God" (ἀλλότριον τῆς Ἐκκλησίας τοῦ Θεοῦ), meaning it is not part of the authentic Christian faith.

        It was "not handed down by the apostles" (οὔτε παραδιδόμενον ὑπὸ τῶν ἀποστόλων), meaning it lacks apostolic authority and is not part of the sacred tradition.

        It is "not anywhere set forth in the Scriptures" (οὔτε ἐμφαινόμενόν που τῶν Γραφῶν), meaning it has no biblical foundation.

    The "Spirit and Power" Interpretation: Origen, consistent with the rest of early Christian interpretation, understood the connection between Elijah and John to be one of "spirit and power" (as described in Luke 1:17), not one of a shared soul. They shared a similar mission, prophetic role, and spiritual intensity as forerunners for the Lord.

    Significance in the "Origenist Controversies": This quote is of immense historical importance because Origen himself was later (posthumously) condemned for heresies, including a complex doctrine of the pre-existence of souls. This very passage is often used by scholars to show that, whatever his speculative theories were about the soul's pre-existence, Origen clearly and firmly rejected the specific doctrine of earthly reincarnation as it was commonly understood (i.e., the transmigration of a single soul into different bodies on earth). He saw it as a non-Christian, un-apostolic, and un-biblical teaching.

fr: Si les païens partisans de la métempsycose, par une conséquence logique de leur doctrine, n'admettent pas que le monde puisse périr, il ne leur reste plus, une fois confrontés aux Écritures qui annoncent clairement sa destruction, qu'à refuser d'y croire ou bien à inventer des arguties pour interpréter les récits de la fin des temps — ce dont ils seront d'ailleurs tout à fait incapables, même s'ils le voulaient.
en: ORIGEN OF ALEXANDRIA But if the Greeks, who introduce the doctrine of transmigration, laying down things in harmony with it, do not acknowledge that the world is coming to corruption, it is fitting that when they have looked the Scriptures straight in the face, which plainly declare that the world will perish, they should either disbelieve them or invent a series of arguments about the interpretation of things concerning the consummation, which even if they wish they will not be able to do [ibid.].
latin: Quod si qui transitum animarum in varia corpora invehunt ethnici, utpote consentanea doctrinæ huic astruentes, mundi interitum necessario non admittunt, superest ut, postquam Scripturis mundi occasum asserentibus palam refragati fuerint, vel fidem iis non habeant, vel verba reperiant quibus ea quæ ad consummationem pertinent explicare possint, quod facere neutiquam poterunt, etiamsi velint.
greek: Εἰ δὲ ἀναγκαίως οἱ τὴν μετενσωμάτωσιν εἰσάγοντες Ἕλληνες, ὡς ἀκόλουθα αὐτοῖς τιθέντες, οὐδὲ φθείρεσθαι βούλονται τὸν κόσμον, ὥρα καὶ τούτους ἀντιβλέψαντας ταῖς ἐκφαινούσαις Γραφαῖς φθαρήσεσθαι τὸν κόσμον, ἢ ἀπιστῆσαι αὐταῖς, ἢ εὐρεσιλογεῖν περὶ διηγήσεως τῶν κατὰ τὴν συντέλειαν, ὅπερ, κἂν βούλωνται, ποιῆσαι οὐ δυνήσονται.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

1. The Immediate Context: Elijah and John the Baptist
The entire chapter is a response to the question of whether John the Baptist was a reincarnated Elijah. Origen firmly rejects this. He argues that John came in the "spirit and power" of Elijah (Luke 1:17), not that Elijah's soul had entered John's body. He explicitly states that the doctrine of transmigration (μετενσωμάτωσις) is "foreign to the Church of God" and not taught by the apostles or found in Scripture.

2. Origen's Core Argument Against Reincarnation
Origen's main weapon against the doctrine of reincarnation is Christian eschatology—the teaching about the end of the world. His logic is as follows:

    The doctrine of transmigration requires an endless or extremely long cycle of rebirths for souls to be purified or punished. This implies a world that is essentially eternal.

    The Christian Scriptures, however, are absolutely clear that "the world will perish" (φθαρήσεσθαι τὸν κόσμον). Passages like "Heaven and earth will pass away" (Matt. 24:35) and "the present form of this world is passing away" (1 Cor. 7:31) affirm a definitive end.

    Therefore, the two systems are fundamentally incompatible. You cannot have both an endless cycle of rebirth and a final consummation of the world.

3. The Significance of Your Quote
The passage you selected is Origen's concluding challenge. He pits the pagan philosophers directly against the authority of Scripture. He says if "the Greeks" (the originators of the transmigration doctrine) want to hold their view, they must confront the Bible's clear teaching about the end of the world. This leaves them with only three losing options:

    Disbelieve the Scriptures: Openly reject Christian revelation.

    Invent an interpretation: Try to explain away the plain meaning of the biblical texts about the end times (εὐρεσιλογεῖν - literally "to be clever with words," to quibble or invent specious arguments).

    Fail: Origen concludes that even if they try the second option, they will be unable to succeed, because the biblical teaching is too clear.

This passage is a powerful example of Origen acting as a staunch defender of biblical doctrine against what he saw as a dangerous and incompatible philosophical import.

fr: Si nous-mêmes, en priant, nous nous penchions avec un soin respectueux sur les Évangiles, nous y trouverions, même dans ce qui semble être commun à tous, une différence et une prééminence considérables dans les paroles adressées à Pierre par rapport à celles qui suivent. La différence, en effet, n’est pas mince : Pierre a reçu les clés non pas d’un seul ciel, mais de plusieurs, afin que tout ce qu’il lie sur la terre soit lié non pas dans un seul ciel, mais dans tous les cieux. Par comparaison, pour la multitude de ceux qui ont lié et délié sur la terre, leurs actes se trouvent liés et déliés non pas dans les cieux, à l’instar de Pierre, mais dans un seul ciel. En effet, leur puissance n’atteint pas celle de Pierre, au point de leur permettre de lier et de délier dans tous les cieux.
en: ORIGEN OF ALEXANDRIA f we were to attend carefully to the Gospels, we should also find, in relation to those things that seem to be common to Peter great difference and a preeminence in the things [Jesus] said to Peter, compared with the second class [of apostles]. For it is no small difference that Peter received the keys not of one heaven but of more, and in order that whatever things he binds on earth may be bound not in one heaven but in them all, as compared with the many who bind on earth and loose on earth, so that these things are bound and loosed not in [all] the heavens, as in the case of Peter, but in only one: for they do not reach so high a stage of power as Peter to bind and loose in all the heavens [ Commentary on Matthew 13:31 (c. A.D. 249)].
latin: Quod si nos quoque attendentes diligenter precaremur Evangeliis, inveniremus et in ipsis, juxta ea quae videntur esse communia, magnam differentiam et praestantiam eorum quae dicta sunt ad Petrum prae secundis.
