St. Pacian shows that the authority and sacramental power given to the Apostles were not meant to die with them but were passed down to their successors, the bishops, for the ongoing life of the Church. It is one of the most important early patristic defenses of the Sacrament of Penance (Reconciliation).

Dans son propre ouvrage, il transmet également d’autres récits des paroles du Seigneur par Aristion, déjà mentionné, ainsi que les traditions de Jean l’Ancien...

en: ST. PAPIAS OF HIERAPOLIS And Papias, of whom we are now speaking, confesses that he received the words of the apostles from those who followed them, but says that he was himself a hearer of Aristion and the presbyter John. At least he mentions them frequently by name, and gives their traditions in his writings. [There are] other passages from his works in which he relates some other wonderful events that he claims to have received from Tradition [fragment in Eusebius's Church History 3:39:7 (c. A.D. 130)].
latin: Alias quoque supradicti Aristionis enarrationes sermonum Domini, et Joannis presbyteri traditiones refert in suis libris. . . .     Idem præterea scriptor alia nonnulla nudæ vocis traditione ad se pervenisse testatur.
greek: Καὶ ἄλλας δὲ τῇ ἰδίᾳ γραφῇ παραδίδωσιν Ἀριστίωνος τοῦ πρόσθεν δεδηλωμένου τῶν τοῦ Κυρίου λόγων διηγήσεις, καὶ τοῦ πρεσβυτέρου Ἰωάννου παραδόσεις...     Καὶ ἄλλα δὲ ὁ αὐτὸς συγγραφεὺς ὡς ἐκ παραδόσεως ἀγράφου εἰς αὐτὸν ἥκοντα παρατέθειται...
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    A Quote Within a Quote: This is the most critical detail. The original work of St. Papias, the Exposition of the Sayings of the Lord (Λογίων Κυριακῶν Ἐξήγησις), is lost. We only know it through fragments quoted by later Church Fathers. This passage is our most important source, where Eusebius (writing in the early 4th century) quotes and discusses Papias (who wrote in the early 2nd century).

    Eusebius's Low Opinion of Papias: It is crucial to note from the text you provided that Eusebius was not a fan of Papias. He explicitly calls him a man "of very limited intelligence" (Σφόδρα γάρ τοι σμικρὸς ὢν τὸν νοῦν). Eusebius's main issue was Papias's belief in a literal, physical thousand-year reign of Christ on earth (chiliasm or millenarianism), which Eusebius considered a misinterpretation of apostolic teaching.

    The "Two Johns": This passage is the primary source for the historical theory of the "two Johns." Papias, as quoted by Eusebius just before this section, distinguishes between what "the Apostles said" and what "Aristion and the presbyter John, the Lord’s disciples, are saying." Eusebius interprets this to mean there were two prominent figures named John active in Asia Minor: John the Apostle and a different man, John the Presbyter. This has been a subject of immense scholarly debate for centuries.

    Oral vs. Written Tradition: The fragment is invaluable for showing the immense importance of oral tradition in the early 2nd-century Church. Papias explicitly states his preference for the "living and abiding voice" over written books. This passage confirms that he included material from this "unwritten tradition" (παραδόσεως ἀγράφου) in his work.

Analysis of the Full Document You Found

You have not just found the quote, but the entire hymn in its scholarly context. Here is a guide to what you're seeing in the images:

    The Legendary Introduction (Image 1):

        The page begins with a prose introduction, first in Old Irish and then in English. This tells the famous story of how the hymn was composed: St. Patrick and his monks were on their way to preach to the High King Laoghaire at Tara, and they chanted this prayer to protect themselves from an ambush. The prayer miraculously disguised them as a herd of deer, which is why it is also famously called "The Deer's Cry" (Fáed Fíada).

    The Main Body of the Prayer (Images 1-4):

        You can see the prayer's structure, invoking strength from different sources: the Trinity, the life of Christ, the ranks of angels, the wisdom of patriarchs, the teachings of apostles, the heavens (sun, moon, lightning), and the earth.

        Image 3 contains the section asking for God's protection: "God's strength to pilot me, God's wisdom to guide me, God's eye to look before me..."

        Image 4 contains the invocation against evils ("against false laws of heathendom, against spells of women and smiths and wizards") and the powerful, repetitive litany that is the heart of the prayer: "Christ with me, Christ before me, Christ behind me..." (Crist limm, Crist reum, Crist íamm...)

    The Conclusion (Image 5):

        This final page shows the end of the "Christ in every eye..." section.

        It then repeats the opening stanza ("Atomriug indiu..."). This is a common feature in hymns and liturgical prayers, using the first stanza as a concluding refrain.

        Finally, it ends with a Latin liturgical prayer: "Domini est salus. Domini est salus. Christi est salus. Salus tua, Domine, sit semper nobiscum. Amen." (Salvation is of the Lord. Salvation is of the Lord. Salvation is of Christ. May your salvation, O Lord, be always with us. Amen.). This was a common closing added to the prayer in the manuscripts.

In summary, you have not only found the single stanza you were looking for but the entire hymn in its scholarly context, complete with its legendary introduction, critical footnotes, and liturgical conclusion. This is an outstanding find.

fr:
Moi, Patrick, pécheur, le plus ignorant et le moindre de tous les fidèles, le plus méprisable aux yeux de beaucoup. J’ai eu pour père Calpornius, un diacre, fils du prêtre Potitus, qui était du village de Bannavem Taberniae. Il y possédait en effet un petit domaine tout près, et c’est là que je fus capturé.

J’avais alors environ seize ans, et j’ignorais le vrai Dieu. Je fus emmené en captivité en Irlande avec des milliers d’autres gens, comme nous le méritions, car nous nous étions éloignés de Dieu, que nous n’avions pas gardé ses commandements et que nous n’avions pas obéi à nos prêtres, qui nous exhortaient pour notre salut.
en: ST. PATRICK I, Patrick, the sinner, am the most rustic and the least of all the faithful had for my father Calpornius, a deacon, son of Potitus, a priest, who belonged to the village of Bannavem Taberniae. . At that time was barely sixteen years of age and I was led into captivity in Ireland with many thousands of persons, in accordance with our desserts, for we turned away from God, and kept not his commandments, and were not obedient to our priests, who were wont to admonish us for our salvation [Confession of St. Patrick (c. A.D. 452)].
latin: Ego Patricius peccator, rusticissimus et minimus omnium fidelium et contemptibilissimus sum apud plurimos, patrem habui Calpornium diaconum, filium quondam Potiti presbyteri, qui fuit in vico Bannavem Taberniae. Villulam enim prope habuit, ubi ego capturam dedi. Annorum eram tunc fere sedecim, et Deum verum ignorabam; et Hiberione in captivitatem adductus sum cum tot milia hominum, secundum merita nostra, quia a Deo recessimus et praecepta eius non custodivimus, et sacerdotibus nostris non oboedientes fuimus, qui nostram salutem admonebant.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Author and Work: St. Patrick (c. 385–461 AD) wrote the Confessio late in his life. It is not an autobiography in the modern sense but a spiritual testament and a defense of his mission in Ireland. He wrote it to justify his episcopacy against detractors (likely from his home church in Britain) who considered him uneducated and unfit for the role.

    "Rusticissimus" (Most Rustic): This is one of the most important words in the entire work. Patrick constantly emphasizes his lack of education and poor Latin skills. His Latin is indeed not the classical prose of Cicero but a form of Late/Vulgar Latin, heavily influenced by the Bible (especially the Vetus Latina, the "Old Latin" version). This self-description is a powerful statement of humility, contrasting his own perceived weakness with the power of God working through him.

    Family and Social Status: Patrick's genealogy is highly significant. His father was a deacon and his grandfather was a priest. This was possible at the time before clerical celibacy was universally enforced in the Western Church. More importantly, it shows that Patrick was not a "rustic" peasant. His father was also a decurion (a town councilor), meaning they were a land-owning, Romanized, and relatively well-off family in Britain. This makes his self-description "rusticissimus" a statement of spiritual, not social, humility.

    Bannavem Taberniae: The exact location of this village is one of the great unsolved mysteries of Patrician studies. Scholars have proposed locations all over western Britain, from Wales to the area near Hadrian's Wall, but no definitive identification has ever been made.

    Theology of Captivity: Patrick's interpretation of his capture is profoundly theological. He does not see it as random misfortune or a mere political event. He views it as a direct and just consequence of his and his people's sinfulness and disobedience. This perspective is central to the Confessio: his enslavement becomes the very means of his spiritual awakening and conversion to the "true God" whom he had previously ignored.

fr:
Car il n'y a pas d'autre Dieu — il n'y en a jamais eu avant et il n'y en aura jamais après — en dehors de Dieu le Père, non engendré, sans commencement, de qui vient tout commencement et qui soutient toutes choses, comme nous l’avons appris ; et son Fils Jésus Christ, dont nous attestons qu’il a toujours été avec le Père, engendré spirituellement auprès de lui d’une manière ineffable avant l’origine du monde, avant tout commencement. Par lui ont été faites les choses visibles et invisibles ; il s’est fait homme et, la mort vaincue, il a été reçu aux cieux auprès du Père.

Et le Père lui a donné tout pouvoir au-dessus de tout nom au ciel, sur terre et aux enfers, et que toute langue confesse que Jésus Christ est Seigneur et Dieu. C’est lui que nous croyons et dont nous attendons la venue prochaine, juge des vivants et des morts, qui rendra à chacun selon ses œuvres. Et il a répandu en nous en abondance l’Esprit Saint, don et gage d’immortalité, lui qui fait de ceux qui croient et obéissent des fils de Dieu et des cohéritiers du Christ, lui que nous confessons et adorons, un seul Dieu en la Trinité de son saint nom.
en: ST. PATRICK [T]here is no other God, nor has there been before now, nor will there be hereafter, except God the Father unbegotten, without beginning, from whom is all beginning, upholding all things, and his Son Jesus Christ, whom we also confess to have been with the Father always before the world's beginning. . .Jesus Christ is the Lord and God in whom we believe and who has poured out the Holy Spirit on us abundantly whom we confess and adore as one God in the Trinity of the sacred name [Confession of St. Patrick 4 (c. A.D. 452)].
latin: Quia non est alius Deus nec umquam fuit ante nec erit post haec praeter Deum Patrem ingenitum, sine principio, a quo est omne principium, omnia tenentem, ut didicimus; et huius filium Iesum Christum, quem cum Patre scilicet semper fuisse testamur, ante originem saeculi spiritualiter apud Patrem inenarrabiliter genitum ante omne principium, et per ipsum facta sunt visibilia et invisibilia, hominem factum, morte devicta in caelis ad Patrem receptum. Et dedit illi omnem potestatem super omne nomen caelestium et terrestrium et infernorum et omnis lingua confiteatur ei quia Dominus et Deus est Iesus Christus, quem credimus et expectamus adventum ipsius mox futurum, iudex vivorum atque mortuorum, qui reddet unicuique secundum facta sua, et effudit in nobis habunde Spiritum Sanctum, donum et pignus inmortalitatis, qui facit credentes et oboedientes ut sint filii Dei et coheredes Christi, quem confitemur et adoramus unum Deum in Trinitate sacri nominis.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Author and Work: St. Patrick (c. 387–461 AD) was a Romano-British bishop and missionary who is credited with bringing Christianity to Ireland. His Confessio is an autobiographical work written late in his life. It is not a theological treatise but a defense of his life's work and a testimony to God's grace, written in response to critics. This creedal passage is embedded within that personal story, making it all the more powerful.

    "Rustic" Latin: Patrick famously apologizes for his lack of formal education and his "rustic" Latin. While the grammar is not classical, his firm grasp of complex theological concepts is undeniable. The raw, heartfelt power of his writing shines through.

    A Personal Creed: This passage is structured as a personal creed that closely echoes the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed. This is historically significant because it demonstrates that the faith being preached in the furthest reaches of the former Roman Empire was the same sophisticated, conciliar faith defined at Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381). Note the direct parallels:

        On the Father: "unbegotten, without beginning, from whom is all beginning"

        On the Son: "with the Father always... before the origin of the world," "through him were made all things visible and invisible," "he was made man," "judge of the living and of the dead."

        On the Holy Spirit: The description of the Spirit as the "gift and pledge of immortality" who makes us "sons of God."

    Theological Significance: This is a clear and unambiguous statement of orthodox Trinitarianism ("one God in the Trinity of the sacred name") and Christology ("Jesus Christ is the Lord and God"). It stands as a powerful testament to the unity of faith across the Christian world in the 5th century, connecting the Church in Ireland directly to the great theological currents of the Mediterranean world.

fr: ...car Jésus Christ est Seigneur et Dieu, en qui nous croyons et dont nous attendons la venue prochaine, juge des vivants et des morts, qui rendra à chacun selon ses œuvres...
en: ST. PATRICK Jesus Christ is the Lord and God in whom we believe, and whose coming we expect will soon take place, the judge of the living and the dead, who will render to everyone according to his works [Confession of St. Patrick 4 (c. A.D. 452)].
latin: ...quia Dominus et Deus est Iesus Christus, quem credimus et expectamus adventum ipsius mox futurum, iudex vivorum atque mortuorum, qui reddet unicuique secundum facta sua...
context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. The Source Document: The Confessio

The passage comes from the Confessio Sancti Patricii (The Confession of St. Patrick). This is not a formal theological treatise but a deeply personal and spiritual autobiography. Patrick wrote it late in his life as a defense of his mission to Ireland, an explanation of his divine calling, and a final testament to the faith that sustained him. The creed-like summary in Section 4 serves as the unshakable foundation for everything he did.
2. A Powerful Creedal Statement

The entire section you provided is a beautifully constructed summary of the orthodox faith, reflecting the language of both Scripture and the early creeds. Patrick is establishing his credentials as a preacher of the one, true Catholic faith. By stating this so clearly, he is showing that the faith he brought to Ireland was not some personal invention but the universal faith of the Church.
3. Rich Biblical Allusions

Patrick’s declaration is woven together from key New Testament passages, which demonstrates his deep immersion in the Scriptures.

    omnis lingua confiteatur ei quia Dominus et Deus est Iesus Christus: This is a direct echo and strengthening of Philippians 2:11, "...and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord (quia Dominus est Iesus Christus)". Patrick's addition of et Deus ("and God") is a powerful, explicit declaration of Christ's divinity, likely reflecting the anti-Arian emphasis of the Church in the 5th century.

    iudex vivorum atque mortuorum: This phrase is taken directly from the Apostles' Creed and is found in Scripture in places like Acts 10:42 and 2 Timothy 4:1.

    qui reddet unicuique secundum facta sua: This is a direct quote from passages concerning the final judgment, such as Romans 2:6 and Matthew 16:27.

4. Historical Context (c. A.D. 452)

Patrick was writing just one year after the monumental Council of Chalcedon (451). While he was geographically isolated on the "edge of the world," his creedal statement is perfectly aligned with the orthodox Trinitarian and Christological faith being affirmed by the universal Church. The full passage you provided is profoundly Trinitarian, clearly distinguishing the Persons while affirming their unity—a faith solidified at the Councils of Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381).
5. St. Patrick's Latin

Scholars note that St. Patrick's Latin is not the polished, rhetorical Latin of a highly educated Roman aristocrat. It is a more rustic, direct, and sometimes grammatically unusual form of Late Latin. This adds to the Confessio's power and authenticity; it is the heartfelt testament of a man of profound faith and action, not a professional scholar.

fr: ...et son Fils Jésus Christ, dont nous attestons qu'il a de toute éternité été avec le Père, engendré avant l'origine des siècles, spirituellement et de manière ineffable auprès du Père, avant tout commencement...
en: ST. PATRICK Jesus Christ, whom we also confess to have always been with the Father always before the world's beginning, spiritually and ineffably [he was] begotten of the Father before all beginning [Confession of St. Patrick 4 (c. A.D. 452)].
latin: ...et huius filium Iesum Christum, quem cum Patre scilicet semper fuisse testamur, ante originem saeculi spiritualiter apud Patrem inenarrabiliter genitum ante omne principium...
context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. Theological Context: A Statement of Nicene Orthodoxy

This is not just a passing statement; it is the core of St. Patrick's Trinitarian faith. The language is deliberately chosen to affirm the orthodox doctrine established at the Council of Nicaea (A.D. 325) and to refute the Arian heresy.

    "semper fuisse" (to have always been): This is a direct counter to the Arian slogan, "There was a time when he [the Son] was not." Patrick asserts the eternal co-existence of the Son with the Father.

    "ante originem saeculi" (before the origin of the world): He emphasizes the Son's pre-existence before all of creation.

    "ante omne principium" (before all beginning): This powerful, almost redundant phrase drives the point home with absolute clarity: there is no conceivable "beginning" before which the Son did not exist with the Father.

    "inenarrabiliter genitum" (ineffably begotten): This shows Patrick's alignment with the orthodox teaching that the eternal generation of the Son is a divine mystery that cannot be fully explained in human language, a point stressed by Church Fathers like St. Gregory of Nyssa.

2. The Full Creed

The paragraph you provided is essentially St. Patrick's personal creed, summarizing the entire economy of salvation:

    The Father: Unbegotten, without beginning, the source of all things.

    The Son: Eternally begotten, Creator of all things visible and invisible, Incarnate, victorious over death, Ascended, and Lord over all creation.

    The Holy Spirit: Poured out as a "gift and pledge of immortality," making believers children of God.

    The Trinity: He concludes by confessing and adoring "one God in the Trinity of the sacred name."

3. "Patrician Latin"

St. Patrick famously refers to himself as unlearned and "most rustic" (rusticus). His Latin is not the polished, classical prose of St. Augustine but is known for its directness, scriptural saturation, and passionate, heartfelt quality. This passage is a prime example. The repetition ("always... before the world's beginning... before all beginning") is not a sign of poor style but of intense, creedal emphasis.
4. Historical Placement

Writing around A.D. 452, Patrick is a contemporary of Pope St. Leo the Great and the Council of Chalcedon (451). His Confessio demonstrates that the core Trinitarian and Christological faith of the Roman world, forged in the great councils, was being preached and believed on the very edge of that world, in Ireland.

fr:
Et c’est là qu’une nuit, en songe, j’entendis une voix qui me disait : « Ton jeûne est bon. Bientôt tu retourneras dans ta patrie. »

Et de nouveau, peu de temps après, j’entendis la réponse qui me disait : « Voici, ton navire est prêt. »

Or, il n’était pas proche, mais se trouvait peut-être à deux cents milles. Je n’y étais jamais allé et n’y connaissais personne. C’est alors que je pris la fuite et quittai l’homme avec qui j’avais passé six ans. Et je me mis en route avec la force de Dieu, qui menait mon chemin vers le bien ; et je ne craignais rien, jusqu’à ce que je parvienne à ce navire.
en: ST. PATRICK [In Ireland] one night I heard in my sleep a voice saying to me, "You fast well: soon you will go to your fatherland." And again, after a very short time, I heard the heavenly voice saying to me, "Lo, your ship is ready." And it was not near at hand, but was distant, perhaps two hundred miles. And I had never been there, nor did I know any person living there. And then shortly took flight and left the man with whom I had been for six years. And I came in the strength of God, who prospered my way for good; and I met with nothing to alarm me untill I reached that ship [Confession of St. Patrick 17 (c. A.D. 452)].
latin:
Et ibi scilicet quadam nocte in somno audivi vocem dicentem mihi: «Bene ieiunas, cito iturus ad patriam tuam».

    Et iterum post paululum tempus audivi responsum dicentem mihi: «Ecce, navis tua parata est.»

    Et non erat prope, sed forte habebat ducenta milia passus. Et ibi numquam fueram nec ibi notum quemquam de hominibus habebam. Et deinde postmodum conversus sum in fugam et intermisi hominem cum quo fueram sex annis. Et veni in virtute Dei, qui viam meam ad bonum dirigebat; et nihil metuebam donec perveni ad navem illam.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Author and Work: The passage is from the Confessio (or "Confession") of St. Patrick, one of only two surviving documents authentically attributed to him. It is not a list of sins like St. Augustine's Confessions, but rather a "declaration" or "testimony" of God's work in his life, written late in his career to defend his mission in Ireland against his detractors in Britain.

    Historical Context: This is the story of Patrick's escape. He had been kidnapped from Roman Britain around the age of 16 and sold into slavery in Ireland, where he worked as a shepherd for six years. This quote describes the divinely inspired moment he decided to flee his master and begin a perilous 200-mile journey to the coast, to a place he had never been, to find a ship he only knew about from a dream.

    The Nature of the Latin: The Latin of the Confessio is famously unpolished and non-classical. Patrick himself apologizes for his lack of education and "rustic" style (rusticitas mea), as his schooling was cut short by his kidnapping. This "Vulgar Latin" or "Hiberno-Latin" is of immense interest to linguists and historians because it provides a rare glimpse into the spoken Latin of the late Roman Empire in the provinces. The grammar is sometimes unusual, but the meaning is powerful and direct.

    Theological Significance:

        Divine Revelation: This passage is a prime example of how Patrick experienced God's direct guidance. God speaks to him in dreams, a common form of revelation in the Bible and early Christian literature.

        Providence and Faith: Patrick attributes his entire escape not to his own cunning, but to the "strength of God" (in virtute Dei) who directed his path. He undertakes an incredibly risky journey based solely on faith in these visions, fearing nothing because he believed God was guiding him. This sets the theme for his entire life and mission.

    Primary Sources:

        Critical Edition: The standard scholarly edition of the Latin text is Ludwig Bieler, Libri Epistolarum Sancti Patricii Episcopi (1952), published by the Royal Irish Academy.

        Accessible Edition: The text is also found in Migne's Patrologia Latina (PL), Volume 53, columns 801-818.

        Online Resources: The Royal Irish Academy's "St. Patrick's Confessio" hyperstack is an outstanding digital resource with the Latin text, multiple translations, and detailed commentary.

fr:
Quelques années plus tard, j'étais de nouveau en Bretagne avec mes parents. Ils m'accueillirent comme leur fils et, après les si grandes épreuves que j'avais endurées, ils me supplièrent de ne plus jamais les quitter.
Et c'est là que je vis, au cœur de la nuit, un homme qui venait comme d'Irlande, du nom de Victoricius, portant d'innombrables lettres. Il m'en donna une, et je lus le début de la lettre, qui portait ce titre : « La Voix des Irlandais ».
Et au moment où je lisais à haute voix le début de la lettre, je crus entendre à l'instant même la voix de ceux qui habitaient près de la forêt de Foclut, qui se trouve près de la mer occidentale. Ils s'écrièrent comme d'une seule voix : « Nous t'en prions, saint jeune homme, viens et marche de nouveau parmi nous. »
J'eus le cœur si profondément touché que je ne pus lire davantage, et c'est ainsi que je m'éveillai. Grâces soient rendues à Dieu, car de très nombreuses années plus tard, le Seigneur leur a accordé ce qu'ils avaient demandé dans leur cri.
en: And once more, after a few years, I was in Britain with my family. . . And there I saw in a vision in the night of a man whose name was Victoricus coming from Ireland with countless letters. He gave me one of them, and I read the beginning of the letter, which was entitled "The Voice of the Irish.* And while I was reading it aloud, I thought I heard the voices of those who dwelled beside the Wood of Foclut [in Ireland], which IS near the Western Sea. And they cried, as with one mouth. "We beseech you, holy youth, to come and walk once more among us!" [ibid., 23].
latin: Et iterum post paucos annos in Britannis eram cum parentibus meis, qui me ut filium susceperunt, et ex fide rogaverunt me ut vel modo ego post tantas tribulationes quas ego pertuli nusquam ab illis discederem. Et ibi scilicet vidi in sinu noctis virum venientem quasi de Hiberione, cui nomen Victoricius, cum epistolis innumerabilibus, et dedit mihi unam ex his, et legi principium epistolae continentem Vox Hiberionacum. Et cum recitabam principium epistolae putabam ipso momento audire vocem ipsorum qui erant iuxta silvam Focluti, quae est prope mare occidentale. Et sic exclamaverunt quasi ex uno ore: «Rogamus te, sancte puer, ut venias et adhuc ambules inter nos». Et valde conpunctus sum corde et amplius non potui legere, et sic expertus sum. Deo gratias, quia post plurimos annos praestitit illis Dominus secundum clamorem illorum.
context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. Context: Patrick's "Macedonian Call"

This vision is the central turning point of the Confessio. After escaping his six-year enslavement in Ireland and returning to his family in Britain, Patrick was living a life of relative comfort. This divine call disrupted that peace and set him on his life's mission. The event is deliberately framed as a parallel to St. Paul's vision of the man from Macedonia in the Bible (Acts 16:9-10), who begs him, "Come over to Macedonia and help us." By echoing this apostolic call, Patrick is placing his own mission to Ireland within the grand tradition of the Apostles, giving it profound theological authority.
2. Key Figures and Places

    Victoricus: This name means "victorious" or "conqueror." He may have been a real person Patrick knew, or a symbolic figure representing Christ's victory. Scholars have noted a Saint Victoricus who was a 4th-century martyr in Gaul, a region Patrick may have visited.

    The Wood of Foclut (Silva Focluti): This is a real, identifiable place. It is generally located in the west of Ireland, near Killala Bay in what is now County Mayo. This is significant because it was likely the area where Patrick was held as a slave. The vision is therefore deeply personal: the very people among whom he had been a captive were now calling him back as their spiritual father.

    "Holy Youth" (Sancte Puer): This phrase is deeply poignant. Patrick was a puer (a boy, a youth) when he was captured and enslaved. The Irish voices in his vision call him back using a term that recalls his time of suffering, but they sanctify it by calling him a "holy youth."

3. The Author and His Work

    St. Patrick (c. 387–461 AD): This work is one of only two surviving texts written by Patrick himself (the other being his Letter to the Soldiers of Coroticus).

    The Confessio: This document is not a modern autobiography or a chronological history. It is a "confession" in the Augustinian sense: a testament to God's grace and a defense (apologia) of his mission. Patrick wrote it late in his life to justify his episcopal work in Ireland against critics (likely from the Church in Britain) who questioned his authority and qualifications. The "Voice of the Irish" vision was his ultimate answer to them: his authority came not from men, but directly from God.

    The Latin: The Latin of the Confessio is famously non-classical. It is often called "Hiberno-Latin" and reflects the speech patterns of someone for whom Latin was a learned, ecclesiastical language, not a native tongue. Its style is earnest, direct, and powerful, but can sometimes be grammatically unconventional.

fr: Que rie et insulte qui voudra, moi, je ne me tairai pas, ni ne cacherai les signes et les merveilles que le Seigneur m’a révélés bien des années avant qu’ils n’adviennent, lui qui connaît toutes choses avant même le commencement des temps.
en: Let those who will. laugh and mock. I will not be silent or conceal the signs and wonders that were shown to me by the Lord many years before they came to pass, since he knows all things even before the world's beginnings [ibid., 45].
latin: Rideat autem et insultet qui voluerit, ego non silebo neque abscondam signa et mirabilia quae mihi a Domino ministrata sunt ante multos annos quam fierent, quasi qui novit omnia etiam ante tempora saecularia.
context:
Additional Details and Context
Author and Work

    Author: Saint Patrick, the 5th-century Apostle of Ireland.

    Work: The Confessio (Latin for "Confession" or "Declaration"). This is one of only two surviving authentic works by Patrick. It is not a systematic theological treatise but a deeply personal and often emotional account of his life and a defense (an apologia) of his episcopal mission to the Irish people.

Immediate Context of the Quote

    This passage comes after Patrick has recounted a series of profound spiritual experiences, including visions and prophecies that he received from God.

    He is writing with his critics in mind—likely more educated and skeptical clerics back in his native Britain who questioned his authority, his learning (his Latin was notoriously rustic), and the legitimacy of his mission.

    He anticipates that they will mock him as an unlearned and presumptuous man for claiming to have received direct revelations from God. This quote is his defiant response to that anticipated scorn.

Theological and Historical Significance

    Defense of Divine Calling: The core of Patrick's argument throughout the Confessio is that his mission was not his own idea but a direct command from God. The "signs and wonders" he mentions are his proof—prophetic knowledge given to him by God long before the events occurred.

    Humility and Divine Providence: Despite the defiant tone ("Let those who will, laugh and mock"), the passage is rooted in humility. Patrick is not claiming any special power for himself. He frames himself as a mere instrument, a witness to what "the Lord ministered to me." He immediately grounds the possibility of prophecy in God's omniscience ("since he knows all things..."), not in his own merit.

    Biblical Language: The phrase "signs and wonders" (signa et mirabilia) is a direct echo of the language used in the Old Testament (e.g., Deuteronomy) and the Acts of the Apostles to describe God's miraculous actions. By using this phrase, Patrick places his own experiences and mission firmly within the tradition of biblical revelation and apostolic work.

Primary Source Citation

    In Migne's collection, you can find this in: Patrologia Latina (PL), Volume 53, column 827.

    For modern scholarly work, the critical editions by Ludwig Bieler or the Royal Irish Academy's Dictionary of Medieval Latin from Celtic Sources are the standard references.

fr: Moi, Patrice, pécheur et sans grande instruction, je confesse avoir été établi évêque en Irlande. Je crois très fermement que j’ai reçu de Dieu ce que je suis. Ainsi, je demeure parmi les barbares, étranger et exilé pour l’amour de Dieu.
en: Patrick, the sinner, unlearned as everybody knows, avow that have been established a bishop in Ireland. Most assuredly I believe that have received from God what I am. And so I dwell in the midst of barbarous heaths, a stranger and an exile for the love of God Letter to the Soldiers of Coroticus 1 (c. A.D. 452)].
latin: Patricius peccator, indoctus scilicet, Hiberione constitutum episcopum me esse fateor. Certissime reor, a Deo accepi id quod sum. Inter barbaros itaque habito proselytus et profuga, ob amorem Dei.
context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. Title and Context of the Letter

    Full Title: Epistola ad milites Corotici (Letter to the soldiers of Coroticus).

    Historical Situation: This is not a calm theological treatise. It is a raw, passionate, and furious letter of protest and excommunication. Coroticus was a Christian British chieftain whose soldiers raided a community of Patrick's newly baptized Irish converts. They slaughtered some and sold others into slavery to non-Christian Picts. Patrick wrote this letter to be read aloud in Coroticus's territory, publicly shaming him and excommunicating him and his soldiers until they repented and freed the captives.

2. Analysis of the Opening Lines

The opening you've selected is powerful because it establishes Patrick's entire identity and the basis of his authority in just a few lines.

    Patricius peccator, indoctus scilicet (Patrick, the sinner, unlearned as everybody knows): This is a key theme in both of Patrick's surviving works (this letter and his Confessio). He was deeply insecure about his lack of formal classical education, as he was captured and enslaved in his youth, interrupting his studies. This phrase is both a genuine expression of humility and a brilliant rhetorical move. He preemptively disarms critics who might attack his rustic Latin or lack of polish.

    a Deo accepi id quod sum (I have received from God what I am): This is the core of his defense. He is admitting, "I am not qualified by human standards, but my authority is not human—it is a direct commission from God." This divine appointment is the foundation for his right to speak and to judge Coroticus's horrific actions.

    proselytus et profuga (a stranger and an exile): These are incredibly potent words. A proselytus is a sojourner or convert living among a foreign people. A profuga is a fugitive or exile. Patrick is emphasizing that he has willingly given up his homeland (Roman Britain), his family, and his status as a Roman citizen (non dico civibus meis... sed civibus daemoniorum - "I say not to my fellow citizens... but to citizens of demons," as he says later in your provided text) to serve God among a people considered "barbarous." This highlights his personal sacrifice and gives his words immense moral weight.

3. Source Citation

    The text you provided with the column markers (0813D) confirms the source. It is from J.-P. Migne's Patrologia Latina, Volume 53, columns 813-814. This is the standard scholarly reference for this work.

fr:
Lignée divine du Poisson céleste, toi qui as reçu parmi les mortels la source immortelle, puise-y avec un cœur pur. Mon ami, ranime ton âme aux eaux divines, aux flots éternels de la Sagesse qui dispense ses richesses. Reçois la nourriture douce comme le miel que donne le Sauveur des saints ; toi qui as faim, mange le Poisson, que tu tiens dans le creux de tes mains.

Maître et Sauveur, fais que je sois rassasié en abondance du Poisson.
Puisse ma mère dormir en paix ; c'est toi que nous supplions, ô lumière des défunts.
Aschandius, mon père, toi qui es si cher à mon cœur,
avec ma tendre mère et mes frères,
dans la paix du Poisson, souviens-toi de ton Pectorius.
en: PECTORIUS OF AUTUN Aschandius, my father. beloved of my heart, with my sweet mother and my brothers, be mindful of your Pectorius abiding in the peace of the Fish [Christ] [Christian Inscriptions no. 42 (Epitaph of Pectorius) (c. A.D. 375)].

context:
The ΙΧΘΥΣ Acrostic: The most famous feature of this epitaph is that the first letter of the first five lines spells out Ι-Χ-Θ-Υ-Σ (IXTHYS), which is Greek for "Fish." This was an early and widespread Christian acronym for:

        Ι – Ἰησοῦς (Iesous - Jesus)

        Χ – Χριστός (Christos - Christ)

        Θ – Θεοῦ (Theou - of God)

        Υ – Υἱός (Huios - Son)

        Σ – Σωτήρ (Soter - Savior)
        So, "Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior."

    Structure: The poem is in two parts.

        The Acrostic Poem (Lines 1-6): This part is a general instruction to a fellow Christian ("friend"). It uses rich symbolic language referring to Baptism ("immortal fountain," "ever-flowing waters") and the Eucharist ("honey-sweet food of the Savior," "eat hungrily, holding the Fish in thy hands"). The "divine offspring of the heavenly Fish" is the baptized Christian.

        The Personal Epitaph (Lines 7-11): Here, the author, Pectorius, speaks in his own voice. He addresses Christ directly ("Master, Savior"), asks for his mother to rest well, and addresses his father, Aschandius. He concludes by asking Christ, the "Fish," to remember him, Pectorius, in His peace.

    Dating and Significance: The inscription is dated anywhere from the late 2nd to the early 4th century AD, making it one of the most important early Christian inscriptions ever found. It provides invaluable evidence for early Christian belief in Christ's divinity, the practice and theology of Baptism and the Eucharist, and the use of the ΙΧΘΥΣ symbol as a profound confession of faith.

fr: En toutes choses, nous t’exhortons, très cher frère, à prêter attention avec obéissance à ce qui a été écrit par le très bienheureux pape de la ville de Rome. Car le bienheureux Pierre, qui vit et préside sur son propre siège, offre à ceux qui la cherchent la vérité de la foi. En effet, dans notre zèle pour la paix et la foi, nous ne pouvons instruire des causes relatives à la foi sans le consentement de l’évêque de Rome.
en: ST. PETER CHRYSOLOGUS We exhort you in every respect, honorable brother. to heed obediently what has been written by the most blessed pope of the city of Rome, for blessed Peter, who lives and presides in his own see, provides the truth of faith to those who seek it. For we, by reason of our pursuit of peace and faith, cannot try cases on the faith without the consent of the bishop of Rome [Letters 25:2 (A.D. 449)].
latin: In omnibus autem hortamur te, frater honorabilis, ut his quae a beatissimo papa Romanae civitatis scripta sunt, obedienter attendas: quoniam beatus Petrus, qui in propria sede et vivit et praesidet, praestat quaerentibus fidei veritatem. Nos enim pro studio pacis et fidei extra consensum Romanae civitatis episcopi causas fidei audire non possumus.
greek: Ἐπί πᾶσι δὲ προτρεπόμεθά σε, ἀδελφὲ τιμιώτατε, ὥστε τοῖς παρὰ τοῦ μακαριωτάτου πάπα τῆς πόλεως Ῥώμης γραφομένοις πειθαρχοῦντως προσέχειν· ἐπειδὴ ὁ μακάριος Πέτρος, ὃς ἐν τῇ ἰδίᾳ καθέδρᾳ καὶ ζῇ, καὶ προκάθηται, δίδωσι τοῖς ζητοῦσι τῆς πίστεως τὴν ἀλήθειαν· Ἡμεῖς γὰρ σπουδῇ τῆς εἰρήνης, καὶ τῆς πίστεως, ἐκτὸς συναινέσεως τοῦ Ῥώμης ἐπισκόπου, πίστεως αἰτίας διαγνῶναι οὐ δυνάμεθα.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    The Historical Context (A.D. 449): This letter is a direct response to an appeal from Eutyches, an archimandrite in Constantinople. Eutyches had just been condemned for heresy (for denying the two natures in Christ) by his local patriarch, St. Flavian of Constantinople. In an attempt to rally support, Eutyches wrote to several influential bishops, including Pope St. Leo the Great in Rome and St. Peter Chrysologus in Ravenna.

    The Author: St. Peter Chrysologus ("Peter of the Golden Words") was the Bishop of Ravenna. At this time, Ravenna was the capital of the Western Roman Empire, making its bishop a very powerful and respected figure, second only to the Pope in Italy.

    The Significance of the Response: St. Peter's reply is a masterclass in orthodox procedure and deference to papal authority. Instead of offering his own theological opinion or taking sides, he does something remarkable: he tells Eutyches to submit to the judgment of the Bishop of Rome.

    Key Theological Points in the Quote:

        Papal Authority: He urges "obedient attention" to whatever has been written by the Pope of Rome.

        The Living Voice of Peter: The authority of the Roman See is not merely historical or administrative; it is theological. St. Peter Chrysologus states that "blessed Peter, who lives and presides in his own see, provides the truth of faith to those who seek it." This is a profound statement of the living Petrine ministry in the Pope.

        Jurisdictional Deference: He declares that he and his see are incompetent to judge "cases on the faith" (causas fidei) without the consent of the Bishop of Rome. This establishes a clear principle: major doctrinal disputes are ultimately settled by the Roman See.

This letter is a powerful piece of evidence from the mid-fifth century, written by a major Western bishop outside of Rome, affirming the unique role of the Pope as the final arbiter in matters of Christian faith, based on the living authority of St. Peter.

fr: Ainsi Pierre, le premier des apôtres, après avoir été de nombreuses fois arrêté, emprisonné et outragé, fut finalement crucifié à Rome.
en: ST. PETER OF ALEXANDRIA Thus Peter, the first of the apostles, having been often apprehended, and thrown into prison, and treated with ignominy, was last of all crucified at Rome [Penance, canon (A.D. 306)1.
latin: Ita Petrus apostolorum primus, sape comprehensus, et custodia traditus, ignominiaque affectus, postremo Romæ crucifixus est.
greek: Οὕτως ὁ πρόκριτος τῶν ἀποστόλων Πέτρος, πολλάκις συλληφθεὶς καὶ φυλακισθεὶς καὶ ἀτιμασθείς, ὕστερον ἐν Ῥώμῃ ἐσταυρώθη.
context:
Additional Relevant Details & Context

This quote is highly significant, but its meaning is fully revealed by the context of the canon in which it appears.

1. The Main Argument of Canon 9:
The primary purpose of this canon is to correct a form of fanatical zeal among some Christians. St. Peter is arguing against those who rashly and voluntarily throw themselves into the hands of the authorities to seek martyrdom. He criticizes those who "as if from a sleep... rush into the contest" without being sought, thereby provoking the persecutors.

2. The Correct Model: Christ and the Apostles:
To counter this misguided zeal, St. Peter presents the proper model for Christian conduct during persecution:

    Jesus Christ: He points out that Jesus often withdrew from those who sought to harm him and did not hand Himself over, but waited for his persecutors to come to him.

    Apostolic Examples: He then cites the great martyrs of the Church as examples of this patient endurance, not reckless self-destruction. They did not seek death, but accepted it when it came as a result of their faithful witness.

3. The Purpose of Your Quote:
The sentence about the Apostle Peter is the climax of a list of proper examples:

    First, Stephen: He was seized (συναρπασθεὶς) by his enemies in Jerusalem.

    Second, James: He was arrested (συλληφθεὶς) by Herod and then beheaded.

    Third, Peter the Apostle: As your quote states, he was repeatedly apprehended and imprisoned before his final martyrdom.

    Fourth, Paul: He was likewise handed over many times and endured countless dangers before being beheaded in Rome.

The key theme is that these heroes of the faith did not turn themselves in. They were arrested, seized, and apprehended. They endured suffering patiently, following the model of Christ. Therefore, your quote serves as a crucial piece of evidence in a larger pastoral argument about the true nature of martyrdom.

4. Historical Significance:
This passage from c. A.D. 306 is an extremely important and early patristic witness from the Christian East (Alexandria, Egypt) affirming the ancient tradition that the Apostle Peter was martyred by crucifixion in Rome.

fr: ...ils arrivèrent à l'église de la très bienheureuse Mère de Dieu et toujours vierge Marie, que lui-même, comme nous avions commencé à le dire, avait fait construire dans un faubourg de la partie occidentale, près des cimetières des martyrs.
en: ST. PETER OF ALEXANDRIA [T]hey came to the church of the most blessed Mother of God, and Ever-Virgin Mary, which, as we began to say, he had constructed in the western quarter, in a suburb, for a cemetery of the martyrs [The Genuine Acts of Peter of Alexandria (A.D. 305)].
latin: ...venerunt in ecclesiam beatissimæ Dei Genitricis semperque virginis Mariæ, quam, ut dicere cœperamus, ipse ob martyrum cœmeteria ad occidentalem partem in quodam prosatio (e) construxerat.
context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. Source and Original Language

    Source: The text you are looking at is the Latin translation of the Acta S. Petri Alexandrini Episcopi (The Acts of St. Peter, Bishop of Alexandria). This version is found in Migne's Patrologia Graeca (PG), Volume 18, column 463.

    Original Language: St. Peter was the Patriarch of Alexandria, and the original account of his martyrdom was written in Greek. The Latin text you have is a translation of that original. The footnote (e) Græcismus, pro suburbio confirms this, explaining that the unusual Latin word prosatio is a loanword from the Greek proasteion (προάστειον), meaning "suburb."

2. Immediate Historical Context

The passage describes the events immediately following the martyrdom of St. Peter of Alexandria (c. 311 A.D.).

    A Dispute: After his execution, a "not small contention" (non parva contentio) broke out among the faithful. One group wanted to bury his body in the sanctuary of St. Mark the Evangelist, where he was martyred. Another group wanted to take him to the church that he himself had built—the one mentioned in your quote.

    Intervention: To prevent the dispute from turning into a riot (pugnæ litigium), a group of officials (called senatorum animosa phalanx) intervened.

    The Journey: They seized the holy relics, placed them in a boat (scapham), and sailed around the Pharos lighthouse to a place called Leucado, finally arriving at the church St. Peter had built.

3. Theological and Historical Significance

This quote is highly valued by historians and theologians for several reasons:

    Early Marian Devotion: It is one of the earliest explicit historical references to a church being formally dedicated to "the most blessed Mother of God, and Ever-Virgin Mary" (beatissimæ Dei Genitricis semperque virginis Mariæ). This provides powerful evidence for a well-developed Marian devotion and the use of the title Theotokos (God-bearer, or Dei Genitrix) more than a century before it was dogmatically defined at the Council of Ephesus in 431 A.D.

    Cult of the Martyrs: The church's purpose as a "cemetery of the martyrs" (martyrum cœmeteria) highlights the profound connection in the early Church between the veneration of the martyrs and the honor given to the Virgin Mary. She was seen as the Queen of Martyrs, the ultimate witness to Christ.

    Historical Realism: The specific geographical details—the "western quarter," the "suburb," the journey by boat around the Pharos—lend a strong sense of authenticity and historical grounding to the account.

fr: Moi, Pionios, j’ai donc écrit à mon tour ce qui précède d’après l’exemplaire antérieur, que j’ai retrouvé après recherche, le bienheureux Polycarpe me l’ayant manifesté par une révélation – comme je le déclarerai dans la suite. J’ai ainsi rassemblé ces textes déjà presque anéantis par le temps, afin que le Seigneur Jésus Christ me rassemble moi aussi avec ses élus dans son royaume céleste. À lui la gloire, avec le Père et l'Esprit Saint, pour les siècles des siècles. Amen.
en: ST. PIONIUS OF SMYRNA I again, Pionius, wrote them from the previously written copy, having carefully searched into them, and the blessed Polycarp having manifested them to me through revelation, even as I shall show in what follows. I have collected these things, when they had almost faded away through the passing of time, that the Lord Jesus Christ may gather me along with his elect into his heavenly kingdom, to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be glory forever and ever. Amen [Martyrdom of Polycarp, copyist note 2 (C. A.D. 250)].
latin: Et posthæc ego Pionius ex suprascriptis hæc exaravi, postquam illa perquisivissem, et beatus Polycarpus ea per revelationem mihi manifestasset, ut in sequentibus declarabo, collegi ea, propemodum ex temporis diuturnitate fatiscentia, ut me quoque cum electis suis in regnum suum cœleste colligat Dominus Jesus Christus, cui sit gloria, cum Patre et Spiritu sancto, in sæcula saeculorum. Amen.
greek: Ἐγὼ δὲ πάλιν Πιόνιος ἐκ τοῦ προγεγραμμένου ἔγραψα, ἀναζητήσας αὐτὰ, κατὰ ἀποκάλυψιν φανερώσαντός μοι τοῦ μακαρίου Πολυκάρπου· καθὼς δηλώσω ἐν τῷ καθεξῆς· συναγαγὼν αὐτὰ ἤδη σχεδὸν ἐκ τοῦ χρόνου κεκμηκότα, ἵνα κἀμὲ συναγάγῃ ὁ Κύριος Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς μετὰ τῶν ἐκλεκτῶν αὐτοῦ, εἰς τὴν οὐράνιον βασιλείαν αὐτοῦ, ᾧ ἡ δόξα, σὺν Πατρὶ καὶ ἁγίῳ Πνεύματι, εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

This short note is packed with historically significant information.

    The Document: The Martyrdom of Polycarp (Martyrium Polycarpi) is a letter written by the church of Smyrna to the church of Philomelium (and other churches) shortly after the martyrdom of their bishop, St. Polycarp, around A.D. 155-160. It is the earliest complete account of a Christian martyrdom outside of the New Testament.

    The Chain of Transmission: The notes you found (from Gaius, Socrates, and Pionius) are not part of the original letter. They are additions by successive copyists that trace the document's history. Your text lays out this incredible provenance:

        The original letter was written by the Church of Smyrna.

        Irenaeus (a disciple of Polycarp) possessed a copy.

        Gaius copied it from Irenaeus's version.

        Socrates (in Corinth) copied it from Gaius's manuscript.

        Pionius then copied it from Socrates's version ("the previously written copy").

    The Identity of Pionius: The author of this final note is almost certainly St. Pionius of Smyrna, a priest who was himself martyred in Smyrna during the persecution of the Emperor Decius, around A.D. 250. This adds a profound layer of meaning: a future martyr, living in the same city, is preserving the story of a famous past martyr.

    The Supernatural Claim ("Revelation"): Pionius makes a remarkable claim. He says he didn't just find the manuscript; the blessed Polycarp "manifested them to me through revelation" (κατὰ ἀποκάλυψιν). He also states that the manuscript was old and fragile, "almost faded away through the passing of time" (σχεδὸν ἐκ τοῦ χρόνου κεκμηκότα - literally "worn out by time"). Pionius believed he was on a divinely inspired mission, guided by the spirit of St. Polycarp himself, to rescue this sacred history from being lost.

    The Concluding Doxology: The note ends with a beautiful and fully-formed Trinitarian doxology: "...to whom [Jesus Christ], with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be glory forever and ever. Amen." This provides clear evidence of a developed Trinitarian formula used in worship and writing by the mid-3rd century.

fr:
Sur cette chaire où Pierre lui-même avait siégé, la grande Rome ordonna à Lin d’être le premier à prendre place.
Après lui, Cletus à son tour prit en charge le troupeau du bercail.
Son successeur, Anaclet, fut établi par le sort.
Lui succède Clément, bien connu des apôtres.
Après lui, Évariste gouverna l’Église sans reproche.
Le sixième, Alexandre, confie le bercail à Sixte,
qui, au terme de son lustre, le transmet à Télesphore, homme éminent et fidèle martyr.
en: POEM AGAINST THE MARCIONITES In this chair in which he himself had sat. Peter in mighty Rome commanded Linus. the first elected. to sit down. After him. Cletus too accepted the flock of the fold. As his successor, Anacletus was elected by lot. Clement follows him, well-known to apostolic men. After him Evaristus ruled the flock without crime. Alexander, sixth in succession, commends the fold to Sixtus. After his illustrious times were completed, he passed on to Telesphorus. He was excellent, a faithful martyr [Poem Against the Marcionites 276-84 (c. A.D. 285)].
latin:
Hac cathedra, Petrus qua sederat ipse, locatum
    Maxima Roma Linum, primum considere jussit.
    Post quem Cletus et ipse gregem suscepit ovilis.
    Hujus Anacletus successor sorte locatus:
    Quem sequitur Clemens; is apostolicis bene notus.
    Evaristus ab hoc rexit sine crimine legem.
    Sextus Alexander Sixto commendat ovile:
    Post expleta sui qui lustri tempora tradit
    Telesphoro; excellens hic erat, martyrque fidelis;
context:
Additional Relevant Details
About the Work

    Title: Adversus Marcionem Carmen (Poem Against the Marcionites).

    Author: The work is attributed to Pseudo-Tertullian. For centuries it was included in the works of Tertullian, but modern scholarship universally agrees he was not the author. The true author remains anonymous.

    Date: The date is debated. Your estimate of c. A.D. 285 falls within the scholarly consensus, which places it somewhere between the 3rd and 5th centuries. Its theological language and structure suggest an earlier date is more likely.

    Source Citation: The column numbers you provided (1077B-1078A) indicate this text is from Volume 2 of Migne's Patrologia Latina (PL 2), which contains the works of Pseudo-Tertullian.

Significance of the Passage

This passage is a powerful early testimony to the doctrine of Apostolic Succession centered on the See of Rome. Its key elements are:

    The Chair of Peter (Hac cathedra): The author explicitly grounds the legitimacy of the Roman bishops in their succession to the specific "chair" where Peter himself sat. This is a very early reference to the concept of the Cathedra Petri.

    An Unbroken Chain: The poem's primary purpose here is to list an unbroken chain of succession from the Apostle Peter. This was a crucial argument used by the early Church against heretics.

    Argument Against Heresy: The poem was written to refute Marcionism. Marcion was a 2nd-century heretic who rejected the Old Testament and created his own, edited canon of Scripture. By listing the historical, verifiable succession of bishops from the apostles, the author demonstrates that the Catholic Church possesses the authentic tradition, while Marcion's teaching is a recent and illegitimate invention.

The Papal List

The list of popes provided here is one of the earliest we have, alongside the famous list from St. Irenaeus of Lyons in his work Against Heresies (Book 3, Chapter 3), written around A.D. 180.

The succession in your text is:

    Peter

    Linus

    Cletus

    Anacletus

    Clement

    Evaristus

    Alexander

    Sixtus

    Telesphorus

This list is remarkably consistent with other early sources. The detail about Telesphorus being a "faithful martyr" is also corroborated by St. Irenaeus, adding to its historical weight. The line "Alexander, the sixth, commends the fold to Sixtus" is slightly confusing, as Alexander is the 6th bishop after Peter, not Sixtus. However, the order of succession is presented correctly.

fr:
Celui qui manipule les paroles du Seigneur pour les plier à ses propres désirs, et qui prétend qu'il n'y a ni résurrection ni jugement, celui-là est le premier-né de Satan.

C'est pourquoi, abandonnant la vanité du grand nombre et les fausses doctrines, revenons à la Parole qui nous a été transmise dès l'origine...
en: ST. POLYCARP OF SMYRNA Whoever perverts the sayings of the Lord for his own desires, and says that there is neither resurrection nor judgment, is the firstborn of Satan. Let us leave the foolishness and the false teaching of the crowd and turn back to the word that was delivered to us in the beginning [Letter to the Philippians 7 (c. A.D. 135)].

context:
Additional Relevant Details

This passage is one of the most famous in early Christian literature outside of the New Testament. Its importance comes from its author, its historical context, and the powerful language it uses.
1. The Author: St. Polycarp of Smyrna

Polycarp (c. 69 – c. 155 AD) was a towering figure of the post-apostolic age. He was a Bishop of Smyrna (modern-day Izmir, Turkey) and, most importantly, a direct disciple of St. John the Apostle. This personal connection to the apostles gave his words immense authority in the early Church. He is a crucial link in the chain of Apostolic Tradition.
2. The "Firstborn of Satan" Anecdote

This fiery phrase was not just a general insult; it appears to have been a specific title St. Polycarp used for the arch-heretic Marcion. According to St. Irenaeus (who was a disciple of Polycarp), a famous encounter took place in Rome:

    "And Polycarp himself replied to Marcion, who met him on one occasion and said, 'Dost thou know me?' 'I do know thee, the firstborn of Satan.'"
    — St. Irenaeus, Against Heresies, 3.3.4

This anecdote shows that the phrase in the letter was a deeply serious condemnation, likely aimed directly at Marcion and his followers, who were active during this period.
3. The Theological Targets: Docetism and Gnosticism

The full text you provided makes it clear what heresies Polycarp is fighting:

    Denial of the Incarnation: The chapter begins, "For whoever does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, is an antichrist." This is a direct attack on Docetism (from the Greek dokein, "to seem"), a Gnostic-leaning heresy that claimed Jesus was a pure spirit who only appeared to be human.

    Denial of the Resurrection and Judgment: The Gnostics and Marcionites generally held a deep contempt for the physical, material world, which they saw as evil or flawed. Consequently, they denied a future bodily resurrection and a final judgment involving the body.

Polycarp links these theological errors directly to a moral failing: "perverting the sayings of the Lord for his own desires." He saw this false teaching not as an honest mistake, but as a satanic corruption of the Gospel.
4. The Appeal to Apostolic Tradition

The second part of your quote is the classic orthodox response to heresy:

    "...Let us leave the foolishness and the false teaching of the crowd and turn back to the word that was delivered to us in the beginning."

This is one of the earliest and clearest articulations of the principle of Apostolic Tradition. For Polycarp and the early Church, the test of true doctrine was not novelty or philosophical sophistication, but its faithful continuity with what the apostles themselves had taught "from the beginning."

fr: En effet, quiconque ne confesse pas que Jésus-Christ est venu dans la chair est un antéchrist ; et quiconque ne confesse pas le témoignage de la croix vient du diable ; et quiconque falsifie les paroles du Seigneur pour les plier à ses propres convoitises, et dit qu'il n'y a ni résurrection ni jugement, celui-là est le premier-né de Satan.
en: ST. POLYCARP OF SMYRNA For whoever does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is Antichrist [1 Jn 4:3], and whoever does not confess the testimony of the cross is of the devil; and whosoever perverts the oracles of the Lord to his own lusts, and says that there is neither a resurrection nor a judgment, he is the firstborn of Satan [Letter to the Philippians (C. A.D. 135)].
greek: Πᾶς γάρ, ὃς ἂν μὴ ὁμολογῇ, Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν ἐν σαρκὶ ἐληλυθέναι, ἀντίχριστός ἐστιν· καὶ ὃς ἂν μὴ ὁμολογῇ τὸ μαρτύριον τοῦ σταυροῦ, ἐκ τοῦ διαβόλου ἐστίν· καὶ ὃς ἂν μεθοδεύῃ τὰ λόγια τοῦ κυρίου πρὸς τὰς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας καὶ λέγῃ μήτε ἀνάστασιν μήτε κρίσιν, οὗτος πρωτότοκός ἐστι τοῦ σατανᾶ.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

This short passage is incredibly rich with historical and theological significance.

1. Historical Context:

    Author: St. Polycarp was the Bishop of Smyrna (modern-day Izmir, Turkey) and, according to his own student St. Irenaeus, he was a direct disciple of the Apostle John. This places him in the generation immediately following the apostles.

    Date: The letter is dated to around A.D. 135, making it one of the earliest Christian documents outside of the New Testament.

    Purpose: He is writing to the church in Philippi to warn them against false teachers who were spreading dangerous doctrines.

2. The Heresies Being Condemned:
St. Polycarp identifies a threefold error that constitutes being the "firstborn of Satan":

    Denying the Incarnation ("Jesus Christ has come in the flesh"): This is a direct attack on Docetism, an early Gnostic heresy. Docetists believed that matter was evil and therefore Christ, being divine, could not have had a real, physical body. They taught he only seemed (Greek: dokeō) to be human. By quoting/alluding to 1 John 4:2-3, Polycarp uses the Apostle John's own teaching to condemn this.

    Denying the Cross ("the testimony of the cross"): This is a logical consequence of Docetism. If Jesus wasn't truly human, his suffering and death on the cross were not real, but an illusion. For Polycarp, denying the reality of the cross is to deny the very act of salvation.

    Denying Resurrection and Judgment: This was another common feature of Gnostic belief systems, which rejected the physical resurrection of the body in favor of a purely spiritual "escape" from the material world. By denying a final judgment, these teachings also promoted moral laxity ("perverts the oracles of the Lord to his own lusts").

3. The "Firstborn of Satan" Anecdote:
This is not just a random insult. It was St. Polycarp's famous, personal description for a specific heretic. His student, St. Irenaeus, records a story of a personal encounter between Polycarp and the notorious heretic Marcion (who also promoted a form of Docetism).

    "And Polycarp himself replied to Marcion, who met him on one occasion, and said, 'Dost thou know me?' 'I do know thee, the first-born of Satan.'"

    —St. Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book 3, Chapter 3, Section 4.

This historical anecdote shows that the strong language in his letter was not just rhetorical; it reflected his personal conviction in face-to-face confrontations with heretics.

4. The Pastoral Response (The Verse You Included):
The verse that immediately follows (7.2) is just as important, as it shows Polycarp's solution:

    Greek (7.2): διὸ ἀπολιπόντες τὴν ματαιότητα τῶν πολλῶν καὶ τὰς ψευδοδιδασκαλίας ἐπὶ τὸν ἐξ ἀρxῆς ἡμῖν παραδοθέντα λόγον ἐπιστρέψωμεν...

    Translation: "Wherefore, leaving the vanity of many and their false teachings, let us return to the word which was delivered to us from the beginning..."

His response to heresy is not just condemnation, but a call to return to the Apostolic Tradition—the faith "delivered to us from the beginning"—and to reinforce it with prayer, fasting, and vigilance.

fr: Demeurez donc fermes sur ces principes et suivez l'exemple du Seigneur, solides et inébranlables dans la foi, pleins d'amour fraternel. Quand vous pouvez faire le bien, ne tardez pas, car l'aumône délivre de la mort. Soyez tous soumis les uns aux autres ; ayez une conduite irréprochable au milieu des païens, afin que par vos bonnes œuvres, vous receviez vous aussi des louanges et que le Seigneur ne soit pas blasphémé à cause de vous. Mais malheur à celui par qui le nom du Seigneur est blasphémé.
en: ST. POLYCARP OF SMYRNA Stand fast, therefore, in these things, and follow the example of the Lord, being firm and unchangeable in the faith, loving the brotherhood [1 Pt 2:17]. . . When you can do good, do not defer it, because "alms delivers from death" [Tb 4:10; 12:9]. Be all of you subject to one another 1 Pt 5:5], having your conduct blameless among the Gentiles [1 Pt 2:12], and the Lord may not be blasphemed through you. But woe to him who blasphemes the name of the Lord [ls 52:5]! [ Letter to the Philippians 10 (c. A.D. 135)].
latin: In his ergo state, et Domini exemplar sequimini, firmi in fide et immutabiles, fraternitatis amatores... Cum potestis benefacere, nolite differre, quia eleemosyna de morte liberat. Omnes vobis invicem subjecti estote, conversationem vestram irreprehensibilem habentes in gentibus, ut ex bonis operibus vestris et vos laudem accipiatis, et Dominus in vobis non blasphemetur. Væ autem illi, per quem nomen Domini blasphematur.
context:
Original Greek Text

The original Greek text for Chapter 10 is lost.

As the note in your source correctly states (Desiderantur Græco... - "The Greek is missing..."), the complete letter of St. Polycarp does not survive in its original Greek. Only Chapters 13 and a portion of Chapter 9 are extant in Greek because they were quoted by the historian Eusebius of Caesarea in his Ecclesiastical History (Book 3, Chapter 36).

The rest of the letter, including the entirety of Chapter 10 that you are looking for, is known to us only through this single, ancient Latin translation. Therefore, it is impossible to provide the original Greek for this specific passage.
English Translation

(Based on the Latin text)

    "Stand fast, therefore, in these things, and follow the example of the Lord, being firm and unchangeable in the faith, loving the brotherhood... When you can do good, do not defer it, because 'alms delivers from death.' Be all of you subject to one another, having your conduct blameless among the Gentiles, so that from your good works you yourselves may receive praise and the Lord may not be blasphemed through you. But woe to him through whom the name of the Lord is blasphemed!"

Additional Relevant Details
1. The Author and His Authority

St. Polycarp (c. A.D. 69–155) was the Bishop of Smyrna (modern-day Izmir, Turkey). He is a towering figure of the post-apostolic age because he was a direct disciple of St. John the Apostle. His letter is a precious link to the teaching of the apostles themselves. It was written around A.D. 135.
2. The Context of the Passage

This passage is the core of St. Polycarp's pastoral exhortation to the Christians in Philippi. Having warned them against the love of money and the heresy of docetism (which denied Christ's true humanity), he moves to a practical summary of the Christian life. The entire chapter is a tapestry woven from New Testament phrases and ethical commands.
3. A Mosaic of Scripture

This short passage is a powerful example of how deeply the first Christians were immersed in the scriptures. Polycarp is not just quoting verses; he is thinking and writing in biblical language. The specific allusions are:

    "loving the brotherhood": A direct echo of 1 Peter 2:17.

    "alms delivers from death": A quotation from the book of Tobit (4:10 and 12:9). This shows the early Church's use and reverence for the Deuterocanonical books of the Old Testament.

    "Be all of you subject to one another": A quotation from 1 Peter 5:5.

    "having your conduct blameless among the Gentiles": A direct quotation from 1 Peter 2:12. The concern for the Church's public witness was paramount.

    "woe to him through whom the name of the Lord is blasphemed": This is a common theme, echoing Isaiah 52:5 as it was used by St. Paul in Romans 2:24.

The heavy reliance on 1 Peter suggests that this epistle was particularly beloved and influential in the churches of Asia Minor.

fr: C'est pourquoi, pour toutes choses, je te loue, je te bénis, je te glorifie par l'éternel et céleste grand prêtre Jésus-Christ, ton Fils bien-aimé, par qui gloire à toi, avec lui et l'Esprit Saint, maintenant et pour les siècles à venir. Amen.
en: ST. POLYCARP OF SMYRNA praise you for all things, I bless you, glorify you, along with the everlasting and heavenly Jesus Christ, your beloved Son, with whom, to you, and the Holy Spirit, be glory both now and to all coming ages. Amen [quoted in Martyrdom of Polycarp 14 (c. A.D. 156) emphasis added].
greek: διὰ τοῦτο καὶ περὶ πάντων σὲ αἰνῶ, σὲ εὐλογῶ, σὲ δοξάζω διὰ τοῦ αἰωνίου καὶ ἐπουρανίου ἀρχιερέως Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, ἀγαπητοῦ σου παιδός, δι’ οὗ σοὶ σὺν αὐτῷ καὶ πνεύματι ἁγίῳ δόξα καὶ νῦν καὶ εἰς τοὺς μέλλοντας αἰῶνας. ἀμήν.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

This short doxology is one of the most important in all of early Christian literature for several reasons:

    Extreme Antiquity: Dating to the mid-second century (c. A.D. 156), this is one of the earliest and clearest extra-biblical examples of a fully formed Trinitarian doxology used in Christian prayer and worship. It demonstrates that the practice of glorifying the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together was already established in the generation immediately following the Apostles.

    Liturgical Form: The structure is highly liturgical and reflects a pattern that would become foundational for Christian prayer. Praise is offered to the Father, through the Son (as High Priest), with the Holy Spirit. This formulation is theologically rich, preserving both the distinction of the divine Persons and their unity in the act of worship.

    High Christology: Jesus is called the "eternal and heavenly High Priest" (ἀρχιερέως). This title, drawn from the Epistle to the Hebrews, affirms Christ's divinity and his unique role as the mediator through whom all true worship reaches the Father.

    Witness to the Holy Spirit's Divinity: The Holy Spirit is included alongside the Father and the Son as the co-recipient of glory. This is a powerful, implicit affirmation of the Holy Spirit's divine status at a very early date, long before the formal definitions of the Council of Constantinople in 381.

    Context of Martyrdom: These are not words from a calm theological treatise; they are the final, climactic words of a man sealing his life's testimony with his death. His prayer is his ultimate act of witness (martyria) to the Triune God for whom he is dying.

fr: Celui qui, en effet, a été justifié et qui, d’impie, est devenu pieux, a reçu le don d’acquérir un mérite, lui qui n’en avait aucun auparavant, afin que ce que la grâce du Christ a initié en lui soit également augmenté par l’effort du libre arbitre, sans que jamais, toutefois, ne vienne à manquer le secours de Dieu, sans lequel nul ne peut progresser ni persévérer dans le bien.
en: ST. PROSPER OF AQUITAINE Indeed, a man who has been justified, who from impious has been made pious, receives a gift, since he had no antecedent good merit, by which gift he may acquire merit. Thus, what was begun in him by Christ's grace can also be augmented by the industry of his free choice, but never in the absence of God's help, without which no one is able to progress or to continue in doing good [Responses on Behalf of Augustine 6 (c. A.D. 431)].
latin: Qui enim justificatus, et ex impio pius factus est, donum accepit, quo, quia nullum praecedens bonum meritum habuit, meritum acquireret. Ut quod in illo gratia Christi coepit, etiam studio liberi augeatur arbitrii, nunquam tamen desit auxilium Dei, sine quo nec proficere, nec perseverare in bono quisquam potest.
context:
Additional Context and Significance

1. The Author and the Work: St. Prosper of Aquitaine (c. 390 – c. 455 AD) was a lay theologian who fiercely defended St. Augustine's doctrines on grace and predestination against a group of monks in Southern Gaul (modern-day France). These opponents are often called "Semi-Pelagians" because while they rejected Pelagianism, they argued that the beginning of faith (initium fidei) was an act of unaided human free will. Prosper's Responses is a direct refutation of their objections.

2. The Context of Chapter 6:

    The Objection: The chapter begins with the Gallic monks' objection: "That God creates in men a will like that of the demons, which by its own movement can will nothing but evil." They are caricaturing Augustine's teaching, suggesting it makes God the author of evil and denies free will.

    Prosper's Initial Response (The text you found): Prosper first clarifies that while wicked men have wills like demons, God is not the author of that evil. The crucial difference is that men can be saved by God's mercy, whereas demons cannot.

    The Pivot to Your Quote: Having dealt with the state of the wicked, Prosper then explains how a person becomes righteous. This is where your quote comes in. It is the heart of the Augustinian synthesis of grace and free will.

3. The Theological Importance of Your Quote:
This passage is a masterfully concise summary of the relationship between grace, free will, and merit.

    Prevenient Grace: "a man who has been justified... receives a gift, since he had no antecedent good merit." This is the core Augustinian principle: God's grace comes first (preveniently), without any prior good works on our part to deserve it.

    Cooperative Grace and Free Will: "by which gift he may acquire merit... what was begun in him by Christ's grace can also be augmented by the industry of his free choice." This is the crucial anti-fatalist point. Once grace has healed and liberated the will, our free choice can and must cooperate with that grace. This cooperation "augments" the work of grace and "acquires merit" (not as a wage owed, but as a further gift from God crowning His own work).

    The Necessity of Ongoing Grace: "but never in the absence of God's help, without which no one is able to progress or to continue in doing good." This refutes the Semi-Pelagian error directly. Even after justification, our free will is powerless to persevere in goodness without the constant, sustaining help of God's grace.

fr:
Et voici qu’un ange du Seigneur se présenta et dit : « Anne, Anne, le Seigneur Dieu a exaucé ta prière : tu concevras et tu enfanteras, et l’on parlera de ta descendance dans le monde entier. »

Et Anne dit : « Le Seigneur mon Dieu est vivant ! Si j’enfante, que ce soit un garçon ou une fille, je l’offrirai en don au Seigneur mon Dieu, et il le servira tous les jours de sa vie. » . . . Or, Marie vivait dans le temple du Seigneur, élevée comme une colombe, et elle recevait sa nourriture de la main d’un ange.
en: PROTOEVANGELIUM OF JAMES And, behold, an angel of the Lord stood by, saying: "Anna, Anna, the Lord has heard your prayer, and you shall conceive, and shall bring forth; and your seed shall be spoken of in all the world." And Anna said: "As the Lord my God lives, if I beget either male or female, I will bring it as a gift to the Lord my God; and it shall minister to him in holy things all the days of its life. And [from the time she was three] Mary was in the temple of the Lord as she were a dove that dwelt there [Protoevangelium of Jamnes 4, 8 (C. A.D. 150)].
greek:
(1) Καὶ ἰδοὺ ἄγγελος Κυρίου ἐπέστη λέγων· Ἄννα, Ἄννα, εἰσήκουσεν Κύριος ὁ θεὸς τῆς δεήσεώς σου· συλλήψῃ καὶ γεννήσεις, καὶ λαληθήσεται τὸ σπέρμα σου ἐν ὅλῃ τῇ οἰκουμένῃ.
