context:
Additional Relevant Details
About the Source Text

    Title: Protoevangelium of James (Protoevangelium Jacobi), sometimes called the Infancy Gospel of James.

    Date & Author: Written anonymously around A.D. 150. It is a work of early Christian piety, not a historical account by the Apostle James.

    Status: It is an apocryphal gospel, meaning it is outside the canon of the New Testament. While not considered divinely inspired Scripture, it was immensely popular and influential in the early Church.

    Purpose: The text was written to satisfy the curiosity of early Christians about the life of the Virgin Mary, which is not detailed in the canonical Gospels. It emphasizes her purity, unique origins, and lifelong consecration to God.

Theological and Liturgical Significance

These specific passages are the foundational source for several major Christian traditions and feasts:

    The Parents of Mary: This text is the only ancient source that gives the names of Mary's parents as Joachim and Anna. The feasts of St. Joachim and St. Anna in both the Catholic and Orthodox Churches derive entirely from this tradition.

    The Presentation of Mary: Anna's vow in Chapter 4—to dedicate her child to serve God in the Temple—is the narrative basis for the Feast of the Presentation of the Blessed Virgin Mary (celebrated on November 21). Chapter 7 of the text describes her being brought to the Temple at age three to fulfill this vow.

    Mary's Purity and Consecration: The description of Mary being "nurtured like a dove" and fed by an angel in the Temple (Chapter 8) powerfully reinforces the belief in her unique holiness and separation from the world from her earliest childhood. This tradition was a cornerstone for the later development of doctrines like the Immaculate Conception.

Analysis of Key Phrases

    λειτουργοῦν αὐτῷ (leitourgoun autō) - "ministering to him": The Greek word for "ministering" is the root of our word "liturgy." Anna's vow is that her child will be dedicated to the official, sacred worship of God in the Temple.

    ὡσεὶ περιστερὰ νεμομένη (hōsei peristera nemomenē) - "nurtured like a dove": This is a very rich image. The dove is a symbol of purity, gentleness, and the Holy Spirit. The Greek word nemomenē means "fed," "nurtured," or "pastured." The phrase suggests not just that Mary lived there, but that she was cared for in a state of perfect innocence and divine protection, which is confirmed by the next clause stating she was fed by an angel.

About Your Edition

The images you provided are from a scholarly critical edition, most likely the famous 19th-century work by Constantin von Tischendorf, Evangelia Apocrypha. The layout, with the reconstructed Greek text at the top and the detailed list of manuscript variations (apparatus criticus) at the bottom, is characteristic of such an edition and represents a very high standard of textual scholarship.

fr:
Voici que Marie avait atteint l’âge de douze ans dans le temple du Seigneur. « Que ferons-nous d’elle, de peur qu’elle ne souille le sanctuaire du Seigneur ? » Et ils dirent au grand-prêtre : « C’est toi qui te tiens devant l’autel du Seigneur. Entre et prie pour elle, et ce que le Seigneur te révélera, nous le ferons. »

Le grand-prêtre, revêtu de l’ornement aux douze clochettes, entra dans le Saint des Saints et pria pour elle. Et voici qu’un ange du Seigneur se présenta à lui et dit : « Zacharie, Zacharie, sors et convoque les veufs du peuple. Qu’ils apportent chacun un bâton, et celui à qui le Seigneur montrera un signe, elle sera sa femme. » . . .

... Joseph prit aussi son bâton, en tout dernier. Et voici qu’une colombe sortit du bâton et se posa sur la tête de Joseph. Et le prêtre dit à Joseph :

« C’est toi que le sort a désigné pour recevoir la vierge du Seigneur et la prendre sous ta garde. » Mais Joseph protesta : « J’ai des fils et je suis un vieil homme, alors qu’elle est une jeune fille ! »
en: And when she was twelve years old a council of the priests was held, which said: "Behold, Mary has reached the age of twelve years in the temple of the Lord. What shall we do with her, lest she defile the sanctuary of the Lord?" And they said to the high priest: "You stand by the altar of the Lord; go in, and pray concerning her; and whatever the Lord shall manifest unto you, that will we do. And the high priest went in, taking the robe with the twelve bells into the holy of holies: and he prayed about her. And behold an angel of the Lord stood by him, and said to him: "Zacharias, Zacharias, go out and assemble the widowers of the people, and let them bring each his rod; and to whomever the Lord shall show a sign, his wife shall she be." And Joseph [was chosen]. . And the priest said to Joseph, "You have been chosen by lot to take into your keeping the Virgin of the Lord." But Joseph refused, saying, "I have children, and am an old man, and she is a young girl" [ibid., 8-9].

context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. Source Identification

    Name: The Protoevangelium of James (meaning "First Gospel of James"). It is also commonly known as the Infancy Gospel of James.

    Author: The text claims to be written by James (implying the "brother of the Lord"), but this is universally rejected by scholars. The author is anonymous.

    Date: It is dated to the mid-2nd century (c. 145-170 AD), making it one of the earliest non-canonical gospels.

    Status: This work is apocryphal. It is not, and has never been, part of the canonical New Testament accepted by any major Christian tradition.

2. Historical and Theological Significance

Despite being non-canonical, the Protoevangelium of James has had an immense and profound influence on Christian piety, art, and liturgy, particularly in shaping traditions surrounding the Virgin Mary.

    Mary's Parents: This is the first text to name Mary's parents as Joachim and Anne. Their story of barrenness and miraculous conception of Mary forms the first part of the book.

    The Presentation of Mary: It contains the famous story of Mary, at age three, being presented by her parents to live in the Temple, an event commemorated in the liturgical Feast of the Presentation (November 21).

    Joseph as an Elderly Widower: This is perhaps the most influential detail from the passage you cited. The depiction of Joseph as an old man and a widower with children from a previous marriage became the dominant tradition in both Eastern and Western Christianity. This conveniently explained the "brothers of Jesus" mentioned in the canonical Gospels (Mark 6:3, Matthew 13:55) as being Joseph's children from his first wife, thereby safeguarding the doctrine of the Perpetual Virginity of Mary.

    Influence on Art: Scenes from this book are staples of Christian art. Giotto's famous fresco cycle in the Scrovegni Chapel, for instance, depicts many events from the Protoevangelium, including the "Test of the Rods" and the betrothal of Mary and Joseph.

    The Nativity Scene: It adds details not found in the canonical Gospels, such as the birth of Jesus taking place in a cave, a tradition still very strong in the East.

Le prêtre dit : « Marie, qu'as-tu fait ? Pourquoi as-tu souillé ton âme et oublié le Seigneur ton Dieu ? »

Elle pleura amèrement en disant : « Le Seigneur mon Dieu est vivant : je suis pure devant lui et je ne connais pas d'homme. »
en: And the priest said, "Mary, why have you done this? Why have you brought your soul low and forgotten the Lord your God?" And she wept bitterly and said, "As the Lord my God lives, I am pure before him, and know not a man" [ibid.].

context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. Immediate Context of the Scene

This confrontation is the climax of a crisis.

    Joseph's Discovery: In Chapter 13, Joseph returns from his work as a builder to find the six-month-pregnant Mary. He is devastated, assuming she has been unfaithful.

    Angelic Reassurance: In Chapter 14, Joseph, like his counterpart in the Gospel of Matthew, has a dream in which an angel reassures him that the child is from the Holy Spirit.

    Public Accusation: However, in Chapter 15, before Joseph can act, a scribe named Annas visits and sees Mary's condition. He reports it to the high priest, leading to both Joseph and Mary being summoned for a formal inquiry. The quote you've selected is the priest's direct accusation of Mary.

2. The Significance of Mary's Response

Mary's defense is a solemn, legal, and theological statement.

    A Solemn Oath: She begins with "As the Lord my God lives..." (Ζῇ κύριος ὁ θεός μου). This is not a casual phrase; it is the most serious form of oath one could take in a Jewish context, invoking God himself as a witness to the truth of the statement.

    Echoes of the Annunciation: Her words, "I know not a man" (ἄνδρα οὐ γινώσκω), are a direct echo of her question to the angel Gabriel in the canonical Gospel of Luke 1:34 ("How will this be, since I do not know a man?"). The author of the Protoevangelium places this same declaration in a new, public, and judicial setting, turning it from a question of confusion into a powerful defense of her purity.

3. The "Trial by Ordeal"

This scene of accusation is not the end of the story. It directly leads to the book's most dramatic and miraculous vindication of Mary's virginity in Chapter 16.

    The Water of the Ordeal: The high priest, unconvinced by their verbal testimony, subjects both Mary and Joseph to the "water of the ordeal of the Lord." This is a practice loosely based on the test for an unfaithful wife described in the Book of Numbers 5:11-31.

    Miraculous Vindication: Both Mary and Joseph drink the water, and when neither suffers any harm, the priest publicly declares them innocent. This miraculous trial serves as God's public testimony to the truth of the Virgin Birth.

4. The Purpose of the Narrative

This entire storyline—the public accusation, Mary's tearful defense, and the miraculous trial—is absent from the canonical Gospels. The author of the Protoevangelium created it to:

    Dramatize the Narrative: It fills in the "gaps" left by Matthew and Luke with a story full of human emotion, conflict, and suspense.

    Defend the Virgin Birth: Most importantly, it serves as a powerful piece of apologetics. By inventing a public trial that ends in a divine miracle, the author provides a definitive, "in-story" refutation of any accusation or slander against Mary's purity and the divine origin of Jesus.        Additional Context and Analysis of the Images

The images you provided contain more than just that one quote. They show the full scene of the accusation, including the priest's subsequent interrogation of Joseph.
1. The Accusation of Joseph (Chapter 16)

The first, smaller image you sent shows the very end of Chapter 16, where the priest turns his accusation towards Joseph. The full accusation begins in the text of the second image and concludes in the first.

Original Greek Text (from Chapter 16):

    καὶ εἶπεν ὁ ἱερεύς· ...μὴ ψευδομαρτύρει ἀλλὰ λέγε τὸ ἀληθές· ἔκλεψας τοὺς γάμους αὐτῆς καὶ οὐκ ἐφανέρωσας τοῖς υἱοῖς Ἰσραήλ, καὶ οὐκ ἔκλινας τὴν κεφαλήν σου ὑπὸ τὴν κραταιὰν χεῖρα ὅπως εὐλογηθῇ τὸ σπέρμα σου. καὶ Ἰωσὴφ ἐσίγησεν.

English Translation:

    And the priest said: "...Do not bear false witness, but speak the truth. You have stolen her marriage and not made it known to the sons of Israel, and you did not bow your head under the mighty hand [of God] so that your seed might be blessed." And Joseph was silent.

Context: The priest's accusation against Joseph is that he must have consummated the marriage secretly, without the proper public rites ("you stole her marriage"), thus violating the sacred trust. Joseph's silence in the face of this charge sets the stage for the divine vindication that is to come.
2. The Nature of the Document You're Viewing

The images are from a critical edition of the Greek text. This is a scholarly version of the text, and it's important to understand its features:

    The Main Text: The larger text at the top of the columns is the editor's reconstructed version of what the original Greek most likely said.

    The Critical Apparatus: The dense block of text at the bottom is the "critical apparatus." This is a highly abbreviated set of notes showing where different ancient manuscripts (often referred to by letters like A, B, D, E, P, etc.) have different words or spellings. For example, it shows which manuscripts might omit a word (om.), add a word (add.), or have a different spelling. This tool is essential for scholars studying the history of the text's transmission.

3. Narrative Flow

By providing these images, you have captured the entire judicial accusation scene:

    Chapter 15: The priest accuses Mary.

    Chapter 15: Mary makes her solemn oath of innocence.

    Chapter 16: The priest accuses Joseph.

    Chapter 16: Joseph remains silent.

This complete scene of public accusation is what necessitates the "Trial by the Ordeal Water" that immediately follows, where God himself must intervene to prove their innocence to the community.

context:
dditional Relevant Details
1. Author and Authenticity: "Pseudo-Ignatius"

This is the most crucial piece of context. The author is not St. Ignatius of Antioch, the apostolic father who was martyred around A.D. 110. The letter you have cited comes from what is known as the "Longer Recension" of the Ignatian letters.

    Authentic Letters (Middle Recension): St. Ignatius wrote seven original letters. These are prized for their early testimony to Christian doctrine.

    Forged Letters (Longer Recension): Around A.D. 350-380, an anonymous author (often identified as an Apollinarian or Arian sympathizer trying to sound orthodox) took the seven authentic letters, heavily interpolated them with later theological language, and forged six additional letters, including this Letter to the Philippians. This collection is called the "Longer Recension."

Therefore, the text you quoted is not from the early 2nd century, but a product of the mid-to-late 4th century.
2. Historical Context: The Arian Controversy

The date (c. A.D. 350) places this text squarely in the middle of the Arian Controversy. The author's language is clearly shaped by the theological debates of his time. He is fighting a war on two fronts:

    Against Arianism/Subordinationism: By insisting that the Son is "God the Word" (Λόγος Θεός), he affirms the Son's full divinity.

    Against Modalism/Sabellianism: By clearly distinguishing between the Father, Son, and Paraclete as "three of equal honor" (τρεῖς ὁμοτίμοις), he rejects the idea that they are merely three modes or manifestations of one Person.

    Against Tritheism: By repeatedly stressing "One God," "One Son," "One Paraclete," and condemning the idea of "three Fathers" or "three Sons," he guards against the charge of polytheism.

3. Theological Analysis of the Full Passage

The fuller text you provided is even more revealing. The author's goal is to present a balanced, orthodox Trinitarianism as understood in the 4th century:

    Unity of God: He starts with the fundamental Jewish and Christian confession from Deuteronomy 6:4, the Shema Yisrael ("The Lord is one"), to ground everything in strict monotheism.

    Distinct Persons: He then systematically names the three distinct persons: Father, Son, and Paraclete.

    Use of the Baptismal Formula: He appeals to the baptismal command in Matthew 28:19 ("baptize in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit") as the ultimate proof of three distinct and divine persons. This was a standard and powerful argument used by the pro-Nicene fathers.

    "Three of Equal Honor" (εἰς τρεῖς ὁμοτίμοις): This is the theological climax. The word homotimos (ὁμότιμος) means "of equal honor" or "of equal rank." It is a powerful anti-Arian statement, asserting that the Son and Spirit are not lesser, subordinate beings but are worthy of the same divine honor as the Father.

fr: Alors qu'elle priait ainsi, le Seigneur dit à sa propre mère : « Réjouis-toi et que ton cœur exulte. Car toute grâce et tout don t'ont été accordés par mon Père qui est dans les cieux, par moi et par l'Esprit Saint. Toute âme qui invoquera ton nom ne sera jamais confondue, mais elle trouvera miséricorde, réconfort, secours et assurance, dans le siècle présent comme dans le siècle à venir, devant mon Père qui est aux cieux. »
en: PSEUDO-JOHN [T]he Lord said to his Mother, "Let your heart rejoice and be glad, for every favor and every gift has been given to you from my Father in heaven and from me and from the Holy Spirit. Every soul that calls upon your name shall not be ashamed, but shall find mercy and comfort and support and confidence, both in the world that now is and in what is to come, in the presence of my Father in the heavens" [Falling Asleep of Mary (c. A.D. 550)].

The Immediate Context (What is Happening)

The context you've captured on pages 108-109 makes this passage even more powerful. Here is the sequence of events:

    Christ Arrives: Jesus appears to his mother as she is preparing for her death.

    Mary's Prayer (Page 108): Mary takes Jesus's hand and offers a long, beautiful prayer. She expresses her humility and then makes a powerful intercession for humanity, asking Christ to grant help to "every person who calls upon or names the name of your handmaiden" (πάντα ἄνθρωπον ἐπικαλούμενον ἢ ὀνομάζοντα τὸ ὄνομα τῆς δούλης σου).

    Christ's Answer (Page 109 - Your Quote): The passage you found is Christ's direct and glorious answer to her specific prayer. He confirms that her request is granted by the Holy Trinity and that her name will indeed be a source of mercy, comfort, and confidence for all who invoke it.

    The Apostles Begin to Sing (End of Page 109): Immediately after this promise, Christ turns to Peter and the other apostles, and they begin to sing hymns, leading into the final moments of Mary's life on earth.

You have successfully navigated through a fascinating apocryphal text and pinpointed the exact passage, along with its rich context.

context:
The Immediate Context

This sentence is the climax of the story of Mary's burial. The context makes the moment even more profound:

    Burial in Gethsemane: The Apostles place Mary's body in a new tomb in Gethsemane.

    Angelic Vigil: For three days, the Apostles do not leave the tomb. They are surrounded by the sound of invisible angels singing and glorifying Christ.

    The Divine Sign: On the third day, the angelic singing suddenly stops.

    The Realization: The silence is the sign. The Apostles understand that the angelic honor guard is no longer needed because the body they were guarding is no longer there. This is how they "knew" that her body had been assumed into heaven.

fr: ... comme lui-même en témoigne par ses prophètes quand il dit : « Je suis Dieu, le premier et celui qui vient après ; et à part moi, il n’existe pas d’autre Dieu. » C’est pourquoi, en envoyant Moïse aux Hébreux, Dieu ne mentionne aucun nom ; c’est au contraire par une certaine forme de participation qu’il enseigne de manière mystique être lui-même le seul et unique Dieu. Car il dit : « Je suis celui qui est »...
en: PSEUDO-JUSTIN [God] himself by his own prophets testifies when he says, "1, God, am the first," and after this, "And beside me there is no other God" [Is 44:6]. On this account, then, God did not mention any name when he sent Moses to the Hebrews, but by a participle he mystically taught them that he is the one and only God [Hortatory Address to the Greeks 21 (C. A.D. 250)].

context:
English Translation and Analysis

Your English translation is a very accurate and faithful rendering of the original Greek. Let's look at it piece by piece:

    "...as he himself by his own prophets testifies when he says, 'I, God, am the first,' and after this, 'And beside me there is no other God' [Is 44:6]."

        This directly translates: ...ὡς καὶ αὐτὸς διὰ τῶν ἑαυτοῦ προφητῶν μαρτυρεῖ λέγων, Ἐγὼ Θεὸς πρῶτος καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα· Καὶ πλὴν ἐμοῦ Θεὸς ἕτερος οὐκ ἔστι.

        This is a direct quotation of Isaiah 44:6 from the Septuagint (the Greek version of the Old Testament).

    "On this account, then, God did not mention any name when he sent Moses to the Hebrews..."

        This translates: Διὰ τοῦτο τοίνυν... οὐδὲ ὀνόματός τινος ὁ Θεὸς, ἀποστέλλων πρὸς τοὺς Ἑβραίους τὸν Μωϋσέα, μέμνηται...

        The author is connecting God's uniqueness (from Isaiah) to the specific way He revealed Himself to Moses.

    "...but by a participle he mystically taught them that he is the one and only God."

        This translates: ...ἀλλὰ διά τινος μετοχῆς ἕνα καὶ μόνον Θεὸν ἑαυτὸν εἶναι μυστικῶς διδάσκει.

        The "participle" (μετοχή - metochē) he refers to is ὁ ὤν (ho Ōn) from Exodus 3:14, which means "The One Who Is" or "The Existing One."

Broader Context from Your Image

The surrounding text in your image provides the full context for the author's argument, which is brilliant:

    God Has No Proper Name: The chapter begins by stating that no proper name can truly be applied to God (Οὐδὲν γὰρ ὄνομα ἐπὶ Θεοῦ κυριολογεῖσθαι δυνατόν). Names are used to distinguish between many different things, but God is absolutely unique and singular.

    God's Self-Revelation: The author argues that God Himself confirms this. When revealing Himself, He doesn't give a "name" like Zeus or Baal. Instead, He reveals His very nature of being: "I am The One Who Is."

    The Contrast: The purpose of this revelation was to sharply contrast the one true, existing God (ὁ ὤν) with the false gods, who are non-existent (τοῖς μὴ οὖσιν). This was a direct lesson for the Hebrews who had been exposed to the polytheism of Egypt.

You have successfully located a classic passage from early Christian apologetics on the nature of God's name and the radical monotheism of the Judeo-Christian faith.

fr:
Ainsi donc, nous, tes serviteurs, avons jugé qu'il était juste que toi qui règnes dans la gloire après avoir vaincu la mort, tu ressuscites le corps de ta mère et l'emmènes avec toi, pleine de joie, au ciel.

Alors le Sauveur dit : « Qu'il en soit fait selon votre parole. »
en: PSEUDO-MELITO therefore it might come to pass by the power of your grace, it has appeared right to US your servants that, as you, having overcome death, do reign in glory, so you should raise up the body of your Mother and take her with you, rejoicing, into heaven. Then said the Savior: "Be it done according to your will" [Passing of the Virgin 16:2- 17:1 (c. A.D. 475)].
latin:
The Apostles' Request (from Chapter 16):

    Sic ergo visum nobis fuerat famulis tuis etiam rectum esse; ut sicut tu, devicta morte, regnas in gloria, ita resuscitans matris corpusculum, tu tecum duceres eam lætam in cœlum.

The Savior's Reply (from Chapter 17):

    Tunc Salvator ait: Fiat secundum verbum vestrum.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Title of the Work: The text is from a highly influential apocryphal work known in Latin as the Transitus Beatae Mariae Virginis ("The Passing of the Blessed Virgin Mary").

    Authorship ("Pseudo-Melito"): The work is "pseudepigraphical," meaning it is falsely attributed to an earlier, famous author to give it more authority. It was attributed to St. Melito of Sardis, a respected bishop from the 2nd century, but scholars universally agree he did not write it. Hence, the author is referred to as "Pseudo-Melito."

    Date and Nature: The text dates from the late 5th or early 6th century (your c. 475 A.D. is a very good estimate). It is an apocryphal work, meaning it is not part of the canonical New Testament. These were popular, devotional stories that arose in the early Church to fill in details about the lives of Jesus, Mary, and the apostles that are not found in the Gospels.

    Historical Significance: This text is one of the most important early written witnesses to the developing Christian belief in the Bodily Assumption of Mary. It shows that by the late 400s, a detailed narrative of Mary's death (or "dormition") and her body being taken into heaven was widespread and popular. It played a significant role in shaping the liturgy and piety surrounding the Assumption for centuries, long before it was formally defined as a dogma by the Catholic Church in 1950.

    Source of Your Text: The formatting of your text (two columns, chapter headings like "CAPUT XVII") is characteristic of J.-P. Migne's Patrologia Latina (PL), the monumental collection of writings from the Church Fathers.

Direct English Translation of the Latin

Here is a literal translation of the extracted Latin text, which you can see aligns perfectly with the quote you were looking for.

    The Apostles' Request:
    "Therefore, it had also seemed right to us, your servants, that just as you, having conquered death, reign in glory, so you, by resurrecting the little body of your mother, should take her with you, rejoicing, into heaven."

    The Savior's Reply:
    "Then the Savior said: Let it be done according to your word."

(Note: The Latin verbum vestrum literally means "your word," which in this context clearly means "what you have requested" or "your will.")

Sous ta tendresse, nous nous réfugions, Mère de Dieu.

mais du danger délivre-nous,

greek:
Ὑπὸ τὴν σὴν εὐσπλαγχνίαν,
καταφεύγομεν, Θεοτόκε.
Τὰς ἡμῶν ἱκεσίας,
μὴ παρίδῃς ἐν περιστάσει,
ἀλλ᾽ ἐκ κινδύνου λύτρωσαι [or ῥῦσαι] ἡμᾶς,
μόνη Ἁγνή, μόνη εὐλογημένη.
context:
Historical and Theological Significance

This small piece of papyrus is monumental for several reasons:

    Earliest Marian Prayer: It is the oldest surviving prayer addressed directly to Mary.

    Early Use of Theotokos: This is the earliest known use of the title Θεοτόκε (Theotoke, the vocative form of Theotokos). Its presence here, in a popular prayer from the 3rd century, demonstrates that the belief in Mary as the "God-bearer" or "Mother of God" was part of Christian piety long before it was formally defined at the Council of Ephesus in A.D. 431. It refutes the idea that the title was a 5th-century theological invention.

    A Prayer for Help: The prayer is a plea for protection and rescue, showing that early Christians looked to Mary as a powerful intercessor in times of danger and persecution (which were rampant in the 3rd century).

The Famous Latin Version

The prayer became immensely popular and has a famous Latin version, known as the Sub Tuum Praesidium, which is still widely used in the Catholic Church today:

    Sub tuum praesidium confugimus, Sancta Dei Genetrix. Nostras deprecationes ne despicias in necessitatibus, sed a periculis cunctis libera nos semper, Virgo gloriosa et benedicta.

fr:
Écoutez, vous tous qui aimez Dieu, les saints mérites
de l'homme bienheureux dans le Christ, l'évêque Patrick :
comment, par ses bonnes actions, il est semblable aux anges,
et, par sa vie parfaite, il est l'égal des apôtres.
en: ST. SECHNALL OF IRELAND Hear, all you who love God, the holy merits of Patrick the bishop, a man blessed in Christ; how, for his good deeds, he is likened to the angels, and, for his perfect life, he is like the apostles [Hymn in Praise of St. Patrick (c. A.D. 444)].
latin:
Audite, omnes amantes Deum, sancta merita
    Viri in Christo beati, Patricii episcopi:
    Quomodo bonum ob actum similatur angelis,
    Perfectamque ob vitam aequatur apostolis.
context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. The Significance of its Early Date (c. A.D. 444)

This is arguably the most important detail. If the traditional dating is correct, this hymn was composed during St. Patrick's own lifetime. This makes it:

    The Earliest Biographical Source: It predates all other accounts of Patrick, including the later, more legendary "Lives." It is a contemporary testament to how his followers viewed him.

    A Work of Apologetics, Not Just Praise: Patrick's own writings, like his Confessio, reveal that his mission was controversial. He faced severe criticism from churchmen back in Britain who questioned his qualifications, his education (he called himself "unlearned"), and his handling of finances. The hymn is a powerful and public defense of Patrick against these charges, written by one of his own disciples.

2. The Theological Weight of the Comparisons

The specific praises chosen by Sechnall are not random compliments; they are carefully selected theological titles that confer immense authority upon Patrick.

    "Likened to the angels" (similatur angelis): In early Christian thought, this signifies more than just being "good." It points to a life of ascetic purity, chastity, and a role as a direct messenger of God (angelos means "messenger"). It frames Patrick's mission as being divinely ordained.

    "Like [or equal to] the apostles" (aequatur apostolis): This is the most powerful claim. To be "equal to the apostles" was to have apostolic authority. It placed Patrick on the same level as the original founders of the Church. This was a direct rebuttal to any critic questioning his legitimacy. It established the Church in Ireland not as a minor, derivative mission, but as one founded by a figure of apostolic stature, with the authority to establish doctrine and ordain clergy.

3. Literary Structure and Style

    Abecedarian Form: The hymn is an abecedarian acrostic. Each of its 23 stanzas begins with a successive letter of the Latin alphabet (A, B, C... Z, omitting J, U, and W as was common). This structure was not just a poetic game; it served several purposes:

        Mnemonic Device: It made the hymn easy for clergy and laity to memorize and teach.

        Symbol of Completeness: Going from A to Z implied a complete and comprehensive account of the saint's virtues.

        Literary Sophistication: It demonstrated that the "unlearned" circle of Patrick could produce Latin poetry that was in line with the continental tradition of Christian poets like Hilary of Poitiers and Ambrose of Milan.

    Metre: The hymn is written in a metre known as trochaic tetrameter, the same metre used by St. Ambrose for his famous hymns. This choice of metre was a deliberate act, connecting the nascent Irish Church to the mainstream of Latin Christian literary and liturgical culture.

4. Primary Manuscript Sources

Our knowledge of this hymn comes from some of the greatest treasures of early Irish Christianity. It is preserved in two main manuscripts:

    The Antiphonary of Bangor (late 7th century): An ancient Irish liturgical book, now housed in the Ambrosian Library in Milan.

    The Book of Armagh (early 9th century): A magnificent manuscript that also contains the earliest copy of St. Patrick's Confessio.

In summary, this brief stanza is a dense and powerful document. It is at once a hymn of praise, a work of political and ecclesiastical defense, a claim to apostolic authority for the Irish Church, and a sophisticated piece of Latin poetry from the very dawn of Irish Christianity.
