fr:
Ferme dans la crainte de Dieu, inébranlable dans la foi,
sur qui, comme sur Pierre, est bâtie l'église ;
il a reçu de Dieu son apostolat,
et les portes de l'enfer ne l'emportent pas contre elle.
en: ST. SECHNALL OF IRELAND Steadfast in the fear of God, and in faith immovable, upon [Patrick] as upon Peter the [lrish] church is built; and he has been given his apostleship by God; against him the gates of hell prevail not [Hymn in Praise of St. Patrick 3 (C. A.D. 444)].
latin:
Constans in Dei timore et fide immobilis,
    Super quem aedificatur ut Petrum ecclesia;
    Cuiusque apostolatum a Deo sortitus est,
    In cuius porte aduersum inferi non praeualent.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

This stanza is a theological bombshell. Sechnall is not just using poetic language; he is deliberately applying the specific promises Christ made to St. Peter in the Gospel of Matthew directly to St. Patrick.
1. The Direct Parallel to Peter (Matthew 16:18)

This is the central and most powerful claim.

    The Text: "Super quem aedificatur ut Petrus ecclesia" ("Upon whom the church is built, as upon Peter").

    The Biblical Source: This is a direct echo of Matthew 16:18, where Jesus says to Peter, "You are Peter (Petrus), and upon this rock (petram) I will build my church (ecclesiam meam)."

    The Audacious Claim: Sechnall is not merely saying Patrick is "rock-like." He is making a direct structural analogy: just as the universal Church is founded on the rock of Peter, the Irish Church is founded on the rock of Patrick. This is a foundational charter for the authority of the Patrician mission and, by extension, the See of Armagh, which Patrick founded. It establishes Patrick not just as a successful missionary, but as the divinely appointed foundation of Irish Christianity.

2. "Apostleship from God"

This line reinforces the claim from the first stanza and makes it even more explicit.

    The Text: "Cuiusque apostolatum a Deo sortitus est" ("And he has been allotted his apostleship from God").

    Divine, Not Human, Authority: This is a crucial defense against Patrick's critics. His authority, his "apostleship," does not come from any human committee, council, or bishop in Britain or Gaul who might have questioned his mission. It was given to him directly by God. The verb used, sortitus est, implies something allotted by divine will or destiny.

    Bypassing the Critics: By framing Patrick's authority as a direct divine commission, Sechnall effectively invalidates all earthly criticism of his mission. To question Patrick is to question God's own choice.

3. The Promise of Indefectibility

Sechnall completes the parallel with Peter by applying the final promise from Matthew 16:18 to Patrick.

    The Text: "Contra quem portae inferi non praevalebunt" ("Against whom the gates of hell will not prevail").

    Divine Protection: The promise that the forces of evil will not overcome the Church built on Peter is here transferred directly to Patrick and his work. This is a profound statement of confidence in the ultimate success and divine protection of the Irish Church.

    Who are the "Gates of Hell"? In the context of 5th-century Ireland, the "gates of hell" would have had a multi-layered meaning. It certainly referred to the forces of paganism that Patrick was battling. However, it could also be interpreted as a defiant statement against the human opponents of his mission. The hymn implies that those who stand against Patrick are siding with the forces that are doomed to fail.

In summary, this stanza is the theological and political heart of the hymn. It is a bold declaration of independence and divine right for the Church founded by Patrick. It establishes him as a new Peter for the Irish people, with a direct commission from God and a divine guarantee of victory over all his enemies, both spiritual and temporal.

fr:
Avec audace, il annonce le nom du Seigneur aux nations,
auxquelles il donne la grâce éternelle du bain de salut.
Pour leurs péchés, il prie Dieu chaque jour,
et pour elles, il immole des victimes dignes de Dieu.
en: ST. SECHNALL OF IRELAND [St. Patrick] proclaims boldly to the [Irish ] tribes the name of the Lord. to whom he gives the eternal grace of the washing of salvation: for their offenses he prays daily unto God; for them also he offers up to God worthy sacrifices [Hymn in Praise of St. Patrick 13 (c. A.D. 444)].
latin:
xiii. Nomen Domini audenter
    Annunciat gentibus,
    Quibus lavacri salutis
    Æternam dat gratiam,
    Pro quorum orat delictis
    Ad Deum quotidie,
    Pro quibus ut Deo dignas
    Immolatque hostias.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

This stanza is particularly significant because it outlines the classical threefold office (tria munera) of a bishop, defining Patrick's ministry in a way that would be understood throughout the universal Church.
1. The Threefold Office of a Bishop (Tria Munera)

This stanza is a perfect, concise summary of the duties of a Christian bishop:

    To Teach (Prophetic Office): Praedicatque Dei nomen gentibus ("And he proclaims the name of God to the tribes"). This is the bishop's primary missionary and teaching duty—to evangelize and instruct. The word gentibus ("to the peoples/tribes") is crucial, as it is the Latin equivalent of the Greek ethne from the Great Commission (Matthew 28:19), framing Patrick's work among the non-Roman Irish as a direct fulfillment of Christ's command.

    To Sanctify (Priestly Office): Quibus aeternam dat gratiam salutis ("To whom he gives the eternal grace of salvation") and Pro quibus hostias Deo dignas offeret ("For whom he offers up to God worthy sacrifices"). This describes the bishop's sacramental role.

        The "grace of salvation" (gratiam salutis), often called the "washing" in translation, directly refers to Baptism.

        The "worthy sacrifices/hosts" (hostias... dignas) is a clear reference to the Eucharist.

    To Govern (Pastoral/Kingly Office): Pro quorum orat delictis Deum quotidie ("For whose offenses he prays daily unto God"). This is the bishop's shepherding role. He is the intercessor for his flock, standing before God on their behalf, praying for the forgiveness of their sins. The adverb quotidie ("daily") emphasizes the constant, paternal care Patrick has for his people.

2. The Sacrificial Nature of the Eucharist

The fourth line is one of the most important pieces of evidence from the early Celtic Church regarding the Eucharist.

    The use of the word hostias (sacrificial victims, hosts) is unambiguous. It shows that, from the very beginning, the Church in Ireland understood the Mass not merely as a commemorative meal, but as a true sacrifice offered by the priest to God for the sins of the people.

    This aligns perfectly with the mainstream patristic and Catholic understanding of the Eucharist and stands as a powerful testament to the orthodoxy of Patrick's mission and the Church he founded.

3. Context of Defending Patrick's Ministry

Like the first stanza, this section serves as a defense of Patrick's legitimacy. By presenting him as the perfect embodiment of the episcopal office—preaching, baptizing, offering the holy sacrifice, and praying for his people—Sechnall is creating an icon of an ideal bishop. This implicitly answers any critics who questioned his qualifications. The message is clear: judge him not by his rustic education, but by his apostolic and priestly works, which are a perfect model of Christian leadership.

fr: Il chante les hymnes, l'Apocalypse et les psaumes de Dieu, qu'il expose pour édifier le peuple de Dieu, à qui il enseigne la loi qu'il professe au sein de la Trinité du saint Nom, et l'unique substance en trois personnes.
en: ST. SECHNALL OF IRELAND Hymns, with Revelation and the Psalms of God [Patrick] sings, and expounds them to edify God's people. This law he holds in the Trinity of the sacred name and teaches one being in three persons [ Hymn in Praise of St. Patrick 22 (C. A.D. 444)].
latin:
Ymnos cum apocalipsi
    salmosque cantat dei
    quosque ad aedificandum
    dei tractat populum
    quem legem in trinitate
    sacri credit nominis
    tribusque personis unam
    docetque substantiam
context:
Additional Relevant Details

This stanza is a compact and powerful statement, designed to establish St. Patrick's credentials as a thoroughly orthodox Catholic bishop, refuting any suggestion that he was an unlearned or heterodox missionary.
1. The Theological Significance of Patrick's Orthodoxy

This is the central point of the stanza. Sechnall is making two crucial claims about Patrick's teaching:

    Liturgical and Scriptural Foundation: Patrick's ministry is rooted in the core texts of Christian worship.

        Hymns and Psalms: These were the heart of the daily liturgical prayer of the Church (the Divine Office). This shows Patrick is not an independent evangelist but a man of the Church's established liturgical life.

        The Apocalypse (Revelation): Mentioning this specific book is significant. It was considered a text of deep mystery and profound theological importance, requiring great skill to interpret. By noting that Patrick not only sings from it but expounds upon it (explanat), Sechnall portrays him as a skilled doctor and teacher, not a simple preacher.

        To Edify God's People: His teaching has a clear purpose: to build up the Church (ad aedificandum populum), a direct echo of St. Paul's language for ministry.

    Precise Trinitarian Doctrine: The last two lines are the most important. They use the precise, technical language of 5th-century Catholic orthodoxy.

        unam substantiam in tribus personis docet ("he teaches one substance in three persons"). This is the cornerstone of the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity as defined by the Councils of Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381). It is the formula used by the Latin Fathers like St. Augustine to combat Arianism and other heresies.

        By stating this so clearly, Sechnall is declaring that the faith Patrick brought to Ireland was not some isolated, "Celtic" version of Christianity, but the one, orthodox, Catholic faith of the universal Church.

2. The Apologetic Context

As with the rest of the hymn, this stanza is a defense. Patrick's critics in Britain viewed him as uneducated and possibly unreliable. This stanza directly counters that perception.

    It proves he is not only literate but a master of Scripture.

    It proves he is not theologically naive but a teacher of the highest mysteries of the faith, using the correct and precise terminology.

    It solidifies his authority by showing that his teaching is in perfect harmony with that of Rome, Alexandria, and Constantinople.

In this one stanza, Sechnall portrays Patrick not merely as a successful missionary but as a pillar of orthodox faith, a learned teacher, and a true successor to the apostles, fully qualified to establish the Church in a new land.

fr: Que faut-il donc faire pour obtenir ces dons, sinon vivre saintement et justement, considérer les réalités de ce monde comme étrangères et ne pas les convoiter ? Car c’est en désirant les posséder que nous nous écartons de la voie de la justice.
en: SECOND CLEMENT By what course of conduct, then, shall we attain these things, but by leading holy and righteous life, and by deeming these worldly things as not belonging to us, and not fixing our desires upon them? For if we desire to possess them, we fall away from the path of righteousness [Second Clement 5 (c. AD. 80)].
greek: τί οὖν ἐστὶν ποιήσαντας ἐπιτυχεῖν αὐτῶν, εἰ μὴ τὸ ὁσίως καὶ δικαίως ἀναστρέφεσθαι καὶ τὰ κοσμικὰ ταῦτα ὡς ἀλλότρια ἡγεῖσθαι καὶ μὴ ἐπιθυμεῖν αὐτῶν; ἐν γὰρ τῷ ἐπιθυμεῖν ἡμᾶς κτήσασθαι ταῦτα ἀποπίπτομεν τῆς ὁδοῦ τῆς δικαίας.
context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. Author, Title, and Genre

    Title: The work is traditionally known as the Second Epistle of Clement (or 2 Clement).

    Author: It is anonymous. Despite the traditional title, modern scholarship is unanimous that it was not written by St. Clement of Rome (the author of 1 Clement). The style, theology, and historical context are all different.

    Genre: It is not actually an epistle (a letter). It is the earliest surviving Christian homily or sermon. The text refers to itself as being read aloud to a congregation after a reading from the Scriptures.

2. Date

    The date you listed, "c. A.D. 80," is too early and is more associated with the time of the authentic First Clement.

    The scholarly consensus places 2 Clement much later, likely in the mid-second century, around A.D. 140–160. This is based on its theological language and its use of texts that were becoming established as Scripture during that period.

3. Context of the Full Chapter

The quote you selected is the powerful ethical conclusion to the argument the author builds in Chapter 5.

    Verse 1: The author urges the listeners to "abandon our sojourn in this world" and do the will of God.

    Verses 2-4: He quotes a saying of Jesus (likely from an apocryphal gospel like the Gospel of the Egyptians or an oral tradition) about being "lambs in the midst of wolves" and not fearing those who can only kill the body.

    Verse 5: He states the core theme: our "sojourn of this flesh in this world is small and short-lived," but the "promise of Christ is great and wonderful," offering the rest of the eternal kingdom.

    Verses 6-7 (Your Quote): Based on this contrast between the temporary present and the promised future, the author asks the logical question: How do we get there? The answer is the ethical command for a holy life marked by detachment from worldly possessions.

4. Theological Significance

    Early Christian Asceticism: This passage is a classic example of early Christian asceticism and world-denial. The material world (τὰ κοσμικὰ) is seen as "foreign" or "alien" (ἀλλότρια) to the true identity of the Christian, who is a pilgrim on the way to the eternal kingdom.

    Ethical and Moral Focus: The homily places a very strong emphasis on righteous conduct (ὁσίως καὶ δικαίως ἀναστρέφεσθαι) as the necessary path to salvation. This moralistic tone is characteristic of much second-century Christian teaching.

    Sojourner Motif: The idea of the Christian as a temporary resident or "sojourner" (παροικίαν) on earth has deep roots in both the Old Testament (e.g., Abraham) and the New Testament (1 Peter 2:11) and became a central theme in early Christian identity.

fr:
Car en faisant la volonté du Christ, nous trouverons le repos ; mais sinon, rien ne nous délivrera du châtiment éternel, si nous désobéissons à ses commandements.
...

...si nous ne gardons pas notre baptême pur et sans tache, avec quelle assurance entrerons-nous dans le royaume de Dieu ? Ou qui sera notre défenseur, si l’on ne nous trouve pas porteurs d’œuvres saintes et justes ?
en: SECOND CLEMENT For if we do the will of Christ, we shall find rest; otherwise, if we disobey his commandments, nothing shall deliver us from eternal punishment. . . . [H]ow can we hope to enter into the royal residence of God unless we keep our baptism holy and undefiled? Or who shall be our advocate, unless we are possessed of works o1 holiness and righteousness? [Second Clement 6 (c. A.D. 80)].
greek:
ποιοῦντες γὰρ τὸ θέλημα τοῦ Χριστοῦ εὑρήσομεν ἀνάπαυσιν· εἰ δὲ μήγε, οὐδὲν ἡμᾶς ῥύσεται ἐκ τῆς αἰωνίου κολάσεως, ἐὰν παρακούσωμεν τῶν ἐντολῶν αὐτοῦ. ...

    ...ἡμεῖς, ἐὰν μὴ τηρήσωμεν τὸ βάπτισμα ἁγνὸν καὶ ἀμίαντον, ποίᾳ πεποιθήσει εἰσελευσόμεθα εἰς τὸ βασίλειον τοῦ θεοῦ; ἢ τίς ἡμῶν παράκλητος ἔσται, ἐὰν μὴ εὑρεθῶμεν ἔργα ἔχοντες ὅσια καὶ δίκαια;
context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. Nature of the Document ("Second Clement")

This text is incredibly important because it is not what its title suggests.

    It is not a letter: The form, style ("Brothers..."), and content identify it as the earliest surviving complete Christian sermon, or homily.

    It is not by St. Clement of Rome: Scholarly consensus is that it is an anonymous work. It was given the name "Second Clement" simply because it was found bound together with Clement's genuine first letter in ancient manuscripts.

2. Dating of the Document

While your source provided a date of c. A.D. 80, modern scholarship places it significantly later, likely in the mid-2nd century (c. 120–160 A.D.). The earlier date is unlikely because the author quotes from apocryphal gospels (like the Gospel of the Egyptians) and seems familiar with a range of canonical New Testament writings that were not yet widely circulated by A.D. 80.
3. Context of the Quote (The "Two Worlds")

The immediate context of your quote, found in the rest of Chapter 6 which you provided, is the classic early Christian theme of the Two Worlds or Two Ages. The preacher sets up a stark contrast:

    This Age: "says adultery and corruption and love of money and deceit" (6:4).

    The Age to Come: "bids farewell to these things" (6:4).

The quote you selected serves as the powerful conclusion to this section: because these two worlds are enemies, our choices have eternal consequences. Our actions determine which world we ultimately belong to.
4. Theological Significance of the Quote

This passage is a window into the intense moral and theological concerns of the 2nd-century Church.

    Post-Baptismal Purity: The line "unless we keep our baptism holy and undefiled" reflects the serious, rigorist view of post-baptismal sin common in the early Church. Baptism was seen as a complete washing, and the Christian life was a struggle to preserve that purity.

    Faith and Works: The sermon places immense emphasis on righteous actions ("do the will of Christ," "works of holiness and righteousness") as the necessary evidence of true faith and the prerequisite for salvation. There is no separation between belief and ethical behavior.

    The Advocate (παράκλητος): The use of the word parakletos (advocate, defender, comforter) is fascinating. While in John's Gospel it refers to the Holy Spirit, here it is used in a legal sense for the final judgment. The preacher's rhetorical question implies that if we lack holy works, no one—not even Christ or the Spirit—can stand up and defend us. Our righteous deeds themselves become our defense.

fr:
Et que personne parmi vous ne dise que cette chair n’est ni jugée, ni ne ressuscite.

Sachez-le : où donc avez-vous été sauvés, où donc avez-vous retrouvé la vue, sinon dans cette chair où vous vous trouviez ?

Nous devons donc garder notre chair comme un temple de Dieu.

Car de la même manière que vous avez été appelés dans la chair, c’est aussi dans la chair que vous viendrez.

En effet, si le Christ, le Seigneur qui nous a sauvés, qui était d’abord esprit, s’est fait chair et nous a ainsi appelés, de la même manière, nous aussi, c’est dans cette chair que nous recevrons la récompense.

Aimons-nous donc les uns les autres, afin de parvenir tous ensemble au royaume de Dieu.
en: SECOND CLEMENT And let no one of you say that this very flesh shall not be judged, nor rise again. Consider in what [state] you were saved, in what you received sight, if not while you were in this flesh. We must preserve the flesh as the temple of God. For as you were called in the flesh, so shall you [be judged] in the flesh. As Christ the Lord who saved US. though ne was first Spirit became flesh, and thus called us, so shall we also receive the reward in this flesh. Let us therefore love one another, that we may all attain to the kingdom of God [Second Clement 9 (c. A.D. 80)].
greek:
Καὶ μὴ λεγέτω τις ὑμῶν, ὅτι αὕτη ἡ σὰρξ οὐ κρίνεται οὐδὲ ἀνίσταται.

        γνῶτε· ἐν τίνι ἐσώθητε, ἐν τίνι ἀνεβλέψατε, εἰ μὴ ἐν τῇ σαρκὶ ταύτῃ ὄντες;

        δεῖ οὖν ἡμᾶς ὡς ναὸν θεοῦ φυλάσσειν τὴν σάρκα.

        ὃν τρόπον γὰρ ἐν τῇ σαρκὶ ἐκλήθητε, καὶ ἐν τῇ σαρκὶ ἐλεύσεσθε.

        εἰ Χριστός, ὁ κύριος ὁ σώσας ἡμᾶς, ὢν μὲν τὸ πρῶτον πνεῦμα, ἐγένετο σὰρξ καὶ οὕτως ἡμᾶς ἐκάλεσεν· οὕτως καὶ ἡμεῖς ἐν ταύτῃ τῇ σαρκὶ ἀποληψόμεθα τὸν μισθόν.

        ἀγαπῶμεν οὖν ἀλλήλους, ὅπως ἔλθωμεν πάντες εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Authorship and Date: Despite its name, this work is not by St. Clement of Rome (the author of 1 Clement). It is an anonymous work. The date you cited (c. A.D. 80) is too early; modern scholarship places it in the mid-2nd century (c. A.D. 140-160). This is very important, as it is not a work from the apostolic age, but from the sub-apostolic period.

    Genre: It is not actually a letter or epistle. It is the earliest surviving Christian homily or sermon. This explains its direct, exhortatory tone ("And let no one of you say..."). It was likely delivered to a congregation after a reading from Scripture.

    Theological Significance of the Passage: This section is profoundly important for several reasons:

        Anti-Gnostic Polemic: Its primary purpose is to combat teachings that viewed the physical body as evil or as a prison for the soul. The author insists that the same flesh we have now is the flesh that will be judged and resurrected.

        "Soma" (Body/Flesh) Christology: The phrase "Christ... though he was first Spirit became flesh" (ὢν μὲν τὸ πρῶτον πνεῦμα, ἐγένετο σὰρξ) is a very early and important Christological formula. It presents a "Spirit-Flesh" model of the incarnation, emphasizing the reality of Christ's human body against docetic claims that he only seemed to be human.

        The Flesh as Temple: The concept of preserving the flesh as a "temple of God" (echoing St. Paul in 1 Corinthians 6:19) is used here to ground Christian ethics. Our hope for future resurrection is directly tied to our moral conduct in the body today.

        Powerful Parallelism: The author builds a beautiful and logical argument based on parallelism:

            You received salvation and sight in this flesh.

            You were called in the flesh, so you will come [to be judged] in the flesh.

            Just as Christ was Spirit and became flesh to save us, so we will receive our reward in this flesh.

This structure makes the argument inescapable: the flesh is integral to every stage of salvation—from initial calling to final reward.

fr:
Il parle de ce jour du Jugement, où l'on verra ceux d'entre nous qui ont vécu dans l'impiété et bafoué les commandements de Jésus-Christ.

Quant aux justes, qui auront mené une vie droite, enduré les tourments et détesté les voluptés de l'âme, lorsqu'ils verront ceux qui se sont égarés et qui ont renié Jésus, en paroles ou en actes, être châtiés par de terribles tourments dans un feu qui ne s'éteint pas, ils rendront gloire à leur Dieu en disant : « Il y aura de l'espérance pour celui qui a servi Dieu de tout son cœur. »
en: It is of the great day of judgment he speaks, when they shall see those among us who were guilty of ungodliness and erred in their estimate of the commands of Jesus Christ. The righteous, having succeeded in enduring the trials and hating the indulgences of the soul, whenever they witness how those who have swerved and denied Jesus by words or deeds are punished with grievous torments in fire unquenchable, will give glory to their God and say, "There will be hope for him who has served God with his whole heart" [ibid., 17].
greek:
τὴν ἡμέραν ἐκείνην λέγει τῆς κρίσεως, ὅταν ὄψονται τοὺς ἐν ἡμῖν ἀσεβήσαντας καὶ παραλογισαμένους τὰς ἐντολὰς Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ.

    οἱ δὲ δίκαιοι εὐπραγήσαντες καὶ ὑπομείναντες τὰς βασάνους καὶ μισήσαντες τὰς ὑδυπαθείας τῆς ψυχῆς, ὅταν θεάσωνται τοὺς ἀστοχήσαντας καὶ ἀρνησαμένους διὰ τῶν λόγων ἢ διὰ τῶν ἔργων τὸν Ἰησοῦν, ὅπως κολάζονται δειναῖς βασάνοις πυρὶ ἀσβέστῳ, ἔσονται δόξαν διδόντες τῷ θεῷ αὐτῶν λέγοντες, ὅτι· Ἔσται ἐλπὶς τῷ δεδουλευκότι θεῷ ἐξ ὅλης καρδίας.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Author and Title: The work known as the Second Letter of Clement is not a letter, nor was it written by St. Clement of Rome (the author of 1 Clement). It is an anonymous work, which is why it is sometimes called "Pseudo-Clement."

    Genre and Date: It is the earliest surviving Christian sermon (or homily). It was likely written in the mid-2nd century, around A.D. 140–160, possibly in either Rome or Corinth.

    Theological Context of the Passage:

        Eschatology: The passage is a vivid depiction of the final judgment and the separation of the righteous from the unrighteous.

        Judgment Within the Church: A crucial point is the phrase τοὺς ἐν ἡμῖν ("those among us"). The author is not talking about pagans but about Christians who failed in their commitment. This reflects a major pastoral concern in the early Church: ensuring that baptism was followed by a life of genuine faith and good works.

        Perseverance: The righteous are defined by their endurance (ὑπομείναντες τὰς βασάνους - having endured the trials/torments) and their asceticism (μισήσαντες τὰς ὑδυπαθείας τῆς ψυχῆς - having hated the soul's pleasures).

        Vindication of the Faithful: The final line, "There will be hope for him who has served God with his whole heart," is the sermon's powerful conclusion. For the righteous who witness the judgment, it is not a moment of smug satisfaction but of profound vindication and relief. Their difficult life of service is proven to have been worthwhile, confirming that their hope in God was justified.

fr:
XIII.
Imposition des mains pour l'ordination des prêtres.

Nous étendons la main, Maître, Dieu des cieux, Père de ton Fils unique, sur cet homme, et nous te prions pour que l'Esprit de vérité vienne sur lui. Accorde-lui le discernement, la connaissance et un cœur bon. Qu'un esprit divin soit en lui, afin qu'il puisse administrer ton peuple, annoncer tes divines paroles et réconcilier ton peuple avec toi, le Dieu inengendré.

Toi qui, de l'esprit de Moïse, as accordé un esprit saint aux élus, donne aussi en partage à celui-ci un esprit saint provenant de l'Esprit de ton Fils unique, comme une grâce de sagesse, de connaissance et de foi droite, afin qu'il puisse te servir avec une conscience pure par ton Fils unique, Jésus Christ.

Par lui, à toi la gloire et la puissance dans l'Esprit Saint, maintenant et pour tous les siècles des siècles. Amen.
en: ST. SERAPION OF THMUIS Accept therewith our hallowing too, as we say, "Holy, holy, holy Lord Sabaoth, heaven and earth are full of your glory." Heaven is full, and full is the earth, with your magnificent glory, Lord of virtues. Full also is this sacrifice, with your strength and your communion; for to you we offer this living sacrifice, this unbloody oblation [Sacramentary of Serapion 13:3 (c. A.D. 350)].
greek:
ΧΙΙΙ.
Χειροθεσία καταστάσεως πρεσβυτέρων.

Τὴν χεῖρα ἐκτείνομεν δέσποτα θεὲ τῶν οὐρανῶν πάτερ τοῦ μονογενοῦς σου ἐπὶ τὸν ἄνθρωπον τοῦτον καὶ δεόμεθα, ἵνα τὸ πνεῦμα τῆς ἀληθείας ἐπιδημήσῃ αὐτῷ· φρόνησιν αὐτῷ χάρισαι καὶ γνῶσιν καὶ καρδίαν ἀγαθήν· γενέσθω ἐν αὐτῷ πνεῦμα θεῖον πρὸς τὸ δύνασθαι αὐτὸν οἰκονομῆσαι τὸν λαόν σου καὶ πρεσβεύειν τὰ θεῖα σου λόγια καὶ καταλλάξαι τὸν λαόν σου σοὶ τῷ ἀγεννήτῳ θεῷ, ὁ χαρισάμενος ἀπὸ τοῦ πνεύματος τοῦ μωσέως ἐπὶ τοὺς ἐκλελεγμένους πνεῦμα ἅγιον· μέρισον καὶ τῷδε πνεῦμα ἅγιον ἐκ τοῦ πνεύματος τοῦ μονογενοῦς εἰς χάριν σοφίας καὶ γνώσεως καὶ πίστεως ὀρθῆς, ἵνα δυνηθῇ σοὶ ὑπηρετῆσαι ἐν καθαρᾷ συνειδήσει διὰ τοῦ μονογενοῦς σου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, δι' οὗ σοὶ ἡ δόξα καὶ τὸ κράτος ἐν ἁγίῳ πνεύματι καὶ νῦν καὶ εἰς τοὺς σύμπαντας αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων ἀμήν.
context:
Analysis: Ordination Prayer vs. Eucharistic Prayer

This is a beautiful and theologically rich prayer that reveals the ancient understanding of the priesthood.

    Its Purpose: To invoke the Holy Spirit upon a man being ordained, equipping him for ministry.

    The Key Actions of a Priest: The prayer defines a priest's role as:

        Governing/Stewarding (οἰκονομῆσαι) the people of God.

        Being an Ambassador (πρεσβεύειν) for the Word of God.

        Reconciling (καταλλάξαι) the people to God.

    Typology: It draws a powerful connection to the Old Testament, referencing how God took the spirit that was on Moses and shared it with the seventy elders (Numbers 11:17, 25).

In summary, while the Eucharistic prayer focuses on the consecration of the bread and wine into the Body and Blood of Christ, this Ordination prayer focuses on the consecration of a man for the service of God's people. Both are central to the sacramental life of the Church, and you have successfully located another key part of this ancient and precious prayer book.

fr:
Prière sur le chrême avec lequel sont oints les baptisés.

Dieu des puissances, secours de toute âme qui se tourne vers toi et se place sous la main puissante de ton Fils unique, nous t’invoquons pour que, par la puissance divine et invisible de notre Seigneur et Sauveur Jésus Christ, tu déploies dans ce chrême une force agissante, divine et céleste.

Ainsi, ceux qui ont été baptisés et qui sont oints de ce chrême, recevant l’empreinte du signe de la croix salvatrice du Fils unique, et étant régénérés et renouvelés par le bain de la renaissance, pourront participer au don de l’Esprit Saint. Affermis par ce sceau, qu’ils demeurent solides et inébranlables, sans dommage et inviolables, à l’abri de toute influence et de tout complot, menant leur vie dans la foi et la pleine connaissance de la vérité jusqu’à la fin, dans l’attente des espérances célestes de la vie et des promesses éternelles de notre Seigneur et Sauveur Jésus Christ. Par lui, à toi la gloire et la puissance dans l’Esprit Saint, maintenant et pour tous les siècles des siècles. Amen.
en: ST. SERAPION OF THMUIS [Prayer for blessing the holy chrism:] "God of powers, aid of every soul that turns to you and comes under your powerful hand in your only-begotten. We beseech you, that through your divine and invisible power of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, you may effect in this chrism a divine and heavenly operation, so that those baptized and anointed in the tracing with it of the sign of the saving cross of the only-begotten as if reborn and renewed through the bath of regeneration, may be made participants in the gift of the Holy Spirit and, confirmed by this seal, may remain firm and immovable, unharmed and inviolate" [Sacramentary of Serapion 25:1 (c. A.D. 350)].
greek:
Εὐχὴ εἰς τὸ χρῖσμα ἐν ᾧ χρίονται οἱ βαπτισθέντες.

Ὁ θεὸς τῶν δυνάμεων ὁ βοηθὸς πάσης ψυχῆς ἐπιστρεφούσης ἐπὶ σὲ καὶ γινομένης ὑπὸ τὴν κραταιάν σου χεῖρα τοῦ μονογενοῦς ἐπικαλούμεθά σε, ὥστε διὰ τῆς θείας καὶ ἀοράτου σου δυνάμεως τοῦ κυρίου καὶ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ ἐνεργῆσαι ἐν τῷ χρίσματι τούτῳ ἐνέργειαν θείαν καὶ οὐράνιον,

ἵνα οἱ βαπτισθέντες καὶ χριόμενοι ἐν αὐτῷ τὸ ἐκτύπωμα τοῦ σημείου τοῦ σωτηριώδους σταυροῦ τοῦ μονογενοῦς, ὡς ἀναγεννηθέντες καὶ ἀνανεωθέντες διὰ τοῦ λουτροῦ τῆς παλιγγενεσίας καὶ οὗτοι μέτοχοι γένωνται τῆς δωρεᾶς τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος καὶ ἀσφαλισθέντες τῇ σφραγῖδι ταύτῃ διαμείνωσιν ἑδραῖοι καὶ ἀμετακίνητοι, ἀβλαβεῖς καὶ ἀσύλοι, ἀνεπηρέαστοι καὶ ἀνεπιβούλευτοι ἐμπολιτευόμενοι ἐν τῇ πίστει καὶ ἐπιγνώσει τῆς ἀληθείας μέχρι τέλους ἀναμένοντες τὰς οὐρανίους τῆς ζωῆς ἐλπίδας καὶ αἰωνίους ἐπαγγελίας τοῦ κυρίου καὶ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ, δι' οὗ σοὶ ἡ δόξα καὶ τὸ κράτος ἐν ἁγίῳ πνεύματι καὶ νῦν καὶ εἰς τοὺς σύμπαντας αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων, ἀμήν.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Author and Source: This prayer is from St. Serapion of Thmuis (a city in the Nile Delta). He was a contemporary, friend, and staunch supporter of St. Athanasius the Great during the Arian crisis of the 4th century. The prayer comes from his Euchologion (a Greek term for a prayer book, later known in the West as a Sacramentary), which is one of the earliest surviving liturgical books.

    Liturgical Context: This is a prayer of consecration for the holy chrism (anointing oil). It would have been prayed by the bishop to bless the oil that would be used for the post-baptismal anointing of the newly initiated. This anointing is the ancient liturgical root of the Sacrament of Confirmation.

    Theological Significance (Epiclesis): The prayer is a powerful epiclesis, a formal calling-down of divine power upon something. Serapion asks God the Father to send His power to "effect in this chrism a divine and heavenly operation." This transforms the oil from a simple element into a vehicle of grace.

    Effects of the Anointing (Sacramental Theology): The prayer is a rich source for understanding the 4th-century theology of this sacrament:

        Linked to Baptism: It is for those "reborn and renewed through the bath of regeneration," explicitly connecting the anointing to the grace of baptism.

        Gift of the Holy Spirit: The anointing makes the recipient a "participant in the gift of the Holy Spirit" (μέτοχοι ... τῆς δωρεᾶς τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος).

        The Seal (Sphragis): The anointing is described as a seal (σφραγίς). This is a profoundly biblical and ancient term for the indelible mark of the Holy Spirit that confirms and protects the believer.

        Grace of Perseverance: The effect of this seal is strength and protection: to remain "firm and immovable, unharmed and inviolate," persevering in faith until the end.

    Anti-Arian Language: The repeated emphasis on the "Only-Begotten" (μονογενής) is characteristic of the Nicene orthodoxy of Serapion and Athanasius, strongly affirming the unique divine Sonship of Christ against the Arian heresy which claimed the Son was a creature.

fr: Assurément, nous ne pouvons le nier : c'est à bon droit que l'on a blâmé la thèse des « fils de Marie », et c'est avec raison que votre sainteté s'est indignée à l'idée qu'un autre enfantement soit issu du même sein virginal d'où le Christ est né selon la chair. Car le Seigneur Jésus n'aurait pas choisi de naître d'une vierge s'il avait estimé qu'elle serait à ce point incontinente qu'elle en vienne à souiller par la semence d'une union humaine ce sanctuaire où fut formé le corps du Seigneur, ce palais du Roi éternel.
en: POPE ST. SIRICIUS I Surely, we cannot deny that regarding the sons of Mary the statement is justly censured, and your holiness rightly abhors it, that from the same virginal womb from which Christ was born. another offspring was brought forth. For neither would the Lord Jesus have chosen to be born of a Virgin if he had judged she would be so incontinent, that with the seed of human copulation she would pollute the generative chamber of the Lord's body, the palace of the eternal king [Letter to Bishop Anysius (A.D. 392)].
latin: Sane non possumus negare de Mariae filiis jure reprehensum, meritoque vestram sanctitatem abhorruisse, quod ex eodem utero virginali, ex quo secundum carnem Christus natus est, alius partus effusus sit. Neque enim elegisset Dominus Jesus nasci per virginem, si eam judicasset tam incontinentem fore, ut illud genitale Dominici corporis, illam aulam Regis aeterni, concubitus humani semine coinquinaret.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

This passage is a crucial early defense of the doctrine of the Perpetual Virginity of Mary from the highest authority in the Western Church.

    Historical Context: The letter is a direct response to the teachings of Bonosus, the Bishop of Sardica (modern-day Sofia, Bulgaria). Bonosus was teaching that Mary had other children with Joseph after the birth of Jesus, a view that challenged her perpetual virginity. This heresy was causing a disturbance in the region of Illyricum (the Balkans), for which Anysius of Thessalonica was the acting papal vicar.

    Theological Argument: Pope Siricius's argument is one of fittingness or propriety. He argues that it is theologically unfitting and inconceivable that the womb sanctified by the Incarnation—the sacred space where the body of Christ was formed—would subsequently be used for ordinary human generation.

    Powerful Imagery: The Pope uses exceptionally strong and majestic language to describe Mary's womb, calling it the "generative chamber of the Lord's body" (genitale Dominici corporis) and, most famously, "the palace/hall of the eternal King" (aulam Regis aeterni). This elevates the discussion from biology to theology, framing Mary's womb as a consecrated and inviolable sanctuary.

    Link to Anti-Christian Polemics: In the sentences immediately following your quote, Siricius argues that this heresy plays directly into the hands of Jewish anti-Christian arguments. He states that denying Mary's perpetual virginity strengthens the polemical claim that Jesus could not have been born of a virgin in the first place, as it attempts to normalize Mary's life and undermine the uniqueness of the Incarnation.

    Canonical Procedure: The letter itself shows the established Church structure of the late 4th century. The bishops of Illyricum, faced with a theological problem, write to the Pope for a definitive judgment (nostram sententiam sciscitari voluistis). The Pope responds with an authoritative teaching, referencing prior councils (the Council of Capua) and affirming the authority of his local representatives.

fr: Grégoire de Nazianze était à la tête de ceux qui professaient la Trinité consubstantielle ; il célébrait les offices dans une petite maison, aménagée en lieu de prière par ses coreligionnaires. Par la suite, cette église est devenue et demeure l’une des plus illustres de la ville, non seulement par la beauté et la grandeur de ses édifices, mais aussi par les bienfaits de manifestations divines éclatantes. En effet, une puissance divine se manifestant en ce lieu a souvent porté secours, pendant la veille comme en rêve, à de nombreuses personnes accablées par la maladie ou les revers de fortune. Or, on croit que cette puissance est la mère du Christ, Marie, la sainte Vierge, car c'est bien ainsi qu'elle se manifeste.
en: SOZOMEN OF CONSTANTINOPLE Gregory of Nazianzen presided over those who maintain the "consubstantiality" of the Holy Trinity, and assembled them together in a little dwelling, which had been altered into a house of prayer by those who held the same opinions and had a like form of worship. It subsequently became one of the most conspicuous in the city, and is so now, not only for the beauty and number of its structures, but also for the advantages accruing to it from the visible manifestations of God. For the power of God was manifested there, and was helpful both in waking visions and in dreams, often for the relief of many diseases and for those afflicted by some sudden change in their affairs. The power was accredited to Mary, the Mother of God, the holy Virgin, for she does manifest herself in this way [Church History 7:5 (c. A.D. 444)].
greek: Γρηγόριος δὲ ὁ ἐκ Ναζιανζοῦ προΐστατο τῶν ὁμοούσιον τριάδα δοξαζόντων, ἐκκλησίαζε δὲ ἐν οἰκίσκῳ μικρῷ παρ' ὁμοδόξων αὐτῷ τε καὶ τοῖς ὁμοίως θρησκεύουσιν εἰς εὐκτήριον οἶκον κατασκευασθέντι. μετὰ δὲ ταῦτα περιφανὴς τῶν ἐν τῇ πόλει νεὼς γέγονεν οὗτος καὶ ἔστιν, οὐ μόνον οἰκοδομημάτων κάλλει τε καὶ μεγέθει, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐναργῶν θεοφανειῶν ὠφελείαις. προφαινομένη γὰρ ἐνθάδε θεία δύναμις ὕπαρ τε καὶ ἐν ὀνείρασι πολλοῖς πολλάκις νόσοις τε καὶ περιπετείαις πραγμάτων κάμνουσιν ἐπήμυνε· πιστεύεται δὲ ταύτην τὴν Χριστοῦ μητέρα Μαρίαν τὴν ἁγίαν παρθένον εἶναι· τοιαύτη γὰρ ἐπιφαίνεται.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

Your passage is historically and theologically significant for several reasons, many of which are explained in the rest of the text you provided (sections 7.5.3-4).

1. The Name of the Church: The Anastasia

Immediately following the quote, Sozomen explains that this little church was famously named the Anastasia (Ἀναστασία), which means "Resurrection." He gives two reasons for the name:

    Theological Reason: This was the place where the Nicene Creed (belief in the homoousion, or "consubstantiality"), which had been effectively "dead" in the Arian-dominated capital of Constantinople, was resurrected by the powerful preaching of St. Gregory.

    Miraculous Reason: Sozomen also recounts a story he heard, in which a pregnant woman fell from an upper gallery during a service and died. After the congregation prayed over her, she was miraculously restored to life (anestē), and the child was also saved.

2. The Preaching of St. Gregory the Theologian

The sermons that St. Gregory of Nazianzen delivered in this tiny, makeshift chapel are among the most important theological works in Church history. They are known as the Five Theological Orations, and they articulated the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity with such profound clarity that they earned him the title "The Theologian."

3. Major Significance for Marian Devotion

This passage is a landmark in the history of Christian piety. It is one of the earliest, clearest, and most explicit accounts from a mainstream historian of:

    Active Marian Intercession: The belief that the Virgin Mary actively appears and intervenes in the lives of the faithful to heal and assist them.

    A Specific Marian Shrine: A particular church being known as a place where one could experience the help of the Virgin Mary.

    Pre-Ephesian Devotion: This account was written before the Council of Ephesus (431), where Mary was formally declared the Theotokos (Mother of God). It shows that powerful devotion and a belief in her intercession were already well-established in the capital city decades earlier.

fr: Notre Dieu n'a pas son origine dans le temps : seul sans commencement, il est lui-même le principe de toutes choses. Dieu est esprit, non un souffle qui pénètre la matière, mais le créateur des esprits matériels et des formes qu'elle contient. Invisible et intangible, il est lui-même le Père de tout ce qui est sensible et visible.
en: TATIAN THE SYRIAN Our God did not begin to be in time: He alone IS without beginning, and he himself is the beginning of all things. God is a Spirit [Jn 4:24], not pervading matter, but the maker of material spirits, and of the forms that are in matter; he iS invisible, impalpable, being himself the Father of visible and invisible things [ Address to the Greeks 4 (c. A.D. 170)].
greek: θεὸς ὁ καθ' ἡμᾶς οὐκ ἔχει σύστασιν ἐν χρόνῳ, μόνος ἄναρχος ὢν καὶ αὐτὸς ὑπάρχων τῶν ὅλων ἀρχή. πνεῦμα ὁ θεός, οὐ διήκων διὰ τῆς ὕλης, πνευμάτων δὲ ὑλικῶν καὶ τῶν ἐν αὐτῇ σχημάτων κατασκευαστής, ἀόρατός τε καὶ ἀναφής, αἰσθητῶν καὶ ὁρατῶν αὐτὸς γεγονὼς πατήρ.
context:
Additional Relevant Details
About the Author and Work

    Tatian the Syrian (c. 120–180 AD): Tatian was a 2nd-century Christian apologist and a student of the great St. Justin Martyr in Rome. His Address to the Greeks is a fierce and sometimes abrasive defense of Christianity, which he presents as a superior "barbarian philosophy." Later in his life, he broke from the orthodox community and founded an ascetic sect known as the Encratites, who were condemned as heretical. However, this work was written during his orthodox period and is a valuable witness to early Christian thought.

Theological Significance of the Quote

This short passage is packed with profound theological statements that contrast Christian doctrine with Greco-Roman paganism and philosophy.

    God's Timelessness and Aseity:

        οὐκ ἔχει σύστασιν ἐν χρόνῳ ("does not have a beginning/constitution in time").

        μόνος ἄναρχος ὢν ("He alone IS without beginning").

        This is a direct attack on pagan mythology, where gods like Zeus and the Olympians had complex birth stories and genealogies. Tatian asserts the Judeo-Christian doctrine of a God who is eternal, uncaused, and stands outside of time. He is the ἀρχή (beginning/principle) of all things, but is Himself ἄναρχος (without beginning).

    God is Spirit (A Critique of Materialism and Stoicism):

        πνεῦμα ὁ θεός ("God is Spirit") is a direct quotation from John 4:24.

        The next phrase, οὐ διήκων διὰ τῆς ὕλης ("not pervading matter"), is crucial. This is a direct polemic against the Stoic philosophical concept of God. The Stoics viewed God (the Logos or pneuma) as a fine, fiery, rational substance that permeated and animated the entire material universe, like a soul in a body.

        Tatian rejects this pantheistic view entirely. For him, God is a transcendent spirit, completely distinct from the matter He creates. He is the maker (κατασκευαστής) of matter and spirits, not a part of them.

    God's Incorporeality and Transcendence:

        ἀόρατός τε καὶ ἀναφής ("invisible and impalpable/untouchable").

        This reinforces the distinction between the Creator and creation. Unlike pagan idols which could be seen and touched, or philosophical principles that were tied to matter, the true God is utterly transcendent and beyond the grasp of the physical senses.

    God as Universal Father/Creator:

        αἰσθητῶν καὶ ὁρατῶν αὐτὸς γεγονὼς πατήρ ("being himself the Father of perceptible/sensible and visible things").

        This phrase is an early echo of the language that would later be formalized in the Nicene Creed ("maker of all things, visible and invisible"). It establishes God's absolute sovereignty as the creator of the entire cosmos, both the material world we can see and the spiritual world we cannot.

fr: Et c'est pourquoi nous croyons qu'il y aura aussi une résurrection des corps, après l'achèvement de toutes choses...
en: TATIAN THE SYRIAN We believe that therel will be a resurrection of bodies after the consummation of all things [Address to the Greeks 6 (C. A.D. 170)].
greek: Καὶ διὰ τοῦτο καὶ σωμάτων ἀνάστασιν ἔσεσθαι πεπιστεύκαμεν μετὰ τὴν τῶν ὅλων συντέλειαν...
context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. Context: Arguing Against Stoic Philosophy

Immediately after this declaration, Tatian contrasts the Christian doctrine of resurrection with the well-known Stoic doctrine of cyclical recurrence.

    Stoic Belief: The Stoics believed that the universe went through endless cycles (palingenesis). The world would be destroyed by fire (ekpyrosis) and then perfectly recreated, with every person and event repeating exactly as before. For Tatian, this was a pointless, deterministic cycle with no ultimate purpose.

    Christian Contrast: Tatian emphasizes that the Christian resurrection is a one-time, final event (ἅπαξ δὲ τῶν καθ' ἡμᾶς αἰώνων πεπερασμένων - "once our age has been completed"). It is not part of an endless cycle. Its purpose is definitive: for the sake of Judgment (χάριν κρίσεως). The judge is not a mythological figure like Minos or Rhadamanthus, but God the Creator Himself.

2. Philosophical Defense of the Resurrection

Tatian anticipates the pagan listener's skepticism and provides a philosophical defense of the resurrection, making two key points:

    The Analogy from Creation: He argues: "Just as I did not exist before I was born... and yet came into being, in the same way, I who was born and then ceased to be through death... will exist again." His logic is that if God can create a person from non-existence once, He can certainly re-create them a second time.

    The Power of God Over Matter: He addresses the common objection about the destruction and scattering of the body. He says that whether his body is destroyed by fire, dissolved in a river, or torn apart by wild beasts, the constituent matter is not lost. It remains preserved in the "storehouses of a rich master" (ταμείοις ἐναπόκειμαι πλουσίου δεσπότου). God, the King, knows where every particle is and can, when He wills, restore the visible substance to its original form.

3. Author and Work

    Tatian the Syrian (2nd Century): Tatian was an Assyrian Christian apologist and a pupil of the famous St. Justin Martyr in Rome.

    Address to the Greeks: This work is a fierce and often sarcastic critique of Greek culture, religion, and philosophy, which Tatian contrasts with the antiquity and rationality of Christianity.

    Historical Significance: While Tatian later fell into heresy (founding the Encratites, who practiced extreme asceticism), this earlier work is considered a valuable witness to the core Christian beliefs of the mid-to-late 2nd century. This passage is one of the clearest an

fr: ...afin que le méchant soit puni à juste titre pour s'être rendu lui-même pervers, et que le juste soit dignement loué pour ses actions vertueuses, pour n'avoir pas, par son libre arbitre, transgressé la volonté de Dieu.
en: TATIAN THE SYRIAN The bad man may be justly punished, having become depraved through his own fault, but the just man may be deservedly praised for his virtuous deeds. since in the exercise of his free choice he refrained from transgressing the will of God [Address to the Greeks' (c. A.D. 170)].
greek: ...ὅπως ὁ μὲν φαῦλος δικαίως κολάζηται δι' αὑτὸν γεγονὼς μοχθηρός, ὁ δὲ δίκαιος χάριν τῶν ἀνδραγαθημάτων ἀξίως ἐπαινῆται κατὰ τὸ αὐτεξούσιον τοῦ θεοῦ μὴ παραβὰς τὸ βούλημα.
context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. Immediate Context: Creation and Free Will

The quote is the climax of Tatian's explanation of God's creation of angels and humans. In the sentences immediately preceding your quote, he states:

    "The Logos, before the creation of men, becomes the Creator of angels. And each of the two orders of created beings was made with free will (αὐτεξούσιον), not having the nature of good in itself... but with this nature being perfected in them by their freedom of choice."

Your quote, therefore, serves as the logical conclusion: because humans and angels were created with free will, they are justly held responsible for how they use that freedom.
2. Theological Significance: A Classic Free-Will Theodicy

This passage is a powerful and early example of a Christian theodicy—an explanation for why a good God permits the existence of evil.

    Against Fatalism: Tatian is writing to a Greek audience steeped in concepts of fate (εἱμαρμένη). He directly contrasts the Christian view of self-determination (αὐτεξούσιον) with Greek fatalism. For Tatian, human actions are not predetermined; they are the result of free choice.

    The Origin of Evil: The quote firmly places the origin of evil not in God, but in the creature's misuse of its freedom. The "bad man" becomes depraved "through his own fault" (δι' αὑτὸν γεγονὼς μοχθηρός). This absolves God of being the author of evil and is a cornerstone of orthodox Christian thought.

    Basis for Just Judgment: Because humans are free, God's judgment is just. It is not arbitrary. Punishment is deserved because the choice to do evil was freely made. Likewise, praise (and reward) for virtue is deserved because the just man chose not to transgress God's will.

fr: Les hommes deviennent pour eux le prétexte de leur apostasie. Car en leur présentant un schéma de la position des astres, à la manière de joueurs de dés, ils ont introduit la fatalité, une doctrine d’une injustice extrême. De fait, celui qui juge comme celui qui est jugé sont l’un et l’autre le produit de la fatalité...
en: TATIAN THE SYRIAN But men form the material of their apostasy. For, having shown them a plan of the position of the stars, like dice players, they introduced fate, a flagrant injustice. For the judge and the judged are made so by fate [Address to the Greeks 8 (c. A.D. 170)].
greek: Ὑπόθεσις δὲ αὐτοῖς τῆς ἀποστασίας οἱ ἄνθρωποι γίνονται. διάγραμμα γὰρ αὐτοῖς ἀστροθεσίας ἀναδείξαντες ὥσπερ οἱ τοῖς κύβοις παίζοντες, τὴν εἱμαρμένην εἰσηγήσαντο λίαν ἄδικον. ὅ τε γὰρ κρίνων καὶ ὁ κρινόμενος καθ' εἱμαρμένην εἰσὶν γεγονότες...
context:
Additional Context and Analysis

The text you provided is a brilliant example of early Christian apologetics. Tatian's goal is to dismantle the philosophical and religious worldview of the Greeks. The quote you selected is the opening salvo in his attack on astrological fatalism.

1. Who are "They"? The Architects of Apostasy:
In the preceding chapters, Tatian has been discussing the fallen angels, or demons (daimones). He argues that these beings, after their own fall, sought to lead humanity astray. So when he says "they introduced fate," he is referring specifically to these demons. For Tatian, astrology and the concept of inescapable fate (heimarmenē) are not neutral philosophical ideas; they are a demonic invention designed to enslave humanity.

2. The Argument Against Fate: The Destruction of Morality:
Tatian’s core objection is that fate is a "flagrant injustice" because it eradicates moral responsibility.

    If a person's actions are predetermined by the stars, then there can be no true justice.

    The "judge" is not acting from reason, and the "judged" is not responsible for their crime. Both are merely puppets of destiny.

    This removes any basis for praise, blame, sin, or virtue, which is precisely the demons' goal.

3. The Analogy of the Dice Players:
This is a powerful and dismissive image. Tatian compares the demons to crooked gamblers.

    They lay out the stars like a game board or a "diagram" (διάγραμμα).

    They introduce "fate" as the arbitrary rules of the game.

    Humans are treated like dice (κύβοι), tossed about with no will of their own, all for the cruel amusement of these demonic spectators. This idea is reinforced later in the chapter when he says the demons watch human tragedy as if it were entertainment in a theater (ὥσπερ ἐν θεάτρῳ τερπωλὴν παρέσχε τούτοις).

4. The Broader Attack in Chapter 8:
After refuting the philosophical concept of fate, Tatian spends the rest of the chapter (as seen in your full text) launching a scathing, sarcastic attack on the pagan gods themselves. He points out their internal contradictions and immoral behavior to show that they are not worthy of worship:

    Contradictory Laws: Rhea demands castration, while Aphrodite delights in marriage.

    Immoral Actions: Athena and Asclepius divide the blood of Medusa, one using it to kill and the other to heal. Hephaestus attempts to rape Athena. Zeus commits incest with his daughter, Persephone.

    Weakness and Subjection: He even argues that the gods themselves, including Zeus, are subject to the same passions and fate as humans, proving they are not divine.

In summary, your chosen quote is the philosophical foundation for Tatian's entire argument in this chapter. He first dismantles the intellectual framework of pagan determinism and then proceeds to mock the absurd and immoral stories of the gods who supposedly operate within that framework.

fr:
Tels sont les démons : ce sont eux qui ont institué le destin. Leur système reposait sur la représentation des animaux. En effet, les reptiles qui rampent sur la terre, les créatures qui nagent dans les eaux et les quadrupèdes des montagnes – animaux avec lesquels ils vivaient, eux qui avaient été chassés de la vie céleste –, ce sont eux qu'ils ont jugés dignes d'un honneur céleste. Leur but était double : qu'on les croie eux-mêmes habitant le ciel, et que, par la disposition des astres, leur conduite insensée sur terre paraisse sensée.

Ainsi, que l'on soit colérique ou travailleur, maître de soi ou sans retenue, pauvre ou riche, tout cela vient de ceux qui ont édicté les lois de la naissance. Car la représentation du cercle du zodiaque est l'œuvre des dieux. Et la lumière de l'un d'eux, lorsqu'elle l'emporte — à ce qu'ils disent —, fausse le jugement des autres, et celui qui est vaincu maintenant a coutume de l'emporter à son tour. Quant aux sept planètes, elles se prêtent à leur jeu, comme des joueurs s'amusant avec des pions.

Quant à nous, nous sommes au-dessus du destin et, au lieu des démons errants, nous avons appris à connaître l'unique Maître qui, lui, n'erre pas.
en: Such are the demons; these are they who laid down the doctrine of fate. Their fundamental principle was the placing of animals in the heavens. For the creeping things on the earth, and those that swim in the waters, and the quadrupeds on the mountains, with which they lived when expelled from heaven-these they dignified with celestial honor, so that they might themselves be thought to remain in heaven, and, by placing the constellations there, might make the irrational course of life on earth appear rational. Thus the high-spirited and he who is crushed with toil, the temperate and the intemperate, the indigent and the wealthy, are what they are simply because of the controllers of their nativity. For the delineation of the zodiacal circle is the work of gods. And, when the light of one of them predominates. as they express it, it deprives all the rest of their honor; and he who now is conquered at another time gains the predominance. And the seven planets are well pleased with them, as if they were amusing themselves with dice. But we are superior to fate, and instead of wandering demons, we have learned to know one Lord who wanders not [ibid., 9].
greek: Τοιοῦτοί τινές εἰσιν οἱ δαίμονες· οὗτοι οἳ τὴν εἱμαρμένην ὥρισαν. στοιχείωσις δὲ αὐτοῖς ἡ ζώωσις ἦν. τὰ γὰρ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς ἑρπετὰ καὶ τὰ ἐν τοῖς ὕδασι νηκτὰ καὶ τὰ ἐπὶ τοῖς ὄρεσι τετράποδα, μεθ' ὧν ἐποιοῦντο τὴν δίαιταν ἔκβλητοι τῆς ἐν οὐρανῷ διαίτης γεγενημένοι, ταῦτα τῆς ἐπουρανίου τιμῆς ἠξίωσαν, ἵνα τε νομισθῶσιν αὐτοὶ διατρίβν ἐν οὐρανῷ καὶ τὴν ἄλογον ἐπὶ γῆς πολιτείαν εὔλογον διὰ τῆς ἀστροθεσίας ἀποδείξωσιν. ὥστε ὁ θυμικὸς καὶ ὁ ἐπίμοχθος καὶ ὁ ἐγκρατευόμενος καὶ ὁ ἀκρατὴς καὶ ὁ πτωχεύων καὶ ὁ πλουτῶν ἐστι τῶν νομοθετησάντων τὴν γένεσιν. ἡ γὰρ τοῦ ζωδιακοῦ κύκλου γραφὴ θεῶν ἐστι ποίημα. καὶ τὸ ἐπικρατῆσαν, ὥς φασιν, ἑνὸς αὐτῶν φῶς τοὺς πλείονας παραβραβεύει, καὶ ὁ νικώμενος νῦν εἰσαῦθις ἐπικρατεῖν εἴωθεν· εὐαρεστοῦσι δὲ αὐτοῖς οἱ ἑπτὰ πλανῆται ὥσπερ οἱ ἐν τοῖς πεσσοῖς ἀθύροντες. ἡμεῖς δὲ καὶ εἱμαρμένης ἐσμὲν ἀνώτεροι καὶ ἀντὶ πλανητῶν δαιμόνων ἕνα τὸν ἀπλανῆ δεσπότην μεμαθήκαμεν.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Author and Context: Tatian (c. 120–180 AD) was an Assyrian Christian apologist and a student of St. Justin Martyr in Rome. His Address to the Greeks is a scathing, satirical, and often angry critique of Greek culture, philosophy, and religion, written to demonstrate the superiority of Christianity, which he calls "our philosophy."

    The Attack on Fate (Heimarmenē): Belief in fate and determination by the stars was pervasive in the Greco-Roman world, especially in popular Stoicism and various mystery religions. Tatian’s claim that "we are superior to fate" was a radical and liberating declaration. It positioned Christianity as a path to true freedom from a deterministic, impersonal cosmos, offering instead a relationship with a personal, sovereign Lord.

    Demonology and Astrology: Tatian presents a clear theory: demons are fallen spiritual beings who, after being cast out of heaven, sought to deceive humanity. They invented astrology by placing the images of the earthly animals they once associated with into the sky as constellations (the Zodiac). This was a trick to make humans believe their lives were governed by these celestial powers (i.e., the demons themselves) rather than by their own free will and the providence of the one true God.

    The Brilliant Wordplay on "Planets": The final sentence contains a masterful pun that is central to the passage's power.

        The Greek word for "planets" is πλανῆται (planētai), which literally means "wanderers," because they appear to wander across the sky relative to the fixed stars.

        Tatian contrasts these "wandering demons" (πλανητῶν δαιμόνων) with the "one Lord who wanders not" (ἕνα τὸν ἀπλανῆ δεσπότην). The word ἀπλανῆ (aplanē) means "not wandering," fixed, steady, and unerring.

        He is therefore contrasting the deceptive, erratic, wandering demons with the one true, stable, and unerring Lord of the universe. This is a powerful rhetorical conclusion.

    Satire in the Rest of the Chapter: The rest of the Greek text you provided (9.2-9.4) continues this mocking tone by listing the ridiculous mythological origins of other constellations (e.g., Erigone's dog, the scorpion that helped Artemis, the Centaur Chiron, etc.), essentially asking, "Was the sky empty before these silly events happened?" This satirical deconstruction of Greek myths is a hallmark of Tatian's style.

fr: Car nous ne déraisonnons pas, Grecs, ni ne débitons de sornettes, en proclamant que Dieu est apparu sous une forme humaine.
en: TATIAN THE SYRIAN We do not act as fools, O Greeks, nor utter idle tales. when we say that God was born in the form of a man [Address to the Greeks 21 (C. A.D. 170)].
greek: Οὐ γὰρ μωραίνομεν, ἄνδρες Ἕλληνες, οὐδὲ λήρους ἀπαγγέλλομεν, θεὸn ἐν ἀνθρώπου μορφῇ γεγονέναι καταγγέλλοντες.
context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. Author and Work

    Tatian the Syrian (c. 120–180 AD): Tatian was a second-century Christian writer and theologian. He was a pupil of the great apologist St. Justin Martyr in Rome. While his early works, like this one, are considered orthodox, he later broke from the mainstream Church and founded an ascetic sect known as the Encratites, who were condemned for their extreme views (such as rejecting marriage and wine).

    Address to the Greeks (Oratio ad Graecos): This work is a classic of early Christian apology. Unlike the more conciliatory tone of his teacher, Justin, Tatian’s address is aggressive, confrontational, and often contemptuous of Greek philosophy, religion, and culture. His goal is to demonstrate the bankruptcy of paganism and the supreme truth and antiquity of Christianity.

2. Immediate Context of the Quote (Chapter 21)

The quote you selected is the opening sentence of a masterful polemical argument. Tatian anticipates the primary objection a sophisticated Greek listener would have: "The idea of God being born in human form is a foolish and absurd fairy tale."

Tatian's strategy is a pre-emptive counter-attack known as the tu quoque ("you too") argument. He essentially says, "You think our story is absurd? Let's look at your own revered myths."

Immediately after your quote, he launches into a list of embarrassing and immoral stories about the Greek gods from their own literature:

    Athena disguising herself as the warrior Deiphobus to trick Hector.

    Apollo, the great god, having to work as a shepherd for a mortal king, Admetus.

    Hera, queen of the gods, visiting Semele disguised as an old woman.

    Asclepius, the god of healing, being killed.

    Heracles, the great hero, burning himself to death.

    Prometheus being punished by a jealous Zeus for helping humanity.

His point is devastatingly clear: The Christian proclamation of the Incarnation, while a profound mystery, is infinitely more noble and credible than the petty, deceptive, and all-too-human stories of the pagan gods.
3. Theological Significance

    A Bold Proclamation: This is one of the earliest, most direct, and unapologetic statements of the Incarnation found in apologetic literature. Tatian isn't trying to soften the message or explain it away philosophically. He uses the strong verb καταγγέλλοντες (katangellontes), which means "we proclaim" or "we announce." It is a term of public, authoritative declaration.

    The Form of a Man: The phrase ἐν ἀνθρώπου μορφῇ (en anthrōpou morphē - "in the form of a man") is a powerful echo of the language used by St. Paul in Philippians 2:7, where Christ Jesus "took the form of a servant" (μορφήν δούλου λαβών).

    A Foundational Claim: Tatian places the Incarnation at the center of the Christian message, presenting it not as a "tale" (λῆρος - lēros, idle talk, nonsense) but as the foundational truth upon which Christianity stands or falls.

fr:
Et il leur dit : « Mais vous, qui dites-vous que je suis ? »
Simon répondit : « Tu es le Christ, le Fils du Dieu vivant. »
Jésus reprit et lui dit : « Heureux es-tu, Simon fils de Jonas, car ce ne sont pas la chair et le sang qui t’ont révélé cela, mais mon Père qui est dans les cieux. Et moi, je te le dis : tu es Pierre, et sur cette pierre je bâtirai mon Église, et les portes du séjour des morts ne l’emporteront pas sur elle. Je te donnerai les clés du royaume des Cieux : tout ce que tu lieras sur la terre sera lié dans les cieux, et tout ce que tu délieras sur la terre sera délié dans les cieux. »
en: TATIAN THE SYRIAN Simon Cephas answered and said. "You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God." Jesus answered and said unto him, "Blessed are you, Simon, son of Jonah: flesh and blood has not revealed it unto thee, but my Father which is in heaven. And say unto thee also, that you are Cephas, and on this rock will I build my Church; and the gates 01 hades shall not prevail against it" [Diatesseron 23 (c. A.D. 170)].
