greek: ܘܐܡܪ ܠܗܘܢ ܐܢܬܘܢ ܡܢܘ ܐܡܪܝܢ ܐܢܬܘܢ ܕܐܝܬܝ. ܥܢܐ ܫܡܥܘܢ ܘܐܡܪ ܠܗ ܐܢܬ ܗܘ ܡܫܝܚܐ ܒܪܗ ܕܐܠܗܐ ܚܝܐ. ܘܥܢܐ ܝܫܘܥ ܘܐܡܪ ܠܗ ܛܘܒܝܟ ܫܡܥܘܢ ܒܪ ܝܘܢܐ ܕܒܣܪܐ ܘܕܡܐ ܠܐ ܓܠܐ ܠܟ ܐܠܐ ܐܒܝ ܕܒܫܡܝܐ. ܐܦ ܐܢܐ ܐܡܪ ܐܢܐ ܠܟ ܕܐܢܬ ܗܘ ܟܐܦܐ ܘܥܠ ܗܕܐ ܟܐܦܐ ܐܒܢܝܗ ܠܥܕܬܝ ܘܬܪܥܐ ܕܫܝܘܠ ܠܐ ܢܚܣܢܘܢܗ. ܘܠܟ ܐܬܠ ܩܠܝܕܐ ܕܡܠܟܘܬܐ ܕܫܡܝܐ. ܘܟܠ ܡܕܡ ܕܬܐܣܘܪ ܒܐܪܥܐ ܢܗܘܐ ܐܣܝܪ ܒܫܡܝܐ. ܘܟܠ ܡܕܡ ܕܬܫܪܐ ܒܐܪܥܐ ܢܗܘܐ ܫܪܐ ܒܫܡܝܐ.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    "Cephas" and "Petra": A Syriac/Aramaic Echo:
    The most striking feature of the Latin version you found is its directness. In Aramaic (and Syriac), the word for "rock" is Kēphā. Jesus names Simon Kēphā and says on this kēphā he will build his church. The pun is perfect.

        Greek creates a slight distinction: Petros (a masculinized name) and petra (the rock).

        The standard Latin Vulgate does the same: Petrus and petram.

        Your Diatessaron text, however, says tu es Petra ("You are Rock"). This is a very literal, un-gendered translation that preserves the force of the original Aramaic/Syriac pun much more directly than the standard Vulgate. This shows the Syriac influence on this version of the text.

    Harmonization of the Gospels:
    The Diatessaron is a "harmony," meaning it weaves the four gospels into one. While this specific passage is almost entirely from Matthew 16, Tatian places it within a sequence of events drawn from Mark and John as well. Your provided text shows this perfectly: it starts with events from Matthew 15 and John 4, transitions to the confession from Matthew 16, and then continues with events from Mark 8.

    Tatian's Importance:
    The Diatessaron was the standard Gospel text used in the Syriac-speaking Church for nearly two centuries. Its existence from such an early date (c. A.D. 170) is powerful evidence for the authority and widespread acceptance of all four canonical Gospels by the mid-second century.   Additional Relevant Details

    This IS the Syriac Quote You Were Looking For: Entry #1268 is the best scholarly reconstruction of the passage from Tatian's Diatessaron that you requested. The Syriac text is the direct source for the English translation you provided.

    The "Kepha" Pun is Clear:
    The Syriac makes the Aramaic wordplay even more explicit than the Latin or Greek:

        ܕܐܢܬ ܗܘ **ܟܐܦܐ** (d-ant hú Kēphā) - "that you are the Rock"

        ܘܥܠ ܗܕܐ **ܟܐܦܐ** (w-‘al hādē Kēphā) - "and upon this rock"
        It uses the exact same word, Kēphā, for both Peter's name and the foundation of the Church. This is the original, powerful force of Jesus's words.

    Understanding the Other Entries (#1269-1276):
    These are called textual variants. They show how other ancient Syriac gospels or writers quoted this passage. For example:

        #1269 & #1270: These are slightly different and abbreviated versions of the same story.

        #1271-1276: These are just tiny fragments of the confession ("You are the Son of the living God," "You are the Messiah," etc.). These might come from other Church Fathers who only quoted a small part of the verse.
        The footnotes at the bottom of the page tell scholars which ancient manuscript or author each of these variants comes from.

Conclusion: You have successfully found the original Syriac text of the passage from Tatian's Diatessaron. The main entry, #1268, is the most complete and authoritative reconstruction based on our best ancient witness, St. Ephrem the Syrian.

fr: Alors Jésus s'approcha et leur dit : « Toute autorité m'a été donnée au ciel et sur la terre. Comme mon Père m'a envoyé, moi aussi je vous envoie. Allez donc dans le monde entier et annoncez mon Évangile à toute la création. Faites de toutes les nations des disciples : baptisez-les au nom du Père, et du Fils, et du Saint-Esprit, et apprenez-leur à garder tout ce que je vous ai commandé. Et voici, je suis avec vous tous les jours, jusqu'à la fin du monde. »
en: TATIAN THE SYRIAN Then said Jesus unto them, "I have been given all authority in heaven and earth; and as my Father has sent me, so I also send you. Go now into all the world, and preach my gospel in all the creation; and teach all the peoples, and baptize them in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit; and teach them to keep all whatsoever commanded you: and lo, I am with you all the days, unto the end of the world" [Mt 28:18-20] [ Diatesseron 55 (c. A.D. 170)].
latin: Tunc ait illis Iesus: Data est mihi omnis potestas in caelo, et in terra: sicut enim misit me Pater meus, ita et ego mitto vos: ite ergo in mundum universum, et praedicate Evangelium meum omni creaturae; et docete omnes gentes, ac baptizate eos in nomine Patris, et Filii et Spiritus sancti: docentes eos servare omnia, quae mandavi vobis: et ecce, ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus, usque ad consummationem mundi.
greek: ܘܩܪܒ ܝܫܘܥ ܡܠܠ ܥܡܗܘܢ ܘܐܡܪ܄ ܐܬܝܗܒ ܠܝ ܟܠ ܫܘܠܛܢ ܒܫܡܝܐ ܘܒܐܪܥܐ. ܐܝܟܢܐ ܕܫܕܪܢܝ ܐܒܝ ܐܦ ܐܢܐ ܡܫܕܪ ܐܢܐ ܠܟܘܢ. ܘܥܒܕܘ ܬܠܡܝܕܐ ܠܟܠܗܘܢ ܥܡܡܐ ܘܐܥܡܕܘ ܐܢܘܢ ܒܫܡ ܐܒܐ ܘܒܪܐ ܘܪܘܚܐ ܕܩܘܕܫܐ. ܙܠܘ ܠܥܠܡܐ ܟܠܗ ܘܐܟܪܙܘ ܣܒܪܬܝ ܒܟܠܗ ܒܪܝܬܐ. ܘܐܠܦܘ ܐܢܘܢ ܕܢܛܪܘܢ ܟܠ ܡܕܡ ܕܦܩܕܬܟܘܢ. ܘܗܐ ܐܢܐ ܥܡܟܘܢ ܐܢܐ ܟܠܗܘܢ ܝܘܡܬܐ ܥܕܡܐ ܠܫܘܠܡܗ ܕܥܠܡܐ.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    The Nature of the Diatessaron:
    The Diatessaron (meaning "Through the Four") is the most important Gospel harmony from the early Church. Written by Tatian the Syrian around A.D. 170, it masterfully weaves the four canonical Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John) into a single, continuous narrative. The passage you selected is a perfect example of this technique.

    How Tatian Harmonized This Passage:
    You can see Tatian's editorial hand at work. He creates a single, powerful command from Jesus by blending phrases from three different Gospels:

        He begins with Matthew 28:18 ("All authority in heaven and earth has been given to me").

        He inserts John 20:21b ("as my Father has sent me, so I also send you").

        He then uses Mark 16:15b ("Go into all the world, and preach my gospel in all the creation").

        He returns to Matthew 28:19-20 for the command to teach, the Trinitarian baptismal formula, and the promise of Christ's perpetual presence.

    The Source of Your Texts (This is fascinating):
    You have provided texts from two different and very important manuscript traditions of the Diatessaron.

        The Latin Text: The long Latin text you provided is from a later Latin translation of an Arabic version of the Diatessaron. The very end of your text tells its incredible story: it was translated from Syriac into Arabic by the famous scholar Abû-l-Pharaģ, from a manuscript written by a disciple of the legendary translator Honain ben Ishac. This shows the complex journey of the text: a likely Greek or Syriac original -> Syriac -> Arabic -> Latin.

        The Syriac Text: The image you provided is from a modern scholarly edition that presents the Syriac text of the Diatessaron, likely reconstructed from St. Ephrem the Syrian's commentary on it, as the original Syriac manuscript is lost. The Spanish translation in the image is a helpful modern guide but, as you can see, is not always a literal word-for-word rendering.

You have pinpointed a crucial passage from one of early Christianity's most influential, though now partially lost, documents.

fr: La condition du Dieu unique impose cette règle : il n'est unique que parce qu'il est seul ; il n'est seul que parce que rien n'existe avec lui. Ainsi, il est aussi le premier, parce que tout est après lui ; et si tout est après lui, c'est que tout vient de lui ; et si tout vient de lui, c'est que tout vient de rien, afin que soit aussi confirmée la parole de l'Écriture : Qui a connu la pensée du Seigneur ? Ou qui a été son conseiller ? Ou qui a-t-il consulté ? Ou qui lui a montré le chemin de l'intelligence et de la science ? Qui lui a donné le premier, pour en être payé de retour ?
en: This rule is required by the nature of the one and only God, who is only one in no other way than as the sole God: and in no other way sole, than as having nothing else [co-existent] with him. So also he will be first, because all things are after him; and all things are after him, because all things are by him; and all things are by him, because they came from nothing: so that reason coincides with the Scripture that says: "Who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? Or with whom took he counsel? Or who has shown to him the way of wisdom and knowledge? Who has first given to him, and it shall be recompensed to him again?" [Rom 11:33-36] [Against Hermogenes 17:1 (C. A.D. 203)].
latin: Unici Dei status hanc regulam vindicat: non aliter unici, nisi quia solius: non aliter solius, nisi quia nihil cum illo: sic et primus erit, quia omnia post illum: sic omnia post illum, quia omnia ab illo: sic ab illo, quia ex nihilo, ut illi quoque Scripturae ratio constet: Quis cognovit sensum Domini? Aut quis illi consiliarius fuit? aut quem consultatus est? aut viam intelligentiae et scientiae quis demonstravit illi? quis tradidit, et retribuetur ei?
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Author and Work: The author is Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus (c. 155 – c. 220 AD), a brilliant and fiery Carthaginian writer often called the "Father of Latin Christianity." The work, Against Hermogenes, is a polemical treatise written around A.D. 203.

    Primary Theological Context: The entire book is an argument against the teaching of Hermogenes, a Christian painter who held a philosophical view common in Greek thought: that God did not create the world from nothing, but rather fashioned it from a pre-existing, co-eternal matter (materia).

    The Core Argument of the Quote: This passage is the heart of Tertullian's refutation. He uses a powerful and concise chain of logic to defend the doctrine of creatio ex nihilo (creation from nothing):

        God is One/Unique (unicus).

        To be truly unique and sole (solus), nothing can be co-eternal with Him.

        If matter were co-eternal, God would not be truly sole.

        Therefore, matter cannot be co-eternal.

        Therefore, all things must be from God (ab illo).

        And if they are from God alone, they must be created from nothing (ex nihilo).

    The Role of Scripture: Tertullian brilliantly uses Romans 11:34-35 as his ultimate proof. He argues that if God had to work with pre-existing matter, He would have been constrained by its properties. He would have effectively needed to "take counsel" with the matter to see what was possible. But St. Paul declares that God is absolutely sovereign and needed no counselor. This proves, for Tertullian, that God was not dependent on any pre-existing substance and created freely, from nothing.

    Significance: This text is a cornerstone of Western Christian theology on the doctrine of creation. It powerfully defends God's absolute sovereignty, omnipotence, and freedom. By refuting the idea of a co-eternal matter, Tertullian also refutes the Gnostic tendency to blame evil on a flawed material principle, insisting instead on the sole causality and goodness of the one God.

fr:
Allez ! Toi qui veux employer au mieux ton zèle pour l'affaire de ton salut, parcours les églises apostoliques. Auprès d'elles, les chaires mêmes des apôtres président encore à leur place ; auprès d'elles, on lit encore leurs lettres authentiques, qui font résonner la voix et rendent présent le visage de chacun d'eux.
L'Achaïe est-elle la plus proche de toi ? Tu as Corinthe. Si tu n'es pas loin de la Macédoine, tu as Philippes, tu as Thessalonique. Si tu peux te rendre en Asie, tu as Éphèse. Si, par ailleurs, tu es proche de l'Italie, tu as Rome, d'où nous vient à nous aussi l'autorité.

Voyons quel lait les Corinthiens ont reçu de Paul ; selon quelle règle les Galates ont été redressés ; ce que lisent les Philippiens, les Thessaloniciens, les Éphésiens ; ce que proclament aussi les Romains, tout proches, à qui Pierre et Paul ont laissé l'Évangile, scellé de leur propre sang.
en: Let us see what milk the Corinthians drank from Paul: to what rule of faith the Galatians were brought for correction; what the Philippians, the Thessalonians, the Ephesians read by it; what utterance also the Romans give, so very near (to the apostles), to whom Peter and Paul conjointly bequeathed the gospel even sealed with their own blood [Against Marcion 4:5 (C. A.D. 209)].
latin: Age iam, qui voles curiositatem melius exercere in negotio salutis tuae, percurre ecclesias apostolicas, apud quas ipsae adhuc cathedrae apostolorum suis locis praesident, apud quas ipsae authenticae litterae eorum recitantur, sonantes vocem et repraesentantes faciem uniuscuiusque. Proxima est tibi Achaia? Habes Corinthum. Si non longe es a Macedonia, habes Philippos, habes Thessalonicenses. Si potes in Asiam tendere, habes Ephesum. Si autem Italiae adiaces, habes Romam, unde nobis quoque auctoritas praesto est. ... Videamus quod lac a Paulo Corinthii hauserint; ad quam regulam Galatae sint recorrecti; quid legant Philippenses, Thessalonicenses, Ephesii; quid etiam Romani de proximo sonent, quibus evangelium et Petrus et Paulus sanguine quoque suo signatum reliquerunt.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

This passage is one of the most famous and important articulations of the early Church's principle of Apostolic Tradition.

    The Context and Argument: Tertullian's opponent, Marcion, had created his own, heavily edited version of the New Testament. He threw out the entire Old Testament and most of the New, keeping only a mutilated Gospel of Luke and ten of Paul's epistles. Tertullian's brilliant counter-argument is to appeal to the public, historical, and verifiable teaching of the churches founded directly by the apostles. He is essentially saying, "You can't just invent your own Christianity. If you want to know the true gospel, go to the source—the apostolic churches. See what they have believed and taught from the very beginning. Their teaching is the authentic one."

    The "Rule of Faith" (Regula Fidei): When Tertullian mentions the "rule" to which the Galatians were corrected, he is referring to the regula fidei, or "rule of faith." This was a summary of core Christian doctrines (like a proto-creed) that was universally taught in the apostolic churches and used as a benchmark to identify and refute heresy.

    The Special Authority of Rome: Notice how Tertullian singles out the Church of Rome for special mention. He calls it the church "from which there comes even into our own hands the very authority." He highlights two unique qualifications for Rome's authority:

        Proximity: They are "so very near" (de proximo), not just in geography for him, but in their direct connection to the chief apostles.

        The Witness of Peter and Paul: Rome is the church where both Peter and Paul preached and, crucially, were martyred. They "bequeathed the gospel even sealed with their own blood." This foundation by the two most prominent apostles and their ultimate witness of martyrdom gave the Church of Rome a preeminent place of honor and authority in the early Christian world.

    Source Citation: You can find the original Latin text in Migne's Patrologia Latina (PL), Volume 2, columns 366-367.

fr:
Concernant la résurrection des morts, il faut d'abord examiner comment on la nie. Sans doute de la même manière qu'aujourd'hui, car la résurrection de la chair trouve toujours des opposants. En effet, de nombreux sages qualifient les âmes de divines et affirment qu'elles survivent à la mort ; le peuple lui-même honore les défunts, précisément dans la conviction qu'ils continuent d'exister. Quant aux corps, il est évident qu'ils finissent par disparaître : soit immédiatement, livrés au feu ou aux bêtes sauvages, soit à la longue, même s'ils ont été conservés avec le plus grand soin. Par conséquent, lorsque l'Apôtre réfute ceux qui nient la résurrection des morts, ce qu'il défend face à eux, c'est précisément ce qui est nié : la résurrection de la chair. Tout l'enjeu est là. Le reste est sans objet.

Dès lors, pour ce qui est de la résurrection des morts, il est indispensable de s'en tenir au sens propre des termes. On ne qualifie de « mort » que ce qui a perdu l'âme qui le faisait vivre. Or, c'est le corps qui perd l'âme, et c'est en la perdant qu'il devient mort. Ainsi, le terme de « mort » ne s'applique qu'au corps. Par conséquent, si la résurrection est celle de ce qui est mort, et que seul le corps est mort, alors la résurrection sera celle du corps. De même, le terme de « résurrection » ne s'applique qu'à ce qui est tombé. On pourrait en effet dire « se relever » de ce qui n'est pas du tout tombé, mais était simplement couché. Mais en réalité, « se relever » ne se dit que de ce qui est tombé, car c'est en se relevant de sa chute qu'on « se re-lève ». Le préfixe « re- » marque en effet la répétition. Nous affirmons donc que le corps tombe à terre par la mort — comme cela se produit effectivement —, conformément à la loi de Dieu. Car il a été dit à l'homme : « Tu es terre, et à la terre tu retourneras. »
en: Touching the resurrection of the dead 1 Cor 15:12], let us first inquire how some persons then denied it. No doubt in the same way in which it is even now denied, since the resurrection of the flesh always has men to deny it. But many wise men claim a divine nature for the soul, and are confident of its undying destiny, and even the multitude worship the dead in the presumption they boldly entertain that their souls survive. As for our bodies, however, it is clear that they perish either at once by fire or the wild beasts, or even when most carefully kept by the passage of time. When, therefore, the apostle refutes those who deny the resurrection of the flesh, he defends, in opposition to them, the precise matter of their denial. that is, the resurrection of the body. You have the whole answer wrapped up in this. All the rest is superfluous. Now on this very point, the resurrection of the dead, it is necessary that the proper force of the words should be accurately maintained. The word dead expresses simply that which has lost the vital principle, by means of which it used to live. Now the body is what loses life, and as the result of losing it becomes dead. To the body, therefore, the term dead is only suitable. Moreover, as resurrection accrues to what iS dead, and dead is a term applicable only to a body, only the body alone has a resurrection incidental to it. So the word resurrection, or rising again, embraces only what has fallen down. "To rise," indeed, can be said of what has never fallen down, but had been lying down. But to rise again" can be said only of what has fallen down; because it is by rising again, in consequence of its having fallen down, that it is said to have re-risen. For the syllable "re" always implies repetition. We say, therefore, that the body falls to the ground by death, as facts show, in accordance with the law of God. For to the body it was said, "Dust you are, and unto dust shall you return" [Against Marcion 5:9 (c. A.D. 209)].
latin:
De resurrectione mortuorum prius est, quomodo negetur, retractare. Sine dubio eodem modo, quo et nunc, quia semper resusurrectio carnis negatores habet. Animas enim et divinas multi sapientes vocant, et superstites affirmant, et vulgus etiam mortuos ita honorat, praesumptione scilicet qua supersint. Corpora vero manifestum est interire, vel statim igni aut bestiis, vel diligentissime quoque reservata postremo tempore. Igitur cum apostolus refutat negantes resurrectionem mortuorum, id ipsum defendit adversus eos, quod negabatur, carnis scilicet resurrectionem. Totum in hoc habes. Superest cetera vacare.

    Tunc igitur, de resurrectione mortuorum, proprietatem vocabulorum necesse est custodiri. Mortuum non dicitur nisi quod animam amisit, de qua vivebat. Corpus est quod amittit animam, et amittendo fit mortuum. Ita mortui vocabulum non competit nisi corpori. Porro si resurrectio mortui est, mortuum autem non est nisi corpus, corporis erit resurrectio. Sic et resurrectionis vocabulum non complectitur nisi quod cecidit. Resurgere enim potest dici et quod omnino non cecidit, sed iacuit. Rursus autem resurgere non dicitur nisi quod cecidit; quia in eo rursus surgit, quod cecidit, ideo resurgit. 'Re-' enim syllaba iterationi praeponitur. Nos igitur dicimus corpus cadere in terram per mortem, sicut et accidit, ex Dei lege. Illi enim dictum est: Terra es, et in terram ibis.
context:
Additional Relevant Details
Context of the Argument

Tertullian is writing against Marcion, a second-century heretic who taught that the God of the Old Testament was a lesser, wrathful "Creator" god, distinct from the supreme, merciful God revealed by Jesus. A key part of Marcion's theology was a hatred of the material world and the flesh, which he saw as the flawed creation of this lesser god. Consequently, he denied the physical incarnation of Christ (promoting a docetic, or phantom-like, view of Jesus) and vehemently rejected the resurrection of the flesh. For Marcion, salvation was the soul's escape from the body, not the redemption of the body.

In Book 5 of Against Marcion, Tertullian is using the Epistles of St. Paul (the only part of the New Testament that Marcion accepted, albeit in a heavily edited form) to dismantle Marcion's own theology. This passage from chapter 9 is a direct assault on Marcion's denial of the bodily resurrection.
Tertullian's Method: A Lawyer's Precision

This passage is a perfect example of Tertullian's legalistic and philological approach to theology. He builds his case like a lawyer in court, based on the precise definition of terms:

    Define "Dead" (Mortuum): He argues that only the physical body truly "loses life" and can therefore properly be called "dead." The soul, he notes, is widely believed to survive.

    Define "Resurrection" (Resurrectio): He makes a brilliant etymological point.

        Surgere (to rise) can apply to anything that gets up.

        Re-surgere (to rise again) can only apply to something that has first fallen. The prefix "re-" implies repetition or restoration.

    The Conclusion: Since only the body dies (falls), only the body can rise again. The term "resurrection of the dead" can logically only mean "resurrection of the body." Any other interpretation does violence to the plain meaning of the words.

The Final Jab: Using Marcion's Hated Scripture

The final sentence is a masterstroke of polemics. By quoting Genesis 3:19 ("Dust you are, and unto dust shall you return"), Tertullian is using the scripture of the Creator God whom Marcion despises to prove the very nature of the body that will be resurrected. He is forcing Marcion to confront the fact that the Christian doctrine of resurrection is inextricably linked to the doctrine of creation found in the Old Testament.

fr: ...l'homme du péché, le fils de la perdition, qui doit être révélé avant la venue du Seigneur, l'adversaire qui s'élève au-dessus de tout ce qu'on appelle Dieu ou qu'on adore, au point de siéger dans le temple de Dieu en se faisant passer pour Dieu ? C'est lui que nous identifions à l'Antichrist, comme nous l'enseignent les prophéties anciennes et nouvelles, et tout particulièrement l'apôtre Jean. Celui-ci dit en effet que de nombreux faux prophètes, précurseurs bien sûr de l'Antichrist, se sont déjà manifestés dans le monde, niant que le Christ soit venu dans la chair et dissociant Jésus — c'est-à-dire le dissociant du Dieu créateur.
en: TERTULLIAN OF CARTHAGE [T]he man of sin, the son of perdition, who must first be revealed before the Lord comes, "who opposes and exalts himself above all that is called God, or that is worshipped; who is to sit in the temple of God, and boast himself as being God?" [2 Thes 2:3-4]. According to our view, he is Antichrist; as it is taught us in both the ancient and the new prophecies, and especially by the apostle John, who says that "already many false prophets are gone out into the world,* the forerunners of Antichrist, who deny that Christ is come in the flesh 1 Jn 4:1-3], and do not acknowledge Jesus [to be the Christ], meaning in God the Creator [ Against Marcion 5:16 (c. A.D. 209)].
latin: ...homo delicti, filius perditionis, qui revelari prius debeat, antequam Dominus veniat, qui adversatur et extollitur supra omne quod dicitur Deus aut quod colitur, ut in templo Dei sedeat, ostentans se quasi sit Deus? Hunc nos Antichristum, sicut et veteribus et novis prophetiis edocemur, et praecipue Joanne apostolo, qui jam antichristi scilicet praecursores, multos pseudoprophetas dicit processisse in orbem, negantes Christum in carne venisse, et solventes Jesum, scilicet in Deo creatore.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

This passage is a brilliant example of Tertullian's polemical genius. He isn't just defining the Antichrist; he is using the doctrine of the Antichrist as a weapon to destroy Marcion's theology.

    The Context: Refuting Marcion's Eschatology: In Book 5, Tertullian is systematically dismantling Marcion's interpretation of St. Paul's letters. Marcion accepted a heavily edited version of Paul's epistles but rejected the Old Testament entirely. He believed the God of the Old Testament (the "Creator") was a harsh, lesser deity, while the Father of Jesus was a different, "Good God" who was previously unknown.

    The Argument's Genius: Tertullian's argument goes like this:

        St. Paul, whom you (Marcion) claim to follow, speaks of a "man of sin."

        This figure will sit "in the temple of God". Tertullian asks Marcion: Whose temple? The "Good God" has no temple on earth; only the Creator God of the Jews does. Therefore, the Antichrist is defined by his opposition to the Creator God.

        Tertullian then masterfully connects Paul's "man of sin" with John's "Antichrist." He points out that the forerunners of Antichrist are those who "deny that Christ has come in the flesh."

        The Knockout Punch: He concludes with the phrase solventes Jesum, scilicet in Deo creatore ("dissolving Jesus, that is to say, in God the Creator"). For Tertullian, to deny the fleshly reality of Jesus (as Marcion and other Gnostics did) was to "dissolve" him from his identity as the Messiah of the Creator God, sent into the Creator's world to fulfill the Creator's prophecies.

    Unity of the Testaments: By showing that the Antichrist's primary rebellion is against the Creator God and His temple, Tertullian proves the unity of the divine plan across the Old and New Testaments. The enemy of Christ is the enemy of the God of Abraham. This directly refutes Marcion's core belief in two separate, opposing gods.

fr: Nous croyons, certes, en un Dieu unique, mais selon cette disposition que nous appelons l'économie : que ce Dieu unique ait aussi un Fils, son Verbe, qui est issu de lui-même, par qui tout a été fait et sans qui rien n'a été fait.
en: We do indeed believe that there is only one God, but we believe that under this dispensation, or, as we say, "divine economy," there is also a Son of this one and only God, his Word, who proceeded from him and through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made [Against Praxeas 2 (c. A.D. 218)].
latin: ...unicum quidem Deum credimus: sub hac tamen dispensatione, quam oeconomiam dicimus, ut unici Dei sit et filius sermo ipsius, qui ex ipso processerit, per quem omnia facta sunt, et sine quo factum est nihil.
context:
Additional Relevant Details & Context

The passage you've highlighted is one of the most important and influential in the history of Western theology for several key reasons:

1. The Heresy Being Fought: Modalism (or Patripassianism)
Tertullian was writing against a teacher named Praxeas. To safeguard the strict monotheism of Christianity, Praxeas taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were not distinct Persons, but simply different "modes" or "masks" of the one God. This led to the conclusion that it was the Father himself who suffered and died on the cross, a heresy known as Patripassianism (from Latin Pater for "Father" and passus for "suffered").

2. Tertullian's Groundbreaking Solution: The Oeconomia
To refute this, Tertullian needed a way to explain how God could be both one and three. He brilliantly borrowed a term from Greek thought and Roman administration:

    Oeconomia (Greek, οἰκονομία): This word literally means "household management" or "stewardship." In a theological context, Tertullian uses it to mean the internal arrangement or divine plan of the Godhead. He argues that the unity of God is not compromised by an internal economy that includes the Son and the Spirit.

    Dispensatio (Latin): This is the Latin equivalent Tertullian uses, meaning "arrangement" or "disposition."

This concept allowed the Church to speak of distinctions within the one God without falling into polytheism.

3. The First Use of "Trinity" in Latin Theology
Just a few lines later in the same chapter you provided, Tertullian gives us one of the earliest clear uses of the Latin word Trinitas (Trinity) in a theological context:

    "...custodiatur oeconomiae sacramentum, quae unitatem in trinitatem disponit, tres dirigens, Patrem, et Filium, et Spiritum Sanctum."

    "...the mystery of the economy is safeguarded, which arranges the Unity into a Trinity, setting forth three: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit."

4. The Language of "One Substance, Three Persons"
This chapter lays the foundation for all subsequent Western Trinitarian theology. Tertullian goes on to introduce the formula that would become standard: one substance (substantia) and three persons. He writes:

    "Tres autem non statu, sed gradu; nec substantia, sed forma... unius autem substantiae..."

    "Three, however, not in condition, but in degree; not in substance, but in form... but of one substance."

In this work, Tertullian essentially created the Latin vocabulary that the Western Church would use for centuries to articulate the doctrine of the Trinity. Your quote is the opening statement of this revolutionary theological argument.

fr:
Quant à nous, qui depuis toujours, et plus encore aujourd’hui, sommes mieux instruits par le Paraclet — celui qui conduit à toute la vérité —, nous croyons bien en un Dieu unique, mais selon cette disposition, que nous appelons « économie », qui veut que ce Dieu unique ait aussi un Fils, son Verbe, qui a procédé de lui-même, par qui tout a été fait et sans qui rien n’a été fait.

Ce Fils a été envoyé par le Père dans la Vierge, et d’elle il est né homme et Dieu, Fils de l’homme et Fils de Dieu, et a été nommé Jésus Christ. Il a souffert, il est mort et a été enseveli selon les Écritures ; il a été ressuscité par le Père, a été repris dans les cieux où il siège à la droite du Père, et viendra juger les vivants et les morts. De là, selon sa promesse, il a envoyé d’auprès du Père l’Esprit Saint, le Paraclet, qui sanctifie la foi de ceux qui croient au Père, au Fils et au Saint-Esprit.

Cette règle de foi a eu cours dès le commencement de l’Évangile, avant même les tout premiers hérétiques, et à plus forte raison avant Praxéas, cet homme d’hier.
en: We, as we always have done (and more especially since we have been better instructed by the Paraclete, who indeed leads men into all truth), believe that there iS only one God, but under the following dispensation, or oikonomia, as it is called, that this one and only God has a Son, his Word, who proceeded from himself, by whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made. We believe he was sent by the Father into the Virgin, and was born of her -being both man and God, the Son of Man and the Son of God, and was called by the name of Jesus Christ; we believe he suffered, died, and was buried, according to the Scriptures, and, after he was raised again by the Father and taken back to heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father, and will come to judge the living and the dead; and that this one God also sent from heaven, according to his own promise, the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, the sanctifier of the faith of those who believe in the Father, and in the Son, and in the Holy Spirit. This rule of faith has come down to us from the beginning of the gospel, even before any of the older heretics [Against Praxeas (Cc. A.D. 218)].
latin: Nos vero et semper, et nunc magis, ut instructiores per Paracletum deductorem scilicet omnis veritatis, unicum quidem Deum credimus: sub hac tamen dispensatione, quam oeconomiam dicimus, ut unici Dei sit et filius sermo ipsius, qui ex ipso processerit, per quem omnia facta sunt, et sine quo factum est nihil: hunc missum a Patre in virginem, et ex ea natum hominem et Deum, filium hominis et filium Dei, et cognominatum Jesum Christum: hunc passum, hunc mortuum et sepultum secundum Scripturas, et resuscitatum a Patre, et in coelos resumptum, sedere ad dexteram Patris, venturum judicare vivos et mortuos, qui exinde miserit, secundum promissionem suam, a Patre Spiritum Sanctum Paracletum, sanctificatorem fidei eorum qui credunt in Patrem et Filium et Spiritum Sanctum. Hanc regulam ab initio Evangelii decucurrisse, etiam ante priores quosque haereticos, nedum ante Praxeam hesternum...

This passage is one of the most important in the history of Trinitarian theology. Here's why:

    The Context: Refuting Monarchianism: Tertullian wrote this book to refute a heretic named Praxeas. Praxeas taught a doctrine known as Modalistic Monarchianism (or Patripassianism), which held that God is a single person who simply reveals himself in different "modes"—sometimes as Father, sometimes as Son. This implied that it was God the Father Himself who suffered and died on the cross. Tertullian's goal is to defend the real distinction of the Persons (Father, Son, Holy Spirit) while fiercely upholding that there is only one God.

    Key Term: Oikonomia / Dispensatio: This is the central concept Tertullian uses to solve the problem. The Greek term oikonomia (which he translates into Latin as dispensatio) literally means "household management" or "plan." Theologically, he uses it to describe God's internal plan or arrangement. There is one God, one divine substance, but within that unity, there is an "economy" or "dispensation" that arranges the unity into a Trinity of distinct persons. This was a revolutionary way of articulating the faith in Latin.

    The Regula Fidei (Rule of Faith): By laying out this creed-like summary, Tertullian is appealing to the Rule of Faith—the core, unwritten apostolic teaching that circulated in the churches before the formal creeds. His argument is that his Trinitarian view is not a new invention but is the ancient, original faith that has been held "from the beginning of the gospel." He contrasts this antiquity with the "novelty" of Praxeas, whom he dismissively calls "of yesterday" (hesternum).

    Influence of Montanism: The phrase "better instructed by the Paraclete" is a clear reference to Tertullian's adherence to Montanism. The Montanists believed in a "New Prophecy" of the Holy Spirit (the Paraclete) that was revealing deeper truths to the Church. Tertullian saw his advanced understanding of the Trinity as a fruit of this new revelation.

    Pioneering Trinitarian Language: Although not in the specific quote you asked for, the text you provided immediately following it contains the first clear articulation in Latin of the language that would define Western Trinitarianism for all time:

        "...custodiatur oeconomiae sacramentum, quae unitatem in trinitatem disponit, tres dirigens, Patrem, et Filium, et Spiritum Sanctum. Tres autem non statu, sed gradu; nec substantia, sed forma... unius autem substantiae..."
        "...the mystery of the economy is safeguarded, which arranges the unity into a Trinity, setting forth three: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Three, however, not in status but in grade; not in substance but in form... but of one substance..."

    Tertullian is the first known Latin writer to use the word Trinitas (Trinity) and to apply the terms substantia (substance) and persona (person) to God, laying the groundwork for all future Latin theology on the subject.

fr:
Cependant, tout en maintenant ce principe, il faut néanmoins, pour l’instruction et l’affermissement de certains, ménager une place à la discussion. Il s’agit d’éviter que chaque doctrine perverse ne paraisse condamnée sans examen, mais par un simple préjugé. C’est le cas surtout de celle-ci, qui prétend détenir la pure vérité en soutenant qu’il n’y a pas d’autre manière de croire au Dieu unique qu’en disant qu’il est lui-même et identiquement le Père, le Fils et le Saint-Esprit.

Comme si, dans notre doctrine, l’Un n’était pas aussi le Tout, puisque de l’Un procède toute chose — en vertu, bien sûr, de l’unité de substance — et comme si, en même temps, n’était pas sauvegardé le mystère de l’Économie, laquelle déploie l’unité en une trinité, en ordonnant les trois : le Père, le Fils et le Saint-Esprit. Trois, cependant, non par la condition, mais par le rang ; non par la substance, mais par la forme ; non par la puissance, mais par l’aspect ; mais d’une seule substance.
en: [S]ome opportunity must be given for reviewing the statements of heretics], with a view to the instruction and protection of various persons; even if only so that it does not seem that each perversion of the truth is condemned without examination, and simply prejudged; especially in the case of this heresy, which supposes that possesses the pure truth, in thinking that one cannot believe in only one God in any other way than by saying that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are the very same Person. As if in this way one were not all, in that all are of one, by unity of substance; while the mystery of the dispensation that distributes the unity into a Trinity is still guarded, placing in their order the three Personsthe Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: three, however, not in condition, but in degree; not in substance, but in form; not in power, but in aspect; yet of one substance [Against Praxeas 2 (c. A.D. 218)].
latin: Sed salva ista praescriptione, utique tamen propter instructionem et munitionem quorumdam, dandus est etiam retractatibus locus: vel ne videatur unaquaeque perversitas, non examinata, sed praejudicata damnari, maxime haec, quae se existimat meram veritatem possidere, dum unicum Deum non alias putat credendum, quam si ipsum eumdemque et Patrem et Filium et Spiritum Sanctum dicat: quasi non sic quoque unus sit omnia, dum ex uno omnia, per substantiae scilicet unitatem; et nihilominus custodiatur oeconomiae sacramentum, quae unitatem in trinitatem disponit, tres dirigens, Patrem, et Filium, et Spiritum Sanctum. Tres autem non statu, sed gradu; nec substantia, sed forma; nec potestate, sed specie: unius autem substantiae.

This passage is extraordinarily important for several reasons, as it introduces key concepts and vocabulary that would define Western Trinitarian theology for centuries.

1. The Heresy of Praxeas (Modalism):
Tertullian is writing against a heretic named Praxeas who taught Modalistic Monarchianism. This heresy "protected" the oneness of God (the monarchia) by claiming that "Father," "Son," and "Holy Spirit" were simply different modes or roles played by the one divine person. This led to the conclusion known as Patripassianism—the idea that God the Father himself was born, suffered, and died on the cross (since He is the Son). Tertullian begins the chapter by summarizing this view: "And so after a time the Father was born, and the Father suffered."

2. The Introduction of Key Latin Vocabulary:
This work is famous for being one of the first, if not the very first, to use specific Latin terms to articulate the doctrine of the Trinity:

    Trinitas (Trinity): Tertullian is one of the earliest Latin writers to use this term to describe the Godhead.

    Substantia (Substance): He uses this term to refer to the single, shared "divine stuff" or "being" of God. There is una substantia (one substance).

    Persona (Person): While not in this specific quote, he uses it throughout the work to refer to the distinct Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. For Tertullian, a Roman lawyer, persona did not mean a self-conscious individual (our modern meaning) but rather a "face," "mask," or a party in a legal case—a distinct entity with a specific role.

3. The Oeconomia (Dispensation or Divine Plan):
Tertullian borrows the Greek word oikonomia (economy) to explain how the one God can exist as three. The oikonomia is God's divine plan or internal arrangement for His own being, by which the "unity is distributed into a Trinity." This concept allows for distinction within God without dividing His substance.

4. The Famous List of Distinctions:
The final sentence of your quote is a masterful piece of theological precision, defining how the Three are distinct:

    "Not in condition, but in degree" (non statu, sed gradu): They are not different in their fundamental state or status of being God, but there is an order or rank (degree) of procession: the Father is the source, from whom the Son proceeds, etc.

    "Not in substance, but in form" (nec substantia, sed forma): This is the core of his argument. They do not have different substances; they are distinct in their presentation or "form."

    "Not in power, but in aspect" (nec potestate, sed specie): There is only one divine power, but it is manifested in three distinct "aspects" or appearances.

You have identified one of the most foundational texts in the history of Western theology, where the language to speak of "one God in three Persons" was first forged.

fr: ...et que soit néanmoins sauvegardé le mystère de l'Économie, qui dispose l'unité en trinité, en présentant les trois : le Père, et le Fils, et le Saint-Esprit. Trois, non par l'état, mais par le degré ; ni par la substance, mais par la forme ; ni par la puissance, mais par l'aspect ; mais d'une seule substance, d'un seul état et d'une seule puissance. Car il y a un seul Dieu, de qui procèdent ces degrés, ces formes et ces aspects, au nom du Père, et du Fils, et du Saint-Esprit.
en: And at the same time the mystery of the divine economy IS safeguarded, for the unity is distributed in a Trinity. Placed in order. the three are the Father, Son, and Spirit. They are three, however, not in condition, but in degree; not in being, but in form; not in power, but in kind: of one being, however, and one condition and one power, because he is one God of whom degrees and forms and kinds are taken into account in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit [ibid.].
latin: ...et nihilominus custodiatur oeconomiae sacramentum, quae unitatem in trinitatem disponit, tres dirigens, Patrem, et Filium, et Spiritum Sanctum. Tres autem non statu, sed gradu; nec substantia, sed forma; nec potestate, sed specie: unius autem substantiae, et unius status, et unius potestatis; quia unus Deus, ex quo et gradus isti et formae et species, in nomine Patris et Filii et Spiritus Sancti deputantur.

Additional Relevant Details & Context

This passage is monumentally important for several reasons. It is one of the earliest instances of a Latin theologian systematically articulating what would become the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity, and in doing so, Tertullian coins or popularizes the essential vocabulary for it.

1. The Author and Work:

    Tertullian of Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 A.D.) is known as the "father of Latin Christianity." He was a brilliant and fiery writer who was the first to produce a large body of Christian literature in Latin.

    Adversus Praxean was written to refute the teachings of a man named Praxeas.

2. The Heresy Being Refuted (Modalistic Monarchianism):

    Praxeas taught a heresy that tried to fiercely protect God's oneness (monarchianism). He argued that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were not distinct persons but simply different modes or "masks" that the one God wears when acting in different ways.

    This led to a conclusion known as Patripassianism (from the Latin Pater for "Father" and passus for "suffered"). If the Son who suffered on the cross is just a "mode" of the Father, then it was God the Father who suffered and died. Tertullian found this absurd and blasphemous.

3. Tertullian's Theological Breakthroughs in This Quote:
Tertullian's genius was to develop a vocabulary that could affirm both God's unity and the real distinction of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

    Oeconomia (Economy): Tertullian borrows this Greek term (which he translates as dispensatio) to refer to the internal "arrangement" or "ordering" of the Godhead. He argues that God is one in His being, but within that unity, there is an internal divine economy of three.

    Trinitas (Trinity): This is one of the first, if not the very first, appearances of the Latin word Trinitas in Christian writing. Tertullian effectively coins the term that would define the doctrine for all subsequent history.

    Una Substantia (One Substance): This is the philosophical bedrock of his argument. He states that the Father, Son, and Spirit are "of one substance" (unius substantiae). This means they share the single, undivided divine being. This is the Latin precursor to the crucial Greek term homoousios ("of the same being") used in the Nicene Creed over a century later.

    Three Persons (Expressed with Early Terminology): To describe the "threeness," Tertullian is still experimenting with language. In this passage, he uses:

        gradus (degree, rank, step)

        forma (form, shape)

        species (kind, appearance)
        He says the three are distinct in these aspects, but they are united in status (condition, state) and potestas (power). Later in the work, he would famously settle on the formula of one substance, three persons (personae), but this quote shows the theological workshop in action.

In summary, this single passage is a landmark moment. Tertullian provides the foundational language and conceptual framework for Western Trinitarian theology, brilliantly defending the mystery of the one God in three distinct persons against a heresy that tried to dissolve those distinctions.

fr: ...car je crois que l'Esprit ne procède que du Père par le Fils.
en: I believe the Spirit to proceed from no other source than from the Father through the Son [ Against Praxeas 4 (c. A.D. 218)].
latin: ...quia Spiritum non aliunde puto, quam a Patre per Filium.
context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. Source and Context

    Author: Tertullian of Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 AD)

    Work: Adversus Praxean (Against Praxeas)

    Chapter: 4

    Approximate Date: c. 213 AD

    Immediate Context: The entire work is a defense of the doctrine of the Trinity against the heresy of Monarchianism (also known as Modalism or Patripassianism). Praxeas taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were merely different "modes" or manifestations of the one God, not distinct Persons. This led to the conclusion that the Father himself must have suffered on the cross (hence "Patripassianism").

In the passage you provided, Tertullian is arguing that the orthodox belief in the Trinity does not destroy the "Monarchy" (the one rule of the one God), as Praxeas claimed.

    He first explains that the Son is not a rival to the Father, because He is "from the substance of the Father" and does nothing without the Father's will.

    He then applies this same principle to the Holy Spirit, whom he calls the "third grade." The Spirit's origin maintains the Monarchy because He comes from a single ultimate source—the Father—but in an ordered way—through the Son.

    Tertullian then brilliantly turns the accusation back on Praxeas, saying that it is Praxeas who destroys the divine order by collapsing the distinct Persons into one.

2. Theological Significance

This quote is one of the most significant early Latin statements on the procession of the Holy Spirit and has been foundational for Western Trinitarian theology.

    Pioneering Language: This work, Against Praxeas, is famous for being one of the first, if not the first, to use the Latin words Trinitas (Trinity), persona (Person), and substantia (substance) in the specific theological sense that would become standard in the West.

    Foundation of the Filioque: The formula a Patre per Filium ("from the Father through the Son") is a direct and crucial precursor to the later Western doctrine of the Filioque ("and the Son"). While not identical to the later formulation, Tertullian's text clearly establishes an active role for the Son in the Spirit's coming-forth from the Father. This concept would be developed by later Latin Fathers like Hilary of Poitiers, Ambrose, and Augustine, eventually leading to the inclusion of the Filioque clause in the Nicene Creed in the West. This clause remains a major point of theological difference between the Catholic and Eastern Orthodox Churches.

You have identified a landmark passage that stands at the very beginning of Latin Trinitarian theology.

fr: C'est ainsi qu'il l'a fait son égal, lui qui, en procédant de lui, est devenu le Fils : le Premier-né, puisqu'engendré avant toutes choses, et l'Unique, puisqu'il est le seul à être engendré de Dieu, issu à proprement parler des entrailles de son cœur même, selon le témoignage que le Père lui-même en donne : « De mon cœur a jailli une Parole excellente. »

A.D. 218)].

This passage is incredibly rich with theological significance. Here’s a breakdown of the context and importance:

1. The Overall Context: Arguing Against Modalism

    Tertullian is writing against a heretic named Praxeas.

    Praxeas taught a doctrine known as Modalism or Patripassianism. This heresy claimed that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were not distinct Persons, but simply different "modes" or "masks" of the one God.

    The logical conclusion of this view was that the Father himself (the Pater) must have suffered (passus) on the cross—hence, "Patripassianism."

    Tertullian's goal in this entire book is to prove that the Son is a distinct Person from the Father, yet without dividing the single divine substance.

2. The Argument in This Specific Passage

Tertullian is explaining how the Word (the Son) can be distinct from the Father without being separate or created out of nothing.

    Exinde eum parem sibi faciens ("Thus does he make him equal to him"): The generation of the Son establishes his equality with the Father. He is not a lesser, secondary being.

    de quo procedendo Filius factus est ("by proceeding from himself he became his Son"): This is the core of the argument. The Son is not "made" in the sense of a creature. He is "made Son" by an eternal procession from the Father's own being. This establishes both their relationship and their distinction.

    primogenitus... unigenitus ("first-begotten... only-begotten"): Tertullian grounds his argument in scriptural titles for Christ (Colossians 1:15, John 1:18, etc.) to show this is not his own invention but the teaching of the apostles.

    proprie de vulva cordis ipsius ("properly from the womb of his own heart"): This is a powerful, anthropomorphic metaphor. It emphasizes that the Son's generation is not a cold, intellectual act but an intimate, substantial procession from the very core of the Father's being. It is a true Sonship, not an adopted or figurative one.

    Eructavit cor meum sermonem optimum ("My heart has issued my most excellent Word"): This is Tertullian's key scriptural proof-text, a quotation from Psalm 45:1 (Psalm 44:1 in the Vulgate). The Latin verb eructavit is very strong, meaning "to belch forth" or "gush out." For Tertullian, this verse is the Father Himself testifying that the Word (Sermo, the Son) comes forth from His own substance, like a word from the heart.

3. Tertullian's Lasting Contribution

This chapter is a prime example of Tertullian's pioneering work in Latin theology. He was one of the first to use the terms that would become standard in the West:

    Substantia (Substance) to describe the one divine "stuff" of the Godhead.

    Persona (Person) to describe the distinct realities of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

This passage is a brilliant articulation of his famous formula: "una substantia, tres personae" (one substance, three persons).

fr:
Tenez-vous-en partout à cette règle que je professe, par laquelle j’atteste que le Père, le Fils et l’Esprit sont inséparables l’un de l’autre ; ainsi, vous saurez reconnaître ce qui est dit et de quelle manière.

Car voici ce que je dis : le Père est autre, le Fils autre, et l’Esprit autre.

Toute personne simple ou mal intentionnée interprète mal cette parole, comme si elle signifiait une diversité et que de cette diversité découlait une séparation du Père, du Fils et de l’Esprit.
en: Bear always in mind that this is the rule of faith I profess; by it I testify that the Father, and the Son, and the Spirit are inseparable from each other, SO you will know in what sense this IS said. My assertion is that the Father IS one, and the Son one, and the Spirit one, and that they are distinct from each other. This statement is taken in a wrong sense by every uneducated and perversely disposed person, as if it meant a diversity, or implied a separation among the Father, and the Son, and the Spirit [ibid., 9].
latin:
Hanc me regulam professum, qua inseparatos ab alterutro Patrem et Filium et Spiritum testor, tene ubique; et ita, quid quomodo dicatur, agnosces.

    Ecce enim dico alium esse Patrem, et alium Filium, et alium Spiritum. Male accipit idiotes quisque aut perversus hoc dictum, quasi diversitatem sonet, et ex diversitate separationem protendat, Patris et Filii et Spiritus.
