context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Author: Tertullian of Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 A.D.)

    Work: De Baptismo (On Baptism)

    Date: c. A.D. 200–206. This is the earliest surviving treatise dedicated entirely to the subject of baptism.

    Citation: De Baptismo, 7

Immediate Context of the Quote

The primary subject of this chapter is not baptism itself, but the post-baptismal anointing with chrism (blessed oil). Tertullian is defending this physical practice against those who might question its spiritual value.

    He first explains that after coming out of the font (de lavacro), Christians are anointed with oil, a practice rooted in the Old Testament anointing of priests like Aaron.

    He argues that just as the physical oil (unctio) runs on the body in a carnal way (carnaliter currit) but produces a spiritual benefit (spiritaliter proficit), the same principle applies to baptism.

    The quote you are looking for is the analogy he uses to prove his point about the anointing. He says, in essence: "Look, we all accept that in baptism there is a physical act—being plunged in water—that produces a spiritual effect—the remission of sins. The anointing works the same way."

Theological Significance

    Sacramental Principle: This is one of the clearest and earliest articulations of the sacramental principle in Christian theology: a visible, physical, "carnal" sign is the means through which an invisible, "spiritual" grace is conferred.

    Anti-Gnostic Polemic: Tertullian is writing in an environment where Gnostic and Marcionite Christians disparaged the material world and the physical body. They would have rejected the idea that something as common as water could save a soul. Tertullian’s bold defense of the "carnal act" of baptism is a direct refutation of this anti-material dualism. He champions the goodness of creation as a vehicle for divine power.

    Tertullian's Style: The phrase is a perfect example of Tertullian's masterful rhetorical style. He loved sharp, memorable antitheses and paradoxes (carnalis actus... spiritalis effectus) to drive home his theological points.

fr: Ensuite, en sortant du bain, nous recevons une onction bénie, conformément à l’ancienne discipline selon laquelle on oignait d’huile au moyen d’une corne pour conférer le sacerdoce, depuis qu’Aaron fut oint par Moïse. C’est de là que le Christ tire son nom : du chrisme, qui est l’onction et qui a donné son nom au Seigneur. Cette onction est devenue spirituelle, parce qu’il a été oint de l’Esprit par Dieu le Père, comme il est dit dans les Actes : *Car en vérité, ils se sont rassemblés dans cette ville contre ton saint Fils, que tu as oint*. Ainsi pour nous, l’onction se répand sur la chair, mais elle porte un fruit spirituel ; de même, l’acte du baptême est charnel, puisque nous sommes plongés dans l'eau, tandis que son effet est spirituel, puisque nous sommes libérés de nos fautes.
en: After this, when we have issued from the font, we are thoroughly anointed with a blessed unction-[a practice derived] from the old discipline, in which on entering the priesthood, men were anointed with oil from a horn, ever since Aaron was anointed by Moses. Thus Aaron is called "Christ," from the "chrism," which is "the unction"; which, when made spiritual, furnished an appropriate name for the Lord, because he was "anointed" with the Spirit by God the Father; as written in the Acts: "For truly they were gathered together in this city against your holy Son whom you have anointed." Thus, too, in our case, the unction runs carnally, but profits spiritually; in the same way as the act of baptism is carnal, in that we are plunged in water, but the effect spiritual, in that we are freed from sins [Baptism (C. A.D. 203)].
latin: Exinde egressi de lavacro perungimur benedicta unctione de pristina disciplina, qua ungui oleo de cornu in sacerdotium solebant, ex quo Aaron a Moyse unctus est. Unde Christus dicitur a chrismate, quod est unctio, quae et Domino nomen accommodavit, facta spiritalis, quia Spiritu unctus est a Deo Patre; sicut in Actis: Collecti sunt enim vero in ista civitate adversus sanctum Filium tuum quem unxisti. Sic et in nobis carnaliter currit unctio, sed spiritaliter proficit, quomodo et ipsius baptismi carnalis actus, quod in aqua mergimur, spiritalis effectus, quod delictis liberamur.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

This short passage is immensely important for several reasons:

1. Historical and Liturgical Significance:

    De Baptismo (c. A.D. 203) is the earliest surviving complete treatise on the sacrament of baptism.

    This passage provides one of our most ancient and explicit descriptions of a post-baptismal anointing in the Latin West. It is a foundational text for understanding the historical development of the Sacrament of Confirmation. It shows that by A.D. 203 in Carthage, the rite of Christian initiation already included an anointing immediately after coming out of the baptismal font.

2. Theological Argument and Method:

    Typology (The "Old Discipline"): Tertullian grounds the Christian practice in the pristina disciplina ("the old discipline" or "ancient practice") of the Old Testament. He creates a direct parallel between the anointing of Christian neophytes and the priestly anointing of Aaron by Moses. This is a classic example of patristic typology, where Old Testament figures and rituals are seen as prefiguring New Testament realities.

    Christological Foundation: The entire meaning of the anointing is rooted in Christ. Tertullian explains the etymology: the name Christus (Christ) comes from chrisma (the anointing). The Christian's anointing is a participation in the anointing of Christ himself, who was anointed not with physical oil, but with the Holy Spirit by the Father. He proves this by quoting the Apostolic prayer in Acts 4:27.

    The Sacramental Principle: This passage contains one of the clearest and earliest articulations of the sacramental principle in Western theology. Tertullian masterfully contrasts the physical action with the spiritual effect:

        Anointing: carnaliter currit unctio (the unction runs carnally/physically) but spiritaliter proficit (it profits spiritually).

        Baptism: carnalis actus (the act is carnal/physical: immersion in water) but spiritalis effectus (the effect is spiritual: freedom from sins).
        This principle—that a visible, material sign conveys an invisible, spiritual grace—became a cornerstone of all subsequent Latin sacramental theology.

fr: Or, lorsqu’il est posé en règle que le salut n’appartient à personne sans le baptême, c’est principalement en vertu de cette déclaration du Seigneur qui dit : « Si quelqu'un ne naît pas de l’eau, il n’aura pas la vie… »
en: [T]he prescript is laid down that "without baptism, salvation iS attainable by none" (chiefly on the ground of that declaration of the Lord, who says, "Unless one be born of water, he has not life") [Baptism 12 (c. A.D. 203)].
latin: Cum vero praescribitur nemini sine baptismo competere salutem, ex illa maxime pronuntiatione Domini qui ait, Nisi natus ex aqua quis erit, non habebit vitam...
context:
Additional Relevant Details

1. The Work's Full Title:
The work is De Baptismo ("On Baptism"). It is one of the earliest surviving Christian treatises dedicated entirely to a single sacrament and is immensely important for understanding early Christian doctrine and practice.

2. The Context: A Major Theological Problem
The entire chapter you provided is a brilliant example of early Christian theology in action. Tertullian isn't just stating a rule; he is immediately addressing a difficult and obvious objection that his opponents ("scrupulous or rather, reckless people" - scrupulosi immo temerarii) were raising against it.

    The Unbreakable Rule: He begins by stating the strict principle (praescribitur) derived from John 3:5: No one can attain salvation without baptism.

    The Thorny Problem: This immediately raises the question: What about the Apostles? The objectors point out that, with the exception of Paul, there is no biblical record of the other apostles being baptized (at least not with Christ's baptism).

    The Dilemma: This creates a logical crisis. Either (a) the rule is broken, and salvation is possible without baptism, or (b) the apostles themselves are not saved.

3. Tertullian's Proposed Solutions
The rest of the chapter is Tertullian's masterful attempt to resolve this dilemma. He offers several possible solutions, showing the depth of early theological reasoning:

    Possibility #1: They Received John's Baptism. He argues that the apostles likely received the baptism of John, which at the time served its purpose of preparing the way for the Lord.

    A Refuted Argument: He mentions and quickly dismisses a rather creative theory that some were putting forward: that the apostles were "baptized" when their boat was tossed by the waves in the storm, and that Peter was "sufficiently immersed" when walking on the water. Tertullian rejects this with a sharp distinction: "...aliud est aspergi vel intercipi violentia maris, aliud tingui disciplina religionis." ("...it is one thing to be sprinkled or caught by the violence of the sea, another to be baptized by the discipline of religion.")

    Possibility #2 (His Main Point): A "Prerogative" of Faith. This is his most profound argument. He suggests that the apostles' unique situation—their direct, personal calling by and intimate familiarity with Jesus—could have conferred upon them a "prerogative that could stand in for baptism" (praerogativa compendium baptismi conferre posset). Their faith itself was salvific, as shown by Jesus's own words, which Tertullian quotes: "Fides tua te salvum fecit" ("Your faith has saved you"). In this unique, foundational case, their immediate and total faith in the person of Christ served the function of baptism.

In essence, Chapter 12 of De Baptismo is a crucial text showing how the early Church grappled with the universal necessity of its sacraments while also making room for God's sovereign freedom and the unique circumstances of salvation history.

fr: ...nul n'obtient le salut sans le baptême...
en: Without baptism, salvation is attainable by none [ibid., 12].
latin: ...nemini sine baptismo competere salutem...
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Author: Tertullian of Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 AD)

    Work: De Baptismo ("On Baptism")

    Chapter: 12

    Context and Nuance (Critically Important): While the phrase nemini sine baptismo competere salutem ("salvation is attainable by no one without baptism") is famously quoted as an absolute statement, the context of the chapter is fascinating and reveals a more nuanced argument.

    Tertullian is not simply stating the rule in a vacuum. He is stating this well-known Christian principle in order to address a difficult objection that was being raised in his time: What about the Apostles?

    The objectors, whom he calls "scrupulous" and "rash," pointed out that there is no record of the Apostles (except for St. Paul) being baptized by Jesus. This created a dilemma:

        If baptism is absolutely necessary for salvation, were the Apostles not saved? (This was unthinkable).

        If the Apostles were saved without baptism, does that mean the rule is not absolute?

    The rest of the chapter you provided is Tertullian's attempt to solve this problem. He considers a few possibilities but ultimately argues that the Apostles had a unique case. Their direct call from Christ and their unwavering faith served as a substitute or a "shortcut" for baptism (compendium baptismi). He states that their "prerogative of being the first chosen and their undivided intimacy [with Jesus] could have conferred the benefit of baptism."

    Therefore, the great irony is that this chapter, which gives us one of the strongest patristic statements on the necessity of baptism, is actually dedicated to arguing for a very specific exception to that rule. The quote itself serves as the premise—the established rule—from which he must then defend the unique status of the Apostles.

fr:
Il existe bien pour nous un second baptême, lui aussi unique : celui du sang. C’est celui dont le Seigneur disait : « Je dois être baptisé d’un baptême », alors qu’il avait déjà été baptisé. Car il était venu par l’eau et par le sang, comme l’a écrit Jean, pour être baptisé par l’eau et glorifié par le sang, et faire ainsi de nous des appelés par l’eau et des élus par le sang.

Ces deux baptêmes, il les a fait jaillir de la blessure de son côté transpercé : pour que ceux qui croiraient en son sang soient lavés par l’eau, et que ceux qui auraient été lavés par l’eau boivent aussi le sang. Tel est le baptême qui remplace celui que l’on n’a pas reçu et restitue celui que l’on avait perdu.
en: We have a second font (itself one with the former) of blood, about which the Lord said, "] have to be baptized with a baptism," when he had been baptized already. For he had come "by means of water and blood" [1 Jn 5:6], just as John has written; that he might be baptized by the water, glorified by the blood-to make us, in like manner, called by water, chosen by blood. These two baptisms he sent out from the wound in his pierced side, in order that they who believed in his blood might be bathed with the water; they who had been bathed in the water might drink the blood. This baptism stands in lieu of being bathed in the font when that has not been received, and restores when lost [ibid., 16].
latin:
Est quidem nobis etiam secundum lavacrum, unum et ipsum, sanguinis scilicet, de quo Dominus, "Habeo," inquit, "baptismo tingui," cum iam tinctus fuisset. Venerat enim per aquam et sanguinem, sicut Ioannes scripsit, ut aqua tingueretur, sanguine glorificaretur. Proinde nos faceret aqua vocatos, sanguine electos.

Hos duos baptismos de vulnere percussi lateris emisit, quia qui in sanguinem eius crederent, aqua lavarentur; qui aqua lavissent, et sanguine potarent. Hic est baptismus qui lavacrum et non acceptum repraesentat et perditum reddit.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

This is a hugely important and influential passage in the history of Christian theology. Here are the key details:

    Author: Tertullian of Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 AD). He was one of the earliest and most significant Christian writers in the Latin language and is often called the "father of Latin Christianity." He was known for his brilliant, fiery, and legalistic style.

    Work: De Baptismo (On Baptism). This is the earliest surviving complete treatise dedicated to the sacrament of baptism. It was likely written around 200 AD to defend the necessity of water baptism against Gnostic groups who rejected it.

    Theological Concept: Baptism of Blood (Baptismus Sanguinis)
    This passage is the classic and foundational text for the doctrine of the "Baptism of Blood." This doctrine addresses a critical pastoral question in the age of persecutions: What is the fate of a catechumen (someone preparing for baptism) who is martyred for Christ before they can be baptized with water?

    Tertullian's Argument:

        A "Second Font": He calls martyrdom a "second font" (secundum lavacrum), but one that is spiritually united with the first.

        Scriptural Basis: He grounds this in Christ's own life and words:

            Luke 12:50: Jesus says, "I have a baptism to be baptized with." Since Jesus was already baptized in the Jordan, Tertullian argues this "second baptism" must be his Passion and death—his "baptism" in his own blood.

            John 19:34: The "two baptisms" (water and blood) flow from the pierced side of Christ on the cross. This image became central to sacramental theology, representing the birth of the Church and its primary sacraments from Christ's sacrifice.

    The Two Functions of the Baptism of Blood:
    The final sentence is the most powerful summary of the doctrine's two purposes:

        non acceptum repraesentat ("stands in lieu of... when that has not been received"): This applies to the catechumen who is martyred. Their martyrdom supplies the grace of the baptism they could not physically receive.

        et perditum reddit ("and restores when lost"): This reflects Tertullian's extremely strict (rigorist) view of post-baptismal sin. He believed that for grave sins committed after baptism (like apostasy), the grace of the sacrament was "lost." For him, martyrdom was the only certain way—a "second baptism"—to have that grace restored. This rigorist stance would later characterize his adherence to Montanism.

fr: Pour les défunts, nous faisons des offrandes le jour anniversaire de leur mort, chaque année.
en: We offer sacrifices for the dead on their birthday anniversaries [the date of death, their birth into eternal life][ Chaplet 3 (A.D. 211)].
latin: Oblationes pro defunctis, pro nataliciis, annua die facimus.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Source: The quote is from the book De Corona Militis (often shortened to De Corona), which translates to The Soldier's Crown or simply The Chaplet. It was written by Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus (Tertullian of Carthage) around A.D. 211.

    Immediate Context: This sentence is part of a longer list of practices that Tertullian presents as universally accepted in the Church but not explicitly commanded in Scripture. His purpose is to defend the authority of unwritten Tradition. The other examples he lists in the same paragraph include:

        Renouncing the devil at baptism.

        Triple immersion in the font.

        Tasting a mixture of milk and honey after baptism.

        Receiving the Eucharist only from the hands of the presiding clergy.

        Receiving the Eucharist in the early morning.

        Not fasting or kneeling on Sundays.

        Making the Sign of the Cross on one's forehead throughout the day.

    Broader Argument: The entire book is an argument against a Christian soldier wearing a laurel wreath (a military award). When challenged to show a scriptural prohibition against it, Tertullian retorts by listing all the beloved and universal customs (like the one you cited) that are also not in Scripture, thereby establishing Tradition as a legitimate source of authority.

    Theological Significance:

        Prayers for the Dead: This is one of the earliest and most explicit non-scriptural references to the Christian practice of making offerings for the deceased. It shows that by the early 3rd century, this was an established and uncontroversial custom.

        "Oblationes": The term "offerings" or "oblations" almost certainly refers to offerings made during the Eucharistic liturgy. This directly connects the remembrance of the dead to the central act of Christian worship.

        "Pro nataliciis": This phrase, meaning "for their birthdays," is profoundly significant. As your original note correctly indicated, it refers to the dies natalis or "heavenly birthday"—the anniversary of a martyr's or a faithful Christian's death, which was celebrated as their day of birth into eternal life. This practice is the ancient root of celebrating saints' feast days.

fr: C’est ainsi que la condition propre de chacune des deux substances a manifesté l’homme et Dieu : d’un côté né, de l’autre non né ; d’un côté charnel, de l’autre spirituel ; d’un côté faible, de l’autre infiniment fort ; d’un côté mortel, de l’autre vivant.
en: Thus the nature of the two substances displayed him as man and God in one respect born, in the other unborn: in one respect fleshly, in the other spiritual; in one sense weak, in the other exceeding strong; in one sense dying, in the other living [The Flesh of Christ 5:6-7 (c. A.D. 210)].
latin: ita utriusque substantiae census hominem et Deum exhibuit: hinc natum, inde non natum; hinc carneum, inde spiritalem; hinc infirmum, inde praefortem; hinc morientem, inde viventem.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Author and Work: This passage is from Tertullian of Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 AD), one of the most brilliant and fiery Latin apologists of the early Church. The work is De Carne Christi, written around A.D. 210-212.

    Historical Context: Tertullian is writing against several Gnostic and Docetic heresies, most notably that of Marcion. Marcion taught that Christ was a purely spiritual being sent by a good, unknown God, and that he only appeared to have a human body (a "phantasm"). He denied the physical birth, suffering, and death of Jesus because he considered all matter, including the human body, to be evil and unworthy of God.

    Theological Significance: This quote is a landmark in the development of Western Christology. It is one of the earliest and clearest articulations of the two natures of Christ in the Latin language. Tertullian uses his famous love for paradox and antithesis to hammer home his point: the single person of Jesus Christ possesses the full and true properties of both divinity and humanity. The series of contrasting pairs—born/unborn, fleshly/spiritual, weak/strong, dying/living—is a powerful rhetorical device used to affirm that Christ's humanity was not an illusion but a reality just as true as His divinity.

    Key Terminology: The use of the word substantia (substance) here is crucial. Tertullian was a pioneer in developing a Latin theological vocabulary. His use of substantia to refer to the distinct divine and human natures, and later persona for the single subject, laid the groundwork for the language that would be formally adopted at the Council of Chalcedon over two centuries later.

fr: Sur ce point aussi, la raison le justifie : Dieu a reconquis son image et sa ressemblance, que le diable avait capturées, par une opération en miroir. Car dans Ève, encore vierge, s’était insinuée la parole qui édifie la mort ; il fallait de même qu'en une vierge soit introduit le Verbe de Dieu qui édifie la vie, afin que ce qui, par ce sexe, était allé à sa perte, soit ramené au salut par ce même sexe. Ève avait cru le serpent, Marie a cru Gabriel. La faute que la première a commise en croyant, la seconde l'a effacée en croyant.
en: But that I may lose no opportunity of supporting my argument from the name of Adam, why is Christ called Adam by the apostle, unless it be that, as man, he was of that earthly origin? And even reason maintains the same conclusion, because it was by just the contrary operation that God recovered his own image and likeness, of which he had been robbed by the devil. For it was while Eve was yet a virgin that the ensnaring word crept into her ear, which was to build the edifice of death. Into a virgin's soul, in like manner, must be introduced that Word of God, which was to raise the fabric of life; sO that what had been reduced to ruin by this sex might by the selfsame sex be recovered to salvation. As Eve had believed the serpent, so Mary believed the angel. The delinquency that the one occasioned by believing, the other by believing effaced [The Flesh of Christ 17 (c. A.D. 210)].
latin: Sed et hic ratio defendit, quod Deus imaginem et similitudinem suam, a diabolo captam, aemula operatione recuperavit. In virginem enim adhuc Evam irrepserat verbum aedificatorium mortis; in virginem aeque introducendum erat Dei Verbum extructorium vitae: ut quod per ejusmodi sexum abierat in perditionem, per eumdem sexum redigeretur in salutem. Crediderat Eva serpenti: credidit Maria Gabrieli. Quod illa credendo deliquit, haec credendo delevit.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Primary Source: Tertullian of Carthage, De Carne Christi, Caput XVII (Chapter 17).

    Patrology Citation: The text you provided is from Migne's Patrologia Latina (PL), Volume 2, columns 782B-782C. The marginal numbers (0782B, 0782C) correspond to the columns in that standard edition.

    Theological Context (Recapitulation): This passage is one of the most brilliant and concise expressions of the theological theme known as Recapitulation. First developed by St. Justin Martyr and masterfully expanded by St. Irenaeus of Lyons, Recapitulation holds that Christ, the New Adam, retraces the steps of the first Adam in order to reverse the Fall.

    The Eve/Mary Parallel: Tertullian applies this principle with stunning rhetorical force to Eve and Mary. The parallel is built on a series of antitheses:

        Eve (a virgin) listened to the word of a fallen angel (the serpent), which was the "builder of death" (aedificatorium mortis).

        Mary (a virgin) listened to the Word of God from a holy angel (Gabriel), which was the "constructor of life" (extructorium vitae).

        Through the female sex (per ejusmodi sexum), ruin entered the world.

        Through the same female sex (per eumdem sexum), salvation was restored.

        Eve's belief in the serpent's word led to sin (credendo deliquit).

        Mary's belief in the angel's word erased that sin (credendo delevit).

    Literary Style: This passage is a prime example of Tertullian's genius as a Latin stylist. He was trained as a lawyer, and his writing is known for its punchy, energetic, and highly rhetorical quality. Notice the powerful parallelism and the final, memorable, almost legalistic summary: Quod illa credendo deliquit, haec credendo delevit. (What the one, by believing, offended, the other, by believing, erased.) This balanced, rhythmic sentence is one of the most famous in all of patristic literature.

    Overall Argument: Within the treatise, Tertullian uses this argument to prove the necessity of the Virgin Birth and the reality of Christ's flesh. He is refuting heretics (like Marcion and Valentinus, whom he mentions just before this quote) who denied that Christ took real human flesh from Mary. Tertullian argues that the Virgin Birth wasn't arbitrary; it was the divinely ordained "rival operation" (aemula operatione) required to undo the damage that began with the virgin Eve.

fr: Nous observons que parmi les arts, certaines professions sont elles aussi exposées à l'idolâtrie. Des astrologues, il n'est même pas besoin de parler. Mais puisqu'un individu, ces jours-ci, a lancé un débat pour défendre son droit de persévérer dans cette profession, je serai bref. Je ne m'attarderai pas sur le fait que l'astrologie honore des idoles, dont elle a inscrit les noms dans le ciel et auxquelles elle a attribué toute la puissance de Dieu ; si bien que les hommes, convaincus d'être régis par le décret immuable des étoiles, ne jugent plus nécessaire de chercher Dieu. Je n'avancerai qu'un seul argument : il s'agit de ces anges, déserteurs de Dieu, amants des femmes, qui ont aussi transmis cet art indiscret et qui, pour cette raison même, ont été condamnés par Dieu.
en: We observe among the arts some professions liable to the charge of idolatry. Of astrologers there should be no speaking even; but since one has recently challenged us, defending his profession on his own behalf, will use a few words. I do not allege that he honors idols, whose names he has inscribed in the heavens, and to whom he has attributed all God's power; but that men, presuming that we are disposed of by the immutable judgment of the stars, think on that account that God is not to be sought after. One proposition lay down: that those angels, the deserters from God, the lovers 01 women, were the discoverers of this curious art, and on that account also condemned by God [Idolatry 9 (c. A.D. 211)].
latin: Animadvertimus inter artes etiam professiones quasdam obnoxias idololatriae. De astrologis ne loquendum quidem est. Sed quoniam quidam istis diebus provocavit defendens sibi perseverantiam professionis istius, paucis utar. Non allego quod idola honoret, quorum nomina coelo inscripsit, quibus omnem Dei potestatem addixit: quod propterea homines non putant Deum requirendum, praesumentes stellarum nos immutabili arbitrio agi. Unum propono, angelos esse illos desertores Dei, amatores foeminarum, proditores etiam hujus curiositatis, propterea quoque damnatos a Deo.
context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. Source and Citation

    Author: Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus (Tertullian of Carthage)

    Work: De Idololatria (On Idolatry)

    Chapter: 9

    Date: c. A.D. 208-211

    Migne Citation: Patrologia Latina (PL) 1, columns 671-673.

2. Context of the Quote

De Idololatria is one of Tertullian's most rigorous and uncompromising works. In it, he argues that a Christian must avoid any and all contact with pagan idolatry, not just in worship but in every aspect of daily life—from one's job to social customs and even speech.

Chapter 9 deals specifically with professions that are incompatible with the Christian faith. Tertullian has already condemned obvious professions like idol-making and now turns to more "intellectual" arts. He begins with astrology, noting that a contemporary debate ("quidam istis diebus provocavit" - "someone has recently challenged us") has forced him to address it directly.
3. Key Theological and Historical Points

    Astrology's Two Great Sins: Tertullian condemns astrology for two main reasons:

        It is Idolatry: It assigns the names of pagan gods (idols) to the stars and attributes to them the power over human life that belongs only to God (omnema Dei potestatem addixit).

        It is Fatalistic: Its core teaching is that human lives are determined by the "immutable judgment of the stars" (stellarum nos immutabili arbitrio agi). This fatalism destroys free will and makes seeking God and repentance pointless (non putant Deum requirendum).

    The Fallen Angels Tradition (The Crucial Point): Tertullian's most striking argument is that astrology was invented and taught to humanity by fallen angels. His reference to "those angels, the deserters from God, the lovers of women" (angelos esse illos desertores Dei, amatores foeminarum) is a direct allusion to the narrative found in the Book of Enoch (specifically 1 Enoch 6-8), an apocryphal Jewish work that was highly influential among early Christians. This text elaborates on the cryptic passage in Genesis 6:1-4, describing how a group of angels called the "Watchers" descended to earth, took human wives, and taught humanity forbidden arts, including sorcery, weaponry, and astrology. For Tertullian, astrology is not just a false science; it is a demonic and condemned art, revealed by condemned beings.

    The Magi and the "Closing" of an Era: The rest of the Latin text you provided is Tertullian's brilliant pre-emptive refutation of the obvious counter-argument: "What about the Magi who followed the star to Christ's birth?" Tertullian argues that this event was a one-time permission that served as a "clausula" (a closing off or conclusion) of that science. After Christ's birth, the art became illicit. He interprets the command for the Magi to return by "another way" metaphorically, meaning they were to abandon their former "sect" or profession.

fr: Quant aux autres déchaînements impies de la luxure, ceux qui s'exercent contre les corps et les sexes en violation des lois de la nature, nous les chassons non seulement du seuil, mais de l'édifice tout entier de l'Église ; car ce ne sont pas là des péchés, mais des monstruosités.
en: [A]lI the other frenzies of passions-impious both toward the bodies and toward the sexes-beyond the laws of nature, we banish not only from the threshold, but from all shelter of the Church, because they are not sins, but monstrosities [Modesty 4 (c. A.D. 220)]
latin: Reliquas autem libidinum furias impias et in corpora et in sexus ultra jura naturae non modo limine, verum omni Ecclesiae tecto submovemus; quia non sunt delicta, sed monstra.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Author and Work: Tertullian of Carthage, De Pudicitia (On Modesty).

    Date and Context: This work was written around A.D. 220, during Tertullian's Montanist period. This is critically important. He had broken away from the mainstream Catholic Church, which he now viewed as too lax, and embraced the rigorist Montanist sect. This treatise is a polemic written against the authority of the Bishop of Rome (likely Pope Callixtus I), who had issued an edict allowing sins like adultery to be forgiven after a period of public penance.

    The Argument of the Quote: In this chapter, Tertullian is creating a hierarchy of sins. He argues that even adultery and fornication are unforgivable by the Church (his strict Montanist position). However, he then establishes a third category of acts that are even worse. These "other frenzies of passions" (reliquas libidinum furias) are those that go "beyond the laws of nature" (ultra jura naturae).

    "Not Sins, but Monstrosities": The key to the passage is the final phrase: quia non sunt delicta, sed monstra. Tertullian argues that these acts are so contrary to the created order that they don't even qualify as mere sins (delicta), which are moral failings. Instead, they are "monstrosities" (monstra), perversions of nature itself.

    Absolute Exclusion: Because of this categorization, the punishment is absolute. While other grave sinners might be allowed to stand at the threshold of the church as penitents, these offenders are to be banished "not only from the threshold, but from all shelter of the Church" (non modo limine, verum omni Ecclesiae tecto submovemus). This reflects the extreme severity of his Montanist views.

    Primary Source Citation: You can find this text in Migne's Patrologia Latina (PL), Volume 2, column 1039.

fr:
Est-ce parce que le Seigneur a dit à Pierre : « C’est sur cette pierre que je bâtirai mon église ; je t’ai donné les clés du royaume des cieux », ou encore : « Tout ce que tu auras lié ou délié sur la terre sera lié ou délié dans les cieux », que tu en déduis que le pouvoir de délier et de lier s’est transmis jusqu’à toi, c’est-à-dire jusqu’à toute église proche de Pierre ?

Qui es-tu pour renverser et altérer l’intention manifeste du Seigneur, qui conférait ce pouvoir à Pierre à titre personnel ? C’est « sur toi », dit-il, « que je bâtirai mon église » ; c’est « à toi que je donnerai les clés », et non à l’église ; c’est « tout ce que tu délieras ou lieras », et non ce qu’ils délieront ou lieront.
en: [T]he Lord said to Peter, "On this rock I will build my Church, I have given you the keys of the kingdom of heaven [and] whatever you shall have bound or loosed on earth will be bound or loosed in heaven" [Mt 16:18-19]. . . . What kind of man are you, subverting and changing what was the clear intent of the Lord when he himself conferred this upon Peter? Upon you, he says, I will build my Church; and I will give to you the keys [Modesty 21 C. A.D. 220)].
latin: Si, quia dixerit Petro Dominus: Super hanc petram aedificabo Ecclesiam meam; tibi dedi claves regni coelestis, vel: Quaecumque alligaveris vel solveris in terra, erunt alligata vel soluta in coelis; idcirco praesumis et ad te derivasse solvendi et alligandi potestatem, id est ad omnem Ecclesiam Petri propinquam; qualis'es evertens atque commutans manifestam Domini intentionem personaliter hoc Petro conferentem: Super te, inquit, aedificabo Ecclesiam meam; et: Dabo tibi claves, non Ecclesiae; et: Quaecumque solveris vel alligaveris, non quae solverint vel alligaverint.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

This passage is one of the most significant and intensely debated in early Christian literature, primarily because of its author, context, and argument.

1. Author and Work:

    Tertullian of Carthage (c. 160 – c. 225 AD), a brilliant and fiery North African lawyer and theologian.

    The work is De Pudicitia (On Modesty), written around A.D. 220. This is a crucial detail because it comes from Tertullian's Montanist period.

2. Historical Context (The Montanist Shift):

    Early in his career, Tertullian was a pillar of the mainstream Catholic Church. However, he later embraced Montanism, a charismatic and extremely rigorist sect that believed in new prophecy and held that the institutional Church was becoming too lax.

    De Pudicitia is a polemical work from this later phase. Tertullian is arguing furiously against a declaration by a Bishop of Rome (very likely Pope Callixtus I) who had issued an edict allowing for the forgiveness of grave sins like adultery and fornication after a period of penance.

    Tertullian, in his Montanist severity, saw this as an unacceptable watering down of Christian discipline. He contemptuously refers to the bishop he is attacking as the pontifex maximus and "psychic" (a carnal man, as opposed to a "spiritual" Montanist).

3. Analysis of Tertullian's Argument:

    The entire point of this passage is to restrict the power of the keys. Tertullian is arguing against the very bishop who claims the Petrine authority to forgive sins.

    A Personal Grant to Peter: Tertullian's argument is that Christ's promise in Matthew 16 was a grant made personally and exclusively to Peter (personaliter hoc Petro conferentem).

    "Upon YOU... To YOU": He dramatically rephrases the promise to emphasize this point: "Super te... aedificabo Ecclesiam meam" ("Upon you... I will build my Church") and "Dabo tibi claves, non Ecclesiae" ("I will give the keys to you, not to the Church").

    The "Spiritual" Church vs. the "Episcopal" Church: At the end of the chapter, Tertullian reveals his Montanist theology. He argues that this power to forgive belongs not to the institutional Church of bishops (ecclesia numerus episcoporum) but to the "Church of the Spirit" (Ecclesia Spiritus), which is embodied in the "spiritual man" (spiritalem hominem)—that is, an apostle or a Montanist prophet.

4. Significance:
This text is a historical landmark. It is one of the earliest detailed commentaries on Matthew 16:18-19. It is historically invaluable because it shows that by A.D. 220, the Bishop of Rome was explicitly using the promise to Peter as the basis for his authority to govern the Church and forgive sins. Tertullian's argument is a powerful piece of evidence for the very claim he is trying to refute.

fr: La discipline dirige l'homme, le pouvoir confère l'autorité. Car le pouvoir est une chose, l'Esprit en revanche est Dieu. Or, qu'enseignait-il ? De ne pas prendre part aux œuvres des ténèbres. Observe ce qu'il commande. Mais qui pouvait pardonner les péchés ? Cela n'appartient qu'à lui seul. Car qui remet les péchés, sinon Dieu seul ? Et bien sûr, les péchés mortels commis contre lui et contre son temple.
en: Discipline governs a man, power sets a seal upon him, apart from the fact that power is the Spirit, but the Spirit is God. What did the Spirit teach? That there must be no communicating with the works of darkness. Observe what he says. Who, moreover, was able to forgive sins? This is his prerogative alone: for "who remits sins but God alone?" And, of course, (who but he can remit) mortal sins, such those committed against himself, and against his temple? [Modesty 21 (c. A.D. 220)].
latin: Disciplina hominem gubernat, potestas adsignat, seorsum quod potestas, spiritus autem Deus. Quid autem docebat? non communicandum operibus tenebrarum. Observa quod jubet. Quis autem poterat donare delicta? hoc solius ipsius est. Quis enim dimittit delicta, ni solus Deus? et utique mortalia quae in ipsum fuerint admissa et in templum ejus.
context:
Additional Details and Context

This is one of the most important and revealing passages in Tertullian's writings. To understand it fully, you must know its context:

    Source and Date: The work is De Pudicitia (On Modesty), written around A.D. 220.

    Author's Stance (Crucial): By this time, Tertullian had broken from the mainstream Catholic Church and become a prominent leader of the Montanists in North Africa. The Montanists (or "New Prophecy") were a rigorist, charismatic movement that believed the Holy Spirit (the Paraclete) was speaking directly through their prophets. This passage is a direct product of his Montanist beliefs.

    The Target of the Argument: Tertullian is writing in fierce opposition to an edict issued by a Bishop of Rome (almost certainly Pope Callixtus I). This bishop had declared that the Church had the authority to forgive even the most serious "mortal sins," such as adultery and fornication, after a period of public penance.

    The Core Argument — Disciplina vs. Potestas: Tertullian is incensed by what he sees as unacceptable laxity. His entire argument in this chapter hinges on a sharp distinction he creates:

        Disciplina (Discipline): This is the authority to teach, govern, and guide the Church. Tertullian says this belongs to the bishops. It is a human, ministerial role.

        Potestas (Power): This is true, divine power. The power to forgive mortal sins, like the power to raise the dead, is a potestas that belongs to God alone.

    Tertullian's Radical Conclusion:

        He argues that while the Apostles wielded this divine potestas, they did so only because they were filled with the Spirit and could prove their divine authority with miracles. He challenges his opponent (the Pope): "Show me your prophetic powers, and I will acknowledge your divine authority" (Exhibe igitur et nunc mihi, apostolice, prophetica exempla, et agnoscam divinitatem).

        He radically re-interprets Matthew 16 ("on this rock... I give you the keys"). He claims this power was given personally to Peter and now belongs only to the "spiritual man" (spiritalem hominem)—that is, a Montanist prophet—and not to the institutional "Church which is a number of bishops" (non ecclesia numerus episcoporum).

In essence, this quote is the heart of a Montanist attack on the developing penitential discipline and episcopal authority of the Catholic Church in the early 3rd century.

fr: En vérité, elle prie pour son âme, et demande pour lui le réconfort dans l'attente et la communion à la première résurrection, et offre le sacrifice aux jours anniversaires de sa mort.
en: A woman, after the death of her husband . . prays for his soul and asks that he may, while waiting, find rest; and that he may share in the first Resurrection. And each year, on the anniversary of his death, she offers the sacrifice [Monogamy 10 (c. A.D. 218)].
latin: Enimvero et pro anima eius orat, et refrigerium interim adpostulat ei, et in prima resurrectione consortium, et offert annuis diebus dormitionis eius.
context:
Additional Details and Context

    Source and Confirmation:

        Author: Tertullian of Carthage (c. 160 – c. 225 AD).

        Work: De Monogamia (On Single Marriage).

        Date: c. 213-218 AD.

        Confirmation: The text you provided is from Chapter 10 of this work. The numbers 0942B and 0942C are column markers from J.-P. Migne's Patrologia Latina, Volume 2, which is the standard collection for Tertullian's writings. Your quote is located at the beginning of column 0942C.

    Theological Argument:

        Tertullian's primary goal in De Monogamia is to argue forcefully against the remarriage of widows. He considers a second marriage to be a form of adultery.

        The passage you've quoted is a crucial part of his proof. He uses the existing, pious practices of a faithful widow to demonstrate that her spiritual bond with her deceased husband is unbroken.

        His logic is: If a widow still prays for her husband's soul, asks for his rest, and offers the Eucharistic sacrifice for him, she is clearly still spiritually united to him. How, then, could she possibly join herself in the flesh to another man without committing a form of spiritual adultery? He uses the Church's accepted practices regarding the dead to bolster his own much stricter conclusion about remarriage.

    Historical and Doctrinal Significance:

        Prayers for the Dead: This is one of the earliest and most explicit non-scriptural witnesses to the Christian practice of praying for the souls of the faithful departed. It shows this was not a later invention but a deeply ingrained custom by the early 3rd century.

        The Eucharistic Sacrifice for the Dead: The word offert ("she offers") is a technical term for the offering of the Eucharistic sacrifice (the Mass). This passage is a cornerstone of historical evidence for the belief that the Eucharist can be offered for the benefit of the dead.

        Early Eschatology: The terminology gives a window into early Christian beliefs about the afterlife:

            refrigerium interim: "rest in the meantime." This refers to a peaceful state for the soul in the intermediate period between individual death and the final judgment.

            in prima resurrectione consortium: "fellowship in the first resurrection." This likely refers to the resurrection of the just who will reign with Christ, as mentioned in the Book of Revelation (Rev. 20:4-6).

    A Note on Tertullian's Montanism:

        It is crucial to know that Tertullian wrote De Monogamia during his Montanist period. Montanism was a charismatic and prophetic movement that embraced a much more rigorous and severe asceticism than the mainstream Catholic Church.

        While the Church permitted the remarriage of widows (as St. Paul does in 1 Corinthians 7), Tertullian, under Montanist influence, condemned it. However, the practices he describes (praying and offering the sacrifice for the dead) were clearly part of the common Catholic tradition he was drawing from, which makes this passage an invaluable historical witness despite the author's schismatic leanings at the time.

fr: ... qu'il y a un Dieu absolument unique, le Créateur du monde ; c'est lui qui a tiré l'univers du néant par son Verbe, émis avant toute chose.
en: [T]here is only one God, and he is none other than the Creator of the world, who produced all things out of nothing through his own Word, first of all sent forth [Prescription Against Heretics 13 (c. A.D. 200)].
latin: ...unum omnino Deum esse, nec alium praeter mundi conditorem; qui universa de nihilo produxerit, per Verbum suum primo omnium emissum.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

This passage is exceptionally important for several reasons. It is not just a passing statement but the beginning of Tertullian's articulation of the Regula Fidei (the "Rule of Faith").

    The Rule of Faith (Regula Fidei):

        The text you provided is one of the earliest and most detailed summaries of the core, non-negotiable tenets of the Christian faith.

        This "Rule of Faith" functioned as a proto-creed. It was the standard of orthodox belief that the Church had received directly from the Apostles. Any teaching that deviated from this Rule was, by definition, heresy.

    The Legal Argument of the Book:

        Tertullian was a trained Roman lawyer, and the title of the book, De Praescriptione Haereticorum, reflects a legal strategy. A praescriptio was a legal maneuver to dismiss a case before hearing its details, based on a preliminary objection.

        Tertullian's argument is that heretics have no legal right to use or debate the Christian Scriptures. The Scriptures belong to the Church because the Church has "title" to them through unbroken succession from the Apostles. The Rule of Faith is the summary of the doctrine that the Church has always taught, proving its ownership and correct interpretation.

    Polemical Significance of the Quote:

        unum omnino Deum esse, nec alium praeter mundi conditorem ("that there is only one God, and he is none other than the Creator of the world"): This was a direct and forceful refutation of the Gnostics and especially Marcion. Marcion taught that the God of the Old Testament, the Creator (Demiurge), was a flawed and wrathful lesser deity, distinct from the loving, supreme God revealed by Jesus. Tertullian insists that the Creator God is the one true God.

        qui universa de nihilo produxerit ("who produced all things out of nothing"): This asserts the doctrine of creation ex nihilo. This distinguished Christian teaching from many pagan philosophies which held that the world was formed from pre-existing, eternal matter. It emphasizes God's absolute sovereignty.

        per Verbum suum primo omnium emissum ("through his own Word, first of all sent forth"): This is a key statement of early Logos theology. The "Word" (Verbum = Greek Logos) is the divine agent of creation. The term emissum ("sent forth" or "emitted") is characteristic of Tertullian's developing Trinitarian language, which was foundational for later Latin theology.

fr: Voici donc la règle de foi, et nous affirmons dès maintenant que c'est elle que nous défendons : il s'agit de croire qu'il n'y a absolument qu'un seul Dieu, et nul autre que le créateur du monde, qui a produit l'univers à partir de rien par son Verbe, émis le premier de tous.
en: Now, with regard to this rule of faith-that we may from this point acknowledge what we defend-it is what prescribes the belief that there is one God. and that he iS none other than the Creator of the world, who produced all things out of nothing through his own Word, first of all sent forth [Prescription Against Heretics 13 (c. A.D. 200)].
latin: Regula est autem fidei, ut jam hinc quid defendamus profiteamur, illa scilicet qua creditur, unum omnino Deum esse, nec alium praeter mundi conditorem; qui universa de nihilo produxerit, per Verbum suum primo omnium emissum.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    The Regula Fidei (Rule of Faith): The passage you've quoted is one of the most important early examples of the Regula Fidei. This was not a fixed, word-for-word creed like the later Nicene Creed, but rather a summary of the core, non-negotiable tenets of the apostolic faith that were taught consistently across all the major Christian churches. Its purpose was to provide a "yardstick" to measure any teaching and quickly identify heresy.

    The Legal Argument of the Book: The book's title, De Praescriptione Haereticorum, is a legal metaphor. In Roman law, a praescriptio was a preliminary objection raised by a defendant to have a case dismissed before it was even heard on its merits. Tertullian's brilliant argument is that heretics have no legal standing to debate the meaning of Scripture. Why? Because the Scriptures are the "property" of the one true Church, which received them from the apostles. The Regula Fidei is the "deed of ownership"—the Church that holds this rule is the rightful heir. Therefore, before a heretic can even begin to argue about a Bible verse, the Church can issue a praescriptio and say, "You have no right to use our book."

    Direct Anti-Heretical Polemic: The specific phrasing of this rule is deliberately targeted at the major heresies of Tertullian's day, especially Gnosticism and Marcionism:

        unum omnino Deum esse, nec alium praeter mundi conditorem ("that there is one God, and that he is none other than the Creator of the world"): This directly refutes the Gnostic and Marcionite belief in a lesser, flawed creator god (the Demiurge) who was distinct from the supreme, unknowable Father revealed by Jesus. Tertullian insists that the God of Creation and the God of Redemption are one and the same.

        qui universa de nihilo produxerit ("who produced all things out of nothing"): This affirms the doctrine of creatio ex nihilo and rejects the pagan philosophical view that God shaped the world from pre-existing, eternal matter.

        per Verbum suum primo omnium emissum ("through his own Word, first of all sent forth"): This introduces the Logos (Word) as the agent of creation. The term emissum ("sent forth" or "emitted") is characteristic of Tertullian's early Trinitarian language, which often used analogies of procession or emanation (like a ray from the sun) to describe the Son's eternal generation from the Father.

    Source Citation: The text you provided with column numbers (0026B) comes from a standard edition, most likely Migne's Patrologia Latina, Volume 2, column 26. This is the classic and most frequently cited source for Tertullian's works

fr: C'est pourquoi ils ont fondé des églises dans chaque cité. Auprès d'elles, les autres églises ont ensuite emprunté — et continuent d'emprunter chaque jour — le surgeon de la foi et les semences de la doctrine pour devenir elles-mêmes des églises. De ce fait, elles sont, elles aussi, considérées comme apostoliques, en tant que descendance des églises apostoliques. Toute lignée doit nécessairement être rattachée à son origine. Par conséquent, ces églises, si nombreuses et si grandes, n'en sont qu'une seule : cette Église première, issue des apôtres, de qui toutes procèdent. Ainsi, toutes sont premières et apostoliques, dès lors qu'elles attestent toutes ensemble de leur unité, tant qu'elles maintiennent entre elles la communion de la paix, le titre de fraternité et le partage des droits de l'hospitalité ; ces liens sacrés n'ont d'autre règle que l'unique tradition d'un même mystère.
en: [The apostles] then in like manner founded churches in every city, from which all the other churches, one after another, derived the Tradition of the faith. and the seeds of doctrine, and are everyday deriving them, that they may become churches. Indeed, it is only on this account that they will be able to deem themselves apostolic, the offspring of apostolic churches. Everything must necessarily revert to its original for its classification. Therefore the churches, although they are so many and so great, comprise but one primitive Church, (founded) by the apostles, from which they all [spring]. In this way all are primitive, and all are apostolic, while they are all proved to be one, in (unbroken) unity [Prescription Against Heretics 20 (C. A.D. 200)].
latin: ...et proinde ecclesias apud unamquamque civitatem condiderunt, a quibus traducem fidei et semina doctrinae, caeterae exinde ecclesiae mutuatae sunt, et quotidie mutuantur ut ecclesiae fiant: ac per hoc et ipsae apostolicae deputantur, ut soboles apostolicarum ecclesiarum. Omne genus ad originem suam censeatur necesse est. Itaque tot ac tantae ecclesiae, una est illa ab Apostolis prima, ex qua omnes. Sic omnes prima, et apostolicae, dum una omnes probant unitatem; dum est illis communicatio pacis, et appellatio fraternitatis, et contesseratio hospitalitatis: quae jura non alia ratio regit, quam ejusdem sacramenti una traditio.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

1. The Author and Work:

    Author: Tertullian of Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 AD), often called the "father of Latin Christianity." He was a brilliant lawyer before his conversion, and his legalistic, precise, and often fiery style profoundly shaped Western theological language.

    Work: De Praescriptione Haereticorum ("The Prescription Against Heretics"), written around A.D. 200. It is one of the most powerful and influential anti-heretical works of the early Church.

2. The Core Argument: "Prescription"
The entire book is a brilliant legal argument. "Prescription" (praescriptio) was a Roman legal term for a procedural objection that could dismiss a case before it was even heard on its merits. A defendant could file a praescriptio to argue that the plaintiff had no legal standing to bring the lawsuit in the first place.

Tertullian applies this to theology: heretics, he argues, have no legal standing to debate the meaning of Scripture. Why? Because the Scriptures belong to the Church. The Church had prior possession of them, received directly from the apostles who received the faith from Christ. Heretics are newcomers, trespassers, and squatters on property that is not theirs. Therefore, the Church doesn't even need to argue Scripture with them; it can simply dismiss their claims on the grounds of "prescription."

3. Context of Chapter 20:
This chapter is the positive side of Tertullian's argument. After establishing that heretics have no claim, he explains who does have the claim: the apostolic churches. This chapter lays out his famous "rule of faith" based on apostolic succession. A church is only legitimate if it can trace its doctrine and lineage back to an original church founded by an apostle.

4. Key Concepts in the Quote:

    Traducem fidei et semina doctrinae: This is a beautiful and powerful metaphor. Tradux in Latin means a vine-shoot or cutting that is planted to propagate a new vine. Semina means "seeds." Tertullian isn't describing the faith as a static list of rules, but as a living, organic thing. The apostles planted the "vine" of faith, and new churches are grown from its cuttings and seeds. This ensures that the new plant is identical to the original.

    Soboles apostolicarum ecclesiarum: "The offspring of apostolic churches." This reinforces the organic, familial metaphor. A church is apostolic because it has a direct, verifiable family lineage.

    Omne genus ad originem suam censeatur: "Every kind must be classified back to its origin." This is the core principle of his argument. To know the true nature of something, you must trace it to its source. The true Church's origin is the apostles; the origin of heresy is some later individual.

    Contesseratio hospitalitatis: The "token of hospitality." This refers to a fascinating practice in the early Church. A tessera was a small token (like a piece of pottery or a seal) that a Christian traveler could carry from their home bishop. When they arrived in a new city, they could present this token to the local bishop to prove they were an orthodox Christian in good standing. This "passport" granted them hospitality and, most importantly, admission to the Eucharist. This was a tangible, practical sign of the "unbroken unity" that bound the apostolic churches together.

fr:
C'est donc ici que nous intervenons, et nous voudrions avant tout faire cette remarque capitale : on ne peut prouver ce que les Apôtres ont prêché — c'est-à-dire ce que le Christ leur a révélé — autrement que par les Églises qu'ils ont eux-mêmes fondées en leur prêchant personnellement, tant de vive voix, comme on dit, que plus tard par leurs lettres.

S'il en est ainsi, il est donc évident que toute doctrine qui s'accorde avec ces Églises apostoliques, mères et sources originelles de la foi, doit être considérée comme la vérité, puisqu'elle détient sans aucun doute ce que les Églises ont reçu des Apôtres, les Apôtres du Christ, et le Christ de Dieu. Inversement, toute doctrine qui contredit la vérité des Églises, des Apôtres, du Christ et de Dieu doit être d'emblée jugée mensongère.

Il reste par conséquent à démontrer si notre doctrine, dont nous avons exposé la règle plus haut, relève bien de la tradition des Apôtres et, par là même, si les autres procèdent du mensonge.
en: [W]hat Christ revealed to them the apostles] can, as must here prescribe, properly be proved in no other way than by those very churches the apostles founded in person, by declaring the gospel to them directly themselves.. If, then, these things are it is also so, it is manifest that all doctrine that agrees with the apostolic churches- those molds and original sources of the faith-must be reckoned for truth, as undoubtedly containing what the (said) churches received from the apostles, the apostles from Christ, Christ from God. All doctrine must be prejudged as false that savors of incompatibility with the truth of the churches and apostles of Christ and God. It remains, then, to demonstrate whether this doctrine of ours, of which we have now given the rule, has its origin in the Tradition of the apostles, and whether all other doctrines do not ipso facto proceed from falsehood [ibid., 21].
latin:
Hic ergo et nos inserimus, et in primis hoc velim graviter praenotaremus, non aliter probari posse quid Apostoli praedicaverint, id est, quid illis Christus revelaverit, nisi per easdem Ecclesias quas ipsi Apostoli condiderunt, ipsi eis praedicando, tam viva, quod aiunt, voce, quam per epistolas postea.

Si haec ita sunt, constat proinde omnem doctrinam, quae cum illis ecclesiis apostolicis, matricibus et originalibus fidei, conspiret, veritati deputandam, id sine dubio tenentem quod ecclesiae ab apostolis, apostoli a Christo, Christus a Deo accepit; omnem vero doctrinam de mendacio praejudicandam, quae sapiat contra veritatem ecclesiarum et apostolorum et Christi et Dei. Superest ergo uti demonstretur, an haec nostra doctrina, cujus regulam supra edidimus, de apostolorum traditione censeatur, et ex hoc ipso, an caeterae de mendacio veniant.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Author: Tertullian of Carthage (c. 160 – c. 225 AD).

    Work: De Praescriptione Haereticorum (often translated as The Prescription of Heretics or On the Prescription Against Heretics), written around A.D. 200.

    The Concept of "Prescription" (Praescriptio): This is the key to the whole book. "Prescription" is a legal term from Roman law, not a medical one. It refers to a legal procedure where a defendant could bar a plaintiff's case from being heard at all by showing a fatal flaw in their claim (e.g., the statute of limitations had passed, or the plaintiff had no legal standing). Tertullian brilliantly applies this to theology. His argument is that heretics have no legal right to even argue from Scripture because the Scriptures belong to the Church, which has prior and continuous possession of them through Apostolic Succession.

    The Argument's Flow:

        Chapter 20 (The text you provided): Tertullian establishes the historical facts. Christ taught the Apostles -> The Apostles preached and founded churches -> All other churches are descended from these original foundations. This establishes the Church's historical pedigree.

        Chapter 21 (The quote you wanted): Tertullian makes his "prescriptive" or legal argument based on those facts. Since the Church has this unbroken chain of custody of the faith (God -> Christ -> Apostles -> Churches), any doctrine that aligns with these apostolic churches is true. Any doctrine that contradicts them is, by that fact alone (ipso facto), false. There is no need to even debate the details of the heretics' scriptural interpretations; their case is thrown out before it begins because they lack the authentic tradition.

    Significance: This passage is one of the most powerful and earliest articulations of the principle of Apostolic Tradition as the rule of faith. It establishes the "apostolicity" of a doctrine as the primary test of its truth. It is a cornerstone of the Catholic and Orthodox understanding of how Christian doctrine is to be preserved and verified.

fr: Quelque chose aurait-il échappé à Pierre, appelé la pierre sur laquelle l'église serait bâtie, lui qui a reçu les clés du royaume des cieux et le pouvoir de délier et de lier dans les cieux et sur la terre ?
en: Was anything withheld from the knowledge of Peter, who is called the rock on which the Church would be built" [Mt 16:18] with the power of "loosing and binding in heaven and on earth? [Mt 16:19]" [Prescription Against Heretics 22 C. A.D. 200)7.

context:
Additional Details and Context

1. Source Confirmation:

    Author: Tertullian of Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 AD)

    Work: De Praescriptione Haereticorum (The Prescription Against Heretics)

    Date: c. A.D. 200

    Location: Chapter 22

2. The Core Argument:
In this chapter, Tertullian is refuting the claims of Gnostic heretics. The Gnostics often argued that they possessed a "secret knowledge" (gnosis) that Christ had passed down secretly, which was unknown to the mainstream Church. To justify this, they would claim one of two things:

    That the Apostles did not know the entire truth (Christ withheld things from them).

    That the Apostles knew the entire truth but did not pass all of it on publicly.

Tertullian attacks the first claim head-on in this passage.

3. The Role of the Quote:
The sentence you highlighted is a brilliant rhetorical question designed to show the absurdity of the Gnostic position. Tertullian's argument is a reductio ad absurdum:

    He asks, "Can anyone of sound mind really believe that the Apostles were ignorant of anything?"

    To prove his point, he uses the chief of the Apostles, Peter, as his prime example. The logic is: If anyone knew the full truth, it must have been Peter.

    He piles on Peter's unique titles and privileges—the Rock on which the Church would be built, the one who received the keys of the kingdom, and the one given the power to bind and loose—to emphasize his foundational importance.

    The implied answer to his question, "Was anything hidden from Peter?" is a resounding and obvious "No!" The very idea, Tertullian suggests, is preposterous. He immediately follows this by asking the same about John, "the beloved disciple."

4. Significance:
This passage is one of the most important and earliest non-biblical Latin testimonies to the unique role and authority of St. Peter. Writing just over a century after the death of the Apostles, Tertullian presents Peter's titles not as points of debate but as well-known, foundational facts of the faith, using them as undeniable proof in his argument against heresy.

fr: Où était alors Marcion, cet armateur du Pont, adepte du stoïcisme ? Où était Valentin, disciple du platonisme ? Car il est bien établi qu'ils ne sont pas si anciens, puisqu'ils vécurent à peu près sous le principat d'Antonin, et qu'ils adhérèrent d'abord à la doctrine catholique au sein de l'église de Rome, sous l'épiscopat du bienheureux Éleuthère. Ils y restèrent jusqu'à ce que leur curiosité toujours inquiète, qui les poussait d'ailleurs à se tenir à l'écart des frères, leur vaille d'être exclus une première, puis une seconde fois...
en: Where was [the heretic] Marcion, that shipmaster of Pontus, the zealous student of Stoicism? Where was Valentinus, the disciple of Platonism? For it is evident that those men lived not so long ago-in the reign of Antonius for the most part-and that they at first were believers in the doctrine of the Catholic Church. in the church of Rome under the episcopate of the blessed Eleutherius, until on account of their ever restless curiosity, with which they even infected the brethren, they were more than once expelled [Prescription Against Heretics 30 (c. A.D. 200)].
latin: Ubi tunc Marcion, ponticus nauclerus, stoicae studiosus? Ubi Valentinus platonicae sectator? Nam constat illos, neque adeo olim fuisse, Antonini fere principatu, et in catholicae primo doctrinam credidisse apud Ecclesiam romanensem, sub episcopatu Eleutherii benedicti, donec ob inquietam semper eorum curiositatem, qua fratres quoque vitabant, semel et iterum ejecti...
context:
Additional Relevant Details

This passage is the very heart of Tertullian's masterful argument against heresy, and understanding its context is key.

    The "Prescription" (Praescriptio): The title of the work is a legal term from Roman law. A "praescriptio" was a preliminary objection that could dismiss a lawsuit before the main arguments were even heard. Tertullian, a trained lawyer, brilliantly applies this to theology. His argument is that we don't even need to debate the heretics on Scripture verse-by-verse. We can dismiss their entire case on a preliminary point: Priority.

    The Argument from Antiquity: Tertullian's core thesis is that truth is by nature older than falsehood. The Catholic Church's teaching is true because it comes directly from Christ through the Apostles. Any teaching that arose later is, by definition, a deviation and a corruption.

    The Quote as Evidence: This passage about Marcion and Valentinus is Tertullian's "Exhibit A." He is using them as prime examples to prove his legal "prescription." His point is devastatingly simple:

        He can name the heretics.

        He can name their philosophical influences (Stoicism, Platonism).

        He can pinpoint the historical period they appeared in ("in the reign of Antoninus").

        Crucially, he can prove they were latecomers. They were not there from the beginning. In fact, they were originally members of the one, true, apostolic Church in Rome.

        He can even name the specific bishop under whom they taught before being expelled: the "blessed Eleutherius" (Pope from c. 174–189 AD).

    The Significance: By providing these specific historical details, Tertullian demonstrates that the heresies of Marcion and Valentinus are innovations. They are not the original faith. The Catholic Church in Rome existed before them, it taught them the original faith, and it had the authority to expel them when they deviated. Therefore, their case is dismissed on the grounds of being a novelty.

    Details from the Rest of the Chapter: The full Latin text you provided adds even more damning detail, mentioning that Marcion was expelled along with the 200,000 sesterces he had donated to the church, and that he later repented but died before he could bring his followers back to the Church. This shows that Tertullian is working with specific historical traditions and records, strengthening his case that the Church's memory and history are the guarantors of true doctrine.

fr:
D'ailleurs, si certaines hérésies osent se rattacher à l’âge apostolique pour donner l’impression d’avoir été transmises par les Apôtres, au prétexte qu’elles existaient à leur époque, nous pouvons leur lancer ce défi : qu’elles exposent donc l’origine de leurs églises ! Qu’elles déroulent la liste de leurs évêques, en suivant la succession depuis l’origine, de sorte que leur tout premier évêque ait eu pour fondateur et prédécesseur l’un des Apôtres, ou l’un de ces hommes apostoliques qui, bien entendu, aura persévéré avec les Apôtres.

C’est en effet de cette manière que les églises apostoliques justifient leur filiation : ainsi, l’Église de Smyrne atteste que Polycarpe y fut établi par Jean, et celle de Rome, que Clément y fut ordonné par Pierre. De même, les autres églises peuvent-elles aussi montrer quels hommes, établis par les Apôtres dans l’épiscopat, elles possèdent comme transmetteurs de la semence apostolique. Que les hérétiques inventent quelque chose de semblable ! Après le blasphème, qu’est-ce qui leur est encore interdit ? Mais même s’ils l’inventaient, cela ne leur servirait à rien. Car leur doctrine elle-même, comparée à celle des Apôtres, manifestera par sa divergence et sa contradiction qu’elle n’a pour auteur ni un apôtre, ni un homme apostolique. En effet, de même que les Apôtres n’auraient pas enseigné des doctrines contradictoires, les hommes apostoliques n’auraient pas non plus transmis un enseignement contraire aux Apôtres – à moins, bien sûr, que ceux qui furent formés par les Apôtres se soient mis à prêcher autre chose !

C’est donc à ce critère que les hérésies seront jugées, par comparaison avec ces églises qui, bien qu’elles ne puissent présenter aucun Apôtre ou homme apostolique comme fondateur — étant beaucoup plus récentes, et de nouvelles étant même fondées chaque jour —, n’en sont pas moins tenues pour apostoliques, parce qu’elles convergent dans la même foi, en vertu de la parenté de leur doctrine. Ainsi, que toutes les hérésies, mises au défi par nos églises selon ce double critère, prouvent donc leur prétendue apostolicité de la manière qui leur conviendra. Mais en réalité, elles ne le sont pas, et ne peuvent prouver ce qu’elles ne sont pas. Elles ne sont d’ailleurs pas accueillies dans la paix et la communion par les églises qui sont, d’une manière ou d’une autre, apostoliques ; et pour cause : en raison de la divergence de leur règle de foi, elles ne sont elles-mêmes en rien apostoliques.
en: But if there be any (heresies) that are bold enough to plant themselves in the midst of the Apostolic Age, that they may thereby seem to have been handed down by the apostles, because they existed in the time of the apostles, we can say: Let them produce the original records of their churches; let them unfold the roll of their bishops, running down in succession from the beginning, in such a way that [that first bishop of theirs] shall be able to show as his ordainer and predecessor one of the apostles or apostolic men-a man, moreover, who continued steadfast with the apostles. For this is the manner in which the apostolic churches transmit their registers: as the church of Smyrna, which records that Polycarp was placed therein by John; as also the church of Rome, which makes Clement to have been ordained by Peter. In exactly the same way the other churches also exhibit [their several worthies], whom, as having been appointed to their episcopal places by apostles, they regard as transmitters of the apostolic seed. Let the heretics contrive something of the same kind. For after their blasphemy, what is unlawful for them [to attempt]? But should they even try to do so, they will not advance step. For their very doctrine, after comparison with that of the a apostles, will declare, by its own diversity and contrariness, that it had as its author neither an apostle nor an apostolic man; because, as the apostles would never have taught things that were self-contradictory, sO the apostolic men would not have taught anything different from the apostles, unless they who received their instruction from the apostles went and preached in a contrary manner. To this test, therefore, will they be submitted for proof by those churches, who, although they don't derive their founder from apostles or apostolic men (as being of much later date, for they are in fact being founded daily), yet, since they agree in the same faith, they are accounted as not less apostolic because they are akin in doctrine. Then let all the heresies, when challenged with these two tests by our apostolic Church, offer proof of how they deem themselves to be apostolic. But in truth they are not. nor are they able to prove themselves to be what they are not. Nor are they admitted to peaceful relations and communion by such churches as are connected with apostles, as they are in no sense themselves apostolic because of their diverse opinions about the mysteries of the faith [ibid., 32].
latin:
Caeterum, si quae audent interserere se aetati apostolicae, ut ideo videantur ab Apostolis traditae, quia sub Apostolis fuerunt, possumus dicere: Edant ergo origines Ecclesiarum suarum: evolvant ordinem episcoporum suorum, ita per successiones ab initio decurrentem, ut primus ille episcopus aliquem ex Apostolis, vel apostolicis viris, qui tamen cum Apostolis perseveraverit, habuerit auctorem et antecessorem.

Hoc enim modo Ecclesiae apostolicae census suos deferunt: sicut Smyrnaeorum Ecclesia Polycarpum ab Joanne conlocatum refert: sicut Romanorum, Clementem a Petro ordinatum edit; proinde utique et caeterae exhibent quos ab Apostolis in episcopatum constitutos apostolici seminis traduces habeant. Confingant tale aliquid Haeretici. Quid enim illis post blasphemiam inlicitum est? Sed etsi confinxerint, nihil promovebunt. Ipsa enim doctrina eorum cum apostolica comparata, ex diversitate et contrarietate sua pronuntiabit, neque apostoli alicujus auctoris esse, neque apostolici; quia sicut Apostoli non diversa inter se docuissent, ita et apostolici non contraria Apostolis edidissent, nisi illi qui ab Apostolis didicerunt aliter praedicaverunt.

Ad hanc itaque formam probabuntur ab illis ecclesiis, quae licet nullum ex Apostolis, vel apostolicis, auctorem suum proferant, ut multo posteriores, quae denique quotidie instituuntur; tamen in eadem fide conspirantes, non minus apostolicae deputantur, pro consanguinitate doctrinae. Ita omnes haereses ad utramque formam nostris Ecclesiis provocatae, probent se quaqua putant apostolicas. Sed adeo nec sunt, nec probare possunt quod non sunt, nec recipiuntur in pacem et communicationem ab Ecclesiis quoquo modo apostolicis, scilicet ob diversitatem sacramenti nullo modo apostolicae.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

1. Name of the Work:
The work is De Praescriptione Haereticorum, which translates to "On the Prescription of Heretics" or, more accurately, "The Prescription Against Heretics."

2. The Central Argument (The "Prescription"):
Tertullian, who was trained as a lawyer in Rome, uses a brilliant legal metaphor. In Roman law, a praescriptio was a preliminary legal objection raised by a defendant to have a case dismissed without even hearing the main arguments. The defendant would argue that the plaintiff had no legal standing to bring the case in the first place (e.g., because of a statute of limitations or a defect in their claim).

Tertullian applies this to theology. He argues that the Catholic Church has prior possession of the truth and the Scriptures. Therefore, heretics have no legal standing to use the Scriptures to argue their case. The Church's long-standing, public, and consistent teaching "prescribes" against them, dismissing their novel claims before the debate even begins.

3. The Twofold Test of Apostolicity:
This chapter lays out a clear, two-part test for any community claiming to be Christian:

    Test 1: Apostolic Succession (Historical Continuity): Can you trace your leadership back to an Apostle? Tertullian issues a direct challenge: "Let them unfold the roll of their bishops" (evolvant ordinem episcoporum suorum). He provides concrete examples: Smyrna traces its bishop Polycarp to the Apostle John, and Rome traces its bishop Clement to the Apostle Peter. This is a public, historical, and verifiable claim that Gnostic groups, with their claims of secret knowledge, could not match.

    Test 2: Apostolic Doctrine (Theological Continuity): Does your teaching match what the Apostles taught? This is the ultimate test. Even if a church is new and cannot physically trace its founder to an Apostle, it is still considered "apostolic" if it shares the same faith. Tertullian calls this the "kinship of doctrine" (pro consanguinitate doctrinae). Conversely, even if heretics could forge a succession list, their doctrine itself, by its "diversity and contrariness" (ex diversitate et contrarietate), would prove they are not apostolic.

4. Key Terminology:

    Apostolici seminis traduces: "Transmitters of the apostolic seed." This is a powerful organic metaphor. The bishops in the apostolic line are not just officeholders; they are the conduits through which the living "seed" of the apostolic faith is passed down through generations.

    Pro consanguinitate doctrinae: "On account of the kinship/blood-relationship of doctrine." This beautiful phrase emphasizes that the unity of the Church is like that of a family, bound together by a shared inheritance of faith.

fr: C'est de cette manière, en effet, que les églises apostoliques présentent leurs titres de succession : ainsi, l'église de Smyrne rapporte que Polycarpe fut établi par Jean ; de même, celle de Rome fait connaître que Clément fut ordonné par Pierre.
en: For this is the manner in which the apostolic churches transmit their registers: as the church of Smyrna, which records that Polycarp was placed therein by John; as also the church of Rome, which makes Clement to have been ordained in like manner by Peter [ibid., 32].
