Additional Relevant Details

    Author: Tertullian of Carthage (c. 160 – c. 225 AD), an early and brilliant Christian author from North Africa, often called the "father of Latin Christianity."

    Work: De Praescriptione Haereticorum ("The Prescription of Heretics"). The title uses a Roman legal term, praescriptio, which was a legal objection or demurrer that could be raised to stop a lawsuit before it even got to the main arguments.

    Date: Written around A.D. 200.

    Context and Significance of the Argument:
    This passage is the core of Tertullian's argument against Gnostic and other heretical groups. He establishes a powerful legal and historical test to determine true Christian doctrine. His argument is:

        The apostles received the full truth from Christ and founded churches.

        They appointed bishops as their successors to hand down this same truth.

        Therefore, any church that can demonstrate an unbroken line of succession from one of the apostles (Apostolic Succession) is guaranteed to hold the authentic apostolic faith.

        Heretical groups, which arose later, cannot produce such a "register" or "census" (census) of their bishops. Therefore, their claim to apostolic truth is invalid from the start, and there is no need to even debate Scripture with them.

    The Power of the Examples:

        Smyrna: Citing Polycarp's appointment by the Apostle John was a powerful move. Polycarp was a revered martyr and a direct link to the apostolic age, making the authority of the churches in Asia Minor undeniable.

        Rome: Mentioning Clement's ordination by the Apostle Peter established the apostolic foundation of the Roman Church as the benchmark for the West. (It is worth noting that other early writers, like St. Irenaeus, place Clement as the third successor after Peter, following Linus and Anacletus. Tertullian's main point, however, is the direct apostolic origin, not the precise numerical order).

A.D. 200)].

context:
Additional Relevant Details

    The Meaning of "Prescription" (Praescriptio): The title of the work is a legal term from Roman law. A praescriptio was a legal objection or demurrer lodged at the beginning of a trial to argue that the opposing party had no legal standing to even bring their case. Tertullian, a trained lawyer, brilliantly applies this concept to theology. His argument is that heretics have no right to debate or interpret the Scriptures because the Scriptures do not belong to them. They are the rightful inheritance of the Church, which received them from the Apostles.

    The Argument from Apostolic Succession: This passage is a classic and foundational statement of the doctrine of Apostolic Succession. Tertullian’s challenge to the heretical sects is simple and devastating: "Show us your origins." He demands that they produce their lists (census) of bishops, tracing a line of succession back to one of the Apostles or an apostolic man. The inability to do so proves they are illegitimate, later innovations.

    Significance of the Specific Examples:

        Smyrna and Rome: Tertullian deliberately chooses two of the most prominent and unimpeachable churches, one in the Greek-speaking East (Smyrna) and one in the Latin-speaking West (Rome), to show that this is a universal standard.

        Polycarp and John: The connection between St. Polycarp of Smyrna and the Apostle John was a cornerstone of the 2nd-century Church's defense against Gnosticism. St. Irenaeus of Lyons, who was a disciple of Polycarp, frequently used this direct, personal link (John -> Polycarp -> Irenaeus) to prove that the Church’s teaching was public and authentic, not a secret tradition as the Gnostics claimed.

        Clement and Peter: This is one of the earliest explicit written statements linking the Church of Rome's authority directly to the Apostle Peter. While other early sources like St. Irenaeus list Clement as the third bishop after Peter (following Linus and Anacletus), Tertullian's statement that he was "ordained by Peter" powerfully affirms the direct Petrine foundation of the Roman See. This doesn't necessarily contradict Irenaeus; it could mean Peter ordained Clement as a bishop for a specific role, even if he did not immediately succeed him as the head of the church.

    Public vs. Secret Tradition: The entire force of Tertullian's argument rests on the public, historical, and verifiable nature of the apostolic succession. The "registers" (census) were public lists. This was a direct counter-attack on the Gnostic claim to a secret, invisible line of "knowledge" passed down from master to disciple. For Tertullian, true Christian authority is visible, historical, and institutional.

fr: Si, par ailleurs, tu es proche de l'Italie, tu as Rome, d'où l'autorité nous est aussi accessible. Bienheureuse Église ! C'est pour elle que les Apôtres ont répandu toute leur doctrine avec leur propre sang ; là où Pierre est assimilé à la passion du Seigneur ; là où Paul est couronné de la même fin que Jean ; là où l'apôtre Jean, après avoir été plongé dans l'huile bouillante sans en souffrir, est exilé sur une île.
en: Since, moreover, you are close upon Italy, you have Rome, from which there comes even into our own hands the very authority of apostles themselves). How happy is its church. on which apostles poured forth all their doctrine along with their blood! Where Peter endures a passion like his Lord's! Where Paul wins his crown in death like John's! Where the apostle John was first plunged, unhurt, into boiling oil, and thence remitted to his island exile! [Prescription Against Heretics 36 (c. A.D. 200)].
latin: Si autem Italiae adjaces, habes Romam, unde nobis quoque auctoritas praesto est. Ista quam felix Ecclesia! cui totam doctrinam Apostoli cum sanguine suo profuderunt; ubi Petrus passioni Dominicae adaequatur; ubi Paulus Joannis exitu coronatur; ubi Apostolus Joannes, posteaquam, in oleum igneum demersus, nihil passus est, in insulam relegatur.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

This passage is highly significant for several historical and theological reasons.

1. Context of the Work (De Praescriptione Haereticorum):
Tertullian, a brilliant Roman-trained lawyer from Carthage, wrote this work around A.D. 200. His argument is a legal one. The term praescriptio was a legal procedure in Roman law used to dismiss a case before it even went to trial. Tertullian’s argument is that heretics have no legal right to argue from the Scriptures because the Scriptures do not belong to them. They belong to the Church, which received them directly from the Apostles.

2. The "Apostolic See" Argument:
In this chapter, Tertullian gives a practical test for finding the true faith: go to the churches founded directly by the Apostles. He tells his reader to survey the great apostolic sees: Corinth in Greece, Philippi in Macedonia, Ephesus in Asia. This establishes a clear principle of apostolic succession as the guarantor of orthodox doctrine.

3. The Special Status of Rome:
When he turns to Italy, his tone becomes one of exceptional praise. Rome is not just another apostolic see; it is uniquely blessed.

    "unde nobis quoque auctoritas praesto est": "from which authority is available to us also." For Tertullian in Carthage (North Africa), Rome was the nearest and most preeminent apostolic authority.

    "Ista quam felix Ecclesia!": "How happy is that Church!" The word felix implies not just happiness but also blessedness, fortune, and fruitfulness.

    "totam doctrinam... cum sanguine suo profuderunt": "poured forth all their doctrine along with their blood." The foundation of the Roman Church is uniquely built upon both the complete teaching and the ultimate witness (martyrdom) of the Apostles.

4. The "Triple Apostolic Crown" of Rome:
The climax of the passage is Tertullian’s enumeration of the apostolic glories of Rome, linking it to the three most prominent apostles:

    Peter: His passion is "made equal to the Lord's" (passioni Dominicae adaequatur), a reference to the tradition that Peter was crucified.

    Paul: He is "crowned with a death like John's" (Joannis exitu coronatur). This refers not to John the Apostle, but to John the Baptist, who was beheaded, just as Paul was according to tradition.

    John the Apostle: Tertullian recounts the ancient tradition that the Apostle John was miraculously saved after being plunged into boiling oil at the Latin Gate in Rome, before being exiled to Patmos. This constitutes a "white martyrdom"—the willingness to die and a miraculous preservation by God.

Conclusion: This passage is one of the earliest and most powerful patristic testimonies to the special dignity of the Church of Rome. Its authority, for Tertullian, rests on its direct connection to the foundational acts of teaching and martyrdom of the "Princes of the Apostles," Peter and Paul, as well as the miraculous witness of John.

fr: En effet, peu leur importent leurs divergences, du moment qu’ils s’unissent pour saper l’unique vérité. Tous sont bouffis d’orgueil, tous promettent la connaissance. Leurs catéchumènes sont parfaits avant même d’être instruits. Leurs femmes hérétiques elles-mêmes, quelle impudence ! Elles qui osent enseigner, débattre, pratiquer des exorcismes, jusqu’à promettre des guérisons.
en: [It matters not to them, however different their treatment of subjects, provided that they can conspire together to storm the citadel of the one truth. All are puffed up, all offer you knowledge. Their catechumens are perfect before they are fully taught. The very women of these heretics, how wanton they are! For they are bold enough to teach, to dispute, to enact exorcisms, to undertake cures [ Prescription Against Heretics 41 (c. A.D. 200)].
latin: Nihil enim interest illis, licet diversa tractantibus, dum ad unius veritatis expugnationem conspirent. Omnes tument, omnes scientiam pollicentur. Ante sunt perfecti catechumeni, quam edocti. Ipsae mulieres haereticae, quam procaces! quae audeant docere, contendere, exorcismos agere, curationes repromittere.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

1. Source and Author:

    Author: Tertullian of Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 AD), a brilliant and fiery Christian writer, often called the "father of Latin Christianity."

    Work: De Praescriptione Haereticorum ("On the Prescription of Heretics").

    Date: Written around A.D. 200.

2. Context of the Work (The "Prescription"):
The title is a legal term. Tertullian, a trained lawyer, makes a brilliant legalistic argument. A "prescription" (praescriptio) in Roman law was a procedural objection that could dismiss a case before it was even heard on its merits. Tertullian argues that the Catholic Church holds the "title deed" to the Christian faith because it can trace its doctrine and leadership in an unbroken line back to the apostles (apostolic succession). Therefore, heretics, who are innovators and latecomers, have no legal standing (praescriptio) to even debate the Church or use its Scriptures. Their case should be dismissed out of hand.

3. Context of Chapter 41:
This chapter is the climax of Tertullian's polemic. Having made his theological and legal arguments, he now turns to a scathing sociological critique. He contrasts the strict order, discipline, and reverence of the Catholic Church with what he portrays as the chaotic, arrogant, and worldly behavior within heretical groups. This quote is the centerpiece of that critique.

4. Analysis of the Quote's Key Points:

    "ad unius veritatis expugnationem conspirent" ("conspire to storm the citadel of the one truth"): Tertullian claims that the only thing heretical sects have in common is their opposition to the Catholic Church. They may disagree wildly with each other, but they unite in their attack on the one, apostolic truth.

    "Omnes tument, omnes scientiam pollicentur" ("All are puffed up, all promise knowledge"): This is a direct shot at Gnostic groups. "Gnosticism" comes from the Greek word gnosis (knowledge). These groups claimed to offer a secret, superior knowledge to a select few, and Tertullian mocks this as pure arrogance.

    "Ante sunt perfecti catechumeni, quam edocti" ("Their catechumens are perfect before they are fully taught"): He contrasts the heretics' "easy initiation" with the rigorous, multi-year process of instruction (the catechumenate) required in the Catholic Church before baptism. He sees their process as shallow and unserious.

    "Ipsae mulieres haereticae, quam procaces!" ("The very women of these heretics, how wanton!"): This is one of the most famous and controversial lines. Tertullian is shocked by the prominent roles women played in some dissident Christian groups (like the Montanists, to whom he would later convert). The activities he lists—teaching, disputing, performing exorcisms, and undertaking cures—were roles that, in the mainstream Church of his time, were increasingly reserved for the ordained male clergy. He presents this empowerment of women as a sign of radical disorder and a breakdown of proper discipline.

fr: En effet, Dieu ne tient pas pour valable le rejet des bonnes œuvres, puisqu'elles sont siennes. Comme il en est l'auteur et le défenseur, il est donc nécessaire qu'il les accueille ; et s'il les accueille, il les récompense aussi.
en: For God, never giving his sanction to the condemnation of good deeds, because they are his own (of which, being the author, he must necessarily be the defender too), IS in like manner the acceptor of them, and if the acceptor, likewise the rewarder [ Repentance 2 (c. A.D. 203)].
latin: Deus enim reprobationem bonorum ratam non habet utpote suorum, quorum cum auctor et defensor sit, necesse est proinde et acceptator; si acceptator, etiam remunerator.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Precise Citation: The passage is from De Paenitentia, Chapter 2. In Migne's Patrologia Latina, it is found in PL 1, column 1230A. The modern critical edition is in Corpus Christianorum, Series Latina (CCSL) 1, page 323.

    Context of the Argument: Tertullian's primary argument in this chapter is to define the proper object of repentance. He is forcefully arguing that repentance is exclusively for sins, never for good deeds. He is likely combatting a mindset where someone might regret doing a good deed if it was met with ingratitude or led to a negative personal outcome. He states this clearly a little later: "Let the ingratitude of men see to it, if it compels repentance even for good deeds... A good deed has God as its debtor, just as an evil one does." (Viderit ergo ingratia hominum, si etiam bonis factis poenitentiam cogit... Bonum factum Deum habet debitorem, sicuti et malum.)

    Theological Significance of the Quote: Your chosen quote is the theological anchor for his entire argument. It explains why one must never repent of a good deed. The logic is as follows:

        Good deeds are fundamentally God's own works ("utpote suorum").

        God is their author (auctor) and their defender (defensor).

        Therefore, to reject or condemn a good deed is to reject something that originates from and is protected by God Himself.

        Because God is their author and defender, He is necessarily also their acceptor (acceptator).

        And because God is a just judge who accepts good deeds, He must also be their rewarder (remunerator).

    To "repent" of a good deed would be to place oneself in opposition to this entire divine economy of creation, defense, acceptance, and reward. It is an illogical and impious act.

fr:
Je présume que la plupart des gens, considérant cette démarche comme un étalage public de leur personne, la fuient ou la remettent de jour en jour, plus soucieux de leur pudeur que de leur salut. Ils ressemblent à ceux qui, atteints d'une maladie aux parties les plus intimes du corps, se dérobent au savoir des médecins et meurent ainsi, consumés par leur honte.

Intolérable, n'est-ce pas, pour leur pudeur, de donner satisfaction au Seigneur offensé et d'être rétablis dans le salut qu'ils ont trahi ! Quelle admirable pudeur que la tienne, en vérité ! Tu lèves le front pour pécher, mais tu le baisses pour supplier.

Pour ma part, je ne laisse aucune place à la honte, car je gagne bien plus à sa disparition. Elle-même, en quelque sorte, semble exhorter l'homme en lui disant : « Ne t'occupe pas de moi ; grâce à toi, il vaut mieux pour moi périr. »
en: Yet most men either shun this work, as a public exposure of themselves, or else defer it from day to day. presume (they are) more mindful of modesty than salvation; just like men who, having contracted some malady in the more private parts of the body, avoid the probing of physicians, and so perish of their own bashfulness. It is intolerable for modesty to make satisfaction to the offended Lord! To be restored to its forfeited salvation! Truly you are honorable in your modesty; bearing an open forehead for sinning, but an abashed one for deprecating! I give no place to bashfulness when I am a gainer by its loss; when it exhorts the man, "Respect not me; it is better that perish through you than you through me" [ Repentance 10 (c. A.D. 203)].
latin: Plerosque tamen hoc opus, ut publicationem sui, aut suffugere, aut de die in diem differre, praesumo; pudoris magis memores quam salutis: velut illi, qui in partibus verecundioribus corporis contracta vexatione, conscientiam medentium vitant, et ita cum erubescentia sua pereunt. Intolerandum scilicet pudori, Domino offenso satisfacere, saluti prodactae reformari. Nae tu verecunda bonus, ad delinquendum expandens frontem, ad deprecandum vero subducens. Ego rubori locum non facio, cum plus de detrimento ejus acquiro, cum ipse hominem quodammodo exhortatur, Ne me respexeris, dicens, per te mihi melius est perire.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Author and Work: Tertullian of Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) was a prolific and brilliant early Christian author from North Africa. He was the first major Christian writer to produce an extensive body of literature in Latin. The work, De Paenitentia (On Repentance), was written around 203 AD, during his orthodox Catholic period before he fully embraced the more rigorist Montanist movement.

    Full Citation: The text you found is from Migne's Patrologia Latina, Volume 1, columns 1245-1246. This is the standard scholarly reference for this work.

    Context of the Quote: This passage is the heart of Chapter 10, where Tertullian addresses the single greatest obstacle to public penance: shame or modesty (pudor). In the early Church, reconciliation for serious post-baptismal sins (like apostasy, murder, or adultery) required a formal, public process known as exomologesis. This involved public confession, wearing sackcloth, fasting, and prostrating oneself before the congregation to ask for their prayers. It was, by design, a humbling and public act.

    Tertullian's Argument: Tertullian is furious with Christians who, out of a false sense of modesty, would rather hide their sin and risk eternal damnation than endure the temporary embarrassment of public penance. His argument is a masterpiece of rhetoric:

        Medical Analogy: He compares the sinner to a person with a disease in a private part of their body who, out of shame, avoids the doctor and dies. For Tertullian, sin is a mortal wound that requires radical treatment, and hiding it out of bashfulness is spiritual suicide.

        Sarcasm and Irony: The line, "Truly you are honorable in your modesty; bearing an open forehead for sinning, but an abashed one for deprecating!" is a classic piece of Tertullian's biting sarcasm. He points out the absurd hypocrisy of being bold enough to sin publicly or privately but too shy to ask for forgiveness.

        Personification: The most brilliant part is his personification of Shame (rubor), which tells the sinner to ignore it and save himself: "It is better that I [shame] perish through you than you [the sinner] perish through me." He argues that sacrificing one's pride is a small price to pay for eternal life.

    Theological Significance: This passage is a vital historical witness to the practice and theology of public penance in the early third-century Church. It underscores the belief that reconciliation is not just a private matter between the soul and God, but an ecclesial act that involves the entire community, which suffers with the sinner and labors for their restoration.

fr: ... il suffirait de cet argument : aucune âme ne peut absolument obtenir le salut si elle n’a pas cru tandis qu’elle est dans la chair. À ce point la chair est le pivot du salut. ... De fait, la chair est lavée, pour que l’âme soit purifiée ; la chair est ointe, pour que l’âme soit consacrée ; la chair est marquée du signe, pour que l’âme aussi soit fortifiée ; la chair est couverte de l’ombre par l’imposition de la main, pour que l’âme aussi soit illuminée par l’Esprit ; la chair se nourrit du corps et du sang du Christ, pour que l’âme aussi se rassasie de Dieu. Ne peuvent donc être séparées dans la récompense, celles que l’œuvre unit.
en: It would suffice to say, indeed, that there iS not a soul that can at all procure salvation, except believe while it is in the flesh, so true is that the flesh is the very condition on which salvation hinges. The flesh. indeed, is washed, that the soul may be cleansed; the flesh is anointed, that the soul may be consecrated; the flesh is signed (with the cross), that the soul may be fortified; the flesh is shadowed with the imposition of hands, that the soul may be illuminated by the Spirit; the flesh feeds on the body and blood of Christ, that the soul may fatten on its God. They cannot then be separated in their recompense when they are united in their service [ Resurrection of the Flesh 8 (c. A.D. 210)].
latin: ...sufficeret illi, quod nulla omnino anima salutem possit adipisci, nisi dum est in carne crediderit: adeo caro salutis est cardo. ... Scilicet caro abluitur, ut anima emaculetur; caro ungitur, ut anima consecretur; caro signatur, ut et anima muniatur; caro manus impositione adumbratur, ut et anima spiritu illuminetur; caro corpore et sanguine Christi vescitur, ut et anima Deo saginetur. Non possunt ergo separari in mercede, quas opera conjungit.
context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. Source and Citation

    Author: Tertullian of Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 AD)

    Work: De Resurrectione Carnis (On the Resurrection of the Flesh)

    Chapter: 8

    Approximate Date: c. A.D. 210-212

    Migne Citation: The text you found, with the marginal numbers like 0806B, confirms it is from Patrologia Latina (PL), Volume 2, columns 805-806.

2. Theological Context: Anti-Gnosticism

This entire treatise is a polemic written against Gnostic and Marcionite heresies. Gnostics viewed the material world, and especially the human body ("the flesh"), as an evil prison for the pure, spiritual soul. They found the Christian doctrine of the resurrection of the flesh to be repulsive and nonsensical. Tertullian’s argument is a brilliant reversal: he contends that the flesh is not an obstacle to salvation but is essential to it.
3. The Famous Maxim: Caro Salutis Est Cardo

The phrase adeo caro salutis est cardo is one of the most famous maxims in all of patristic literature.

    Caro: The flesh, the body.

    Salutis: Of salvation.

    Est: Is.

    Cardo: The hinge of a door.

A literal translation is "Therefore, the flesh is the hinge of salvation." It means that the entire plan of salvation swings upon the flesh. Without the Incarnation (God becoming flesh), there is no salvation. And, as this passage argues, without the flesh participating in the sacraments, the soul cannot receive grace.
4. Early Evidence for the Sacraments

This passage is a treasure trove of information about the sacramental life of the Church in North Africa around A.D. 200. Tertullian lists a series of physical, sacramental actions performed on the body and links each one to a corresponding spiritual effect on the soul.

    caro abluitur (the flesh is washed): This is Baptism.

    caro ungitur (the flesh is anointed): This refers to the post-baptismal anointing with chrism, a central part of what would become Confirmation (Chrismation).

    caro signatur (the flesh is signed): This is the Sign of the Cross, made upon the forehead during the baptismal and confirmation rites.

    caro manus impositione adumbratur (the flesh is overshadowed by the laying on of hands): This is the Imposition of Hands, a key liturgical act for conferring the Holy Spirit, associated with Confirmation and Ordination.

    caro corpore et sanguine Christi vescitur (the flesh feeds on the body and blood of Christ): This is a clear and unambiguous reference to the Eucharist.

The concluding sentence—Non possunt ergo separari in mercede, quas opera conjungit ("Therefore, they cannot be separated in their reward, whom their works unite")—is the logical capstone: since the body and soul work together for salvation, they will be rewarded together in the resurrection.

fr: À ce point, la chair est le pivot du salut. En somme, quand l'âme est unie à Dieu, c'est la chair qui rend cette union possible. Ainsi, la chair est lavée pour que l'âme soit purifiée ; la chair est ointe pour que l'âme soit consacrée ; la chair est marquée du signe pour que l'âme aussi soit fortifiée ; la chair est ombrée par l'imposition des mains pour que l'âme aussi soit illuminée par l'Esprit ; la chair se nourrit du corps et du sang du Christ pour que l'âme aussi se nourrisse de Dieu.
en: [T]here is not a soul that can at all procure salvation, except it believe while it is in the flesh, so true iS it that the flesh is the very condition on which salvation hinges. And since the soul is, in consequence of its salvation, chosen to the service of God, it is the flesh that actually renders it capable of such service. The flesh, indeed, is washed [in baptism], that the soul may be cleansed. The flesh is shadowed with the imposition of hands [in confirmation], that the soul may be illuminated by the Spirit; the flesh feeds [in the Eucharist] on the body and blood of Christ, that the soul may fatten on its God [ Resurrection of the Flesh 8 (c. A.D. 210)].
latin: ...adeo caro salutis est cardo. Denique cum anima Deo allegitur, ipsa est quae efficit ut anima allegi possit. Scilicet caro abluitur, ut anima emaculetur; caro ungitur, ut anima consecretur; caro signatur, ut et anima muniatur; caro manus impositione adumbratur, ut et anima spiritu illuminetur; caro corpore et sanguine Christi vescitur, ut et anima Deo saginetur.
context:
Additional Details and Context

You have pinpointed one of the most important passages in early Christian theology for several reasons:

    Theological Context: Anti-Gnosticism: Tertullian's primary target in this work are Gnostic and Marcionite heretics who held the physical body in contempt. They saw the flesh as an evil prison for the pure, spiritual soul and believed salvation was an escape from the body. Tertullian’s argument is a radical affirmation of the goodness of the flesh as created by God and as the instrument of salvation.

    Sacramental Theology: This passage is a foundational text for Western sacramental theology. Tertullian masterfully uses a series of parallel phrases to show the inseparable link between the physical, visible action of the sacraments and the invisible, spiritual grace they impart. He lists:

        Baptism: The flesh is washed (caro abluitur) so the soul can be cleansed (ut anima emaculetur).

        Confirmation/Anointing: The flesh is anointed (caro ungitur), signed (caro signatur), and overshadowed by the laying on of hands (caro manus impositione adumbratur) so the soul can be consecrated, fortified, and illuminated by the Spirit.

        Eucharist: The flesh feeds on the body and blood of Christ (caro corpore et sanguine Christi vescitur) so the soul can be fattened on God (ut et anima Deo saginetur).

    The Key Phrase: "Caro salutis est cardo": This is one of Tertullian's most famous and brilliant phrases.

        Literal Meaning: "The flesh is the hinge of salvation."

        Significance: A cardo was the pivot or hinge on which a heavy Roman door swung. Tertullian’s metaphor is powerful: the entire weight of our salvation—a massive, spiritual reality—turns upon the physical reality of the flesh. The soul's destiny hinges on what the body does, experiences, and believes. Without the flesh, there is no access to the salvation offered through the Incarnate Christ and his sacraments. This single phrase demolishes the Gnostic worldview.

fr: Par conséquent, aie confiance qu'il a tiré tout cela du néant, et tu connais Dieu en croyant à une telle puissance.
latin: Igitur confide illum totum hoc ex nihilo protulisse, et Deum nosti, fidendo quod tantum Deus valeat.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Author: Tertullian (Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus, c. 155 – c. 220 AD). The reference to "Paracletus per prophetidem Priscam" (the Paraclete through the prophetess Prisca) is a clear indicator, as Tertullian was an adherent of the Montanist movement.

    Work: De Resurrectione Carnis (On the Resurrection of the Flesh).

    Chapter: 11 (Caput XI).

    Argumentative Context: This passage is a cornerstone of Tertullian's defense of the bodily resurrection. His primary goal is to prove that God has the power to reconstitute the human body after death. To do this, he employs an a fortiori argument (from the greater to the lesser).

    Theological Point: Tertullian introduces the doctrine of creatio ex nihilo (creation out of nothing) as the ultimate demonstration of God's omnipotence. His logic is that if God was powerful enough to create the entire universe from absolute nothingness, then He is more than powerful enough to perform the "lesser" miracle of re-creating a human body from its pre-existing, though scattered, material.

    Direct Link to Resurrection: Tertullian makes this connection explicit later in the same paragraph with another powerful statement:

        Sive enim ex nihilo Deus molitus est cuncta, poterit et carnem, in nihilum perductam, exprimere de nihilo.
        (This second quote directly links God's power to create all things from nothing with his power to bring back the flesh, even if it has been reduced to "nothing," from that same nothingness.)

fr: Ainsi, ce qui n'est pas dans la chair ne peut non plus être pris en compte pour le salut. À tel point que la chair est le pivot du salut. Et lorsque l'âme s'unit à la chair en vue du salut, c'est la chair qui rend cette union possible. De fait, la chair est lavée, pour que l'âme soit purifiée ; la chair est ointe, pour que l'âme soit consacrée ; la chair est marquée du signe, pour que l'âme soit elle aussi fortifiée ; la chair est placée sous l'ombre de l'imposition des mains, pour que l'âme soit elle aussi illuminée par l'Esprit ; la chair se nourrit du corps et du sang du Christ, pour que l'âme se repaisse elle aussi de Dieu.
en: And so the flesh shall rise again, wholly in every man, in its own identity, in its absolute integrity. Wherever it may be, it is in safe keeping in God's presence, through that most faithful "mediator between God and man, (the man) Jesus Christ" [1 Tm 2:5], who shall reconcile God to man, and man to God; the spirit to the flesh, and the flesh to the spirit [Resurrection of the Flesh 63 c. A.D. 210)].
latin: Itaque quae in carne non est, nec in salutem potest computari. Adeo caro salutis est cardo. Et cum anima carni ob salutem annectitur, caro est quae efficit ut anima annecti possit. Plane caro lavatur, ut anima emaculetur; caro ungitur, ut anima consecretur; caro signatur, ut et anima muniatur; caro manus impositione adumbratur, ut et anima spiritu illuminetur; caro corpore et sanguine Christi vescitur, ut et anima de Deo saginetur.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    The Core Argument ("Caro salutis est cardo"): The passage you selected is the beautiful illustration of the chapter's main thesis, which is summed up in the iconic phrase that comes just before it: "Adeo caro salutis est cardo"—"So true is it that the flesh is the hinge of salvation." A cardo is a hinge or a pivot point; Tertullian is arguing that the entire system of salvation pivots on the reality and goodness of the human body.

    Anti-Gnostic Polemic: Tertullian wrote this entire book to combat Gnostic heresies. Gnostics universally despised the material world and the physical body, seeing it as an evil prison for the pure, spiritual soul. They believed salvation was the escape of the soul from the flesh. Tertullian's argument is a direct and devastating refutation of this idea.

    Sacramental Theology: This passage is one of the most important early witnesses to the practice and theology of the sacraments in the Western Church. Tertullian's rhetorical strategy is to list the physical, tangible actions of Christian initiation and life to prove his point:

        "Caro lavatur" (The flesh is washed): Refers to Baptism.

        "Caro ungitur" (The flesh is anointed) and "caro signatur" (the flesh is signed): Refers to post-baptismal anointing and the sign of the cross (Confirmation).

        "Caro manus impositione adumbratur" (The flesh is overshadowed by the laying on of hands): Also refers to Confirmation/the gift of the Spirit.

        "Caro corpore et sanguine Christi vescitur" (The flesh feeds on the body and blood of Christ): Refers to the Eucharist.

    The Logic: His logic is irrefutable: If the flesh were evil and irrelevant to salvation as the Gnostics claim, why would God use profoundly physical means (water, oil, hands, bread, and wine) to save the soul? The fact that God sanctifies the soul through the flesh proves the goodness and essential role of the flesh in God's plan. The body is not a prison to be escaped, but an instrument to be sanctified.

fr: De plus, nous annonçons un jugement fixé par Dieu après la mort, selon les mérites de chacun.
en: Again, we [Christians] affirm that a judgment has been ordained by God according to the merits of every man [ To the Nations 19 (A.D. 197)].
latin: Item judicium annuntiamus a Deo pro cujusque meritis post interitum destinatum.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Author and Work: The quote is from Tertullian of Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 AD), one of the most brilliant and fiery of the early Latin Church Fathers. The work is his early apologetic treatise Ad Nationes (To the Nations), written around A.D. 197.

    Immediate Context (The "Tu Quoque" Argument): This passage is a prime example of Tertullian's masterful and aggressive apologetic style. In this chapter, he is refuting pagan mockery of core Christian beliefs—specifically the resurrection of the dead and the final judgment. His strategy is not just to defend Christian doctrine but to turn the tables by demonstrating that pagans hold similar, yet often less rational, beliefs. This is a form of the tu quoque ("you also") argument.

    The Comparison: Immediately after stating the Christian belief in a final judgment by God based on merits, Tertullian points out the pagan parallel:

        "Id vos Minoi et Radamantho adscribitis..."
        ("This you ascribe to Minos and Rhadamanthus...")

    He is reminding his pagan audience that their own mythology includes judges of the dead in the underworld. He continues the comparison by noting that Christians believe the wicked will go to eternal fire and the righteous to a place of delight, which directly parallels the pagan concepts of Pyriphlegethon (the river of fire) and Elysium (the paradise for heroes).

    Rhetorical Goal: Tertullian's point is devastatingly effective: "How can you mock us for believing in a final judgment when your own poets, myths, and even philosophers affirm a similar, though less perfect, version of the same idea?" He forces his opponents to either condemn their own traditions or concede that the Christian belief is not as absurd as they claim. This method of using an opponent's own sources against them was a hallmark of his apologetic works.

fr: Ainsi, dans l’arsenal des médecins, il y a l’instrument qui, par son mécanisme de torsion, force d’abord les parties secrètes à s’ouvrir. Il y a le scalpel annulaire, avec lequel on découpe les membres à l’intérieur, au prix d’une décision angoissante. Il y a le crochet émoussé, qui sert à extraire toute cette œuvre du crime par un accouchement violent. Il y a même une aiguille de bronze, qui guide l’égorgement lui-même : un brigandage à l’aveugle. On l’appelle ἐμβρυοσφάκτην, le « tueur d’embryon », un nom tiré de sa fonction infanticide, puisqu’il est destiné à supprimer un enfant sans aucun doute vivant. Hippocrate en possédait un, tout comme Asclépiade, Érasistrate, le grand dissecteur Hérophile, et même le plus humain d'entre eux, Soranus. Tous étaient en effet convaincus que le fœtus est un être vivant et, prenant en pitié une enfance si profondément malheureuse, ils préféraient le tuer avant, pour éviter qu’il ne soit lacéré vivant.
en: [A]mong surgeons' tools there is a certain instrument formed with nicely adjusted flexible frame for opening the uterus and keeping it open; is further furnished with an annular blade, by means of which the limbs within the womb are dissected with anxious but unfaltering care; its last appendage being blunted or covered hook, with which the entire fetus is extracted by a violent delivery. There is also a copper needle or spike, by which the actual death is managed in this furtive robbery of life: from its infanticide function, they give it the name of embruosphakté, the slayer of the infant, which was of course alive. Such apparatus was possessed both by Hippocrates, and Asclepiades, and Erasistratus, and Herophilus, that dissector of adults, and the milder Soranus himself, who all knew well enough that a living being had been conceived, and pitied this most luckless infant state, which had first to be put to death, to escape being tortured alive [ Treatise on the Soul 25 (C. A.D. 210)].
latin: Itaque et inter arma medicorum et organon est quo prius patescere secreta coguntur, tortili temperamento, cum anulocultro quo intus membra caeduntur, anxio arbitrio; cum hebete unco, quo totum facinus extrahitur violento puerperio. Est etiam aeneum spiculum, quo jugulatio ipsa dirigitur, caeco latrocinio: ἐμβρυοσφάκτην appellant, de infanticidii officio, utique viventis infantis peremptorium. Hoc et Hippocrates habuit, et Asclepiades, et Erasistratus, et majorum quoque prosector Herophilus, et mitior ipse Soranus, certi animal esse conceptum, atque ita miserti infelicissimae hujusmodi infantiae, ut prius occidatur, ne viva lanietur.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

Author, Work, and Date:

    Author: Tertullian of Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 AD), one of the most brilliant and fiery of the early Latin Christian writers.

    Work: De Anima (On the Soul), a detailed treatise arguing for the Christian understanding of the soul against various philosophical and heretical views.

    Date: Written around A.D. 210.

Context of the Argument:
The entire purpose of Chapter 25 is to refute the pagan philosophical idea (held by Stoics and some Platonists) that the soul only enters the body at the moment of birth, with the first breath. Tertullian is arguing passionately that the soul is present from the moment of conception.

The Power of this Specific Passage:
This quote is the climax of his argument from empirical evidence. His logic is a masterful piece of rhetoric:

    The Opposing View: His opponents claim the fetus in the womb is not an ensouled, living human being.

    Tertullian's Evidence: He points to the grisly, but real, medical practice of embryotomy—a procedure used to save a mother's life during an obstructed birth by dismembering the fetus in the womb.

    The Killer Proof: He describes the surgical instruments in graphic detail. The most damning piece of evidence is the Greek name for one of the tools: ἐμβρυοσφάκτης (embruosphaktēs).

        embryon (ἔμβρυον) = embryo, fetus

        sphaktēs (σφάκτης) = slayer, sacrificer, murderer (from the verb sphazō, "to slay" or "to slaughter").

    The Conclusion: The very name of the instrument—the "embryo-slayer"—proves his point. You cannot "slay" or "murder" something that is not alive. By using this term, the most famous physicians of antiquity (Hippocrates, Soranus, etc.) implicitly admitted that the fetus was a living being. Therefore, the philosophical theory that life begins at birth is contradicted by the practical knowledge and terminology of their own medical experts.

In short, Tertullian uses the grim reality of ancient obstetrics as an undeniable proof that the unborn child was considered a living being, thereby demolishing the arguments of his opponents.

fr: Or, nous reconnaissons la vie dès la conception, car nous revendiquons l'âme dès la conception. Dès lors en effet, la vie est là où est l'âme.
en: Now we allow that life begins with conception, because we contend that the soul also begins from conception; life taking its commencement at the same moment and place that the soul does [ibid., 27].
latin: Porro vitam a conceptu agnoscimus, quia animam a conceptu vindicamus. Exinde enim vita, quo anima.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Author: Tertullian of Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 AD)

    Work: De Anima ("On the Soul")

    Chapter: 27 (Caput XXVII)

    Date: c. A.D. 210-213

Theological Context: The Doctrine of Traducianism

This passage is a cornerstone of Tertullian's argument for a doctrine known as Traducianism. The central question of the chapter is: When and how does the soul originate?

    Tertullian's Position (Traducianism): Tertullian argues that the human soul is transmitted (or "handed down," Lat. traducere) from the parents to the child at the moment of conception, just as the body is. He believed the soul was corporeal (though of a very fine substance) and was contained within the parental seed. In this view, the soul and body are generated simultaneously. Your quote is the climax of this argument: life begins at conception because the soul is present from conception.

    Alternative Views: This stood in contrast to two other major theories:

        Creationism: The belief that God creates each individual soul ex nihilo (from nothing) and infuses it into the body at some point after conception (e.g., at "quickening" or at birth). This became the more dominant view in Western theology.

        Pre-existence: The Platonic idea, championed by Origen, that souls exist in a spiritual realm before being united with a body as a form of punishment or trial. This view was later condemned as heretical.

Significance of the Passage

    Foundation for Original Sin: Traducianism provided a very clear mechanism for the transmission of Original Sin. If the soul itself is generated from the parents' souls, it would naturally inherit their fallen nature.

    Early Christian Pro-Life Stance: This quote is one of the most powerful and explicit statements from the early Church Fathers on the personhood of the unborn. By equating the beginning of life with the beginning of the soul at the moment of conception, Tertullian provides a robust philosophical and theological foundation for the belief that abortion is the termination of a human life.

    Christological Problems: While influential, Traducianism was ultimately viewed with caution by the wider Church, in large part because of the theological problem it posed for the soul of Jesus Christ. If Christ's human soul were "traduced" from Mary, it would seem to imply an inheritance of a fallen human nature, which was unacceptable.

fr: ...de peur qu'il ne t'accuse devant Dieu le Juge d'être un fraudeur, un transgresseur du pacte ; que le juge ne te livre alors à l'ange de l'exécution, et que celui-ci ne te fasse jeter dans la prison des enfers, d'où tu ne seras libéré qu'après avoir soldé jusqu'à la plus petite faute par un retard de la résurrection. Quel sens plus juste, quelle interprétation plus vraie ?
en: [T]hat allegory of the Lord [Mt 5:25-26] . is extremely clear and simple in its meaning: [Beware unless, as] a transgressor of your agreement, before God the judge . . . he deliver you over to the angel who is to execute the sentence, and he commit you to the prison of hades, out of which there will be no dismissal until the smallest even of your delinquencies be paid off in the period before the resurrection. What can be a more fitting meaning than this? What a truer interpretation? [ Treatise on the Soul 35 (c. A.D. 210)].
latin: ...ne te ut fraudatorem, ut pacti transgessorem judici Deo objiciat... et judex te tradat angelo executionis, et ille te in carcerem mandet infernum, unde non dimittaris, nisi modico quoque delicto mora resurrectionis expenso. Quid his sensibus aptius? quid his interpretationibus verius?
context:
Additional Relevant Details

This passage is a brilliant example of Tertullian's polemical and exegetical style, and it is a text of immense theological significance.

1. The Immediate Context: Refuting Gnostic Reincarnation

    As the full text you provided shows, Tertullian is not writing in a vacuum. He is directly refuting the Gnostic heretic Carpocrates.

    Carpocrates and his followers used the parable from Matthew 5:25-26 to support their doctrine of metempsychosis (reincarnation). They taught that the "prison" was the physical body, and that the soul had to be reincarnated repeatedly until it had "paid the last penny" by committing every possible type of act, good or evil, to exhaust its worldly experience and achieve liberation.

    Tertullian mocks this interpretation as absurd, calling Carpocrates a "magician and a fornicator" (magus... fornicarius).

2. Tertullian's Orthodox Interpretation

Tertullian offers what he calls the "clear and simple" orthodox interpretation of the allegory:

    The Adversary: The Devil (diabolum), with whom Christians have made a pact (in baptism) to renounce him.

    The Judge: God (judici Deo).

    The Angel of Execution: The angel who carries out God's sentence (angelo executionis).

    The Prison: Hades/The Underworld (carcerem infernum). This is not the final Hell of the damned, but the temporary abode of the dead awaiting the final judgment.

    Paying the Debt: This refers to a period of purification for smaller sins or delinquencies (modico quoque delicto). This satisfaction is made during the "delay before the resurrection" (mora resurrectionis expenso).

3. Theological Significance: An Early Witness to Purgatory

This passage is one of the most important and explicit early patristic texts contributing to the development of the doctrine of Purgatory in the Latin West.

    Tertullian clearly articulates a belief in an intermediate state after death but before the final resurrection.

    In this state, souls who are saved but still have minor faults (modico... delicto) must undergo a form of purification or satisfaction.

    He explicitly states that one cannot be released from this "prison" of Hades until this satisfaction for even the smallest offenses is complete.

While Tertullian does not use the word "purgatory" and his theology is not identical to the later, fully developed medieval doctrine, his interpretation of this biblical passage lays a clear and undeniable foundation for it. His argument is that after death, there is a cleansing process for the saved that prepares them for their eventual entry into heaven at the resurrection.

fr: Car la loi de Moïse elle-même ne soumet l’auteur d’un avortement à la peine du talion que lorsqu’il s’agit déjà d’un être humain.
en: The Law of Moses, indeed, punishes with due penalties the man who shall cause abortion [ Ex 21:22-24] [ibid., 37].
latin: Nam et Moysis lex tunc aborsus reum talionibus judicat, cum jam hominis est caussa.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Source: The text is from Tertullian's treatise De Anima ("On the Soul"), written around A.D. 210. The quote is found in Chapter 37.

    Author: Tertullian of Carthage (c. 160 – c. 225 AD) was a prolific early Christian author and one of the most important apologists of his time. He was the first major Christian author to write in Latin.

    Context of the Argument: This quote is not a standalone statement. Tertullian's primary argument in this chapter is about ensoulment—the point at which a developing fetus becomes a human being with a soul. He is arguing against philosophical theories that posited ensoulment at a much later stage, or even at birth.

        Immediately preceding your quote, he states: "Ex eo igitur foetus in utero homo, a quo forma completa est." ("Therefore, the fetus in the womb is a human from the time its form is complete.")

        He then uses the Law of Moses as legal proof for his theological and philosophical claim. His logic is that the Mosaic Law would not prescribe such severe penalties for causing an abortion if the fetus were not already considered a human being ("cum jam hominis est caussa" - "since it is already the case of a human being").

    Note on the Legal Reference: The word talionibus is highly significant. It refers to the lex talionis, the law of retaliation ("an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth, a life for a life") found in Exodus 21:23-25. By stating that the law judges the one who causes an abortion with talio, Tertullian is interpreting the biblical text to mean that the life of the unborn child is valued as a human life, deserving of the highest legal protection.

fr: Car Dieu seul est sans péché, et le seul homme sans péché est le Christ, parce que le Christ est aussi Dieu.
en: God alone is without sin. The only man who is without sin is Christ; for Christ is also God [ Treatise on the Soul 41 (C. A.D. 210)].
latin: Solus enim Deus sine peccato, et solus homo sine peccato Christus, quia et Deus Christus.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Source: Tertullian of Carthage, De Anima ("On the Soul"), Chapter 41.

    Date: Circa A.D. 210.

    Standard Citation: Migne, Patrologia Latina (PL) 2, 720B. The numbers 0720B and 0720C in your provided text are the column markers from Migne's edition.

Context and Significance

This quote is one of the most powerful and concise statements in early Latin theology regarding Christology (the nature of Christ) and Hamartiology (the doctrine of sin).

    Immediate Context: In this chapter, Tertullian is arguing that the human soul, since its origin, possesses a natural flaw or "corruption" (ex originis vitio). However, he balances this by stating that the soul also retains an innate and divine goodness that is "obscured" but never fully "extinguished." This leads him to the conclusion that even the worst people have some good in them, and even the best have some evil (in pessimis aliquid boni, et in optimis nonnihil pessimi).

    The Ultimate Exception: The quote you selected serves as the absolute and singular exception to this universal human condition. While all other humans are a mixture of good and evil, Tertullian presents two beings who are entirely without sin: God and the man who is also God, Jesus Christ.

    Powerful Christological Formula: The statement is a brilliant piece of theological logic. It affirms both Christ's sinlessness and his divinity, making the latter the explicit cause of the former. The structure of the sentence is almost a syllogism:

        Major Premise: God alone is without sin.

        Minor Premise: Christ is God.

        Conclusion: Therefore, Christ is the only man without sin.

This formulation was highly influential and provided a clear, memorable expression of orthodox teaching on the unique nature of Christ.

fr: Il n’est pas permis à la femme de parler dans l’assemblée, ni d’enseigner, ni de baptiser, ni d’offrir, ni de s’attribuer la moindre charge masculine, et à plus forte raison l’office sacerdotal.
en: It is not permitted for a woman to speak in the church [1 Cor 14:34- 35], but neither [is it permitted her] . . to offer, nor to claim to herself a lot in any manly function, not to say sacerdotal office [Veiling of Virgins 9 (c. A.D. 209)].
latin: Non permittitur mulieri in ecclesia loqui, sed nec docere, nec tinguere, nec offerre, nec ullius virilis muneris, nedum sacerdotalis officii sortem vindicare.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Author and Work: The author is Tertullian of Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 AD), one of the most brilliant and rigorous of the early Latin Church Fathers. The work, De Virginibus Velandis, was written around 209 AD, during his Montanist period. Montanism was known for its charismatic prophecy (including from women) but also for its extreme moral and disciplinary rigor, which is clearly on display here.

    The Core Argument of Chapter 9: The entire point of this chapter is to argue that the ecclesiastical disciplines that apply to a mulier (a woman, often implying a married woman) also apply with equal or greater force to a virgo (a consecrated virgin). Tertullian is refuting any idea that a virgin's special status might grant her exemptions or privileges not afforded to other women in the Church. His logic is: if a married woman must be veiled and silent, how much more so a virgin who has dedicated herself to humility?

    Breakdown of the Prohibited Functions: The list Tertullian provides is a detailed and sweeping prohibition of female participation in key church functions, moving from the general to the highly specific:

        loqui (to speak): A direct reference to St. Paul (1 Cor 14:34).

        docere (to teach): A reference to 1 Timothy 2:12.

        tinguere (to baptize): A clear statement against women administering the sacrament of baptism. This was a significant issue in the early Church, which Tertullian addresses elsewhere as well.

        offerre (to offer): This refers specifically to the offering of the Eucharistic sacrifice. It is a direct prohibition against a woman acting in the role of a priest at the altar.

        ullius virilis muneris... sortem vindicare (to claim for herself a lot in any manly function): A broad, catch-all phrase covering any role or duty considered to be masculine within the Church's structure.

        nedum sacerdotalis officii (let alone the sacerdotal office): This is the ultimate and most explicit point. Nedum is a powerful Latin word meaning "much less" or "not to say." He concludes his list by stating that if the lesser functions are forbidden, the priestly office itself is completely out of the question.

    Source Citation: The text you provided correctly identifies the source as Chapter 9 of the work. In Migne's Patrologia Latina, this passage is located in Volume 2, column 902A.

fr:
C'est donc à juste titre que, lorsqu'il a donné le pain, il n'a pas dit : « Ceci est le symbole de mon corps », mais : « Ceci est mon corps ». De même, lorsqu'il a donné la coupe, il n'a pas dit : « Ceci est le symbole de mon sang », mais : « Ceci est mon sang ». Il voulait en effet que, après l'accueil de la grâce et la venue de l'Esprit, nous ne considérions plus ces éléments selon leur nature, mais que nous les recevions comme le corps et le sang de notre Seigneur.

En effet, le corps de notre Seigneur lui-même ne possède pas par sa propre nature l'immortalité ni le pouvoir de la conférer ; cela lui fut donné par l'Esprit Saint. Lors de sa résurrection d'entre les morts, il reçut une union intime avec la nature divine, et devint immortel et l'instrument qui confère l'immortalité aux autres.
en: When [Christ] gave the bread he did not say. "This is the symbol of my body," but, "This IS my body." In the same way, when he gave the cup of his blood he did not say, This is the symbol of my blood," but, "This is my blood." For he wanted us to look upon the [eucharistic elements] after their reception of grace and the coming of the Holy Spirit not according to their nature, but to receive them as they are, the body and blood of our Lord. We ought not to see [the elements] merely as bread and cup, but as the body and blood of the Lord, into which they were transformed by the descent of the Holy Spirit [Catechetical Homilies 5:1 (c. AD. 410)].
latin: It is with justice, therefore, that when He gave the bread He did not say : " This is the symbol of my body," but: * This is my body likewise when He gave the cup He did not say: "This is the symbol of my blood but : This is my blood," because He wished us to look upon these (elements) after their reception of grace and the coming of the Spirit, not according to their nature, but to receive them as if they were the body and the blood of our Lord. Indeed, even the body of our Lord does not possess immortality and the power of bestowing immortality in its own nature, as this was given to it by the Holy Spirit ; and at its resurrection from the dead it received close union with Divine nature and became immortal and instrumental for conferring immortality on others.
context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. The Author and His Work

    Theodore of Mopsuestia (c. 350 – 428 AD): He was a bishop and a leading theologian of the Antiochene School, known for its focus on literal-historical biblical interpretation. His work is a prime example of the theology of the pre-Ephesian era.

    The Catechetical Homilies: This work was lost for over 1,500 years. It was a series of instructions for catechumens preparing for baptism. Its rediscovery in a Syriac manuscript by Alphonse Mingana in the early 20th century was a monumental event in patristic studies, providing a direct window into the liturgical and sacramental life of the 4th-5th century Church in Syria.

2. Profound Theological Significance

This passage is one of the most important patristic texts on the Eucharist for several reasons:

    Explicit Realism: Theodore forcefully rejects a purely symbolic interpretation. His direct contrast—"He did not say 'symbol'... but 'This IS'"—is an unambiguous affirmation of what is now called Eucharistic realism. This was particularly significant coming from the Antiochene school, which is sometimes stereotyped as being less "mystical" than the Alexandrian school.

    The Role of the Holy Spirit (Epiclesis): Theodore's explanation is a classic example of Eastern Eucharistic theology. He states clearly that the change in the elements occurs "by the descent of the Holy Spirit." This invocation of the Spirit to effect the transformation is known as the Epiclesis, and it remains a central and explicit part of all Eastern Christian liturgies.

    Transformation ('eštaḥlap): The Syriac word for "transformed" is a form of the root ܫ-ܚ-ܠ-ܦ (Š-Ḥ-L-P), which means to change, alter, or exchange. It is a very strong term, equivalent to the Greek metabolē (μεταβολή). This indicates a real, objective change in the elements, not merely a change in their significance. It is a powerful precursor to later, more systematic theological definitions of the Eucharistic change.

3. Historical Context

    Although Theodore's Christological teachings were posthumously condemned at the Second Council of Constantinople in 553, his writings, particularly on the sacraments and liturgy, remained enormously influential, especially within the Church of the East (often called the Nestorian or Assyrian Church), where he is revered as "The Interpreter." His Eucharistic theology is a foundational part of their tradition.

fr: Donc, lorsqu’on demande : « Marie est-elle mère de l’homme ou mère de Dieu ? », nous devons répondre : « Les deux ». Le premier par nature, le second par relation. Mère de l’homme par nature, car c’est bien un homme qui était dans le sein de Marie et qui en est sorti ; mère de Dieu, car Dieu était dans l’homme qui naquit, non qu’il fût circonscrit en lui selon la nature, mais parce qu’il était en lui selon une relation de volonté.
en: THEODORE OF MOPSUESTIA When, therefore, they ask, "Is Mary mother of man or Mother of God?" we answer, "Both!" The one by the very nature of what was done and the other by relation. Mother of man because it was a man who was in the womb of Mary and who came forth from there, and the Mother of God because God was in the man who was born The Incarnation 15 (C. A.D. 410)].
latin: cum ergo interrogent, ‘hominis genetrix aut Dei genetrix Maria?’ dicatur a nobis, ‘utraque’—unum quidem natura rei, alterum autem relatione. hominis enim genetrix natura, quia homo erat in uentre Mariae, quia et processit inde; Dei autem genetrix, quia Deus erat in homine nato, non in illo circumscriptus secundum naturam, sed quod in eo erat affectu uoluntatis.
greek: ὅταν τοίνυν ἐρωτῶσιν ‘ἄνθρωποτόκος ἢ θεοτόκος ἡ Μαρία,’ λεγέσθω παρ’ ἡμῶν ‘ἀμφότερα’· τὸ μὲν γὰρ τῇ φύσει τοῦ πράγματος, τὸ δὲ τῇ ἀναφορᾷ. ἀνθρωποτόκος μὲν γὰρ τῇ φύσει, ἐπείπερ ἄνθρωπος ἦν ὁ ἐν τῇ κοιλίᾳ τῆς Μαρίας, ὡς καὶ προῆλθεν ἐκεῖθεν· θεοτόκος δέ, ἐπείπερ θεὸς ἦν ἐν τῷ τεχθέντι ἀνθρώπῳ, οὐκ ἐν αὐτῷ περιγραφόμενος κατὰ τὴν φύσιν, ἐν αὐτῷ δὲ ὢν κατὰ τὴν σχέσιν τῆς γνώμης.
context: Additional Relevant Details

fr: Et à quoi bon de longs discours, quand on peut confondre le mensonge en quelques mots ? En effet, nous veillons à ce que ceux qui, chaque année, s’approchent du très saint baptême apprennent la foi exposée à Nicée par les saints et bienheureux Pères. Puis, en les initiant aux mystères comme il nous a été prescrit, nous les baptisons au nom du Père, et du Fils, et du Saint-Esprit, en prononçant chaque nom séparément.
en: THEODORET OF CYR [W]hat need is there of many words, when it is possible to refute falsehood in few? We provide that those who year by year come up for holy baptism should carefully learn the faith set forth at Nicaea by the holy and blessed Fathers; and initiating them as we have been bidden, we baptize them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, pronouncing each name singly [Letters 145 (A.D. 450)].
latin: Et quid longa oratione uti opus est, cum paucis mendacium refellere liceat? Eos enim qui ad sacrosanctum baptisma singulis annis accedunt, fidem Nicææ a sanctis Patribus expositam ediscere jubemus: et instituentes eos, sicut jussi sumus, baptizamus in nomine Patris et Filii et Spiritus sancti, singulariter unumquodque nomen proferentes.
greek: Καὶ τί δεῖ μακρηγορεῖν, ἐξὸν συντόμως διελέγξαι τὸ ψεῦδος; Τοὺς γὰρ καθ᾽ ἕκαστον ἔτος τῷ παναγίῳ προσιόντας βαπτίσματι, τὴν ἐκτεθεῖσαν ἐν Νικαίᾳ παρὰ τῶν ἁγίων καὶ μακαρίων Πατέρων πίστιν ἐκμανθάνειν παρασκευάζομεν· καὶ μυσταγωγοῦντες αὐτοὺς ὡς προσετάχθημεν, βαπτίζομεν εἰς τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ Πατρὸς, καὶ τοῦ Υἱοῦ, καὶ τοῦ ἁγίου Πνεύματος, ἑνικῶς ἑκάστην προσηγορίαν προσφέροντες.
context:
Additional Relevant Details
Context of the Letter

This letter is a passionate work of self-defense. Theodoret, a leading figure of the Antiochene school of theology, was under fierce attack from his theological opponents of the Alexandrian school (led by the successors of St. Cyril). They were accusing him of Nestorianism—specifically, of teaching "two Sons" because he insisted on maintaining the distinction between Christ's divine and human natures after the Incarnation.
Theodoret's Argument

Theodoret's defense strategy in this letter is not just to argue theology, but to appeal to his actual, verifiable pastoral practice as a bishop. The quote you selected is the climax of this practical argument. He is essentially saying: "You accuse me of heresy? Look at what I actually do in my church every single year. My actions prove my orthodox faith."
The Power of the Quote

    Appeal to the Nicene Creed: His first line of defense is to state that he requires all catechumens to learn the Nicene Creed. In the 5th century, adherence to the faith of Nicaea was the absolute benchmark of orthodoxy. By grounding his teaching in this universally accepted creed, he immediately aligns himself with the tradition of the "holy and blessed Fathers."

    Appeal to the Baptismal Formula: His second line of defense is the core of the Christian faith: the act of baptism. He states that he baptizes exactly as commanded, using the universal Trinitarian formula. This demonstrates his belief in the consubstantial Trinity.

    The Crucial Detail: "Pronouncing each name singly": This is a brilliant and subtle theological point.

        ἑνικῶς ἑκάστην προσηγορίαν (Greek) / singulariter unumquodque nomen (Latin)

        By emphasizing that he pronounces each name—Father, Son, Holy Spirit—individually and singly, he proves that he believes in the real distinction of the three divine Persons. This refutes any charge of Sabellianism (or modalism), a heresy that claimed the Father, Son, and Spirit were just different "modes" of a single person.

        This orthodox Trinitarian practice serves as irrefutable proof against the slander that he holds an unorthodox Christology. His argument is that a correct understanding of the Trinity is the foundation for a correct understanding of the Incarnation of the Son.

fr:
Il est sans principe, car il est inengendré ; il est immuable, car il est immortel. Il est appelé Dieu parce qu’il a tout établi sur son propre fondement stable, et parce qu’il « court ». Or, courir, c’est se mouvoir, agir, nourrir, veiller, gouverner et donner la vie à toutes choses.
Il est Seigneur, parce qu’il domine l’univers ; Père, parce qu’il est avant toutes choses ; Créateur et Artisan, parce qu’il est le fondateur et l’auteur de l’univers ; Très-Haut, parce qu’il est au-dessus de tout ; Tout-Puissant, parce que c’est lui qui maîtrise et embrasse toutes choses.
En effet, les hauteurs des cieux, les profondeurs des abîmes et les confins du monde sont dans sa main, et il n’existe aucun lieu pour son repos. Car les cieux sont son ouvrage, la terre est son œuvre, la mer sa création ; l’homme est son modelage et son image. Le soleil, la lune et les étoiles sont ses éléments, créés pour marquer les signes, les temps, les jours et les années, afin de servir les hommes.
Et c’est du néant que Dieu a fait exister toutes choses, afin que par ses œuvres on puisse connaître et comprendre sa grandeur.
en: ST. THEOPHILUS OF ANTIOCH And he is without beginning, because he is unbegotten; and he is unchangeable, because he is immortal. And he is called God [Theos] because he established [tetheikenai] all things with a security that he himself provided; and on account of théein, for théein means running, and moving, and being active, and nourishing, and foreseeing, and governing, and making all things alive. But he is Lord, because he rules over the universe; Father, because he is before all things; fashioner and maker, because he is creator and maker of the universe; the highest, because of his being above all; and Almighty, because he rules and embraces all. For the heights of heaven, and the depths of the abysses, and the ends of the earth are in his hand and there is no place where he rests. For the heavens are his work, the earth is his creation, the sea is his handiwork; man iS his formation and his image; sun, moon, and stars are his elements, made for signs, and seasons, and days, and years, that they may serve and be slaves to man; and all things God has made, out of things that were not into things that are, in order that through his works his greatness may be known and understood [ To Autolycus 1:4 (c. A.D. 181)].
latin: Caret principio quia ingenitus est: immutabilis est quatenus immortalis. Deus dicitur, διὰ τὸ τεθεικέναι, id est quia omnia in sua ipsius stabilitate posuit, et διὰ τὸ θέειν, quod idem est ac currere et movere, et operari, et nutrire, et providere, et gubernare et vivificare omnia. Dominus est quia omnibus dominatur; Pater, quia ante omnia; conditor et creator, quia omnia condidit et creavit; altissimus, quia supra omnia; omnipotens, quia omnia tenet et complectitur. Nam excelsa cœlorum, et profunda abyssorum, et termini orbis terræ, sunt in manu ejus; nec est locus in quo moretur et quiescat. Est enim cœlum ejus opus, terra et mare ejus opificium, homo ejus figmentum et imago. Sol, luna et stellæ sunt ejus elementa, in signa et tempora, et dies et annos condita, ut ministrent et serviant hominibus. Atque omnia Deus fecit, cum antea non essent, ut ex operibus cognoscatur et intelligatur ejus majestas.
greek: Ἄναρχος δέ ἐστιν, ὅτι ἀγέννητός ἐστιν· ἀναλλοίωτος δὲ, καθότι ἀθάνατός ἐστι. Θεὸς δὲ λέγεται διὰ τὸ τεθεικέναι τὰ πάντα ἐπὶ τῇ ἑαυτοῦ ἀσφαλείᾳ, καὶ διὰ τὸ θέειν· τὸ δὲ θέειν ἐστὶν τὸ τρέχειν, καὶ κινεῖν, καὶ ἐνεργεῖν, καὶ τρέφειν, καὶ προνοεῖν, καὶ κυβερνᾷν, καὶ ζωοποιεῖν τὰ πάντα. Κύριος δέ ἐστι διὰ τὸ κυριεύειν αὐτὸν τῶν ὅλων· πατὴρ δὲ διὰ τὸ εἶναι αὐτὸν πρὸ τῶν ὅλων· δημιουργὸς δὲ καὶ ποιητῆς διὰ τὸ αὐτὸν εἶναι κτίστην καὶ ποιητὴν τῶν ὅλων· ὕψιστος δὲ διὰ τὸ εἶναι αὐτὸν ἀνώτερον τῶν πάντων· παντοκράτωρ δὲ, ὅτι αὐτὸς τὰ πάντα κρατεῖ καὶ ἐμπεριέχει. Τὰ γὰρ ὕψη τῶν οὐρανῶν, καὶ τὰ βάθη τῶν ἀβύσσων, καὶ τὰ πέρατα τῆς οἰκουμένης, ἐν τῇ χειρὶ αὐτοῦ ἐστιν· καὶ οὐκ ἔστι τόπος τῆς καταπαύσεως αὐτοῦ. Οὐρανοὶ μὲν γὰρ ἔργον αὐτοῦ εἰσιν, γῆ ποίημα αὐτοῦ ἐστι· θάλασσα κτίσμα αὐτοῦ ἐστιν· ἄνθρωπος πλάσμα καὶ εἰκὼν αὐτοῦ ἐστιν. Ἥλιος καὶ σελήνη καὶ ἀστέρες στοιχεῖα αὐτοῦ εἰσιν, εἰς σημεῖα καὶ εἰς καιροὺς καὶ εἰς ἡμέρας καὶ εἰς ἐνιαυτοὺς γεγονότα, πρὸς ὑπηρεσίαν καὶ δουλείαν ἀνθρώπων· καὶ τὰ πάντα ἐκ τοῦ μὴ ὄντος εἰς τὸ εἶναι ἐποίησεν ὁ Θεός, ἵνα διὰ τῶν ἔργων γινώσκηται καὶ νοηθῇ τὸ μέγεθος αὐτοῦ.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Etymological Argument: Theophilus's explanation for the name "God" (Θεός - Theos) is a classic example of ancient etymology. He derives it from two verbs: τίθημι (tithēmi, aorist stem the- meaning "to place, establish") and θέω (theō, meaning "to run, be active"). While not linguistically accurate by modern standards, this method was common in philosophy and apologetics. It allowed Theophilus to pack profound theological meaning into the very name of God, presenting Him as both the stable foundation of reality and the active, immanent power sustaining it.

    Creatio ex Nihilo (Creation from Nothing): The line "καὶ τὰ πάντα ἐκ τοῦ μὴ ὄντος εἰς τὸ εἶναι ἐποίησεν ὁ Θεός" ("and all things God has made, out of things that were not into things that are") is one of the clearest and earliest explicit statements of the doctrine of creatio ex nihilo in Christian literature. This was a radical departure from the prevailing Greek philosophical view that the universe was shaped from pre-existing, eternal matter.

    Apophatic Theology (Negative Theology): The passage begins by describing God by what He is not or what He is without: "without beginning" (ἄναρχος - anarchos), "unchangeable" (ἀναλλοίωτος - analloiōtos). This method of speaking about God by denying limitations is a foundational element of Christian theology.

    Natural Theology: The final clause, "in order that through his works his greatness may be known and understood," is a direct echo of Romans 1:20. Theophilus is making a classic natural theology argument: the visible creation serves as a signpost pointing to the invisible Creator's power and majesty. This was a crucial point of engagement with pagan thought.

    Catalog of Divine Attributes: Theophilus provides a list of divine titles (Lord, Father, Creator, Highest, Almighty) and explains what each one means in relation to the world. This catalog format became a standard way for the Church Fathers to systematically teach about the nature of God.

fr:
Car Dieu ressuscite ta chair, pour la rendre immortelle avec ton âme. Alors, devenu immortel, tu verras l’Immortel, si maintenant tu crois en lui ; et c’est alors que tu reconnaîtras avoir parlé de lui injustement.

Mais tu ne crois pas que les morts ressuscitent. Quand cela arrivera, alors tu croiras, que tu le veuilles ou non ; et ta foi te sera comptée comme une incroyance, si tu ne crois pas maintenant.
en: ST. THEOPHILUS OF ANTIOCH For God will raise your flesh immortal with your soul; and then, having become immortal, you will see the immortal, i now you believe in him; and then you will know that you have spoken unjustly against him. But you do not believe that the dead are raised. When the resurrection takes place, then you will believe, whether you want to or not: and your faith shall be reckoned for unbelief, unless you believe now [To Autolycus 1:7-8 (C. A.D. 181)].
latin:
Excitat enim tuam carnem cum anima immortalem Deus, ac tunc factus immortalis immortalem videbis, si nunc ei credideris; tunc etiam cognosces te contra illum inique locutum esse.

    Sed mortuos excitari non credis. Cum res eveniet, tunc credes, velis nolis; sed tua fides in incredulitatis loco deputabitur, nisi nunc credas.
greek:
Ἀνεγείρει γάρ σου τὴν σάρκα ἀθάνατον σὺν τῇ ψυχῇ ὁ Θεός· καὶ τότε γενόμενος ἀθάνατος τὸν ἀθάνατον ὄψει, ἐὰν νῦν πιστεύσῃς αὐτῷ· καὶ τότε ἐπιγνώσῃ, ὅτι ἀδίκως κατελάλησας αὐτοῦ.

    Ἀλλὰ ἀπιστεῖς νεκροὺς ἐγείρεσθαι. Ὅτε ἔσται, τότε πιστεύσεις θέλων καὶ μὴ θέλων· καὶ ἡ πίστις σου εἰς ἀπιστίαν λογισθήσεται, ἐὰν μὴ νῦν πιστεύσῃς.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Author and Work: St. Theophilus of Antioch (died c. A.D. 183-185) was the sixth bishop of Antioch. His apology, To Autolycus (Ad Autolycum), is his only surviving work. It is addressed to a learned pagan friend named Autolycus who was skeptical of Christianity and ridiculed its doctrines.

    Date: The work is dated to approximately A.D. 181, making it a very early and important witness to Christian belief in the 2nd century.

    Context of the Passage: Theophilus is directly responding to Autolycus's demand to "show me your God." Theophilus argues that one cannot see God with physical eyes unless the "eyes of the soul" are opened by faith. This leads to the passage you cited, where he explains that the ultimate vision of God is eschatological—it will happen after the resurrection, when believers are made immortal.

    Theological Significance:

        Bodily Resurrection: This is a remarkably clear and early affirmation of the resurrection of the flesh (σάρκα / carnem). Theophilus explicitly states that God will raise the flesh immortal together with the soul, a direct refutation of Gnostic and other philosophical views that denigrated the body and imagined a purely spiritual salvation.

        Faith and Vision: The passage establishes a core Christian principle that faith precedes sight and understanding. Belief in the present life (ἐὰν νῦν πιστεύσῃς / si nunc ei credideris) is the necessary condition for the beatific vision in the next.

        Apologetic Warning: Theophilus uses the doctrine as a powerful warning. For the skeptic, belief will become unavoidable at the resurrection ("then you will believe, whether you want to or not"), but at that point, it will be too late. This forced "faith" of the judgment day will be counted as the "unbelief" of this life.

    Source: The layout of the page you provided, with parallel Greek and Latin columns and detailed scholarly notes, is characteristic of major patristic collections, most famously Jacques-Paul Migne's Patrologia Graeca (PG), Volume 6.

fr: Et toi, ne veux-tu pas être oint de l'huile de Dieu ? C'est bien pour cette raison que nous sommes appelés Chrétiens, parce que nous sommes oints de l'huile de Dieu.
en: ST. THEOPHILUS OF ANTIOCH [A]re you unwilling to be anointed with the oil of God? We are called Christians on this account, because we are anointed with the oil of God [ To Autolycus 1:12 (c. A.D. 181)].
latin: tu vero non vis ungi oleo Dei? Nos enim ideo Christiani vocamur, quod Dei oleo ungamur.
greek: σὺ δὲ οὐ βούλει χρισθῆναι ἔλαιον Θεοῦ; Τοιγαροῦν ἡμεῖς τούτου εἵνεκεν καλούμεθα Χριστιανοί, ὅτι χριόμεθα ἔλαιον Θεοῦ.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Author and Work: The passage is from St. Theophilus, the sixth bishop of Antioch, and is found in his only surviving work, the apology Ad Autolycum (To Autolycus), written around A.D. 181. The work is a defense of the Christian faith addressed to his learned pagan friend, Autolycus.

    The Central Wordplay (Etymology): This is one of the earliest and clearest patristic explanations of the meaning of the name "Christian." The entire argument is a beautiful play on Greek words derived from the verb χρίω (chriō), meaning "to anoint."

        Χριστός (Christos): This is the Greek word for "Anointed One," a direct translation of the Hebrew "Messiah."

        Χριστιανός (Christianos): The name for a follower of Christ.

        χρῖσμα (chrisma): The anointing or the oil itself.
        Theophilus is explaining to Autolycus that the name "Christian" is not a slur or a meaningless label, but a title that describes their very being: they are the "anointed people" because they belong to the Anointed One and are themselves anointed with the "oil of God."

    Theological Significance (The "Oil of God"): The "oil of God" (ἔλαιον Θεοῦ) is a metaphor for the Holy Spirit. By being "anointed" with this oil, Christians are consecrated, set apart for God, and share in the very life and mission of Christ. While written before the full development of sacramental theology, this passage is a foundational text for understanding the spiritual reality behind the physical anointing with oil (chrism) in the sacraments of Baptism and Confirmation (Chrismation).

    Context of the Argument: In the full chapter you provided, Theophilus masterfully argues that anointing is a universal principle of goodness, beauty, and utility. He asks Autolycus:

        What ship is useful without being caulked (anointed with pitch)?

        What house is beautiful without being plastered?

        What athlete competes without being anointed with oil?

        What created thing is beautiful unless it is polished (anointed)?

        Is not the very air "anointed" with light and spirit?
        His final question, which is part of your quote—σὺ δὲ οὐ βούλει χρισθῆναι ἔλαιον Θεοῦ; ("Are you unwilling to be anointed with the oil of God?")—is the powerful climax of this rhetorical argument, designed to make the Christian anointing seem not strange, but natural, necessary, and supremely desirable.

fr:
Car celui qui a donné la bouche pour parler, a façonné l’oreille pour entendre et a créé les yeux pour voir, examinera toutes choses et portera un juste jugement, en rendant à chacun la récompense de ses mérites. À ceux qui, par leur persévérance dans le bien, cherchent l’incorruptibilité, il accordera en don la vie éternelle, la joie, la paix, le repos et une multitude de biens, « que l’œil n’a pas vus, que l’oreille n’a pas entendus et qui ne sont pas montés au cœur de l’homme ».

Quant aux incrédules, aux méprisants, à ceux qui sont rebelles à la vérité pour obéir à l’injustice, lorsqu’ils se seront souillés d’adultères, de débauches, de relations charnelles entre hommes, de cupidité et d’abominables idolâtries, il y aura pour eux la colère et la fureur, la détresse et l’angoisse. Et à la fin, le feu éternel s’emparera de telles personnes.
en: ST. THEOPHILUS OF ANTIOCH For he who gave the mouth for speech, and formed the ear to hear, and made the eye to see, will examine all things, and will judge righteous judgment, rendering merited awards to each. To those who by patient continuance in well-doing [Rom 2:7] seek immortality, he will give life everlasting, joy, peace, rest, and abundance of good things, which neither has eye seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man to conceive [1 Cor 2:9].
