But to the unbelieving and despisers, who obey not the truth, but are obedient to unrighteousness, when they have been filled with adulteries and fornications, and filthiness, and covetousness, and unlawful idolatries, there shall be anger and wrath, tribulation and anguish [Rom 2:8-9], and at the last everlasting fire shall possess such men [ To Autolycus 1:14 (c. A.D. 181)].
latin: Nam qui dedit os ad loquendum, ac aures finxit ad audiendum et oculos ad videndum, excutiet omnia et justum feret judicium, suam cuique pro meritis mercedem tribuens. Iis quidem qui secundum patientiam boni operis incorruptionem quærunt, donabit vitam æternam, gaudium, pacem, quietem, multitudinem bonorum, quæ nec oculus vidit, nec auris audivit, nec in cor hominis ascendit. Incredulis autem et superbis, et iis qui non acquiescunt veritati, credunt autem iniquitati, cun repleti fuerint adulteriis, scortationibus, puerorum stupris, avaritia et infandis simulacrorum cultibus, erit ira et indignatio, tribulatio et angustiæ, ac tandem tales ignis æternus detinebit.
greek: Ὁ γὰρ δοὺς στόμα εἰς τὸ λαλεῖν, καὶ πλάσας οὖς εἰς τὸ ἀκούειν, καὶ ποιήσας ὀφθαλμοὺς εἰς τὸ ὁρᾷν, ἐξετάσει τὰ πάντα καὶ κρινεῖ τὸ δίκαιον, ἀποδιδοὺς ἑκάστῳ κατὰ ἀξίαν τῶν μισθῶν. Τοῖς μὲν καθ' ὑπομονὴν διὰ ἔργων ἀγαθῶν ζητοῦσι τὴν ἀφθαρσίαν δωρήσεται ζωὴν αἰώνιον, χαρὰν, εἰρήνην, ἀνάπαυσιν, καὶ πλήθη ἀγαθῶν, ὧν οὔτε ὀφθαλμὸς εἶδεν, οὔτε οὖς ἤκουσεν, οὔτε ἐπὶ καρδίαν ἀνθρώπου ἀνέβη· τοῖς δὲ ἀπίστοις, καὶ καταφρονηταῖς καὶ ἀπειθοῦσι τῇ ἀληθείᾳ, πειθομένοις δὲ τῇ ἀδικίᾳ, ἐπὰν ἐμφύρωνται μοιχείαις, καὶ πορνείαις, καὶ ἀρσενοκοιτίαις, καὶ πλεονεξίαις, καὶ ταῖς ἀθεμίτοις εἰδωλολατρείαις, ἔσται ὀργὴ, καὶ θυμὸς, θλίψις καὶ στενοχωρία· καὶ τὸ τέλος τοὺς τοιούτους καθέξει πῦρ αἰώνιον.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Author and Work: The author is St. Theophilus, the sixth bishop of Antioch, writing around A.D. 181. The work, Ad Autolycum (To Autolycus), is a three-part Christian apology written to his educated pagan friend, Autolycus, to defend the Christian faith against pagan misunderstandings and to persuade him of its truth.

    Immediate Context: In this chapter, Theophilus has been urging Autolycus to abandon his disbelief. He uses his own conversion as an example and points to the fulfillment of prophecies in the Hebrew Scriptures as proof of their divine origin. He exhorts Autolycus to study these Scriptures so he can "escape the eternal punishments, and obtain the eternal blessings of God." The passage you selected is the detailed description of those punishments and blessings.

    A Mosaic of Scripture: This passage is a masterful example of how early Church Fathers integrated the language of the New Testament into their own writing. Theophilus is not just paraphrasing; he is weaving together a powerful tapestry of direct biblical allusions to give his warning apostolic authority:

        Romans 2:7: "To those who by patient continuance in well-doing seek... immortality, [God will give] eternal life."

        1 Corinthians 2:9: "...what no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the heart of man imagined..." (which itself is a reference to Isaiah 64:4).

        Romans 2:8-9: "But for those who... do not obey the truth, but obey unrighteousness, there will be wrath and fury... tribulation and anguish."

    Theological Significance: This passage is a clear, early witness to the Christian doctrine of the Final Judgment. It emphasizes God as both the Creator (who formed the mouth, ear, and eye) and the Righteous Judge who holds His creation accountable. It presents a stark vision of the "Two Ways"—the path of faithful obedience leading to unimaginable heavenly reward, and the path of disbelief and immorality leading to eternal punishment.

fr: Si toi aussi tu le veux, étudie avec zèle les Écritures prophétiques ; elles te guideront avec plus de clarté pour échapper aux châtiments éternels et obtenir les biens éternels de Dieu. Car Celui qui a donné la bouche pour parler, façonné l’oreille pour entendre et créé les yeux pour voir, examinera toutes choses et jugera avec justice, en rendant à chacun la récompense de ses mérites. À ceux qui, par la persévérance dans les bonnes œuvres, recherchent l’incorruptibilité, il accordera la vie éternelle, la joie, la paix, le repos et une multitude de biens que l’œil n’a pas vus, que l’oreille n’a pas entendus et qui ne sont pas montés au cœur de l’homme. Mais quant aux incrédules, aux orgueilleux, à ceux qui désobéissent à la vérité pour obéir à l’injustice, et qui se souillent d’adultères, de débauches, d’actes contre nature, de cupidité et des cultes abominables des idoles, sur eux viendront la colère et la fureur, la tribulation et l’angoisse ; et à la fin, le feu éternel les retiendra captifs.
en: But do you also. if you please, give reverential attention to the prophetic Scriptures, and they will make your way plainer for escaping the eternal punishments, and obtaining the eternal prizes of God. For he who gave the mouth for speech, and formed the ear to hear, and made the eye to see, will examine all things, and will judge righteous judgment, rendering merited awards to each. To those who by patient continuance in well-doing [Rom 2:7] seek immortality, he will give life everlasting, joy, peace, rest, and abundance of good things, which neither has eye seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man to conceive [1 Cor 2:9]. But to the unbelieving and despisers, who obey not the truth. but are obedient tc unrighteousness, when they have been filled with adulteries and fornications, and filthiness, and covetousness. and unlawful idolatries, there shall be anger and wrath. tribulation and anguish [Rom 2:8-9], and at the last everlasting fire shall possess such men [ To Autolycus 1:14 (c. A.D. 181)].
latin: Tu quoque, si tibi ita videtur, lege studiose propheticas Scripturas, ac lucem illarum tutiorem habebis ducem ut fugias æterna supplicia, et perpetua Dei bona consequaris. Nam qui dedit os ad loquendum, ac aures finxit ad audiendum et oculos ad videndum, excutiet omnia et justum feret judicium, suam cuique pro meritis mercedem tribuens. Iis quidem qui secundum patientiam boni operis incorruptionem quærunt, donabit vitam æternam, gaudium, pacem, quietem, multitudinem bonorum, quæ nec oculus vidit, nec auris audivit, nec in cor hominis ascendit. Incredulis autem et superbis, et iis qui non acquiescunt veritati, credunt autem iniquitati, cun repleti fuerint adulteriis, scortationibus, puerorum stupris, avaritia et infandis simulacrorum cultibus, erit ira et indignatio, tribulatio et angustiæ, ac tandem tales ignis æternus detinebit.
greek: Εἰ δὲ βούλει καὶ σὺ, ἔντυχε φιλοτίμως ταῖς προφητικαῖς Γραφαῖς· καὶ αὐταί σε τρανότερον ὁδηγήσουσι πρὸς τὸ ἐκφυγεῖν τὰς αἰωνίους κολάσεις, καὶ τυχεῖν τῶν αἰωνίων ἀγαθῶν τοῦ Θεοῦ. Ὁ γὰρ δοὺς στόμα εἰς τὸ λαλεῖν, καὶ πλάσας οὖς εἰς τὸ ἀκούειν, καὶ ποιήσας ὀφθαλμοὺς εἰς τὸ ὁρᾷν, ἐξετάσει τὰ πάντα καὶ κρινεῖ τὸ δίκαιον, ἀποδιδοὺς ἑκάστῳ κατὰ ἀξίαν τῶν μισθῶν. Τοῖς μὲν καθ' ὑπομονὴν διὰ ἔργων ἀγαθῶν ζητοῦσι τὴν ἀφθαρσίαν δωρήσεται ζωὴν αἰώνιον, χαράν, εἰρήνην, ἀνάπαυσιν, καὶ πλήθη ἀγαθῶν, ὧν οὔτε ὀφθαλμὸς εἶδεν, οὔτε οὖς ἤκουσεν, οὔτε ἐπὶ καρδίαν ἀνθρώπου ἀνέβη· τοῖς δὲ ἀπίστοις, καὶ καταφρονηταῖς καὶ ἀπειθοῦσι τῇ ἀληθείᾳ, πειθομένοις δὲ τῇ ἀδικίᾳ, ἐπὰν ἐμφύρωνται μοιχείαις, καὶ πορνείαις, καὶ ἀρσενοκοιτίαις, καὶ πλεονεξίαις, καὶ ταῖς ἀθεμίτοις εἰδωλολατρείαις, ἔσται ὀργὴ, καὶ θυμὸς, θλίψις καὶ στενοχωρία· καὶ τὸ τέλος τοὺς τοιούτους καθέξει πῦρ αἰώνιον.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Context: This passage is the culmination of St. Theophilus's argument to his educated pagan friend, Autolycus. Autolycus had demanded, "Show me your God." Theophilus explained that God is seen not with physical eyes but with the "eyes of the soul," which must first be cleansed of sin. This quote serves as a direct, pastoral exhortation: the way to cleanse one's spiritual eyes and escape eternal punishment is to diligently study the prophetic Scriptures.

    Apologetic Method: This is a classic example of 2nd-century Christian apologetics. Theophilus points Autolycus not to complex philosophy (though he uses it elsewhere) but to the authority and clarity of the Hebrew prophets. For the early Church, the Old Testament was the foundational proof of Christian claims.

    Biblical Allusions: The passage is a remarkable tapestry of New Testament quotations and allusions, demonstrating how deeply the apostolic writings had already formed the theological language of the Church by the late 2nd century.

        Romans 2:7-9: The entire structure of the final judgment—reward for the righteous who persevere and wrath for the disobedient—is a direct paraphrase of St. Paul's words in this chapter.

        1 Corinthians 2:9: The description of the eternal reward ("which neither has eye seen, nor ear heard...") is a direct quotation of St. Paul, who was himself likely alluding to Isaiah 64:4.

    Early Christian Eschatology: This is a very clear and early summary of the Christian doctrine of the "Two Ways"—the path of life and the path of death—and their eternal consequences. It powerfully outlines the Church's teaching on the final judgment, heaven, and hell.

fr: De même, les trois jours qui ont précédé les luminaires sont les figures de la Trinité : de Dieu, de son Verbe et de sa Sagesse.
en: It is the attribute of God, of the most high and almighty and of the living God, not only to be everywhere, but also to see and hear all; for he can in no way be contained in place. The three days before the stars were created are types of the Trinity: God, his Word, and his Wisdom [ To Autolycus 2:15 (c. A.D. 181)].
latin: Similiter tres illi dies, qui ante luminaria fuerunt, imago sunt Trinitatis, Dei, ejus Verbi, ejusque Sapientiae.
greek: Ὡσαύτως καὶ αἱ τρεῖς ἡμέραι τῶν φωστήρων γεγονυῖαι τύποι εἰσὶν τῆς Τριάδος, τοῦ Θεοῦ, καὶ τοῦ Λόγου αὐτοῦ, καὶ τῆς Σοφίας αὐτοῦ.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Source and Context: This passage is from Book 2, Chapter 15 of To Autolycus. Theophilus is providing a Christian commentary on the creation account in Genesis. He is arguing against pagan philosophy by showing the divine order and wisdom of creation. The entire chapter is a work of typology, where elements of the creation story are interpreted as "types" or prefigurements of deeper spiritual realities.

    Theological Significance: This passage is exceptionally important for two reasons:

        First Use of the Word "Trinity": This is the first known instance in extant Christian literature where the Greek word Τριάς (Trias), translated as Trinitas in Latin and "Trinity" in English, is explicitly used to refer to God. St. Theophilus is therefore credited with coining the term that would become central to Christian theology.

        Early Trinitarian Formula: The formula he uses—God, his Word, and his Wisdom (Θεός, Λόγος, Σοφία)—is a very early and not-yet-standardized expression of the Trinity. Later, the formula would be solidified as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Theophilus's use of "Wisdom" (Sophia) for the third person is a fascinating glimpse into the development of Trinitarian language.

    The Argument: Theophilus's argument is that God deliberately ordered creation to teach profound truths. He claims that God created vegetation on the third day, before creating the sun on the fourth day, precisely to refute philosophers who would later claim that plants derive their life from the sun rather than from God. In this same typological way, the three days that existed before the creation of the sun (a type of God) and moon (a type of man) are themselves a type of the Trinity.

fr: Le quatrième jour, les luminaires furent créés. En effet, Dieu, dans sa prescience, prévoyait les vaines théories des philosophes : ils allaient soutenir que les productions de la terre provenaient des luminaires, afin de rejeter Dieu. C’est pourquoi, pour que la vérité soit manifeste, les plantes et les semences furent créées avant les luminaires. Car ce qui vient après ne peut créer ce qui l’a précédé.
en: On the fourth day the luminaries were made; because God, who possesses foreknowledge, knew the follies of the vain philosophers, that they were going to say that the things that grow on the earth are produced from the heavenly bodies, sO as to exclude God. In order that the truth might be obvious, the plants and seeds were produced prior to the heavenly bodies, for what iS posterior cannot produce what is prior [ To Autolycus 2:15 (c. A.D. 181)].
latin: Quarto die facta sunt luminaria. Deus enim cum omnia provideat, nugas vanorum philosophorum perspiciebat, qui dicturi erant a luminaribus esse quidquid in terra gignitur, ut Deum ex animis tollerent. Quare ut veritas pateret, creatæ sunt plantæ et semina ante luminaria. Porro quod posterius est non potest ea quæ sunt priora facere.
greek: Τετάρτῃ ἡμέρᾳ ἐγένοντο οἱ φωστήρες. Ἐπειδὴ ὁ Θεὸς προγνώστης ὤν, ἐπίστατο τὰς φλυαρίας τῶν ματαίων φιλοσόφων, ὅτι ἔμελλον λέγειν ἀπὸ τῶν στοιχείων εἶναι τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς φυόμενα πρὸς τὸ ἀθετεῖν τὸν Θεόν. Ἰν᾿ οὖν τὸ ἀληθὲς δειχθῇ, προγενέστερα γέγονεν τὰ φυτὰ καὶ τὰ σπέρματα τῶν στοιχείων. Τὰ γὰρ μεταγενέστερα οὐ δύναται ποιεῖν τὰ αὐτῶν προγενέστερα.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Author and Work: The author is St. Theophilus, who was the bishop of Antioch in the late 2nd century. The work, Ad Autolycum (To Autolycus), is the only one of his writings to survive. It is a work of Christian apologetics addressed to his educated pagan friend, Autolycus, to defend the reasonableness and superiority of the Christian faith.

    Theological Argument (Polemic against Determinism): Theophilus's argument is a direct attack on the astrological and naturalistic philosophies prevalent in the Greco-Roman world.

        The Target: His mention of "vain philosophers" refers to those who taught that the heavenly bodies (luminaria / στοιχεία - which can mean both "elements" and "heavenly bodies") governed life and growth on earth. This belief removed God as the direct, active Creator and subjected the world to an impersonal, deterministic fate ruled by the stars.

        God's Pedagogical Creation: Theophilus presents a powerful idea: God did not just create, He created in a specific order for a specific purpose. He arranged the sequence of creation (plants on Day 3, sun and moon on Day 4) as a divine lesson plan to preemptively refute this future philosophical error. Creation itself is an argument against atheism and determinism.

        Appeal to Logic: The final sentence—"what is posterior cannot produce what is prior"—is a direct appeal to simple, irrefutable logic. An effect cannot precede its cause. This was a way of showing Autolycus that the Christian account is not only divinely revealed but also logically superior to pagan alternatives.

    Significance: This passage is a prime example of how the early Church Fathers read Genesis. For them, it was not merely a scientific or historical chronicle in the modern sense, but a profound theological polemic against the pagan cosmologies of their time. The very structure of the creation week was seen as a divine argument for God's sovereignty, freedom, and direct involvement in His creation.

fr: En outre, Dieu a béni les créatures issues des eaux, afin que cela soit aussi un signe : tous ceux qui s'approchent de la vérité, sont régénérés et reçoivent la bénédiction de Dieu, obtiendront la pénitence et la rémission des péchés par l'eau et le bain de la régénération.

A.D. 181)].

context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Author and Work: Saint Theophilus of Antioch, Ad Autolycum (To Autolycus), Book 2, Chapter 16. Theophilus was the sixth bishop of Antioch, a major center of early Christianity. This work is an apology written to a learned pagan friend named Autolycus to defend the Christian faith.

    Date: c. A.D. 181. This places the text firmly in the 2nd century, making it a very early and valuable witness to Christian doctrine and biblical interpretation.

    Theological Significance:

        Typology: This passage is a classic example of early Christian typology. Theophilus sees the blessing of the sea creatures in the Genesis creation account (Genesis 1:22) not merely as a historical event, but as a prefigurement—a "sign" (δεῖγμα / signum)—that points forward to the sacrament of Baptism.

        Early Baptismal Theology: It is an exceptionally clear and early testimony to the Church's understanding of Baptism. Theophilus explicitly connects the physical element of water with the spiritual graces of "repentance and remission of sins."

        Key Terminology: He uses the phrase "washing of regeneration" (λουτροῦ παλιγγενεσίας / lavacrum regenerationis), a direct echo of Titus 3:5. This demonstrates the deep scriptural roots of the Church's sacramental language from a very early period. The terms "born again" (ἀναγεννωμένους / regenerantur) also connect directly to the language of the New Testament (e.g., John 3:3-5, 1 Peter 1:23).

fr:

Même si une certaine durée nous avait échappé — mettons 50, 100 ou même 200 ans —, il ne s'agirait pas pour autant de milliers ou de myriades d'années, comme l'ont prétendu Platon, Apollonius et les autres dans leurs écrits mensongers.
Et de fait, il est possible que nous ne connaissions pas avec exactitude le nombre total des années, car les mois et les jours excédentaires n'ont pas été rapportés dans les livres sacrés.

[f even a chronological error has been committed by us. of, for example, fifty or one hundred, or even two hundred years, yet not of thousands and tens of thousands, as Plato and Apollonius and other mendacious authors have hitherto written. And perhaps our knowledge of the whole number of the years IS not quite accurate, because the odd months and days are not set down in the sacred books [ibid., 3:28].

context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Author and Work: St. Theophilus, Bishop of Antioch (died c. A.D. 183-185). The work is his only surviving writing, an apology titled Ad Autolycum (To Autolycus), written around A.D. 181.

    Context of the Quote: This passage is the culmination of Theophilus's primary argument in Book 3. He is responding to the common pagan criticism that Christianity is a new and therefore untrustworthy religion. His defense is built on proving the immense antiquity of the Hebrew prophets and their sacred writings compared to the most ancient Greek historians and philosophers.

    The Polemical Purpose:

        Antiquity as Truth: For Theophilus, demonstrating that Moses wrote centuries before the Trojan War, and that the biblical timeline is older than any other, is paramount to proving its truthfulness.

        History vs. Myth: He contrasts the sober, year-by-year biblical chronology with the fantastical, multi-myriad-year timelines found in writers like Plato (who wrote of ancient Atlantis) or Apollonius of Rhodes. He labels their accounts "mendacious" (lying) myths, while presenting his own as verifiable history.

        Rhetorical Honesty: The admission of a potential minor error ("50 or 100, or even 200 years") is a clever rhetorical device. It makes him appear careful, reasonable, and honest, strengthening his claim that he is dealing with factual history, not wild invention. He even provides a logical reason for the slight imprecision—the unrecorded "odd months and days."

    Significance: This is the earliest surviving detailed Christian chronology of the world. Theophilus's work is a foundational text for the genre of the Christian world-chronicle, which would later be perfected by historians like Julius Africanus and, most famously, Eusebius of Caesarea. His goal was to create a universal history that placed biblical events on a firm timeline that could be synchronized with and proven superior to secular Greek and Roman history.

fr: Voilà pourquoi la Vierge demeure jusqu'à ce jour immortelle, elle que Celui qui a habité en elle a fait passer dans les lieux de son assomption.
en: TIMOTHY OF JERUSALEM Therefore the Virgin is immortal to this day, seeing that he who had dwelt in her transported her to the regions of her Assumption [Homily on Simeon and Anna (c. A.D. 500)].

context:
Additional Relevant Details and Context

The context you have captured in this image is extremely important. The author, Timothy of Jerusalem, presents the Bodily Assumption of Mary as the correct theological alternative to a different, incorrect theory about her death.

    The Starting Point: The "Sword of Sorrow"
    The passage begins by analyzing Simeon's prophecy to Mary: "And a sword will pierce your own soul" (Καὶ σοῦ δὲ αὐτῆς τὴν ψυχὴν διελεύσεται ῥομφαία).

    Refuting an Incorrect Interpretation
    Timothy notes that some people have misinterpreted this prophecy to mean that Mary died a physical, violent death as a martyr. He explicitly refutes this idea:

        Greek: ἔνθεν τινὲς ἔδοξαν τὴν τοῦ Κυρίου μητέρα ξίφει θανάτῳ μαρτυρικὸν ἀπενέγκασθαι τέλος... ἔχει δὲ οὐχ οὕτως.

        Translation: "Hence some have thought that the mother of the Lord suffered a martyr's end by the sword of death... but it is not so."

    The Theological Argument
    He argues that a physical sword (ῥομφαία χαλκευτικὴ) divides the body, but it cannot cut the soul. Therefore, the prophecy cannot be about a literal martyrdom.

    The Assumption as the Correct Conclusion
    It is immediately after refuting the martyrdom theory that he presents the Assumption as the truth. The word ἐξ ὧν (ex hōn - "from which" or "whence") or the Latin unde ("whence," "therefore") shows that his statement about the Assumption is the logical conclusion of his argument:

        Argument: Since she did not die a martyr's death by the sword, what happened to her?

        Conclusion: Therefore, the Virgin is immortal to this day, because Christ, who dwelt in her, transported her to the heavenly regions of the Assumption.

    The True Meaning of the "Sword"
    After establishing the Assumption, Timothy returns to the prophecy to explain its true meaning. The "sword" was the immense pain and sorrow (ὀδύνην) that pierced her soul, particularly when she thought she had lost her Son (referencing the Finding in the Temple, which he begins to discuss immediately afterward).

In summary, you have not only found the quote but have also captured its entire argumentative framework. Timothy of Jerusalem uses the Bodily Assumption of Mary as a direct refutation of the theory of her martyrdom.

fr: Alors, tout en étant sur terre, tu contempleras que c'est Dieu qui gouverne dans les cieux ; alors tu commenceras à parler des mystères de Dieu. Alors tu aimeras et admireras ceux qui sont châtiés pour leur refus de renier Dieu. Alors tu condamneras la tromperie et l'égarement du monde, quand tu auras compris ce qu'est la véritable vie au ciel, quand tu mépriseras cette mort qui n'est qu'une apparence ici-bas, et que tu redouteras la mort véritable, celle qui est réservée à ceux qui seront condamnés au feu éternel, lequel tourmentera jusqu'à la fin ceux qui lui auront été livrés. Alors tu admireras ceux qui endurent pour la justice le feu d'un moment, et tu les proclameras bienheureux, quand tu auras connu cet autre feu.
en: Then you will see, while still on earth, that God in the heavens rules over [the universe]; then you will begin to speak the mysteries of God; then will you love and admire those who suffer punishment because they will not deny God; then will you condemn the deceit and error of the world when you will know what it is to live truly in heaven, when you will despise what is here esteemed to be death, when you will fear what is truly death, which is reserved for those who shall be condemned to the eternal fire. which will afflict those even to the end who are committed to it Then will you admire those who for righteousness's sake endure the fire that is but for a moment, and will count them happy when you will know the nature of that fire To Diognetus 10 (c. A.D. 160)].
latin: Tunc perspicies, in terra degens, Deum in cælis mundum, velut aliquam rempublicam, gubernare, tum mysteria Dei loqui incipies: tunc eos qui puniuntur quod abnegare Deum nolint, et diliges et miraberis: tunc imposturam mundi et errorem damnabis, cum vere in cœlo vivere didiceris; cum ejus quæ hic mors esse censetur, contemptor esse; et mortem, quæ revera est mors, formidare coeperis, quæ servatur iis qui ad ignem æternum damnabuntur, qui sibi traditos afficiet supplicio ad finem usque. Tunc admirationi tibi erunt qui pro justitia ignem patiuntur; tunc beatos prædicabis, cum ignem illum cognoveris.
greek: Τότε θεάσῃ τυγχάνων ἐπὶ γῆς, ὅτι Θεὸς ἐν οὐρανοῖς πολιτεύεται· τότε μυστήρια Θεοῦ λαλεῖν ἄρξῃ· τότε τοὺς κολαζομένους ἐπὶ τῷ μὴ θέλειν ἀρνήσασθαι Θεὸν, καὶ ἀγαπήσεις καὶ θαυμάσεις· τότε τῆς ἀπάτης τοῦ κόσμου καὶ τῆς πλάνης καταγνώσῃ, ὅταν τὸ ἀληθῶς ἐν οὐρανῷ ζῆν ἐπιγνῷς· ὅταν τοῦ δοκοῦντος ἐνθάδε θανάτου καταφρονήσῃς, ὅταν τὸν ὄντως θάνατον φοβηθῇς, ὃς φυλάσσεται τοῖς κατακριθησομένοις εἰς πῦρ τὸ αἰώνιον, ὃ τοὺς παραδοθέντας αὐτῷ μέχρι τέλους κολάσει. Τότε τοὺς ὑπομένοντας ὑπὲρ δικαιοσύνης θαυμάσεις τὸ πῦρ τὸ πρόσκαιρον, καὶ μακαρίσεις, ὅταν ἐκεῖνο τὸ πῦρ ἐπιγνῷς.
context:
Additional Details and Context

    Work: Epistle to Diognetus (Greek: Πρὸς Διόγνητον Ἐπιστολή).

    Author: Anonymous. The author is unknown, though various figures from the early Church have been suggested. He was clearly a highly educated and eloquent writer.

    Date: The date is uncertain, but it is generally placed in the 2nd century (c. A.D. 130–200), making it a precious example of early Christian apologetics. Your date of c. A.D. 160 is a very reasonable estimate.

    Original Language: The epistle was written in elegant, classical Greek. The Latin version you provided is a standard early translation.

    Context of the Quote: Chapter 10 is the climax of the epistle's argument. After explaining who Christians are (Chapter 5-6) and the divine origin of their faith (Chapter 7-8), the author describes the profound benefits of accepting this faith. The chapter begins by explaining that faith leads to an imitation of God's own goodness (imitatio Dei). The passage you selected is the powerful conclusion, describing the radical shift in perception that this new life brings: the believer begins to see earthly life from a heavenly perspective.

    Theological Significance: This passage is rich with early Christian themes:

        Realized Eschatology: The believer begins to experience the realities of heaven ("you will see, while still on earth...").

        Veneration of Martyrs: It shows a deep love and admiration for those who suffer for their faith, seeing their temporary suffering in light of eternal realities.

        The Two Deaths: It makes a sharp distinction between physical death, which is now despised, and true, spiritual death (eternal fire), which is to be feared.

    Unique Manuscript History: This is one of the most fascinating aspects of this text. The Epistle to Diognetus survived into the modern era in a single 13th-century manuscript. Tragically, this sole manuscript was destroyed during the Franco-Prussian War when the municipal library of Strasbourg, where it was housed, was shelled and burned in 1870. All modern editions of the text are based on copies made by scholars before the original was lost.

fr:
C'est pour cela qu'il a envoyé le Verbe, afin qu'il se manifeste au monde...
Celui qui est depuis le commencement, qui est apparu nouveau et s'est révélé ancien...
Celui qui est de toute éternité, aujourd'hui reconnu comme Fils.
en: TO DIOGNETUS [The Father] sent the Word, that he might be manifested to the world. . This is he who was from the beginning, who appeared as if new, and was found old. This is he who, being from everlasting, is today called the Son [ To Diognetus 11 C. A.D. 160) emphasis added].

greek: Οὗ χάριν ἀπέστειλε λόγον, ἵνα κόσμῳ φανῇ... Οὗτος ὁ ἀπ' ἀρχῆς, ὁ καινὸς φανείς, καὶ παλαιὸς εὑρεθείς... Οὗτος ὁ ἀεὶ, σήμερον Υἱὸς λογισθείς.
context:
Additional Details and Context

    The Work: The Epistle to Diognetus is an anonymous masterpiece of early Christian apologetics, likely written in the mid-to-late 2nd century (c. A.D. 150-180). It is highly regarded for its elegant Greek prose and profound theological insights.

    The Manuscript and the Missing Word "Old": This is a crucial detail. The single surviving Greek manuscript for this text was destroyed in a fire in 1870. In that manuscript, there was a gap, or lacuna, in the text. The Greek text literally read: ...ὁ καινὸς φανείς, καὶ . . . εὑρεθείς... (...who appeared new, and ... was found...). The word for "old" (παλαιός) is a famous and universally accepted scholarly emendation (a proposed correction) first suggested by the 16th-century scholar Henri Estienne (Stephanus). It is accepted because it creates a beautiful and theologically rich paradox ("new yet old") that is perfectly in keeping with the author's style. The Latin translation (vetus) reflects this emendation.

    Key Theological Concepts:

        Pre-existence of the Word: The phrases "from the beginning" (ἀπ' ἀρχῆς) and "He who is everlasting" (ὁ ἀεὶ) are powerful affirmations of the Son's eternal existence before his incarnation, echoing the prologue of John's Gospel.

        Paradoxical Revelation: The author loves paradox. The eternal Word "appeared new" in the Incarnation, yet he is "found old" because he is the ancient, pre-existent Creator. This theme of newness and timelessness is central to the chapter.

        "Today Called the Son": The phrase σήμερον Υἱὸς λογισθείς ("today reckoned/regarded as Son") does not imply that he only became the Son at a certain point in time. Rather, it signifies that his eternal Sonship is manifested and proclaimed in time within the history of salvation. It is a clear allusion to Psalm 2:7 ("You are my Son; today I have begotten you"), a foundational text for early Christian understanding of Jesus's divine identity.

fr: Alors, la crainte de la Loi est chantée, et la grâce des prophètes est reconnue, et la foi des Évangiles est affermie, et la tradition des apôtres est préservée, et la grâce de l'église tressaille.
en: TO DIOGNETUS Then the fear of the Law is chanted, and the grace of the prophets is known, and the faith of the Gospels is established, and the Tradition of the apostles IS preserved, and the grace of the Church exults [To Diognetus 11 (C. A.D. 160)].
latin: Deinde metus legis decantatur, et prophetarum gratia cognoscitur, et Evangeliorum fides stabilitur, et apostolorum traditio custoditur, et Ecclesia gratia exsultat.
greek: Εἶτα φόβος νόμου ᾄδεται, καὶ προφητῶν χάρις γινώσκεται, καὶ Εὐαγγελίων πίστις ἵδρυται, καὶ ἀποστόλων παράδοσις φυλάσσεται, καὶ Ἐκκλησίας χάρις σκιρτᾷ.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Work and Author: The Epistle to Diognetus is a celebrated work of early Christian apologetics. The author is anonymous, though he describes himself as a "disciple of the Apostles." The date you provided (c. A.D. 160) is a common scholarly estimate, placing it firmly in the 2nd century among the works of the Apostolic Fathers.

    Original Language: The original language of the epistle is Greek. The Latin text you have is a standard, ancient translation.

    Context of the Quote: This beautiful sentence comes at the climax of Chapter 11. The author has just described how the eternal Word (Logos), who appeared new in the world, enriches the Church and expands grace in the saints. The quote is a magnificent, five-part summary of the harmonious elements that constitute the life and understanding of the Church.

    Theological Significance: The quote provides a powerful snapshot of 2nd-century Christian self-understanding:

        φόβος νόμου ᾄδεται (fear of the Law is chanted): This shows the Old Testament Law is not discarded but is understood with reverence ("fear") and integrated into the Church's life, likely through liturgical reading ("chanted").

        προφητῶν χάρις γινώσκεται (grace of the prophets is known): The prophecies of the Old Testament are now understood in their true light, as a gift ("grace") pointing to Christ.

        Εὐαγγελίων πίστις ἵδρυται (faith of the Gospels is established): The apostolic accounts of Jesus are the firm foundation of Christian belief.

        ἀποστόλων παράδοσις φυλάσσεται (Tradition of the apostles is preserved): This is a key phrase. Παράδοσις (Gr.) / Traditio (Lat.) refers to the authoritative body of teaching "handed down" from the Apostles. Its preservation is seen as essential to the Church's identity.

        Ἐκκλησίας χάρις σκιρτᾷ (grace of the Church exults): The result of this harmony is a dynamic, living community. The Greek verb σκιρτᾷ (skirta) is particularly vibrant; it means "to leap" or "bound," famously used to describe John the Baptist leaping in his mother's womb (Luke 1:41). It conveys a sense of exultant, active joy.

fr: Je constate que la question a été débattue entre frères sur la conduite à tenir à l'égard de ceux qui, bien qu'ayant été baptisés dans l'hérésie, l'ont ensuite quittée et reviennent en suppliants à l'Église de Dieu, accomplissant leur pénitence de tout leur cœur et, comprenant enfin que leur erreur est condamnable, implorant d'elle le secours du salut. La question est de savoir si, conformément à la plus ancienne coutume et à la tradition ecclésiastique, il suffirait, après ce baptême qu'ils ont bel et bien reçu au-dehors, que l'évêque leur impose seulement la main pour qu'ils reçoivent l'Esprit Saint, et si cette imposition de la main leur conférerait un signe de foi renouvelé et accompli.
en: TREATISE ON RE-BAPTISM [Ut has been asked among the brethren what course ought specially to be adopted towards the persons of those who baptized in heresy and subsequently departing from their heresy, and fleeing as supplicants to the Church of God, should repent with their whole hearts, and only now perceiving the condemnation of their error, implore from the Church the help of salvation. .. . [A]ccording to the most ancient custom and ecclesiastical tradition, it would suffice, after that baptism that they have received outside the Church . . that only hands should be laid upon them by the bishop for their reception of the Holy Spirit, and this imposition of hands would afford them the renewed and perfected seal of faith [Treatise on Re-Baptism (C. A.D. 257)].
latin: Animadverto quaesitum apud fratres quid potius observari oportet in personam eorum qui in haeresi quidem... sint tincti; postmodum inde digressi, et suppliciter ad Ecclesiam Dei advolantes, totis praecordiis poenitentiam agerent; et erroris sui damnationem nunc demum intelligentes auxilium salutis ab ea implorarent;     ...utrum vetustissima consuetudine ac traditione ecclesiastica, post illum quod foris quidem... accceperuut Baptisma, tantummodo imponi eis manum ab episcopo ad accipiendum Spiritum sanctum sufficeret, et haec manus impositio signum fidei iteratum atque consummatum... eis praestaret:
context:
Context: What the Rest of Your Latin Text Says

The portion of your Latin text that follows the quote you were looking for is the author setting up the entire debate. He explains:

    The Alternative Position: He contrasts the ancient tradition with the other view being debated: an vero etiam iteratum Baptisma his necessarium esset — "or whether, on the other hand, a repeated Baptism would be necessary for them."

    The Author's Frustration: He immediately shows his own position. He states that this "new question" (nova quaestione) would never have arisen if everyone had just contented themselves with the "venerable authority of all the Churches" (venerabili Ecclesiarum omnium auctoritate) and practiced humility.

    Condemnation of Innovation: He strongly condemns those who are challenging the ancient custom, accusing them of disrupting the peace of the Church and acting out of pride and a desire for "empty glory." He even says they are bringing shame upon Mother Church.

    The Plan for the Treatise: He concludes by stating his purpose: to gather all the relevant passages from Holy Scripture (quaecumque sanctarum Scripturarum... capitula... congeremus) to demonstrate the "most healthy and peaceful custom" (consuetudinem saluberrimam atque pacificam) to all the brethren.

fr: En effet, lorsque, par l'imposition des mains de l'évêque, l'Esprit Saint est donné à chaque croyant, c'est à la manière des Apôtres qui, pour les Samaritains, après le baptême de Philippe, leur imposèrent la main et leur conférèrent ainsi l'Esprit Saint...
en: [Bly imposition of the bishop's hands the Holy Spirit is given to everyone who believes, as in the case of the Samaritans, after Philip's baptism, the apostles did to them by laying on of hands [Acts 8:14-177: in this same way they conferred on them the Holy Spirit [ibid., 3].
latin: Nam cum per manus impositionem episcopi datur unicuique credenti Spiritus sanctus, sicut Apostoli circa Samaritanos post Philippi Baptisma manum eis imponendo fecerunt, et hac ratione Spiritum sanctum in eos contulerunt...
context:
Additional Context from Your Provided Text

The full passage you posted is a brilliant piece of theological reasoning. Here is the flow of the argument:

    The Opponent's Position: The author begins by imagining an opponent (representing the Cyprianic view) quoting Jesus in John 3:5: "Nisi quis denuo natus fuerit ex aqua et Spiritu, non potest introire in regnum coelorum" ("Unless one is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of heaven"). The opponent uses this to argue that water baptism and the reception of the Holy Spirit are an inseparable package.

    The Author's Agreement (with a twist): The author then says, "No one among us is so insane or stubborn as to dare contradict this." He agrees that, ideally and in the normal practice of the Church (rebus integris), this is true.

    The Crucial Distinction: Then he makes his key point: "But if in the New Testament we find that these things... are sometimes found in a way divided and separated (divisa ac separata)... let us see if they can sometimes stand alone."

    The Prime Example (Your Quote): He then presents his "Exhibit A" for this separation: the case of the Samaritans in Acts 8. They received water baptism from Philip but did not receive the Holy Spirit until Peter and John came and laid hands on them. This, for the author, is the scriptural proof that the gift of the Spirit (conferred by a bishop's hands) can be separated from, and can complete, an earlier water baptism.

fr: ...mais si, au contraire, il a été conféré par des étrangers, qu'on y remédie dans la mesure où l'affaire le peut et le permet : car l'Esprit Saint n'est pas hors de l'Église, et la foi non plus ne peut être saine, non seulement chez les hérétiques, mais aussi chez ceux qui sont établis dans le schisme. C'est pourquoi, à ceux qui font pénitence...
en: TREATISE ON RE-BAPTISM [O]utside the Church there is no Holy Spirit. Sound faith moreover cannot exist, not only among heretics, but even among those who are established in schism [Treatise on Re-Baptism 10 (c. A.D. 257)].
latin: ...si vero ab alienis traditum fuerit, ut potest hoc negotium et ut admittit, corrigatur: quia Spiritus sanctus extra Ecclesiam non sit, fides quoque non solum apud haereticos, verum etiam apud eos qui in schismate constituti sunt sana esse non possit. Idcircoque poenitentiam agentibus...
context:
Context of the Passage

This is a fascinating and historically important text. The anonymous author of the Treatise on Re-Baptism is arguing for a position that differs from that of St. Cyprian of Carthage.

    The Problem: Someone has been baptized with water in the name of Jesus, but by a heretic or a schismatic. What should the Catholic Church do when that person wants to become a member?

    St. Cyprian's Position: All sacraments outside the true Church are invalid. Therefore, the person must be completely re-baptized.

    The Author's Position (in your text): The author argues for a middle way. He says the invocation of Jesus' name is a powerful act that should not be repeated. However, he agrees that the Holy Spirit is missing from the heretical baptism.

    The Solution: Therefore, the person should not be re-baptized with water. Instead, the Church should "supply" what was missing by having a bishop lay hands on the person to confer the Holy Spirit.

The sentence you found is the author's theological justification for this practice: The reason we need to lay on hands is precisely because "outside the Church there is no Holy Spirit," and therefore a "sound faith" could not have been present in the original schismatic ceremony.

fr: Toute cette masse, Dieu l'a façonnée en six jours pour l'ornement de sa majesté ; quant au septième jour, c'est par une bénédiction qu'il l'a . . . consacré.
en: ST. VICTORINUS OF PETTAU God produced that entire mass for the adornment of his majesty in six days; on the seventh he consecrated it with a blessing [ Creation of the World (c. A.D. 270)].
latin: COGITANTI mihi, una cum animo meo conferenti, de fabrica mundi istius, in quo clausi tenemur, etiam velocitas fabricae istius haec est; sicut in libro Moysis continetur, quem de conditione ipsius scripsit, qui Genesis appellatur. **Totam molem istam, Deus sex diebus in ornamento majestatis suae expressit, septimo quibus benedictione . . . consecravit.** Idcirco igitur, quoniam septenario numero dierum...
context:
Context and Significance

This sentence serves as the thesis statement for the entire short treatise, De Fabrica Mundi (On the Creation of the World).

    Location: As the opening declaration, it sets the theme. Victorinus immediately establishes the framework of the seven days of creation as his starting point.

    Numerology: The rest of the treatise is a fascinating and highly symbolic exploration of numbers, especially the numbers seven, four, and twelve. He uses this opening statement about the seven days to launch into a discussion of how these key numbers structure not only creation but all of salvation history (e.g., the four Gospels, the four rivers of Paradise, the seven spirits of God, the twelve apostles, the twenty-four elders).

fr:
Ce sixième jour est appelé parasceve, c'est-à-dire la préparation du royaume ; c'est en effet ce jour-là qu'il a parachevé Adam, qu'il a fait à son image et à sa ressemblance. C'est d'ailleurs pour cette raison qu'il a achevé ses œuvres avant de créer les anges et de façonner l'homme, de peur que ceux-ci ne s'attribuent faussement le rôle d'auxiliaires. C'est aussi en ce jour que, en raison de la Passion du Seigneur Jésus-Christ, nous observons une station pour Dieu ou un jeûne.

Le septième jour, il se reposa de toutes ses œuvres, le bénit et le sanctifia. Ce jour-là, nous avons coutume de prolonger notre jeûne, afin que le jour du Seigneur, nous puissions nous approcher du pain dans l'action de grâces. Et cette prolongation du jeûne du vendredi a lieu afin de ne pas sembler observer le sabbat avec les Juifs, un sabbat que le Christ lui-même, Seigneur du sabbat, déclare par ses prophètes que son âme déteste ; sabbat qu'il a lui-même aboli par son corps en ce jour...
en: ST. VICTORINUS OF PETTAU This sixth day [Friday] is called parasceve, that IS to say, the preparation of the kingdom. For he perfected Adam, whom he made after his image and likeness. But for this reason he completed his works before he created angels and fashioned man, lest they should falsely assert that they had been his helpers. On this day also, on account of the Passion of the Lord Jesus Christ, we make either a station to God, or a fast. On the seventh day he rested from all his works, and blessed it, and sanctified it. On the former day we are accustomed to fast rigorously, that on the Lord's Day we may go forth to our bread with thanksgiving. And let the parasceve become a rigorous fast, lest we should appear to observe any Sabbath with the Jews, which Christ himself, the Lord of the Sabbath, says by his prophets that "his soul hates" [Is 1:13-14]; which Sabbath he in his body abolished [Creation of the World (A.D. 270)].
latin: Hic dies sextus parasceve appellatur, praeparatio scilicet regni; Adam enim quem ad imaginem et similitudinem suam consummavit. Idcirco autem prius opera sua consummavit, quam angelos creavit, et hominem fabricavit, ne forte adjutores se fuisse falsa dictione asseverant. Hoc quoque die ob passionem Domini Jesu Christi aut stationem Deo, aut jejunium, facimus. Die septimo requievit ab omnibus operibus suis, et benedixit eum et sanctificavit. Hoc die solemus superponere; idcirco, ut die Dominico cum gratiarum actione ad panem exeamus. Et parasceve superpositio fiat, ne quid cum Judaeis sabbatum observare videamur, quod ipse Dominus sabbati Christus per prophetas suos odisse animam suam dicit; quod sabbato corpore suo resolvit...
context:
Context and Analysis

You've found a very important passage from one of the earliest Latin exegetes.

    Typology: Victorinus masterfully links the sixth day of Creation (the making of Adam) with the sixth day of Redemption (Christ's Passion on Good Friday). For him, Friday (Parasceve, "Preparation") is a day of perfecting and preparing.

    Early Christian Practice: The text is a priceless witness to Christian worship in the 3rd century. It clearly describes the practice of fasting on Friday in memory of the Passion.

    The "Superpositio": This was a technical term for a "rigorous fast." It meant extending the Friday fast through all of Saturday, breaking it only at the Sunday liturgy. This practice was specifically designed to distinguish the Christian observance from the Jewish Sabbath, which was a day of feasting and rest. Victorinus's explicit statement—ne quid cum Judaeis sabbatum observare videamur ("lest we should appear to observe any Sabbath with the Jews")—is a powerful statement of developing Christian identity.

    Lord of the Sabbath: He reinforces this distinction by quoting the Old Testament prophets (Isaiah 1:13-14) to show that God Himself was displeased with mere formal observance, and then stating that Christ, as "Lord of the Sabbath," fulfilled and "abolished" its old requirements in his own body.

fr:
J'ai donc souvent cherché avec beaucoup d'ardeur et la plus grande attention auprès de très nombreux hommes qui excellaient par leur sainteté et leur doctrine, par quel moyen je pourrais, selon une règle pour ainsi dire générale et constante, distinguer la vérité de la foi catholique de la fausseté de la perversion hérétique. De la quasi-totalité d'entre eux, j'ai toujours reçu cette réponse : si moi-même ou n'importe qui d'autre voulait démasquer les impostures des hérétiques qui surgissent, éviter leurs pièges et conserver une foi saine et intacte, il devait, avec l'aide du Seigneur, affermir sa foi par un double moyen : premièrement, par l'autorité de la loi divine, et ensuite, par la tradition de l'église catholique.

Ici, quelqu'un demandera peut-être : puisque le canon de l'Écriture est parfait et qu'il se suffit amplement à lui-même en toutes choses, pourquoi est-il nécessaire d'y joindre l'autorité de l'interprétation ecclésiale ? La raison en est que l'Écriture sainte, en raison de sa profondeur même, n'est pas comprise par tous dans un seul et même sens. Ses paroles sont interprétées de manières différentes par les uns et les autres, de sorte qu'on pourrait presque dire qu'il y a autant d'interprétations que de lecteurs. En effet, Novatien l'expose d'une manière, Sabellius d'une autre, Donat d'une autre ; d'une autre encore Arius, Eunomius, Macédonius ; d'une autre Photin, Apollinaire, Priscillien ; d'une autre Jovinien, Pélage, Célestius ; et enfin, d'une autre encore, Nestorius. C'est pourquoi, face à de si nombreux et si tortueux replis de l'erreur, il est absolument nécessaire que la ligne d'interprétation prophétique et apostolique soit dirigée selon la norme du sens ecclésial et catholique.

De même, au sein de l'église catholique elle-même, il faut veiller avec le plus grand soin à nous en tenir à ce qui a été cru partout, toujours et par tous. Voilà en effet ce qui est véritablement et proprement catholique, comme l'indiquent la force et la signification même de ce mot, qui embrasse la quasi-totalité des choses de manière universelle.
en: ST. VINCENT OF LERINS I have often then inquired earnestly and attentively of very many men eminent for sanctity and learning, how and by what sure and universal rule may be able to distinguish the truth of Catholic faith from the falsehood of heretical pravity; and I have always, and in almost every instance, received an answer to this effect: That whether I or anyone else should wish to detect the frauds and avoid the snares of heretics as they rise, and to continue sound and complete in the Catholic faith, we must, the Lord helping, fortify our own belief in two ways: first, by the authority of the divine law, and then, by the Tradition of the Catholic Church. But here someone perhaps will ask, "Since the canon of Scripture is complete, and sufficient of itself for everything, and more than sufficient, what need is there to join with it the authority of the Church's interpretation?" For this reason-because, owing to the depth of Holy Scripture, all do not accept it in one and the same sense, but one understands its words in one way, another in another; so that seems to be capable of as many interpretations as there are interpreters. For Novatian expounds it one way, Sabellius another, Donatus another, Arius, Eunomius, Macedonius, another, Photinus, Apollinarius, Priscillian, another, lovinian, Pelagius, Celestius, another, and lastly, Nestorius, another. Therefore, it is very necessary, on account of so great intricacies of such various error, that the rule for the right understanding of the prophets and apostles should be framed in accordance with the standard of ecclesiastical and Catholic interpretation. Moreover, in the Catholic Church itself, all possible care must be taken, that we hold that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all. For that is truly and in the strictest sense Catholic, which, as the name itself and the reason of the thing declare, comprehends all universally [Notebooks 2:4-6 (c. A.D. 434)].
latin:
Saepe igitur magno studio et summa attentione perquirens a quamplurimis sanctitate et doctrina praestantibus viris quonam modo possim certa quadam et quasi generali ac regulari via catholicae fidei veritatem ab haereticae pravitatis falsitate discernere, hujusmodi semper responsum ab omnibus fere retuli, quod sive ego, sive quis alius vellet exsurgentium haereticorum fraudes deprehendere laqueosque vitare, et in fide sana sanus atque integer permanere, duplici modo munire fidem suam, Domino adjuvante, deberet: primùm scilicet divinae legis auctoritate, tum deinde Ecclesiae catholicae traditione.

    Hic forsitan requirat aliquis: Cum sit perfectus Scripturarum Canon, sibique ad omnia satis superque sufficiat, quid opus est ut ei Ecclesiasticae intelligentiae jungatur auctoritas? Quia videlicet Scripturam sacram pro ipsa sua altitudine non uno eodemque sensu universi accipiunt, sed ejusdem eloquia aliter atque aliter alius atque alius interpretatur; ut pene quot homines sunt, tot illinc sententiae erui posse videantur. Aliter namque illam Novatianus, aliter Sabellius, aliter Donatus exponit, aliter Arius, Eunomius, Macedonius; aliter Photinus, Apollinaris, Priscillianus, aliter Jovinianus, Pelagius, Caelestius; aliter postremo Nestorius. Atque idcirco multùm necesse est, propter tantos tam varii erroris anfractus, ut propheticae et apostolicae interpretationis linea secundum Ecclesiastici et Catholici sensus normam dirigatur.

    In ipsa item Catholica Ecclesia magnopere curandum est ut id teneamus quod ubique, quod semper, quod ab omnibus creditum est. Hoc est etenim vere proprieque catholicum, quod ipsa vis nominis ratioque declarat, quae omnia fere universaliter comprehendit.
context:
Additional Detail and Context
Author and Work

St. Vincent was a fifth-century monk and priest who lived in the renowned monastery on the island of Lérins (off the southern coast of modern-day France). He wrote the Commonitorium (meaning "Memorandum" or "Notebooks") around the year 434, under the pseudonym "Peregrinus" (pilgrim). Its purpose was to create a practical, reliable guide for distinguishing authentic Christian doctrine from heresy.
Historical Context

St. Vincent was writing in a period of intense theological turmoil.

    The Council of Ephesus (431) had just condemned Nestorius for his teachings on the nature of Christ.

    Debates were raging over the complex teachings of St. Augustine on grace and predestination, which had arisen in response to the Pelagian heresy.

    Older heresies like Arianism were still a recent and painful memory.

Vincent saw "novelties" cropping up everywhere. His goal was not to innovate but to establish a clear, conservative principle for preserving the faith that had been handed down from the apostles.
Breakdown of the Argument

This famous passage contains a three-step argument that is both brilliant and foundational for Catholic and Orthodox theology.

    The Twofold Rule: Vincent establishes that a Catholic must fortify their faith with two sources of authority: Scripture (divinae legis auctoritate) and Tradition (Ecclesiae catholicae traditione). This immediately sets him against any notion that Scripture can be interpreted in a vacuum.

    The Problem of Interpretation: He masterfully anticipates the objection: "Isn't Scripture sufficient on its own?" His answer is a resounding "no," not because Scripture is flawed, but because its depth allows for it to be twisted. He proves his point by listing a "rogue's gallery" of heretics—from Arius to his contemporary, Nestorius—who all used Scripture to justify their errors. Therefore, Scripture requires an authoritative interpretive key.

    The Vincentian Canon: This leads to his most celebrated formulation—the threefold test for identifying authentic Catholic Tradition. The true faith is that which has been believed:

        Everywhere (quod ubique) - This is the test of Universality or Ecumenicity.

        Always (quod semper) - This is the test of Antiquity or Apostolicity.

        By All (quod ab omnibus) - This is the test of Consent or Consensus.

This principle, often called the "Vincentian Canon," became the gold standard for theological orthodoxy. A doctrine is not an innovation if it can be shown to have been held by the whole Church, from the earliest times, with the universal consent of the Church Fathers.
Legacy and Enduring Influence

This passage is one of the most quoted texts from the patristic era because of its clarity and utility.

    It was highly influential during the Counter-Reformation, as the Council of Trent reaffirmed the dual authority of Scripture and Tradition against the Protestant principle of sola Scriptura.

    It perfectly encapsulates the Orthodox Church's understanding of Holy Tradition as the proper context for interpreting Scripture.

    It was famously adopted by Anglican theologians (most notably John Henry Newman before his conversion to Catholicism) as a pillar of the via media (the "middle way"), which sought a path between Roman Catholicism and Protestantism based on the faith of the ancient, undivided Church.

fr: Nestorius, en revanche, atteint de la maladie opposée à celle d'Apollinaire, alors qu'il feint de distinguer deux substances dans le Christ, introduit soudain deux personnes. Et, par un crime inouï, il veut qu'il y ait deux fils de Dieu, deux Christs : l'un Dieu, l'autre homme ; l'un né du Père, l'autre né de sa mère. C'est pourquoi il affirme que sainte Marie ne doit pas être appelée Théotokos, mais Christotokos, car d'elle n'est pas né le Christ qui est Dieu, mais celui qui était homme.
en: ST. VINCENT OF LERINS Nestorius, whose disease iS of an opposite kind, while pretending that he holds two distinct substances in Christ, brings in of a sudden two Persons, and with unheard of wickedness would have two sons of God, two Christs one God, the other man, one begotten of his Father, the other, born of his Mother. For which reason he maintains that St. Mary ought to be called not Theotokos the Mother of God], but Christotokos [the Mother of Christ], seeing that she gave birth not to the Christ who is God, but to the Christ who is man [Notebooks 12:35 C. A.D 434)].
latin: Nestorius autem contrario Apollinari morbo, dum sese duas in Christo substantias distinguere simulat, duas introducit repente personas, et inaudito scelere duos esse vult filios Dei, duos Christos, unum Deum, alterum hominem, unum qui ex Patre, alterum qui sit generatus ex matre. Atque ideo asserit sanctam Mariam non Theotocon, sed Christotocon esse dicendam: quia scilicet ex ea non ille Christus qui Deus, sed ille qui erat homo, natus sit.
context:
Additional Detail and Context
The "Rogues' Gallery" of Heretics

In this section of the Commonitorium, St. Vincent is providing concrete examples to illustrate his main thesis. He has just explained that even great teachers can fall into error, and that God allows this to "test" the faith of the Church. To demonstrate this, he briefly outlines the errors of three major heretics: Photinus, Apollinaris, and Nestorius. His summary of their teachings is a masterclass in precision and clarity.
The Heresy of Apollinaris (The "Opposite Disease")

To explain the error of Nestorius, Vincent first brilliantly describes its opposite, the heresy of Apollinaris.

    Apollinaris's Error: Apollinaris taught that in the Incarnation, the divine Word (Logos) took the place of the human rational soul in Jesus. In his view, Christ had a human body and a human "animal soul," but his mind and will were purely divine.

    The Consequence: This heresy "mutilates" Christ's humanity. It results in a being who is not fully human and not fully divine, but a strange fusion or mixture of the two. Apollinaris's error was one of confusion and fusion of the natures.

The Heresy of Nestorius (A Heresy of Separation)

Vincent describes Nestorianism as the contrario morbo—the "contrary disease." If Apollinaris confused the natures, Nestorius separated them too radically.

    Nestorius's Error: Nestorius, the Patriarch of Constantinople, insisted on a sharp distinction between Christ's human nature and his divine nature. While this was orthodox in principle, he took it so far as to imply that there were not only two natures but two distinct persons in Christ: the divine Person (the Son of God) and a separate human person (the man Jesus).

    The Consequence: According to Nestorius, these two persons were united only by a moral bond or a "conjunction of wills," not in a true, single personal identity (the "hypostatic union"). Vincent powerfully summarizes this outcome as the belief in "two sons of God, two Christs." There was the eternal Son begotten of the Father, and the human son born of Mary. These were not one and the same Person.

The Crucial Distinction: Theotokos vs. Christotokos

This deep theological error had a very practical and public consequence, which became the flashpoint of the controversy: the title of the Virgin Mary.

    Theotokos (θεοτόκος): The traditional and orthodox title, meaning "God-bearer" or "Mother of God." This title affirms that the Person Mary carried in her womb and gave birth to is, in fact, God the Son. It is a direct statement about the identity of Jesus Christ: He is one divine Person with two natures.

    Christotokos (χριστοτόκος): The title Nestorius insisted upon, meaning "Christ-bearer" or "Mother of Christ." For Nestorius, this was the more accurate term because Mary gave birth only to the human person Jesus, who was the "temple" or "vehicle" for the divine Son. This title reflects his belief in two separate persons.

St. Vincent correctly identifies that this debate over Mary's title was not primarily about Marian devotion; it was the clearest possible test of one's Christology. What you call Mary reveals who you believe Jesus to be. By rejecting Theotokos, Nestorius revealed his heretical belief in two separate Christs. This heresy was formally condemned at the Council of Ephesus in 431, just a few years before Vincent wrote his Commonitorium.

fr: Car le Dieu tout-puissant, qui veut que tous les hommes soient sauvés et que nul ne périsse, ne trouve rien en nous de plus agréable que le fait qu'un homme, après l'amour qu'il Lui doit, aime son prochain, et qu'il ne fasse pas à autrui ce qu'il ne voudrait pas qu'on lui fît. Cet amour, donc, nous et vous nous le devons plus particulièrement les uns aux autres qu'aux autres peuples, nous qui croyons en un seul Dieu et le confessons — bien que de manière différente — et qui chaque jour le louons et le vénérons comme Créateur des siècles et gouverneur de ce monde.
latin: Nam omnipotens Deus, qui omnes homines vult salvos facere, et neminem perire, nihil est quod in nobis magis approbet quam ut homo post dilectionem suam hominem diligat, et quod sibi non vult fieri, alii non faciat. Hanc itaque charitatem nos et vos specialibus nobis quam cæteris gentibus debemus, qui unum Deum, licet diverso modo, credimus et confitemur, qui eum Creatorem sæculorum et gubernatorem hujus mundi quotidie laudamus et veneramur.
